2.1.28.2. Depot Maintenance Additional Requirements. Unplanned depot losses recouped in subsequent years may be financed with prior year funds from the customer provided all other criteria associated with prior year upward obligations are met.

2.1.28.3. Contingency or Emergency Operations. Fund managers may waive pricing and financing requirements to facilitate Department operations during times of war or other national emergencies. Notification of Fund Managers actions must be provided in writing to the Revolving Funds and Integration Director within 30 days of the event.

2.1.29. Public-Private Partnerships at DWCF Depot Maintenance Activities

2.1.29.1. Pricing guidance and requirements for sales of goods and services by DoW depot maintenance activities to private entities engaged in public-private partnerships are set forth in section 10. In general, such prices are subject to the requirements with the exception that the prices may be based upon the most recent actual and projected costs applicable to the workload, rather than upon approved stabilized billing rates. Rates and prices to private entity partners may also be tailored to include only those direct and indirect production overhead costs that contribute to the finished product or service. However, full General and Administrative (G&A) costs will continue to be allocated on the same basis as for DoW customers.

2.1.29.2. Fixed pricing of sales to private party entity partners, including multiyear fixed price agreements, is authorized when production costs can be reasonably predicted and the risk of future operating losses is not significant. Such fixed prices may include provisions for adjustments to accommodate the effect of scope-of-work changes, annual inflation, and specified contingencies. When future production costs or risks cannot be reasonably predicted, cost reimbursable pricing is more appropriate.

2.1.30. Revolving Funds – Capital Budgeting

2.1.30.1. Budgetary resources for capital investments will be separately identified in an approved capital budget. Capital investments, such as unspecified minor construction, automatic data processing equipment or software, and other equipment, will be justified within the capital budget. Refer to section 10 for additional information regarding capital budgeting. Once the Revolving Funds activity capitalized an asset, the asset will continue to be reported as a capital asset and depreciated until the book value of the asset reaches zero or its salvage value, as appropriate. See Volume 4 for additional information regarding accounting policy for capitalization thresholds.

2.1.30.2. Depreciation. All capital assets owned by activities in the Fund will be depreciated or amortized by the individual Component business area. Depreciation will be on a straight-line basis and based on the acquisition cost, less residual value when residual value is expected to be 10 percent or more of the acquisition cost, including installation and related costs. Refer to Volume 4, for additional information regarding accounting policy for depreciation.

2.1.31. Revolving Funds - Base Support

2.1.31.1. Interservice and intragovernmental support agreements, as identified in DoDI 4000.19, is reimbursable by the Revolving Fund activity to the extent that the specified support for the activity increases the host activity’s direct costs (i.e., incremental direct cost). Costs associated with common use infrastructure are non-reimbursable, except for support provided solely for the benefit of one or more tenants. Support costs that are charged to a tenant Revolving Fund activity (i.e., reimbursable cost) must be measurable and directly attributable to the Revolving Fund activity. Indirect costs will not be included in reimbursement charges, except those included in stabilized rates charged for Revolving Funds mission products and services. Host activities (suppliers of base support) are permitted to waive reimbursement from tenants who use or benefit from available support without appreciably increasing the host activities’ costs (i.e., revenues would be less than the anticipated expense of billing and disbursing funds).

2.1.31.2. Revolving Fund activities that use any of the common base support functions identified in DoDI 4000.19 (Interservice and Intragovernmental Support) are to reimburse host activities for this support. Reimbursement for Revolving Funds mission products and services (e.g., depot supply, depot maintenance, public works center services, information processing, communications, and software development) must be based on the approved stabilized rate. Other support incidental to the Revolving Fund activity’s primary mission or purpose will be budgeted and reimbursed based on direct costs measurable and directly attributable to the Revolving Fund activity. Only the incremental change in cost attributable to the Revolving Fund activity (incremental direct cost) must be chargeable to the Revolving Fund activity. Indirect costs are not to be included as a cost to the Revolving Fund activity.

2.1.31.3. Refer to section 10 for additional information regarding base support budget exhibits.

2.1.32. Revolving Funds - Dual Funded Organizations

2.1.32.1. A dual funded organization is an organization that is funded (including reimbursable funding) by both Revolving Fund and other appropriations or accounts. In those instances where a function is funded with a combination of both Revolving Fund and appropriated funds, the function initially will be funded in its entirety either by the Revolving Fund or by appropriated funds. The determination of whether the particular function initially will be funded by the Revolving Fund or appropriated funds will be based on the predominance of definable units of measure for the function. Examples of definable units of measure include workload, productive hours, outputs, or ultimate use. The appropriation or account initially funding the function must be reimbursed by the other account(s) at the same unit of measure as was used to determine the initial funding source. The amount of reimbursement must be determined based on the relative portion of that unit of measure attributable to each part of the organization (or funding source) involved.

2.1.32.2. This policy does not change the policy for reimbursement for base support services provided by the Revolving Fund to tenant activities. The DoDI 4000.19 and
section 2.1.31 provide guidance for funding base support services.

2.1.33. Prohibition on Parking of Funds

10 U.S.C. § 2773b specifically prohibits a DoW officer or employee from directing the designation of funds for a particular purpose in the President’s Budget submission, or in the budget justification materials submitted in support of the budget, with the knowledge or intent that such funds will not be used for the designated purpose. Further, violation of this prohibition will be treated as a violation of the Antideficiency Act.

2.1.34. Use of O&M Funds under Contingency Construction Authority (CCA)

Pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 2804, the criteria and procedures for the use of O&M funds under CCA (also known as Section 2808 Authority) are listed in Volume 3, section 15.

2.2    Program and Budget Review Submission

2.2.1. The internal annual Planning, Programming, Budgeting, and Execution (PPBE) process will guide the Department’s strategy development, identification of needs for military capabilities, program planning, resource estimation and allocation, acquisition, and other decision processes. The PPBE process will continue to be the single link throughout the DoW that integrates and influences all internal decision processes. The annual budget will include the Strategic Planning Guidance (SPG), a Joint Programming Guidance (JPG), a Program Review, and a Budget Review. Program Decision Memoranda (PDMs) will implement Program Review decisions. Program Budget Decisions (PBDs) will implement Budget Review decisions.

2.2.2. The OUSW(C) and the Director of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation (DCAPE) guidance memorandum transmitted in the Spring of each year will provide specialized instructions such as program basis for the estimates, key assumptions to be used, and special supporting material requirements. In addition, “supplementary instructions” memoranda issued on an “as needed” basis (usually in July/August) will be limited to specific instructions which amplify guidance included in the OUSW(C) memorandum and in this volume. The use of other memoranda to transmit program and budget guidance will be restricted to new or nonrecurring requirements.

2.2.3. The Director of National Intelligence (DNI) will issue the guidance for development of the National Intelligence Program (NIP) and the NIP program and budget review submission. Additional details are found in section 16.

2.2.4. The instructions for submitting certain summary schedules are provided in the Volume 2 procedures. The instructions for back-up material tailored to each appropriation or fund category are provided in subsequent sections. Materials required by OMB Circular No. A‑11, which are not otherwise required by Volume 2, will be submitted in accordance with that Circular, unless specific exception is granted by the OMB.

2.2.5. The OUSW(C) will provide a budget work schedule on a memorandum at the beginning of each budget formulation cycle. This schedule will show the dates and processes to be used for planning the various phases involved in the formulation process.

2.2.6. Program and budget review exhibits will be identified in the program and budget review guidance for each submission cycle. In most cases, submissions will include data input through the OUSW(C) budget formulation systems. The process is addressed in Volume 2 procedures.

2.2.7. Pursuant to 31 U.S.C. § 1105, the DoW prepares in advance of the required President’s Budget (PB) submission to Congress. The OUSW(C) and DCAPE provide technical guidance for the program and budget data submission requirements. These offices maintain and administer web-based applications for a timely and consistent submission process.

2.2.8. All program and budget estimates, submission formats and required exhibits are found in Volume 2 procedures.

2.3 CCMD Business Rules (Joint Task Assignment Process (JTAP))

2.3.1. Financial Management Arrangements

As a business rule governing financial management arrangements between CCMD Support Agents (CCSAs) and CCMDs, the OSW will establish initial funding for new CCMD missions. The OSW will establish and provide funding for new missions assigned by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary as part of the JTAP process and in conjunction with the PPBE processes. CCSAs must maintain funding for the directed CCMD missions and adjust CCMD accounts across the FYDP consistent with the OSW/OMB approved inflation indices. CCMDs will be subjected to a proportionate share (on a percentage basis) of total CCSA reductions from undistributed congressional and/or OSW general reductions.

2.3.2. Adjustments of Funds

All Service business and efficiency reductions require prior CCMD or OSW approval to ensure they do not impede the conduct of directed missions. CCSAs will pre-coordinate any Service-initiated reductions to CCMD resources with the CCMD s during each phase of the PPBE process for all years in the FYDP, and Service-initiated reductions will not be applied to any CCMD funds without the prior approval of the CCMD or the OSW staff. OUSW(C), OSW CAPE, Joint Staff, CCMDs and CCSAs will meet annually to validate, and adjudicate as necessary, all adjustments to CCMD resources. The OUSW(C) will review and coordinate CCSA budget exhibits that specifically pertain to CCMD resources with CCMDs prior to approval and publication to ensure that CCSAs have fully complied with PBD or PDM direction.

2.3.3. Visibility of CCMD Directed Missions and Other Costs

CCSAs must ensure adequate visibility of CCMD directed missions and other costs for each O&M funded CCMD. A minimum of two Sub Activity Groups (SAG)s within each MILDEP’s active components’ O&M appropriation will be established as Mission Funding (one or more SAGs) and Headquarters and Headquarters Support Funding (single SAG). Budget and execution structure for USTRANSCOM will continue to follow the normal Working Capital Fund business area structure. The United States Special Operations Command and the United States Cyber Command budget structures are not governed by the guidance in section 2.2.

title: Section 3.0: Military Personnel Appropriations
content:
3.0    MILITARY PERSONNEL APPROPRIATIONS

Military Personnel and Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund Contribution appropriations finance statutory military pay, allowances, and entitlements; Retired Pay Accrual (RPA); Thrift Savings Plan (TSP) Service member and matching contributions; Continuation Pay (CP); special and incentive pays; permanent change of station (PCS) entitlements; and the required MERHCF contribution for Active and Reserve Component Service members. Program and budget estimates must reflect the most current military personnel strength plans provided by the Military Departments, including projected average strength for each fiscal year. Estimates must also reflect statutory pay rates, statutory formulas, and compensation policies issued by the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Personnel and Readiness. Detailed exhibit requirements are provided in the Volume 2 procedures.

title: Section 4.0: Operation and Maintenance Appropriations
content:
4.0    OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE APPROPRIATIONS

Operation and Maintenance appropriations support baseline and overseas operations. Refer to the Volume 2 procedures for detailed guidance.

title: Section 5.0: Procurement Appropriations
content:
5.0    PROCUREMENT APPROPRIATIONS

5.1    Preparations

5.1.1. General Guidance. This section provides guidance for the preparation of procurement appropriation backup material required to support the Budget Estimates Submission (BES) and the President’s budget request. The procurement accounts should also submit applicable exhibits required by other sections of this volume. The Components will also submit any exhibits required by the OMB Circular No. A‑11.

5.1.2. Specific Guidance. The budget justification material should be unclassified. All classified material must be submitted separately. Components must include a P-40 Budget Justification exhibit for special access programs (SAPs) that are not labeled as secret. The P-40 exhibits for SAPs must only include funding streams and cite the following justification: “This program is reported in accordance with 10 U.S.C. § 119(a)(1) in the Special Access Program Annual Report to Congress.” All other (non-intel and non-SAP) classified funding requests must be identified (submit a one page P-40 exhibit) within unclassified justification budget materials. Refer to Volume 2 procedures for exhibit formats, templates, and additional instructions.

5.2    Transmittal Clearance

MILDEPs and Defense Agencies are responsible for clearing the justification material with the Washington Headquarters Services, Defense Office of Prepublication and Security Review, prior to transmittal to OMB and the congressional committees.

title: Section 6.0: Research, Development, Test and Evaluation Appropriations
content:
6.0    RESEARCH, DEVELOPMENT, TEST AND EVALUATION APPROPRIATIONS

6.1    General Guidance

Unless otherwise specified, this guidance applies to all RDT&E appropriations and to all budgets. The budget justification material should be unclassified. All classified material must be submitted separately. Components must include a R-2 RDT&E Budget Justification exhibit for special access programs (SAPs) that are not labeled as secret. The R-2 exhibits for SAPs must only include funding streams and cite the following justification: “This program is reported in accordance with 10 U.S.C. § 119(a)(1) in the Special Access Program Annual Report to Congress.” All other (non-intel and non-SAP) classified funding requests must be identified (i.e., submit a one page R-2 exhibit) within unclassified justification budget materials.

6.2    RDT&E Budget Activities

The RDT&E budget activities are broad categories reflecting different types of RDT&E efforts. The categories are provided in subparagraphs 6.2.1 through 6.2.8 below. The acquisition milestones identified in the definitions are established by DoWI 5000.02, “Operation of the Adaptive Acquisition Framework.” Acquisition program developmental criteria and administrative requirements for each milestone are set forth in this instruction.

6.2.1. Budget Activity 1, Basic Research. Basic research is systematic study directed toward greater knowledge or understanding of the fundamental aspects of phenomena and of observable facts without specific applications towards processes or products in mind. It includes all scientific study and experimentation directed toward increasing fundamental knowledge and understanding in those fields of the physical, engineering, environmental, and life sciences related to long-term national security needs. It is farsighted high payoff research that provides the basis for technological progress. Basic research may lead to: (a) subsequent applied research and advanced technology developments in Defense-related technologies, and (b) new and improved military functional capabilities in areas such as communications, detection, tracking, surveillance, propulsion, mobility, guidance and control, navigation, energy conversion, materials and structures, and personnel support. Program elements in this category involve pre-Milestone A efforts.

6.2.2. Budget Activity 2, Applied Research. Applied research is systematic study to understand the means to meet a recognized and specific need. It is a systematic expansion and application of knowledge to develop useful materials, devices, and systems or methods. It may be oriented, ultimately, toward the design, development, and improvement of prototypes and new processes to meet general mission area requirements. Applied research may translate promising basic research into solutions for broadly defined military needs, short of system development. This type of effort may vary from systematic mission-directed research beyond that in Budget Activity 1 to sophisticated breadboard hardware, study, programming and planning efforts that establish the initial feasibility and practicality of proposed solutions to technological challenges. It includes studies, investigations, and non-system specific technology efforts. The dominant characteristic is that applied research is directed toward general military needs with a view toward developing and evaluating the feasibility and practicality of proposed solutions and determining their parameters. Applied Research precedes system specific technology investigations or development. Program control of the Applied Research program element is normally exercised by general level of effort. Program elements in this category involve pre‑Milestone B efforts, also known as Concept and Technology Development phase tasks, such as concept exploration efforts and paper studies of alternative concepts for meeting a mission need.

6.2.3. Budget Activity 3, Advanced Technology Development (ATD). This budget activity includes development of subsystems and components and efforts to integrate subsystems and components into system prototypes for field experiments and/or tests in a simulated environment. Budget Activity 3 includes concept and technology demonstrations of components and subsystems or system models. The models may be form, fit, and function prototypes or scaled models that serve the same demonstration purpose. The results of this type of effort are proof of technological feasibility and assessment of subsystem and component operability and producibility rather than the development of hardware for service use. Projects in this category have a direct relevance to identified military needs. Advanced Technology Development demonstrates the general military utility or cost reduction potential of technology when applied to different types of military equipment or techniques. Program elements in this category involve pre-Milestone B efforts, such as system concept demonstration, joint and Service-specific experiments or Technology Demonstrations and generally have Technology Readiness Levels of 4, 5, or 6. (For further discussion on Technology Readiness Levels, see the Assistant Secretary of War for Research and Engineering’s Technology Readiness Assessment (TRA) Guidance.) Projects in this category do not necessarily lead to subsequent development or procurement phases but should have the goal of moving out of Science and Technology (S&T) and into the acquisition process within the FYDP. Upon successful completion of projects that have military utility, the technology should be available for transition.

6.2.4. Budget Activity 4, Advanced Component Development and Prototypes (ACD&P). Efforts necessary to evaluate integrated technologies, representative modes, or prototype systems in a high fidelity and realistic operating environment are funded in this budget activity. The ACD&P phase includes system specific efforts that help expedite technology transition from the laboratory to operational use. Emphasis is on proving component and subsystem maturity prior to integration in major and complex systems and may involve risk reduction initiatives. Program elements in this category involve efforts prior to Milestone B and are referred to as advanced component development activities and include technology demonstrations. Completion of Technology Readiness Levels 6 and 7 should be achieved for major programs. Program control is exercised at the program and project level. A logical progression of program phases and development and/or production funding must be evident in the FYDP.

6.2.5. Budget Activity 5, System Development and Demonstration (SDD). System Development and Demonstration (SDD) programs have passed Milestone B approval and are conducting engineering and manufacturing development tasks aimed at meeting validated requirements prior to full-rate production. This budget activity is characterized by major line item projects, and program control is exercised by review of individual programs and projects. Prototype performance is near or at planned operational system levels. Characteristics of this budget activity involve mature system development, integration, demonstration to support Milestone C decisions, conducting live fire test and evaluation, and initial operational test and evaluation of production representative articles. A logical progression of program phases and development and production funding must be evident in the FYDP consistent with the Department’s full funding policy.

6.2.6. Budget Activity 6, RDT&E Management Support. This budget activity includes management support for research, development, test, and evaluation efforts and funds to sustain and/or modernize the installations or operations required for general research, development, test, and evaluation. Test ranges, military construction, maintenance support of laboratories, operation and maintenance of test aircraft and ships, and studies and analyses in support of the RDT&E program are funded in this budget activity. Costs of laboratory personnel, either in-house or contractor operated, would be assigned to appropriate projects or as a line item in the Basic Research, Applied Research, or ATD program areas, as appropriate. Military construction costs directly related to major development programs are included in this budget activity.

6.2.7. Budget Activity 7, Operational System Development. This budget activity includes development efforts to upgrade systems that have been fielded or have received approval for full rate production and anticipate production funding in the current or subsequent fiscal year. All items are major line item projects that appear as RDT&E Costs of Weapon System Elements in other programs. Program control is exercised by review of individual projects. Programs in this category involve systems that have received approval for Low Rate Initial Production (LRIP). A logical progression of program phases and development and production funding must be evident in the FYDP, consistent with the Department’s full funding policy.

6.2.8. Budget Activity 8, Software and Digital Technology Pilot Programs

6.2.8.1. Software and Digital Technology Pilot Program requirements for funding in BA 8 include software, electronic tools, systems, applications, resources, acquisition of services, business process re-engineering activities, functional requirements development, technical evaluations, and other activities in direct support of acquiring, developing, deploying, sustaining, enhancing, and modernizing Software Digital Technology Pilot Programs.

6.2.8.2. Pilot programs may purchase Commercial off the Shelf (COTS) software, tools, and services necessary to meet the program’s requirements.

6.2.8.3. Software and Digital Technology Pilot Programs may be nominated to Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment. Approved pilot program nominations will be submitted with the President’s Budget request.

6.2.8.4. A system project participating in the Pilot Program may be removed from BA 8 if the project has not been successful in meeting criteria established for the Pilot Program.

6.3    Establishing RDT&E Program Elements

6.3.1. The program element is the primary data element in the FYDP and is the major aggregation, at which RDT&E efforts are organized, budgeted, and reviewed. All funding associated with a major system new start must be identified in a unique program element. Requests to establish program elements should be forwarded to OSW CAPE for coordination and approval.

6.3.2. In general, the coding symbology identifies the RDT&E budget activity for the program element. Program elements in RDT&E budget activities 1 through 6 will have “06” in the first two positions; “06” indicates it is part of Major Force Program 6, Research and Development. The third and fourth position will identify the specific budget activity (e.g., 0602 is an RDT&E budget activity 2 program element). Program elements in RDT&E budget activity 7 reflect the Major Program of the fielded system in the first two positions (e.g., “01” indicates a strategic system).

title: Section 7.0: Military Construction/Family Housing Appropriations
content:
7.0    MILITARY CONSTRUCTION/FAMILY HOUSING APPROPRIATIONS

7.1    Applicable Accounts

This section provides guidance for budget formulation and congressional justification of Military Construction (MILCON), Family Housing, Homeowners’ Assistance Program (HAP), North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) Security Investment Program, Family Housing Improvement Fund (FHIF), Military Unaccompanied Housing Improvement Fund (MUHIF), and Military Housing Privatization Initiative (MHPI) Investments and Credit Financing appropriations. This section also covers specific back-up material requirements for these accounts and provides additional specific guidance for the back-up material required for MILCON, Family Housing, Homeowners’ Assistance Program and NATO Security Investment Program appropriations.

7.2    Family Housing Program Policies and Guidelines

7.2.1. Policy

7.2.1.1. It is DoW Policy: 1) to provide Military Family Housing for military families and for eligible civilian families only when suitable housing in the community does not exist; 2) to provide for the housing and support services, as authorized by law, that are necessary to meet the requirements of the DoW; 3) that the program must be financed and managed in the most cost effective and efficient manner possible in order to support these requirements and to maximize the use of available program resources; 4) that the program must include the provision of assistance to all military personnel and certain eligible civilians in locating and utilizing privately owned housing including leasing; 5) that the program must include, within available resources, the provision of Government-owned or leased family housing and furnishings (referred to as Defense Family Housing Property); and 6) that the program must include the efficient and effective financial and program management of Defense Family Housing Property, including acquisition, privatization, operation, improvement, maintenance, debt financing, leasing, and family housing support programs.

7.2.1.2. The Family Housing Program encompasses Military Family Housing as defined and authorized by the provisions of 10 U.S.C. Chapter 169 and includes all DoW Component family housing in the Defense Family Housing Property Account, leases of real property utilized by DoW Components for family housing, and associated family housing support services programs.

7.2.2. Responsibilities

7.2.2.1. The USW(A&S) is responsible for program management as set forth in the DoDI 4165.63, and DoD Manual (DoDM) 4165.63, which also addresses Unaccompanied Housing. 10 U.S.C. § 2851a established the Assistant Secretary of War for Energy, Installations, and Environment (ASW(EI&E)) as the DoW Chief Housing Officer (CHO). The CHO oversees family and unaccompanied housing under the jurisdiction of the DoW or acquired or constructed under the MHPI. The Office of the Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Housing (ODASW(H)) carries out the day-to-day responsibilities of the CHO with respect to the creation and administration of policies and processes regarding privatized, DoW-owned, and DoW-controlled family and unaccompanied housing. The ODASD(H) also has responsibility for overseeing the HAP. The USW(C) is responsible for financial management, program budget policies, program accounting policies, and financial reporting. As prescribed by the USW(C), the Director, Defense Finance and Accounting Service, is responsible for central accounting and financial reporting for the program. As prescribed by DoDI 4165.63, the Secretaries of the MILDEPs and the Directors of the Defense Agencies are responsible for execution of the program for personnel under their respective jurisdictions, including program and financial management, accounting and reporting.

7.2.2.2. In the financial management and execution of the program, DoW Components must conduct program budget formulation, presentation, and execution in accordance with the guidance and provisions contained in this section and adhere to the program accounting and financial reporting guidance and provisions contained in Volume 4.

7.2.3. Family Housing Objectives, Procedures, and the Administration / Management of Program Funds.

Refer to Volume 2 procedures for the appropriate instructions.

7.3    Uniform Budget and Fiscal Accounting Classification

7.3.1. MILCON Appropriations. Accomplish programming, budgeting, financing, and accounting for the MILCON Program under an account structure uniformly used for these purposes by all DoW Components. The uniform account structure and scope of each account prescribed for the administration of the MILCON Program are as follows:

7.3.1.1. Major Functional Category: Construction. The Immediate Subordinate Accounts include: Major Construction, Minor Construction, Design,

7.3.1.2. Major Functional Category. NATO Security Investment Program includes contributions for the United States share of the cost of multilateral programs for the acquisition and construction of military facilities and installations (including international military headquarters) and for the related expenses for the collective defense of the North Atlantic Treaty Area. 10 U.S.C. § 2806 pertains to contributions for NATO Security Investment Program.

7.3.1.3. Immediate Subordinate Account: Minor Construction. Includes any construction project not otherwise authorized by law having a cost equal to or less than $9,000,000. Minor construction projects costing more than $750,000 may not be carried out unless 10 U.S.C. § 2805 requirements are met. This includes advance approval by the Secretary concerned, and notification to the Congress if the project amount is more than $4,000,000. An unspecified MILCON project costing not more than $4,000,000 may be funded from appropriations available for O&M.

7.3.1.4. Immediate Subordinate Account: Design. Includes architectural and engineering services, construction design, working drawings, specifications and estimates for construction projects. 10 U.S.C. § 2807 pertains to architectural and engineering services and construction design.

7.3.2. Family Housing. DoW Components will use the uniform account structure established for programming, budgeting, financing and accounting for the family housing program. Administer the account structure to provide program and financial control of the family housing program consistent with applicable statutes. The uniform account structure and scope of each account for the family housing program are as follows:

7.3.2.1. Major Functional Category: Construction. The Immediate Subordinate Accounts include: New Construction (by Installation and Project), Construction Improvements (formerly Post Acquisition Construction), and Design.

7.3.2.2. Major Functional Category: O&M. The Immediate Subordinate Accounts include: Operation (Subaccounts: Management, Services, Furnishings, and Miscellaneous) Housing Privatization Support, Maintenance of Real Property Facilities, Leasing, Utilities, and Mortgage Insurance Premiums (or also known as Servicemen’s Mortgage Insurance Premiums).

7.3.2.3. Major Functional Category: FHIF. Includes activities required for family housing in connection with the MHPI program planning, execution, accounting and financial reporting, and administration of contracts entered under the authorities of 10 U.S.C. Chapter 169, Subchapter IV.

7.3.2.4. Major Functional Category: MUHIF. Includes activities required for unaccompanied housing in connection with the MHPI program planning, execution, accounting and financial reporting, and administration of contracts entered under the authorities of 10 U.S.C. Chapter 169, Subchapter IV.

7.3.3. Homeowners’ Assistance Fund, Defense Responsibilities

7.3.3.1. The Department of the Army, which has been assigned the overall responsibility for the administration and management of the DoW HAP by DoDD 4165.50E, will submit budget estimates.

7.3.3.2. Each Component is responsible for including sufficient resources in its budget to fund HAP costs related to the Component’s actions associated with base closures, realignments, and force reductions. Develop the level of resources required to fund HAP costs in consultation with the Army, HAP executive agent. Separately identify and submit budget estimates for HAP costs in the Component' Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) submissions for HAP costs associated with realignments and closures and in the O&M submission for non- BRAC related HAP costs.

7.3.4. NATO Security Investment Program Responsibilities

The OUSW(A&S) has been assigned overall responsibility for the oversight and management of the NATO Security Investment Program by DoDD 2010.05, thereby responsible for submitting the corresponding budget estimates.

7.3.5. NATO Security Investment Program Expansion Costs

Refer to Volume 2 procedures for the appropriate submission and instructions.

7.3.6. FHIF/MUHIF Program

Refer to Volume 2 procedures for the appropriate submission and instructions.

7.3.7. MHPI Investments and Credit Financing

7.3.7.1. The Federal Credit Reform Act of 1990 and OMB Circular No. A-11 require credit financing and investment information for privatization projects to be reflected in the President’s budget. OMB Circular No. A-11, Part 5, Section 85 (Federal Credit) explains the credit financing information required for the President’s budget. On an annual basis, OMB sends out Budget Data Requests (BDR) for Credit Re-estimates, MAX Schedule updates, and Credit Supplemental Reporting information for the President’s Budget (for PY, CY, and BY).

7.3.7.2. Annually, the OUSW(C), Program Budget, MPC and the ODASD(H) jointly issue a “Consolidated MHPI Data Call for the Fiscal Year 20BY President’s Budget” that supports the upcoming OMB BDRs for both Federal credit and non-credit financing aspects of MHPI, including the development of the Fiscal Year (FY) 20CY Credit Subsidy Re-estimates, Credit Supplement Report Exercise information, and OMB MAX A-11 database inputs for the FY20 BY President’s Budget (PB). OUSW(C) P/B MPC will retain responsibility for providing OMB with required MHPI Federal credit and non-Federal credit data for the FY 20BY PB. ODASD(H) will perform OSD-level reviews of MHPI programmatic data and related files, providing technical instructions with corresponding templates and feedback to the Services regarding their submissions to OUSW(C) P/B MPC.

7.3.8. For procedures covering applicable appropriations/program funds in subparagraphs
7.3.1 to 7.3.7 and budget formulation, refer to the appropriate section of the Volume 2 procedures.

title: Section 8.0: Base Realignment and Closure Appropriations
content:
8.0    BASE REALIGNMENT AND CLOSURE APPROPRIATIONS

8.1    Authority

Defense Authorization Amendments and Base Closure and Realignment Act, Public Law (PL) 100-526, established the Defense Base Closure Account (Part I) as a mechanism to provide the required funding to implement the approved recommendations of the Base Closure and Realignment Commissions. PL 101-510, Title XXIX, Defense Base Closure and Realignment Act of 1990, established Base Closure Account 1990 (Part II), the FY 2002 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) established the DoD Base Closure Account 2005 (BRAC 2005), and
Section 2711 of the FY 2013 NDAA established the DoD Base Closure Account, which directed the transfer of remaining balances from all three previous BRAC accounts. Funding approved by Congress in these Accounts is appropriated and authorized in a lump sum amount and may be spent for construction, planning and design, civilian severance pay, civilian permanent change in station, transportation of things, and other costs related to the realignment or closure of the subject bases. The management structure of the program is described below.

8.2    Guidance

8.2.1. The Assistant Secretary of War (Sustainment) is responsible for issuing policy for management of the BRAC program and overseeing the DoW Components’ execution of the program.

8.2.2. To properly account for and manage appropriated fund resources, the DoD Base Closure Accounts were established on the books of the Treasury to aid the DoW Components in the closure and realignment of certain military installations. Treasury has assigned account symbol 097-0103 to identify the DoD Base Closure Account - Part I, 097X0510 to identify DoD Base Closure Account 1990 - Part II, Part III, and Part IV, 097X0512 to identify DoD Base Closure Account 2005, and 097X0516 to identify DoD Base Closure Account (consolidated).

8.2.3. The USW(C) makes funds available to DoW Components based on their official financial plans. Financial plans are prepared by DoW Components in cooperation with and at the direction of the program manager, the ASW(Sustainment). The DoW Components’ financial plans and the subsequent allocation of funds are supported by detailed, line-item military and family housing construction justification. Separate narrative explanations for other planned expenditures are also submitted to the USW(C) in sufficient detail to support the DoW Component’s financial plan. Each DoW Component is allocated funds based upon its official budget justification and financial plan.

8.2.4. All closures and realignments must be completed no later than the end of the six- year implementation period beginning on the date on which the President transmitted to Congress the report containing the recommendations of such closures or realignments.

8.2.5. Section 2711 of FY 2013 NDAA established a new appropriation (097X0516) as DoD Base Closure Account. Funds in this account shall be available only to incur new obligations for environmental restoration, property management and disposal, and other caretaker costs at closed or realigned installations and for the purpose of recording, adjusting and liquidating obligations properly chargeable to the account under 31 U.S.C. § 1553. With the enactment of the FY 2014 NDAA (PL 113-66, dated December 26, 2013), the previous DoD BRAC accounts (097X0510 and 097X0512) remain as no-year accounts, and must be accounted for similarly to an expired appropriation. Unobligated balances from 0510 and 0512 accounts were transferred to the new BRAC account (0516) in January 2014.

8.3    Fiscal Accounting Classification

The account classification structure for the Base Closure Account, Defense is prescribed in Volume 12, section 13.

title: Section 9.0: Facilities Sustainment and Restoration/Modernization
content:
9.0    FACILITIES SUSTAINMENT AND RESTORATION/MODERNIZATION

9.1    Authority

9.1.1. Facility Sustainment Restoration and Modernization is covered under the following accounts: Operation and Maintenance Appropriations, Research, Development, Test, and Evaluation Appropriations, Defense Working Capital Funds, Military Construction appropriations, Transfer or Disposal of DoD Real Property, Lease of DoD Real Property, and DoD Overseas Military Facility Investment Recovery Account.

9.1.2. For appropriation specific policy refer to appropriation section of this document.
Section 4 provides guidance related to Operation and Maintenance costs and O&M exhibits.
Section 6 provides guidance related to Research, Development, Test, and Evaluation appropriations, Section 7 provides guidance related to Military Construction, and Section 10 provides guidance related to the Defense Working Capital Fund.

9.1.3. Additional details are provided in Volume 2 procedures.

title: Section 10.0: Defense Working Capital Budget Justification Analysis
content:
10.0    DEFENSE WORKING CAPITAL BUDGET JUSTIFICATION ANALYSIS

10.1    Intragovernmental Revolving Funds

The DoW operates five Defense Intragovernmental Revolving Funds, which comprises many accounts, sub-accounts, and activity groups.

10.1.1. The Intragovernmental Revolving Fund accounts consist of the:

10.1.1.1. Defense Working Capital Fund (DWCF), which includes:

Department of the Army Working Capital Fund (WCF);

Department of the Navy WCF;

Department of the Air Force WCF;

Defense Commissary Agency (DeCA) WCF;

Defense-Wide Working Capital Fund (DWWCF)

Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) WCF

Defense Information Services Agency (DISA) WCF

Defense Finance and Accounting Service (DFAS) WCF

10.1.1.2. Building Maintenance Fund (BMF);

10.1.1.3. Pentagon Reservation Maintenance Revolving Fund (PRMRF);

10.1.1.4. Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) WCF; and

10.1.1.5. National Defense Stockpile Transaction Fund (NDSTF).

10.1.2. This section also applies to the s Surcharge Collections, Sales of Commissary Stores, Defense account (DeCA Surcharge Fund). This trust fund, managed by DeCA, is subject to apportionment by the OMB. The Revolving Funds Directorate administers the Annual Operating Budget (AOB) for the DeCA Surcharge Fund upon apportionment. Refer to section 11 for additional information regarding the DeCA Surcharge Fund.

10.1.3. Authoritative Guidance. The National Security Act of 1947, as amended 10 U.S.C. § 2208, and other provisions of 10 U.S.C. § 131 provide the Department’s revolving fund authority. The BMF, and DCSA WCF were established under 10 U.S.C. § 2208 as separate and distinct revolving funds and therefore are not part of the DWCF. The PRMRF was established by the 1991 NDAA and codified in 10 U.S.C. § 2674. The NDSTF was codified in 50 U.S.C. § 98h while the DeCA Surcharge Fund was codified in 10 U.S.C. § 2484(d)(h).

10.2    Defense Revolving Funds

10.2.1. Cash Management Policy

10.2.1.1. Cash Balance. DoW Components must maintain a positive cash balance sufficient to meet operating, capital investment, and other justified requirements throughout the year and to support continuing requirements into the subsequent year. Each DoW Component and subordinate activity, command, or business line must establish a cash requirement based on business events, trends, activities, and risks relevant to its operations and manage that cash balance in compliance with all applicable laws and guidelines at the lowest level where transactions occur. This process is formalized through the DoW Component’s required submission of budget exhibits (Fund-13, and Fund-13b) that outline plans to maintain cash balances within a required operating range and above a specified lower control limit at the end of each budget year. Cash managers at all levels should use available mitigation strategies to control cash flow, such as negotiating the timing of customer order receipts, controlling the timing of supplier disbursements; and requesting policy waivers, like an out of cycle rate adjustment, from the OUSW(C) Revolving Funds Director to maintain/or reduce the cash balance.

10.2.1.2. Cash Thresholds. All DoW Components will construct required cash plans using specific methods as outlined in the associated DoW Revolving Fund, Fund-13 Exhibit procedure guidance.

10.2.1.3. Cash Transfers. Transfers of cash between RF activities, whether directed internally by the Components, departmental guidance, or congressional direction, will be included in all the affected activities’ budget (Fund-13). Cash transfers between Military Department’s WCFs (e.g., Army to Air Force) or between the DWCF and appropriation-funded activities require Congressional approval.

10.2.2. Advance Billings

10.2.2.1. The total amount of advance billings executed by the Department for a fiscal year may not exceed the amount specified in 10 U.S.C. § 2208 (l) or as amended by public law. 10 U.S.C. § 2208, paragraph (l)(4) provides that advance billing for background investigations and related services performed by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency is not subject to Section 2208’s congressional notification requirements and dollar limitations. 10 U.S.C. § 2208, paragraph (I)(3)(B) provides that advance billing for relief efforts following a declaration of a major disaster or emergency under the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act is not subject to Section 2208’s dollar limitations.

10.2.2.2. Components may use advance billings of customers as a cash mitigation strategy. The OUSW(C) or the MILDEP, as applicable, must notify Congress in writing within 30 days after the end of the month in which the advance billing occurred. The notification must explain the reasons for the advance billing, as well as an analysis of the effects of the advanced billing on both military readiness and the customer. Military Departments must send this notification directly to Congress and provide a copy to the Revolving Fund Directorate, while Defense Agencies must submit their requests to the Revolving Fund Directorate to notify Congress on their behalf.

10.2.2.3. With the exception of the DCSA, advance billing requires authorization within the activity’s AOB. Components must request this authority and, if approved, the Advanced Billing Authority will be added to their AOB as a note disclosure. The note disclosure must explicitly state the amount the cumulative total of the advance billing is related to a declaration of a major disaster or emergency under the Stafford Act.

10.2.2.4. Advance payments received from non-federal entities are not subject to 10 U.S.C. § 2208, advance billing limitations, and are required by Volume 11. The billing of customers by Supply Management Activities upon shipment rather than delivery is also not subject to the advance billing limitations.

10.2.3. Capital Investment Program (CIP) Policy

10.2.3.1. The legal requirements related to the CIP are found in 10 U.S.C. § 2208, paragraphs (k), (m), and (o). The legal requirements for unspecified minor military construction projects are found in 10 U.S.C. § 2805.

10.2.3.2. With the exception of major military construction and items listed in subparagraphs 10.2.3.3, 10.2.3.4., and 10.2.3.8, acquisition of all capital assets for use by activities within the revolving funds can be financed using contract authority. Components may not use the CIP to establish a new or expand an existing organic capability except as specifically justified in the President’s Budget Request (Exhibit Fund-9b, “Capital Investment Justification”).

10.2.3.3. Revolving Fund activities outside the DWCF that are not authorized contract authority (e.g. the PRMRF) must build the full cost of capital investments into their rate structure to ensure funds are available prior to obligation.

10.2.3.4. The CIP consists of the following four major categories of assets:
(1) Automated Data Processing Equipment (ADPE); (2) Non-ADPE Equipment; (3) Software Development, whether internally or externally developed; and 4) Minor Construction.

10.2.3.5. The RF Capital Budget specifically excludes the following items, which must be financed by appropriated funds.

10.2.3.5.1. Major Range and Test Facility (MRTF) installations (equipment and minor construction) that meet the DoW Investment capitalization criteria in accordance with 10 U.S.C. § 2208, paragraph (k);

10.2.3.5.2. Military and tenant support functions;

10.2.3.5.3. Major weapons systems (such as aircraft, ships, tanks, barges, etc.), and general-purpose passenger type vehicles;

10.2.3.5.4. Equipment and minor construction projects for mobilization requirements, but not used during peacetime operations;

10.2.3.5.5. Equipment initially procured and usually furnished as part of a weapons system and/or support system including modifications (includes initial common support equipment for depot maintenance support of new weapons systems);

10.2.3.5.6. Materiel is normally funded by appropriated funds and provided to contractors as Government-Furnished Materiel (GFM). The customer must use appropriated funds to purchase the GFM and provide it at no cost to the WCF;

10.2.3.5.7. Minor construction projects for non-RF activity or military support functions;

10.2.3.5.8. Construction and facility investment projects that exceed the amount specified in 10 U.S.C. § 2805 for funding under O&M appropriations;

10.2.3.5.9. Environmental projects financed or submitted for funding by the applicable Environmental Restoration Transfer appropriation;

10.2.3.5.10. Capital Investments for morale, welfare, and recreation activities; and

10.2.3.5.11. Such other exclusions as may be approved by the USW(C).

10.2.3.6. RF activities are authorized to use the CIP to purchase capital assets meeting the criteria in 10 U.S.C. § 2208, paragraph (k). The AOB permits an RF activity to obligate contract authority to purchase capital assets prior to receiving funded customer orders and collecting cash from customers. Those obligations must be funded by offsetting collections since cash does not come with contract authority. Unobligated Contract Authority does not carry into the subsequent fiscal year.

10.2.3.7. As an administrative control of resources subject to the rules of the Antideficiency Act, which is codified in 31 U.S.C. §§ 1341, 1342, and 1517, the AOBs provide a specific amount of contract authority for the CIP. Therefore, obligations may not exceed the amount provided on the AOB.

10.2.3.8. The RF customers may procure capital assets through direct appropriations for use by a RF activity. However, these assets remain the property of the customer and will be recorded as General Property, Plant, and Equipment (GPP&E) on the customers financial statements; the capital asset will not be recorded as GPP&E assets on revolving fund financial statements unless the asset is transferred to RF ownership.

10.2.3.9. WCF activities must recover costs to purchase capital assets by including a Capital Investment Recovery (CIR) factor in rates billed to customers. The revenue collected from the CIR is used to liquidate the contract authority used to procure the CIP asset. If the WCF activity does not have enough revenue to fully liquidate the contract authority, it must, at a minimum, liquidate enough to cover any cash outlays related to CIP. In addition to the CIR, a capital surcharge might be applied to collect cash for the capital outlay if the existing minimum balances are not sufficient to provide adequate budgetary resources to offset budgetary claims.

10.2.3.10. The following budget exhibits are required to document an activity’s capital budget request: (1) Exhibit Fund-9a, “Capital Investment Summary”; (2) Exhibit Fund-9b, “Capital Investment Justification,” and (3) Exhibit Fund-9c, “Capital Budget Execution.”

10.2.3.11. Each proposed CIP project must be reviewed to ensure that it satisfies the required criteria for justification and backup.

10.2.3.11.1. The acquisition of a capital asset meets the Department’s long- range planning and programming objectives and satisfies a documented need for capability to perform valid operations, functions, or services that cannot be performed as effectively or economically using existing equipment and facilities or by contract.

10.2.3.11.2. The acquisition of a capital asset complies with policies and regulations governing the acquisition and management of facilities, special tooling, and special test equipment as established by DoDD 4275.5, “Acquisition and Management of Industrial Resources,” as well as other applicable policies and regulations governing the lease and acquisition of equipment and facilities.

10.2.3.11.3. The workload projections used to justify capital purchases take into account the results of inter-service decisions, workload posture planning decisions, readily available commercial alternatives, and other reasonable options available for accomplishing applicable workload.

10.2.3.11.4. The acquisition of a capital asset accomplishes the objective for which it is justified. The criteria are: improved efficiency (savings) or effectiveness of operations; replacement of unsafe (locally determined by an authorized safety representative), beyond economical repair, or inoperative and unusable assets; and environmental, hazardous waste reduction, or regulatory agency (state, local, or Federal) mandated requirements.

10.2.3.12. A formal pre-investment economic analysis or cost comparison analysis must be completed and maintained by the originating office prior to capital budget submissions, reprogramming requests, or project substitutions across the four investment categories (ADPE, Non-ADPE, Software, and Minor Construction).

10.2.3.12.1. Formal economic analyses are required for projects of $5,000,000 or more, while cost comparison analyses are required for projects under $5,000,000.

10.2.3.12.2. Cost comparison analyses (under $5,000,000) must be prepared in constant base-year dollars, presenting yearly differential costs for up to a 6-year evaluation period.

10.2.3.12.2.1. Documentation must define objectives, functional processes, workload projections, feasible alternatives, total/differential costs, expected monetary benefits, assumptions, estimating methods, and data sources.

10.2.3.12.2.2. The payback period, expressed in tenths of years, is the primary economic ranking indicator.

10.2.3.12.3. Formal economic analyses ($5,000,000 or more) must be prepared on a net present value (NPV) basis over the project’s expected economic life, displaying costs in constant, discounted, and current dollars. This analysis must comply with applicable DoW or Component guidance as well as functional program guidance.

10.2.3.12.3.1. Documentation requires the same core elements as a cost comparison analysis, plus sensitivity/uncertainty analysis of key parameters and the identification of both intangible and quantifiable benefits (outputs achieved per investment dollar).

10.2.3.12.2. The Benefit-to-Investment Ratio (BIR) is the primary ranking indicator—calculated using discounted constant dollars as an index value rounded to two decimal places, where a BIR greater than one indicates the project is cost-beneficial and larger ratios indicate greater advantage—and must compare alternatives in terms of all expected monetary benefits (including whole and partial manpower productivity savings and other cost avoidance) over the total project life under evaluation, with the payback period considered as a secondary ranking factor.

10.2.3.12.4. The Savings-to-Investment Ratio (SIR) must be calculated using discounted dollars for Automated Information Systems to compare actual budget savings against investment costs.

10.2.3.12.5. A post-investment analysis is required upon project completion to evaluate actual costs and benefits against initial projections.

10.2.3.12.6. Exemptions from these requirements apply to environmental, hazardous waste, or regulatory mandates, higher DoW or Component authority directives that preclude alternatives, or specific DoW waivers (e.g., equipment age/condition replacement criteria).

10.2.3.13. Internal Use Software as defined in DoDI 5000.76 must be budgeted and capitalized as part of the hardware it runs on. In contrast, systems application software must be budgeted for separately, either as a direct expense or as a capital investment if it meets the criteria for a capital asset, with all new acquisitions and improvements budgeted on a per-project basis. The costs associated with the software development phase are capitalized as part of the capital budget. The preliminary design (e.g., costs prior to Milestone 0, Concept Exploration and Definition, etc.) and post implementation costs (e.g., Data conversions, application maintenance, training, documentation, etc.) are expensed as part of the operating budget. Furthermore, in accordance with 10 U.S.C. § 2222 and DoDI 5000.75, those with projected spending over $250 million or more over the FYDP for Priority Defense Business Systems or $25 million or more for Fourth Estate Defense Business Systems over the FYDP, must be approved by the Defense Business Council (DBC) and obtain certification by the DoW CIO before any funds can be obligated.

10.2.3.13.1. To account for the potential unpredictability in costs and scheduling during the development phase, any software initially planned or developed outside a Revolving Fund activity may not transfer into the revolving fund until both the preliminary design and developmental phases are completed, and the software has entered full production in the post implementation phase. This ensures that only software that is fully developed and operational is transferred into the RF. Once transferred, the fully recoverable costs will be expensed as part of the operating budget.

10.2.3.13.2. Only include those software development or acquisition efforts for the benefit of the activity in the RF capital budget submissions. Software developed or acquired for a specific customer order should be charged to and reimbursed by the requesting customer.

10.2.3.13.3. Software projects may be accomplished in modules. A module is an application that may be operated or used independent of other modules within a system. Where an entire system consists of more than one severable module, request funding for each severable module in the year that the module is started. Funding requests must be sufficient to complete the module. If several modules make up a complete ADP system, show the cost of all modules related to the system.

10.2.3.14. Unspecified minor military construction projects costing more than the threshold established in 10 U.S.C. § 2805 must be funded within the DoW Component’s Military Construction appropriation.

10.2.3.14.1. However, under 10 U.S.C. § 2805(c), O&M funds can be used for unspecified minor construction projects costing not more than the threshold established therein is available for RF-funded unspecified minor construction. Projects that have estimated costs that exceed the thresholds established in 10 U.S.C. § 2208 and not been previously documented in the budget (Exhibit Fund-9b, “Activity Capital Investment Summary”) must be approved through the Congressional notification process or in a subsequent budget and displayed as an adjustment on the Exhibit Fund-9c, “Capital Budget Execution.” The approval will be reflected in the Component’s Annual Operating Budget.

10.2.3.14.2. Laboratory Revitalization Program projects must be for the revitalization and recapitalization of Defense laboratories owned by the U.S. and under the jurisdiction of the SecWar or a MILDEP. In accordance with 10 U.S.C. § 2805, paragraph (d)(3) any projects using the Laboratory Revitalization Program requires the concerned Secretary to provide the appropriate Congressional committees a 14-day notification prior to obligation of funds. Fund activities designated to participate in the DoW Laboratory Revitalization Program must obtain prior approval from the Director or Deputy Director for Revolving Funds for all projects estimated to exceed the thresholds established in 10 U.S.C. § 2208 so that those projects can be specifically identified in the capital program within the AOB prior to project execution.

10.2.3.14.3. Capital investment costs financed in the minor construction portion of the capital budget include project planning and design costs associated with minor construction projects. Planning and design costs are not included as part of the statutory threshold for minor construction projects.

10.2.3.15. DoW Components may reprogram RF capital funds between their sub-activities, or CIP categories and their projects within the DoW component. There is no minimum or maximum limit on this type of reprogramming. Capital reprogramming between CIP categories and projects within the same RF sub-activity does not require the written approval of the OUSW(C) Revolving Funds Director or Deputy Director in the form of a signed AOB. The following approval levels, and dollar threshold, apply to changes to projects approved in the capital budget including reprogramming, substitutions, cancellations, and additions:

10.2.3.15.1. Fund managers may approve transfers between the ADP Equipment and Software categories or among their individual projects once they obtain certification from the approval authority as directed in the guidance displayed in DoDI 5000.75.

10.2.3.15.2. Fund managers may approve transfers between the Non-ADP Equipment and Minor Construction categories or among their individual projects.

10.2.3.15.3. CIP transfers between DWCF activities within a DoW Component (e.g., supply to non-supply) must be approved by the Director or Deputy Director for Revolving Funds, in the form of a signed AOB, before the transfer is executed.

10.2.3.15.4. Components must charge capital obligation adjustments to the program year cited in the President’s Budget for the original project. The prior year capital investment program limitation is equal to actual obligations on September 30 of that fiscal year plus adjustments approved by the OUSW(C) Revolving Funds Director or Deputy Director to the prior year program. Fund managers may request approval to carry over authority for any unobligated capital projects before the end of the fiscal year.

10.2.3.15.5. Capital obligation authority may be adjusted for prior year within scope increases provided that there is contract authority available to finance the increase. Before making such increases, the Component must have equal off reductions (deobligations) of current year capital authority to finance the prior year increase. Prior approval from the Director or Deputy Director for Revolving Funds is only required if cumulative adjustments exceed 20 percent of the total CIP budget of the current fiscal year. All adjustments should be documented in the activity’s next AOB but will not require a new AOB solely for such documentation.

10.2.3.15.6. For current fiscal year capital projects that will not obligate by September 30, components must request in writing permission to carry over these projects via a memo to the Director or Deputy Director for Revolving Funds. If the Director or Deputy Director for Revolving Funds approves the request in a signed memorandum, the approved carry over amounts for projects not obligated by the end of the fiscal year will be carried forward to the next fiscal year’s AOB.

10.2.4. Mobilization/Surge Costs and War Reserve Materiel

10.2.4.1. War Reserve Materiel. The DWCF activities must identify all costs related to maintaining a capacity to meet mobilization requirements. These costs are not considered normal operating costs and may be reimbursed by direct appropriations so that customer rates are not burdened by contingency requirements. Obligations for the procurement of war reserve materiel must be funded by a direct appropriation to the WCF with one exception; if Congress is notified, and a cost recovery rate is included in the rates, contract authority may be used. Such appropriated amounts for secondary items must be reflected as a separate goal within the applicable Supply Management or Commissary Resale activity AOB. Use the SM-6 “War Reserve Materiel” exhibit to justify War Reserve Materiel Requirements.

10.2.4.2. Unutilized and Underutilized Plant Capacity. Unutilized/Underutilized Plant Capacity (UPC) represents costs associated with maintaining facilities to meet surge capacity needed for mobilization or war. The UPC is a mobilization requirement budgeted in and funded by Operation and Maintenance appropriated funds of the DoW Component responsible for the activity’s management. Do not include UPC costs in the WCF rate structure. As a general rule, UPC funding includes the pro-rata facilities support costs for any month in which
1) mobilization facilities are not used or 2) facilities are used 20 percent or less of available workdays.

10.2.4.2.1. Mobilization expenses related to UPC may include both maintenance and labor costs related to mobilization.

10.2.4.2.2. Each non-supply DWCF activity should prepare a UPC Budget
Exhibit (Fund-30). This exhibit documents total capacity, Unutilized Capacity Index, justification, and cost used in developing the request for UPC. All non-supply DWCF activities should complete the three capacity-index metrics found in Part I of the exhibit. Any non-supply activity requesting UPC funding will also complete the funded UPC line in Part I and the UPC justification in Part II of the exhibit.

10.2.4.2.3. Industrial Mobilization Costs. The Army established a category of costs that includes both UPC and underutilized facilities cost called “Industrial Mobilization Cost.” The Army will use the Exhibit Fund-30, “Underutilized Plant Capacity” to justify their Industrial Mobilization Costs.

10.2.4.3. Airlift Readiness Account (ARA). The U.S. Transportation Command (USTRANSCOM) must maintain sufficient airlift capability to respond to transportation requirements for a wide variety of mobilization conditions. This requirement exists in both peacetime and contingency environments. To the extent customer revenue is insufficient to support the costs of maintaining this capability; the Air Force must provide appropriated funds from the ARA. USTRANSCOM will coordinate with military services and Combatant Commanders to understand airlift workload requirements and adjustments to workload projections on a routine basis. USTRANSCOM must provide the Air Force with the budgeted ARA amount that will be part of the Transportation Working Capital Fund Budget Estimate Submission (BES) and President’s Budget with enough lead time for the Air Force to incorporate in its budget submissions. The Air Force must submit a matching amount in its BES and President’s Budget submission within its Operation & Maintenance account. USTRANSCOM must submit the Fund- 8, “Air Mobility Command Common User Services” exhibit to justify the ARA requirement. The USTRANSCOM will record as a funded order and revenue.

10.2.5. Military Personnel

10.2.5.1. Components must use the civilian-equivalent rates provided by the OUSW(C) Revolving Funds Director to price military labor at WCF activities. The difference between the civilian-equivalent costs, included in the WCF budget, and the actual military personnel cost must be budgeted directly in the appropriate military personnel appropriation.

10.2.5.2. The amount expensed for military personnel by WCF activities and the amount reimbursed to the appropriate military personnel appropriation must equal the amount budgeted. No adjustments will be made to the WCF cost of operations to reflect the actual cost of military personnel employed by WCF activities. Military Departments having military personnel assigned to other Components, must provide to each Component the number of work years that should be included in the WCF budget submission. The WCF activities that augment their manpower requirements with National Guard or Reserve personnel, to include those participating in the Personnel Force Innovation program, must reimburse the appropriate military personnel appropriation at the WCF civilian-equivalency rates.

10.2.6. Full Recovery of Costs and the Setting of Prices

10.2.6.1. Managers of RF activities within each Component will set their prices based on full cost recovery, including all general and administrative support. Prices are established by the budget process and are represented at the aggregate level in the form of a composite rate. Prices and corresponding rates should remain fixed during the year of execution (exceptions are listed in Volume 11). Prior to execution, Components will conduct a review of prices changes for all National Item Identification Numbers to mitigate any unintended impact on customer buying power. Customers may request price challenges in accordance with DoDM 4140.01 Volume 9,
section 6.2 and dispute bills between DoW Components in accordance with the process outlined in DoW FMR Volume 11. This stabilized price policy serves to protect customers from unforeseen inflationary increases and other cost uncertainties and better assures customers that they will not have to reduce programs to pay for potentially higher -than-anticipated prices. In turn, this policy allows activities to execute the budgeted program level and permits a more effective use of RF resources.

10.2.6.2. Except in unusual circumstances, prices for the budget year will be set to break even over the long run at the sub-activity level. Generally, this means that prices will be set to achieve an AOR of zero in the budget year, provided that cash and budgetary resources are available to support the adjustments. If unusual circumstances have put a severe strain on cash such that projected cash levels are below the lower limit of the operating range, the RF activity may consider planning for a positive AOR in the budget year. However, the AOR balance will either be off-set in the budget by deferring the AOR balance into the subsequent budget year or as a nonrecoverable AOR in the Fund-14. In budget execution, activities will incur either a positive or negative operating result. Accordingly, activities will adjust their budget year prices by increasing their rates to recover actual or projected losses of budgetary resources or decreasing their rates for the customers to account for excess cash resources or projected budgetary gains to customers. An activity may request recovery of AOR outside the budget year. This request must be included in the budget submission and must demonstrate that the alternative recovery period will not adversely affect the cash balance of the activity. A phased recovery schedule must be provided with the budget.

10.2.6.3. WCF rules for pricing and operating loss recovery or gain distribution may be waived or deferred if one or more of the following conditions exist.

10.2.6.3.1. Fund Liquidity: Component fund managers must maintain a positive cash balance throughout the year. The cash requirement developed on the exhibit, Fund 13b, Cash Requirements, provides a management guide for maintaining cash sufficiency.

10.2.6.3.2. Depot Maintenance Additional Requirements: If Component cash balances are projected to be sufficient by the end of the budget year, depot maintenance activities will recoup losses and return gains in the budget year. However, if cash balances will be outside the cash operating range, an out-of-cycle rate adjustment or surcharges may be directed, to restore cash to appropriate levels, at any time in accordance with subparagraph 10.2.6.3.1. Components may recoup unplanned depot losses in subsequent years with prior year resources. Prior to employing this financing method, components must notify the OUSW(C) Revolving Funds Director in writing of actions being taken and provide evidence all other criteria for prior year upward obligations are met.

10.2.6.3.3. A WCF activity operating overseas may experience significant operating losses or gains due to changes in foreign currency exchange rates. The WCF activities are not eligible to participate directly in the Foreign Currency Fluctuations, Defense (FCF,D) (97-X-0803) and the Foreign Currency Fluctuations – Construction, Defense (FCF-C,D) (97-X-0801) accounts.

10.2.6.3.4. In addition to spreading contract costs when developing rates for all customers, the RF activities may incur and recover costs for contracts awarded specifically to fill the requirements of one customer by charging that customer an amount equivalent to the RF activity’s expense in funding, awarding, and administering the contract. During the year, price changes must be in accordance with Volume 11, section 25.

10.2.6.3.5. Unbillable costs and operational losses that cannot be billed to an identifiable customer or that were generated from unforeseen cost overruns are to be treated as costs in the fiscal year in which the costs were incurred. The resulting operating losses must be included in calculating net and accumulated operating results.

10.2.6.3.6. Unless approved in writing by the Director or Deputy Director for Revolving Funds as an out-of-cycle rate adjustment, the prices must be consistent with the rates set for all activity products, goods, or services approved during the budget review and documented in a memorandum signed by the USW(C), or designated representative.

10.2.6.3.7. Users must pay for the goods and services provided by all WCF activities, including deployment or other emergency response for military or humanitarian assistance. Consistent with this policy, third party collections for transportation provided in response to a Request-for-Assistance (RFA) from another government agency are prohibited. The Military Department that controls the equipment or personnel is responsible for reimbursing USTRANSCOM. It is then the responsibility of the Military Department that accepted the RFA to collect any required reimbursements due that Military Department by the requesting government agency.

10.2.6.3.7.1. The only exception to this policy is when the Joint Chiefs of Staff orders USTRANSCOM to transport non-U.S. equipment or personnel, such as for non-reimbursed support to the United Nations. In these specific cases, the costs are covered by the respective military branches: the Army pays for Surface Deployment and Distribution Command, the Navy for Military Sealift Command, and the Air Force for Air Mobility Command. While billing can be centralized for convenience, invoices must be forwarded to the responsible Military Department within 30 days of the mission’s start. These departments are required to pay all bills, including those for transportation, in a timely manner.

10.2.6.3.7.2. This guidance does not apply to contingency operations designated by the SecWar as a “National Contingency Operation” under 10 U.S.C. § 127. These operations are governed by separate rules, which are issued at the time of their designation

10.2.6.3.8. Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC)-Related Costs. Costs incurred in implementing the recommendations of the BRAC Commissions will be funded by the appropriate BRAC account and are not to be included in the rates and costs of businesses within the Fund. The WCF activities may incur BRAC expenses prior to receiving an allocation of BRAC funding; however, all costs properly charged against the BRAC account must be reimbursed with BRAC funds. The WCF activities may not expend funds prior to complying with the notification requirements imposed by law with respect to the obligation of BRAC funds. The BRAC account must reimburse all costs incurred by WCF activities to carry out BRAC prior to the end of the fiscal year in which costs were incurred. Prior year, current year, or budget year operating losses in WCF are not to be budgeted in the base closure accounts. Costs attributable to base closure actions at WCF activities to be budgeted in BRAC may include:

10.2.6.3.8.1. BRAC directed reductions-in-force, separation incentives, plant closures, layaway or custody costs, or other BRAC-related expenses, such as all costs not associated with a valid work order during the year of closure.

10.2.6.3.8.2. Environmental restoration and mitigation, to include reducing, removing, and recycling hazardous waste, and removing unsafe building debris.

10.2.6.3.8.3. Planning, to include conducting such advance planning and design as may be required to transfer from an activity being closed to another military installation.

10.2.6.3.8.4. Outplacement assistance in relocating, training, or providing other necessary assistance to civilian employees employed by the Department at installations being closed.

10.2.6.3.8.5. Community programs, to include economic adjustment assistance to a community in which the closed base is located, or community planning assistance to the community to which functions will be transferred as a result of closure of a military installation.

10.2.6.3.9. BRAC and WCF Rates. Overhead, not specific to BRAC and not in support of producing goods or services for customers, will be financed in the year the costs are incurred with the Components’ Operation and Maintenance (O&M) appropriations. The WCF losses occurring in years prior to closure will be recovered through the rate structure to the extent that there are new customer orders. When there are no new customer orders in the budget year, the Component responsible for the activity incurring the loss will finance, as a pass through from O&M appropriations to the WCF, all overhead not included in rates supported by ongoing work or prior year losses to be recovered in the budget year. All costs at a closing activity in the year of closure that are not associated with a valid work order or are not valid BRAC costs are O&M costs and must be budgeted in the fiscal year when they will be incurred.

10.2.6.3.10. BRAC-Related Permanent Change of Station (PCS) Moves for WCF Activities. Costs incurred to recruit and hire civilian personnel (including associated PCS costs) to fill vacant positions at an activity that is being transferred from a closing or realigning installation to another military installation in accordance with a BRAC recommendation may properly be considered BRAC costs under the Base Closure and Realignment Act of 1990.
