As a matter of Department policy, however, BRAC funds will not be used for such costs except in the case of WCF activities, which may temporarily charge such costs against the WCF, provided the WCF is reimbursed with BRAC or O&M funds by the end of the fiscal year in which the costs are incurred.

10.2.6.3.11. Eligible and Ineligible Costs. BRAC accounts are intended to cover specific expenses directly related to the closure or realignment, including:
(a) reductions -in -force and separation incentives; (b) environmental restoration and hazard removal; (c) planning and design for transferring functions; (d) outplacement and training assistance for civilian employees; and (e) economic and planning assistance for affected communities. However, BRAC funds cannot be used to cover prior, current, or budget-year operating losses within the WCF.

10.2.6.4. Funding of Civilian Voluntary Separation Incentive Program will be financed and included in stabilized rates for civilian separation incentive requirements of assigned employees unless they must be offered because of a directed BRAC action, in which case the appropriate BRAC account will fund the civilian separation incentive.

10.2.6.5. WCF activities operating as tenants must reimburse the host installation for any base support services listed in Exhibit Fund-22, but only to the extent that their presence directly increases the host’s costs. This reimbursement must follow the guidelines outlined in DoDI 4000.19 for support agreements. Costs for WCF mission products and services (e.g., depot supply, depot maintenance, facility engineering services, information processing, communications, and software development) should be based on the approved stabilized rate. However, for other incidental support, the WCF activity can only be charged for the measurable, incremental direct costs it creates. Overhead costs cannot be passed on to the WCF activity. All budgeted costs for these services, whether from the host or tenant perspective, must be documented on Exhibit Fund-22 in the fall budget submission.

10.2.6.6. The labor costs for first-line supervisors – those in official positions directly overseeing non-supervisory employees – are typically charged as an indirect production cost to the cost center they manage. However, there are two exceptions. First, if a supervisor’s entire time is dedicated to a single project, their costs are handled differently. Second, if a supervisor is temporarily assigned to perform direct, hands-on work, their time must be classified as direct labor and charged to the specific job order. This policy does not apply to subordinate leaders like “crew chiefs” or “team leaders.” For more detailed guidance on labor cost accounting, refer to Volume 11.

10.2.6.7. A management headquarters is a discrete organization or part of an organization that has authority over the management of the WCF activity. The OSD and Service Departmental activities normally do not have this direct responsibility. All the major systems/logistics organizations in the Services include headquarters elements directly supporting WCF activities that should be funded or reimbursed by the WCF activities.

10.2.6.8. Costs for discrete WCF management headquarters organizations and parts of organizations that perform direct WCF management headquarters functions can be financed directly in the WCF or reimbursed by the WCF activity (whichever is more practical). In addition, Components may allocate significant costs for common support functions, such as counsel or personnel services, at WCF management headquarters to other users based on workload percentages in those functions.

10.2.6.9. Dual-Funded Organizations are organizations that are funded (including reimbursable funding) by both the WCF and other appropriations or accounts. In instances where a non-management headquarters function is funded with a combination of WCF and General Fund (GF), the function initially will be funded in its entirety by either the WCF or GF, based on the preponderance of definable units of measure for the function (e.g., workload, productive hours, outputs, or ultimate use).

10.2.6.9.1. The entity that initially funds a shared function should be reimbursed by the other users for their proportional share of the cost. The reimbursement amount is based on the same metric (e.g., workload, hours) used to determine who paid the initial cost.

10.2.6.9.2. Initial Funding Rule. The part of the organization (or funding source provided) initially funding the function should be reimbursed for appropriate amounts by other parts of the organization (or financing sources or customers) involved, based on the unit of measure that was used to determine which organization or funding source would provide initial funding; and the amount of reimbursement should be based on the relative portion of that unit of measure attributable to each part of the organization or funding source involved. If the part of an organization that is within the WCF accounts for more than 50 percent (e.g., 60 percent) of the unit of measure for a function shared with the part of the organization funded through appropriated funds, then the WCF portion of the organization initially would fund all of the costs of performing that function. However, the applicable part of the organization funded through General Funds would reimburse the WCF for, and be allocated, the remainder of the costs (e.g., 40 percent).

10.2.6.9.3. This policy does not apply to base support services. The reimbursement amount for these services provided by the WCF to tenant activities must be determined according to the policies outlined in DoDI 4000.19.

10.2.6.10. When an RF activity purchases a capital asset that is also used by a GF entity, the RF activity must capitalize the asset and bill the GF user at a rate that recovers both capital investment and operating costs. Conversely, if a GF entity purchases an asset that is also used by an RF activity, the GF entity will capitalize it and may bill the RF activity for operating costs, but it is strictly prohibited from billing for the asset’s depreciation.

10.2.6.11. When a work order or project is canceled or reduced in scope after a DWCF activity has commenced work or incurred costs, the RF activity should charge the customer for the direct and indirect production costs incurred, plus the applied overhead plus costs associated with the cancellation or reduction. Volume 11 provides specific guidance for the types of directly associated cancellation or reduction costs that can be charged to customers.

10.2.6.12. Write-offs of unusual or infrequently occurring losses are not chargeable against AOR and should not be recovered through increases in customer rates unless recovery of a cash loss or outlays is required and in accordance with accounting policies. Examples of unusual or infrequently occurring losses not recovered in rates include losses resulting from the disposal or divestiture of capital budget items that have not been fully depreciated at the time they are taken out of service due to BRAC action; or losses associated with systematic inventory reductions by disposal of assets associated with force drawdowns. Only unusual or infrequently occurring write-offs that require a cash resource will be separately identified in the Component’s budget submission using the Fund-14, “Revenue and Expenses” exhibit.

10.2.6.13. Net Operating Results (NOR) Adjustments. There are instances where additional adjustments to the Fund-14 and NOR are required. For example: Cash Transfers in and out of the fund not directly related to operational performance (Direct Appropriations associated with natural disasters, humanitarian relief, pandemics, cash infusions, and reprogramming actions e.g., transfers in/out) may use below-the-line adjustments to the NOR to adjust for transfers that are not directly related to operational performance and subsequently does not support returning or collecting AOR.

10.2.6.14. All requests (to include justification) for NOR and/or AOR non-recoverable or deferred adjustments must be submitted in writing via a memorandum format to the FMOA Director for approval prior to or concurrent with the Budget Estimate Submission.

10.2.6.15. Methods for Rate Setting for RF Activities. All DWCF activities will establish rates using the following a multiple step process detailed in Volume 2 procedures.

10.2.6.15.1. Percentage Markup on Cost. A cost recovery percentage is applied to the purchase or repair cost of secondary supply items to recover overhead costs and other pricing adjustments. This method is typically used for supply management DWCF activities.

10.2.6.15.2. Direct Labor Hour (DLH). A specific dollar value, including all direct costs, overhead, and other pricing adjustments, is charged per DLH associated with the completion of a customer order. This method is typically used for industrial DWCF activities (i.e., depot maintenance, ordnance, and research and development).

10.2.6.15.3. Specific Unit of Output. RF activities that provide services via numerous outputs that do not have a common measure for calculation will establish separate rates for each output. When multiplied by projected customer workload for each output, the rates will produce revenue that approximates, to the extent possible, recovery of the full cost, including approved adjustments, of providing the specific outputs (e.g., transportation, finance and accounting, information systems, and base support). This includes direct systems reimbursement.

10.2.6.16. Standard Fuel Price (SFP). During the budget development cycle, the Revolving Funds Directorate will establish the standard fuel price (SFP) for use by the Defense agencies and military departments to develop their fuel estimates for the budget. The Revolving Funds Directorate will use the OMB economic assumptions (EA) and the refined product costs experienced by the department to develop the SFP. The SFP consists of the refined fuel cost and the non-product cost, which includes cost for Sustainment, Restoration and Modernization (SRM), terminal operations, transportation, operations and product losses. During the year of execution, the SFP may be set at the budgeted rate or may be adjusted due to updated economic assumptions from OMB, the latest refined product cost experienced by the Department, changes in projected product costs, or the DLA Energy cash balance. The OUSW(C) must approve the SFP that will be used for the budget and changes thereafter.

10.2.7. Public-Private Partnerships at Depot Maintenance Activities

10.2.7.1. Guidance. Conditions for the sale of goods and services to non-DoW entities must be based on specific statutory authority. Pursuant to the authority granted to the SecWar by 10 U.S.C. § 2208(h) to prescribe regulations for DWCF activities and the use of inventories, this DoW guidance clarifies existing legal authority applicable in specific circumstances. The guidance set forth in this section:

10.2.7.1.1. May not be used to compete for non-defense related work;

10.2.7.1.2. Does not apply when otherwise precluded by public law;

10.2.7.1.3. Does not apply to products or services produced under work-share arrangements in which a DoW sponsor assigns work and separately funds the DoW depot maintenance activity and the private sector entity; and

10.2.7.1.4. May be used for sales to private sector entities only when the transaction is part of an arrangement that is officially recognized as a depot maintenance public -private partnership.

10.2.7.2. Sales Prices. To minimize potential DoW operating losses or gains, sales prices to private sector entities in depot maintenance public-private partnership relationships may be tailored to the most recent actual and projected costs, rather than the approved stabilized billing rates charged to DoW customers (10 U.S.C. § 2474). Tailored rates or prices charged for sales to private sector partners, if used, must ensure full cost recovery for the work involved in producing the specific products and services. Such tailored rates and prices must include: (a) all direct costs,
(b) production or shop overhead costs that contribute to the final product and (c) a full allocation of General and Administrative (G&A) overhead costs, distributed on the same basis as for DoW customers. (Since G&A overhead costs cannot be attributed to specific products or services, there is no basis to include or exclude specific items of cost from prices charged to customers.). Exceptions to DWCF pricing policy for sales to private sector parties in depot maintenance partnership arrangements, do not change the requirement that sales prices include unfunded costs, as prescribed in Volume 11.

10.2.7.3. Fixed Pricing. The DoW is authorized to sell goods and services to private sector partners using a fixed-price model, which can include multi-year agreements, provided that the work is well-defined and costs are predictable. This practice helps private partners forecast their expenses and allows for better use of DoW maintenance depot capacity. For projects where costs are uncertain, a cost-reimbursable model is more appropriate. Additionally, the DoW may accept incremental advance payments when the scope and risk associated with a contract make it a suitable option. Multiyear fixed price agreements are authorized when future production costs can be reasonably predicted and the potential for future losses and gains are minimal. Prices may be fixed at a predetermined level taking into account future year escalation factors like pay rate changes, general inflation, and the number of units produced. Multiyear fixed price agreements may also incorporate other pricing techniques such as establishment of a base price with provisions for economic price adjustments to accommodate inflation.

10.2.8. Military Clothing Items and Individual Equipment

The DLA Supply Management Activity procures military clothing and equipment (uniforms, combat equipment, tents, tool sets and kits, hand tools, and cleaning equipment and supplies) and bills users at standard prices. The Military Services are responsible for budgeting these items through the appropriate channels: the Military Personnel appropriation for new clothing bag items and the O&M appropriation for new organizational equipment. These budgets must be sufficient to cover the initial purchase and inventory, although funds can be reprogrammed if items are needed before the budget is formally approved. A replacement item is considered “new” if its cost increases by more than 10 percent compared to the item it replaces.

10.3    Budget Justification Material

Each Revolving Fund will submit justification material to the OUSW(C), Revolving Funds Directorate, in preparation for submitting the President’s budget request to the Congress following a review and approval by the OUSW(C) and the OMB. The following chart provides the required exhibits by Revolving Fund activity:

title: Section 11.0: Offsetting Receipts
content:
11.0    OFFSETTING RECEIPTS

11.1    Program and Budget Submission

Each MILDEP must include offsetting receipts in their annual program and budget submission. Refer to Volume 2 procedures for instructions consistent with the provisions of the OMB Circular No. A-11.

11.2    Accounting Policies

Refer to Volume 11 for guidance relating to the DoW accounting for offsetting receipts.

title: Section 12.0: Defense Health Program
content:
12.0    DEFENSE HEALTH PROGRAM

The Defense Health Program appropriation encompasses three sub-accounts: Operations and Maintenance (O&M); Procurement; and Research, Development, Test, and Evaluation (RDT&E). Program and budget estimates must reflect the most current actual execution and rigorous projections across the three periods of availability for each fiscal year. Detailed exhibit requirements are provided in Volume 2 procedures.

title: Section 13.0: Defense Environmental Restoration
content:
13.0    DEFENSE ENVIRONMENTAL RESTORATION

13.1    Applicability

The MILDEPs and applicable Defense Agencies with Defense Environmental Restoration Program (DERP) requirements use transfer account appropriations to fund DERP eligible cleanup activities at active installations and Formerly Used Defense Sites (FUDS) properties. Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) appropriations to fund cleanup activities are addressed in
section 7.

13.2    Environmental Restoration Account

This section directs readers to applicable guidance covering program and budget formulation for the Department’s combined Program and Budget Review and congressional justification for Environmental Restoration Account (ERA) appropriations. Readers are also directed to guidance for programming, budgeting, and performance data necessary to meet reporting requirements, respond to congressional concerns, and conform to OMB guidance to link the Department’s budget to the DERP performance goals for active installations and FUDS properties.

13.3    Eligible Appropriations

The appropriations eligible to receive funds from the Defense Environmental Restoration Transfer Accounts and their corresponding source for specific policies are O&M, Procurement, and RDT&E.

13.4    Procedures

All program and budget estimates, submission formats and required exhibits are found in Volume 2 procedures.

title: Section 14.0: Drug Interdiction and Counter-Drug Activities
content:
14.0    DRUG INTERDICTION AND COUNTER-DRUG ACTIVITIES

14.1    DoW Counternarcotics Budget Activities

The DoW Counternarcotics program provides appropriation for four budget activities, as listed in sections 14.1.1 through 14.1.4. The funds are appropriated to the Department’s Central Transfer Account (CTA) titled “Drug Interdiction and Counter-Drug Activities, Defense.” Although appropriated as an O&M account, the CTA has the authority to transfer funds to other appropriations (e.g., RDT&E or Procurement) for execution. This centralized structure supports unified budgeting and oversight while enabling execution across the entire range of DoW MILDEPs, CCMDs, and Combat Support Agencies.

14.1.1. Counter-Narcotics Support. This budget activity includes detection and monitoring of aerial and maritime transit, and countering the production, trafficking, and use of illegal drugs into the United States.

14.1.2. Drug Demand Reduction Program. This budget activity includes prevention, education, and outreach to ensure the dangers of drug abuse and misuse within the DoW are understood, prevented, identified, and treated to keep the fighting force at the highest levels of readiness.

14.1.3. National Guard Counter-Drug Program. This budget activity support State National Guard assistance to Federal, State, tribal, and local law enforcement agencies, and community-based organizations in efforts to disrupt and degrade illicit drug production and trafficking within the United States.

14.1.4. National Guard Counter-Drug Schools. This budget activity funds the operation of five National Guard counter-drug schools, which provide counter-drug and related counter transnational organized crime courses of instruction to Federal, State, local and community-based organizations from the 50 states, three territories, and the District of Columbia.

14.2    Responsibilities

The Office of the Deputy Assistant Secretary of War (Counternarcotics and Global Threats) (ODASW(CNGT)) is responsible for all submission requirements for this program. DoW Components are responsible for providing all needed input to ODASW(CNGT), consistent with the submission requirements and due dates established by ODASW(CNGT).

14.3    Procedures

All program and budget estimates, submission formats and required exhibits are found in Volume 2 procedures.

title: Section 15.0: Overseas Cost Report
content:
15.0    OVERSEAS COST REPORT

Section 8125 of the Fiscal Year 1989 DoD Appropriations Act (PL 100-463), as codified in 10 U.S.C. § 113, requires that the DoW separately identify the amounts necessary for payment of all personnel, operations, maintenance, facilities, and support costs for all DoW overseas military units and the costs of supporting all dependents who accompany DoW personnel outside the United States. Refer to the Volume 2 procedures for guidance on OP-53 Exhibit (Overseas Funding) requirements.

title: Section 16.0: Intelligence Programs/Activities
content:
16.0    INTELLIGENCE PROGRAMS/ACTIVITIES

16.1    National Intelligence Program (NIP)

16.1.1. NIP Scope. The NIP provides integrated intelligence that covers broad aspects of national policy and national security. The portion of the NIP contained in the DoW Budget contributes substantially to meeting Defense intelligence requirements and may also contain programs/activities in support of elements of the United States Government outside the DoW.

16.1.2. NIP Classification. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) determines classification of U.S. Intelligence funding and manpower information, pursuant to EO 12958, Section 1.5(c); EO 12333, Section 1.5(g), and the DNI’s authorities under the National Security Act of 1947.

16.1.2.1. NIP resource information in all DoW databases must be classified as shown in subparagraphs 17.1.2.2 thru 17.1.2.5 unless other specific NIP program guidance in effect requires higher classification. NIP resource information for military construction and family housing for defense agencies are exempt and must be maintained and presented as unclassified.

16.1.2.2. Information which, standing alone or in aggregate, reveals any Program Element (PE) total or DoW Component total funding or manpower requirements of any program in the NIP will be classified SECRET.

16.1.2.3. Information that permits the disclosure of any PE total or the funding or manpower requirements of any program in the NIP, for example, through a subtractive process, will be classified SECRET.

16.1.2.4. Whenever NIP funding and manpower information is combined with other unclassified programs in such a way as to effectively mask the NIP resource PE total, such combined resource PE total may be treated as unclassified.

16.1.2.5. Forward requests for clarification of the foregoing classification guidance to the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Intelligence and Security (OUSW(I&S)). The OUSW(I&S) will coordinate questions of application with the ODNI and disseminate responses to all interested DoW Components.

16.1.3. NIP Budget Submissions. DoW Components with NIP Special Program Codes (SPCs) will prepare and provide NIP Congressional Budget Justification Books (CBJB) in accordance with guidance provided by the ODNI. Coordinate Decision Documents affecting elements of the NIP with the ODNI, the OUSW(C) and the OUSW(I&S). The OUSW(C), Program/Budget (P/B), Investment Directorate will ensure that the DNI Chief Financial Officer (CFO) has an opportunity to review and provide comments.

16.1.3.1. The DoW Components will implement ODNI’s Intelligence Community Directive 104 and Military Personnel Resources Programming and Budgeting Policies and Procedures when developing NIP military personnel cost estimates for the budget submission.

16.1.3.2. The CBJB will incorporate an Intelligence Community (IC) project to PE crosswalk exhibit at the R-1, P 1, and OP-1 levels to help satisfy continuous congressional budget reconciliation and visibility requirements. DoW Components must continue to show steady, measurable progress toward achieving fully captured, whole, distinct, NIP data elements for all appropriations RDT&E; Procurement (PROC); O&M; MILCON; and Military Personnel (MILPERS)) identified by NIP SPC. NIP resources will not be shared or aligned to Non-NIP PEs.

16.1.3.3. The ODNI will deliver one hardcopy and compact disk (CD) of NIP program and budget materials prescribed by the ODNI to the OUSW(C), P/B, Investment Directorate, Pentagon, Room 3C749, at the same time they are delivered to the OMB.

16.1.4. NIP Classified Appeals

16.1.4.1. Classified appeals may supplement actions included in the overall Defense Appeal where security considerations have dictated a less than complete justification. Prepare classified appeals at the appropriate level of classification to fully explain and justify the action. The ODNI will determine the appeals format and content.

16.1.4.2. Classified appeals will be consistent with the SecWar policy direction as articulated by the OUSW(C) and, in the case of appeals to legislative provisions, also as articulated by the Office or the General Counsel and the Deputy SecWar. Coordinate all NIP appeals with the OUSW(I&S), the OUSW(C) and the OMB before release to the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence (HPSCI), the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, the House Appropriations Committee (HAC), and the Senate Appropriations Committee (SAC).

16.2    Military Intelligence Program (MIP)

16.2.1. MIP Scope. The MIP consists of programs, projects, or activities that support the SecWar’s intelligence, counterintelligence, and related responsibilities as outlined in DoDD 5205.12. This includes those intelligence and counterintelligence programs, projects, or activities that provide capabilities to meet warfighters’ operational and tactical requirements more effectively. The term excludes capabilities associated with a weapons system whose primary mission is not intelligence, along with all, programs, projects, and activities under the NIP.

16.2.2. MIP Classification. MIP projects, individual PEs and line items may be classified or unclassified according to content, unless disclosure of such a total would allow derivation of classified totals. The total DoW funding for MIP is classified SECRET. Intelligence project resource data will be sorted, aggregated, and used in different ways. It is essential that DoW Components comply with DoW Financial Management Sensitive Activities Security Classification Guidance and the OUSW(I&S) and the OUSW(C) receive DoW Component current SCGs to avoid inadvertent, unauthorized disclosure of classified information. Additionally, DoW Components are responsible for reviewing and validating their project level classification and include SCG compliance statements in their Congressional Justification Book (CJB) validation memorandum submitted to OUSW(I&S).

16.2.3. MIP Budget Submissions

16.2.3.1. The OUSW(I&S) will provide complementary MIP CJB guidance. The CJB is a functional aggregation of the MIP portion of the DoW request, containing program justification and resource highlights that must be consistent with and directly auditable to all DoW justification materials (e.g., R-2, P-40, OP-5) and any other DoW justification books that address the same resources.

16.2.3.2. The OUSW(I&S) will task DoW Components annually to provide SCG for each project, along with a citation of the source of classification and any other security classification guidance unique to the organization that may be pertinent to the MIP.

16.2.3.3. Each DoW Component identified in DoDD 5205.12, with resources delineated by SPC 296, 355, 365, or 398 will prepare DoW justification materials for each appropriation. Classified justification materials will contain sufficient detail needed to fully justify the classified portion of the request, without the use of supplemental justification materials.

16.2.3.4. The CJB will incorporate a MIP project to PE crosswalk exhibit at the R-1, P 1, and O-1 levels to help satisfy continuous congressional budget reconciliation and visibility requirements. DoW Components must comply with achieving fully captured, whole, distinct, MIP data elements for all appropriations (RDT&E, PROC, O&M, MILCON, and MILPERS) identified by SPC 296, 355, 365, or 398. MIP resources will not be shared or aligned to non-MIP PEs.

16.2.3.5. DoW Components will submit one hardcopy and PDFs of their classified R-2, P-40 or OP-5 and the OUSW(I&S) will deliver one final MIP hardcopy and PDFs of all volumes directly to the OUSW(C), P/B Investment Directorate, Pentagon, Room 3C749, at the same time as the unclassified details. The OUSW(C) will review and combine all DoW Component classified exhibits (SECRET and TOP SECRET) as a classified Defense-wide volume
exhibit before releasing to OMB.

16.2.4. MIP Classified Appeals

16.2.41. Classified appeals may supplement actions included in the overall Defense Appeal where security considerations have dictated a less than complete justification. Prepare classified appeals at the appropriate level of classification necessary to fully explain and justify the action. Unclassified MIP appeals will follow normal procedures per additional guidance.

16.2.4.2. Classified Appeals will be completely consistent with the SecWar policy direction as articulated by the OUSW(C) and, in the case of appeals to legislative provisions, also as articulated by the Office of the General Counsel and the Deputy SecWar. The OUSW(I&S) will prepare classified appeals for the MIP and must coordinate with the OUSW(C), the ODNI CFO and the OMB before release to the House Armed Services Committee, Senate Armed Services Committee, HAC, and SAC, and HPSCI.

title: Section 17.0: Information Technology (Including Cyberspace Activities)
content:
17.0    INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (INCLUDING CYBERSPACE ACTIVITIES)

17.1    Office of Primary Responsibility

Within the office of the Chief Information Officer (CIO) of the DoW, the Deputy CIO for Resources and Analysis (DCIO(RA)) is responsible for collecting, assembling, and reporting of the Department’s Information Technology and Cyberspace Activities (IT/CA) budget for the purposes of submitting complete and accurate IT/CA justification materials to the OMB and the Congress. DoW CIO DCIO(RA) will issue annual supplemental guidance that addresses detailed and amplifying submission requirements, relevant changes, and submission due dates.

17.2    Applicability

The IT/CA budget submission materials apply to the Office of the SecWar (OSW), the MILDEPs (including their National Guard and Reserve Components), the Joint Staff, the CCMDs, the DoW Inspector General, the Defense Agencies and Field Activities, the Joint Service Schools, the Defense Health Program, and the Court of Military Appeals.

title: Section 18.0: Other Special Analyses
content:
18.0    OTHER SPECIAL ANALYSES

This section introduces DoW budget formulation and congressional back-up information requirements for various special interest areas not covered in the preceding sections. The exhibit requirements cover resources crossing DoW appropriations and are generally functional in nature. Exhibits are required for program review, budget review, and congressional justification/presentation submissions. Detailed information on submission requirements, exhibit or material preparation, and special instructions on the review processes are provided in Volume 2 procedures.

18.1    Combating Terrorism

The data collected for Combating Terrorism through reporting process will be used to comply with congressional and OMB reporting requirements. The Department will also use the data to evaluate the Components’ combating terrorism efforts during program and execution reviews. Office responsibilities and definitions specific to Combating Terrorism are provided in Volume 2 procedures.

18.2    Major Range and Test Facility Base

The Major Range and Test Facility Base (MRTFB) exhibit formats submitted in support of the Program and Budget Review submission are the same as those submitted to the Director, DoW Test Resource Management Center (TRMC) in support of the President’s Budget except that the President’s Budget submission will not include updates to any of the Direct (User) funding or MILCON information on any exhibit to include Exhibit 2D, Source of Direct Funds, in whole. This guidance applies to the activities included in the MRTFB, as defined in DoDD 3200.11. Budget estimates will be in accordance with the applicable funding policy for the required appropriation or account.

18.3    Test and Evaluation Funding

The DOT&E is charged with oversight of the DoW T&E resources and funding of T&E by each major DoW program. Modifications to the instructions in Volume 2 procedures, requests for deviations from their provisions, or requests for their clarification or applicability should be directed to and coordinated with DOT&E and OUSW(C) Program and Budget.

18.4    Financial Management Activities

Information on funding levels for financial management activities is required for oversight and review of component resources devoted to these activities and to ensure that their use is in accordance with the government-wide 5-year financial management plan prepared by OMB as required by the Chief Financial Officers Act of 1990. It fulfills the requirements outlined in OMB Circular No. A-11, Sections 130 and 150, which govern apportionment reporting and administrative control of funds.

18.5    Federal Credit Programs

Credit programs in the DoW consist of direct loans and guaranteed loans. Submission requirements and definitions specific to the DoW credit programs are provided in Volume 2 procedures. Agencies can also refer to OMB Circular No. A-11 for a more detailed explanation of terminology and budget instructions.

18.6    Other Interest Areas

The Congress or OMB has prioritized areas of special interest that require submission of additional budget justification material, with requirements extending beyond a single appropriation. The list and corresponding instructions for these exhibits are provided either in Volume 2 procedures or OUSW(C) guidance for the budget review and/or the President’s Budget submission.

title: Section 1.0: General
content:
1.0    GENERAL

1.1    Overview

1.1.1. Volume 3 provides general guidance on the execution of the budget, specifically for availability and use of the budgetary resources, for the Office of the Secretary of War (OSW). Budget policy memoranda issued throughout the year, special instructions, and nonrecurring requirements unique to that year’s budget cycle will provide any necessary changes or revisions to this standing document. The provisions of Volume 3 apply to all DoW military and specified civil functions.

1.1.2. Volume 3 also provides budget policies; general guidance on supporting material, and budget execution submission formats in addition to specific guidance by appropriations, programs, and activities. Required budget exhibits and formats, corresponding instructions, procedures, and automated submission requirements can be found in the Volume 3 Supplemental Document.

1.2    Purpose

This volume provides budget execution policies, exceptions to policies, and proposed changes, specifically related to the availability and use of budgetary resources. This volume also contains guidance for governing budget execution business rules and financial management arrangements. The scope and provisions in this volume apply to the OSW, the Military Departments (MILDEPs), the Defense Agencies, the Combatant Commands, and any other Defense Agencies or DoW Field Activities (hereafter referred to as “Components”) that manage program and budget resources.

1.3    Authoritative Guidance

Refer to the authoritative guidance document.

title: Section 2.0: Apportionment / Reapportionment and Funds Distribution
content:
2.0    APPORTIONMENT / REAPPORTIONMENT AND FUNDS DISTRIBUTION

2.1    Responsibilities

2.1.1. Office of Management and Budget (OMB). The administrative control of all government funds is legally mandated through an apportionment process, as required by 31 U.S.C. §§ 1512 and 1513. The OMB manages and approves these apportionments at the Treasury appropriation fund symbol (TAFS) level. All appropriation requests must follow the guidance in OMB Circular No. A-11, Section 120, which also identifies certain exemptions. OMB may grant additional exemptions under its authority in 31 U.S.C. § 1516.

2.1.2. OUSW(C)/Program and Budget (P/B). Following OMB's approval, the OUSW(C) P/B allocates funds to the Military Services and Defense Agencies for execution. The OUSW(C)

P/B is responsible for the initial distribution of all funds to Military Services and Defense Agencies. This is accomplished via funds authorization documents (FADs) after the funds have been apportioned. The assigned OUSW(C) P/B analyst for each appropriation account will allocate funds to the Military Services and/or the Defense Agencies via FADs. Funds in transfer- only accounts are not available for obligation or outlay and are not distributed directly. Instead, they are moved to the recipient appropriation's FAD using the reprogramming procedures outlined in section 6 (Reprogramming of DoW Appropriated Funds).

2.1.3. OUSW(C) Program and Financial Control (P&FC) Directorate. The OUSW(C) P&FC manages the complete apportionment lifecycle. It submits all requests to OMB and processes all approved apportionments. All appropriations must be apportioned unless exempt per OMB Circular No. A-11 or 31 U.S.C. § 1516. P&FC processes authorized exemptions and maintains a comprehensive list of exempt accounts for the DoW.

2.2    Provisions

2.2.1. Accounts must be reapportioned before obligating any upward adjustment of budgetary resources that is greater than $400,000 or 2 percent, whichever is lower. Unobligated balances in unexpired accounts must be reapportioned every year. Expired accounts are not apportioned, and transfer-only accounts are generally exempt from apportionment. Refer to the OMB Circular No. A-11, Section 120. All reapportionments must be validated against the most current SF 133 (Report on Budget Execution and Budgetary Resources).

2.2.2. For Surcharge Collections, Sales of Commissary Stores - Trust Revolving Fund, the 10 U.S.C. § 2685 permits obligation of anticipated proceeds from the adjustments or surcharges authorized by 10 U.S.C. § 2685.

2.2.3. OMB automatically apportions certain funds in accordance with OMB Circular No. A-11 Section 120.41 for newly enacted appropriations in accordance with the Interim Apportionment Authority for Initial Appropriations Act.

2.2.4. If an appropriations act is not signed into law by October 1, Congress may pass a Continuing Resolution (CR) to temporarily fund government operations. Multiple CRs may be necessary, and each must be signed by the President to become law, until the final annual appropriations act is passed.

2.2.5. Apportionments to record the sale and replacement of assets under Section 21 of the Apportionments and the Arms Export Control Act require actions codified at 22 U.S.C. § 2761.

2.2.6. For rescissions and deferrals, available budgetary resources may be withheld from obligation or expenditure through impoundment, either permanently (rescission) or temporarily (deferral) under conditions set forth in 31 U.S.C. § 1512 and the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act (2 U.S.C. §§ 683 and 684). Refer to OMB Circular No. A-11 for information and definitions of rescissions and deferrals.

title: Section 3.0: Appropriation Transfer Authorities
content:
3.0    APPROPRIATION TRANSFER AUTHORITIES

Congress grants authority for the transfer of funds between appropriations, with most DoW transfers occurring in accordance with the annual Appropriations Act and the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). The Secretary of War (SecWar) also possesses General Transfer Authority (GTA) for unforeseen, high-priority military needs, provided the item was not previously denied by Congress and Congress is promptly notified. OMB approval may also be required depending on the legal source of authority. To ensure timely action, the Office of the Under Secretary of War (Comptroller) (OUSW(C)) maintains and publishes periodic status reports on transfer actions.

3.1    Responsibilities and Authorizations

3.1.1. DoW Components must formally submit all proposals to transfer funds to the OUSW(C) and state the specific statutory authority that permits the action. Once approved, the originating DoW Component is fundamentally responsible for executing transfers.

3.1.2. The SecWar provides the ultimate authority and amounts for most transfers, contingent upon the existence of certain conditions as provided in DoD Directive (DoDD) 5118.03. This authority may be delegated to the USW(C). Furthermore, all transfer documents processed to the Treasury must cite the legal authority for the transfer, including any required determinations or approvals.

3.1.3. A transfer cannot be executed without the required approval from the OMB.

3.2    Authority for Transfers Affecting Budget Availability

3.2.1. Congressionally Directed Transfers. The DoW Appropriations Act provides direct authority for DoW Components to execute specified fund transfers.

3.2.2. GTA. The SecWar may transfer funds for unforeseen, high-priority military needs, provided the item was not previously denied by Congress.

3.2.3. Transfers Between Working Capital Funds. Transfers between working capital funds are permitted, but no funds may be obligated for war reserve materials without prior Congressional notification.

3.2.4. Transfer of Military Construction (MILCON) Appropriations. The SecWar has the authority to transfer MILCON funds to other MILCON or Family Housing accounts, where they must be used for the same purpose and time period.

3.2.5. Transfer Accounts. The DoW recognizes certain accounts (e.g., Environmental Restoration, Drug Interdiction and Counter-Drug Activities) established by law as dedicated "Transfer Accounts."

3.2.6. Transfer of Funds and Personnel for Functional Transfers Within the DoW. When a function is reassigned within the DoW, the necessary funds and personnel positions may also be transferred, and the funds must be used for their original purpose as established under the authority of 10 U.S.C. §§ 125 and 126.

3.2.7. Transfer of Funds for Functional Transfers Between Government Agencies. In accordance with the authority granted by 31 U.S.C. § 1531, the DoW adheres to the legal framework governing the transfer of appropriations when a function is moved to or from another federal agency.

3.2.8. Limitation on Transfer of Funds to Other Departments and Agencies. Pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 2215, DoW policy prohibits the transfer of funds designated for military functions to any other federal department or agency. This policy applies to transfers made under any provision of law enacted after November 29, 1989. An exception to this policy is permitted only when the transfer is certified to be in the national security interest of the United States.

3.3    Transfer Provisions

3.3.1. Reprogramming Actions. A reprogramming action (DD 1415) must be executed for any non-congressionally directed fund transfer that results in an increase or decrease between DoW appropriations.

3.3.2. Processing of Treasury Non-Expenditure Transfers (NETs). The mechanism for moving funds between accounts at the Treasury for an approved transfer is the Treasury Non- Expenditure Transfer (NET). NETs between DoW accounts will not be processed without a directing memorandum from the OUSW(C). However, this policy does not require prior OUSW(C) approval for certain exceptions, including functional transfers initiated by a non-DoW agency or transfers of obligational authority to a designated transfer account in another agency. The directing OUSW(C) memorandum serves as the official policy instrument for the transfer, must contain all information necessary for proper execution and reporting, and will confirm which office is responsible for any required Congressional notification.

3.3.3. Notification to Congress. DoW policy mandates compliance with all statutory requirements for reporting transfers to Congress. For functional transfers, a distinction applies: the transfer of funds under 10 U.S.C. § 126 does not require Congressional notification. However, the transfer of the function itself, pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 125, must be reported to Congress if it results in the substantial reduction or elimination of a major weapons system.

3.3.4. Apportionment and Reapportionment Schedules. In accordance with OMB Circular No. A-11, DoW policy requires all transfers to be reflected on the Apportionment and Reapportionment Schedule (SF 132). While certain specified transfers (e.g., Foreign Currency Fluctuations, Environmental Restoration) result in automatic apportionment for the gaining and losing accounts, those accounts designated as "only for transfer" are exempt from apportionment, as specified in OMB Circular No. A-11, section 120.5.

3.3.5. Guidance on SF 133 Treatment. With agreement from OUSW(C) and OMB, transfers may be anticipated on the SF 133 report once all statutory requirements are met, even before the NET action is complete. This is an exception to standard guidance in OMB Circular No. A-11.

3.3.6. Funding Authorization Documents (FAD). Program adjustments from transfers must be reflected in a FAD, as determined by the OUSW(C)'s cognizant P/B appropriation director.

title: Section 4.0: Functional Transfers
content:
4.0    FUNCTIONAL TRANSFERS

4.1    Statutory Authority

Under 10 U.S.C. § 125, the SecWar is authorized to transfer, reassign, consolidate, or abolish any function within the Department. When this occurs, 10 U.S.C. § 126 permits the transfer of associated appropriations and civilian employees, provided the SecWar determines they are needed and the President grants approval (as delegated to the OMB).

4.2    Provisions

4.2.1. Fund Adjustments. DoW policy dictates that current-year functional transfer funding adjustments should primarily be reimbursable. Direct fund transfers are only to be requested when reimbursement presents serious burdens or significant financial amounts.

4.2.2. Transfer of Funds. DoW policy requires the receiving DoW Component to initiate a fund transfer request when necessitated by a functional transfer under 10 U.S.C. § 125. The request must comply with the requirements of 10 U.S.C. § 126 and be based on a mutually agreed- upon amount between the involved DoW Components.

title: Section 5.0: Special Military Construction/Family Housing Fund Release Procedures
content:
5.0    SPECIAL MILITARY CONSTRUCTION/FAMILY HOUSING FUND RELEASE PROCEDURES

5.1    Fund Approval

It is the policy of the DoW that fund approval for military construction and family housing construction accounts must be formally requested by the cognizant MILDEP. The cognizant MILDEP must submit a request to the OUSW(C) P/B, Military Personnel and Construction Directorate.

5.2    OUSW(C) Review

It is the policy of the OUSW(C) to issue a formal fund approval to the requesting Component after its review, granting obligational authority corresponding to the amounts approved.

5.3    Document Approval

It is a critical DoW policy that the final fund approval document limits a Component’s authority to incur obligations. No obligations may be incurred prior to the receipt of this document or in amounts that exceed the authority granted within it.

5.4    Submission Requirements

It is DoW policy that a formal fund release request is required under several specific circumstances: for the initial fund authorization, to request the release of funds previously placed on withhold by OUSW(C), and to provide support for an approved apportionment/reapportionment schedule (SF 132) or a formal above-threshold reprogramming action.

title: Section 6.0: Reprogramming and DoW Appropriated Funds
content:
6.0    REPROGRAMMING AND DOW APPROPRIATED FUNDS

6.1    Transfer Authority

The DoW requires specific transfer authority for any movement of funds between appropriations or their legal subdivisions. This authority is established through several distinct mechanisms.

6.1.1. General Transfer Authority (GTA). This is contained in the annual DoW Appropriations Act (e.g., Section 8005 of Public Law 119-75). GTA is also authorized in the annual National Defense Authorization Act (e.g., Section 1001 of Public Law 119-60). The use of GTA is subject to the SecWar’s determination that the action is in the national interest and requires approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). OMB concurrence on the use of GTA is documented on a SecWar Determination letter.

6.1.2. Foreign Currency Fluctuations (FCF). Policy also provides specific FCF authority through public laws (e.g., Public Law 95-457 and 10 U.S.C. § 2779).

6.1.3. Special Transfer Authorities. Policy recognizes additional special transfer authorities for unique situations, as provided in various Sections of Title 10 U.S.C. (e.g., 10 U.S.C. § 127a), other annual defense acts, and specific authorities for Intelligence Programs.

6.2    General Reprogramming Policies

6.2.1. DoW’s Three-Form Process Policy. The DD Form 1414 establishes the financial baseline, detailing the budget's complete history and footnoting all items of special congressional interest. To execute changes, the DD Form 1415 is used to either request prior congressional review for fund realignments or to document internal transfers for audit purposes. Finally, for transparency, a cumulative DD Form 1416 report is submitted to show the final program status after all adjustments; this report is provided quarterly for Procurement and RDT&E appropriations and annually for Military Personnel and Operation and Maintenance (O&M) appropriations.

6.2.2. Reprogramming Actions Submitted for Congressional Review. The DoW submits certain reprogramming actions for congressional review. These reprogramming actions enable the DoW to adapt funding to emergent, unforeseen operational requirements, urgent procurement needs, technology advancement opportunities, or other critical mission requirements in the execution of DoW programs. Further, it is expressly prohibited to request reprogramming into an effort that has been denied by Congress. However, this prohibition does not apply to the entire line-item of a congressional denial; only the specific effort. A DD Form 1415-1, Prior Approval Reprogramming, is required by DoW policy for actions that: increases the procurement quantity of a major end item (unless specifically authorized by congressional language, in which case a DD 1415-3 is used); affects an item designated as a matter of special congressional interest; or uses GTA (unless reclassification of a program is required for proper execution of an appropriation). Pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 2214 and the annual Appropriations Act, GTA itself has limitations and may only be used under the "higher priority" conditions. In rare instances involving the movement of funds between special interest items within the same line item, policy allows for a letter notification to Congress instead of a formal DD 1415-1

6.2.3. Internal Reprogramming Actions. The DoW must use a DD Form 1415-3, Internal Reprogramming, as an audit-trail document for several types of internal fund movements that do not require prior congressional review. This policy applies to three main areas.

6.2.3.1. First, it applies to the reclassification of funds to a different line item, program element, or appropriation for proper execution, so long as the substance of the program remains unchanged. If such a reclassification uses GTA (as defined in the annual appropriation bill), then the signed Letter Apportionment satisfies the same intent as a Secretary of War Determination Letter and OMB concurrence is satisfied through the approved apportionment.

6.2.3.2. Second, it applies to reprogramming funds to or from designated Transfer Accounts, such as Environmental Restoration, Drug Interdiction and Counter-Drug Activities, and Foreign Currency Fluctuations, which are generally exempt from the use of GTA.

6.2.3.3. Third, policy dictates the use of a DD 1415-3 for approving increases to procurement quantities for major end items when the action falls below the threshold for a prior review reprogramming.

6.3    Congressional Notification

6.3.1. Letter Notifications to Congress. The DoW requires advance letter notification to Congress before initiating certain below-threshold actions that do not otherwise require a formal prior review reprogramming. This policy applies to:

6.3.1.1. The creation of new procurement line items or development programs costing less than $20 million and $10 million, respectively;

6.3.1.2. The initiation of safety programs or modifications costing less than $20 million; and

6.3.1.3. The termination of procurement or RDT&E programs that also fall below these same $20 million and $10 million thresholds, as long as the parent program element or line item is not entirely eliminated.

6.3.1.4. This policy also extends to identifying specific line items to satisfy other congressionally established transfer notification requirements.

6.3.2. Failure to Provide Proper Notification. Recurring general provisions in DoW Appropriations Acts prohibit the use of reprogrammed funds to initiate a new program, project, or activity. An exception is made only if the program must be undertaken immediately in the interest of national security and after prior written notification is provided to the congressional defense committees.

6.4    Approvals and Responsibilities

6.4.1. Congressional Committee Approval of DD 1415 Requests. As a matter of policy, DoW requires congressional defense committees’ review before a Prior Approval Reprogramming Action (DD 1415-1) can be implemented. A critical aspect of this policy is the strict prohibition against obligating or committing funds for a requested reprogramming prior to receiving this congressional review. Furthermore, DoW policy prohibits using a series of below-threshold reprogramming actions as a workaround to finance an increase that was specifically denied by Congress. However, policy does permit the use of below-threshold authority to finance increases that were approved by Congress but could not be funded during the initial implementation due to a lack of approved sources, provided the action does not violate other reprogramming limitations.

6.4.2. OMB Approval. For prior approval actions, OMB must approve the transmittal before it is sent to the congressional defense committees.

6.4.3. OUSW(C), Deputy Comptroller, Program/Budget (P/B). The SecWar’s determination authority on transfers due to national interest is delegated to the Deputy Comptroller, P/B. The OUSW(C) sends OMB-approved transmittals to the congressional defense committees. After Congress responds and implementation is finalized, the OUSW(C) is responsible for obtaining the formal OMB apportionment for the transfer and issuing a formal implementation memorandum to the DoW Components to document the action and authorize its execution. This policy ensures that a clear, official record exists before any funds are moved and that all necessary documentation, such as transfer authorizations and approval documents, are properly disseminated.

6.4.2. DoW Components. The DoW Assistant Secretary (Financial Management and Comptroller) of a MILDEP or the Comptroller of a Defense Agency must formally submit all proposed DD 1415 reprogramming actions. Policy dictates that these actions must be submitted electronically and are due by the 5th workday of the month for inclusion in the monthly submission. DoW Components must address the following requirements:

6.4.2.1. Required DD Forms, Formats, and Templates. The SecWar has delegated the authority to signal reprogramming actions to the USW(C). The OUSW(C) Program and Financial Control Directorate manages the reprogramming process. Refer to the Supplemental Document for the required DD Forms, formats, and templates.

6.4.2.2. Notification – Investment Programs. When a prior approval reprogramming for investment programs is required to initiate a new start or to terminate a program, a copy should also be provided to the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment. The following DoW policies apply when considering a prior approval for a new start.

6.4.2.2.1. RDT&E. A new start program for RDT&E involves the creation of a new program element or project, or major component thereof, not previously justified by the Department and funded by Congress through the normal budget process.

6.4.2.2.2. Procurement. A new start program for Procurement involves the creation of a new procurement line item or major component thereof, not previously justified by the Department and funded by Congress through the normal budget process.

6.4.2.2.3. MILPERS and O&M. Due to the characteristics of Military Personnel and Operation and Maintenance programs, new starts seldom occur in those appropriations. New starts in these appropriations would be significant new programs, efforts, or activities that have not been explicitly justified to the Congress in budget justification material.

6.4.2.2.4. Follow-on Funding. The Department will not approve a new start reprogramming request unless follow-on funding for the subsequent fiscal years is already budgeted or programmed.

6.4.2.2.5. Extension Exception. Extending an ongoing, previously justified RDT&E or Procurement effort into a subsequent fiscal year does not constitute a new start; rather it is treated as a continuation of the prior-year program.

6.4.2.3. Notification – National Intelligence Program (NIP) or Military Intelligence Program (MIP). For any reprogramming action that involves NIP or MIP resources, policy requires coordination with the Office of the Director for National Intelligence (ODNI) and the Under Secretary of War for Intelligence and Security. Pursuant to 50 U.S.C. § 3024(d)(1)(B), consultation with the ODNI Chief Financial Officer is required before reprogramming funds are made available for the MIP. To ensure transparency without compromising security, any reprogramming action posted publicly must not identify intelligence resources. A separate statement in the transmittal letter must clarify if such resources are affected.

6.4.2.4. Annual Omnibus. Any reprogramming actions submitted outside of the annual Omnibus must be limited to critical, unforeseen, and time-sensitive requirements.

6.4.2.5. Clearance for Public Posting. Since all reprogramming actions are posted on the public website after implementation is complete, the final documents (i.e., DD 1415-1 Prior Approval, DD 1415-3 Internal Reprogramming, and Letter Notifications to Congress) must receive clearance from the Defense Office of Prepublication and Security Review.

6.5    Other DoW Reprogramming Policies

6.5.1. Alternate Letters or Revised Actions for New Sources. The DoW allows for the submission of new funding sources if a congressional committee concurs with a reprogramming increase but denies the proposed sources. However, policy strictly prohibits submitting alternate sources for increases that were denied by the committees, except in the most unusual circumstances. The USW(C) has the authority to appeal a committee's decision on a reprogramming action. Any subsequent action related to a reprogramming, including appeals or proposals for new sources, is subject to the same formal procedures as the original submission.

6.5.2. Withdrawal of Reprogramming Actions. It is the policy of the DoW that if a reprogramming action submitted to Congress is no longer required, it may be formally withdrawn from consideration. This policy applies when circumstances change, such as when too much time has passed for the action to be executed or when the proposed funding sources are needed for higher-priority reprogramming. Policy dictates that the withdrawal notification must provide a sufficient rationale to the congressional committees to justify retracting the original request.

6.5.3. DD 1416, Report of Programs. The DD Form 1416, Report of Programs, is the official DoW report reflecting the status of all programs after enacted budgets, supplementals, rescissions, and all reprogramming actions are incorporated. To ensure financial consistency, DD 1416 data must reconcile with the DD 1002 report. For procurement programs aggregated into an "Items Less Than $5 Million" line item, any cost growth must be accommodated within that line's total below-threshold reprogramming authority (not to exceed the $20 million or 20 percent limit). The basis for calculating below-threshold percentage decreases in Procurement and RDT&E appropriations is the original appropriation adjusted for any enacted supplementals and rescissions. Reimbursable program or order amounts are not required unless reimbursable funding was used for the direct program.

6.5.4. Reprogramming of Intelligence Resources. DoW policy for reprogramming intelligence resources is divided into two categories:

6.5.4.1. NIP. Pursuant to 50 U.S.C. § 3024, the DNI has final approval authority to approve fund transfers and all such actions require prior approval from the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence (HPSCI), Senate Select Committee on Intelligence (SSCI), House Appropriations Committee (HAC), and Senate Appropriations Committee (SAC).

6.5.4.2. MIP. Standard DoW reprogramming policies apply, with additional specific guidance in DoDD 5205.12. Pursuant to 50 U.S.C. § 3024(d)(1)(B), OUSW(C) must consult with the DNI's Chief Financial Officer before reprogramming any MIP funds, Finally, to satisfy 50 U.S.C. § 3094 and as a matter of committee relations, the Department provides the SSCI with information copies of any reprogramming actions occurring into or within the MIP.

6.5.5. Reprogramming of Special Access Programs (SAP). The annual DoW Appropriations Act states: "Funds appropriated by this Act may not be used to initiate a special access program without prior notification 30 calendar days in session in advance to the congressional defense committees." This means that to start a new SAP, the DoW must inform the relevant congressional committees at least 30 legislative days before doing so.

6.5.6. Below-Threshold Reprogramming Actions. DoW policy allows Components to use below-threshold reprogramming for unforeseen, high-priority requirements. These cumulative actions must net to zero and are prohibited from exceeding established monetary thresholds or initiating new start programs. Using this authority to fund an increase specifically denied by Congress is prohibited. However, it may be used to fund an increase that Congress approved but could not be implemented due to a lack of sources, provided this is done with advance written notification and does not violate other limitations. A policy exception to the normal thresholds also exists for funding adjustments related to canceled accounts, as governed by 31 U.S.C. § 1551 et seq.

6.5.7. Replacement Of Items Sold From Inventory. This section is applicable to items sold to foreign governments under the Arms Export Control Act, 22 U.S.C. § 2761. Sales to domestic buyers (Federal or non-Federal) are governed by Title 41 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 102-39.

6.5.7.1. Current budget policy prohibits using proceeds from asset sales to acquire a non-like replacement item (one not of identical type, model, and series) without obtaining congressional review. The DoW secures this requisite approval by submitting a prior approval reprogramming action to the congressional defense committees.

6.5.7.2. The DoW treats the replacement of certain small-dollar-value items sold from inventory as a “like replacement,” even if the replacement is not of the identical type, model, and series. This policy applies only if all of the following conditions are met: the original item has a unit cost of less than $5,000; the replacement is an improved model of the same end item that performs the same warfighting capability; and procuring the replacement does not cause the inventory objective presented to Congress to be exceeded. This policy is intended to reduce unnecessary paperwork. Finally, policy dictates that the amount applied toward the replacement item may not be increased beyond the proceeds generated from the sale of the original item.

6.5.7.3. It is the policy of the DoW that a prior approval reprogramming action is required when an item sold from inventory is replaced with an item that is not identical (i.e., not a "like replacement"). Policy permits such a replacement only if the new item is a later series or modified version of the same basic model, or if it is an acceptable substitute used against the same inventory objective. If congressional review is obtained, the offsetting collections from the sale may then be used to procure the replacement. Furthermore, in accordance with OMB Circular No. A-11, the procurement of such a replacement item must be classified as a direct obligation.

6.5.7.4. When seeking congressional concurrence to use proceeds for non-like replacement items, Components must submit the DD 1415-1 as a distinct, stand-alone reprogramming request. This can be done either as a separate submission or as a separate part within the regular monthly reprogramming action, but it must not be combined with other types of reprogramming requirements.

6.5.8. Reprogramming Policy for Closing Appropriation Accounts (31 U.S.C. § 1551 et seq).

6.5.8.1. Out-of-Scope Contract Changes. It is DoW policy that when currently available appropriations are used to fund out-of-scope contract changes, normal reprogramming procedures and thresholds apply. Policy dictates that these changes be funded from the current corresponding program line. If no such line exists, a new one will be created, and the standard reprogramming threshold procedures for new starts will apply. Any existing line item can serve as the funding source, but it will also be subject to normal reprogramming thresholds.

6.5.8.2. Canceled Appropriation Accounts. DoW policy allows currently available appropriations to fund obligations that would have been properly chargeable to a now-canceled account. This is strictly limited by policy to one percent of the current appropriation or the unexpended balance of the canceled account, whichever is lower. Critically, policy dictates that normal reprogramming procedures and thresholds do not apply to these specific actions. All such charges must be reflected in a line item titled "Canceled Appropriation Account Adjustments" on the DD 1416, Report of Programs.

6.5.8.3. Expired Appropriations. It is DoW policy that an expired appropriation remains available for recording, adjusting, and liquidating obligations properly chargeable to it until the account is officially closed under the authority of 31 U.S.C. § 1552. This includes funding within-scope contract changes. Pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 8683, specific policy, allows expired O&M, Navy appropriations to be used for certain scope changes in ship overhaul and repair. For the Shipbuilding and Conversion, Navy (SCN) appropriation, policy allows for additional obligations to be incurred after the normal 5-year availability period for final-stage construction work, as typically provided by language in the annual DoW Appropriations Act (e.g., Section 8075 of Public Law 113-235). Further, investment appropriations lose their line- item character in the expired period. Therefore, upward obligation adjustments may be made citing sources from other line-items within the same appropriation.

title: Section 7.0: Reprogramming of Military Construction and Family Housing Appropriated Funds
content:
7.0    REPROGRAMMING OF MILITARY CONSTRUCTION AND FAMILY HOUSING APPROPRIATED FUNDS

7.1    General Policy

The DoW has flexibility from Congress to adjust funding for approved military construction and family housing programs to meet changing conditions. However, the DoW must seek approval from the relevant congressional committees for these reprogramming actions. Such adjustments are typically required to respond to emergencies, replace damaged facilities, accommodate price increases, or implement specific congressional provisions. This process ensures that while DoW missions are supported, the use of appropriations remains consistent with congressional intent.

7.2    Authority and Approval

7.2.1. The OUSW(C) must approve all proposed reprogramming actions for military construction and family housing.

7.2.2. Prior congressional approval is mandatory for significant actions, including cost increases that exceed 25 percent of the project's base or $6 million (whichever is less), any funding increase to a project previously reduced in scope by Congress, and for specific circumstances like emergency construction under 10 U.S.C. § 2803 or the restoration of damaged facilities under
10 U.S.C. § 2854.

7.2.3. Prior approval is generally not required for actions below the thresholds specified in Section 7.2.2, projects funded by Environmental Restoration accounts, when cost increases are solely due to final contractor claim settlements, or when reprograming funds between or among family housing operation and maintenance accounts (though a new FAD for family housing remains required under specific conditions).

7.2.4. The policy strictly prohibits reprogramming requests for projects that are unauthorized, have been specifically denied by Congress, or attempt to initiate major unauthorized programs.

7.2.5. The policy also permits split-year funding, allowing a project to be financed with funds from multiple program years, and provides a mechanism for the OUSW(C) to appeal unfavorable congressional committee decisions.

7.3    Procedures

Refer to Volume 3 Supplemental Document for guidance on the appropriate submission and instructions.

title: Section 8.0: Standards for Recording and Reviewing Commitments and Obligations
content:
8.0    STANDARDS FOR RECORDING AND REVIEWING COMMITMENTS AND OBLIGATIONS

This section prescribes the requirements for determining the amount and accounting period in which commitments and obligations must be recorded under various circumstances. Departmental standards for recording transactions in the execution level budgetary accounts are in
Section 12.

8.1    Recording of Commitments

A commitment must cite a Standard Line of Accounting (SLOA) in accordance with Volume 1 and must be recorded in the general ledger in accordance with the United States Standard General Ledger (USSGL) Standard Financial Information Structure (SFIS) Transaction Library in Volume 1.

8.2    Validating Commitments

When drafting contracts, procurement officials may modify the description of deliverable goods and services or contract line-item structure used on a funded purchase request. However, if these changes are substantial, there is a risk the goods and services procured no longer align with the purpose set forth in the purchase request for which the commitment was certified. To mitigate this risk, certifying officials must conduct an automated pre-award validation with the contract issuing organizations to validate that committed funds remain available and suitable for the draft award’s intended purpose. This check must also ensure that the data in the accounting and procurement systems are sufficiently aligned to facilitate line-item traceability between commitments and obligations, to facilitate payment. The structure must support posting obligations and line items with different accounting treatments that must be segregated. This transaction may be performed via the Global Exchange system using system agnostic data standards.

8.3    Obligation Responsibilities

31 U.S.C. § 1501, “Documentary Evidence Requirement for Government Obligations,” directs that amounts must be recorded as obligations only when supported by documented evidence. The office that incurs an obligation must provide, within five calendar days of the date the obligation is incurred, a copy of the obligating document(s), via electronic mail, fax, or other documented means, to the office responsible for recording the obligation. The office that is responsible for recording the obligation must record the obligation in the official accounting records within five calendar days of receipt of such documentation, information, or data. Timely and accurate recording of obligations facilitates the disbursing officer’s ability to verify fund availability before authorizing a timely payment.

8.4    Recording Obligations

8.4.1. All business and financial events resulting in an obligation must cite a SLOA in accordance with Volume 1 and must be recorded in the general ledger in accordance with the SFIS Transaction Library in accordance with Volume 1.

8.4.2. When recording obligations under this section, utilize the following principles:

8.4.2.1. Documented Evidence. An amount must be recorded as an obligation only when supported by documentary evidence of the transaction. A verbal order or agreement must be reduced to writing before the obligation may be recorded. When the amount is not known or cannot be feasibly ascertained at the time it is recorded, the best estimate must be used. Document the best estimate to include relevant inputs, assumptions, and calculations. In accordance with Volume 1, retain evidence to support the transaction.

8.4.2.2. Ten-Day Rule. Record obligations in the official accounting records at the time a legal obligation is incurred, i.e., contract is signed. In all instances, obligations must be recorded within 10 calendar days following the day that an obligation is incurred (to include obligations incurred when invoices are overpaid or duplicate payments are made). Notwithstanding the ten-day rule, record all obligations (per line of accounting) in the official accounting records in the same month in which the obligation is incurred. If an obligation is not recorded within the specified timeframe, follow section 8.16.

8.5    Recording Contract Obligations

Offices generating contract obligations in the form of a contract, order, or modification; must provide official evidence of the obligations, and other supporting documents, to the office responsible for recording the obligation, via electronic format as defined in the Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS) Procedures, Guidance, and Information (PGI) 204.201, and in accordance with the SFIS data elements required in Volume 1, and posting logic in Volume 1. Load obligations manually, within five calendar days from the signature date on the contract or contract modification, based on the official obligating documents in the Electronic Document Access System, if the transactions fail to upload electronically. If the contract contains errors, omissions or deficiencies that prevent posting, a Contract Deficiency Report must be created to document the deficiency and request corrective action in accordance with PGI 204 270-2.

8.5.1. Contracts or Orders for Goods, Supplies, or Services to Meet Bona Fide Need. DoW Components must determine that the goods, supplies, or services required under contracts, or orders placed obligating an annual or multiple year appropriation, are intended to meet a bona fide need of the period for which funds were appropriated. Additionally, a buying activity’s project order must serve a bona fide need that exists in the fiscal year in which the project order is issued; otherwise, a valid obligation is not accomplished. Bona fide need generally is a determination of the buying activity and not that of the selling/performing activity. A selling activity must refuse to accept a project order if it is obvious the project order does not serve a need existing in the fiscal year in which issued. Such determinations must consider estimated current consumption; the requirements that may be foreseen for future years based upon the procurement lead-time; authorized stock levels; and authorized mobilization reserves. It is not intended that the bona fide need of the fiscal year rule be construed to preclude procurement lead-time. If, a provision of law makes such appropriations available for payments under contracts for specified services for periods beyond the period for which the appropriation otherwise is available, the contract for such services extending into the ensuing period (fiscal year) may be charged to the appropriation current at the time that the contract is signed. Obligate funds for each option period after funds become available. Obligations must be consistent with all normal limitations on the obligation of appropriated funds, such as the bona fide needs rule, period of availability, and type of funds. See Volume 11.

8.5.1.1. Execution Requirements Under Contracts or Orders. Contracts entered into or orders placed for goods, supplies, or services must be executed only with bona fide intent that the contractor (or other performing activity) must commence work and perform the contract without unnecessary delay.

8.5.1.2. Execution of Standard Commercial Items. For standard commercial items readily available from other sources, the bona fide needs rule cannot be satisfied based on the delivery, production or manufacturing lead-time exception to the bona fide needs rule if the materials were obtainable by another source before funds expired. See Volume 11.

8.5.1.3. Delivery Withhold. If the contractor is directed to withhold delivery until after the lead-time, then there is not a bona fide need for the item in the current fiscal year and funds for the next fiscal year must be used.

8.5.2. Service Contracts. Service contracts may be either severable or non-severable. Services are generally chargeable to the appropriation current at the time the services are rendered. The contract is thereby, established in a manner that defines the contractors level of responsibility to provide a specified level of effort for a stated period. The determination to charge the appropriation current on the date the contract is let, or to charge the funds current at the time services are rendered, depends upon whether the services are “severable” or “entire.” A contract that is considered entire or non-severable is charged to the fiscal year current when it was let even though performance may extend into the next fiscal year. Service contracts that are considered severable must be charged to the fiscal year in which the services are rendered and may not cross fiscal years, absent statutory authority. There is no precise formula or rule that determines whether a contract is severable or entire. Each case must be determined by the terms and circumstances involved. Non-severable services may occur at a contract line item level as defined in DFARS 204.7101. Refer to the Volume 3 Supplemental Document for severable and non- severable services guidance.

8.6    Determining Scope of Work Changes

8.6.1. Responsibilities for Making Determinations. In making a determination, the contracting officer must apply appropriate provisions of the FAR, the DFARS, legal principles applicable to scope changes, and the provisions of this Regulation.

8.6.2. Standards for Making Determinations. Statutes and DoW policies for the use of appropriations limit the period of availability to fund new obligations.

8.6.3. Increases in Quantities. Changes in the quantity of the major items called for in a contract generally are a change in contract scope and not authorized under the “Changes” clause.

8.6.4. Increases in Required Levels of Service Performance. Any modification of a service contract requiring additional deliverable services is a change in scope.

8.7    Due Diligence
