Fund holders, entrusted by components (buyer/receiving organizations) with administrative subdivisions of funds, ensure appropriated funds are used consistently with the intent, time, purpose, amount, and bona fide need for which the funds were provided. Fund holders must exercise due diligence in committing, obligating, de-committing, and de-obligating funds and generating inter- and intra-governmental orders through prescribed practices and oversight of documentation including contract, invoice, disbursement, and relevant supporting information. Fund holders must effectively collaborate with mission stakeholders including accountants, contracting officers, program managers, and logistics personnel.

8.8    Recording Judgment Fund Obligations

The Judgment Fund is available for court judgments and Justice Department compromise settlements of actual or imminent litigation against the government. Judgment Fund awards and settlement must be funded on a non-reimbursable basis for various types of litigation identified in 31 U.S.C. § 1304, “Judgments, Awards, and Compromise Settlements.” Section 1304 and the Contract Disputes Act of 1978, 41 U.S.C. § 7108, “Payment of Claims,” provide that awards and settlements involving appropriated fund contracts are payable from the Judgment Fund, subject to reimbursement from agency appropriations. The Fund also is available for awards and settlements involving discriminatory conduct by an Agency (such as DoW) under statutes identified in the Notification and Federal Employee Antidiscrimination and Retaliation Act of 2002,” commonly known as the No FEAR Act. Reimbursement of No FEAR Act Judgments. As provided for in 5 CFR § 724, Subpart A, DoW Components must reimburse the Judgment Fund for all judgments resulting from discrimination and No FEAR Act claims covered under authority of 5 U.S.C. § 2301. Reimbursements under the No FEAR Act include reimbursements for payments of judgments, awards, or settlements with respect to discrimination and whistleblower protection cases.

8.9    Recording Government-Wide Commercial Purchase Card Obligations

Record obligations for Government-Wide Commercial Purchase Cards in the amounts placed for orders for goods or services. For additional information on purchase cards, see the DoW Government Charge Card Guide.

8.10 Intra-Governmental Requisitions and Orders Placed with DoW Components or Other U.S. Government Agencies

The Treasury’s G-Invoicing system is used to negotiate, broker, and electronically store the General Terms and Conditions (GT&C) and activity between buyers and sellers for inter- and intra- governmental reimbursable transactions. The standard Interagency Agreement form is comprised of two forms, the GT&C (FS Form 7600A) and the Order Requirements and Funding Information (Order) (FS Form 7600B). When trading partners enter orders in the G-Invoicing system, the partners leverage data in the common repository to improve accuracy in accounting and reporting. Refer to the Volume 3 Supplemental for guidance on Reimbursable Procurement, Direct Cite Procurements, Reimbursable Orders with other DoW Activities, and Modifying Reimbursable Orders.

8.11 Orders Placed with (Or Through) Defense Working Capital Fund Activities

The DoW has authority under 10 U.S.C. § 2208 and 2210, to establish Defense Working Capital Fund (DWCF) activities to finance inventories of its supply chain management business areas and provide working capital for industrial and commercial type activities. Activities funded through DWCFs perform work for others under several different authorities. These authorities include the Project Order Act for depots, the Economy Act for reimbursable and direct citation procurements, and supply management operations (stock fund operations) that use DWCF contract authority to acquire assigned items of supply for other DoW Components. Direct citation orders placed with a DWCF must adhere to Volume 11 requirements. DWCF activities performing commercial type services charge stabilized rates rather than charges based on Economy Act actual cost methodologies. Activities performing DWCF operations can identify the transactional authority for work performed for others. Under 10 U.S.C. § 2208 and 2210, the DWCF is used for two different types of activities to include stock funds (supplies) plus goods and services. An order placed with a DWCF activity may only be for a bona fide need of the period for which the buying activity’s appropriation is available.

8.12    Personal Services and Benefits Obligations

8.12.1. Obligations Recorded for Payments to Military and Civilian Employees. Record obligations for the amounts payable to military services members and civilian employees in the month in which earned. These obligations must be supported by written administrative determinations of the amounts of the liabilities incurred for personal services based on payroll or personnel records .

8.12.2. Obligations Recorded for Subsistence In Kind. Record an obligation for subsistence in kind based on requisitions and orders, or on a written administrative determination of the estimated cost of subsistence furnished by others.

8.12.3. Obligations Recorded for Annual and Sick Leave of DoW Employees. Obligate annual leave for Department employees when it becomes due and payable as terminal leave or when otherwise specifically authorized by law, rather than at the time the leave is earned. Sick leave is obligated, costed, and paid when used.

8.12.4. Obligations Recorded for Severance Pay to U.S. Government Civilians and Foreign National Employees. Record obligations for severance pay for U.S. Government civilian employees and foreign national employees (such as those German nationals covered by the German Tariff Agreement) on a pay period by pay period basis; that is, at the time the severance pay becomes payable, regardless of the time it is disbursed.

8.12.5. Obligations Recorded for Severance Pay Under Specified Conditions

8.12.5.1. Record obligations for severance pay after an employee has been separated and specified conditions (such as those set forth in the German Tariff Agreement) have been met. The organization that terminates the employment of such individuals is responsible for recording and reporting the severance pay obligation. If the liability for any form of severance pay is significant, reasonable estimates must be made and an unfunded liability recorded and reported in accordance with the Governmentwide Treasury Account Symbol Adjusted Trial Balance System.

8.12.5.2. In accordance with other foreign country contracts and agreements, certain foreign national employees earn a separation allowance, also sometimes called “severance pay” in some contracts and agreements, from inception of or during their employment. See the Volume 3 Supplemental for information.

8.13    Permanent Change of Station Obligations Recorded

At the time Permanent Change of Station (PCS) orders are issued for civilian and military personnel, record obligations against current appropriations for all U.S. Government authorized reimbursable expenses incidental to relocation and for estimated bookings of household goods movement and storage. The only exception is the obligation of costs for non-temporary contract commercial storage of household goods, which must be obligated either in the period in which the service is rendered or to the appropriation current at the contract award. Record an adjustment to the obligation based on the costs itemized on the traveler’s settlement voucher.

8.14    Temporary Duty Travel Obligations Recorded

Tentative obligations for temporary duty travel must be recorded from written administrative determinations, based on the travel authorizations issued, for the estimated transportation to be purchased and the estimated reimbursement to be earned by the traveler for per diem allowances, use of privately owned vehicles, and incidental travel expenses. When travel is performed under a blanket authorization (with the itinerary not definite), the amount of the tentative obligation recorded in the current month must not exceed the estimate of the travel expenses to be incurred to the end of the current month. When the period covered by the travel authorization extends beyond the end of the fiscal year, and the travel costs are being paid by means of an annual appropriation or the final year of availability of a multiple year appropriation, the amount of the recorded obligation must be the cost of transportation purchased and reimbursements earned to the end of the fiscal year.

8.15    Other Obligations

8.15.1. Loan Agreements. As required by 2 U.S.C. § 661, new direct loan obligations may be incurred only to the extent that budget authority to cover costs is provided in advance. When a direct loan obligation is incurred, its cost (i.e., the estimated long-term cost of the loan to the government) is obligated against the “program account” established for the loan program. Actual funding of the direct loan is made through a revolving, non-budget “financing account.” Refer to Treasury’s BFS, USSGL Credit Reform Accounting guidance for detailed guidance covering obligation and disbursement of funds for direct and guaranteed loans.

8.15.2. Grants and Subsidies Obligations Recorded. Record the obligation amount of a grant or subsidy when supported by documentary evidence as directed in the Volume 3 Supplemental.

8.15.3. Bid Protests or Other Challenges. Pursuant to the provisions of 31 U.S.C. § 1558, funds available at the time of protest or other action filed in connection with a solicitation for, proposed award of, or award of such contract, remain available for obligation for 100 calendar days after the date on which the final ruling is made on the protest or other action. See The Volume 3 Supplemental Document for more information on bid protests and other challenges.

8.15.4. Foreign Currency Fluctuations.

8.15.4.1. The Foreign Currency Fluctuations Appropriation was established to eliminate losses or gains to programs caused by fluctuation of specified foreign currency exchange rates from rates used in budget formulation. DWCF foreign currency fluctuations are absorbed by the incurring DWCF business area, not the foreign currency account. Contractual obligations or other obligations payable in the specified foreign currencies may not be adjusted until disbursements are made from the appropriation account involved. See Volume 6.

8.15.4.2. When foreign currencies not specified in the Foreign Currency Fluctuations Appropriation account are involved, any adjustments to cost at the time of payment must be supplemented with adjustments made at year-end and may be made at any other time a significant change occurs in order to avoid over or under obligation of an allotment.

8.15.5. Security Guard and Firefighting Services

8.15.5.1. 10 U.S.C. § 2465 prohibits the obligation or expenditure of appropriated funds for the purpose of entering into a contract for the performance of firefighting or security guard functions at any military installation or facility in the U.S., including Alaska and Hawaii. See the Volume 3 Supplemental Document for exceptions to this prohibition.

8.15.5.2. 10 U.S.C. § 2687, the Defense Base Closure and Realignment Act of 1990, as amended, authorizes special procedures for providing security guard (or firefighting) services 180 days before an installation closes under the Base Realignment and Closure initiative.

8.16    Unrecorded Obligations

8.16.1. Dollar Threshold for Obligations Identified as Not Recorded. Apply the following guidance when the accounting office identifies an obligation incurred but not recorded in the official accounting records, and the accounting office is in possession of a valid obligating document (as specified in paragraph 8.16.2).

8.16.2. Document Verification

8.16.2.1. The accounting office must verify the document was not previously recorded under the applicable obligation reference number indicated.

8.16.2.2. The accounting office must verify if the obligation was recorded at an amount less than the face value of the obligating document or Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) representation.

8.16.3. Recording

8.16.3.1. DFAS must immediately record an obligation if the dollar amount is $2,500 or less.

8.16.3.2. If the dollar amount is greater than $2,500, the accounting office must provide the appropriate DoW Component financial manager with a copy of the obligating document(s) via e-mail, fax, upload, or use other means (retaining proof of transmission and receipt of the notification), to document the official document repository. Allow 10 calendar days for the financial manager to record the obligation or demonstrate the obligation was previously recorded. The accounting office must record the obligation on behalf of the financial manager if, within 10 calendar days, the financial manager has accounted for the obligation, the obligation is accurate, the applicable obligation was not previously recorded, or has not recorded the obligation in the accounting records.

8.16.3.3. Whenever the accounting office records an obligation for any amount, the appropriate funds holder must be notified immediately but not later than 10 calendar days of the obligation being recorded. This notification must be via e-mail, fax, electronic upload, or other documented means used for the document repository. Additionally, whenever the accounting office records an obligation, the recording must be uniquely identified, formally approved by the individual designated to provide approval authority, and cross-referenced to the obligating document. The processed obligating document must be similarly annotated. It is acceptable for an automated system to identify the source of a DFAS recorded obligation.

8.16.3.4. DoW Components must promptly record all obligations consistent with standards set forth in section 3.0. The over-recording and under-recording of obligated amounts is equally improper, as either makes it impossible to determine the actual status of an appropriation and may lead to violations of the Antideficiency Act. Over-recording and under-recording will also call into question the accuracy of agency financial statements and the propriety certifications on reports of obligations provided to Congress pursuant to 31 U.S.C. § 1108(c) and 1501(b).

8.16.4. Expired Funds. If the agency has incurred a valid, unrecorded obligation in the prior year, prior year funds must be used. Current appropriations are not available to fund this obligation. If insufficient funds remain in the prior years’ appropriation, the agency must seek a supplemental or deficiency appropriation and must further consider the possibility the Antideficiency Act (31 U.S.C. § 1341) has been violated.

8.17    Internal Controls

8.17.1. Departmental Responsibilities. In accordance with its responsibility for implementing effective internal controls, the Assistant Secretaries and Comptrollers must establish standard procedures for Departmental/Agency level monitoring and review of all obligations and commitments. These reviews must be formally documented in Standard Operating Procedures
(SOP).

8.17.2. Funds Holder Responsibilities

8.17.2.1. For the buyer/receiving component, the funds holder must review and validate commitments and obligations as financial transactions occur.

8.17.2.2. Quarterly, the fund holder must reconcile all obligations incurred during the period to include amounts recorded in the general ledger to contracting system records and/or obligating documents such as contracts and modifications.

8.17.2.2.1. The fund holder must document and investigate all differences.

8.17.2.2.2. The fund holder must alert the financial managers of any variances. The financial manager must review the funds holder’s documentation and assess whether an adjustment to the general ledger is required.

8.17.2.3. The use of “bulk” (estimated) obligations requires periodic monitoring and reconciliation of estimated obligations to the related disbursement transactions and the recording of appropriate adjustments to the estimated obligations based on the disbursement amounts. Limit the use of bulk obligations as Antideficiency Act violations may occur in the absence of adequate procedures for monitoring and reconciling disbursements.

8.17.2.3.1. Bulk obligations must not be used for materiel requisitioned by Defense Logistics Management Standards or Military Standard Logistics Systems transaction processing. Establishing an obligation for the proper amount for each line item under a unique requisition document number is essential for the timely and automated processing of interfund and non-interfund bills at the detail, line item level. Failure to do so may delay processing and increase workload for both DFAS and Component personnel.

8.17.2.3.2. DoW Components that establish business processes for requisitioning outside their customer’s Component sponsored supply system, via internet ordering applications, must provide automated processes for their customers to record line item obligations for each requisition. DoW Components that authorize personnel to initiate orders outside of the Component sponsored supply system must incorporate source of supply automated processes for establishing line item obligations for each requisition.

8.17.3. Supporting Documentation. Prior to recording an obligation, the financial manager responsible for the official accounting records of the funds holder must have supporting documentation. Information on supporting documentation can be found in the Volume 3 Supplemental Document.

8.17.4. Segregation of Duties. To ensure proper internal controls within the responsible financial management office, the duty of approving, certifying, and recording an obligation or order acceptance must be separate from posting a receiving report(s) and certifying acceptance and payment(s) for that obligation. In instances where Management determines that segregation of duties is not practical, additional mitigating controls must be identified and implemented in accordance with Volume 5.

8.17.5. Antideficiency Act Violations. When the financial manager records an obligation in accordance with this policy and it results in an apparent Antideficiency Act violation, that office immediately must initiate research to include consulting with the funds holder. See the Volume 3 Supplemental for more guidance.

8.18    Review of Dormant Accounts

8.18.1. 31 U.S.C. § 1554 mandates an annual certification of unliquidated obligations (ULOs). DoW Components will implement and maintain a documented internal process for the regular, risk-based review of dormant commitments and ULOs. The risk-based review aligns our internal controls with federal law, which mandates an annual certification of ULOs, and with the risk-based assessment principles championed by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and the Government Accountability Office (GAO). DoW Components must also review their Unfilled Customer Orders (UFCOs). UFCOs reviews are to monitor your reimbursable activities.

8.18.2. While Components have the flexibility to design their own procedures, the process must, at a minimum, prioritize the review of dormant transactions based on risk factors such as:

Age: Transactions with no activity for more than 90 days; Materiality: High-dollar value transactions relative to the Component's overall ULO and UFCO balance; Other Risk Indicators: Transactions with known issues, problematic contract types, or those approaching their expiration or cancellation date.

8.18.3. Documentation: Components are not required to submit a report of this activity to OUSW(C) but must maintain sufficient documentation of their risk-based review process and remediation actions for audit purposes.

title: Section 9.0: Accounting Requirements for Expired and Closed Accounts
content:
9.0    ACCOUNTING REQUIREMENTS FOR EXPIRED AND CLOSED ACCOUNTS

9.1    Expired Accounts

Both the obligated and unobligated balances of an expired DoW appropriation must remain available for the purpose of recording, adjusting, and liquidating obligations that are properly chargeable to that specific account until it is officially closed.

9.2    Closed/Cancelled Accounts

In accordance with 31 U.S.C. § 1552(a), any collections authorized for a DoW appropriation but not received before the account is closed must be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. For indefinite appropriations, policy derived from 31 U.S.C. § 1555 dictates that the account must be closed if no disbursements have been made for two consecutive fiscal years and the President or SecWar determines its purpose has been fulfilled.

9.3    Contract Change Provisions

The DoW must differentiate between contract changes and other obligation adjustments. Adjustments for items such as incentive fees or inflation are not considered contract changes and may be charged to applicable expired (but not yet canceled) accounts. For contract changes resulting from a contracting officer's final decision under the Contract Disputes Act, the policy is to apply the specific obligation adjustment rules. If a litigation judgment is paid from the Judgment Fund, it creates a new agency obligation to reimburse the fund. A specific policy, authorized by 10 U.S.C. § 8683, permits the use of expired appropriations for new obligations to cover unusual cost overruns on ship overhauls, maintenance, and repair. This authority is limited and cannot be used beyond the fifth fiscal year following the appropriation's expiration.

9.4    Shipbuilding and Conversion, Navy

The DoW Shipbuilding and Conversion, Navy (SCN) appropriation, while normally available for obligation for five years, is subject to a period of "extended availability." This policy, established through language in the annual appropriation act, allows for new obligations to be incurred after the initial five-year period for limited purposes, such as engineering services, tests, and other work required in the final stages of ship construction. The official period of availability for the entire appropriation is ultimately determined by the latest Obligation Work Limiting Date (OWLD) for the last vessel funded by that specific SCN appropriation. After this date, the appropriation enters a standard five-year expired status before cancellation.

9.5 Obligation Adjustment for a Contract Change Greater Than $4 Million

An obligation must be adjusted for a contract change on an expired appropriation, where the contractor must perform additional work, and can only be incurred after approval from the Under Secretary of War (Comptroller) (USW(C)). This approval is required if the obligation would cause the total charges for a single program, project, or activity to exceed $4 million in a fiscal year. Policy grants a specific exception for the Secretary of the Navy, who may treat this limitation as $10 million for Navy Operation and Maintenance funds used for ship overhauls.

9.6 Obligation Adjustment for a Contract Change Equal to or Greater than $25 Million

It is the policy of the DoW that any obligation adjustment of $25 million or more in a fiscal year, which is for a contract change on an expired appropriation requiring additional contractor work, is subject to special handling. This policy requires that the USW(C), as the designee of the SecWar, must first submit a formal notice of intention to the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. The obligation may not be incurred until 30 days have passed from the submission of this notice, provided no committee has registered a disapproval. The policy also mandates that this notice must include the legal basis and policy reasons for making the obligation.

9.7    Replacement Contracts

The DoW must permit the use of expired funds to finance a replacement contract only if a specific set of conditions is met. First, there must be a continuing bona fide need for the goods or services, and the original contract must have been made in good faith. Second, the original contract must have been terminated either for default or for the convenience of the Government under specific circumstances (e.g., a court order or a formal determination that the award was improper due to explicit evidence that the award was erroneous and the determination is documented with appropriate findings of fact and of law). Third, the replacement contract must be for the same size and scope as the original and must be executed without undue delay. If any of these conditions are not met, policy dictates that current year funds must be used. Furthermore, if a replacement action will cause the obligation to exceed the unliquidated balance of the original contract by $4 million, it is policy that the action must first be approved by the USW(C). If the excess amount is $25 million or more, policy requires that a notice of intention be submitted to the congressional oversight committees at least 30 days prior to obligating the funds.

9.8 Obligation Adjustments or Payments from Current Appropriations for Closed/Cancelled Accounts

The DoW must use a sub-class account when using current appropriations to pay for obligations from a closed/canceled account. This policy mandates that such obligations are only recorded in the current account when payment is imminent in the current fiscal year. To ensure transparency, these adjustments must be clearly identified on the DD 1416, "Report of Programs." However, policy dictates that no formal reprogramming action is required for these specific adjustments, even if they cause a line item to exceed its normal reprogramming threshold.

9.9 Current Appropriations Used for Expired Appropriations with Insufficient Obligation Authority

If an expired appropriation has a negative unliquidated balance (insufficient funds), an obligation or adjustment may be charged by the DoW to a current appropriation for the same purpose. However, policy strictly prohibits charging a current appropriation if a sufficient balance actually exists in the expired account. If a subsequent review finds that sufficient funds were, in fact, available in the expired account, any charge made against the current account must be reversed. Furthermore, policy dictates that this action can only be taken if the obligation is not properly chargeable to any other current DoW appropriation under the transitional provisions of 31 U.S.C. § 1553(b)(1). Finally, the total amount charged to a current appropriation under this policy may not exceed an amount equal to one percent of the total appropriation for that current account.

9.10    Collection Credits After an Account is Closed/Cancelled

Valid accounts receivables with negative unliquidated obligations must not be written off simply because an associated appropriation has closed or canceled. Policy dictates that these proprietary accounts must be maintained until the debt is either settled by the debtor or properly closed in accordance with the guidance in Volume 4. Furthermore, as required by 31 U.S.C. § 1552, if collections that were authorized to be credited to an account are received after that account has closed, it is policy that those funds must be deposited into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts.

9.11 Exceptions to an Account’s Period of Availability for Adjusting and Liquidating Obligations

9.11.1. All appropriation accounts are subject to standard closure and cancellation requirements unless specifically exempted by statute. In accordance with 31 U.S.C. § 1557, a provision in an appropriations act can exempt an account and fix its period of availability for expenditure only for a specific FY. To be valid, such a statutory provision must identify the specific account, state that it remains available for recording and adjusting obligations and explicitly extend the availability of its obligated balances. Policy dictates that this special authority should only be requested when historical data shows that paying old balances from current funds would regularly exceed the one percent limitation or would severely impact the current program. In the absence of a specific legislative extension, it is DoW policy that Components may request a re-appropriation of closed/canceled balances, and any resulting re-appropriation is to be treated as new budget authority.

9.11.2. Availability for expenditure of a specific account may be changed only through specific legislation. This authority should only be requested when historical data shows that paying old balances from unexpired funds would regularly exceed the one percent limitation or would severely impact a current program. In the absence of specific legislative authority to extend an account, it is DoW policy that Components may request a re-appropriation of closed/canceled balances. Policy dictates that the receipt of a re-appropriation is to be treated as adding new budget authority.

9.12    Antideficiency Act Violations

DoW Components must investigate and report potential Antideficiency Act (ADA) violations when limitations are exceeded. An ADA violation can occur when an obligation from an expired account with insufficient funds is charged to a current appropriation. Detailed ADA investigation and reporting policy is specified in Volume 14.

9.13    Control, Reporting, and Certification Requirements

9.13.1. In accordance with 31 U.S.C. § 1554(a), any audit requirement, limitation on obligations, or reporting requirement applicable to an appropriation continues to apply even after its period of availability for new obligations has expired and after the account has been officially closed. If an appropriation act contains a limitation on the obligation of funds for a program, project or activity, or other purpose; that limitation continues during the five-year period after the period of availability for new obligations expires. DoW policy also mandates that Components must establish and test internal controls to ensure an adequate review of obligated balances, as required by OMB Circular No. A-123, Appendix A. Proper general ledger controls must be maintained for all valid unpaid obligations and accounts receivable in closed/canceled accounts. Policy dictates that closed/canceled obligations can only be posted to unexpired accounts when a disbursement is imminent in the current year. All related records must be maintained according to the policy in Volume 1.

9.13.2. Under the provisions of 31 U.S.C. § 1554, the SecWar (or his designee) must submit a comprehensive annual report to the President and the Secretary of the Treasury concerning the status of appropriation accounts (unliquidated obligations, unobligated balances, closed/cancelled balances, and adjustments). This report must include an itemization of appropriation accounts, a descriptive list of each appropriation, details of payments made from current accounts for closed account obligations (per 31 U.S.C. § 1553), and identification of all balances that were closed/canceled on September 30th (per 31 U.S.C. § 1552(a)). The report must also identify any indefinite appropriations that were closed because their purpose was fulfilled (per 31 U.S.C. § 1555). A key policy element is the requirement for a certification from the DoW Components that all obligated balances reflect properly existing obligations and that all expenditures were proper.

9.14    Other Requirements

9.14.1. Apportionment Procedures. The SF 132, "Apportionment and Reapportionment Schedule," must include a footnote stating that up to one percent of the original appropriation or the unobligated balance, whichever is less, may be used for obligation adjustments from closed/canceled accounts. If a supplemental appropriation is enacted, a reapportionment of this one percent amount may be requested.

9.14.2. Unliquidated Obligations. All unliquidated balances in expired accounts must be reviewed prior to an account's closure, and any amount not supported by documentary evidence must be de-obligated. Financial and program managers at all levels are responsible for ensuring all transactions are appropriately concluded. This includes ensuring that if services or materials remain undelivered at the time of expiration, they are subsequently delivered or, if not, that action is taken to terminate the contractual obligations to maintain the integrity of the funds. Furthermore, policy requires that uncompleted contracts, uncollected receivables, and uncollected travel or pay advances must be actively reviewed to ensure their validity.

9.14.3. Payments After Closure/Cancellation of Appropriations. Payment against a closed/canceled appropriation is prohibited until the disbursing office obtains a currently available appropriation from the funding activity. Finally, the write-off of an uncollectible reimbursement receivable is treated as a reclassification to a direct program obligation, and the specific accounting entries can be found in the DoW USSGL Transaction Library.

9.14.4. Closing/Cancelling an Account with a Negative Balance. DoW Components must clear the negative balance and establish a receivable for the amount of the negative balance before the account can be closed.

9.14.5. Accounting for Uncollectible Accounts Receivable in Closed/Cancelled Accounts. When an appropriation account is closed or canceled, the corresponding budgetary accounts for its accounts receivable must also be closed, and this action does not change the total obligations within those budgetary accounts. A key policy is the treatment of uncollectible receivables: the write-off of an uncollectible reimbursement receivable must be treated as a reclassification of that obligation from the reimbursable program to a direct program obligation.

9.14.6. Correction of Reporting Errors in Closed/Cancelled Accounts. The DoW must permit the correction of two specific categories of errors in closed/canceled accounts: clerical errors (such as misplaced decimals or transposed digits) and errors made in classifying a payment prior to account closure that were not discovered until after. In accordance with OMB Circular No. A-11, section 130.16, policy requires that certain complex correction requests must be supported by a written, standalone legal opinion from the Component's Office of General Counsel. This applies when the request involves the redistribution of offsetting collections or gross outlays between a closed Treasury Appropriation Fund Symbol (TAFS) and an expired TAFS.

title: Section 10.0: Unmatched Disbursements, Negative Unliquidated Obligations, and In-Transit Disbursements
content:
10.0    UNMATCHED DISBURSEMENTS, NEGATIVE UNLIQUIDATED OBLIGATIONS, AND IN-TRANSIT DISBURSEMENTS

10.1    Matching Disbursements to Obligation

A disbursement must be matched to its corresponding, detail-level obligation and recorded as promptly as current systems and business practices permit. Many obligations and disbursements are matched automatically via the Department’s various system interfaces. However, some obligations and disbursements are required to be manually matched, mainly due to non-automated processes or the rejection of transactions by automated systems. When a disbursement is recorded in the accounting system but not matched to an obligation, the disbursement results in a UMD. When a disbursement is recorded in the accounting system and is matched to an obligation, but the amount of the disbursement exceeds the amount on the recorded obligation, the amount of the disbursement in excess of the applicable obligation results in a NULO. After performing due diligence research IAW section 1105, obligations must be established and recorded for all UMDs and NULOs no later than September 30 of the year that the cited appropriation is scheduled to be closed regardless of the date that the disbursement was made. Fund holders must participate in the resolution of both UMDs and NULOs as both affect funds availability and have Antideficiency Act (ADA) implications. UMDs and NULOs must be also be included in the Dormant Accounts Review.

10.1.1. UMD and NULO Research Requirement. Research and correction actions must begin as soon as it is apparent that a disbursement transaction has resulted in a UMD or a NULO. The accounting office involved must immediately determine whether the disbursement is a valid charge to the fund holder, and whether a matching obligation transaction is recorded under a different or incorrect document number. If the disbursement is not a valid charge to the fund holder, the accounting office and the fund holder must reject the disbursement. If a matching obligation is recorded under an incorrect document number, the fund holder must immediately correct the document number, thus allowing for the proper matching of the disbursement to its corresponding, detail-level obligation. If an accounting adjustment affects a contract payment, contract reconciliation must be performed IAW Volume 10.

10.1.2. Record an Obligation for Unresolved UMDs and NULOs. Immediately notify the fund holder of applicable UMDs or NULOs. If research efforts fail and the condition is not corrected, advise the fund holder of the requirement to establish a matching obligation within the timeframes delineated in paragraph 110501. If the fund holder fails to record an obligation, the accounting office must elevate the issue IAW subparagraphs 110501.A.3 or 110501.B.4 as applicable.

10.1.3. Establish Obligations for UMDs and NULOs at the Transaction Level. Disbursements must be matched to their corresponding obligation at the detail transaction level. After performing due research, obligations recorded for UMDs and NULOs must be recorded at the detail transaction level as follows:

10.1.3.1. An obligation in the amount of the disbursement must be recorded at the transaction level for UMDs.

10.1.3.2. An obligation adjustment in the amount of the disbursement in excess of the applicable obligation must be recorded at the transaction level for NULOs.

10.2    Overaged UMDs/NULOs

10.2.1. Current and Expired Accounts

10.2.1.1. Unobligated overaged NULOs and UMDs have the first claim to the unobligated balances in any of the current and expired accounts. New obligations, or new upward obligation adjustments, may be executed only when and to the extent that there is an unobligated balance remaining in an account after all overaged NULOs and UMDs have been obligated. Thus, no new obligations or obligation adjustments may be incurred in the account to the extent that unobligated balances in such accounts are zero, or overaged NULOs and UMDs (if they are obligated) when added to obligated balances, would exceed the availability in such accounts.

10.2.1.2. DoW Components may continue to research overaged NULOs and UMDs without the need to initiate an investigation of a potential ADA violation.

10.2.1.3. If an account is obligated fully (but not overobligated) and has unresolved overaged NULOs and UMDs that, if obligated, would exceed the availability in an account, payments may continue, provided the account is not in danger of exceeding the unexpended balance (resulting in an overdisbursement). If an overdisbursement occurs, payments from the account must stop immediately, and the DoW Component involved must accomplish actions required for a potential ADA violation IAW Volume 14.

10.2.1.4. Should a new obligation or obligation adjustment be incurred in an account that has been obligated fully as a result of unresolved, overaged UMDs or NULOs, such an obligation must be recorded even though it will result in recorded obligations in excess of available resources.

10.2.1.5. Must not be construed as authorizing a delay in (1) the recording of an executed obligation that would result in an overobligation or (2) the requirement to conduct an investigation of a potential ADA violation that results from any action other than the sole requirement to obligate amounts for UMDs and NULOs.

10.2.3. Accounts Closed/Scheduled to Close at Fiscal Year-End

10.2.3.1. Obligations must be established no later than September 30 by all DoW Components for all UMDs, NULOs and in-transit transactions in appropriations scheduled to close at the end of the current fiscal year.

10.2.3.2. If such obligations result in obligations in an excess of available funds, the DoW Components must resolve the negative balance and report to Treasury within two months but no later than the end of the current fiscal year.

10.2.3.3. If the account is not returned to a positive balance within 60 days, the DoW Component involved must accomplish actions required for initial identification and investigation of a potential ADA violation IAW Volume 14.

10.2.3.4. Each administrative subdivision of an appropriation carries with it the responsibility for any potential or actual ADA violation. A DoW Component has the right to modify the number or level of administrative subdivisions within an appropriation before the closure of an appropriation. However, once an appropriation closes, no further modification or change may be made in the number or level of administrative subdivisions. Further, the modification of number or level of subdivision does not override the requirements in Volume 6 regarding the level of reporting on the Appropriation Status by Fiscal Year Program and Subaccounts (Accounting Report Monthly 1002).

10.2.3.5. A new cash disbursement, which would be chargeable (both as to purpose and amount) to an appropriation except that the appropriation is closed, must be paid from an appropriation that currently is available for the same purpose. However, a proposed payment may not exceed the:

10.2.3.5.1. Unexpended balance of the closed appropriation.

10.2.3.5.2. Unobligated balance of the currently available appropriation charged.

10.2.3.5.3. One percent limitation, discussed in subparagraph 110402.F.

10.2.3.6. The cumulative amount of payments charged to a currently available appropriation, because the original appropriation(s) that otherwise would have been charged has been closed, may not exceed one percent of the total amount appropriated to the currently available appropriation being charged. If it exceeds the one percent limit, the office funding the proposed payment (contract) must contact the Military Department Assistant Secretary for Financial Management and Comptroller (FM&C) or Defense Agency Comptroller for referral to the OUSW(C), Deputy Chief Financial Officer (DCFO) for appropriate disposition.

10.2.3.7. Corrections of payments involving closed appropriations must be processed as inter- and intra-appropriation adjustments. Such corrections generally do not require the obligation of currently available funds or deposits to the Treasury miscellaneous receipts account if the payment occurred before the closure of the applicable appropriation, or appropriations available for new obligation already have been charged properly.

10.2.3.8. Inter- and intra-appropriation adjustments to correct accounting records must not be accomplished by using a cash disbursement or cash collection.

10.2.3.9. A potential ADA violation must be reported and a preliminary investigation initiated if posting an adjustment to a current, expired or closed appropriation would result in either (1) a negative unobligated balance or (2) disbursements that are in excess of the amount appropriated, at either the appropriation level or a portion thereof that has been subdivided. See Volume 14 for ADA investigations and reporting requirements.

10.2.3.10. Perpetual balances of unobligated amounts and unliquidated amounts must be maintained for each closed appropriation. If the unobligated balance or unexpended balance in a closed appropriation is negative, a potential ADA violation has occurred and must be reported and investigated.

10.2.3.11. All disbursements and collections, or adjustments to disbursements and collections, involving current, expired, or closed appropriations, must be reported to Treasury. However, a correction in which both the debit and credit entry cite a closed appropriation is not reported to Treasury.

10.2.4. Expenditure Controls. The DoW Components must work with accounting and disbursing offices to implement effective controls to prevent over-expenditures in accounts that may be in an over-obligated position or that have UMD or NULO balances that exceed the unobligated balance in the account. This action is necessary because normal controls for determining expenditure availability are based on the unexpended balance of the obligations.

10.3    Request to Discontinue UMD/NULO Research

10.3.1. Research Decision

UMDs and NULOs may continue to be researched notwithstanding the obligation of funds. For transactions of $2,500 or less, the decision to continue (or discontinue) research is at the discretion of the fund holder. For transactions over $2,500, the Military Department Assistant Secretaries (FM&C) or Defense Agency Comptroller, may require the fund holder to continue research action. If continued research is required of the fund holder, written approval to discontinue research must be obtained from the Military Department Assistant Secretaries (FM&C) or Defense Agency Comptroller for transactions over $2,500. However, once the required obligation or obligation adjustment has been recorded for a UMD or NULO, DFAS must discontinue reporting the UMD or NULO regardless of whether research efforts continue.

10.3.2. Reporting Continued Research Efforts

After the research is accomplished by the accounting office and the fund holder, and the researched UMDs and NULOs are properly resolved, and/or required obligations or obligation adjustments are recorded, further research or reporting of such UMDs or NULOs is not required. If a fund manager and/or the accounting office later identify the need for an additional adjustment or correction and provide the appropriate adjusting/correcting document, the appropriate adjustment/correction must be recorded.

10.4 Correction/Posting Disbursements – Foreign Military Sales Trust Fund

Special Notification Requirements

10.4.1. If the accounting office has not been able to resolve the transactions after discovery of the UMD or NULO condition, the transactions must be forwarded to the fund holder for resolution. For FMS, both the Defense Security Cooperation Agency (DSCA) and the fund holder must be involved in the resolution. Notify the fund holder that he or she must fund the transaction if the transaction is not properly matched within the specified timeframes. If required, prepare a draft case modification for DSCA countersignature.

10.4.2. Due to FMS case management requirements, disbursements and disbursement adjustments involving FMS funds must be coordinated with DFAS. DFAS will establish notification and approval procedures.

10.5    Processing In-Transit Disbursements

Required Documentation

10.5.1. The applicable disbursing office or entitlement activity must use either electronic or hard copy-based processes to provide detailed supporting documentation (supplemental information) to the applicable disbursing center, accounting center, or accounting office. If adequate detailed accounting data is transmitted electronically, it is not necessary to forward paper copies unless specifically requested for a particular transaction.

10.5.2. The applicable disbursing office or entitlement activity must ensure that each in- transit disbursement transaction is supported by documentation that identifies the disbursing office and/or entitlement activity, cycle number, voucher number, appropriation/fiscal year, sub- allocation holder identifier, amount, accounting office code, obligation document number, and other information that identifies the obligation, as applicable.

10.6    Reporting Requirements

10.6.1. Data Collection Requirements. DFAS is responsible for collecting and consolidating data and reporting on the amounts and the status of UMDs, NULOs, and in-transit disbursements.

10.6.2. Monthly Reporting Requirements. The DoW Component accounting offices must transmit a status report identifying all disbursement transactions that have not been matched to an obligation to DFAS Headquarters monthly. DFAS will specify the format and detail reporting requirements.

10.7    Record Retention

DoW Components, and supporting accounting offices, must maintain an audit trail with adequate records to substantiate all transactions, amounts and actions taken with respect to the research and clearing of UMDs, NULOs, and in-transit disbursements. This includes but is not limited to determinations that selected transactions meet the criteria for discontinuing further research, and detail and summary records of adjustments. Components must maintain these records to ensure an adequate audit trail and to respond to inquiries from organizations internal and external to the Department. See Volume 1 for DoW policy on record retention.

title: Section 11.0: Policies Governing the Use of the “Feed and Forage” Authority of Section 3732, Revised Statutes (41 U.s.c. § 6301)
content:
11.0    POLICIES GOVERNING THE USE OF THE “FEED AND FORAGE” AUTHORITY OF SECTION 3732, REVISED STATUTES (41 U.S.C. § 6301)

11.1    General Policies

11.1.1. 41 U.S.C. § 6301 authorizes MILDEPs to incur obligations for certain necessities (e.g., clothing, subsistence, medical supplies) beyond available appropriations, not exceeding current fiscal year needs.

11.1.2. 10 U.S.C. § 2204 requires the SecWar to approve scheduled obligation rates to prevent overdrafts and deficiencies, though it does not prohibit legally authorized deficiencies.

11.1.3. Volume 14 (implementing 31 U.S.C. § 1517(a)) establishes the basic administrative control system for appropriations. This system aims to restrict obligations and expenditures to available amounts or apportionments, and to fix responsibility for violations.

11.2    Provisions

11.2.1. The DoW must strictly limit its use of the authority granted by 41 U.S.C. § 6301 to emergency circumstances only. The demands of these circumstances must be such that immediate action is imperative and cannot be delayed long enough to obtain sufficient funds through normal means. Furthermore, this emergency authority will not be used to circumvent the system of administrative controls for appropriations established under 31 U.S.C. § 1517(a).

11.2.2. It is not considered practicable to define specifically the conditions and circumstances which conceivably could constitute an emergency. Each instance in which the authority of 41 U.S.C. § 6301 will be used must be determined on a case-by-case basis.

11.3    Funds Administration

Funds will be administered according to the system of administrative controls in Volume 14. This ensures that responsible officials can take timely action to prevent over- obligation of any fund subdivision, regardless of the authority granted by 41 U.S.C. § 6301.

11.4    Over-obligation

11.4.1. The over-obligation of any apportioned appropriation or fund, or any subdivision thereof, for procurement of those items in paragraph 11.1 is considered a violation of the Antideficiency Act. Two exceptions include over-obligations made during an emergency in accordance with established provisions, provided that: (1) procurements do not exceed the necessities required to relieve the emergency, and (2) these necessities do not exceed the needs of the current fiscal year.

11.4.2. When the authority of 41 U.S.C. § 6301 is used to create an over-obligation, the responsible individual must certify in writing that three specific conditions existed. These conditions are: an emergency existed within the spirit and intent of 41 U.S.C. § 6301; the over- obligation was created to meet the necessities of the period; and it was not feasible to obtain sufficient funds in advance.

11.4.3. The over-obligation must be certified and fully disclosed in the fiscal reports to the next higher level of command, indicating that the over-obligation was incurred under authority of
41 U.S.C. § 6301.

11.5    Reporting Procedures

Refer to the Supplemental Document for details on reporting all obligations incurred under
41 U.S.C. § 6301.

title: Section 12.0: Receipt and Distribution of Budgetary Resources – Department Level
content:
12.0    RECEIPT AND DISTRIBUTION OF BUDGETARY RESOURCES – DEPARTMENT LEVEL

12.1    Appropriations

Congress grants appropriations as the legal authority to incur obligations and make Treasury payments for specified purposes. An appropriations act is the most common form of budget authority and must be explicitly stated, not inferred. The availability of an appropriation is determined by its period of availability, phase of availability, and the specified amount.

12.1.1. Period of Availability. The time in which budget authority is available to incur new obligations. This period of availability is categorized into several types. One-Year (Annual) Authority is the budget authority that is available for obligation only during a single, specified fiscal year, such as that for most Operations and Maintenance appropriations. Multiple Year (Multi-Year) Authority is budget authority that is available for a period longer than one fiscal year, such as for RDT&E (most are 2 years) or Procurement (3 years), Shipbuilding and Conversion, Navy appropriation (5 years), and Military construction appropriations (5 years). No-year Authority is budget authority which remains available for obligation indefinitely and Congressionally Directed Spending, which occurs when Congress designates a portion of an appropriation for a particular purpose through legislative language within an appropriation.

12.1.2. Phases of Availability. All annual and multi-year appropriations pass through three distinct phases of availability. First is the current or unexpired phase, during which the budget authority is available for incurring new obligations, making new grants, signing new contracts, and making disbursements to liquidate the obligations. The current or unexpired phase continues for the set period of availability. No-year authority remains current until fully obligated and disbursed or returned to the general fund of the Treasury. This is followed by the expired phase, a five-year period where funds are no longer available for new obligations but can be used to adjust and liquidate existing ones, although legislation can extend this period. Finally, the appropriation enters the canceled phase. At this point, no payments can be made from the canceled appropriation, and any remaining balance is canceled. On September 30 of the fifth fiscal year after the period of availability for obligation ends for a fixed appropriation account, the account must be closed and any remaining balance is canceled (whether obligated or unobligated). Policy does allow for an exception, per 31 U.S.C. § 1553, where valid obligations from a canceled account may be paid from a current appropriation, if these payments are strictly limited to one percent of the total current appropriation or are not chargeable to another expired account.

12.1.3. Determination of Amount. DoW policy recognizes that the amount of budget authority is determined by legislative language and falls into two categories. Definite Authority is the most common and is granted as a specific sum or a "not to exceed" amount. Indefinite Authority does not state a specific sum; instead, the amount is determined by a variable factor, such as the receipts collected from a certain source, the specific amount of which is determinable only at some future date, or it may appropriate such sums as may be necessary for a given purpose.

12.1.4. Reappropriations. Statutory authority that extends the availability of unobligated budget authority that has expired or is about to expire.

12.1.5. Exceptions. Contract authority is an exception to the general rule that appropriations provide budget authority for new obligations. It allows obligations for a specific purpose, time, and amount, as defined by statute, but remains unfunded and lacks a Treasury cash balance. Agencies must always replace or liquidate contract authority using subsequent budgetary resources, typically through offsetting collections credited to the Defense Working Capital Fund (DWCF). The liquidating appropriation itself does not grant new obligational authority.

12.1.6. Continuing Resolution (CR). A continuing resolution (CR) is a joint resolution that provides continuing appropriations for a fiscal year when regular appropriation bills have not been passed and a program's appropriations are about to or have expired, or when the President has vetoed congressionally passed appropriations bills. A CR does not appropriate a specific sum but instead makes funds available under the same terms and conditions as the prior year's appropriation act, though it may establish new conditions. Funding is available for obligation only until the CR's specified end date or until the regular appropriation is enacted, whichever comes first. For detailed guidance, refer to OMB Circular No. A-11, Section 123.

12.1.7. Funding Lapse or Gap. A lapse in an agency’s appropriations occurs when Congress fails to enact regular appropriations, a CR, or needed supplemental appropriations.

12.1.8. Appropriation Warrants. The DoW must recognize that an Appropriation Warrant, issued by the Secretary of the Treasury, is the official document that establishes the amount and period of availability of funds an agency is authorized to withdraw from the Treasury following the enactment of an appropriation. Policy dictates that under a Continuing Resolution (CR), warrants are generally not issued until the regular appropriation bill is passed. An exception to this policy is made for long-term or full-year CRs, or for those covering specific mandatory federal payments, as detailed in the Treasury Financial Manual (TFM) Volume 1, Part 2, Chapter 2000.

12.1.9. Classification of Appropriations. All departmental-level appropriations and other budgetary resources must be classified by appropriation account, fiscal year, and any obligation or expenditure limitations. This classification must be at the level of detail required by OSW for appropriation and fund status reporting, as specified in Volume 6. The policy is to classify appropriations in various ways based on their purpose, such as by time period, spending limits, or authorized programs and availability to incur obligations. The official representation of this classification is the appropriation account symbol.

12.1.10. Recording an Appropriation. DoW policy states that an appropriation is not available as a financing source or budgetary resource until it has been apportioned by OMB. As soon as funds are made available for apportionment (even if a Treasury Warrant has not been issued or the full amount has not been apportioned), it is policy to recognize them in the capital as "unexpended appropriations" and among assets as "funds with Treasury." Policy further dictates that this "unexpended appropriations" account should be reduced as appropriations are used and adjusted for any other changes, such as rescissions or transfers. These accounting principles are governed by the Federal Accounting Standards Advisory Board (FASAB) Handbook, specifically the Statement of Federal Financial Accounting Standards (SFFAS) 7.

12.2    Apportionments and Reapportionments

12.2.1. The DoW must adhere to the apportionment process, which is the OMB-approved plan to allocate budgetary resources as defined by 31 U.S.C. § 1513(b). An apportionment is legally binding, and policy dictates that any obligation or expenditure that exceeds an apportionment is an Antideficiency Act violation (per 31 U.S.C. § 1517) and must be reported. Policy also requires that apportionments cannot be obligated until the amounts have been formally allotted according to OMB-approved funds control regulations. Programs must be apportioned and executed in accordance with all applicable laws, and obligations must be reconciled against the fiscal year in which the expenses were incurred. Not all appropriations are apportioned. Policy recognizes that some budgetary resources may be withheld pending rescission, deferred, or are otherwise exempt.

12.2.2. Special Circumstances. During a Continuing Resolution (CR), policy requires agencies to adhere to OMB apportionments in the same way they do for regular appropriations. Typically, OMB will automatically apportion funds under a CR. For indefinite budget authority, if actual available amounts are less than anticipated, it is policy to deduct the difference from the apportioned amounts unless a different treatment is specified or a reapportionment is initiated. Per OMB Circular No. A-11 (Section 120), a downward reapportionment for reduced budgetary resources is not required unless OMB specifically directs it.

12.3    Contract Authority – Other Budgetary Authorizations

12.3.1. Congress finances federal programs by granting budgetary authority, which enables agencies to incur financial obligations that lead to government outlays. As defined by the Congressional Budget Act, budgetary authority encompasses not only appropriations but also contract authority, borrowing authority, and spending authority from offsetting collections.

12.3.2. Contract authority, granted by Congress through an authorizing statute, allows an agency to incur obligations in advance of an appropriation. These obligations are typically liquidated by anticipated receipts or offsetting collections. Per 41 U.S.C. § 6301, no expenditures can be made against these obligations until funds are either specifically appropriated or otherwise become available. Contract authority can be current or permanent, definite or indefinite, and its period of availability will align with the fiscal year covered by the appropriation act. Definite authority is a legally prescribed amount of new authority for the fiscal year. Authority is considered definite when the law provides a specific ceiling or a "not to exceed" amount. Indefinite authority is not predetermined; instead, the amount of authority is equal to the new obligations incurred during the fiscal year. Though typically accounted for through a no-year appropriation, it must be apportioned each fiscal year. Current authority requires congressional appropriations action on the request for new budget authority for the year involved. Permanent authority becomes available through standing law without further congressional appropriation once the budget is transmitted. Permanent indefinite authority is open-ended in both period and amount, with examples including 31 U.S.C. § 1304 (Payment of Judgments) and 31 U.S.C. § 1322(b)(2) (Refunding Erroneous Collections). Guidance for emergency military procurement (per 41 U.S.C. § 6301 and FAR), Working Capital Fund authority, and foreign military sales also fall under this category.

12.4    Transfer of Funds

When legally authorized, budgetary authority can be withdrawn from one appropriation and credited to another account or a working fund. Such a transfer is recorded as either an expenditure transfer (involving an outlay) or a nonexpenditure transfer (not involving an outlay). These transfers between appropriations, which must always be authorized by law, are used to redistribute unobligated balances for reasons such as reorganizations, congressionally authorized funding changes, or shifts in the purpose of the funds.

12.4.1. Anticipated Transfers. Appropriation transfers can be anticipated and recorded in advance. An anticipated transfer itself grants no obligation authority; it is treated as authority available for apportionment and prior-year authority and current-year authority are kept separate. Obligation authority only becomes available after the transfer is accomplished and the funds are apportioned by OMB. An agreement must be maintained between the transferring and receiving accounts, and both must record the transfer in the same accounting period. Once a transfer is accomplished, budgetary and proprietary control shifts to the receiving appropriation.

12.4.2. Expenditure Transfer. This is a transfer typically made when it benefits the transferring account. Policy dictates how these transfers are recorded: as an obligation and an outlay in the transferring account, and as an offsetting collection or receipt in the receiving account. Since expenditure transfers are treated as payments and collections, they are not applicable to departmental-level accounting entities. An expenditure transfer includes withdrawals and credits not defined as nonexpenditure, transfers between budgetary and nonbudgetary Treasury accounts such as general fund accounts and deposit accounts, and adjustments to correct errors in previous expenditure transactions.

12.4.3. Nonexpenditure Transfers. This is a transaction that does not involve an outlay but is instead recorded as a decrease in budget authority or unobligated balances in the transferring account and a corresponding increase in the budgetary authority or unobligated balances gaining account. This type of transfer category includes two specific types of actions: a transfer of estimates, which is a proposal to shift the funding of an activity between budget accounts without transferring the actual budgetary resources, and an allocation, which is a legally authorized delegation of authority from one agency to another to obligate funds.

12.4.4. Reprogramming. Shifting of funds for purposes other than those originally specified by Congress or to reclassify funds for proper execution.

12.4.4.1. Below Threshold Reprogramming Action. Action that provides DoW Components with the flexibility to realign funds within congressionally prescribed limits, and approved funding to satisfy unfunded requirements.

12.4.4.2. Above Threshold Reprogramming Actions. Action of reallocating funds when established congressional approval thresholds are exceeded, which requires prior approval from congressional committees. In addition, the Department uses internal reprogramming actions to transfer funds from various accounts that Congress has established with its own specific transfer authority (e.g., Environmental Restoration) or to realign/transfer funds for proper execution of a congressionally approved program.

12.5    Reappropriations

Congressional action that continues the availability of all or part of the unobligated portion of budget authority that has expired or would otherwise expire. Policy dictates that reappropriations of expired balances are to be recorded as new budget authority in the year they become available. If the balance in the losing appropriation is insufficient to cover the transfer, the reappropriation may be delayed or canceled. Decisions to delay or not make a reappropriation transfer require written notification to the USW(C), within five working days of the determination. It is also policy that reappropriations providing funds to a fiscal year for which they were not previously available constitute new budget authority and therefore require a Treasury Warrant. Reappropriations of unexpired balances or those that take effect in a future fiscal year are reported as balance transfers in the year they become newly available for obligation. Unobligated balances must be withdrawn in the losing accounts from operating activities. However, an exception is made when the operating activity includes both the gaining and losing accounts and the intent is simply to extend the availability of funds for the same purpose. In this case, a formal withdrawal is not required.

12.6    Internal Fund Distributions

Apportionments are subdivided and formally distributed through a hierarchy of allotments, sub allotments, allocations, and suballocations. Detailed requirements for these subdivision levels are established in Volume 14, in accordance with OMB Circular No. A-11, Appendix H. A critical policy is that any formal subdivision of funds must carry with it all the same statutory and other limitations that were applicable to the original apportionment. Policy also requires that all formal distributions of funds must be made in writing, with the specific format determined by the issuing entity.

12.7    Interagency Distributions

For distributions of budgetary resources between agencies (interagency distributions), it is policy to use separate accounts to track the distribution and ensure the recipient agency is responsive to the issuing agency. From a consolidated accounting standpoint, policy mandates that both the issuing and receiving agencies must record the distribution in the same accounting period. Reference Volume 11 for overarching policies regarding policies work performed or materials provided between the DoW and other Federal Agencies.

12.8    Withdrawals and Expired Balances

Withdrawal as an administrative action to remove unobligated funds from availability, as distinct from a legal rescission by Congress. A Restoration is the administrative action to make those withdrawn funds available again. A key policy, based on 31 U.S.C. § 1555, is that funds can only be withdrawn when an account closes; budget authority cannot be withdrawn from open accounts.

12.8.1. Expired Balances. Expired balances retain their fiscal year identity for five years. During this time, it is policy that the unobligated balance can only be used to adjust obligations that were incurred when the appropriation was available; it cannot be used for new obligations. After the five-year period, any remaining balances must be transferred to account 4350, Canceled Authority. A strict policy is that canceled amounts cannot be restored.

12.8.2. Nature of Expired Authority Account. Account 465000, Allotments – Expired Authority, is not a fund balance. Its purpose is to serve as a budgetary resource to ensure valid obligations from expired accounts can be met without requiring new congressional action. While transfers in and out of this account do not affect the Treasury's cash position, related proprietary transactions do impact the Fund Balance with Treasury (account 101000).

12.9    Indefinite Appropriations

It is the policy of the DoW to recognize indefinite appropriations as a type of appropriation where a definite amount is not stated but is instead determined by subsequent events, such as the collection of receipts. An example of this is the receipts under the Federal Account Symbol and Title 5095.001, Sale of Hunting and Fishing Permits, Military Reservations, are permanently appropriated for the Army to spend under appropriation account 21X5095, Wildlife Conservation, Military Reservations, Army. Policy dictates that these funds, even if based on the collection of receipts, cannot be accessed until the Treasury issues a warrant or the authorized amount may be specified as the amount obligated for a specific purpose. It is also policy that anticipated amounts from indefinite appropriations must be reported as "anticipated budgetary resources" until the funds are realized. A critical element of this policy is that these anticipated balances, while reported on the SF 133, should not be recorded as currently available for obligation.

12.10    Other Account Adjustments and Closing

12.10.1. Account Adjustments. At the end of the availability period, all undistributed or unobligated budget authority at the execution level must be returned to the departmental level for financial reporting.

12.10.2. Notification from Lower Levels. It is the policy of the DoW that the departmental-level accounting entity must be informed of specific adjustments and account balances from intermediate and execution levels for financial reporting purposes, as specified in Volume 6. This policy ensures transparency and accuracy in financial reporting across all levels.

12.10.3. Account Closing. At year-end, the Treasury requires specific post-closing entries to be made to certain accounts. These closing transactions are critical for financial management, serving to establish beginning balances for accounts with no fiscal year activity and to zero out balances that recorded current-year activity. For direct funds, record unobligated budget authority for unexpired appropriations, close unobligated balances to expired authority, reduce realized appropriations by rescinded appropriations, and close both accomplished and realized appropriation transfers. No closing entries must be made for the reimbursable program at the departmental level.

title: Section 13.0: Receipt and Distribution of Budgetary Resources Intermediate-Level
content:
13.0    RECEIPT AND DISTRIBUTION OF BUDGETARY RESOURCES INTERMEDIATE-LEVEL

13.1    Standards for Recording and Distribution

Many DoW Components, like the Military Departments, are structured in three or more echelons. Budget authority for General Fund direct appropriations is recorded at the Department level (Headquarters), issued to intermediate-level organizations (Major Commands), and then distributed to execution-level organizations (field level) for program implementation. This section sets the standards for recording the receipt and distribution of direct budgetary resources using intermediate-level accounts. These accounts track fund distributions (like allotments) from the Department level to intermediate organizations and then down to execution activities. The guidance in this section does not apply to two-tiered structures (e.g., Defense-wide appropriations) or to reimbursable budget authority, which is covered in Volume 11.

13.2    Required Notification and Reporting

The intermediate-level accounting activity must notify the department-level accounting entity of direct program authority that is not distributed to the execution-level (account 456000, Funds Available for Allotment). After preparation of the prescribed budget execution reports, accounting entries must be made, at the expiration of the period of availability (PoA) for obligation, to close expended amounts to the authorizing account for the expenditures and to withdraw any remaining program authority.

title: Section 14.0: Receipt and Distribution of Budgetary Resources – Execution Level
content:
14.0    RECEIPT AND DISTRIBUTION OF BUDGETARY RESOURCES – EXECUTION LEVEL

Execution-level budgetary and proprietary accounts track the receipt of funds from higher authorities, such as the OSW, and their subsequent distribution, including the subdivision of the allotment (sub allotment, allocation, or suballocation) between a major command and an execution-level activity or among execution-level activities. This section establishes the standards for recording these financial activities, including allotments, commitments, and obligations, which often require entries in both budgetary and proprietary accounts. This section outlines the accounting standards for receiving and executing allotments, commitments, obligations, reimbursements, and borrowing authority.

14.1    Budget Execution Requirements

According to DoW policy, formal subdivisions of budgetary authority, such as allotments, sub allotments, allocations, and suballocations authorize the receiving entity to incur obligations up to a specified amount. These subdivisions must include the same statutory limitations and availability constraints as the original apportionment from the OMB. To ensure congressional intent is met, accounting entities are required to track the obligations and expenditures of any funds designated for a specific purpose.

14.2    Budgetary Commitments

An agreement with the OMB requires commitment accounting for Procurement, Military Construction, and Research, Development, Test, and Evaluation (RDT&E) appropriations. However, this is not required for small purchases if they are not significant to the overall management of funds. While commitment accounting is optional for Operation and Maintenance, military personnel, and revolving fund accounts, agencies may use it if it proves cost-effective. All commitments represent an administrative reservation of funds, and any outstanding commitments must be closed or canceled by the end of the period when the appropriation is available for new obligations, as they cannot exist in an expired appropriation account.

14.3    Obligations

Obligations are legally binding commitments that will require payments. They represent the amounts of orders placed, contracts awarded, and services received which will require payment in the same or future period. These amounts also include obligations that organizations did not previously record and adjustments for any differences between previously recorded obligations and the actual payments made to liquidate them. Furthermore, any reductions or cancellations of prior-year obligations in no-year and unexpired multi-year accounts must be reported in budget execution reports, see Volume 6.

14.4    Reimbursements and Refunds

14.4.1. Reimbursable obligations are those financed by offsetting collections for goods and services provided, which must be authorized by law to be credited to a specific appropriation or fund account. The USW(C) authorizes this reimbursable authority through budget formulation and statutory authorization of the budget. Generally, unless an exception applies, collections are deposited into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. To record an obligation and an outlay in the current fiscal year for returned cash advances, other offsetting collections, or special or trust fund receipts received in a prior fiscal year, follow the guidelines in OMB Circular No. A-11.

14.4.2. Refunds, such as those for overpayments or payments made in error, are treated as reductions to previously recorded expenditures. Any amounts collected that exceed the refund amount, such as interest or penalties, must be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. It is important to note that items returned to Defense Working Capital Fund (DWCF) supply activities are classified as recoveries, not refunds. Except for refunds, agencies must deposit such collections in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts unless a law authorizes the deposit to an appropriation or fund. Agencies may credit refunds related to the use of Government purchase and travel cards, as well as Government travel arranged by Government Contracted Travel Management Centers, to the Operation and Maintenance and Research, Development, Test, and Evaluation accounts that are current when they receive the refunds. Volume 11 contains the general policy statements regarding work performed or materials provided between the DoW and other Federal agencies.

14.4.3. Anticipated Reimbursements. Anticipated reimbursements are estimates of funds expected to be earned during the fiscal year and are subject to OMB apportionment based on customer orders or services received or provided. This authority does not grant the power to incur obligations; a customer order must be formally accepted to create obligational authority, unless specifically authorized by statute. The allotment of anticipated reimbursable authority only provides the authority to accept reimbursable orders, not to obligate funds. It is the accepted customer order that provides the actual obligation authority. With written approval from the OMB a DoW Component can treat its reimbursable authority as “automatic,” which removes the need for it to be specifically allotted.
