OMB approval is granted when the criteria for automatic apportionment are met, as outlined in Volume 3.

14.4.4. Customer Orders. Obligational authority is established only when a customer order is formally accepted in writing. Volume 11outlines the written requirements used to document these requests and acceptances. Unfilled customer orders represent the value of accepted agreements within the U.S. Government to provide goods and services on a reimbursable basis. While an allotment of reimbursable authority is necessary to accept orders, it does not grant obligational authority on its own. For transactions with the public, payment must be collected in advance unless a specific statute permits otherwise. When handling reimbursable orders between federal agencies, if both entities use multi-year appropriations, the performing agency must record the obligation against its own multi-year account with a corresponding period of availability. However, if the agencies' appropriation accounts have different lifecycles (e.g., a one-year appropriation filling a multi-year order), the transaction must be handled in accordance with OMB Circular No. A-11. For specific guidance on Economy Act orders, refer to Volume 11.

14.4.5. Unearned Revenue. Unearned revenue is payment received before goods or services are delivered.

14.5    Earned Reimbursements

An earned reimbursement is recognized when a performing organization renders actual or constructive performance on a reimbursable order. At this point, compound entries are made to record performance and earnings in both budgetary and proprietary accounts. Generally, all cost elements outlined in Volume 11 must be recovered through these reimbursements, although other DoW issuances may authorize different billing prices.

14.6    Borrowing Authority

Borrowing authority is a form of budget authority that allows an entity to incur obligations and make payments for specified purposes using borrowed money. When the U.S. Government acquires property subject to a mortgage, the mortgage balance is included in the accrued expenditures. Conversely, when it sells a property and a buyer assumes the mortgage, that balance is included in accrued revenues. The government may also hold a second mortgage, which is treated as revenue from the sale. Officials must ensure that the total acquisition cost of the property and the mortgage assumed align with Volume 6.

14.7    Account Adjustments

14.7.1. At the end of the fiscal year, DoW Components must ensure their obligational authority and recorded obligations are accurately stated based on the most current information available. This involves a thorough review and adjustment of all open financial transactions.

14.7.2. Adjustments to Expiring Accounts. At fiscal year-end, all outstanding commitments in expiring appropriation accounts must be canceled, as commitments are not permitted in expired accounts. For completed customer orders, any obligational authority from reimbursable authority that exceeded the actual cost of performance must be restored. Any earned amounts that remain uncollected from an expiring account must be moved to a miscellaneous receipt account for future deposit. Additionally, any unused cash advances from non-Federal customers must be returned.

14.7.3. Adjustments to Canceled Appropriation Accounts. Officials must cancel all obligations (undelivered orders and unpaid obligations) and uncollected reimbursements before making normal closing entries.

14.7.4. Report Preparation and Closing. After completing all adjustments, prepare budget execution reports as specified in Volume 6. Once the reports are finished, close the obligational and reimbursable authority.

14.8    Expired and Canceled Accounts

For five years after an appropriation expires for new obligations, its remaining balances can be used to adjust and liquidate obligations properly chargeable to that account. On September 30th of the fifth fiscal year, any remaining obligated and unobligated balances must be canceled, rendering them unavailable for any purpose. If an obligation needs to be paid from a canceled appropriation, it can be charged to a current appropriation available for the same purpose. However, the total of all such payments from the current appropriation is limited to the lesser of the unexpended balance of the canceled, the unexpired, unobligated balance of the currently available appropriation, or one percent of the original amount of the current appropriation.

14.9    Expired Authority

Expired authority includes both unobligated balances and obligated but unliquidated balances in appropriations where the period for incurring new obligations has ended. Separate accounts must be maintained for each expired appropriation for five years after its period of availability for obligation ends.

14.10    Canceled Authority

On September 30th of the fifth fiscal year after an appropriation's period of availability ends, the agency must close the fixed appropriation account and cancel any remaining balance (whether obligated or unobligated) in the account must be closed, and any remaining balance is canceled. After this point, the funds are no longer available for any obligation or expenditure. However, the obligational status of the canceled account must be continuously maintained. Any collections that were authorized but not received before the account was closed must be deposited into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. If it becomes necessary to pay an obligation from a canceled account, a current appropriation available for the same purpose may be used. When using a current appropriation to pay for an obligation from a canceled appropriation, the payment is limited to the lesser of: The unexpended balance of the canceled appropriation; the unexpired, unobligated balance of the current appropriation; or one percent of the current appropriation being charged. If payments exceed this 1 percent limit, the agency must seek additional authority from Congress. Furthermore, if cash collections do not cover reimbursable obligations from a canceled account, those obligations must be paid using the direct unobligated authority that existed in the account when it was closed.

title: Section 15.0: Accounting Requirements for Military Construction Projects
content:
15.0    ACCOUNTING REQUIREMENTS FOR MILITARY CONSTRUCTION PROJECTS

A military construction project encompasses all necessary work to create a complete and usable facility or a complete and usable improvement to an existing facility, including any portion specifically authorized by law. The authority to carry out such a project includes a broad scope of activities, such as surveys and site preparation; the acquisition, conversion, rehabilitation, and installation of facilities; the acquisition and installation of equipment and appurtenances integral to the project; the acquisition and installation of supporting facilities like utilities; and all planning, supervision, administration, and overhead incident to the project.

15.1    Authorization Requests

Guidance for submitting military construction projects for authorization is provided by the Assistant Secretary of War for Energy, Installations, and Environment (ASW(Sustainment)), in conjunction with the OUSW(C). Authorization requests are limited to work expected to be executed within the requested fiscal year. These requests must be supported by detailed data on the project's physical capacity, estimated costs, and location. This information must be accompanied by comparative data on existing property and future projects, along with details on approved missions and forces. Finally, the request must distinguish the portion of the project for immediate authorization from any portion being deferred.

15.2    Authorization Guidance and Restrictions

Congressional authorization acts for major construction programs typically set cost limits for each installation or type of work. Overruns may be authorized within stated percentages, provided the total appropriation is not exceeded. Major construction projects require specific authorization in a military construction authorization act unless the work is carried out under other legal authorities, such as those provided in 10 U.S.C. § 2803-2805. Conversely, minor military construction projects cannot exceed the statutory cost limits defined in 10 U.S.C. § 2805 without specific Congressional approval. The general authority to carry out a military construction project is provided by 10 U.S.C. § 2802.

15.3    Appropriation Requests

The authorization and appropriation process for individual Military Family Housing projects is governed by 10 U.S.C. Chapter 169, Subchapter II. Military construction appropriations are generally available for obligation for five fiscal years. All appropriation requests must be consistent with existing or pending authorizations and must include specific budget estimates for projects requiring legislative authorization. For reprogramming, all requests must align with the amounts appropriated for specific projects, and the total reprogrammed amount cannot exceed the total annual appropriation. Funds may be sourced from projects completed under budget; however, the amount available for reprogramming from any single project is limited to the new total cost that was included in the estimate provided to Congress.

15.4    Obligation and Expenditure Restrictions

In accordance with DoW policy, all appropriated funds are subject to regulations regarding the administrative control of funds and the provisions of the Antideficiency Act. An adequate system of funds control must be established to ensure projects are executed consistently with their authorized purpose and within available funding. While the cost estimate for a project approved by Congress is not a separate statutory cost limitation, any major physical or financial changes to previously approved projects must be reported in advance to the House and Senate Appropriations Committees and the House National Security and Senate Armed Services Committees for their approval after proper clearance within the Department and OMB. Limitations are applied at the project level for major construction and at the budget activity level for minor construction, planning, and design. DoW Components have limited authority to realign resources between projects, and all separate cost limitations imposed by congressional or administrative action must be observed at every level of program execution.

15.4.1. Intergovernmental Construction Work or Services

15.4.1.1. When performing construction or services for another DoW Component or federal agency, Military Departments must use reimbursable agreements under the Economy Act whenever practical. This requires using the latest versions of the standard Interagency Agreement forms (FS Form 7600A and FS Form 7600B), which must mandate periodic billings supported by cost documentation. All DoW Components must also comply with Federal Intragovernmental Data Standards, whether using Treasury’s G-Invoicing system, other enterprise systems, or completing the forms manually.

15.4.1.2. In accordance with DoW policy, any Construction Agent wishing to use suballotments instead of the standard FS Forms 7600A/B must first submit a detailed action plan to the Deputy Chief Financial Officer (DCFO) and receive approval. If approved, the agent is then required to adhere to strict financial management and reporting standards to ensure financial integrity, auditability, and proper accounting for all project costs from funding receipt through asset transfer and contract close-out. This includes using independently validated financial systems, providing complete and reconciled monthly trial balances to customers and the Defense Finance and Accounting Service (DFAS), and maintaining full transparency of their end-to-end business processes for all military construction projects.

15.4.1.2.1. To ensure financial integrity, use independently validated financial management systems that are compliant with both the Federal Information System Controls Audit Manual (FISCAM) and the Federal Financial Management Improvement Act (FFMIA). The system must meet all relevant control objectives, including both Information Technology General Controls and application controls to be FISCAM Compliant. The system must meet federal financial management system requirements (e.g., the OMB Circulars A-127 and A-130), applicable federal accounting standards (e.g., SFFAS, OMB Bulletin 19-03), and the U.S. Standard General Ledger (USSGL) at the transaction level to be FFMIA Compliant.

15.4.1.2.2. Monthly, U.S. Standard General Ledger (USSGL) and Standard Financial Information Structure (SFIS) compliant trial balances must be provided to each customer and to the Defense Finance and Accounting Service (DFAS), which include both budgetary and proprietary accounts. These trial balances must be reconciled to the suballotment universe of transactions; end-to-end feeder systems such as contract writing, entitlement, and Accountable Property Systems of Record; the Defense Departmental Reporting System (DDRS) unadjusted and adjusted trial balances; and Program Budget Accounting System funding authorizations.

15.4.1.2.3. For both major and minor Military Construction projects, you must provide comprehensive end-to-end business process and system walkthroughs, including process flows and narratives. This documentation must cover the entire project lifecycle, from the receipt of funding through the final asset transfer and contract close-out. Crucially, the process must demonstrate how all direct and indirect costs are accumulated in a construction-in-progress account, in accordance with SFFAS 6, "Accounting for Property, Plant, and Equipment." Furthermore, you must provide supporting transaction documents, such as contracts, invoices, or receiving documents, rate settlement calculations, DoD (DD) Form 1354, Transfer and Acceptance of DoW Real Property, and support for DDRS or accounting system Journal Vouchers, within five days of a customer request. Finally, you are required to work with customer auditors to identify and correct any audit findings, including those related to the system.

15.4.1.3. Provide a reconciliation of progress billings to actual construction in progress and provide sufficient supporting documentation for the reconciliation at least monthly.

15.4.1.4. DoW Construction Agents may perform work or services for another DoW Component or other Federal agency (i.e. Federal Emergency Management Agency) when construction or services work is a response to an emergency, under suballotments.

15.4.1.5. Funding for construction work by the transfer of appropriation accounts or by advances of funds is prohibited. Direct citation of funds (i.e. direct charge by the performing unit and/or activity to the funds of the ordering unit and/or activity) is also prohibited.

15.4.2. When work is performed on a reimbursable basis under a construction appropriation, all activities must conform to established policies. Reimbursements earned are considered an additional source of obligational authority for the appropriate budget program. Cost limitations for the performance of work must be strictly observed as defined by the terms of the customer orders received. The management and control of reimbursable programs, including budgeting and use of funds, is retained at the Military Department level.

15.4.3. The authority for the Army, Navy, and Air Force to procure architectural and engineering (A&E) services for public works and utilities projects is provided by 10 U.S.C. § 7540, 8612, and 9540. These statutes limit the cost of A&E services from outside sources to no more than 10 percent of the project's estimated cost. This 10 percent limitation excludes costs for activities such as design reviews, advertisements, preparation of invitations for bids, requests for proposals, land survey, soils and/or other investigations and model studies, determination of program or project requirements, design development criteria, environmental impact statements and supporting data, or travel and per diem.

15.5    Planning and Design

Under 10 U.S.C. § 2807, the Secretary is authorized to obtain architectural and engineering (A&E) services and perform construction design for military construction, family housing projects, and projects undertaken in connection with the authority provided under 10 U.S.C. § 2854 not otherwise authorized by law. These design activities can proceed without specific congressional authorization for the project, as long as the estimated design costs do not exceed $1 million. If the estimated costs for these services exceed $1 million, the Secretary must notify the appropriate congressional committees before obligating funds. The funds can only be obligated after a 14-day waiting period following this notification pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 480. This requirement applies to both active and reserve components.

15.6    Scope of a Military Construction Project

In accordance with DoW policy, all land acquisitions, regardless of their cost, are categorized as military construction projects. A military construction project encompasses all construction or authorized contributions required to create a complete, usable facility or an improvement to an existing one, as specifically authorized by law. Military construction project funding includes only equipment that is installed in and becomes a permanent part of the real property. All production equipment and movable equipment are specifically excluded from military construction project funding.

15.6.1. Construction work must be consolidated into single projects under specific conditions. All construction on a real property facility that serves the same or a related functional purpose must be treated as a single project. For multi-use facilities, all concurrent construction in contiguous areas must also be treated as a single project, even if the functions are unrelated. Similarly, any construction common to the facility as a whole or to areas with related purposes is considered one project. An exception exists for multi-use facilities, where construction may be divided into separate projects, but only if each resulting project can be clearly defined and produces a complete and usable facility.

15.6.2. When construction is performed concurrently with repair or maintenance work as part of an integrated undertaking, the construction portion may be treated as a separate project. When this occurs, the construction portion becomes subject to all cost limitations, notification requirements, and other regulations that apply to standard construction projects.

15.6.3. In accordance with DoW policy, the decision to define related construction efforts as either a single project or multiple projects requires formal approval at the highest level within the respective Military Department. This ensures strategic oversight and proper scoping of construction work.

15.7    Certifications of Costs

A formal certification of costs is required for all military construction projects. This document must detail the project's total cost, with breakdowns for each structure and by category: planning and design, supervision, construction, and real property installed equipment (RPIE). It must also identify the funding sources, including the fund type and lines of accounting, and the responsible funding organization. To formally transfer accountability, the certification must be signed by authorized representatives from both the construction agent and the acquiring entity, typically the Real Property Accountable Officer. A copy of the completed certification must be retained for record-keeping.

15.8    Project Files

A project file must be maintained for every construction project, serving as a complete historical record from its inception to completion. The construction agent is responsible for holding these historical project files and is required to provide copies to the acquiring entity.

15.9    Military Construction Projects

Specified military construction projects, or "major military construction," include any acquisition, construction, addition, expansion, extension, conversion, alteration, or replacement of facilities that exceed the legal maximum for a minor construction project, or any project, regardless of cost, approved as a specific line item in the Military Construction budget request. A major construction project includes surveys, demolition, and site preparation; the acquisition, conversion, rehabilitation and installation of facilities and integral equipment; the installation of supporting facilities and utilities; and all associated supervision, administration, overhead, and design support. Specifically excluded from major construction are those activities identified as minor construction, planning and design, or supporting activities.

15.10    Unspecified Minor Military Construction

15.10.1. Projects involving acquisition of new construction, addition, expansion, extension, alteration, conversion, replacement, or installation to permanent or temporary facilities (excluding family quarters) are considered minor construction when their cost does not exceed the statutory limits specified in 10 U.S.C. § 2805 (Active Components) or 10 U.S.C. § 18233a (Reserve Components), and they are not included as a specific line item in the budget request.

15.10.2. For other than family housing facilities, when the cost of a project is less than the amount specified in 10 U.S.C. § 2805, the project must be financed from unspecified minor construction appropriations; operations and maintenance (O&M) appropriations; research, development, test and evaluation (RDT&E) appropriations; working capital fund resources; or other resources, as appropriate. The funding source does not influence the financial statement capitalization requirements.

15.10.3. Minor construction projects previously disapproved or deleted by Congress from being proposed under minor construction authority. Each project must result in a complete real property facility or improvement. The policy also mandates that, to the maximum extent possible, each project must align with the installation master plan. Full disclosure of the project's relationship to the master plan and any further planned construction is required. Lastly, the policy strictly prohibits incremental construction through a series of minor projects.

15.10.4. Congressional notification is required before starting certain minor construction projects. For projects exceeding the cost limits in 10 U.S.C. § 18233a, funds cannot be obligated until the appropriate congressional committee approves the project. For unspecified minor construction projects costing more than $2 million, as defined in 10 U.S.C. § 2805, the Secretary concerned must notify the appropriate committees of Congress of the decision to undertake the project, including its justification and estimated cost. A mandatory waiting period must be observed after notification before work can begin.

15.10.5. When determining if a project qualifies as minor construction under 10 U.S.C. § 2805, planning and design costs are excluded. DoW Components cannot use materials, supplies, items of installed capital equipment on a non-reimbursable basis for their own minor construction projects. Prerequisites for establishing a project include identifying the result and its correlation with the installation master plan. While absolute criteria for defining a separate minor construction project are not prescribed, any project undertaken must be consistent with the statute's intent.

15.11    Emergency and Contingency Construction

In accordance with DoW policy, 10 U.S.C. § 2808 grants the SecWar the authority to undertake military construction projects during a declared war or a national emergency that requires the use of the Armed Forces. These projects must be necessary to support the use of the Armed Forces and may only be funded using the total amount of unobligated military construction funds, including those for family housing. The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff must certify that any such project is consistent with theater basing plans and operational requirements. Any subsequent increases to the estimated project costs require coordination with the OUSW(C). This emergency authority automatically terminates at the end of the war or national emergency. Additional guidance is contained in DoDD 3025.18 and DoDD 4270.5.

15.11.1. Emergency Construction. Under the authority of 10 U.S.C. § 2803 and as further guided by DoDD 4270.5, the Secretaries of the Military Departments and Directors of Defense Agencies may carry out emergency major construction projects after notifying Congress. This authority is strictly reserved for projects that are vital to national security, health, safety, or the environment, and where the urgency is so great that deferral to the next Military Construction Authorization Act would be inconsistent with those interests. Emergency construction projects must be financed with unobligated military construction funds, and the maximum amount that can be obligated by each Military Department in a fiscal year is established in 10 U.S.C. § 2803. These projects are subject to the same restrictions and cost treatment as major construction projects. It is important to note that there is no provision for emergency construction for the Reserve Components.

15.11.2. Contingency Construction. 10 U.S.C. § 2804 and annual Military Construction Appropriation Acts authorize projects of an urgent nature to be funded from the Contingency Construction Account without specific prior congressional authorization. A project financed under this authority requires a determination that deferring it to the next Military Construction Authorization Act would be inconsistent with national security or the national interest. The use of this authority requires approval by the SecWar and written notification to the appropriate committees of Congress. Additional policy guidance is contained in DoDD 4270.5, and further requirements for the use of these funds in the U.S. Central Command and U.S. Africa Command Areas of Responsibility are prescribed in an OUSW(C) policy memorandum.

15.12    Environmental Response Actions

In accordance with DoW policy, the authority for environmental response actions is provided under 10 U.S.C. Chapter 160. The SecWar or the Secretary of a Military Department may carry out an environmental restoration project if it is determined to be necessary under Chapter 160 or the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 (CERCLA). Any construction, development, conversion, or extension of a structure, and any installation of equipment, included in an environmental restoration project may not be considered military construction. The sole source of funds for these activities is the Environmental Restoration Account (Treasury Fund Symbol ***X0810), except for certain Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) sites, which must use the applicable DoW base closure account. It is policy that funds from an Environmental Restoration Account cannot be used for the payment of fines or penalties except as provided in 10 U.S.C. § 2703.

15.13    Restoration or Replacement of Damaged or Destroyed Facilities

Under the authority of 10 U.S.C. § 2854, the Secretaries of the Military Departments and the SecWar may repair, restore, or replace a facility that has been damaged or destroyed, even if specific legislative authorization and appropriation have not been provided for that purpose. These restoration or replacement projects must be financed using unobligated funds from existing appropriations.

15.14    Defense Access Roads

Under the authority of 23 U.S.C. § 210, the defense access roads program allows the federal government to fund its fair share of highway improvements essential for national defense. This includes providing access to military reservations and defense industry sites, replacing public highways closed by military activities, and repairing highway damage caused by military maneuvers or the construction of missile sites. The program also covers ensuring missile routes can support transporter-erector vehicles and repairing damage from recurrent flooding and sea- level fluctuation that impacts access to a military installation. Defense access roads, including bridges and tunnels, provide access to military reservations, to defense industries and defense industry sites, and to the sources of raw materials when such roads are certified as important to the national defense by the SecWar or such other official as the President may designate. However, roads located entirely within the boundaries of a military reservation are not eligible for these funds and must be financed through other military construction programs, emergency construction, or minor construction programs, as applicable. Similarly, projects on the regular Federal-Aid Primary System are generally not eligible.

15.15    Relocatable Buildings

Under DoD Instruction 4165.56, relocatable buildings may be acquired and used within DoW when they are the most feasible and economical solution for short-term facility needs (typically 5 years or less) arising from peak missions, deployments, or other urgent requirements. They may also be used when the duration of a requirement is uncertain or when a recurring mobile need exists, such as the need to move a field office to different sites on a training range. Relocatable buildings can be classified as either personal property (equipment) or real property. As Personal Property, they are acquired with O&M, RDT&E, or Procurement funds. Costs for setup, disassembly, maintenance, and transport are treated as expenses and charged to appropriate appropriations. As Real Property, they are funded with either O&M or Military Construction funds, depending on the total acquisition cost, which includes the completely assembled building and all site work. Buildings that do not meet the definition of "relocatable" must be acquired as military construction. Site preparation for relocatable buildings that results in real property improvements is classified as construction.

15.16    Efforts Financed by Military Construction Appropriations

15.16.1. Funded Costs. In accordance with DoW policy, major design and construction costs are funded from applicable military construction appropriations. These costs include all materials, services, transportation, and labor (excluding U.S. military labor) relevant to the project. This funding also covers Real Property Installed Equipment (RPIE), unless it was obtained on a non-reimbursable basis from another federal entity. Additionally, identifiable installation overhead, supervision and inspection charges from USACE or NAVFAC, travel and per diem for personnel, planning and design costs for specified major construction projects, and the cost of remediating unknown environmental contamination within the project's footprint are all included. The policy also allows for the inclusion of costs for the operation and maintenance of government equipment used on the project.

15.16.2. Overhead Expenses. All military construction program overhead expenses, including work for others, are initially financed from the performing military construction appropriation and then distributed to the respective projects. This overhead includes costs for personal services and support, contract administration, program and project management (including post-construction evaluation), technical direction, land planning studies or reports, appraisal, and title search after congressional authorization of a land acquisition or exchange, and any other project management and administration costs not otherwise specified.

15.16.3. Reimbursable Project Costs. In accordance with DoW policy, the appropriation that is financing a construction project is required to reimburse any other appropriation that initially covered its costs. This ensures that all project costs are ultimately charged to the correct funding source.

15.17 Related Costs Financed by Other than Military Construction Appropriations

15.17.1. Unfunded Costs. Unfunded costs" that contribute to a military construction project must be capitalized as part of the property's value, even though they are financed by appropriations other than military construction and are not reimbursed. These unfunded costs include expenses financed from military personnel appropriations, the depreciation of government-owned equipment calculated at an hourly rate per Volume 11, and unfunded civilian fringe benefits as prescribed in Volume 11. They also encompass gifts, in-kind considerations, and materials or Real Property Installed Equipment (RPIE) obtained as non-reimbursable from other federal entities. However, DoW Components are prohibited from using their own materials or equipment on their own minor construction projects on a non-reimbursable basis. Additionally, when determining compliance with cost limits for minor construction projects under 10 U.S.C. § 2805, planning and design costs are specifically excluded.

15.17.2. Advance Planning. Activities are performed before a construction project receives its funding and design authorization of a construction project by the military component. These activities are not to be performed under the authority for military construction project planning and design (such as 10 U.S.C. § 2807). Advance planning costs are explicitly excluded when determining compliance with cost limits for minor construction projects. For accounting purposes, advance planning costs are to be expensed in the period they are incurred. Advance planning activities include, but are not limited to: Developing project requirements and master plans; Exploring project alternatives and creating rough drawings; Conducting management studies, conceptual analyses, and site studies; Developing and validating project documentation; and Preparing engineering analyses and environmental impact assessments.

15.17.3. Minor Construction. For minor construction projects (excluding family housing) that cost less than the limit in 10 U.S.C. § 2805, funding must come from appropriate sources such as unspecified minor construction, O&M, RDT&E, or working capital fund appropriations.

15.17.4. Family Housing. All family housing construction projects must be funded from applicable family housing appropriations. Refer to Volume 2.

15.17.5. Equipment and Relocatable Items. Items classified as movable equipment, not integral to a facility, must be financed from O&M, RDT&E, Procurement, or working capital fund appropriations. This includes production, technical, and training equipment, as well as relocatable items like prefabricated screens, partitions, and false floors. The cost of any building alterations required to install this movable equipment, including temporary wall or roof removal and secondary utility connections, must also be funded from these same appropriation sources.

15.17.6. Recycling Programs. Projects for pollution abatement, energy conservation, and occupational safety and health may be funded from sources other than the military construction appropriation. This is permissible when the project cost is derived from recyclable material sales, as per Volume 11 and 10 U.S.C. § 2577, and does not exceed 50 percent of the statutory maximum for minor construction projects.

15.18    Recognition and Reporting Requirements

15.18.1. Acceptance of Real Property. The acceptance and transfer of real property, both within DoW and between other federal agencies, must be formally documented. The DD Form 1354 is designated as the basic source document for this process. To execute this policy, the process for documenting real property acceptance and transfer is detailed in Unified Facilities Criteria (UFC) 1-300-08.

15.18.2. Accounting Recognition. Under DoW policy, capitalization is the process of recognizing the total costs of property, plant, and equipment in the financial records. An asset is capitalized if it has an estimated useful life of two years or more, is not intended for sale in the ordinary course of operations, is acquired or constructed for use by the entity, and its recorded cost meets or exceeds the DoW capitalization threshold (Refer to Volume 4). All significant costs related to the construction or acquisition of an asset, including unfunded costs and all costs incurred after project approval and funding authorization, must be capitalized. The source of funding has no bearing on this requirement. Costs incurred during the advance planning phase are not capitalized; they must be expensed in the period they are incurred. Similarly, if a project is abandoned, all costs incurred up to that point must be expensed.

15.19    Financial Reporting

15.19.1. Accounting Entries. The U.S. Standard General Ledger (USSGL) must be used in all DoW accounting systems to summarize and report costs and obligations for all appropriations and funds. The management of any activity performing a construction project is responsible for ensuring that all significant costs, both funded and unfunded, are recorded for the project and that all costs subject to capitalization are included in the real property asset accounts property records, and reports submitted to the OSW and the Congress. The policy also mandates that cost accounting systems for construction projects must be integrated as a subsidiary ledger of the general accounting system. Furthermore, policy for managerial cost accounting is prescribed in Volume 4.

15.19.2. Financial Reports. DoW policy requires that accounting records be designed to allow for the accurate and timely summarization of financial transactions from a single, unified system of accounts. The data produced must be in the formats prescribed for official budget and financial reports. Additionally, these records must be designed and maintained in a way that facilitates audits of project amounts.

title: Section 16.0: Trust Funds
content:
16.0    TRUST FUNDS

16.1    Applicability and General Information

This section highlights the policies applicable to trust funds. Current accounts include the
(1) National Security Education Trust Fund and the (2) Surcharge Collections, Sales of Commissary Stores, Defense. The complete list of fund accounts and titles is available via the Federal Account Symbols and Titles (The FAST Book) at: https://fiscal.treasury.gov/accounting/fast-book. Section 20 of OMB Circular No. A-11 provides additional information on related terms and concepts. Refer to the Supplemental Documents for DoW execution responsibilities and other requirements.

16.2    Authority

Trust Funds are authorized to incur obligations and expend receipts that OMB has exempted from apportionment. However, the National Security Education Trust Fund and the Surcharge Collections, Sales of Commissary Stores, Defense trust revolving fund, are subject to apportionment by OMB. Each trust fund must be viewed as a unique fund in light of any special provisions in the trust agreement or the enabling legislation. Trust funds have been assigned account symbols between 8000 and 8999. Within this range, trust revolving funds have been assigned symbols between 8400 and 8499.

16.3    Provisions

16.3.1. The Corpus. The term “corpus” commonly refers to the resources available as capital in a fund. Capital resources are provided to commence or increase the size of a fund. The initial corpus is usually provided by a direct appropriation to form a nucleus of resources used to acquire items needed to perform the mission of a fund. Existing resources, transferred as capitalized assets, may also serve the same purpose as an appropriation to start, increase the size, or replace significant losses of a public enterprise or trust fund.

16.3.2. Revenues. DoW trust funds generate revenues from the sale of goods or services to customers. Customer reimbursements replenish the corpus for resources obligated and expended to fulfill the customers’ orders.

16.3.3. Apportionment. For trust funds that OMB apportioned, the ability to incur obligations is limited to the amount officially apportioned. Budgetary resources and authority available for apportionment include new budget authority, unobligated balances available from the prior fiscal year, spending authority from offsetting collections, recoveries of prior year obligations, restorations, and contract authority.

16.3.3.1. The apportionment of spending authority, commonly referred to as “reimbursable authority,” reflects anticipated reimbursements. It does not authorize a trust fund to obligate its apportioned reimbursable program in excess of the funded orders received from within the Federal Government and advances received for orders outside the Federal Government.

16.3.3.2. Assets. Physical assets such as inventories or buildings and equipment are not budgetary resources because they do not provide a direct monetary source for outlays that liquidate budgetary transactions (i.e., obligations). Therefore, such assets do not increase the amount of obligation authority available when calculating unobligated balances.

16.3.3.3. Contract Authority. Contract authority provides legal authority to enter into contracts and incur obligations before budgetary resources are available. Obligations incurred using contract authority may not be liquidated until funded by offsetting collections or other budgetary resources. The apportionment limits the amount of contract authority available for obligation.

16.3.3.4. Antideficiency Act. Incurring or authorizing obligations in excess of apportioned budgetary resources is a potential violation of the Antideficiency Act that must be reported with DoDD 7200.1. This reporting requirement applies even if the fund holds other unapportioned resources or other assets greater than the amount of the deficiency.

16.3.3.4. To avoid these violations, each DoW Component using a fund to finance activities is responsible for maintaining a positive cash balance and restricting obligations to the amount authorized in its AOB or FAD. The OUSW(C) will evaluate Component requests to adjust obligation limits based on the merit of the justification, as long as Congress has not imposed a specific limitation. When a fund's financial execution deviates significantly from its plan, management actions must be taken to either bring execution back into alignment with the plan or revise the plan to reflect more realistic expectations.

title: Section 17.0: Defense Working Capital Funds
content:
17.0    DEFENSE WORKING CAPITAL FUNDS

17.1    General Purpose and Sources of Funds

Under the authority of 10 U.S.C. § 2208, the Defense Working Capital Fund (DWCF) is established to provide goods and services to other DoW activities and authorized non-DoW entities. The customers of the DWCF may include any DoW element, non-DoW federal agencies, and, when authorized by law, private parties, foreign governments, state and local governments, and certain U.S. manufacturers assemblers, or developers authorized by 10 U.S.C. §§ 2208(h), 2563, and 7543. Direct appropriations (such as Procurement or O&M) may be used to start a DWCF activity, fund readiness costs not related to its operating mission, or to increase its size or replace significant losses. Direct appropriations can also be provided for specific purposes like war reserve materiel or overseas contingency operations and expanded inventory requirements, or other purposes as approved by the OUSW(C) Director, Revolving Funds and Integration (RFI). While a direct appropriation increases the Fund Balance with Treasury (FBwT) and budgetary resources, it does not impact the cumulative results of operations. These direct appropriations may be available for obligation in subsequent fiscal years. Alternatively, existing resources from other accounts may be transferred to a working capital fund as capitalized assets for the same purposes. The receipt of the appropriation provides an immediate infusion of cash to the FBwT and the appropriation amount used must be accounted for and reflected on accounting records (AR 1307) and budgetary reports (SF 133).

17.2    Revenues

The DWCF generates revenues predominantly from appropriations used by federal agencies to purchase goods or services. The DWCF uses the revenue collected from these “customers” to pay for the resources required to produce the specific goods or service documented on the customer order. That is, the DWCF uses resources from funded customer orders to replenish its corpus for resources expended to fulfill those customer orders.

17.3    Customer Orders

Customer orders (funded requests for goods or services) provide budgetary resources necessary to finance operations for non-supply management activities, and to liquidate contract authority. Budgetary resources are recognized from customer orders that obligate budgetary resources of another federal government activity, and from cash advances from non-federal customers, to include orders from non-appropriated fund instrumentalities. Customers ordering from the DWCF must adhere to all statutory limitations on their appropriated funds. Placing an order with the DWCF does not expand or change the original appropriation's availability, and customers cannot use the DWCF to indirectly perform actions they are not permitted to do directly. The ordering activity holds the primary responsibility for determining the applicability of the funds they cite on an order. However, if instances arise when it is apparent that the ordering appropriation is not appropriate for the purpose provided, then the DWCF activity should return the order with a request for an applicable appropriation citation. 10 U.S.C. § 2208 restricts cash advances to the DWCF from federal government activities to $1 billion and only when operating resources significantly fall below outlay requirements.

17.4    Obligation authority

Obligation authority is the authority to incur costs, on behalf of the federal government, that will result in a disbursement from the FBwT. The OMB apportions obligation authority to the OUSW(C) via an SF 132, Apportionment and Reapportionment Schedule. This authority, which is limited to the amount approved during the budget review plus any in-year amendments, is requested by the OUSW(C) RFI Directorate. The approved apportionment restricts the authority to incur obligations and serves as the source document for the Annual Operating Budget (AOB). Budgetary resources available for apportionment include budget authority (direct appropriations), unobligated balances brought forward (i.e., unfilled customer orders), spending authority from offsetting collections (i.e., Reimbursements for goods and services provided and/or other income), recoveries of prior year obligations, restorations, and contract authority.

17.4.1. When an activity receives budgetary resources from more than one source (spending authority from offsetting collections, direct appropriation, contract authority), the receiving activity must maintain records that will enable it to control and report separately the transactions relating to each type of source (per OMB Circular No. A-11). Budgetary resources may be received at any level of an organization from the individual activity up to the Departmental level.

17.4.2. Federal customer orders and cash advances generate spending authority from offsetting collections (Reimbursable Authority). These budgetary resources are apportioned from the OMB to DWCF non-supply management activities for operating costs. The acceptance of a customer order requires that the performing entity agree in writing to perform the work for the customer entity. The apportionment of reimbursable authority applies to DWCF (97X4930) non- supply activities and all other DoW Revolving Funds.

17.4.2.1. The apportionment of reimbursable authority is considered “anticipated” and a DWCF non-supply management activity may not obligate more than the total amount of orders received from Federal entities plus advances received for orders from authorized entities external to the Federal government (i.e. state, local, and foreign governments). Specific authorization to obligate above orders received and cash advances may be approved by a signed AOB if other resources are available at the DWCF sub-account level. A DWCF activity should not obligate above all resources available to that specific entity without prior approval of the OUSW(C) Director, RFI, to ensure that budgetary resources are available at the sub-account level.

17.4.2.2. The anticipated reimbursable program authority does not provide obligation authority. Therefore, a non-supply activity should not obligate more than what has been accepted in customer orders and other financing resources available. Recording anticipated reimbursable program authority only documents that reimbursable orders will be accepted. The accepted reimbursable order provides obligation authority. The total amount of anticipated reimbursable authority is recorded on the AOB for reconciling purposes.

17.4.2.3. The AOB does not restrict the amount of reimbursable orders that can be accepted. Reimbursable orders may exceed the anticipated amount without recording a negative anticipated order on the SF 133. Activities should request a new AOB when customer orders in the year of execution are expected to exceed the anticipated amount or obligations are expected to exceed the current authorization.

17.4.2.4. With respect to DWCF budget execution, contract authority is only used in supply management operations and capital investment programs. Contract authority must be apportioned. For supply management operations, if reimbursements from offsetting collections exceed apportioned contract authority, the difference cannot be obligated unless additional contract authority is issued by OMB because such operations are not provided automatically apportioned reimbursable authority. This may be characterized as either an unapportioned balance of a revolving fund or a restrictive withholding. The unapportioned balance preserves a portion of the fund’s capital so it may continue to revolve or represent those resources not scheduled for obligation within a fiscal year. Prior year de-obligations of contract authority are automatically re-apportioned to the DWCF in the current year. Prior year de-obligation of contract authority used for a capital investment program (CIP) may only be used to cover additional costs in programs for that specific fiscal year and may not be used to cover additional current year costs unless approved in writing by the OUSW(C) Director, RFI.

17.5    Antideficiency Act

The incurring of obligations (or authorizing the incurrence of obligations) in excess of apportioned budgetary resources and other financing resources must be reported as a potential violation of the Antideficiency Act, as required in Volume 14.

17.5.1. Commitments for goods or services to be obligated in the following year may be incurred in excess of apportioned budgetary resources only if obligations are not incurred in excess of apportioned budgetary resources. There is no restriction on commitment amounts for DoW revolving fund activities.

17.5.2. The AOB also includes administrative restrictions on the use of obligation authority specific to that activity’s operation.

17.6    Assets

Physical assets such as inventories or buildings and equipment are not considered budgetary resources because they do not provide a direct monetary source for outlays that liquidate budgetary transactions (obligations). Such assets, therefore, do not increase the amount of obligation authority available when calculating unobligated balances. Changes in inventory valuation and unexpected gains in inventory (such as items being found on an installation) do not generate budgetary resources but are currently accounted for in the Net Operating Result (NOR) on the (AR) 1307 report. The NOR for budget purposes must reconcile budgetary resources and claims against those resources (obligations).

17.7    Execution Requirements

17.7.1. SF 132 Apportionment. The SF 132 provides the legal authority to incur obligations against the receipt of customer orders or contract authority in anticipation of receipt of customer orders. Details and explanations on preparing the SF 132 can be found in OMB Circular No. A-11, Preparation, Submission and Execution of the Budget.

17.7.1.1. The DWCF is apportioned new budget authority in the form of direct appropriations, unobligated balances brought forward, spending authority from offsetting collections and contract authority. The FBwT is not apportioned because the financing resources have already been encumbered by obligations and the unencumbered balance is factored into unobligated balances brought forward.

17.7.1.2. All other revolving funds outside of the DWCF are apportioned spending authority from offsetting collections and unobligated balances brought forward.

17.7.2. Contract Authority. Contract authority is the legal authority to enter into contracts and incur obligations before budgetary resources are available. The initial apportionment of contract authority for a fiscal year is typically the operating budget for supply management activities, and for both supply and non-supply management activities is the CIP reflected in the budget year column of last year’s President’s budget.

17.7.2.1. Supply management activities receive contract authority for a variability target, which represents an amount of contract authority to be held in reserve by the OUSW(C) to ensure continuity of operations for fluctuations in materiel costs and/or increased customer orders. The OUSW(C) provides requested adjustments from the initial apportionment to OMB, reflecting revised estimates displayed in the current year column of the President’s budget submission most recently provided to Congress. The OUSW(C) may also request other adjustments that reflect significant changes experienced in budget execution.

17.7.2.2. Contract authority is available for obligation within the fiscal year for which it is provided. Contract authority is unfunded and, therefore, obligations incurred through use of contract authority may not be liquidated (i.e., paid) until funded by offsetting collections or other resources credited to the DWCF. Contract authority does not authorize outlays; the activity reports it on the SF 133 to ensure obligations do not exceed apportioned amounts from OMB. Budgetary resources should be sufficient at the DWCF activity level to ensure disbursements are funded.

17.7.3. Annual Operating Budget. The OUSW(C) RFI Directorate issues initial AOBs for each Component’s DWCF activities prior to the beginning of the fiscal year. The AOB identifies an operating budget, operating results, unit cost targets, and capital investment limitations (subject to 31 U.S.C. § 1517) for each DWCF activity.

17.7.3.1. Each Component/Agency is responsible for taking actions to remain solvent and allow operations (disbursements) to continue. It is a potential violation of the Antideficiency Act (31 U.S.C. § 1517) if the FBwT is below zero at the sub-account level.

17.7.3.2. Non-supply management activities will maintain a positive budgetary resource balance (i.e., obligations will not exceed budgetary resources). Obligations exceeding total budgetary resources available to non-supply management activities, and obligations exceeding issued contract authority on the AOB, are potential violations of the Antideficiency Act
(31 U.S.C. § 1517).

17.7.3.3. Cash balances may be used when negative operating results are authorized on the AOB or by action of the OUSW(C) RFI Directorate. However, the AOB of a DWCF activity does not authorize it to use cash balances associated with another DWCF activity financed within the same DWCF sub-account. It is the responsibility of the DoW Component to ensure that adequate financing or budgetary resources have been allocated to a specific DWCF activity, and to obtain timely authorization for negative operating results for non-supply management activities.

17.7.3.4. In addition to statutory restrictions, the Department may further restrict budget authority through apportionment or administrative action. These administrative limitations cannot alter statutory restrictions but can only further constrain the purpose, amount, or time for which budgetary resources may be used. DoW Components must adhere to these administrative divisions of resources and/or a subdivision of budgetary resources provided to a DWCF activity. When an administrative limitation is imposed, obligations must remain below that limit even if they are lower than the total available budgetary resources. Any such limitation must be clearly stated in a signed, written document.

17.7.3.5. If a DWCF activity has insufficient budgetary resources, the manager cannot assume that funds exist elsewhere within the sub-account. Instead, the manager must request an increase in authority from the OUSW(C) Director, RFI, and defer any additional obligations until sufficient resources are available.

17.7.3.6. Segregation of Budgetary Resources. When an activity receives budgetary resources from more than one source, the receiving activity must maintain records which will enable it to control separately the transactions relating to each source.

17.7.3.7. Claims Against Budgetary Resources. To accurately determine budgetary resources available for obligation, a DWCF entity must use its budgetary accounts, as proprietary accounts alone are insufficient. Non-budgetary assets like inventory and even a positive FBwT do not guarantee availability, as these resources may be encumbered by existing claims such as accounts payable or undelivered orders and unpaid accrued expenditures. Similarly, some budgetary accounts, like anticipated customer orders, do not represent a budgetary resource available for obligation. The true balance of budgetary resources available for obligation, which accounts for administrative restrictions and other withheld amounts, can be determined from the data reported on the SF 133.

17.7.4. Budgetary Resources. Key principles govern the management of budgetary resources within the DWCF. Earned reimbursements are the amount of customer orders that have been filled. In the case of orders from the public, including state and local governments, the amount is limited to the amount of the cash advance received. Earned reimbursements should not exceed the amount of individual customer orders and letters of intent, commanders’ orders, congressionally mandated actions, and other emergency situations. It is also a policy that obligations cannot be incurred unless available resources—such as apportioned contract authority, direct appropriations, or accepted customer orders—exceed the proposed obligation. Incurring obligations beyond available resources may constitute a violation of the Antideficiency Act. Finally, when authorized, non-expenditure transfers of funds will either increase or decrease the available budgetary resources, depending on the direction of the transfer. Detailed guidance on the Report of Budgetary Execution and Budgetary Resources (SF 133) can be found in Appendix F of OMB Circular No. A-11.

17.7.5. DFAS Reporting. The DFAS Accounting Report (AR) 1307 is the official internal document for financial accounting and the source for annual financial statements. The amounts on its Statement of Financial Position and Statement of Cash Flows must reconcile to the SF 133. For supply activities, Part VII of the report provides budgetary, accounting, and inventory data used to develop internal benchmarks and metrics for operational effectiveness and efficiency.

17.7.6. Execution Review. The financial performance of each DWCF activity is subject to formal review by OUSW(C) leadership. This review compares the activity's operational results to its plans for disbursements, collections, revenue, expenses, net operating results, and unit costs. The purpose of this policy is to ensure that financial operations are proceeding according to plan. If significant deviations are identified, management action may be required to either bring execution back into line with the plan or revise the plan to be more consistent with current and realistic financial expectations.

17.7.7. Adjusting Component Resources. Components may request adjustments to their targets or capital budget limitations from the OUSW(C) RFI Directorate based on budget execution. These requests will be evaluated on their merits, and unless precluded by congressional limitations, will be approved or disapproved.

title: Section 1.0: General
content:
1.0    GENERAL

1.1    Purpose

Volume 4 provides accounting policies, general guidance on supporting material, and specific guidance by appropriations, programs, and activities for the Office of the Secretary of War (OSW). Accounting policy memoranda issued throughout the year, special instructions, and nonrecurring requirements unique to that year’s budget cycle will provide any necessary changes or revisions to this standing document. The provisions of Volume 4 apply to the OSW, the Military Departments, the Defense Agencies, the Combatant Commands, and any other Defense Field Offices or Activities (hereafter referred to as “Components”) that manage programs. Volume 4 Supplemental contains corresponding instructions and procedures.

1.2    Authoritative Guidance

Refer to the Volume 4 authoritative guidance document on the FMR webpage.

1.3    Definitions

Refer to the Glossary on the FMR webpage.

1.4    Procedures

Refer to the Supplemental document listed throughout this volume.

title: Section 2.0: Financial Control of Assets
content:
2.0    FINANCIAL CONTROL OF ASSETS

2.1    Asset Characteristics

An asset has two essential characteristics: it embodies probable future economic benefits or services, and the Department of War (DoW) owns or controls access to these benefits, allowing it to obtain, deny, or regulate access for other entities. The Component must record entries for accounting events for assets simultaneously in both the proprietary and budgetary accounts.

2.2    Noncash Assets

Noncash assets are valued promptly, once DoW acquires, takes possession, or exercises accounting control. For purposes of this paragraph, promptly means by the entity’s fiscal year- end.

2.3    Entity Versus Non-Entity Assets

DoW Components report entity assets separately from non-entity assets in the financial statements. DoW Components use entity assets in their operations. The DoW Component determines how entity assets are used and must use them to meet statutory obligations. DoW Components may hold non-entity assets but not use them in their operations. A DoW Component may act as a fiduciary by maintaining non-entity assets for the Treasury, other government agencies, or non-federal entities. DoW Components must report both entity and custodial or managed non-entity assets in the financial statements. However, DoD Components must not recognize fiduciary non-entity assets on the Balance Sheet, according to SFFAS 31; refer to the Volume 4 Supplemental for more information.

2.4    Intragovernmental Versus Public Transactions

Transactions with other Non-DoW Federal Agencies and other DoW Components create intragovernmental assets. Similarly, transactions with non-federal entities create public assets, where "public" refers to domestic and foreign persons and organizations outside the U.S. Government.

title: Section 3.0: Accounting for Cash and Fund Balances with Treasury
content:
3.0    ACCOUNTING FOR CASH AND FUND BALANCES WITH TREASURY

3.1    Cash

Recognize cash, including imprest funds, as an asset in accordance with Statement of Federal Financial Accounting Standards (SFFAS) 1. The Component must translate foreign currencies into U.S. dollars at the exchange rate on the financial statement date. Use the appropriate accounts to record transactions for Fund Balance with Treasury (FBwT) or foreign currency transactions. Refer to the USSGL Treasury Financial Manual (TFM) Supplement and the DoW USSGL Transaction Library.

3.2    Funds Held Outside of Treasury (FHOT)

Cash and Investments Held Outside of the Treasury (CIHO), also known as FHOT. Report entity and non-entity cash in accordance with SFFAS 1. Deposit funds from non-federal sources in anticipation of an order (that is, an advance) should be classified in accordance with SFFAS 31.

3.3    Restricted Cash

Laws, regulations, or agreements impose cash deposit restrictions. All non-entity cash has restrictions. Entity cash may also be subject to restrictions for specific purposes, and financial reports must disclose the reasons and nature of these restrictions.

3.4    Foreign Currency

Account for foreign currencies in subsidiary accounts separate from U.S. currency. Report foreign currencies at the U.S. dollar equivalent using the exchange rates prescribed by the Secretary of the Treasury. Disclose in the financial statement notes that foreign currency is not freely exchangeable. Accounting entities may prepare financial statements for their use. These entity-level statements will be translated into U.S. dollars when used to prepare departmental financial statements. See Volume 6 for additional foreign currency information.

3.5    Reconciliation

3.5.1. All federal agencies must reconcile their FBwT account with the detailed transactions posted to the general ledger on a regular and recurring basis. Additionally, all federal agencies must compare the FBwT balance with the available funds recorded on the Central Accounting Reporting System (CARS) Account Statement. This ensures all disbursements, collections, and intragovernmental transactions in CARS have supporting Agency Location Code (ALC)/ Disbursing Station Symbol Numbers (DSSN) details. This policy ensures the integrity and accuracy of the FBwT balance, which represents the available funds authorizing an entity to make expenditures and pay liabilities. Agencies must promptly disclose, identify, resolve, and correct all errors, losses, and gains. They can consider the reconciliation complete only after they identify all differences, assign accountability, explain any differences, and record the necessary adjustments.

3.5.2. Undistributed amounts are amounts reported to the Treasury that have not been posted to the appropriate obligation in a Component’s general ledger or vice versa. Undistributed amounts can result from timing, invalid LOA, or invalid TAS information, among other reasons. Unsupported undistributed amounts are not yet researched/reconciled to supporting documentation. A "forced balance entry" made into a suspense account to match the Treasury's control total cannot be considered by an agency as an adequate reconciliation of the FBwT USSGL accounts 101000 and 109000. Policy strictly requires that personnel research all differences at the detail-voucher level to identify the underlying causes. For further guidance, refer to the Financial Audit Manual, Volume 2; Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Circular No. A-136; and the Volume 4 Supplemental.

3.6    Universe of Transactions (UoT)

The FBwT UoT comprises all valid funding, disbursements, collections, and transfers within a specific period. These transactions directly affect appropriation account balances as reported to Treasury, recorded in the entity's general ledger, and presented in its financial reports.

3.7    Deposit Fund Activity

Deposit fund activities are external to the budget process and are reviewed by Auditors during the DoW's FBwT reconciliation. Collections for these funds originate from the public and are unrelated to prior U.S. Government obligations. The DoW Treasury Index (TI) (defined in the Federal Account Symbols and Titles (FAST Book) designates the entity responsible for reporting the deposit fund liability, irrespective of the funds' source. To support accurate DoW financial statements and prevent commingling of rights or obligations, the Treasury component holding the funds must report the liability.

3.8    TI-97 Deposit Fund Liabilities Account

DoW Components must review deposit fund accounts quarterly to ensure the funds align with legal authority and maintain a positive balance, taking corrective action when necessary. If a disbursing officer over-disburses a fund, they must promptly report an Antideficiency Act (ADA) violation to OMB. When establishing deposit accounts with the Treasury, the responsible DoW entity must track, reconcile, and report all activity on the standalone financial statements of TI-97 Components. This requirement applies if the activity meets Treasury criteria, is material to a Component that prepares standalone financial statements (per OMB Bulletin 24-01 or statute), and has support from a unique statutory authorization. The DoW Office of Inspector General (OIG) will track, reconcile, report, and audit any deposit fund activity not meeting these criteria as part of the DoW consolidated audit. Refer to the Volume 4 Supplemental for more information.

3.9    Accounting for Cash and Investments Held Outside of Treasury

DoW policy, guided by TFM Chapter 3400 (FHOT), dictates the accounting and reporting for all CIHO. Components may temporarily hold cash using any DoW Treasury Appropriation Fund Symbol, subject to the restrictions noted in TFM Chapter 3400 and Volume 5. They must record all CIHO transactions, including Burden Sharing funds, using USSGL transaction code B150 and the FHOT Business Event Type Code, and report them on financial statements per Volume 6. Components are responsible for the oversight and monitoring of all FHOT. In this reconciliation, the Component must align the cash it reports on the Statement of Accountability with the CARS Account Statement and its own internal accounting records and financial statements. Component-level Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) must detail the roles of service providers.

3.10    Cash Audits and Reviews

Managers supervising personnel who handle cash must maintain appropriate accounting and internal controls to ensure that all disbursements and collections are lawful, proper, and accurate. Policy requires auditors to conduct both announced and unannounced audits to verify personnel properly account for funds, do not exceed requirements, and protect them from loss or misuse. It is management's responsibility to assess vulnerability and determine audit frequency in accordance with DoD Instruction (DoDI) 5010.40. Furthermore, policy mandates that managers must investigate and report any unauthorized use, irregularity, or improper accounting for a cash fund.

3.11    Defense Revolving Fund

The Defense Working Capital Funds (DWCF) FBwT (account 097X4930) is an intragovernmental revolving fund with five Treasury sub-accounts. Each sub-account entity and the activities below it must report their FBwT. The Defense-wide DWCF centralizes funds for Defense Agencies: entities with excess collections contribute to the pool, while those with excess disbursements draw from it. Additional cash management policy is in Volume 2. Program Managers may realign DWCF balances to activity or installation levels but are strictly prohibited from transferring more than the available balance at the transferring DWCF Sub-Allocation Holder Identifier (SAHI). Cash at the Treasury account level must always be sufficient to pay liabilities.

Revolving fund cash management responsibilities are detailed in Volume 2. Personnel must immediately investigate and report any transaction causing a negative balance as a possible ADA violation as prescribed in Volume 14 and 31 United States Code (U.S.C.) § 1341.

3.12    FBwT Transactions

3.12.1. The current FBwT equals the fiscal year's (FY) opening balance plus cumulative collections, appropriations, and transfers-in, minus cumulative withdrawals, transfers-out, and disbursements. Record a collection or disbursement when documentary evidence, such as a Treasury Statement of Differences (SOD) or a voucher, provides support. For Revolving Fund activities, 10 U.S.C. § 2208(m) mandates that Components segregate cash collections and disbursements between operating programs and capital programs. (Refer to Volume 2 for more details).

3.12.2. Record customer advances or prepayments as a liability, per SFFAS 1 and OMB Circular No. A-11. Offsetting collections credited to expenditure accounts automatically offset outlays and budget authority. For more information, refer to Volume 3.

3.13    Reconciliation Roles and Responsibilities.

3.13.1. Under Secretary of War (Comptroller) (OUSW(C)) ODCFO, Financial Systems Modernization and Innovation (FSM&I) Directorate is responsible for the design, development, operation, and maintenance of the Advana FBwT application (see Volume 1).

3.13.2. Defense Finance and Accounting Service (DFAS) is responsible for ensuring the accuracy and integrity of FBwT reporting and reconciliation. This includes a policy mandate for DFAS to ensure that information submitted to Treasury on the Standard Form (SF) 224 and SF 1219 for ALC/DSSNs where DFAS is the Designated Agent matches Treasury records. A key policy is that all Cash Management Report (CMR) reconciling items and variances must be cleared within 60 business days unless they are deemed immaterial in total, with materiality being defined by SFFAS 1 as an omission or misstatement likely to influence a reasonable person's judgment.

3.13.3. Components are responsible for the accurate management of their FBwT. This includes ensuring the accuracy of transaction information reported to Treasury on forms such as the SF 224 and SF 1219 for ALCs that serve as the Designated Agent. A fundamental policy is to ensure a valid LOA is present on all original obligating documents throughout the procure-to-pay process. Furthermore, the relationship between Components, FSM&I, and DFAS must be formalized through documented support agreements, such as Memorandums of Agreement (MOAs) or Service Level Agreements, in accordance with DoDI 4000.19.

3.13.4. Reconciliation Requirements

3.13.4.1. Treasury requires monthly reconciliation of FBwT accounts to Treasury- reported as outlined in TFM Volume I, Part 2, Chapter 5100 and its Supplement. At the same time, audit issue guidance is provided in the Government Accountability Office (GAO)/ Council of the Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency Financial Audit Manual.

3.13.4.2. DoW Components, in conjunction with DFAS, must perform detailed monthly reconciliations of their FBwT accounts (USSGL 101000 and 109000). This reconciliation must be comprehensive, performed at the voucher level, and encompass all fiscal years, all fund types, all TI-097 SAHIs, and all activity, including suspense accounts. Policy dictates that Components acting as ALC Designated Agents are responsible for correcting any differences between their submissions to Treasury and DFAS within 15 business days of being notified. Furthermore, a key policy is that both DFAS and DoW Components must demonstrate they have effective controls in place to ensure that amounts reported to Treasury reconcile with both disbursing and accounting systems.

3.13.5. Treasury Budget Clearing (Suspense) Accounts

Budget Clearing Accounts are temporary TAS established by the Bureau of the Fiscal Service (BFS) to temporarily hold unidentified transactions with a reasonable presumption that the funds belong to a federal agency. A critical policy is that effective FBwT reconciliations depend on the timely clearing of these Treasury suspense accounts. Policy also dictates that DoW Components are ultimately responsible for maintaining transaction records in general ledgers.

3.13.6. Reconciliation of FBwT for Comparison of Transactions

3.13.6.1. The DoW must compare transactions at a detailed level sufficient to specifically identify differences when reconciling FBwT to support accurate FBwT general ledger accounts and Treasury totals.

3.13.6.2. Components must comply with all operational requirements and deadlines for transaction reconciliation. A monthly, voucher-level reconciliation is mandatory, with a strict deadline of 30 calendar days following the end of the month being reconciled. Policy requires that Components have established processes to assign, track, age, research, and resolve all differences monthly at the voucher-level detail. A key policy is that all undistributed amounts, suspense items, and SOD balances must be cleared within 60 business days. For any items exceeding this timeframe, it is policy that the reason for the delay must be investigated and documented. Finally, policy mandates that both Service Provider supervisory and Component reviews and approvals must be completed within 10 business days after all identified differences are resolved.

3.13.6.3. Components are required to address all critical areas and key control points in the end-to-end FBwT reconciliation process. A key performance indicator for this policy is that Components must achieve a 99 percent complete match rate each month for each of these key control points.

3.13.7. FBwT – CARS Account Statement Reconciliation

Component must reconcile transactions to the beginning balance, net activity, and ending balance on the CARS Account Statement. However, this specific policy requirement does not currently apply to Defense Agencies and Field Activities that are part of shared TAS. For those TI-97 components, the policy is that they must reconcile their FBwT balances individually to the internal TI-97 CMR, with support from DFAS as their service provider. It is DFAS's responsibility under this policy to reconcile the totals of all TI-97 components to the Treasury.

3.13.8. Undistributed Collections and Undistributed Disbursements

3.13.8.1. Undistributed collections and undistributed disbursements must be recorded and reported at the lowest organizational level.

3.13.8.2. Undistributed transactions at the sub-account level must be researched and cleared within 60 business days, with no unidentified balances remaining at year-end. Policy also dictates that Component-level undistributed adjustments should be limited at year-end by completing all necessary research and reconciliation.

3.13.8.3. It is the policy of the DoW that DFAS must identify all collections and disbursements at the lowest identifiable level.

3.13.8.4. Undistributed collections and disbursements must accurately reflect the proper FBwT as contained in finance network reports.

3.13.9. Requirement for Written Procedures

Components must maintain current written SOPs, narratives, and process maps in accordance with the Managers’ Internal Control Program (as outlined in DoDI 5010.40). This policy ensures the proper documentation of reconciliation processes. A key policy also requires that these SOPs include evidence of dated supervisory review and approval, certifying that it is correct and accurate. Furthermore, policy mandates that written procedures differentiate the journal entry for unsupported undistributed amounts from those that can be supported, as this practice is essential for efficient cash reconciliation management and audit support.

3.13.10. Expenditure and Receipt Accounts Annual Review
