All expenditure and receipt accounts reported by the Treasury must be reviewed and validated annually to ensure the TAS are valid.

3.14    TI-97 Deposit Fund Liabilities

TI-97 Deposit Fund Liabilities Account Structures. Refer to the Volume 4 Supplemental.

3.15    FBwT Balances Brought Forward

Supporting FBwT Balances Brought Forward (formerly Annex 1). Refer to the Volume 4 Supplemental.

title: Section 4.0: Investments and Other Assets
content:
4.0    INVESTMENTS AND OTHER ASSETS

4.1    Accounting Policy for Investments and Other Assets

DoW investments and other assets must be recognized and recorded in accordance with SFFAS 1. Accounting events must be reported according to the requirements in TFM Chapter 4300 and OMB Circular A-136 using the accounting entries specified in the DoW Standard Chart of Accounts (SCOA) and Standard Financial Information Structure (SFIS) Transaction Library, unless otherwise stated.

4.2    Investments and Other Assets

DoW is authorized to invest in Federal securities, which include non-marketable par value Treasury securities, market-based Treasury securities, marketable Treasury securities, and securities issued by other Federal entities. Use “Other Assets” to record the value of assets not otherwise classifiable to a specific asset account. Establish applicable subsidiary accounts as necessary to meet management and reporting needs. Source documents for entries to this account include receiving reports and journal vouchers.

4.3    Nonmarketable Par Value Treasury Securities

Nonmarketable par value Treasury securities are special-issue debt securities that the U.S. Treasury issues to federal entities at face value (par value).

4.4 Market-Based Treasury Securities Expected to Be Held to Maturity

Market-based Treasury securities expected to be held to maturity are debt securities that the U.S. Treasury issues to federal entities without statutorily determined interest rates. Their prices and interest rates mimic the terms of marketable Treasury securities.

4.5    Market-Based Treasury Securities

Marketable Treasury securities, including Treasury bills, notes, and bonds, are initially offered to the public by the Treasury and can then be bought and sold on securities exchanges. Their bid and ask prices are publicly quoted by the marketplace.

4.6    Recognition of Investments in Federal Securities

The policy for accounting for securities dictates that when an acquisition is made in exchange for nonmonetary assets, the acquired securities must be recognized at the fair market value (FMV) of either the securities acquired or the assets given up, whichever is more definitively determinable. If the acquisition cost differs from the security's face value, it must be recorded at the acquisition cost, with any premium or discount treated as a contra account to the debt security. Specifically, Treasury securities are to be carried at their acquisition cost, adjusted for any amortization as explained in SFFAS 1. For all other investments, the policy mandates they be carried on the Balance Sheet at acquisition cost adjusted for the amortization of any premium or discount, with two exceptions: market value must be used if there is an intent to sell the securities before maturity or if there has been a reduction in value that is considered more than temporary.

4.7    Disposition of Treasury Securities

DoW Components must maintain a subsidiary account for each trust fund that invests in U.S. Treasury securities. The disposition of a U.S. Treasury security may result in a gain or loss. A comparison of principal proceeds, the book value of a U.S. Treasury security, and any remaining unamortized premium or discount will determine whether there is a gain or loss. Unless otherwise provided for by law, securities held by DoW trust funds are U.S. Treasury securities. The Treasury issues no certificates.

4.8    Interest and Amortization

The disposition of a U.S. Treasury security may result in a premium or discount. If a premium or discount exists, the carrying amount, or original purchase cost, of the investments must be adjusted in each reporting period to reflect the amortization of the premium or discount. Premiums and discounts must be amortized over the life of the Treasury security using the interest method. The amount of amortization of discount or premium is the difference between the effective interest recognized for the period and the nominal interest for the period as stipulated in the Treasury security. Income derived from U.S. Treasury securities other than Treasury bills must be the interest stated on the face of the securities adjusted for the amortized premium or discount. For Treasury bills, the difference between the purchase price and the price received at sale or maturity is income. Source documents for entries to this account must include amortization schedules and journal vouchers.

4.9    Use of Other Investments

4.9.1. When authorized, an investment under the provisions of 10 U.S.C § 2875 may take the form of an acquisition of a limited partnership interest, a purchase of stock or other equity instruments, a purchase of bonds or other debt instruments, or any combination of such forms of investment.

4.9.2. The DoW is authorized to invest in joint ventures with private developers for military housing construction and improvement under the Military Housing Privatization Initiative (MHPI), in accordance with 10 U.S.C § 2875. These long-term partnerships, known as Public- Private Partnerships (P3s) or Alternative Financing Arrangements, are defined as risk-sharing arrangements or transactions lasting more than five years between public and private sector entities.

4.10    Reporting Other Investments

P3s for the MHPI can be financed through appropriated funds, non-appropriated funds, third-party financing, or private capital. All MHPI financing events and relevant disclosures must be reported in the DoW financial statements to ensure transparency regarding project financial conditions.

4.11    Recognition and Measurement of Other Investments

4.11.1. A comprehensive evaluation of each operating agreement and a full assessment of the relationship with each partner organization must be conducted for MHPI agreements and P3s. The evaluation will support the determination of the appropriate accounting treatment for each MHPI project. A majority ownership interest exists when an organization has over 50 percent of the voting rights or net residual assets. If an entity is expected to assume more than 50 percent of another entity’s expected losses or gains, it should either consolidate or disclose that entity. Refer to SFFAS 47. An entity that effectively controls another through investment decisions and economic benefits, yet is exposed to less than 50% of its losses or gains, is generally subject to disclosure rather than consolidation. Military Departments are responsible for monitoring, reporting on, and disclosing the financial condition and significant risks of their equity investments in MHPI entities. Per SFFAS 47, an organization is considered a consolidation entity based on a holistic assessment of four main characteristics: it is (1) financed by non-exchange revenue, (2) governed by Congress or the President, (3) imposes risks and rewards on the federal government, and (4) provides goods and services on a non-market basis. Not all characteristics must be met for this classification. Entities that are deemed consolidation entities are considered federal reporting entities and must apply GAAP as defined by SFFAS 34.

4.11.2. After applying SFFAS 47 guidelines, disclosures for MHPI projects must be evaluated under SFFAS 49. Their purpose is to help users understand the nature and risks of P3s, direct loans, and loan guarantees. Disclosures for reporting entities must detail the nature of their relationship, the relevant activities during the period, and their future exposure to risks and rewards. Disclosure entities, which often provide goods and services on a market basis (i.e., at prices set in a competitive marketplace between willing buyers and sellers), differ from consolidation entities. Although the GAAP hierarchy for federal reporting may not fully apply, information from disclosure entities remains crucial for accountability and federal financial reporting objectives. Refer to SFFAS 49 for guidance. The Military Departments and DFAS must use established accounting transaction codes in the DoW Transaction Library to record the primary accounting entries to recognize P3 contributions and any collections received upon dissolution of an arrangement that are not available for use without further Congressional action. Refer to the tables within the procedural guidance. The Military Department is required to obtain all agreements and supporting documentation for its equity investments in MHPI Limited Partnerships (LPs) and Limited Liability Companies (LLCs). This documentation is essential for supporting operating, lockbox, and revenue agreements, as well as transactions related to investment dissolution, the sale of government shares, or any other financial activities involving DoW equity investments. Additionally, the Military Departments must provide the DFAS with details of any other financially impactful transactions. Refer to Volume 4 Supplemental, Tables 4- 3 to 4-8, for more details. Footnote disclosures are also required, including equity-method income/loss, descriptions of termination or default events, and supporting documentation for each disclosure.

4.12    Ground Lease

A ground lease may be provided with property and cash to an LP/LLC to facilitate property development. This ground lease is not treated as a separate transaction from the initial property transfer because they are highly interdependent; the project's success relies on the lease, and the commitment to build is a material inducement for the lease, often for a nominal rent. In accordance with the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) 606, because the property transfer and ground lease are not distinct services, no separate accounting entries are required for the ground lease. Instead, the FMV of the ground lease is considered an integral part of the property's total FMV.

4.13    Recognition and Measurement of Direct Loans

See Volume 12 for additional guidance on the recognition and measurement of direct loans, the liability associated with loan guarantees, and the cost of direct loans and loan guarantees.

title: Section 5.0: Receivables
content:
5.0    RECEIVABLES

5.1    Recognition

Receivables must be recognized in accordance with SFFAS 1. The Component must establish a receivable when it does not receive payment in advance or at the time it recognizes revenue. Receivables must be recorded during the month they are earned from the sale of goods and services or when an event determines a debt is owed to DoW. Accounting records for receivables must include all transactions that occurred during the reporting period. Any events not previously recorded due to error or oversight must be recorded immediately. Accounts receivable and unfilled orders without an advance must be recognized as valid budgetary resources when they are from other federal entities. Conversely, policy dictates that absent specific statutory authority, accounts receivable and unfilled orders without an advance from public/non-federal entities must not be recognized as valid budgetary resources. Components must maintain all supporting documentation for receivables within the applicable accounting system, and these records must be retained in accordance with the guidance in their DoW Component records retention requirements.

5.2    Advance Payments

In general, an advance payment is required for public orders, including state and local governments, except for fuel, as the sale of petroleum products to the public is covered by fuel purchasing agreements. An advance equivalent to the actual or estimated cost of goods and services must accompany the order. If amounts are sufficient, Military Departments may use their own appropriated fund budgetary resources to perform a reimbursable order for a NAFI without an advance. However, they must not recognize budgetary resources for the order until the account receivable is paid. An advance payment from foreign governments for FMS is held and recorded in the FMS Trust Fund or investment accounts that can be drawn on to meet the foreign government’s FMS obligations. Under the statutory authority of 22 U.S.C. § 2767, the DoW may record a budgetary resource for non-federal orders without an advance. However, a critical element of this policy is that Components must receive prior approval from the OUSW(C) before accepting the order and recording the budgetary resource. Additional information regarding budgetary resources may be found in Volumes 3, 4, and 11 for DWCF’s policy on receipt of advances on orders from public/non-federal entities.

5.3    Collection of Receivables

Proactively pursue the collection of all receivables from DoW Components, federal agencies, and the public. A receivable is normally due 30 days from the date of the invoice or demand letter, unless a different due date is established by statute, contract, or a notice of indebtedness. The responsible office must initiate collection actions as soon as payment becomes due. For more information on due process, refer to Volume 16. Funds must be collected in the appropriation that earned the funds, or in the case of a refund, into the appropriation from which the excess payment was made, unless otherwise specified by law. In accordance with 42 U.S.C. § 2651, amounts recovered from a liable third party for a service member's injury or disease must be credited to current operating funds. Funds recovered for medical care are credited to the facility that provided the care or activity that provided the care and treatment, while funds recovered for loss of duty are credited to the service member's assigned command, activity, or unit. In accordance with 10 U.S.C. § 1095, collections from third parties for medical services must be recorded in the fiscal year they are received, regardless of when the service was provided. Any agency that receives collections after an appropriation has been canceled must deposit them into Treasury Account 3200.

5.4    Allowance Account and Aging

The Component must estimate and record an allowance for uncollectible accounts receivable for both public and intragovernmental customers. However, policy explicitly states that no such allowance will be recorded for non-loan interest, penalties, or administrative (IPA) charges. The aging of receivables (delinquency) begins one day after the due date for both public and intragovernmental receivables.

5.5    Interest Penalties, and Administrative Receivables

The DoW assesses IPA charges on delinquent debts. The full amount of a delinquent debt is defined as the sum of the principal, accrued program interest, and any other penalties or administrative charges. Per 31 U.S.C. § 3717, interest must be recognized on outstanding accounts receivable against persons and entities. Policy dictates that interest accrues from the first day of delinquency and continues to accrue until it is officially waived or the debt is closed. However, debts owed by other federal agencies are exempt from these IPA charges. All interest receivables are to be classified as non-entity receivables. It is also a key accounting policy that companies must record an interest receivable when they earn the income, not when they receive it. The detailed IPA policy can be found in Volume 16.

5.6    Payment Application

The Federal Claims Collection Standards, 31 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 901.9(f), mandate the application of partial or installment payments.

5.7    General Ledger Accounting

Receivables must be developed, maintained, and reported using USSGL accounts, with the first six digits conforming to the USSGL chart. DoW mandates the use of its SCOA, which, along with accounting transactions for collections and receivables, is detailed in the DoW USSGL Transaction Library available on the SFIS webpage.

5.8    Internal Controls

The DoW must adhere to the internal control standards prescribed in DoDI 5010.40 when establishing and collecting receivables. This includes maintaining major categories of receivables to ensure clear and full disclosure (debtor, amount, age, and type of debt). Policy requires that subsidiary records be reconciled to the control accounts monthly. Furthermore, it is policy that proper internal controls must ensure the accurate and timely recording of transactions, appropriate documentation and retention, authorization only by personnel acting within their scope of authority, and effective management. A critical policy mandates the separation of duties for authorizing, processing, recording, reviewing transactions, and handling related assets, ensuring no single individual controls all key aspects of a transaction.

5.9 Erroneous, Invalid, and Unsubstantiated Accounts Receivable

Adjust the accounting records and return any funds collected to the debtor if it is determined that no debt was owed and that it should not have been classified as accounts receivable. If a billing Component cannot produce the necessary evidence to establish a receivable and voluntary repayment is not obtained, it is policy to reverse the original entries. The Component must remove all erroneous, invalid, and unsubstantiated accounts receivable from the general ledger. Any internal control failures or process weaknesses identified during research must be addressed and corrected.

5.10    Canceled Appropriations

Accounts Receivable Offices (AROs) must retain all outstanding receivables in residual records even after an appropriation cancels. Even with canceled appropriations, the DoW must continue to pursue the collection of outstanding receivables. When a receivable is collected after its associated appropriation has canceled, the procedure dictates that the collection is recorded in Treasury miscellaneous receipt account 3200, "Collections of Receivables From Canceled Accounts."

5.11    Nonappropriated Fund Instrumentalities Receivables

Classify receivables from NAFIs as public transactions. A key policy is that, except for individual debt, delinquent NAFI debt will not be referred to the Debt Management Office (DMO) or to the Treasury for collection assistance. Refer to Volumes 13 and 16 for more information on NAFI debt.

5.12    Foreign Military Sales Receivables

Classify receivables from the FMS Trust Fund (appropriation 97 11X8242) as federal transactions, while other Security Assistance receivables, such as those from the Foreign Military Financing Program (appropriation 11(FY) 1082), are to be recorded and reported as intragovernmental. A key policy is that delinquent FMS accounts receivable will not be referred to the DMO or Treasury for collection assistance. Refer to Volumes 15 and 16 for more information on FMS debt.

5.13    Non-FMS Foreign Government Receivables

The ARO will initiate initial billings for non-FMS foreign government accounts receivable. See Volume 16 for additional information.

5.14    Retention of Documentation

Supporting documentation for all actions taken on each accounts receivable must be maintained.

5.15    Undistributed Collection Balances

All undistributed collection balances held in Treasury suspense accounts F3875 and F3885 must be analyzed and reconciled monthly. Policy dictates that all differences must be cleared within 60 days, except for specific suspense accounts identified by Treasury as exempt from this requirement. For any items that remain unresolved beyond 60 days, it is policy to conduct an investigation and document the reason for the delay.

5.16    Public Receivables

Receivables due from the public are DoW claims (or claims from another federal entity) against non-federal entities, including individuals and organizations outside the U.S. Government. These receivables arise from sales of goods/services when no advance payment is received, or from refunds due to the DoW. Credit management and debt collection policies and procedures are delineated across several volumes of the DoW FMR. Specifically, Volume 16 addresses debt collection from individuals, and Volume 5 covers policies and procedures for the physical loss of funds, including investigations into accounts receivable resulting from improper payments. For collecting debts from military members or civilian employees through salary offset, refer to Volumes 7 and 8. These volumes also cover the collection of child support, alimony, or commercial debts via garnishment or involuntary offset. Commercial or contractor debt collection policies are in Volume 16 supplemented by the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Subpart 32.6, which prescribes procedures for contract debts, interest charges, deferrals, and compromises. Finally, policies for collecting debts from foreign entities are provided in Volume 16.

5.17    Receivables from the Sale of Goods and Services to the Public

Upon receiving a collection voucher, the ARO must record in accordance with the Volume 4 Supplemental.

5.18    Refunds Receivable

Refunds to appropriations represent amounts collected from outside sources for payments made in error, overpayments, or adjustments for previous amounts disbursed. These refunds must be directly related to previously recorded expenditures and serve as reductions to those expenditures. Policy dictates that there is no separate account for refunds receivable in the USSGL; instead, refunds receivable are treated as accounts receivable, and DoW Components must recognize and report them in their financial statements. Refunds received must be deposited to the credit of the appropriation or fund account that was charged with the original obligation. Examples of refunds receivable include, but are not limited to: salary overpayments; overpayments to commercial concerns due to erroneous billings, incorrect invoices, or contract default; amounts due for rejected/returned items; recovery due on canceled contractual services for unused portions; advance travel payments for canceled travel; amounts payable for "due U.S." travel vouchers; amounts due from advance payments for contractual purposes; and amounts due from employees on leave without pay for their share of benefits. Refer to OMB Circular A-11 for additional details.

5.19    Collection Actions

The DoW must age all accounts receivable to manage collection actions properly. A receivable is considered due 30 days from the date of the invoice or demand letter, unless a different due date is established by statute, contract, or a notice of indebtedness. Policy dictates that uncollected public vendor debts and individual out-of-service debts under $25 are not referred for further collection action and must be collected or written off within one year of delinquency, unless mandated otherwise by public law. In accordance with the Debt Collection Improvement Act and the Digital Accountability and Transparency Act, all valid and legally enforceable public receivables over 120 days are delinquent to the Treasury for collection. Several exceptions to this requirement include debts that are in litigation, part of an asset sales program, with a private collection contractor, collected via internal offset, or foreign government or NAFI debts. Terminating a collection action on a debt returned by the Treasury as uncollectible for debts under $100,000 requires coordination with the Fund Holder. For debts between $100,000 and $500,000, Treasury approval is required. For debts of $500,000 or more, termination of collection action must be approved by the Department of Justice. For additional detailed guidance, refer to Volume 16.

5.20    Establishment of Allowance for Loss on Accounts Receivable

5.20.1. AROs must recognize and record projected debt losses for public and intragovernmental accounts receivable in the general ledger by setting up an allowance for uncollectible accounts. This policy ensures that receivables are recognized at their net realizable value (NRV) by accurately estimating potential losses.

5.20.2. An allowance for estimated uncollectible receivable amounts must be recognized when it is "more likely than not" (meaning more than a 50 percent chance of loss) that the receivables will not be totally collected, as required by SFFAS 1. This policy applies to both intragovernmental and nonfederal/public entity receivables, as clarified by Technical Bulletin (TB) 2020-1. Furthermore, an allowance for loss on accounts receivable must be re-estimated annually and whenever new information indicates that the latest estimate is no longer accurate.

5.20.3. Losses due to uncollectible receivables must be measured through a systematic methodology based on an analysis of groups of receivables, with the option to isolate individual receivables for a separate allowance calculation. The total allowance for loss on accounts receivable will be the sum of these individual and grouped calculations. Any provision to increase or decrease this allowance will result in an adjustment to nonexchange revenue rather than a bad- debt expense. For receivables under $100,000, policy requires separating them into groups with similar risk characteristics. The methodology for determining the percentages applied to these groups must be based on the history of bad-debt expense over the last three years and applied consistently from year to year. Exceptions to this three-year average due to abnormal circumstances must be approved by the OUSW(C). For each receivable of $100,000 or more, the policy mandates an individual analysis to determine the loss allowance. Components with a low number of receivables or a large number of small dollar receivables may lower the $100,000 threshold for individual analysis, provided the methodology remains consistent.

5.20.4. For intragovernmental receivables, entities must not recognize an allowance for uncollectible accounts for debts up to and including two years delinquent. After two years, or if the debt is older, DoW policy mandates a 100 percent allowance for uncollectible intragovernmental accounts. For public debt, policy is to allow no allowance for uncollectible accounts (0 percent) for aging categories less than 90 days. Conversely, a 100 percent allowance is applied to public debt in aging categories with a maturity greater than 2 years. When one Component sub-allots funds to another, policy dictates that the Component executing the funds is responsible for establishing the allowance for loss on accounts receivable. Finally, it is policy that receivable write-offs must be processed through the allowance for uncollectible accounts.

5.21    Write-off and Close-Out of Public Accounts Receivable

According to governing policy, largely derived from OMB Circular A-129, any public delinquent debt that has not been collected within two years must be written off, unless a specific justification is documented and approved by OMB and Treasury. This policy strictly prohibits the write-off of intergovernmental receivables. To write off a public receivable, the Component must debit the allowance for uncollectible accounts and credit the receivable account; policy forbids a direct write-off. After a write-off, the debt must be classified as either "Currently Not Collectible" (CNC) or "Closed-Out." To be classified as CNC, a public debt must be $25 or more, all prior collection actions must have been pursued, and it must be deemed cost-effective to continue collection efforts. CNC debts must be maintained in an inactive administrative file, remain eligible for Treasury's collection programs, and continue to be reported on the Treasury Report on Receivables (TROR). Once a debt is closed out, it is considered final and cannot be reactivated, barring any further administrative or legal action, though the government can still accept voluntary repayments. Furthermore, the DoW is responsible for reporting these canceled debts to the Internal Revenue Service when they meet reporting criteria, with the DFAS Enterprise Solutions and Standards Vendor Pay Tax Office handling this for vendor and contractor debts. Refer to Volumes 4 and 16 Supplemental documents.

5.22    Intragovernmental Receivables

5.22.1. Receivables due from DoW Components or other federal entities are intragovernmental receivables and must be reported separately from receivables due from public entities in the financial statements. All materials sold or services furnished between government entities must be formally authorized and documented in a support agreement. Any uncollected amounts from these reimbursable sales are to be recorded as accounts receivable. A key policy distinction for these intragovernmental transactions, governed by the Economy Act, is the handling of budgetary resources. Unlike orders from non-federal entities, DoW organizations with reimbursable authority may recognize a budgetary resource immediately upon accepting a funded order from another federal agency. This is because the customer agency obligates its own funds at the time of order placement. Consequently, this policy allows DoW organizations to incur obligations to fill such orders without requiring an advance payment or burdening their own budgetary resources. Refer to Volume 11 for more information on intragovernmental receivables.

5.22.2. DoW Performing Entity Responsibilities

The performing entity (seller) is fundamentally responsible for ensuring that all costs for completed work are promptly recorded as revenue and receivable, and that these amounts are quickly billed and collected from the ordering entity. This policy of timely recording is critical to enable Treasury to perform its required intragovernmental eliminations. Furthermore, a critical policy prohibits DoW activities from performing new reimbursable work for any federal agency that is 90 days or more in arrears on previous payments; however, this restriction can be waived by the OUSW(C) if deemed in the national interest. Policy also dictates that any disputed charges be reviewed promptly and that all obligations and accrued expenditures be supported by a reimbursable agreement or other proof of payment due. For detailed accounting guidance, personnel are directed to refer to official manuals such as the TFM Volume 1.

5.22.3. DoW Ordering Agency Responsibilities

The ordering agency has the primary responsibility for ensuring that all charges for a performing activity are valid. This means amounts due must directly correspond to the reimbursable orders and must be substantiated by a supporting order, contract, and evidence of performance. A key policy is that any identified internal control failures or process weaknesses discovered during research must be formally addressed and corrected to prevent future errors. All evidence from this research must be documented and maintained by the organization.

5.22.4. Management of Collection Actions

All aging accounts receivable transactions are eligible for collection actions, with the delinquency date set to one day after the initial due date. All charges from transactions within the DoW or with other federal agencies must be recorded as accounts receivable in the month they are earned. To streamline billing, DoW prohibits providers from accepting G-Invoicing Inter-Agency Agreement Forms 7600A/B if the interfund billing system can be used, and it forbids manual billing unless specifically approved by the Deputy Chief Financial Officer (DCFO). Regarding disputes, a buyer is generally prohibited from charging back or rejecting a charge unless authorized by the formal dispute resolution process. An exception exists for Intra-Governmental Payment and Collection (IPAC) transactions, which can be rejected within 30 days, but only for four valid reasons: billing for more than the agreed amount, duplicate/erroneous billing, lack of supporting documentation, or an expired 7600A/B or appropriation. For transactions outside the DoW, IPAC is the preferred billing and collection method. If an IPAC transaction is rejected, policy requires that the receivable be reestablished and that adjustments be made to the appropriation’s FBwT.

5.22.5. Non-Interfund Dispute Process

5.22.5.1. The ARO is responsible for managing all intragovernmental debt within the DoW, a process overseen by the OUSW(C). A critical policy is that this type of debt cannot be referred to an external debt collection activity. The full settlement of any disputed charge must be completed within a strict 180-day timeline from the date of the original charge. For disputed amounts of $2,500 or less, the buyer may accept the charge without dispute or dispute it only if the process is cost-effective. For larger disputes, the buyer and seller work together for the first 60 days to find a solution, with assistance available from DFAS. If unresolved, the buyer assembles a formal dispute package for the seller with assistance from DFAS. If a dispute resolution concludes that the buyer does not have to pay, the seller must adjust their financial records accordingly: for current fiscal year activity, revenue must be decreased, expenses and direct obligations must be increased; for material receivables from a prior year, a prior period adjustment must be used; and for immaterial prior year receivables, current year revenues can be reduced.

5.22.5.2. Disputes between the DoW and other federal agencies must be handled in accordance with I-TFM-2-4700. Dispute resolution will involve the program offices, the accounting offices, the contracting officer, and the agency’s CFO, as appropriate. A MOA will be signed by the CFOs of each department and agency to acknowledge that department’s or agency’s active participation in the dispute resolution process. All disputes must be documented in writing with clear reasoning. Trading partners are strictly prohibited from charging back or rejecting transactions that comply with I-TFM-2-4700, and they may not create new transactions to circumvent it. Disputes are categorized into two types: those arising from differing accounting treatments and those from contractual disagreements. A key policy for contractual disputes is that the buyer may establish a monetary threshold of no more than $100,000 per order. If a disputed amount is under this threshold and the buyer chooses not to pursue the dispute, they are obligated to pay the amount. Missing indicative data (such as order numbers, TAS, BETC, amounts, or BPN numbers for both trading partners) on a transaction constitutes a valid cause for a contractual dispute.

5.22.5.3. DoDI 1015.15 requires certain categories of NAFIs to reimburse appropriated funds (APF) for goods and services provided. This relationship must be formalized in a reimbursement agreement, such as a Memorandum of Understanding, and signed by authorized representatives from both the APF and NAFI. At a minimum, this agreement must define either the fixed price for the goods and services or the methodology for determining that price. Policy dictates that the due date for any bill is 30 days from the bill's date. A key financial policy is that while Military Departments may use their own appropriated funds to perform work for a NAFI without an advance, they are prohibited from recognizing any budgetary resources for that order until the NAFI has actually paid the account receivable.

5.23    Reporting Receivables Due From the Public

Components must submit the quarterly TROR. The ARO, in conjunction with the Component, must report public receivables in accordance with the TROR guidance on the Treasury website.

5.24    Reporting Receivables in DoW Financial Statements

Accounts receivable must be reported on the quarterly financial statements. A key aspect of this policy is ensuring data integrity through reconciliation. Public accounts receivable balances reported on the financial statements must be reconciled with the corresponding balances in the Governmentwide Treasury Account Symbol (GTAS) system (non-Federal attribute). These balances must also be reconciled with the amounts reported on the TROR. Furthermore, a fundamental policy for consolidated reporting is that all intragovernmental accounts receivable balances must be eliminated.

5.25 Crediting and Accounting for Disputed Collections Under the Contract Disputes Act of 1978

5.25.1. When a contractor pays a debt but simultaneously disputes it (or indicates they will), that collected amount cannot be accounted for as a final settlement. As soon as a collection is made under a disputed status, interest, penalties, and any other administrative fees immediately cease to accrue. A designated Treasury deposit account must be credited with the collected funds and hold them pending the final disposition of the contractor's dispute. Furthermore, there must be continuous, mutual communication among the responsible disbursing officer, the DMO, the contracting officer, and any other relevant authorities regarding all actions affecting these disputed collections.

5.25.2. In accordance with 10 U.S.C. § 3863, disputed collections received and credited must be separately accounted for and remain available, regardless of the closing of an appropriation or fund account, for payment of any settlement of the claim by the parties, any judgment rendered in the contractor’s favor on an appeal of the decision on the claim to the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals (ASBCA), or any judgment rendered in the contractor’s favor in an action on that claim in a court of the U.S. Availability of the disputed collection expires 90 days after the expiration of the period for bringing an action on that claim in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims under section 41 U.S.C. § 7104(a), if within those 90 days, no appeal on the claim is commenced at the ASBCA and that no action on the claim is commenced in a court of the U.S.

5.25.3. If not expiring, then availability of the disputed collected amounts expires in the case of a settlement of a claim, 90 days after the date of the settlement or in the case of a judgment rendered on the claim in an appeal to the ASBCA or an action in a court of the U.S, 90 days after the date on which the judgment becomes final and rendered not appealable.

5.25.4. While a disputed amount is being separately accounted for, it can only be obligated or expended for the purpose of settling that specific claim. If it is determined that all or part of the collection is repayable to the contractor, including payment or adjustment of interest or fees, whether by settlement or judgment, that amount must be disbursed promptly to the contractor. This includes prompt reimbursement to the Treasury Judgment Fund, if applicable. The foregoing disbursed amounts must be charged to the deposit account X6501. A critical financial policy dictates the source of funds for interest payments: any interest that has accrued since the collection and is ordered to be paid as part of the final resolution must be charged to a currently available appropriation account.

5.25.5. Upon the expiration of the availability period for a disputed collection, any funds that have not been obligated or expended must be withdrawn and credited to the appropriate accounts. If an amount was credited to the deposit account for an appropriation or fund account that closed for reasons other than those described under 31 U.S.C. § 1552(a) or 31 U.S.C. § 1555, then the principal amount collected must be properly credited to that appropriation or fund account and an adjustment made of the amounts of the contract(s) for which the disputed collection arose. Any amounts for interest and fees must be credited to the appropriate Treasury Miscellaneous Receipts accounts. A core principle of this policy is that the records for the closed appropriation and any associated unclosed contracts must be adjusted to accurately reflect the outcome, ensuring that all obligated and unobligated balances are correct.

title: Section 6.0: Inventory and Related Property
content:
6.0    INVENTORY AND RELATED PROPERTY

This section provides DoW accounting guidance for inventory, Operating Materials and Supplies (OM&S), and stockpile materials. Management must ensure that all related transactions are recorded in the general ledger in accordance with requirements from the Department of the Treasury and other federal mandates. Furthermore, adequate supporting source documentation, such as contracts, invoices, and receiving reports, payment vouchers, material-return documents, transfer documents, inventory documents, issue and shipping documents, sales records, and documented gains and losses, must be retained for all entries. Tangible items with a useful life of two or more years not intended for consumption or sale in the ordinary course of operations and intended to be used or available for use are classified as General Equipment. Refer to Volume 6 for detailed requirements on preparing and presenting notes to the financial statements for Inventory and Related Property. Except for provisions related to the National Stockpile Fund (NSF), all of the provisions in this section apply to the Working Capital Fund (WCF). Except for provisions related to Inventory, Supply Management Activities, and Stockpile Materials, all provisions in this section apply to the General Fund (GF).

6.1    Valuation Concepts

6.1.1. Historical cost includes all appropriate purchase, transportation, and production costs incurred to bring items to their current condition and location and excludes abnormal costs. Abnormal costs are expenses that significantly exceed the standard cost to purchase and place a new item with similar features and useful life into service (e.g., excessive handling, expedited delivery, and rework costs due to defects or errors). Expense abnormal costs in the period in which they are incurred. For donated, repaired, or remanufactured items, policy dictates that the Component must value them at their fair value when they become serviceable. Recognize differences between fair value and any amounts surrendered in exchange for the item as a gain or loss.

6.1.2. Inventory valuation requires that ending balances and the cost of goods sold must be determined by applying one of three cost flow assumptions: First-In, First-Out; Weighted Average Cost; or Moving Average Cost (MAC). As a policy alternative, any other valuation method compliant with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) is permissible, provided that its results reasonably approximate one of the three specified historical cost methods.

6.2    Net Realizable Value (NRV)

DoW Components must write down the value of any inventory, OM&S, or stockpile materials that are classified as Excess, Obsolete, and Unserviceable (EOU) to their expected NRV. Excess stock exceeds the demand or requirements for normal operations. Stock becomes obsolete when changes in technology, laws, customs, or operations make it unusable, while damaged stock is considered unserviceable if disposal is more economical than repair. In these cases, as well as for stockpile materials experiencing permanent decline, damage, or decay, DoW Components are required to write down their value to the estimated NRV. NRV is defined as the estimated recoverable amount from selling or disposing of an item, after accounting for any associated costs. It is also policy that when items are transferred to the Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) Disposition Services (except those handled through a Qualified Recycling Program), the NRV is generally considered to be zero, as no proceeds are typically received. Refer to Defense Logistics Manual
4000.25 for details on how to dispose of EOU using DLA Disposition Services.

6.3    Held for Repair

Inventory or OM&S Held for Repair may be accounted for using either the Allowance Method or the Direct Method. Regardless of the method chosen, a core policy is that management must retain supporting documentation for the estimated repair costs, in accordance with their DoW Component records retention requirements. Refer to Volume 4 Supplemental for information on the approved methods.

6.4 Alternative Valuation Methodologies for Establishing Opening Balances

6.4.1. An alternative valuation method, guided by SFFAS 48 and Technical Release (TR) 18, is available for establishing opening balances for Inventory, OM&S, and stockpile materials. However, this option can be used only once per line item for each reporting entity and is intended solely to establish and document those initial balances. For serially managed items, such as grocery and household product inventories, the specific identification method may be used. Using this method, the Component directly links each identifiable item to its precise cost. Before using this alternative method, a DoW Component must validate that it is fully prepared to comply with all accounting requirements, including the recognition, measurement, presentation, and disclosure rules outlined in SFFAS 3.

6.4.2. When a component cannot apply the historical cost approach outlined in SFFAS 3 to establish opening balances for inventory, OM&S, or stockpile materials, it is acceptable to use a "deemed cost" as a substitute for the reporting period. Deemed cost is an acceptable valuation method for the reporting period when the reporting entity makes an unreserved assertion that its financial statements, or one or more line items within inventory, OM&S, and stockpile materials, are presently fairly in accordance with GAAP. An unreserved assertion is an unconditional statement. Deemed cost may be determined using a variety of methods, including Standard (Selling) Price, Fair Value, Latest Acquisition Cost, or Replacement Cost. It can also be based on an Estimated Historical Cost, which uses reasonable estimation techniques, or the Actual Historical Cost, which is the original price paid for the asset. See Volume 4 Supplemental for more information on these methodologies.

6.4.3. When using a deemed cost to establish opening balances, a component must identify and report all valuation methods in its financial statement notes and retain supporting documentation, including any necessary sampling techniques. A critical step is to adjust any existing gains or losses in related allowance accounts to zero. Once established, this new opening balance is considered consistent with SFFAS 3 requirements and is integrated into ongoing inventory calculations, such as a MAC, with no future distinction required. Record the difference between the prior value adjusted for any related allowance account value and the new deemed cost must be recorded as a prior period adjustment due to a change in accounting principles, with the adjustment made to the beginning balance of cumulative results of operations in the statement of changes in net position for the period that the change is made, in accordance with the reporting requirements under paragraph 13 of FASAB SFFAS 21. Finally, the nature of this change and its effect on balances in the current period must be disclosed in the financial statements, but this disclosure need not be repeated in subsequent periods unless the statements are presented for comparative purposes.

6.5    Inventory - (Applicable to WCF Only)

6.5.1. Recognition of Inventory

Components recognize inventory at the point they receive title or take delivery of the goods, as specified by the contract or agreement. Title may be received at the origin (FOB shipping point) upon shipment, or at the destination (FOB destination) upon physical delivery. Additionally, constructive delivery can occur when contract terms stipulate that title has been transferred to the recipient even before the physical items arrive.

6.5.2. Reconciliations

All Components are required to maintain accurate inventory records, necessitating a comprehensive reconciliation between their general ledger inventory line items and detailed inventory accountability records at least quarterly. This policy further dictates that all such reconciliations must encompass data from all relevant Enterprise Resource Management system modules (such as Warehouse, Inventory, and Financial Management) and extend to all inventory owned by the entity, irrespective of its physical custody (e.g., inventory managed by contractors or the DLA). A fundamental policy outcome is that any discrepancies identified must be researched and resolved in a timely manner, and that, subsequently, appropriate system and business process controls must be implemented to reduce future errors proactively.

6.5.3. Physical Inventory Counts

Activities are required to conduct physical counts of their inventories at least annually, generally as of the fiscal year-end, in accordance with the Defense Logistics Management Standards Volume 2. Note that auditors will likely attend and observe counts for any inventories that management has deemed material. Following the count, the general ledger must be adjusted to reflect any differences found between the ledger balances and the physical inventory. All adjustments must be supported by developed and maintained audit documentation. For inventory held by contractors, the necessary documentation, such as receipts, shipments, losses, and disposals, is available in the Procurement Integrated Enterprise Environment Government Furnished Property Module. Invoices occasionally list fewer or more items ordered than the actual count of inventory items received. If resolving the difference is not economical, record a loss or gain.

6.6    War Reserve Materiel (WRM)

WRM is a strategic stockpile of essential items and munitions intended to sustain military operations until resupply is available. This inventory includes operating and training stocks in addition to regular peacetime assets. Financially, WRM is primarily funded through direct appropriations to the WCF; however, critical items such as ammunition and major end items are funded through the procurement appropriations of the Components and Defense Agencies. Although it is held in reserve by DoW Components, its acquisition and storage are indistinguishable from regular inventory. The policy allows for this materiel to be transferred to the U.S. Armed Forces without reimbursement to meet mobilization needs, and it also permits DoW Components to sell WRM if authorized. The value of these reserve items is recorded using the same accounting principles as peacetime inventory.

6.7    Work-In-Process

WCF manufacturing activities must record all operating costs for tasks lasting more than one month in a "work-in-process" (WIP) account. This is required to accurately segregate long- term costs from current period expenses, ensuring compliance with GAAP. The inventory WIP account is used to accumulate all direct and indirect costs, including General & Administrative expenses, required to complete a job or customer order. Related costs attributed to an order include costs for additions, alterations, improvements, rehabilitations, and replacements of fixed assets; maintenance costs; manufacturing or fabricating costs for an end item or product; and costs of producing an output. Upon completion or termination of an order, all related costs must be transferred out of the WIP account, and billing must occur immediately, regardless of customer acceptance. A gain or loss must be recognized if the final costs differ from customer funding, and any probable losses must be recognized proportionally over the life of the contract. If an order terminates prior to completion, the Component must expense the accumulated costs.

6.8    Supply Management Activities - (Applicable to WCF Only)

6.8.1. Supply Management Activities manage inventory held for sale to other DoW Components or activities and items procured for sale to members of the Armed Forces and other individuals or organizations when authorized by legislation, including the Army, Navy, Air Force, DLA, and the Defense Commissary Agency for commissary resale. This guidance also applies to DLA Disposition Services, which handles redistribution or disposal of items, including sales to the public and other Federal customers. Examples of items managed by supply management activities include food, military clothing, fuel, and preventive medicine. Supply Management Activities also cover Depot Maintenance or Industrial Operations activities that use items to produce goods or services for a fee. The USW(C) and the Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment (USW(A&S)) may designate items for procurement by supply management and reassign management responsibility between DoW Components.

6.8.2. A supply management activity is authorized to sell items to a broad range of entities, including other federal government activities, DoW-sponsored nonappropriated funding programs, and State Department-sponsored employee commissaries located outside the U.S. Sales are also authorized for foreign governments with established contractual relationships, federal government contractors holding specific purchasing contracts or utilizing the Replenishment Parts Purchase or Borrow Program, and members of the Armed Forces and other individuals legally authorized to purchase commissary and clothing items. Additionally, the activity can sell to private-sector purchasers, state or local governments purchasing non-excess property, provided such sales are authorized by law, and to any other entity specifically authorized by duly appointed officials. Refer to 40 U.S.C. Chapter 5, Section 503.

6.9    Issues Without Reimbursement

6.9.1. Issue or Transfer. DoW Components may not issue or transfer a supply management activity item without a funded customer order unless specifically authorized in the following section. DoW Components will not account for these events in the same manner as a normal sale, except when they need to establish an allowance for loss on accounts receivable.

6.9.2. Domestic Civil Emergency. DoW officials may issue a supply management activity item without immediate reimbursement when they provide an immediate response to save lives, prevent human suffering, or mitigate great property damage within the U.S. by temporarily employing the resources under their control in accordance with DoD Directive (DoDD) 3025.18.

6.9.3. Civil Disturbances. Upon specific authorization by the President in accordance with applicable law, a supply management activity may issue an item without immediate reimbursement when action is taken to control a civil disturbance in accordance with the policies and procedures provided in DoDD 3025.18.

6.9.4. Foreign Disaster Relief (FDR). A supply management activity item may be issued without immediate reimbursement when the State Department is responsible for initiating and financing FDR efforts, as authorized by the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. Within the DoW, the Director of the Defense Security Cooperation Agency (DSCA) serves as the lead for the FDR program's management and budget matters. Furthermore, the Commander of the U.S. Transportation Command is responsible for ensuring that DoW activities can support the transportation requirements of FDR operations. All procedures related to issuing supply management materiel for FDR are to be performed in accordance with DoDD 5100.46.

6.9.5. North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) Country. A NATO country may receive a supply management activity item without reimbursement under a replacement-in-kind arrangement. Nonreimbursable issues under this authority are changed to a reimbursable activity within 12 months if not replaced by the NATO country.

6.9.6. Military Emergency. Under emergency provisions in 10 U.S.C. § 127, the Secretary of War (SecWar), the Inspector General of the DoW, or the Secretary of a military department (within their department) may issue a supply management activity item without immediate reimbursement. The issuing Secretary or the Inspector General may certify the amount of any advisable expenditure without specifying it, and this certificate suffices to cover the expenditure. The SecWar may waive the description requirement due to extraordinary circumstances affecting the national security of the U.S. When funding becomes available to cover the costs of the emergency, the supply management activity receives reimbursement for outstanding accounts receivable.

6.9.7. War Reserve Assets (WRA). A supply management activity may issue an item designated as WRA, without a funded customer order, when it has approved the issuance to satisfy the requirements for mobilizing the U.S. Armed Forces.

6.9.8. Deficiencies in War Reserve Requirements. A supply management activity item may be issued, without reimbursement, when an item is issued to satisfy war reserve requirement deficiencies or between activities within the supply management activity.

6.9.9. Items Nearing End of Shelf Life. If a supply management activity item is not a WRA, the personnel responsible may issue the item at any price or without reimbursement when the item has 6 months or less of remaining shelf life, and the item manager approves the item to be issued on a less-than-cost basis.

6.9.10. Logistical Management Transfers. Logistical management transfers or reassignments occur when funding appropriations for an item change.

6.9.11. Logistical Management Transfers Between Supply Management Activities. Supply management activities transfer inventory on hand without reimbursement. However, wholesale and retail supply activities are authorized to reimburse each other when on-hand retail inventory is transferred back to the wholesale item manager’s inventory control points, in accordance with DoW credit policies.

6.10    Loans and Leases

6.10.1. Supply management activities may only lend or lease items specified in this section for the stated purpose. Accountability for inventory on loan remains with the activity that lends the material, and it is valued in the same manner as inventory on hand. The recipient must cover all transportation, packing, crating, and handling costs associated with borrowing or leasing the item. Additionally, the recipient must pay all costs necessary to restore the item to its original condition upon returning it, or pay for the item if it is not returned within the approved loan or lease period.

6.10.2. Property may be lent or leased to the following recipients:

6.10.2.1. DoW Funded Customers. Supply management activities may lend an item to a DoW funded customer for a maximum of 120 days to support an approved training exercise, a military emergency, or a natural disaster.

6.10.2.2. U.S. Secret Service. Supply management activities may lend an item to the U.S. Secret Service for a maximum of 120 days for purposes prescribed under the policies and procedures in DoDD 3025.13.

6.10.2.3. Civilian Law Enforcement Officials. DoDI 3025.21 prescribes the DoW regulations for supporting civilian law enforcement agencies, ensuring such support is consistent with military preparedness and legal limitations. The Under Secretary of War for Policy governs the defense support of civilian law enforcement agencies and coordinates policy with Federal departments and agencies, State, local, and tribal agencies, and DoW Components. Supply management activities may lend equipment, base facilities, or research facilities to a civilian law enforcement activity for up to 120 days for purposes prescribed by the policies and procedures in DoDI 3025.21.

6.10.2.4. State and Local Governments. Supply management activities may lend an item to a state or local Government for up to 120 days for a specific purpose, per DoDI 3025.21.

6.10.2.5. National Veterans’ Organizations. Supply management activities may lend items (e.g., cots, blankets, pillows, mattresses, bed sacks, and other supplies) to a recognized national veterans’ organization to support a national or state convention or a regional youth athletic or recreational tournament sponsored by the veterans’ organization under the authority of
10 U.S.C. § 2551.

6.10.2.6. American National Red Cross. Supply management activities may lend an item to an organization formed by the American National Red Cross for instruction and practice needed to aid the Army, Navy, or Air Force in time of war under the authority of 10 U.S.C. § 2552. Supply management activities require the immediate return of equipment loaned.

6.10.2.7. Inaugural Committee. Supply management activities may lend an item to the Presidential and the congressional Joint Inaugural Committee to support an inauguration of the President of the United States for a maximum period of nine days beyond the inauguration ceremony under the authority of 10 U.S.C. § 2553.

6.10.2.8. Boy Scout Jamborees. Supply management activities may lend cots, blankets, commissary equipment, flags, refrigerators, and other equipment to the Boy Scouts of America for the use of Scouters and officials attending any national or world Boy Scout Jamboree under the authority of 10 U.S.C. § 2554. Services and expendable medical supplies may be furnished without reimbursement.

6.10.2.9. Shelter for the Homeless, Incidental Services. Under 10 U.S.C. § 2556, the Secretary of a Military Department may make installations available to shelter the homeless in cooperation with state, local, and charitable organizations. Incidental services such as utilities, bedding, security, transportation, facility renovations, minor repairs, and property liability insurance can also be provided, provided they do not interfere with military preparedness. Excess DoW items can only be issued to shelters.

6.10.2.10. Humanitarian Relief. Supply management activities may make nonlethal excess supplies available for transfer to the Secretary of Homeland Security for its distribution for humanitarian relief, domestic emergency assistance, and homeless veterans’ assistance under the authority of 10 U.S.C. § 2557.

6.10.2.11. Foreign Countries or International Organizations. Supply management activities may lease or loan an item to an eligible foreign country or international organization under the authority of the Arms Export Control Act. The Director, DSCA, oversees DoW's worldwide security cooperation efforts, ensuring the timely transfer of defense articles and services to meet strategic objectives. DSCA also holds fiduciary responsibility for the financial management of the FMS Trust Fund and reporting for its security cooperation programs. Refer to Volume 15 and DoDD 5105.65.

6.10.2.12. Other Leases. Supply management activities may lease or loan a non‑excess supply management activity item to an organization when the SecWar or the Secretary of a Military Department has determined that the item is under control of the Secretary, not needed for DoW use during the proposed lease period, and the lease will promote the national defense or public interest under the authority of 10 U.S.C. § 2667. The lease may not exceed five years, unless the Secretary concerned determines that a lease for a longer period will promote national defense or be in the public interest. Additional lease conditions are covered within Volume 12.

6.11    Government Furnished Material (GFM)

GFM may be issued by the item manager to a contractor, another DoW, or a Federal government activity to be maintained as stock for issue, consumption, or repair. When the Component issues GFM to a contractor, the GFM becomes subject to the requirements of the FAR and Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement.

6.12    Supply Management Activity Transfers

6.12.1. Assistant Secretary of War for Sustainment oversees procedures to optimize supply support resources between providers and customers, establishes integrated materiel management processes to reduce redundant items, and provides timely support to customers.

6.12.2. Transfers In Without Reimbursement. A supply activity may assume management responsibility and capitalize supply inventories that were financed by other appropriations and funds as permitted by 10 U.S.C. § 2208 and DoD Manual (DoDM) 4140.26. A supply management activity may receive capital from the SecWar by capitalizing inventories but not make credits to an appropriation-funded activity for capitalized inventories as provided in 10 U.S.C. § 2208. However, stock withdrawal authorizations may be approved.

6.12.3. Transfers of Reimbursable Procurements. The supply management activity may record a liability for an item transferred from a non-WCF account only if (1) the item is undelivered at the time of the transfer, and (2) the transferring organization’s obligation for the item resulted from a reimbursable order from a customer. The customer must transfer appropriated funds to the supply management activity to liquidate the liability.

6.12.4. Stock Withdrawal Authorizations. A transferring activity may not have funds to purchase an item after transferring an item from an appropriation-funded activity to a supply management activity. Therefore, the transferring activity may request that the USD(C) approve an authorization for issues without reimbursement, as part of the formal budget submission to Congress. The supply management activity must issue items on a reimbursable basis when the fiscal year has passed. The supply management activity must record a stock withdrawal authorization as a transfer-out, a reduction of inventory held for sale, and the difference is reported as a realization of holding gain/loss.
6.12.5. Logistical Management Transfers. Logistical management transfers occur when changes are made to the funding appropriation for an item.

6.13    Depot Level Reparables

6.13.1. Reparables are items that have reached the end of their lifecycle but can be restored or remanufactured. Reparables are considered when the computed inventory level requirements are met. The Department's depot-level repair program for inventory replenishment and resale acts as a remanufacturing process for financial management and accounting purposes.

6.13.2. Exchange Transaction. Many DoW Components obtain items for remanufacturing through an exchange transaction. In this transaction, they sell a serviceable item at the standard price in exchange for (1) cash and (2) an item that needs rebuilding or repair (carcass). The supply management team may record two separate transactions to represent the financial event or bill the customer at the exchange price, which is the standard price minus any credit if the requisitioning activity states that a reparable item will be returned. If the impaired item (carcass) has not been received at the time of the exchange, the organization records the item as “Inventory Held for Repair (Remanufacture Due In).” Serviceable Depot Level Reparables are recorded at historical cost. If the customer does not return a reparable item within 90 days of the exchange sale for continental United States (CONUS) customers or within 120 days for customers outside the continental United States (OCONUS), the supply management team must reverse the credit they previously allowed and bill the customer.

6.13.3. Supply management activities may place orders and obligate funds for repair/remanufacture work placed with a contractor or a government repair facility. The carcass will remain in the Supply Management activity “Inventory Held for Repair (Remanufacturing)” account while the item is repaired/remanufactured.

6.13.4. The Department’s depot-level repair program for inventory replenishment and resale acts as a remanufacturing process for financial management and accounting purposes.

6.14    Return of Items to the Supply Management Activity

6.14.1. A customer within the Federal Government, including DoW contractors, may return an item to a supply management activity according to 22 U.S.C. § 2761. The proceeds will be credited to current applicable appropriations and will be available for expenditure for the same purposes as those appropriations. Customers cannot receive inventory credits for returns because inventory is capitalized.

6.14.2. The Arms Export Control Act permits the return of defense articles from a foreign country or international organization under specified conditions if the defense article was previously transferred to that country or organization under 22 U.S.C. § 2761, is not significant military equipment (as defined in 22 U.S.C. § 2794), and is fully functioning without needing repair or rehabilitation.

6.14.3. According to 10 U.S.C. § 2208(g), a department, activity, or agency may return supplies to working-capital funds, and it can charge the appraised value to that working-capital fund.

6.14.4. An item manager may grant credit for a returned item after receipt, inspection, and classification of the item. A return that stratifies to a war reserve inventory requirement does not qualify for credit. The amount of the credit for the return of a fully serviceable consumable or reparable item or the return of a carcass when not part of an exchange transaction and within the approved acquisition objective level must not exceed the current standard price of the returned item less the current fiscal year’s approved cost recovery elements. If the supply management activity granted credit before taking ownership or receiving the returned item, and if the item is not received within 90 days from a CONUS customer or 120 days from an OCONUS customer, the supply management activity must bill the customer for the credit it previously recorded. Additionally, the stockage point may choose to bill the customer for costs incurred due to the non- receipt of the item. The supply management activity may grant a credit to a customer at standard price for defective items when a customer's quality deficiency report has been validated, including specification defects. Credits may be applied against future customer demands for items in the current fiscal year, or credited directly to the customer's current-year available funds.

6.14.5. The supply management activity must fund transportation and other shipping costs for items approved for return from customers. Shipping costs include packing, crating, handling, transportation, port loading, and unloading. The supply management activity must not fund shipping and transportation costs for items that have not been approved for customer return.

6.14.6. Return of an item, whether issuable or not issuable, reverses the sale’s effect on the Cost of Goods Sold. Activities record receipt of a returned item regardless of whether the customer receives credit.

6.15    OM&S - (Applicable to General Fund (GF) and WCF)

6.15.1. OM&S Types

6.15.1.1. OM&S consists of tangible personal property that organizations consume in their normal operations. Title 41, section 101-8.705 of the CFR defines a normal operation as the “operation of a program or activity without significant changes that would inhibit meeting objectives”. OM&S applies to GF and WCF. OM&S includes Held for Use, Held in Reserve for Future Use, EOU, Held for Repair, In Development, In Transit, and Long Range Ballistic Missiles (LRBM). OM&S excludes inventory, stockpile materials, and items acquired for use in constructing real property or in assembling equipment. Refer to the supporting Volume 4 Supplemental for details supporting OM&S Types.

6.15.1.2. LRBMs, including Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles and Submarine Launched Ballistic Missiles, must be reported as OM&S for financial reporting purposes. These missiles are considered OM&S because they are frequently used, are consumable and cannot be reused after consumption, are similar in nature to other missiles classified as OM&S, and are broken down and stored as separate parts. Nuclear warheads remain the property of the Department of Energy (DOE). DOE reports the warheads as OM&S.

6.15.2. Recognition and Valuation of OM&S

The consumption method of accounting for the recognition of expenses must be applied for OM&S. If OM&S (1) are not significant amounts, (2) are in the hands of the end user for use in normal operations, or (3) it is not cost-beneficial to apply the consumption method of accounting, then the purchases method may be applied to OM&S. An end user is any component of a reporting entity that obtains goods for direct use in the component’s normal operations. Generally, material at an end user is not transferred to another location for consumption. Components of a reporting entity, including contractors, that maintain or stock OM&S for future issuance are not end users.

6.15.2.1. Consumption Method. Recognize and report OM&S as assets on the balance sheet when produced or purchased. The contract between the buyer and the seller determines when title passes. If the contract between the buyer and the seller is silent regarding passage of title, title is assumed to pass upon delivery of the goods. The contract terms determine whether delivery is made or constructive delivery occurs. Under the Consumption method, OM&S are valued at historical cost or on a basis that reasonably approximates historical cost. Valuation must be adjusted for EOU or expected repair. In addition, alternative valuation methodologies may be used to establish beginning balances.

6.15.2.2. Purchases Method. Expense OM&S when produced or purchased. This method is an alternative to the consumption method and requires formal justification.

6.16    Stockpile Materials - (Applicable To Revolving Fund Only)

The National Defense Stockpile, authorized by the Strategic and Critical Stock Piling Act (50 U.S.C. Subchapter III), holds materials essential for national defense or conservation, to avoid reliance on foreign sources during emergencies. While National Defense Authorization Acts permit the buying and selling of specific materials (including medicine) and set quantity and revenue levels for selling material, no new acquisitions are allowed if more than 99% of the current inventory is already authorized for sale.

6.16.1. Roles and Responsibilities

6.16.1.1. The DLA Strategic Materials Directorate administers the acquisition, storage, management, and disposal of inventory (including medicine) currently maintained in the National Defense Stockpile Transaction Fund (NDSTF). The NDSTF’s Treasury Federal account symbol is 97X4555. The NDSTF is a continuing fund that finances the operations of the National Defense Stockpile and Defense National Stockpile Center (DNSC).

6.16.1.2. DLA records and reports stockpile materials within the NDSTF. The NDSTF’s Treasury Federal account symbol is 97X4555.

6.16.1.3. The DFAS maintains accounting requirements and procedures, performs financial and general ledger accounting, and prepares external accounting reports for the NDSTF.

6.16.2. Recognition and Valuation of Stockpile Materials

Stockpile materials are accounted for using the consumption method and are reported as assets when produced or purchased.

6.16.3. Material Acquisition

All acquisitions of material for the National Defense Stockpile are proposed in the Annual Materials Plan, which is subject to approval by Congress and the subsequent authorization of funding. Material purchase contracts are recorded as obligations against the current-year acquisition program and reflect the contract date. Additional costs, including initial testing, increase the material's cost for inventory valuation purposes.

6.16.4. Material Upgrade

The Annual Material Plan includes the program for upgrading existing National Defense Stockpile material. Contractors perform the upgrade services, and DoW Components obligate funds from the current-year budget for the program.

6.16.5. Material Disposals

Various materials in the National Defense Stockpile may become obsolete or exceed current defense stockpiling needs. The National Defense Stockpile Act authorizes the disposal of such material within the Annual Material Plan and as authorized within the budget program for the NDSTF.

6.16.6. Exchange Transactions

Materials can be offered as like material, as payment in kind, or in exchange for other material, for amounts due for material upgraded or acquired. These transactions are accounted for as exchange disposals, and the original cost of the material is removed from inventory and recorded as the cost of exchange disposals. All sales and disposals are billed shortly after the sales agreement is made, or as of the scheduled delivery or pickup time for the material. Credits earned for material received and accepted by the DNSC are used to pay for material shipped when it is disposed of during an exchange settlement.

6.16.7. Inventory Adjustments

Inventory adjustments are made when necessary due to events such as physical counts, material movements, or disposals. All adjustments must be documented and approved by the appropriate authorities such as the DNSC Administrator, delegated inventory officials, or a board of survey, depending on the adjustment's nature and size, before they are recorded in the accounting system.

6.16.8. Research Grants

The NDSTF receives appropriations to award grants to universities, colleges, and research institutions.

6.16.9. Relationship of General Ledger Accounts to Logistic Supply Condition Codes and Stratifications. Refer to Volume 4 Supplemental section 6.16.9 for more information on supply condition codes.

title: Section 7.0: General and Right-to-Use Property, Plant and Equipment (GPP&E)
content:
7.0    GENERAL AND RIGHT-TO-USE PROPERTY, PLANT AND EQUIPMENT (GPP&E)

GPP&E consists of tangible assets that: have an estimated useful life of two years or more; are not intended for sale in the ordinary course of operations; and are acquired or constructed to be used or available for use by the entity. Account for GPP&E in accordance with FASAB SFFAS 6, “Accounting for Property, Plant, and Equipment.”

7.1    REAL PROPERTY

The United States Standard General Ledger (USSGL) contains the real property general ledger accounts listed in Volume 1, and the DoW USSGL Transaction Library specifies the accounting entries. Unless otherwise stated, this section applies to all DoW Components, both GF and WCF activities.
