7.1.1.6. Valuation

7.1.1.6.1. Recorded cost includes all amounts paid to bring the asset to its form and location suitable for its intended use. The recorded cost for capitalized assets is depreciated or expensed depending on the acquisition cost. Non-capital assets are expensed when acquired and do not depreciate. Capitalization does not depend on whether the Component uses appropriated funds or WCFs.

7.1.2. Method of Acquisition or Transfer Determines Recorded Cost. Refer to Volume 4 Supplemental section 7.1.2 for more information.

7.1.3. Alternative Valuation for Establishing Opening Balances

7.1.3.1. Applicability and Considerations. This section applies for the reporting period when the reporting entity is presenting financial statements, or one or more line items, following GAAP promulgated by FASAB either (1) for the first time or (2) after a period during which existing systems could not provide the information necessary for producing such GAAP- based financial statements without using the alternative methods. The SFFAS 50 alternative valuation for establishing opening balances for General PP&E is available only once per line item to each reporting DoW Component. Therefore, prior to establishing opening balances, the DoW Components must validate that they are prepared to account for and comply with the SFFAS 6 recognition, measurement, presentation, and disclosure requirements for real property.

7.1.3.2. Deemed Cost - Existing real property assets (RPAs) with deemed cost equal to or over the current real property capitalization threshold and remaining book values are recorded as a part of the opening balance. DoW Components must apply the applicable capitalization threshold to their entire population of real property retroactively, irrespective of the capitalization thresholds in effect for years prior to October 1, 2013. DoW Components must include all relevant prior period adjustments and note disclosures in their annual financial statements in accordance with SFFAS 50. DoW Components must perform additional analytical procedures to identify assets that have been improperly capitalized or expensed. Examples include searching for RPAs with values of $0 or $1, or reviewing for an erroneous additional zero that incorrectly places the asset above the capitalization threshold. DoW Components using the deemed cost methodology must include a disclosure in their financial statements. The disclosure must describe the alternate valuation method used to establish the financial statement opening balances. Include an unreserved assertion that one or more line items are presented fairly in accordance with GAAP. The disclosure does not need to specifically identify the amount of the deemed cost of real property included in the opening balances.

7.1.4. Recognition

7.1.4.1. DoW Components must recognize Real Property Assets (RPAs) for financial statement accountability. RPAs that meet or exceed the established capitalization thresholds must be capitalized and depreciated/amortized. The DoW capitalization threshold for real property is $15,000,000 for General Fund (GF) and $1,000,000 for Working Capital Fund (WCF) activities. Transitional Guidance: Components adopting these thresholds must coordinate with the ODCFO for specific application instructions. Components are eligible to retain existing balances below the Departments capitalization threshold, or apply a lower threshold for component-level reporting, with DCFO approval. Capitalization thresholds may be applied prospectively for components with established opening balances, whereas entities that establish opening balances using deemed cost must apply them retrospectively. Components must review Construction-in-Progress (CIP) projects and make appropriate adjustments during adoption.

7.1.4.2. Recognition Responsibility

7.1.4.2.1. DoW Components must report real property facilities located on their installations. Under 10 U.S.C. § 2682, the SecWar designates the military department's jurisdiction over real property facilities. DoW Components with jurisdiction over RPAs report the assets on the GF financial statements. (see FASAB TB 20172). 10 U.S.C. § 2674 and DoDD
5110.04 delegate jurisdiction over its facilities to Washington Headquarters Services (WHS). The DoW Components’ WCF financial statements include real property if the WCF has jurisdiction over a specific installation. The RPA Command Claimant Code identifies the Service organization that has direct command authority over an RPA. This code must be reviewed whenever tenant agreements change. The RPA Financial Reporting Organization Code identifies the organization responsible for reporting and depreciating the original asset, capital improvement, or both on its financial statements.

7.1.4.2.2. The Host Installation must report real property on its financial statements where the RPA is located, or as identified on the OSW-approved Enduring Location Master List for real property outside the U.S. The OSW identifies jurisdiction in the consolidated real property database. The Office of the Assistant Secretary of War (OASW) Acquisition and Sustainment (A&S) (Energy, Installations and Environment) maintains and manages the database. The OASW A&S helps resolve financial reporting responsibility disputes between Host Installations. Non-DoW entities report their funded RPAs located on a DoW installation.

7.1.4.2.3. One reporting DoW Component must treat assets assigned to/from another reporting DoW Component as transfers of assets per SFFAS 7.

7.1.4.2.4. Financial reporting responsibility includes all aspects of financial reporting and disclosures, including footnote disclosures, Deferred Maintenance & Repair (DM&R), and other RSI.

7.1.4.2.5. Financial reporting documentation must establish the reporting entity’s rights and obligations. Records reflecting the Host Installation jurisdiction, inter- and intra-agency agreements, and host-tenant relationships are examples.

7.1.4.2.6. The DoW’s and the Federal Government’s overall accounting records must not be duplicative. Where doubt exists as to which DoW Component recognizes the RPA, the DoW Components involved must reach agreement on which entity records the asset for financial reporting purposes. If an agreement cannot be reached, the involved parties must refer the matter to OASW (Sustainment) for resolution. Requesters must accompany requests for resolution with adequate supporting documentation and submit them through the DoW Component Financial Management and Comptroller.

7.1.5. Treatment. For the treatment of real property, refer to the Volume 4 Supplemental document.

7.1.6. Construction In Progress. The Funding DoW Components must report construction costs for a capital asset anticipated to meet the capitalization criteria of the Host Installation in CIP until the capital asset is complete. Once complete and placed in service, the Host Installation reports and depreciates the asset on the GF’s financial statements. The WCF financial statements report real property if it has jurisdiction over a specific installation.

7.1.7. Intra-DoW Transfers. Both parties must agree to and document the transfer (e.g., DD Form 1354). The transferor must provide adequate and appropriate supporting documentation for financial statement reporting. Financial reporting information must be maintained with the asset throughout its lifecycle. When DoW Components have different capitalization thresholds, previously capitalized assets by the transferring DoW Component remain capitalized and will depreciate after transfer, regardless of the new financial reporting entity’s capitalization threshold. Assets previously expensed by the transferring DoW Component must remain expensed within the new entity. The receiving DoW Components must include the assets in their Accountable Property System of Record (APSR) as accountable real property.

7.1.8. Memorandum of Agreement. All DoW Component tenants must have a MOA with the Host Installations. An MOA establishes rights and obligations between the Host Installation and the DoW Component using the RPA. All tenants must maintain a list of occupied real property facilities and facilities for which operations, maintenance, or improvement is the tenant’s responsibility (see DoDI 4000.19 for DoW policy on intra-departmental support).

7.1.9. WCF Capital Recovery Rate and Accounting Treatment. Refer to the Volume 4 Supplemental.

7.1.10. Inter-Entity Costs

7.1.10.1. SFFAS 55 requires recognition of significant inter-entity costs among and between federal agencies by business-type activities (e.g., WCFs). Unless otherwise directed by the OMB, non-business-type activities may elect not to recognize inter-entity costs, but personnel benefits and U.S. Department of the Treasury (Treasury) Judgment Fund settlements must be recognized. DoD elected not to recognize imputed costs and corresponding financing, aside from the exceptions stated in this subparagraph.

7.1.10.2. WCFs or other business-like activities must impute costs. These imputed costs include depreciation expense, estimated depreciation expense for WCF-funded RPAs and improvements subsequently posted to the GF, and depreciation expense or other costs for assets not funded by the WCF. See the ODCFO SFIS webpage for imputed costs journal entries (transaction code E402). The decision tree in the Volume 4 Supplemental document illustrates what RPA-related costs must be imputed and reported by a DoW Component for business-type activity (e.g., WCF). Accounting for imputed costs in the decision tree applies only to business- type activities (e.g., WCFs).

7.1.11. Accounting for Real Property Outside of the U.S.

7.1.11.1. As used in this section, U.S. means the 50 States of the U.S., the District of Columbia, and the commonwealths, territories, and possessions of the U.S. DoW Components occupy and use real property facilities outside of the U.S. DoW’s rights to real property outside of the U.S. are different from those within the U.S. For financial reporting purposes, a DoW Component that occupies and uses facilities outside of the U.S. is covered by paragraph 7.1.11.2 and the Supplemental.

7.1.11.2. The Host Installation financial statements report DoW real property that is not located on a DoW installation (including property located on an installation of a host nation) identified on the OSW-approved Enduring Location Master List (which the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Policy maintains and manages) when all of the criteria are met. See Volume 4 Supplemental for the required criteria in Section 7.1.11.

7.1.12. Disclosure Requirements for Land and Permanent Land Rights.

7.1.12.1. DoW Components must disclose, in the notes to their financial statements, referencing the Balance Sheet, the number of acres of General PP&E land and permanent land rights (where the types of land rights are conducive to measurement in acres) held as of the period of their first audited financial statement. This acreage amount must be reported separately from the DoW Component’s Stewardship Land. There are no disclosure requirements for General PP&E land rights that are not measured in acres when establishing opening balances. The disclosure requirements for land and permanent land rights must be presented in accordance with SFFAS 59. Existing disclosures must continue.

7.1.12.2. DoW Components must disclose the number of acres of General PP&E land and land rights measured in acres held at the beginning of each reporting period, the number of acres added during the period, the number of acres disposed of during the period, and the number of acres held at the end of each reporting period.

7.1.13. Capital Improvements. For Land and Permanent Land Rights, capital improvements are covered in the Volume 4 Supplemental document.

7.1.13.1. The DoW Component that reports the improved RPA reports capital improvements (including leasehold improvements).

7.1.13.2. Maintenance and repair costs are not considered capital improvements, regardless of the capitalization threshold.

7.1.14. Depreciation

7.1.14.1. The recorded cost of real property and capital improvements must be depreciated over the shorter of (1) the period benefited, or (2) the asset’s useful life. Depreciation is the systematic and rational allocation of the recorded cost of an asset, less its estimated salvage/residual value, over its estimated useful life.

7.1.14.2. Capitalized amounts, as well as associated amounts of accumulated depreciation and depreciation expense, must be reflected in DoW financial statements. Recognize depreciation expense for all capitalized general PP&E. Estimates of useful life for RPAs must consider factors such as usage, physical wear and tear, and technological change. To compute depreciation on DoW RPAs, specific useful lives are prescribed.

7.1.14.3. The placed-in-service date (PISD) triggers the depreciation calculation (regardless of whether it is used). Depreciation is generally based on the Month Available for Service method. The month the asset was available for use is used to calculate depreciation expense for the first year.

7.1.14.4. Components must use only the straight-line method of depreciation for RPAs. Straight-line depreciation expense is calculated as the recorded cost (less salvage value, if applicable) divided by the asset’s useful life based on the useful lives.

7.1.14.5. If an asset remains in use longer than its estimated useful life, it must be retained in the APSR, as well as the accounting records, and reflect both its recorded cost and accumulated depreciation until disposition of the asset.

7.1.14.6. WCF activities must depreciate RPAs in accordance with this section guidance, whether such assets are procured through the WCF activity’s Capital Purchase/Investment Program budget or depreciation is included in rates charged to customers. The WCF activities may recognize and depreciate assets differently for financial statement reporting purposes than for WCF rate development and budget presentation. All WCF real property depreciation must be expensed on the Statement of Net Cost, included in accumulated depreciation amounts on the Balance Sheet, and reported in the “Defense Working Capital Fund Accounting Report (Monthly) 1307 (AR(M)1307).” Depreciation recorded on real property that was neither acquired nor replaced through the use of DWCF resources must be classified as non- recoverable for rate-setting purposes and reported on the AR(M)1307. DWCF rates charged to customers are based on guidance in Volume 2 and Volume 11.

7.1.14.7. Annex 1 Scenarios I and II in the Volume 4 Supplemental document illustrate the depreciation methodology for capital improvements and the underlying RPA.

7.1.14.8. Impairment. For more information on impairment, refer to the Volume 4 Supplemental document.

7.1.15. Removal/Disposal

7.1.15.1. FASAB TR 14 defines removal from service as an event that terminates the use of a real property asset. Removal from service may occur due to various factors, such as damage or obsolescence, or because the asset is identified as excess to mission needs. For a removal to be considered permanent, two business events must occur: (1) the asset’s use is terminated, and (2) there is documented evidence of the decision to permanently remove the asset from service. If only one of these two events has occurred, the action is considered an other-than- permanent removal.

7.1.15.2. If an asset no longer provides service in the entity's operations, but the DoW Component has not permanently removed it from service, the Component must account for the asset as an 'other than permanent' removal. Continuing low-level maintenance provides evidence of this 'other than permanent' removal status. The value of these assets does not change, and the Component must continue to depreciate them.

7.1.15.3. The DoW Component no longer depreciates assets it has permanently removed from service. A permanent removal occurs when the DoW Component documents its decision to dispose of an asset. Upon permanent removal, the Component must remove the recorded cost and accumulated depreciation/amortization from the accounts and record the asset at its NRV (see SFIS webpage Transaction Code C613). NRV is the estimated amount the Component can recover from selling or otherwise disposing of an item, less the estimated costs of completion, holding, and disposal. The Component must recognize any difference between the Net Book Value (NBV) and the asset's expected NRV as a gain or loss. The Component must also evaluate the expected NRV at the end of each fiscal year and recognize any change as a gain or loss.

7.1.15.4. When an asset is sold, donated, or demolished, the asset must be written off, and the difference between disposal proceeds and the asset’s NBV must be recognized as a gain or loss. The legally enforceable disposal obligation date is the disposal date. It is the demolition contract’s start date. For transfers to a non-DoW entity and sales, it is the instrument endorsement or the operation end date, whichever comes later. For natural disasters, it is the date of complete loss.

7.1.16.3. Physical Inventories of Real Property

7.1.16.3.1. The Military Departments and WHS must reconcile, at least annually, their real property inventory records with all other DoW Components that occupy, operate, or maintain facilities or land for which the Military Departments or WHS have real property accountability. This reconciliation ensures both parties maintain accurate records of the asset’s use, location, and basic characteristics. In the final review, the host installation must ensure it accurately reports all assets in its APSR.

7.1.16.3.2. DoW Components must perform an inspection of each RPA record, including a physical inspection of each RPA, every 5 years; however, RPAs designated with historic status must be reviewed and physically inspected every 3 years and reported in accordance with DoDI 4715.16. Assets identified with RPA Historic Status Code - “Eligible for the purposes of a Program Alternative – ELPA” do not require inspection every 3 years, and may follow the regular 5-year inspection schedule in accordance with DoDI 4165.14.

7.1.16.4. Deferred Maintenance & Repairs

7.1.16.4.1. FASAB SFFAS 42 defines Deferred Maintenance and Repairs (DM&R) as maintenance and repairs that the Component did not perform when scheduled, instead delaying them to a future period. DM&R includes preventive maintenance; replacement of parts, systems, or components; and other activities the Component must perform to preserve or maintain the asset in working condition.

7.1.16.4.2. Measurement

7.1.16.4.2.1. The values reported for DM&R must be consistent with the Facility Condition Index ratings and Facility Plant Replacement Values.

7.1.16.4.2.2. DoW Components must determine acceptable condition standards and which DM&R measurement methods to apply. They must consistently apply these condition standards and measurement methods. If the DoW Components determine that changes are necessary, they must document the rationale for the change(s) and the related impact on the DM&R estimate.

7.1.16.4.2.3. DoW Components must measure DM&R for capitalized, non-capitalized, and fully depreciated real property. They must include DM&R for inactive real property when they report the asset with an operational status of 'caretaker' or 'non- functional.' The DM&R measurement must account for both funded and unfunded delayed maintenance and repairs. The Component must ensure the data does not include DM&R funded with NAFs' commissary surcharge or from non-DoW sources.

7.1.16.4.3. Required Supplemental Information. The Host Installation reporting real property must report DM&R material amounts as RSI. See Volume 6 for required RSI reporting.

7.1.16.5. Financial Statement Disclosure Reporting and Representation Requirements.

7.1.16.5.1. DoW Components reporting real property must reference the Balance Sheet note disclosing information about the reported RPAs.

7.1.16.5.2. The management representation letter provided to the IPA (for audited DoW Components), and the financial statement notes must fully and completely disclose how reported real property complies with this section’s policies.

7.1.16.5.3. DoW Components must disclose in the financial statement notes when a host nation/foreign government provides real property without reimbursement, and that the financial statements do not contain amounts for these properties. The agreement’s general nature must be disclosed. The host nation/foreign government’s geographic location must not be disclosed.

7.1.16.5.4. In accordance with SFFAS 55, DoW Components must disclose in the financial statement notes that inter-entity (imputed) costs are recognized for business-type activities (if applicable), employee benefits, and claims to be settled by the Treasury Judgment Fund. Other federal entities provide these goods and services at no cost or at a cost less than the full cost, as applicable. Unreimbursed costs of goods and services other than those identified in the preceding sentence are not included in DoW financial statements.

7.1.16.5.5. Refer to Volume 6 for additional disclosure reporting requirements.

7.2    GENERAL EQUIPMENT

7.2.1. Accounting for General Equipment

Transferred Equipment. Transfers of equipment must adhere to the cost recorded for general equipment transferred from another DoW Component or Federal agency as the cost recorded on the transferring entity’s books for the general equipment, net of any accumulated depreciation (i.e., net book value). To prevent intergovernmental transaction elimination issues, the receiving DoW component must ensure the transfer-in amount it records aligns with the document it received from the transferring agency. If the receiving DoW Component cannot reasonably ascertain those amounts, the cost of the asset will be its fair value at the time of transfer. Accountability for general equipment transferred between entities must comply with DoDI
5000.64. Refer to DoDI 1225.06 for equipment transfers by entities other than DoW and Reserve Components.

7.2.2. Valuation. Refer to the Volume 4 Supplemental.

7.2.3. Alternate Valuation Methods for Establishing Opening Balances.

7.2.3.1. The alternative valuation methods for establishing opening balances for general PP&E are available only once to each reporting entity. Therefore, prior to the establishment of opening balances for general equipment, DoW Components must validate that they account for and comply with the recognition, measurement, presentation, and disclosure requirements for general equipment at historical cost in accordance with FASAB SFFAS 6, as amended by SFFAS 50. Components must prepare and retain documentation to support compliance with the recognition, measurement, presentation, and disclosure requirements to meet audit requirements. When a Component cannot apply historical cost as outlined in SFFAS 6, Deemed Cost is acceptable to estimate the initial amounts (historical cost) to establish the opening balances for general equipment.

7.2.3.2. When evaluating general equipment for the purpose of establishing opening balances, DoW Components must apply the applicable capitalization threshold to their entire population of general equipment retroactively.

7.2.3.3. DoW Components must calculate a gross value and an accumulated depreciation value for General Equipment assets when establishing opening balances using Deemed Cost.

7.2.3.4. DoW component reporting entities applying deemed cost in establishing opening balances for general PP&E must disclose in the notes to their financial statements that they used an alternative valuation method and describe the methods used in the first reporting period in which the reporting entity makes an unreserved assertion that its financial statements, or one or more line items, are presented fairly in accordance with GAAP. An unreserved assertion is an unconditional statement. Financial statements or, as applicable, reports on line items of subsequent periods need not repeat this disclosure, unless the financial statements for which deemed cost was applied in establishing opening balances are presented for comparative purposes. No disclosure of the distinction or breakout of the amount of deemed cost of general PP&E included in the opening balance is required.

7.2.3.5. Refer to the Volume 4 Supplemental for deemed cost estimates.

7.2.3.5.1. Replacement Cost. The amount required for an entity to replace the remaining service potential of an existing asset in a current transaction at the reporting date, including the amount that the entity would receive from disposing of the asset at the end of its useful life.

7.2.3.5.2. Estimated Historical Cost (initial amount). A reasonable estimate of historical (acquisition) cost.

7.2.3.5.3. Fair Value. The amount at which an asset or liability could be exchanged in a current transaction between willing parties, other than in a forced or liquidation sale.

7.2.3.6. DoW Components that anticipate substantial use of replacement cost or fair value methodologies for equipment valuation must contact the OUSW(C))/ ODCFO and the Office of the Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Logistics prior to committing significant resources to these methods.

7.2.3.7. Refer to the Volume 4 Supplemental for estimated historical cost.

7.2.4. Recognition

7.2.4.1. Recognition requires appropriate accounting treatment (expense or capitalization with depreciation) and reporting of capitalized amounts and accumulated depreciation on the DoW Component’s financial statements.

7.2.4.2. Recognition Responsibility. The entity that has accountability for a general equipment asset, as defined in DoDI 5000.64, has financial reporting responsibility for that asset from purchase or construction, upon transfer of title (receipt, delivery, or acceptance), and through disposal, or when another entity takes physical accountability for the asset.

7.2.4.3. Recognition Uncertainty. The DoW and the Federal Government must ensure that the accounting records are not duplicative. In situations where doubt exists about which DoW Component must recognize an item, the DoW Components involved must reach an agreement with the other applicable DoW Components or Federal agencies on which entity will record the item for financial reporting purposes. Disputes between DoW Components regarding accountability for an asset under DoDI 5000.64 guidelines may be resolved by contacting the Office of the Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Logistics.

7.2.4.4. Recognition Timing. Recognition of general equipment for financial reporting purposes must occur upon delivery to the acquiring DoW Component. Delivery occurs when the title passes to the customer. Delivery or constructive delivery must be made in accordance with the contract terms.

7.2.4.5. Capitalization Thresholds. The DoW capitalization threshold for general equipment is $15,000,000 for General Fund (GF) and $500,000 for Working Capital Fund (WCF) activities. DoW Components must capitalize general equipment with a recorded cost that equals or exceeds these applicable thresholds, provided the asset has a useful life of at least two years, and depreciate the cost over its useful life. Conversely, Components must expense general equipment with a recorded cost below the applicable threshold or with a useful life of less than 2 years, except for items acquired as part of a qualifying bulk purchase. Transitional Guidance: Components adopting these thresholds must coordinate with the ODCFO for specific application instructions. Capitalization thresholds may be applied prospectively for components with established opening balances, whereas entities that establish opening balances using deemed cost must apply them retrospectively. Components are eligible to retain existing balances below the Departments capitalization threshold, or apply a lower threshold for component-level reporting, with DCFO approval.

7.2.4.6. DoW Components must capitalize special tooling, special test equipment, and other similar equipment items that meet or exceed the appropriate capitalization threshold with a useful life of at least two years at the time of delivery. Per SFFAS 6, general equipment must be recognized when title passes to the acquiring entity or when it is delivered to the entity or an agent of the entity. The component must recognize the general equipment acquired by the contractor on behalf of the DoW Component, for which the Government will ultimately hold title.

7.2.4.7. Bulk Purchases.

7.2.4.7.1. Each DoW Component must establish guidance on applying DoW capitalization thresholds to its bulk purchases. DoW Components must document their rationale for the accounting treatment of bulk purchases and retain the documentation for audit purposes in accordance with their DoW Component records retention requirements.

7.2.4.7.2. For financial accounting, a bulk purchase is a single contractual/purchase arrangement of multiple like general equipment items within a fiscal year. For bulk purchases made under a single, multi-year contractual/purchase arrangement, DoW Components must consider aggregate purchases on a fiscal-year basis.

7.2.4.7.3. The DoW Component must consider whether period costs on the Statement of Net Costs would be materially overstated and/or asset values on the Balance Sheet would be materially understated by expensing bulk purchases. SFFAS 1 defines materiality as the degree to which an item's omission or misstatement in a financial statement makes it probable that the judgment of a reasonable person relying on the information would have been changed or influenced by the omission or the misstatement. To determine materiality, the DoW Component must exercise appropriate and reasonable professional judgment.

7.2.4.7.4. In the instance where more than one DoW Component has the authority to place orders under the same contractual/purchase arrangement, the component must consider only those orders it funds for purposes of bulk purchase evaluation and not those funded by other DoW Components.

7.2.4.8. CIP. Funding DoW Components must report and record constructed general equipment in the CIP account (when expected to meet capitalization criteria of the component that will own the asset) until they complete and place it in service, at which time they must transfer the balance to the general equipment USSGL account. The CIP account accumulates costs of new construction of general PP&E and capital improvements while the asset is under construction. CIP accounts include all costs incurred in construction (i.e., direct labor, direct materials, supervision, inspection, and overhead).

7.2.4.9. Accounting for General Equipment Outside of the United States. The “United States” is defined as the 50 States of the United States, the District of Columbia, and the commonwealths, territories, and possessions of the United States. DoW’s rights to general equipment outside of the United States may be different from those within the United States. For financial reporting purposes, a DoW Component that uses general equipment outside of the United States must adhere to the following guidance:

7.2.4.9.1. DoW Components must recognize a general equipment asset on their financial statements in accordance with the guidance provided throughout the other provisions of this section if the DoW Component purchases the general equipment asset outside of the host nation/foreign country to which it is bringing the general equipment.

7.2.4.9.2. DoW Components must evaluate any foreign legal restrictions or terms of any agreement with the host nation/foreign government to determine the accounting treatment if a DoW Component both purchases and uses the general equipment in the foreign country as follows:

7.2.4.9.3. If a general equipment acquisition is not funded/purchased by DoW but instead provided by the host nation/foreign government and the terms and use of the general equipment are set out in an agreement between the DoW Component and the host nation/foreign government, the DoW Component will recognize the general equipment as a right- to-use leased asset. Refer to Volume 4 Supplemental section 7.3.

7.2.4.9.4. SFFAS 4 and SFFAS 55 address imputed costs between Federal agencies. The concept of imputed costs does not apply to activities between a DoW Component and a host nation/foreign government. Therefore, a DoW Component will not record imputed costs for the use of general equipment, for which it does not pay directly or pay through reimbursement, provided by international organizations (e.g., NATO) or host nations/foreign governments.

7.2.4.9.5. The DoW Component must record accountable general equipment it uses in an APSR, including those that have not been capitalized for accounting and financial reporting purposes in accordance with DoDI 5000.64.

7.2.4.9.6. The DoW Component must record an expense for any maintenance and sustainment costs that they incur or will incur relating to the general equipment paid for. Maintenance and sustainment costs refer to costs that do not meet the criteria for capitalization of an improvement.

7.2.5. Capital Improvements are modifications, modernizations, upgrades, remanufacturing, and enhancements and must be capitalized when the improvement increases the asset's useful life by two or more years, or increases the asset's capability, or increases its capacity or size, and when the cost of the improvement equals or exceeds the capitalization threshold. If capital improvements do not meet these two criteria, they must be expensed. If the capital improvement extends the useful life of the underlying general equipment asset by two years or more, the DoW Component must capitalize and depreciate the improvement alongside the original general equipment over the revised estimated useful life. If the costs of capital improvements do not extend the useful life of an existing general equipment asset but enhance its capacity and have a useful life of two years or more, the DoW Component must capitalize and depreciate these costs over the lesser of the estimated useful life of the improvement or the remaining estimated economic useful life of the underlying general equipment asset.

7.2.6. Depreciation

7.2.6.1. Depreciation is the systematic and rational allocation of the recorded cost of an asset, less its estimated salvage or residual value, over its estimated useful life. The DoW entity must depreciate the recorded cost of capitalized general equipment and capital improvements.

7.2.6.2. Capitalized amounts, as well as associated amounts of accumulated depreciation and depreciation expense, must be reflected in DoW financial statements. The depreciable basis of an asset is the recorded cost reduced by the asset’s salvage value (if applicable).

7.2.6.3. The event that triggers the calculation of depreciation is the date of receipt shown on the asset receiving document in cases where no installation is required; the date installed (if required); or the date the asset is available for use, also known as the acceptance date.

7.2.6.4. If an asset remains in use longer than its estimated useful life, it must be retained in the APSR, as well as the accounting records, and reflect both its recorded cost and accumulated depreciation until disposition of the asset.

7.2.6.5. WCF activities must depreciate general equipment assets in accordance with the guidance in this section for financial reporting purposes without regard to whether assets are procured through a WCF activity’s Capital Purchase/Investment Program budget or whether depreciation for such assets is included in rates charged to customers.

7.2.6.5.1. The recognition of general equipment assets and depreciation of such assets by WCF activities may differ for financial statement reporting purposes from amounts used for WCF rate development and budget presentation.

7.2.6.5.2. DWCF rates charged to customers are based on guidance in Volume 2 and Volume 11.

7.2.7. Impairment - Refer to the Procedures document for more information.

7.2.8. Removal/Disposal

7.2.8.1. FASAB TR 14 paragraph 8 defines removal from service as an event that terminates the use of a general equipment asset. Removal from service may occur because of a change in the manner or duration of use, a change in technology, obsolescence, damage from natural disasters or use in operations, or identification as excess to mission needs. Permanent removal from service is evident from the DoW Component’s documented decision to dispose of an asset by selling, scrapping, recycling, donating, or demolishing the asset.

7.2.8.2. Removals from service must be considered other than permanent unless the asset’s use is terminated and there is documented evidence of the DoW Component’s decision to permanently remove the asset from service, or if only one of the two business events has occurred, permanent removal from service has not occurred.

7.2.8.3. When an asset is disposed of (e.g., by selling, scrapping, recycling, donating, or demolishing the asset), the asset must be written off, and the difference between any disposal proceeds and the asset’s net book value must be recognized as a gain or loss. Disposals of general equipment will be conducted in accordance with DoDM 4160.21.

7.2.8.3.1. The disposal start date is the calendar date of a legally enforceable and recognizable obligation to complete the disposal action. For demolitions, this represents the demolition contract’s start date. For transfers to a non-DoW entity and sales, this represents the date on which the instrument is endorsed, or the operation is ceased, whichever comes later. For natural disasters, this represents the actual incident date if the asset is a complete loss.

7.2.8.3.2. All disposals or retirements must be supported as of the date the general equipment leaves the custody of the DoW Component to provide an adequate audit trail for the disposal of the asset. The execution of certain disposal events will generate financial or administrative accountability transactions.

7.2.8.4. Plant clearance officers follow the direction of the FAR Subpart 45.6, Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS) Subpart 245.6, and DFARS Procedures, Guidance, and Information (PGI) 245.602-70. Following the plant clearance officer’s acceptance of an inventory disposal schedule, the property must be screened for reutilization DoW- wide. Surplus personal property with commercial value that is processed through the reutilization screening process without success may be sold. Proceeds of any sale of surplus property are to be credited to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, unless otherwise provided by statute or the contract or any subcontract thereunder authorizing the proceeds to be credited to the price or cost of the work per 40 U.S.C. § 571 and § 574, FAR 45.604-3.

7.2.9. Additional Considerations

7.2.9.1 Use of Canceled TAS, Refer to the Volume 4 Supplemental.

7.2.9.2 Documentation Requirements
7.2.9.2.1. Financial transactions in the accounting system, general ledger accounts, the APSR, and/or other systems must be supported by source documents affecting the Component’s investment in the general equipment.

7.2.9.2.2. All general equipment acquisitions, whether by purchase, transfer from other agencies, donation, or other means, must be supported as of the date of delivery and acceptance (including acceptance where constructive receipt has occurred) by the DoW Component.
7.2.9.2.3. Items must be assigned a dollar value (i.e., acquisition cost) when recording the general equipment item in the APSR and/or accounting system. The dollar value must be supported by appropriate documentation describing the reasons for changes in asset value or physical attributes resulting from a new acquisition or capital improvement.

7.2.9.2.4. DoW Components must retain supporting documents for the cost of general equipment assets in accordance with their DoW Component records retention requirements. Documentation (original documents and/or hard and electronic copies of the originals) must be maintained in a designated location during the applicable retention period to support audit compliance.

7.2.9.2.5. The APSR and/or other systems must be designed to support procurement and utilization decisions, including decisions related to identifying potential excess general equipment that may be available for reuse, transfer to other DoW Components, or made available for disposal in accordance with current DoW regulations and other regulatory requirements.

7.2.9.3. Physical Inventories of General Equipment

7.2.9.3.1. DoW Components must perform periodic physical inventories of general equipment in accordance with DoDI 5000.64.

7.2.9.3.2. All DoW Components (i.e., Military Departments, Washington Headquarters Service, and Other Defense Organizations) must reconcile their APSR to their financial statements (or to their trial balance if financial statements are not required to be prepared) quarterly.
7.2.9.3.3. While conducting physical inventories, DoW components should consider if any general equipment shows potential evidence of impairment and if any general equipment does not appear to be in use, where it has not been used for a significant period.

7.2.9.4. Deferred Maintenance and Repairs. For more information, refer to the Volume 4 Supplemental document.

7.2.9.5 Disclosure Requirements

7.2.9.5.1. DoW Components with general equipment must reference a note on the Balance Sheet that discloses information about the reported general equipment assets. Note 1 of the financial statements must include a disclosure related to the DoW Component’s general equipment reporting accounting policy. DoW Components must state that they are financially reporting on property for which they have accountability, in accordance with DoDI 5000.64. Additionally, DoW Components must disclose that they may use assets to complete their mission that are reported in the financial statements of another DoW Component. See Volume 6 for the specific disclosure requirements.

7.2.9.5.2. DoW Components must disclose in the notes to the financial statements those instances where they are using general equipment provided by a host nation/foreign government without reimbursement by DoW to the host nation/foreign government, as applicable, that (1) The DoW Component is utilizing general equipment provided by and owned by a host nation/foreign government in its operations OCONUS without reimbursement by DoW to the host nation/foreign government The DoW Component is utilizing general equipment provided by and owned by a host nation/foreign government in its OCONUS operations without reimbursement by DoW to the host nation/foreign government, and there are no amounts recorded in the financial statements related to these assets, and (2) the general nature of the agreement with the host nation/foreign government is not intended or recommended to disclose the geographic location of the foreign government/host nation.

7.3    ACCOUNTING FOR LEASES

This policy outlines DoW's accounting for leases, covering instances in which DoW is both a lessee and a lessor, in accordance with SFFAS 54. This policy does not apply to leases of internal use software (IUS), leases of assets under construction, or budgetary accounting for capital leases and lease purchases, as detailed in OMB Circular A-11.

7.3.1. Short-Term Leases (Non-Intragovernmental)

7.3.1.1. Lessee Treatment of Short-Term Leases. A DoW Component, as the lessee, must recognize short-term lease payments as an expense based on the payment provisions of the contract or agreement and standards regarding recognition of accounts payable and other related amounts. The DoW Component (lessee) must recognize an asset if payments are made in advance of the reporting period to which they relate or liability for rent due and unpaid at the end of the reporting period to which they relate. Rental increases, rental decreases, lease incentives, and lease concessions must be recognized when incurred as increases/reductions to lease rental expenses.

7.3.1.2. Lessor Treatment of Short-Term Leases. A DoW Component, as the lessor, must recognize short-term lease payments as revenue based on the payment provisions of the contract or agreement and standards regarding recognition of accounts receivable and other related amounts. The DoW Component (lessor) must recognize a liability if payments are received in advance of the reporting period to which they relate or an asset for rent due and to be received after the reporting period to which they relate. Rental increases, rental decreases, lease incentives, and lease concessions must be recognized when incurred as increases/reductions to lease rental income.

7.3.2. Contracts or Agreements That Transfer Ownership

If a contract or agreement (a) transfers ownership of the underlying asset to a lessee by the end of the term and (b) does not contain termination options (other than a non-probable cancellation clause), then the lessee must report it as an asset purchase, or the lessor must report it as a financed asset sale. For this purpose, options to purchase the underlying asset prior to the transfer of ownership are not considered options to terminate.

7.3.3. Intragovernmental Leases

7.3.3.1. Any lease, regardless of the lease term, that meets the definition of an intragovernmental lease must follow the following accounting and disclosure guidance.

7.3.3.2. Lessee Treatment of Intragovernmental Leases

7.3.3.2.1. Lease Payments. A DoW Component, as the lessee must recognize lease payments, including lease-related operating costs (for example, maintenance, utilities, and taxes) paid to the lessor, as expenses based on the payment provisions of the contract or agreement and standards regarding recognition of accounts payable and other related amounts. Prepaid rent or rent payable must be recognized as an asset or liability, respectively, and an expense must be recognized in the appropriate reporting period based on the specifics of the lease provisions.

7.3.3.2.2. Leasehold Improvements. Leasehold improvements that meet or exceed the capitalization threshold and are placed in service at or after the beginning of the lease term must be amortized over the useful life (the normal operating life in terms of utility to the lessee) of the leasehold improvement, but no longer than the expected lease term. This recognition is consistent with PP&E capital improvements outlined in SFFAS 6.

7.3.3.2.3. Disclosures. A DoW Component as the lessee must disclose the following regarding intragovernmental lease activities (which may be grouped for purposes of disclosure): (1) a general description of significant intragovernmental leasing arrangements, including general lease terms with any applicable specific intragovernmental requirements; and
(2) annual lease expense in total and by major underlying asset category.

7.3.3.3. Lessor Treatment of Intragovernmental Leases

7.3.3.3.1. Lease Payments. A DoW Component, as the lessor must recognize lease receipts, including lease-related operating costs (for example, maintenance, utilities, or taxes) received from the lessee as income based on the provisions of the contract or agreement and standards regarding recognition of accounts receivable and other related amounts. Rent paid in advance, or a lease receivable, must be recognized as a liability or asset, respectively, and income must be recognized in the appropriate reporting period based on the specifics of the lease provisions.

7.3.3.3.2. Lessor Improvements. Lessor improvements, which are elements of the leased property that meet or exceed the capitalization threshold, must be capitalized and depreciated by the lessor over their useful life. This accounting treatment aligns with the lessor’s handling of PP&E and is consistent with the capital improvement guidelines outlined in SFFAS 6.

7.3.3.3.3. Disclosures. Lessors must disclose the following regarding intragovernmental lease activities (which may be grouped for purposes of disclosure): (1) a general description of significant leases; and (2) future lease payments that are to be received to the end of the lease term for each of the five subsequent fiscal years and in five-year increments thereafter.

7.3.3.4. Other Considerations for Lessees and Lessors

7.3.3.4.1. Fixed Rental Increases/Decreases. Rental increases/decreases may be fixed in the lease and take place over time (for example, be based on such factors as anticipated increases/decreases in costs or anticipated appreciation/depreciation in property values, but the amount of the increase/decrease is specified in the lease), or they may be contingent on future events.

7.3.3.4.2. Variable Rental Increases/Decreases. Rental increases/decreases may also be variable and based on future changes in specific economic factors on which lease payments are based, for example, future sales or usage activity levels or future inflation/deflation (tied to a specific economic indicator where the specific amount of the change is not known).

7.3.3.4.3. Treatment of Rental Increases/Decreases, and Lease Incentives/Concessions. Rental increases/decreases and lease incentives/concessions must be recognized by the lessee and lessor when incurred as increases/reductions to lease rental expense and income, respectively.

7.3.3.4.4. Initial Direct Lease Costs. Initial direct lease costs incurred by the lessee must be expensed when incurred. Initial direct lease costs incurred by the lessor must be expensed when incurred.

7.3.4. Lessee Recognition, Measurement, and Disclosure for Leases Other than Short- Term Leases, Contracts or Agreements that Transfer Ownership, and Intragovernmental Leases.

7.3.4.1. At the commencement of the lease term, a DoW Component as the lessee must recognize a lease liability and a leased asset for leases other than short-term leases, contracts, or agreements that transfer ownership, and intragovernmental leases that meet the capitalization thresholds. For leases that do not meet the capitalization threshold, a lease expense must be recognized in the current period.

7.3.4.2. Lease Liability. A lessee must initially measure the lease liability at the present value of payments expected to be made during the lease term.

7.3.4.3. Variable payments must be recognized as an expense in the reporting period in which those payments are incurred. However, any portion of these variable payments that is fixed in-substance must be included in the lease liability.

7.3.4.4. Interest Rate. The future lease payments must be discounted using the interest rate the lessor charges the lessee. If the interest rate is not stated in the lease, it must be based on the interest rate on marketable Treasury securities at the commencement of the lease term (or at the subsequent financial reporting date), with a similar maturity to the term of the lease (as determined by the Treasury).

7.3.4.5. Remeasurement of Lease Liability. The lessee must remeasure the lease liability at subsequent financial reporting dates if one or more of the following changes have occurred at or before that financial reporting date, based on the most recent lease contract or agreement before the changes, and if the changes individually or in the aggregate are expected to significantly affect the amount of the lease liability since the previous measurement.

7.3.4.6. Lease Asset. A lessee must initially measure the lease asset as the sum of the following:

7.3.4.6.1. The amount of the initial measurement of the lease liability;

7.3.4.6.2. Lease payments made to the lessor (e.g., prepaid rents) at or before the commencement of the lease term, less any lease incentives; and

7.3.4.6.3. Initial direct lease costs that are necessary to place the lease asset into service.

7.3.4.6.4. A lease asset must be amortized systematically and rationally over the shorter of the lease term or the useful life of the underlying asset, except as provided in the following subparagraph.

7.3.4.6.5. If a lease contains a purchase option that the lessee has determined is probable of being exercised, the lease asset must be amortized over the useful life of the underlying asset. However, if the underlying asset will be capitalizable and non-depreciable in the reporting period the purchase option is expected to be exercised, the lease asset must not be amortized. If the underlying asset will be non-capitalizable in the reporting period the purchase option is expected to be exercised, the lease asset must be amortized over the remaining lease term.

7.3.4.6.6. The lease asset generally must be adjusted by the same amount when the lease liability is remeasured. However, if this change reduces the carrying value of the lease asset to zero, any remaining amount must be reported in the statement of net cost as a gain. Changes arising from amendments to a lease contract or agreement must be accounted for under the provisions of lease terminations and modifications.

7.3.4.6.7. Leased assets are subject to SFFAS 44, Accounting for Impairment of General Property, Plant, and Equipment Remaining in Use. Refer to volume 4 Supplemental for more information.

7.3.4.7. Lease Term. The lease term for a lessee is the noncancelable period of the lease, plus any probable additional periods, based on all relevant factors, that it will be included. This includes periods covered by a lessee's option to extend the lease if it is likely they will exercise it. It also includes periods following a lessee's option to terminate the lease if it is probable they will not exercise that option.

7.3.4.8. Disclosure Requirements for Lessees

Lessees must disclose lease activities (which may be grouped for purposes of disclosure), other than short-term leases, contracts or agreements that transfer ownership, and intragovernmental leases.

7.3.5. Lessor Recognition, Measurement, and Disclosures for Leases Other than Short- Term Leases, Contracts or Agreements that Transfer Ownership, and Intragovernmental Leases

7.3.5.1. At the commencement of the lease term, a DoW Component as the lessor must recognize a lease receivable and unearned revenue for leases other than short-term leases, contracts or agreements that transfer ownership, and intragovernmental leases. The lessor must report any initial direct lease costs it incurs as an expense of the period.

7.3.5.2. Lease Receivable. A lessor initially must measure the lease receivable at the present value of lease payments to be received for the lease term, reduced by any provision for uncollectible amounts.

7.3.5.3. Variable payments based on the future performance of the lessee or usage of the underlying asset must not be included in the measurement of the lease receivable. Rather, those payments must be recognized as revenue in the reporting period to which those payments relate. However, any payments that are fixed in-substance must be included in the lease receivable.

7.3.5.4. Amounts to be received under residual value guarantees (that are not fixed in-substance) must be recognized as a receivable and revenue when (a) a guarantee payment is required (as agreed to by the lessee and lessor) and (b) the amount can be reasonably estimated. Amounts to be received for the exercise price of a purchase option or penalty for lease termination must be recognized as a receivable and revenue when those options are exercised.

7.3.5.5. Interest Rate. The future lease payments to be received must be discounted using the interest rate the lessor charges the lessee. If the interest rate is not stated in the lease, it must be based on the interest rate on marketable Treasury securities at the commencement of the lease term (or at the subsequent financial reporting date), with a similar maturity to the term of the lease (as determined by the U.S. Department of the Treasury).

7.3.5.6. A lessor must remeasure the lease receivable if certain changes occur that are expected to affect its amount significantly. These triggers include a change in the lease term, a change in the interest rate the lessor charges, or the resolution of a contingency that fixes previously variable payments. When remeasuring due to a change in the lease term or interest rate, the lessor must also update the discount rate. Additionally, if a remeasurement is already triggered, the receivable must be adjusted for any significant change in an index or rate used for variable payments, though a change in an index or rate by itself does not require remeasurement. It is important to note that changes resulting from an amendment to the lease contract are handled separately under the provisions for lease modifications and terminations.

7.3.5.7. Unearned Revenue

7.3.5.7.1. A lessor must initially measure the unearned revenue to include the following: (1) the amount of the initial measurement of the lease receivable, and (2) lease payments received from the lessee at or before the commencement of the lease term that relates to future periods (for example, the final month’s rent), less (3) any lease incentives paid to, or on behalf of, the lessee at or before the commencement of the lease term.

7.3.5.7.2. A lessor subsequently must amortize the unearned revenue, recognizing it as earned revenue, systematically and rationally over the term of the lease. The unearned revenue generally must be adjusted using the same amount as the change resulting from the remeasurement of the lease receivable. However, if the change reduces the carrying value of the unearned revenue to zero, any remaining amount must be reported in the statement of net cost as a loss.

7.3.5.8. Underlying Asset. A lessor must not derecognize the asset (PP&E) underlying the lease. A lessor must continue to apply other applicable guidance to the underlying asset, including depreciation and impairment. However, if the lease contract or agreement requires the lessee to return the asset in its original or enhanced condition, a lessor must not depreciate the asset during the lease term.

7.3.5.9. Lease Term. The lessor's lease term consists of the noncancelable period plus any additional periods where there is significant evidence that the lessor will act to extend the term. This includes periods covered by a lessor's option to extend, if evidence suggests they will exercise it, and periods following a lessor's option to terminate, if evidence suggests they will not exercise it. When determining the total term, options must be evaluated chronologically, with the lessee's options being considered first. If a decision is made not to add a period based on one option, subsequent options are considered.

7.3.5.10. Disclosure Requirements for Lessors. Lessors must disclose lease activities (which may be grouped for purposes of disclosure), other than short-term leases, contracts or agreements that transfer ownership, and intragovernmental leases.

7.3.6. Lease Incentives and Lease Concessions

7.3.6.1. Lease incentives and lease concessions reduce the amount that a lessee is required to pay for a lease. For leases other than short-term leases and intragovernmental leases, lease incentives and lease concessions that provide payments to, or on behalf of, a lessee at or before the commencement of a lease term are included in the initial measurement by directly reducing the amount of the lease asset.

7.3.6.2. Lease incentive and lease concession payments to be provided after the commencement of the lease term must be accounted for by lessees and lessors as reductions of lease payments for the periods in which the incentive or concession payments will be provided. Those payments must be measured by lessees consistently with the lessee's lease liability and by lessors consistently with the lessor's lease receivable. Accordingly, lease incentive and lease concession payments to be provided after the commencement of the lease term are included in the initial measurement and any remeasurement if they are fixed or fixed in-substance, whereas variable or contingent lease incentive or lease concession payments are not included in the initial measurement.

7.3.6.3. Lessor improvements that are made to or on behalf of the lessee without additional cost to the lessee must be accounted for by the lessee and the lessor consistent with other lease incentives and lease concessions. As leasehold improvements are paid for (financed) by the lessee, leasehold improvements would not be considered a lease incentive or concession received from the lessor.

7.3.7. Contracts or Agreements with Multiple Elements

7.3.7.1. Lessors and lessees may enter into contracts or agreements that contain multiple elements, such as a contract or agreement that contains both a lease element and a non- lease element, or a lease that contains multiple underlying assets.

7.3.7.2. If a lessor or lessee enters into a contract or agreement that contains both a lease and non-lease elements (such as maintenance services for the building), the lease and non- lease elements must be accounted for as separate contracts or agreements unless the contract or agreement if any prices for individual elements appear to be unreasonable or it is not practicable to determine the best estimate for price allocation for some or all elements in a contract or agreement. In this instance, some or all elements in a contract or agreement must be accounted for as a single lease unit.

7.3.7.3. If a lease involves multiple underlying assets and the assets have different lease terms, the lessor and lessee must account for each underlying asset as a separate lease element. An exception exists if the contract or agreement does not include prices for individual elements or if any of those prices appear to be unreasonable.

7.3.7.4. To allocate the contract or agreement price to the different elements, lessors and lessees must first use any prices for individual elements that are included in the contract or agreement, as long as the price allocation does not appear to be unreasonable based on the terms of the contract or agreement and professional judgment, maximizing the use of observable information, for example, using readily available observable stand-alone prices.

7.3.7.5. If multiple elements are accounted for as a single lease unit, the accounting for that unit must be based on the primary lease element within that unit. For example, the primary lease element’s lease term must be used for the unit if the lease elements have different lease terms.

7.3.8. Contract or Agreement Combinations

7.3.8.1. Contracts or agreements that are entered into at or near the same time with the same counterparty must be considered to be part of the same lease contract or agreement if either of the following criteria is met: (1) the contracts or agreements are negotiated as a package with a single objective; and (2) the amount of consideration to be paid in one contract or agreement depends on the price or performance of the other contract or agreement.
7.3.8.2. If multiple contracts or agreements are determined to be part of the same lease contract or agreement, that contract or agreement must be evaluated in accordance with the guidance for contracts or agreements with multiple elements.

7.3.9. Lease Terminations and Modifications

7.3.9.1. Provisions of a lease contract or agreement can be amended while in effect, with common changes including price adjustments, term extensions or reductions, and the addition or removal of an underlying asset. The Component treats an amendment as a lease modification unless the lessee’s right to use the asset decreases, in which case it considers the amendment a partial or full lease termination. In contrast, exercising an existing option, such as an option to extend or terminate the lease, is not considered an amendment but instead follows the guidance for remeasurement.

7.3.9.2. Lease Terminations. The lessee and lessor must account for an amendment during the reporting period resulting in a decrease in the lessee’s right to use the underlying asset (for example, the lease term is shortened, or the number of underlying assets is reduced) as a partial or full lease termination.

7.3.9.3. Lease Modifications. A lease modification is treated as a new, separate lease if it adds an asset not included in the original agreement and the corresponding increase in lease payments is reasonable. If the modification is not accounted for as a separate lease, both the lessee and lessor must adjust their accounting.

7.3.10. Subleases

A sublease involves three parties: the original lessor, the original lessee (who becomes the sub-lessor), and the new lessee. The original lessor and the new lessee continue to apply general lessor and lessee guidance, respectively. Additionally, the lessor transactions related to the sublease must be disclosed separately from the lessee transactions related to the original lease.

7.3.11. Sale-Leaseback Transactions

7.3.11.1. Sale-leaseback transactions involve the sale of an underlying asset by the owner and a lease of the property back to the seller (original owner). A sale-leaseback must include a transaction that qualifies as a sale to be eligible for sale-leaseback accounting. A sale-leaseback transaction that does not include a transaction that qualifies as a sale must be accounted for as a borrowing by both the seller-lessee and the buyer-lessor. Refer to SFFAS 7.

7.3.11.2. In a sale-leaseback transaction, the sale and lease portions are treated as separate transactions. The difference between the capital asset's carrying value and its net sale proceeds is typically reported as unearned revenue or deferred expense, recognized systematically over the lease term in the statement of net cost. However, if the lease qualifies as short-term, this difference must be recognized immediately.

7.3.11.3. A sale-leaseback transaction is considered to have off-market terms if there is a significant difference between: (a) the sales price and the estimated fair value of the asset; or (b) the present value of the contractual lease payments and the estimated present value of what the lease payments for that asset would be at a market price, whichever of the two differences is more readily determinable.

7.3.11.4. A seller-lessee must disclose the terms and conditions of sale-leaseback transactions as part of the disclosures required of a lessee. A buyer-lessor must disclose the terms and conditions as part of the disclosures required of a lessor.

7.3.12. Lease-Leaseback Transactions

In a lease-leaseback transaction, an asset is leased by one party (first party) to another party and then leased back to the first party. A lease-leaseback transaction must be displayed in the financial statements as a net transaction. Both parties to a lease-leaseback transaction must disclose the amounts of the lease and the leaseback separately.
