7.3.14. Intragovernmental Leasehold Reimbursable Work Agreements

7.3.14.1. For intragovernmental reimbursable leasehold work agreements, the customer-lessee is normally expected to be the predominant beneficiary of the acquisition, construction, improvement, and/or alteration to the underlying asset.

7.3.14.2. The provider-lessor would not be expected to derive significant residual economic benefits or services from such reimbursable work under these types of agreements. The provider-lessor must expense the costs incurred for the reimbursable work and recognize the amounts received as reimbursement as intragovernmental revenue.

7.3.14.3. However, for acquisitions, construction, improvements, and/or alterations under an intragovernmental reimbursable leasehold work agreement with an expected useful life beyond the remaining lease term and for which the provider-lessor is expected to derive a significant level of residual economic benefits and services from the reimbursable work, the customer-lessee would not be considered the predominant beneficiary. The customer-lessee and provider-lessor must refer to the following guidance.

7.3.14.3.1. Customer-Lessee. Federal entity that pays for the acquisition, construction, or improvement of an asset provided by a "provider-lessor" on a reimbursable basis. Initially, the customer-lessee must recognize an intragovernmental reimbursable work asset for the amount payable for reimbursable work acquisition, construction, improvement, and/or alteration costs. This asset is then amortized as an expense systematically over the shorter of the remaining lease term or the useful life of the asset or improvement. Customer-lessees are also required to disclose a general description of their significant reimbursable work agreement activities.

7.3.14.3.2. Provider-lessor. Federal entity that handles the acquisition, construction, or improvements of an underlying asset for a customer-lessee on a reimbursable basis. Initially, the provider-lessor must recognize an intragovernmental unearned revenue liability for the amount receivable for this work. This liability is then recognized as revenue systematically over the shorter of the remaining lease term or the useful life of the asset or improvement. Additionally, provider-lessors are required to disclose a general description of their significant reimbursable work agreement activities.

7.3.15. Additional Considerations

7.3.15.1. Standard General Ledger Accounts

The USSGL accounts used to report DoW lease entries are provided in the Transaction Library and Standard Reporting Chart of Accounts available on the Office of the DCFO SFIS web page.

7.3.15.2. Recognition Uncertainty

When there is uncertainty as to which DoW Component should record an item, the involved parties must first attempt to reach an agreement. If they cannot, the matter must be referred to the ODCFO, OUSW(C) for resolution, accompanied by adequate supporting documentation submitted through the Financial Management and Comptroller (FM&C) of the submitting Military Department or Defense Agency. As a general rule, the DoW Component that procures a leased item of PP&E is the one that must initially record the transaction. However, if a different DoW Component ultimately uses and benefits from that leased asset, the responsibility for recognizing the lease asset must be re-evaluated.

7.3.15.3. Bulk Acquisitions Through Leases

To determine proper recognition of bulk acquisitions through leases, the acquisition cost of all like items leased under multiple leases with a single lessor within a fiscal year must be totaled, and the resulting total must be considered against the lease criteria for capitalization and the capitalization threshold.

7.3.15.4. Accounting for OCONUS Real Property Leases and Managed by the Department of State.

For real property leases that are managed by the Department of State, the Department of State’s Bureau of the Comptroller and Global Financial Services will provide relevant lease data to any agencies that occupy real property overseas and will allocate the residential housing pool lease balances (i.e., liability, corresponding right to use asset, and amortization) across the participating agencies.

7.3.15.5. Use of Canceled TAS

Capitalized assets must be reported and remain in GTAS even after the original purchasing TAS has expired and been canceled.

7.3.15.6. Supporting Documentation

DoW Components must support all financial transactions related to leases with source documents reflecting every transaction that affects their investment in the leased asset. The Component must maintain this documentation from the date it takes custody of the asset, link it to the appropriate unique identifier(s), and retain it so it is readily available in accordance with Volume 1. The documents must include sufficient information on the physical quantity, location, and unit cost of the underlying PP&E to support changes in the lease asset's value or physical attributes resulting from new leases, leasehold improvements, impairments, modifications, and terminations. These records must identify and classify PP&E that the Component has capitalized and must enable periodic, independent verification through physical inventories. Furthermore, the Component must integrate and reconcile the Accountable Property System of Record (APSR) with its accounting systems, USSGL accounts, and physical counts. This accountability extends to all PP&E the Department possesses, including leased property held by contractors, and the Component must also account for any improvements made to these leased assets.

7.3.15.7. Physical Inventories of PP&E

DoW Components must perform periodic physical inventories of real property and general equipment in accordance with DoDI 4165.14 and DoDI 5000.64, respectively.

7.3.15.8. Reporting Requirements

DoW Components with leased PP&E must reference a note on the Balance Sheet that discloses information about the reported assets. See Volume 6 for the specific reporting requirements.

7.3.15.9. Environmental Liabilities/Cleanup Costs

The lease agreement must clearly identify the party responsible for environmental liabilities/cleanup costs.

7.4    INTERNAL USE SOFTWARE

This details the DoW accounting policy for IUS, which is a subset of General PP&E. General PP&E, per SFFAS 10, includes IUS and consists of tangible and intangible assets that (1) have an estimated service life of two years or more; (2) are not intended for sale in the ordinary course of business; and (3) are intended to be used or available for use by the entity. The IUS general ledger accounts are listed in the government-wide USSGL contained in Volume 1. The accounting entries for these accounts and the DoW SCOA are specified in the DoW USSGL. Unless otherwise stated, this section is applicable to all DoW Components, including WCF activities.

7.4.1. “Software” includes the application and operating system programs, procedures, rules, and any associated documentation pertaining to the operation of a computer system or program. Most often, software is an integral part of an overall system(s) having interrelationships between software, hardware, personnel, procedures, controls, and data. IUS is software that is acquired or developed to meet the entity’s internal or operational needs (intended purpose). It is a stand-alone application, or the combined software components of an information technology system that can consist of multiple applications, modules, or other software components integrated and used to fulfill the entity’s internal or operational needs (software type).

7.4.2. IUS can be purchased from commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) vendors and be ready for use with little or no changes, internally developed by employees of DoW, including new software and existing or purchased software that is modified with or without a contractor’s assistance; or contractor-developed software that a DoW Component paid a contractor to design, program, install, and implement, including new software and the modification of existing or purchased software.

7.4.3. IUS includes software that is used to operate an entity’s programs (e.g., financial and administrative software, including that used for project management), used to produce the entity’s goods and to provide services (e.g., maintenance work order management and loan servicing); and developed or obtained for internal use and subsequently provided to other Federal Entities with or without reimbursement.

7.4.4. Integrated (embedded) software is not IUS.

7.4.4.1. IUS excludes computer software that integrates with and is necessary for operating General PP&E, rather than performing an application.

7.4.4.2. Software that a DoW Component uses in conjunction with equipment is distinct from integrated or embedded software. The Component can consider this software as IUS if it meets the following criteria: the Component developed the software separately from the equipment; the equipment does not require the software to perform its core purpose and functions; and the Component does not know the quantity of equipment items on which it will install the software.

7.4.4.3. Additionally, the Component may treat software as a separate IUS asset, rather than as integrated or embedded software, when it develops the software separately and installs it on several assets at different times. For example, the Component can treat anti-ballistic missile software that it installs on multiple radar systems at different times as a separate IUS asset, provided the software meets the capitalization threshold.

7.4.4.4. DoW Components may purchase IUS as part of a package of products and services (e.g., training, maintenance, data conversions, reengineering, site licenses and rights to future upgrades and enhancements). They must allocate costs based on the relative fair values of the IUS and the services if the costs are not readily separable between the IUS and the services on the invoice. They must capitalize the cost of the IUS (assuming it meets the capitalization criteria) and expense the cost of the training/maintenance. They must expense non-IUS costs (e.g., training and maintenance services) that are not susceptible to allocation between maintenance and relatively minor enhancements.

7.4.5. USSGL Accounts

7.4.5.1. The DoW Components must record IUS transactions to general ledger accounts in the financial statements required by the Treasury and other reporting requirements mandated by Congress and OMB. The USSGL Transaction Library outlines detailed posting transactions, and the DoW SCOA provides detailed account descriptions. The DoW SCOA is located on the ODCFO SFIS webpage.

7.4.5.2. DoW Components may elect to create subaccounts within their general ledger systems to track software under development at a detailed level; however, the internal subaccounts must summarize to one USSGL/DoW account.

7.4.5.3. Management must retain adequate supporting source documentation for entries in accordance with Volume 1.

7.4.6. Valuation

Record the acquisition and other costs necessary to make the software operable.

7.4.7. Alternative Valuation Methodology for Establishing Opening Balances

7.4.7.1. Establishing Opening Balances for IUS

7.4.7.1.1. The alternative valuation method for establishing opening balances for IUS described in FASAB SFFAS 50: Amending SFFAS 6, SFFAS 10, SFFAS 23, and Rescinding SFFAS 35 is available only once to each reporting entity. Therefore, prior to the establishment of IUS opening balances, DoW Components must validate that they are prepared to account for and comply with the recognition, measurement, presentation, and disclosure requirements for IUS in accordance with FASAB SFFAS 10.

7.4.7.1.2. DoW Components must identify any IUS that they have capitalized prior to establishing opening balances, including capitalized development costs. All DoW Components that have not previously undergone a financial statement audit in which they received an unmodified (i.e., “clean”) audit opinion will exclude the value of all IUS, including development costs, from opening balances of General Property, Plant, and Equipment on their Balance Sheet. A DoW Component that has received a “clean” audit opinion should continue to account for IUS, including development costs, in accordance with FASAB SFFAS 10 and will not reduce their balances to zero.

7.4.7.1.3. Entries in the DoW Component accounting systems/records to record IUS opening balances at zero are subject to the reporting requirements under paragraph 13 of FASAB SFFAS 21, Amendment of SFFAS 7. Accordingly, reflect the entries as a change in accounting principle. Document and support any adjustments to assist ongoing audit efforts.

7.4.7.2. Financial Statement Disclosure Requirements

DoW Components that adjust their opening IUS balances must disclose in their financial statements that they used an alternative valuation method in establishing their opening balances.

7.4.7.3. Prospective Accounting for IUS

7.4.7.3.1. DoW Components must capitalize IUS costs for IUS in-service and IUS in development in accordance with the provisions of FASAB SFFAS 10 after recording the opening balances at zero. This capitalization requirement includes IUS development costs incurred after the establishment of opening balances for projects started prior to the establishment of opening balances. DoW Components must have sufficient source documentation to support the capitalized amounts of IUS based on actual historical cost. DoW Components must apply the provisions of FASAB SFFAS 10 regarding amortization and impairment to any unamortized capitalized cost of the IUS.

7.4.7.3.2. DoW Components must fully implement the systems, internal controls, processes, and procedures to be compliant with accounting for IUS under FASAB SFFAS 10. They must also periodically review and update the documentation of the systems, processes, and procedures as needed.

7.4.8. Recognition

7.4.8.1. DoW Components must recognize all acquired IUS for accountability and financial reporting purposes. Recognition requires the proper accounting treatment (expense or capitalization with amortization) and the reporting of capitalized amounts and accumulated amortization on the appropriate DoW Component’s financial statements.

7.4.8.2. Recognition Responsibility

7.4.8.2.1. The DoW Component’s financial reporting responsibility can be determined using two-tier criteria:

7.4.8.2.1.1. Exclusive/sole Use. When a DoW Component is the exclusive/sole user of capitalized IUS, it will report the IUS on its Balance Sheet. If there is no exclusive/sole user, the DoW Component must apply the second criteria.

7.4.8.2.1.2. Control. If an exclusive/sole user does not exist, the DoW Component that controls the IUS will have financial reporting responsibility. Evidence of control can include funding the software maintenance, exercising access control, and prioritizing enhancements.

7.4.8.2.2. DoW Components that possess and/or control IUS items that materially contribute to the Component’s mission must maintain accounting and financial reporting for such items, regardless of the organization that originally acquired or provided the funding for the items. If a DoW Component prepares financial statements, it must appropriately recognize IUS in its financial statements.

7.4.8.3. Recognition Uncertainty

To prevent duplicative accounting records, DoW Components must agree as to which entity will recognize an item when there is doubt. The process and terms of this agreement must be formally documented in a MOA, which will then serve as the official supporting documentation. If DoW Components cannot reach an agreement, they must refer the matter to the ODCFO, OUSW(C) for resolution. DoW Components must submit requests for resolution with adequate supporting documentation to assist in resolving the matter, and they should send these requests through the FM&C of their respective Military Department or Defense Agency.

7.4.8.4. Recognition Timing

7.4.8.4.1. Recognition of the COTS IUS for financial reporting purposes must occur no later than the technical acceptance of the software.

7.4.8.4.2. Record IUS in development anticipated to meet capital criteria in the IUS in Development account during the design, development, and testing phases. DoW Components must recognize the IUS asset, transfer capital costs to the IUS account, and establish accountability in the APSR after completing technical acceptance testing.

7.4.8.4.2.1. Larger and more complex software systems, such as Enterprise Resource Planning systems, are developed and placed in service over time. After successfully testing a module or component of a software project, the Component must move costs from IUS in Development to IUS and begin amortization.

7.4.8.4.2.2. If the use of a module is dependent on the completion of another module(s), move costs from IUS in Development to IUS when both that module and the other module(s) have successfully completed testing.

7.4.8.4.3. For IUS assets acquired by a contractor on behalf of a DoW Component, recognize the software upon completion of the technical acceptance testing by the contractor performing the service, or by the DoW Component. Record contract financing payments (e.g., progress payments, performance-based payments, and commercial interim payments) made to a contractor prior to completion of final technical acceptance testing in a Software in Development account until the IUS is placed in service. Capitalize upon completion of technical acceptance testing.

7.4.8.5. Capitalization Threshold, Criteria, and Cost Treatment

7.4.8.5.1. The current IUS capitalization threshold for all DoW Components is $250,000. However, DoW Intelligence Community Entities may elect to use a capitalization threshold of $1 million. The capitalization threshold described above is for financial reporting purposes.

7.4.8.5.2. DoW Components must apply the treatment of costs based on the nature of the costs incurred, not the exact sequence of the work.

7.4.8.5.3. The capitalized costs of internally developed software should be limited to costs incurred:

7.4.8.5.3.1. After the DoW Component authorizes and commits to a software project and believes that it is more likely than not that the project will be completed and the software will be used to perform the intended function(s), and it will have an estimated service life of two years or more; and

7.4.8.5.3.2. After the completion of the planning and requirements phase (i.e., project evaluation, concept testing, and evaluation of alternatives) as evidenced by a documented approval decision.

7.4.8.5.4. Technical acceptance testing is testing undertaken to verify if a software product meets technical specifications. Capitalize technical acceptance testing costs after technical acceptance; expense operational testing, evaluation, and other functional testing.

7.4.8.5.5. Capitalize the amounts paid to a COTS vendor for the software.

7.4.8.6. Documentation

7.4.8.6.1. DoW Components must assign a dollar value (i.e., recorded cost) to the IUS when recording the acquisition of IUS in the APSR and/or accounting system. Appropriate documentation must be available to support the dollar value.

7.4.8.6.2. To establish proper PP&E financial control when acquiring IUS from another DoW Component or Federal Agency, the acquiring DoW Component must request from the losing DoW Component or other Federal Agency, the necessary source information and financial transfer documents, to include a unique identifier(s) for the software(s); location; original acquisition cost(s); cost of enhancements; the date the software was developed, or acquired; the estimated useful life; the amount of accumulated amortization; and other relevant information linked to that software. If this information is not available, the gaining and losing entities must develop and document a reasonable estimate to support the financial transfer of the software.

7.4.8.6.3. Capitalized IUS costs must have sufficient supporting documentation, including support for costs incurred in the development of the IUS. DoW Components must provide narratives, software architectural documentation, user manuals, and other similar documents to substantiate whether they treat the IUS as separate IUS assets, supporting the functionality of the components/modules of a software system.

7.4.8.7. Joint Ventures

If two or more entities, including at least one entity outside of the DoW, develop the IUS through a joint venture, the DoW Component must capitalize the IUS asset if it meets the criteria for capitalization, based on its share of the development cost in relation to the capitalization threshold. The DoW Component only capitalizes the portion it funded if it meets the criteria for capitalization.

7.4.8.8. Bulk Purchases of Software Applications/Programs

7.4.8.8.1. Bulk purchases must be considered if they materially affect the fiscal year financial statements during which they were purchased. Bulk purchases of software with an aggregate cost that exceeds the capitalization threshold must be capitalized.

7.4.8.8.2. When multiple acquisitions of the same IUS application(s)/programs (for example, spreadsheets, word processing programs, etc.) or modules or components of a software system are made as part of a single contract within a fiscal year, the purchases must be added together to determine whether they meet the capitalization threshold. Purchases made on a single contract during separate fiscal years are to be considered separately. DoW Components must not split bulk purchases into multiple transactions with the intent of avoiding capitalization.

7.4.8.8.3. Bulk purchases of licensed IUS with terms less than two years in length do not need to be considered for capitalization.

7.4.8.9. Software Licenses

7.4.8.9.1. Software licenses grant the license holder the right to use the software for a specific time period. After this period expires, the license holder must renew the license or purchase a new one to continue using the software. License agreements to use software come in many forms and vary in length of the license period. Software licenses can be term or perpetual.

7.4.8.9.1.1. Term licenses provide DoW Components the right to use IUS for a specified period of time. Capitalize or expense term-licensed IUS.

7.4.8.9.1.2. Perpetual software licenses allow the DoW Component to use the software indefinitely in exchange for an upfront cost, which they can pay as a one-time payment or finance over a set period. Apply capitalization criteria if the license is perpetual to determine whether to capitalize or expense.

7.4.8.9.2. The IUS can be expensed if the license term is less than two years, the license cost (excluding any maintenance agreements) is less than the capitalization threshold, or the aggregate cost of a bulk license purchase (excluding any maintenance agreements) is less than the capitalization threshold.

7.4.8.9.3. A license agreement may include executory costs for maintenance and technical support. DoW Component judgment should apply in determining what portions of license fees are attributable to software capitalizable costs versus executory costs. DoW Components may also want to consider having each license agreement specifically identify the various costs throughout the license life cycle, for example, initial license, maintenance, and enhancement.

7.4.8.9.4. Additional guidance regarding accounting for license agreements includes:

7.4.8.9.4.1. Expense maintenance costs agreed to as part of the initial license agreement in the period they are incurred;

7.4.8.9.4.2. Expense “True-up” costs associated with unlimited license agreements or enterprise licenses that may occur (depending on the agreement terms) at the end of each year to reconcile and account for the actual quantity of users; and

7.4.8.9.4.3. Expense software upgrades from annual maintenance and security assurance agreements; do not capitalize as enhancements or separate assets.

7.4.8.10. Cloud and Other Subscription-Based Services

7.4.8.10.1. A cloud computing service is any resource that is accessible over the Internet. It has the following essential characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service.

7.4.8.10.2. When a DoW Component pays regular subscription fees to access and use software from a non-DoW entity, it should expense subscription costs in the period incurred. This scenario is a service and does not constitute an IUS asset for the DoW Component.

7.4.8.10.3. A subscription arrangement using a cloud with a non- DoW entity can result in DoW-owned IUS if the using DoW Component takes possession, or can take possession of a software application without incurring a significant penalty. DoW Components must capitalize this IUS if it meets the capitalization criteria.

7.4.8.10.4. When a cloud or subscription arrangement exists between DoW Components, the Component that owns the software will report it as IUS. The subscribing DoW Component(s) will expense any fees paid for the service in the period incurred.

7.4.8.10.5. If a cloud computing arrangement includes a software license, the customer must account for the software license element of the arrangement consistent with the acquisition of other software licenses. SFFAS 10 is not applicable to a cloud computing arrangement that does not convey a contractual right to the IUS or to ones that do not include an IUS license. The entity that develops and owns the software, platform, or infrastructure used in the cloud computing arrangement would account for the software development in accordance with SFFAS 10. If the funding to develop cloud computing is shared among entities without clear ownership, the service provider entity that receives funding and is responsible for maintaining the software, platform, or infrastructure must account for the software in accordance with SFFAS 10 and the full cost/inter‑entity cost requirements of SFFAS 4.

7.4.8.11. Shared Services

7.4.8.11.1. Shared services is a mission or support function provided by one business unit to other business units within or between organizations. The funding and resourcing of the service is shared, and the providing entity effectively becomes an internal/external service provider.

7.4.8.11.2. There are three types of shared service structures in the Federal Government:

7.4.8.11.2.1. Intra-agency. Intra-agency shared services include those provided within the boundaries of a specific organization, such as a Federal Department or Agency, to that organization’s internal units. Intra-agency shared services would be those between one DoW Component and another DoW Component.

7.4.8.11.2.2. Inter-agency. Inter-agency shared services are those provided by one Federal Organization to other Federal Organizations that are outside of the provider’s organizational boundaries. Inter-agency shared services would be those between one DoW Component and another Federal Agency/Organization outside of DoW.

7.4.8.11.2.3. Commercial. Commercial shared services are those provided by private vendors.

7.4.8.11.3. For intra-agency shared services, a cost allocation methodology could be developed in accordance with SFFAS 4. For inter-agency shared services and commercial shared services, the service provider entity that owns (receives funding/responsible for maintaining) the software must account for the software in accordance with SFFAS 10. In the event that the entity receiving the service (the customer) has the contractual right to take possession of the software at any time during the hosting period without significant penalty, and it is feasible for the customer to either run the software on its own hardware or contract with another party unrelated to the vendor to host the software. The customer must account for the software in accordance with SFFAS 10.

7.4.8.11.4. If the shared service arrangement includes a software license, the DoW Component must account for the software license element of the arrangement consistent with the acquisition of their other software licenses. SFFAS 10 is not applicable to a shared service arrangement that does not convey a contractual right to the IUS or to ones that do not include an IUS license.

7.4.8.12. Accountable Records of IUS

DoW Components must establish accountable records for all government IUS. Account for IUS that meet the criteria for capitalization in an APSR. DoW Components must also establish and maintain accountability records for IUS that do not meet the criteria for capitalization in either an APSR or approved managerial system through disposition or transfer. Managerial systems must contain all general data elements contained in a data-compliant APSR. In addition, managerial systems must document controls and procedures in place that are sufficient to withstand potential audit scrutiny and support the audit requirement of a complete universe of assets. The primary Accountable Property Officer (APO) or designated delegate should grant managerial system approval. See DoDI 5000.76.

7.4.9. IUS Enhancements

7.4.9.1. DoW Components must capitalize an enhancement that increases the capability of the IUS when its cost meets or exceeds the capitalization threshold.

7.4.9.2. Evaluate modules together as one enhancement if one module is dependent upon another to function. DoW Components must amortize all costs of an enhancement that they have capitalized based on the IUS capitalization criteria, including any costs they carry over or allocate from the original software, over the enhancements' estimated useful life, which should not exceed five years.

7.4.9.3. DoW Components must begin to accumulate costs for enhancements when these enhancements are more likely than not to produce new capabilities; and the project phase in which the costs are being incurred and the nature of the cost meet the criteria for capitalization treatment; and the estimated total cost of the enhancement meets the IUS capitalization threshold.

7.4.9.4. DoW Components must separately account for enhancements in a manner that allows them to specifically identify and support each capitalized enhancement made to the IUS.

7.4.9.5. Expense an enhancement to IUS that meets or exceeds the capitalization threshold to correct a design flaw, and in effect doubles its useful life, in the period incurred, unless the enhancement adds new capabilities to the software. However, the useful life of the IUS is subject to adjustment and must reflect the enhancement.

7.4.9.6. Expense the cost of minor enhancements resulting from ongoing systems maintenance or incurred solely to repair a design flaw without adding additional capabilities in the period incurred. Examples of minor enhancements include updating data tables, web-enabling, customizing reports, or changing graphic user interfaces. Expense enhancements that extend the useful life of the software without adding significant capabilities. However, in instances where the useful life of IUS is extended, DoW Components must adjust the amortization.

7.4.9.7. A specific software development project may include expenditures for enhancements and maintenance that the Component cannot easily separate but can reasonably and consistently allocate. As one approach, the Component can use a ratio based on the projected work hours for development phase activities relative to other types of work. The Component must apply this ratio to determine which expenditures to capitalize, provided the expenses meet the other capitalization criteria. The Component must apply this basis for allocating costs consistently and in accordance with GAAP.

7.4.9.8. Retain documentation related to IUS enhancement decisions, such as the justification for capitalizing the enhancement, a change of useful life, and the amount to capitalize.

7.4.9.9. Only capitalize the cost of enhancements to more than one IUS asset as identified by a unique identifier, when performed under a single contract or work order that cannot be specifically identified by asset, if the allocated cost per IUS equals or exceeds the appropriate DoW capitalization threshold and the enhancements are more likely than not to add additional capability to the existing software.

7.4.9.10. When a single IUS undergoes more than one enhancement as part of a single overall effort to increase its functionality and/or useful life, the Component must capitalize the sum of the enhancement costs if the total equals or exceeds the appropriate DoW capitalization threshold. The Component must follow this requirement even when it funds the enhancements separately. The Component must capitalize the enhancements once it determines that it is more likely than not that the enhancements will result in significant new capabilities.

7.4.10. Maintenance and Repair

7.4.10.1. Maintenance and repair costs are not capital enhancements, regardless of whether the cost equals or exceeds the DoW capitalization threshold. Maintenance and repairs are activities directed toward keeping IUS assets in an acceptable condition so that they continue to provide services and achieve their expected useful life.

7.4.10.2. When determining whether to capitalize the IUS, do not include the costs of maintenance agreements purchased with a software license in the historical cost of the IUS. If DoW Components cannot distinguish maintenance costs from the cost of the license itself, they must use reasonable and documented estimating methods. Do not capitalize upgrades included in annual maintenance and security assurance agreements.

7.4.11. Amortization

7.4.11.1. Amortization is the systematic and rational allocation of the acquisition cost of an IUS over its estimated useful life. During the planning phase of IUS development, the DoW Component must determine the useful life based on how long it expects the IUS to provide economic benefit or service potential. The Component must document its decision regarding the useful life, a decision it must make with input from personnel who are familiar with the software’s technical characteristics and planned use. For IUS acquired for R&D with no alternative future use, the Component must amortize the cost over the period of the project, as opposed to applying the normal life-cycle amortization.

7.4.11.2. DoW Components must amortize the recorded cost of capitalized IUS and enhancements to IUS. They must also reflect these capitalized amounts, as well as the associated accumulated amortization and amortization expense, in their financial statements.

7.4.11.3. DoW Components must document the PISD for both acquired IUS and developed IUS. Documentation of PISDs is critical in determining when to start amortization of capitalized IUS costs. IUS is considered placed in service when final technical acceptance testing is completed. The point at which this milestone is reached can vary for different types of software acquisitions.

7.4.11.4. When replacing the IUS with new software, expense the unamortized cost of the old IUS when the new IUS successfully completes testing. No adjustments will be made to the previously recorded amortization. Treat any additions to the book value or changes in useful life prospectively. Account for the change during the period of the change and future periods.

7.4.11.5. Account for all IUS in an APSR.

7.4.11.6. The program office must retain proper supporting documentation to justify the estimated useful life of the program.

7.4.11.7. In the case of IUS assets, after the successful completion of the final technical acceptance testing, the calculation of amortization is based on the date the asset is installed and placed in service (regardless of whether it is actually used).

7.4.11.8. DoW policy permits the use of only the straight-line method of amortization. Calculate straight-line amortization expense based on the recorded cost divided equally among accounting periods during the software’s useful life based on recovery periods. The salvage value for all capitalized IUS for the DoW Components should be zero.

7.4.11.9. Retain the IUS asset in APSR if it remains in use longer than its estimated useful life, as well as the accounting records, and reflect both its recorded cost and accumulated amortization until disposition of the software.

7.4.11.10. WCF activities are required to recognize and amortize IUS assets without regard to whether such assets are procured through a WCF activity’s Capital Purchase/Investment Program budget or whether amortization for such assets is included in rates charged to customers. The recognition of IUS assets and the amortization of such assets by WCF activities therefore may be different for financial statement reporting purposes than the amortization amounts used for WCF rate development and budget presentation. All IUS asset amortization of WCF activities must be recognized as an expense on the Statement of Net Cost, reflected in the Statement of Changes in Net Position, included in accumulated amortization amounts on the Balance Sheet, and reported in the “Defense Working Capital Fund Accounting Report [Accounting Report (Monthly) 1307] (AR(M)1307).” Accounting Report 1307 is described in Volume 6. Amortization recorded on IUS assets that were not acquired nor will be replaced through the use of DWCF resources must be classified as non-recoverable for rate-setting purposes and reported appropriately on the AR(M)1307. DWCF rates charged to customers are based on guidance in Volume 2 and Volume 11.

7.4.12. Impairment

7.4.12.1. The Component must recognize and measure an impairment when one of the following events occurs and is related to post-implementation/operational IUS assets:

7.4.12.1.1. The IUS asset is no longer expected to provide substantive service potential and will be removed from service; or

7.4.12.1.2. A significant reduction occurs in the software’s or software module’s capabilities, functions, or uses.

7.4.12.2. If the impaired software is to remain in use, the loss due to impairment must be measured as the difference between the book value and either:

7.4.12.2.1. The cost to acquire software that would perform similar remaining functions (i.e., the unimpaired functions) or, if that is not feasible;

7.4.12.2.2. The portion of the book value attributable to the remaining functional elements of the software.

7.4.12.3. Recognize the loss upon impairment and reduce the book value of the asset accordingly. If amounts cannot be determined, the DoW Component should continue to amortize the book value over the remaining useful life of the software. Document and retain this decision and associated analyses.

7.4.12.4. If the DoW Component removes the impaired IUS asset from use, it must measure the loss as the difference between the book value and the NRV, if any. The Component must recognize the loss upon impairment and reduce the asset's book value accordingly. Finally, the Component must transfer the NRV, if any, to an appropriate asset account and hold it there until it disposes of the software and realizes the amount.

7.4.12.5. When a DoW Component determines it is more likely than not that it will not complete a developmental software project, the Component must stop capitalizing costs and must immediately expense any costs it has already capitalized for that project.

7.4.12.6. When an IUS developmental software project is suspended pending management’s evaluation as to whether to resume or terminate the project, the software development cost may remain capitalized in an IUS in Development account (USSGL 183200) as long as it is more likely than not that the developmental software project will eventually be completed and that the cost incurred or expected to be incurred meets the capitalization threshold. Reevaluate the status of the project periodically and write off capitalized costs if management concludes that it is more likely than not that the software will not be placed in service in the future.

7.4.12.7. Recognize and report the loss from impairment, if any, in the Statement of Net Cost in the period in which the DoW Component concludes that the impairment is both (1) a significant decline in service utility and (2) expected to be permanent. Include such losses in program costs or costs not assigned to programs. A general description of the IUS for which an impairment loss is recognized, the nature (e.g., damage or obsolescence) and amount of the impairment, and the financial statement classification of the impairment loss must be disclosed in the notes to the financial statements in the period the impairment loss is recognized if the amount is significant to the financial statements.

7.4.12.8. Report the impairment loss net of any associated recovery of the NRV when the recovery and loss occur in the same fiscal year. Report recoveries in subsequent fiscal years as revenue or other financing source, as appropriate. Disclose the amount and financial statement classification of recoveries in the notes to the financial statements.

7.4.12.9. Account for the costs incurred to replace or restore the lost service utility of impaired IUS remaining in use in accordance with applicable standards (i.e., recognized according to the nature of the costs incurred and the appropriate capitalization threshold).

7.4.13. Removal/Disposal

7.4.13.1. In TR 14, FASAB defines removal from service as an event that terminates the use of a General PP&E asset. DoW Component Heads must establish and maintain effective policies and procedures for the removal (disposal or transfer) of IUS assets.

7.4.13.2. If an IUS’s normal use is terminated (i.e., it no longer provides service in the operations of the entity) but the DoW Component has not yet decided to permanently remove the IUS from service, the removal from service is considered other than permanent. Other than permanent removal from service is evidenced by activities such as continuing low-level maintenance to sustain the IUS in a recoverable status or until reutilization efforts are exhausted.

7.4.13.3. If (1) an IUS’s use is terminated and (2) the DoW Component has documented its decision to permanently remove the IUS from service, the removal from service must be accounted for as permanent. Permanent removal from service is evident from the DoW Component’s documented decision to dispose of an IUS by selling, recycling, or donating the IUS.

7.4.13.4. When an IUS is disposed of (e.g., by selling, recycling, donating, or destruction), the IUS must be written off from the financial records and financial statements, and the difference between any disposal proceeds and the IUS’s net book value must be recognized as a gain or loss.

7.4.13.5. Upon authorized disposition, APOs are responsible for ensuring that all IUS asset dispositions and transfers are properly recorded in the APSR or managerial system, including updating the asset's status to "Disposed," recording the date and method of disposition. The reason for disposition or transfer of IUS assets must be properly documented. The APO retains all supporting documentation per record retention policies. Refer to DoDI 5000.76 for additional information.

7.4.14. Additional Considerations

7.4.14.1. Use of Canceled TAS. Capitalized assets are required to be reported and remain in GTAS after the original purchasing TAS has expired and been canceled. If a capitalized asset has not been moved to a “C” TAS, GTAS will provide a “C” TAS on the GTAS Super Master Account File (SMAF) for each fund family represented on the SMAF. The system-generated “C” TAS will have three components: the three-digit agency identifier, availability type “C”, and a four-digit main account. All DoW Components must use the “C” availability type TAS to report capitalized assets. Assets may be moved to a C TAS at any time from the purchase date to the date the original purchasing fund is canceled. Refer to the TFM, Part 2, Chapter 4700.

7.4.14.2. Supporting Documentation. Entries to record financial transactions in accounting system general ledger accounts and/or the supporting subsidiary accountable property records and/or systems must:

7.4.14.2.1. Be supported by source documents that reflect all transactions affecting the DoW Component’s investment in the IUS.

7.4.14.2.2. Support all acquisitions, whether by purchase, transfer from other agencies, donation, or other means, as of the date the DoW Component takes custody of the IUS with supporting documents.

7.4.14.2.3. Support all disposals or retirements as of the date the IUS leaves the custody of the DoW Component to provide an adequate audit trail for the disposal of an asset. The execution of certain disposal events will generate financial or administrative accountability transactions.

7.4.14.2.4. Retain documents that support the recorded cost of IUS assets by the DoW Component in accordance with their DoW Component records retention requirements. Maintain documentation in a readily available location during the applicable retention period to permit the validation of information pertaining to the asset, such as the purchase cost, purchase date, and cost of enhancements. The documentation must also be linked to the appropriate unique identifier(s).

7.4.14.3. Include sufficient information indicating the quantity. location, and unit cost of the IUS. Designate the accountable property records to be of maximum assistance in making procurement and utilization decisions, including decisions related to identifying potential excess IUS that may be available for reuse, transfer to other DoW Components, or made available for disposal in accordance with current DoW regulations and other regulatory requirements.

7.4.14.4. Identify and classify IUS that were capitalized, recorded in the APSR and accounting system, and reported in the financial statements.

7.4.14.5. Be based on the same documents to ensure that entries to the accounting and accountable property records are the same. This will ensure that the property accountability records are integrated and subsidiary to the accounting system, and those records can be reconciled with the accounting system.

7.4.14.6. Include documents used to accumulate the cost of developmental projects. Each document must be linked to the appropriate asset unique identifier.

7.4.14.7. Include all IUS possessed by the Department (to include property held by others) and IUS of others held by DoW through seizure, forfeiture, loss, or abandonment.

7.4.14.8. Provide information to identify and account for capitalized enhancements to IUS.

7.4.15. Reporting Requirements

DoW Components with IUS should reference a note on the Balance Sheet that discloses information about the reported IUS assets. See Volume 6 for the specific reporting requirements.

7.5    HERITAGE ASSETS, MULTI-USE HERITAGE ASSETS, AND STEWARDSHIP
LAND

7.5.1. This section establishes the accounting policy and requirements for financial control over heritage assets, multi-use heritage assets, and stewardship land. Volume 1 discusses the applicable general ledger accounts listed in the USSGL. The DoW USSGL Transaction Library contains both the DoW SCOA and the accounting entries for these PP&E accounts. DoW Components must recognize all acquired heritage assets, multi-use heritage assets, and stewardship land for accountability (in accordance with DoDI 4165.14, DoDI 4165.70, and DoDI 5000.64) and financial reporting purposes. Unless otherwise stated, all DoW Components, including WCF activities, must follow this section.

7.5.2. Heritage Assets

7.5.2.1. Heritage assets are PP&E that experts consider unique due to their historical or natural significance, cultural, educational, or artistic importance, or significant architectural characteristics.

7.5.2.2. Heritage assets consist of (1) collection-type assets, such as objects gathered and maintained for exhibition (e.g., museum collections, art collections, and library collections); and (2) non-collection-type assets (e.g., memorials, monuments, buildings, and archeological sites). Cultural resources and historic properties, defined in DoDI 4715.16, may be categorized as heritage assets for financial reporting purposes if they have the attributes of heritage assets described in this definition.

7.5.2.3. Heritage assets are generally expected to be preserved indefinitely.

7.5.2.4. The cost or value must not serve as a factor when deciding if an asset must be classified as a heritage asset.

7.5.2.5. If a particular asset is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, it is heritage in nature. If it is not listed on the National Register of Historic Places, refer to cultural resources and collections policies, published registers, and consult with DoW subject matter experts (i.e., the DoW cultural resources or museum staff) when making this assessment. Designation of a PP&E asset (including such assets as museum, library, and art collections) as a heritage asset can be done at any time in its life cycle, based on the application of evaluation criteria by qualified staff.

7.5.2.6. Historic significance may be identified if a property/asset meets at least one of the following criteria adapted from the National Register of Historic Places as determined by the relevant DoW Component with concurrence by the relevant State Historic Preservation Officer, or as determined by the guidelines of the National Register of Historic Places in 36 CFR, Part 60, Section 60.4:

7.5.2.6.1. Association with historic events or activities that have made a significant contribution to the broad patterns of history (e.g., battles, development of military technology, prehistoric cultural patterns);

7.5.2.6.2. Association with the lives of significant historic persons (e.g., important military leaders, political leaders, inventors);

7.5.2.6.3. Distinctive design or physical characteristics of a type, period, or method of construction (e.g., work representative of a particular approach to military design or a particular type or style of architecture or engineering); or that represents the work of a master (e.g., work of a master architect, landscape architect, planner, or engineer); or that possess high artistic values (e.g., artwork that a recognized artist commissioned to commemorate military history); or that represents a significant and distinguishable entity whose components may lack individual distinction (e.g., a formative example of standardized planned military housing); or

7.5.2.6.4. Have yielded or may be likely to yield important information about prehistory or history (e.g., an archeological site on a military installation).

7.5.2.7. Ordinarily, cemeteries, birthplaces, or graves of historical figures, properties owned by religious institutions or used for religious purposes, structures that have been moved from their original locations, reconstructed historic buildings, properties primarily commemorative in nature, and properties that have achieved significance within the past 50 years are not considered eligible for the National Register. However, such properties will qualify if they are integral parts of districts that meet the criteria, or if they fall within the following categories:

7.5.2.7.1. A religious property deriving primary significance from architectural or artistic distinction or historical importance; or

7.5.2.7.2. A building or structure removed from its original location but which is significant primarily for architectural value, or which is the surviving structure most importantly associated with a historic person or event; or

7.5.2.7.3. A birthplace or grave of a historical figure of outstanding importance if there is no appropriate site or building directly associated with their productive life.

7.5.2.7.4. A cemetery which derives its primary significance from graves of persons of transcendent importance, from age, from distinctive design features, or from association with historic events; or

7.5.2.7.5. A reconstructed building when accurately executed in a suitable environment and presented in a dignified manner as part of a restoration master plan, and when no other building or structure with the same association has survived; or

7.5.2.7.6. A property primarily commemorative in intent if design, age, tradition, or symbolic value has invested it with its own exceptional significance; or

7.5.2.7.7. A property achieving significance within the past 50 years if it is of exceptional importance.

7.5.2.8. As contrasted with multi-use heritage assets, heritage assets are not used predominantly in general government operations. Heritage assets having an incidental (i.e., not significant or predominant) use in government operations are not considered and are not classified as multi-use heritage assets; they are simply heritage assets.

7.5.2.9. Some heritage assets will meet the definitions of, and be considered and reported as, both heritage assets and stewardship land. Such reporting would not be considered duplication as the type of information reported on the physical unit would be different for each category of stewardship asset (i.e., heritage assets and stewardship land).

7.5.3. Acquisition/Valuation

Expense the cost of acquiring heritage assets in the period incurred. The cost must include all costs incurred to bring the asset to a form and location suitable for its intended use.

7.5.4. Recognition and Measurement

7.5.4.1. Recognize the cost of acquiring, improving, reconstructing, or renovating heritage assets on the Statement of Net Cost for the period in which the cost is incurred. Include all costs incurred to bring the asset to its current condition and location.

7.5.4.2. Do not recognize revenue for heritage assets acquired through donation or devise (a will or clause of a will disposing of property).

7.5.4.3. Transfers of heritage assets from one DoW Component to another or to another Federal agency do not affect the net cost of operations or net position of either entity.

7.5.5. Removal/Disposal

Heritage Assets can be removed from service or otherwise disposed of.

7.5.6. Disclosure Requirements

The DoW Component that has control over the heritage asset must report information about the heritage assets in its financial statement note disclosures as set forth in SFFAS 29. Disclosures must include physical units of measure.

7.5.7. Multi-Use Heritage Assets

7.5.7.1. Heritage assets may in some cases serve two purposes: (i) a heritage function and (ii) a government operations function. In cases where a heritage asset serves two purposes, and the predominant use of the asset is in general government operations, officials must consider and classify the heritage asset as a multi-use heritage asset.

7.5.7.2. The costs of acquisition, improvement, or renovation of multi-use heritage assets must be capitalized as general PP&E and depreciated if the costs equal or exceed the DoW capitalization threshold. Expenses are the costs that do not equal or exceed the capitalization threshold.

7.5.7.3. Assets classified as multi-use heritage assets and acquired through donation or devise must be recognized as general PP&E at the fair value of the assets at the time received, and the amount must be recognized as non-exchange revenues as defined in SFFAS 7.

7.5.7.4. When a Federal entity transfers a multi-use heritage asset to another (including between DoW Components or between a DoW Component and another Federal entity), the receiving entity must recognize it as a transfer-in and an additional financing source. The transferring entity must recognize a transfer-out. The receiving entity must record the value at the transferring entity’s net book value for the multi-use heritage asset.

7.5.7.5. Capital improvements or enhancements to multi-use heritage assets must be capitalized in accordance with general PP&E.

7.5.7.6. The recorded cost of capitalized multi-use heritage assets must be depreciated in accordance with the general PP&E guidance.

7.5.7.7. Multi-use heritage assets are subject to the same impairment ruleset as general PP&E.

7.5.7.8. Multi-use heritage assets must be removed and disposed of in accordance with the general PP&E guidance.

7.5.8. Disclosure Requirements

Multi-use heritage assets require additional descriptive information in the heritage asset note disclosure as set forth in SFFAS 29. Multi-use heritage assets are to be reported in both the principal financial statements (in dollars) as general PP&E and in the heritage asset note disclosure (in physical units). Disclosures must include physical units of measure.

7.5.9. Use of Canceled TAS

Multi-use heritage assets are required to be reported in the Treasury’s GTAS.

7.5.10. Stewardship Land

7.5.10.1. Stewardship land includes both public domain and acquired land and land rights owned by the Federal Government intended to be held indefinitely but not acquired for or in connection with the acquisition or construction of real property facilities. Stewardship land also includes areas reserved, managed, planned, used, or acquired for forests and parks, recreation and conservation, and wildlife habitat and grazing. It encompasses land used for the conservation or preservation of cultural and historic sites, for ancillary revenue-generating activities like mineral development, and as buffer zones for security, flood management, and noise and viewsheds. While DoW stewardship lands support environmental conservation, they also support military readiness. To prepare for global challenges, soldiers conduct training in deserts, forests, wetlands, and coastal areas.

7.5.10.2. Land rights such as easements or rights-of-way that are for an unspecified period of time or unlimited duration are considered permanent land rights in perpetuity. Temporary land rights are those land rights that are for a specified period of time or limited duration.

7.5.10.3. The DoW defines “Acquired for or in connection with the acquisition or construction of real property facilities” as land or land rights acquired with the intent to construct general PP&E, and land or land rights acquired in combination with general PP&E. DoW or a DoW Component must account for and report land and land rights they own and acquired for or in connection with real property facilities as general PP&E. They must expense the cost of acquiring stewardship land in the period incurred. This cost must include all expenses necessary to bring the asset to a form and location suitable for its intended use.

7.5.11. Recognition and Measurement

7.5.11.1. Recognize the cost of the acquisition of stewardship land as an expense on the Statement of Net Cost for the period in which the cost is incurred. The cost must include all costs to prepare stewardship land for its intended use (e.g., grading the land or razing a building).

7.5.11.2. In some cases, land may be acquired along with existing facilities. Consult with Component cultural resources staff to determine how to treat the acquisition cost of the facility. Facilities to be used in operations must be treated as an acquisition of stewardship land if the value of the facility is insignificant, or its acquisition is merely a byproduct of the acquisition of the land. Facilities of significant value that have an operating use (e.g., a constructed hotel or employee housing block) must be treated as general PP&E (real property or multi-use heritage assets) by identifying the cost attributable to the facilities and segregating it from the cost of stewardship land acquired.

7.5.11.3. Do not recognize revenue for stewardship land acquired through donation or devise.

7.5.11.4. Transfers of stewardship land from one DoW Component to another or to another Federal agency do not affect the net cost of operations or net position of either entity.

7.5.12. Removal/Disposal

Stewardship land can be removed from service and subject to disposal.

7.5.13. Disclosure Requirements

7.5.13.1. Land classified as stewardship land is reported as basic information within the financial statements of the DoW Component responsible for such land and subject to units of measure.

7.5.13.2. All heritage assets, multi-use heritage assets, and stewardship land acquired by DoW Components must be recognized for accountability (in accordance with DoDI 4165.14, DoDI 4165.70, and DoDI 5000.64) and financial reporting purposes.

7.5.14. Supporting Documentation

7.5.14.1. Entries to record financial transactions in accounting system general ledger accounts and the APSR and/or other systems, as well as information to be included in financial statement note disclosures, must be supported by source documents that reflect all transactions affecting the DoW Component’s stewardship investment in the PP&E.

7.5.14.2. All acquisitions, whether by purchase, transfer from other agencies, donation, or other means, must be supported as of the date the DoW Component accepts the heritage assets, multi-use heritage assets and/or stewardship land. Documentation, where applicable, must be readily available to support the changes in asset value or physical attributes as a result of new acquisition or capital improvement.

7.5.14.3. When definitive documentation for stewardship land and/or heritage assets is not available, management must identify and use alternative methods for supporting management’s assertions for these assets.

7.5.14.4. All disposals or retirements must be supported as of the date the PP&E leaves the custody of the DoW Component to provide an adequate audit trail for the disposal of the asset. The execution of certain disposal events will generate financial or administrative accountability transactions.

7.5.15. Policies and Procedures

DoW Components must document the identification, categorization, and method used to physically quantify the assets to ensure consistent reporting for all similar heritage assets and stewardship land.

7.5.16. Physical Units of Measure

Physical units of measure are necessary to meet disclosure requirements described in
SFFAS 29.

7.5.17. Accountable Property System of Record

The APSR and/or other systems must be designed to support procurement and utilization decisions, including decisions related to identifying general PP&E that may transfer to other DoW Components, or made available for disposal in accordance with current DoW regulations and other regulatory requirements.

7.5.18. Physical Inventories

DoW Components must perform periodic physical inventories of heritage assets and multi‑use heritage assets in accordance with DoDI 5000.64 and DoDI 4165.14. Periodic physical inventories of stewardship land must be performed in accordance with DoDI 4165.14.

7.5.19. Deferred Maintenance and Repairs

7.5.19.1. DM&R refers to scheduled or necessary maintenance that an organization has postponed. In general, personnel perform maintenance and repairs to keep assets in an acceptable condition. These activities include preventive maintenance and the replacement of parts or systems to preserve the asset. However, these activities specifically exclude those that expand an asset's useful life, capacity, or capability, or otherwise upgrade it for significantly different or greater uses.

7.5.19.2. DoW Components must determine acceptable condition standards and which DM&R measurement methods to apply. Condition standards and measurement methods must be consistently applied. If the DoW Component determines that it must make changes, it must document the rationale and any impact the changes will have on the DM&R estimates.

7.5.19.3. Amounts for DM&R may be measured using condition assessment surveys, life‑cycle cost forecasts, or other similar methods.

7.5.19.4. Disclosure Requirements

DoW Components must report material amounts of DM&R in the notes to the financial statements. Refer to Volume 6.

title: Section 8.0: Advances
content:
8.0    ADVANCES

A Component may issue advances or prepayments for anticipated expenses or for goods and services not yet received. These amounts are reduced when related goods or services are received, contract terms are met, progress is made under a contract, or anticipated expenses are realized. Per 31 U.S.C. § 3324, law or the President specifically authorizes advances. For financial reporting, these transactions are treated as assets and liabilities, with intragovernmental transactions accounted for separately. All advances and prepayments must be supported by a detailed audit trail with information to show the period the advances were made, the budget authority for the advances, the period the advances were liquidated, and the related approving authorities.

8.1    Accounting for Advances and Prepayments

8.1.1. Advances and prepayments must comply with the law or regulation requirements. Organizations or individuals (other than DoW employees requesting travel advances) requesting advances must demonstrate that all external financing sources have been exhausted before DoW Components authorize an advance. Prepayments are recurrent transactions that do not provide financing as a precondition of performance.

8.1.2. Accounting activities must account for and segregate capitalized assets and expenses into separate line items. Record advances and prepayments paid out as assets. Record advances and prepayments received as liabilities.

8.1.3. A receivable is established when revenue is recognized, and payment has not been received in advance.

8.1.4. Amounts of advances and prepayments that are subject to refund (for example, a settled travel claim indicating the traveler owes part of the advance to the government) must be transferred to accounts receivable.

8.1.5. A quarterly review of dormant accounts is required for sound internal controls to increase each DoW Component’s ability to use available appropriations before they expire and ensure remaining open obligations are valid and liquidated before the appropriations are canceled. This increases mission readiness for the DoW.

8.2    Recoveries and Adjustments

Components must recover unneeded and unused balances as soon as information indicates they are excess to the original purposes. Unused advance and prepayment recoveries received the same year as the original obligation are recorded as recoupments. Collections are recoveries of unused advances and prepayments of prior-year obligations. Refer to the SFIS to decompose DoW USSGL accounting transactions for recoveries and adjustments.

8.3    Contract Financing Payments

The Government authorizes disbursements of monies to a contractor prior to the acceptance of supplies or services for contract financing payments in accordance with FAR 32.001. Contract financing payments include advance payments, performance-based payments, commercial advances, interim payments, progress payments based on cost, progress payments based on a percentage or stage of completion, and interim payments under a cost reimbursement contract. Contract financing payments are more fully discussed in Volume 10.

8.4    Grant Awards and Cooperative Agreements

DoW Components account for advance payments to award recipients (including amounts drawn against letters of credit) until the recipient has performed under the grant or agreement. Once the recipient has performed, the assisting agency must record an expense equal to the cost of the services performed or costs incurred and reduce the advance account by a like amount.

Periodically, the advances must be reconciled with the supporting transaction documentation. Refer to Volumes 10 and 12.

8.5    Advances to Foreign Countries

As authorized by 10 U.S.C. § 2396, DoW appropriations may be used to make advance payments to foreign countries. These advances can be used to comply with local laws and ministerial regulations of a foreign country, pay for rent, tuition, and public utilities, or provide funds to a friendly nation's military for their pay, allowances, and necessary supplies and services.

8.6    Advances in Military Pay

Military pay advances, which cover allowances for subsistence and housing, are authorized only to alleviate financial hardship for members who are mobilized, ordered to a distant station, or deployed on a ship for over 30 days. For complete details, refer to Volume 7.

8.7    Advances in Civilian Pay

Refer to Volume 8 for civilian personnel pay advances including foreign post assignment advances, advance payments to evacuees, newly hired employees, and employees relocating within the U.S. or its territories.

8.8    Advances as Imprest Funds

Imprest Funds are cash advances from a Disbursing Officer to a cashier, charged against a specific LOA. Although considered "Cash Held Outside of Treasury," they are treated as "entity cash" because they are tied to an entity's specific LOA.

8.9    Travel Advances

A commander- or supervisor-approved travel order must be issued before military members or civilian personnel travel unless an urgent or unusual situation prevents prior issuance. Do not authorize cash travel advances unless an exception is granted. Record the maximum advance amount authorized on the travel order. The traveler must not exceed the limit specified in the travel order. Personnel who are not eligible for a Government Travel Charge Card may obtain travel advances only via electronic funds transfer. The commander or supervisor, in coordination with the Disbursing Officer, may authorize cash advances in limited situations where no other process is available to accomplish the mission. A DoW traveler must submit a travel claim voucher within five working days of return.

8.10    Inventory Bid Deposits

Bid deposits for inventory sales are recorded as advances. The advance account is relieved either by recording sales proceeds upon delivery to successful buyers or by refunding the deposit and canceling the sale.

title: Section 9.0: Liabilities
content:
9.0    LIABILITIES

A liability is a probable future outflow or sacrifice of resources stemming from past transactions or events. This includes amounts owed for received items or services, incurred expenses (like personnel costs), assets where title has transferred (even if in transit), ongoing shipbuilding costs, and cash received but not yet earned. Liabilities also encompass obligations that the Component incurs from grants, pensions, benefits, awards, and other forms of indebtedness.

9.1    Recognition Criteria

Pursuant to SFFAS 5, liability recognition begins by determining if the event is transaction- based (exchange or nonexchange) or other. Refer to the procedural guidance. Liabilities from government-related events are recognized when the resource outflow is probable and measurable. Contingent liabilities are either recorded/reported as liabilities or disclosed in footnotes, based on their probability and the capability to estimate resource outflow.

9.2    Reporting and Disclosures

As required by SFFAS 1, intragovernmental liabilities must be reported separately from those with nonfederal entities. Accounting events must be recorded in accordance with the DoW USSGL Transaction Library and reported in accordance with the regulations promulgated by the Treasury and the OMB. In line with OMB Circular A-136, liabilities are classified into three categories: covered by budgetary resources, not covered by budgetary resources, and not requiring budgetary resources. The Component must disclose any liabilities not covered by budgetary resources. Refer to Volume 6.

title: Section 10.0: Accounts Payable
content:
10.0    ACCOUNTS PAYABLE

10.1    Accounts Payable Recognition – General

DoW Components must recognize an accounts payable liability for unpaid goods upon accepting title, whether delivered or in transit. For commercially available goods, accounts payable generally arises upon physical delivery, receipt, and formal title transfer. However, for custom-built facilities or equipment, recognition occurs upon formal acceptance. Accounts payable must be accurately recorded and properly documented, with 48 CFR §§ 52.247.29 –
52.247.49 governing recording timing. If exact amounts are unavailable at quarter-end, Components must estimate the accounts payable. Economically justified discounts, whether contractual or on invoices, should be applied when recognizing accounts payable (refer to Volume 10 for details). Audit evidence of "receipt" must document the items/services, quantities, date received, and authorizing official's signature. This evidence must also include calculations or the basis for estimated accrued amounts. Sensitive information, such as Personally Identifiable Information or proprietary data, may be redacted or aggregated. Finally, robust internal controls for all transactions (intragovernmental, interfund, and public) must be developed, implemented, and validated. Receipt and acceptance of goods and services must be performed and documented solely by authorized personnel.

10.2    Accounts Payable Recognition – Estimating the Accrual

10.2.1. Estimate and record an accrual when definitive amounts or invoices are not available, but the requirements for recording an accounts payable liability exist. The Component must reverse the estimate and record a more definitive amount when more complete data becomes available.

10.2.2. Components must have effective controls in place to ensure that a payable is not duplicated when an invoice is subsequently received for the same procured goods or services.

10.2.3. Show the calculations and data used to compute the amounts in the supporting documents (or mechanized program(s) used for the accrual estimates). This documentation must also identify who prepared the estimate, the date prepared, and who received and reviewed/approved the estimate. Ensure that the documentation is of sufficient quality to allow an external auditor to understand and verify the basis, value, and rationale for the recorded amount. Maintain this documentation for auditors to validate that the review was performed and approved by management.

10.3    Accounts Payable Recognition – Quarterly Accruals

10.3.1. To assist in developing more accurate financial statements, at least quarterly, Components must accrue all procurements in which DoW has received a measurable benefit from, or ownership title to, but have not been documented due to the lack of a receiving report or invoice. If the Component cannot obtain all necessary information from the contracting representatives within the 21 days allowed for the preparation of quarterly financial statements, the Component must use the best available information to estimate the accrual.

10.3.2. Components must also accrue temporary duty (TDY) travel taken, not yet disbursed, or otherwise accounted for as an accounts payable liability at least quarterly. Additionally, Components must record an accounts payable liability for TDY travel that crosses two or more accounting quarters on an estimated/proportional basis, if significant. Record the accrued liability in the applicable accounting period, supported with appropriate documentation (or mechanized programs) that clearly shows the calculations and data used to compute the liability amount.

10.3.3. Components must accrue Permanent Change of Station (PCS) travel taken, not yet disbursed, or otherwise accounted for as a liability, as an accounts payable liability at least quarterly. Additionally, Components must record an accounts payable liability for PCS travel that crosses two or more accounting quarters on an estimated/proportional basis, if significant. Accrue the liability in the applicable accounting period. Support the liability with appropriate documentation (or mechanized programs) that clearly shows the calculations and data used to compute the amount.

10.3.4. Fixed-price construction contracts containing progress payment provisions based upon the percentage or stage of completion require special consideration when recording the accounts payable liability. The accounts payable accrual must include any amounts being withheld from the contractor pending acceptance and completion, or for other contract administration reasons, as per the terms of the contract. The contracting officer or their designee must maintain the supporting documentation and be prepared to provide it to DFAS or auditors to support the accounts payable amount. The Component acquires an asset during each accounting period based on constructive or de facto receipt and thus must recognize/record an accounts payable during each accounting period to reflect the accumulation of that asset.

10.4    Accounts Payable Recognition – Availability of Funds

Components must not delay recognizing an accounts payable liability pending the availability of funds. The Components must disclose the accounts payable not covered by budgetary resources in the financial statement notes. (Refer to Volume 6). A potential violation of the ADA may exist if the payable amount exceeds the total availability of funds. Refer to Volume 14 for the financial management policy regarding an ADA violation.

10.5    Intragovernmental Purchases

10.5.1. Procuring a good or service from another DoW Component or Federal entity is an intragovernmental purchase under the TFM Chapter 4700. Payables due to Components or other Federal entities are intragovernmental payables and must be reported separately from payables due to public entities. Note that OMB Circular A-11 uses the term “intergovernmental” for transactions between or among accounts of Federal entities and that transactions with non- appropriated fund instrumentalities are reported as transactions with the public. The Treasury considers both interdepartmental and intradepartmental transactions to be subsets of intragovernmental transactions.

10.5.2. Components must record accounts payable liability for intragovernmental purchases in the appropriate accounting period to recognize the receipt of goods or services ordered regardless of the document used in placing the order (e.g., Forms 7600A and 7600B, MIPR, project order, or Reimbursable Work Order (RWO)). Components must ensure the liability is recorded during the accounting period that the benefit was received and not delayed pending receipt of a corresponding interagency billing or subsequent payment thereof. Documentation supporting the amount recorded must clearly show the basis (description of the good, quantity, and amount; for services, description of the service, labor hours, and amount) for the payable amount recorded (e.g., MIPR, project order, RWO, reciprocal agreement) and proof of receipt. The documentation must also be of sufficient quality to allow an independent third party, such as an external auditor, to understand and verify the basis, value, and rationale for recorded amounts.

10.5.3. DoW Components must ensure an accounts payable liability is also recorded when the goods are received, or the buying DoW Component has gained title to an asset.

10.6    Late Payment Interest

Components must record in accounts payable an amount for prompt payment interest and other penalties incurred on late payments as required under terms of the non-federal contract. Refer to Volume 10 for the policy on late payment interest and penalties.

10.7    Refunds Due

DoW Components must record an accounts payable liability to reflect the refunds due but not paid at the end of the reporting period, when applicable.

10.8    Monetary Credits
