10.8.1. If the DoW entity exercises this authority, it must also record an accounts payable liability during the period the benefit from the property or services is received. When monetary credits are used for exchange transactions, the DoW entity must record an accounts payable liability equal to the value of the monetary credit.

10.8.2. Specific statutes authorize DoW entities to issue monetary credits as compensation for property or services received from non-federal entities. These monetary credits give the seller the agreed-upon value of the acquired property or received service. The credit holder may apply them later to reduce an amount owed (by the holder) in other, sometimes unrelated, transactions with the government.

10.8.3. Components must ensure the documentation supporting the accounts payable entry specifically identifies the property or services received, the date received, the name and signature of the DoW receiving official, and includes the bilateral agreement between the non‑federal entity and designated DoW representative establishing the agreed-upon value. Components must also ensure the documentation is of sufficient quality to allow an independent third party, such as an external auditor, to understand and verify the basis, value, and rationale for the recorded amount.

10.9    Closed Appropriations

When an appropriation account is closed, any remaining balance in the account must be canceled and unavailable for obligation or expenditure for any purpose. However, legitimately incurred obligations that have not been paid at the time an appropriation is canceled must be reinstated to canceled payables and paid out of a current unexpired appropriation that is available for obligation for the same purpose as the closed account.

10.10    Liquidating Accounts Payable

Accounts payable recorded when a particular good or service is received must be liquidated when the liability created by the payable is settled.

10.11    Reviewing Accounts Payable Balances

10.11.1. The accounting office must review and reconcile all accounts payable balances to the transaction detail level in supporting accounting systems each quarter.

10.11.2. The accounts payable recorded for acceptable final performance on a contract or order must remain in the account until liquidated through proper payment, or until receipt of contractual or legal documents that remove the remaining liability. Continued non-receipt of an invoice on firm-fixed-price contracts may extinguish the contractor’s right to payment and relieve DoW’s obligation to pay for the un-invoiced goods or services. Components must ensure the accounts payable amounts written off contain sufficient documentation to allow an independent third party, such as an external auditor, to verify the basis, value, and rationale for the write-off. Refer to Volume 3 for a policy associated with dormant commitments and unliquidated obligations eligible for closeout on physically complete contracts.

10.11.3. The accounting office must investigate accounts payable debit balances over $100. These debit (abnormal) balances may result from any number of circumstances (e.g., duplicate payments and unrecorded accounts payable). Components must fully document subsequent adjustments to correct the abnormal balance. This documentation must be available for review by the independent auditors if necessary. If the investigation of a debit balance discloses an overpayment or under-recouped funds related to a contract or vendor payment, the accounting office must coordinate with the responsible entitlement and disbursing offices to pursue collection or recoupment. Refer to Volume 10 for additional details.

10.11.4. If the accounting office cannot match a performance report or invoice with a corresponding obligation, a breakdown of fund control processes and a material weakness in internal controls may exist. If posting a transaction to accounts payable does not disclose a corresponding obligation, this may be evidence that either a contract has not been awarded or a posting error has occurred.

10.11.5. These transactions are defined as, and based on the USSGL Crosswalk, map to the accounts payable line of the balance sheet. Refer to Volume 3 for disbursements in-transit policy.

10.12    Accounts Payable Document Retention

All documentation in support of accounts payable entries and adjustments must be readily available for review by auditors, management, and other DoW Component financial management personnel. The documentation retention policy is contained in the DoW Component records retention office.

title: Section 11.0: Personnel Related Liabilities
content:
11.0    PERSONNEL RELATED LIABILITIES

11.1    Accounting Policy

In accounting for personnel-related liabilities, adhere to established standards by updating entries based on current pay adjustments, leave balances, benefit levels, and changes in benefit rules. Available budgetary resources do not limit accrued personnel-related amounts. DoW Components must calculate imputed costs based on the annual Office of Personnel Management (OPM) Benefits Administration Letter for the Civil Service Retirement System (CSRS), Federal Employees Retirement System (FERS), Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and Federal Employee Group Life Insurance Program. Refer to Volume 6 for required financial statement disclosure guidance.

11.2    Accounting for Personnel Entitlements

11.2.1. Accrue the DoW military and civilian employees’ cost of services, including overtime, when a pay period does not coincide with the end of an accounting period.

11.2.2. Record probable and estimable annuities, adjudicated claims, and benefit payments as of the end of the applicable accounting period.

11.2.3. Accrue bonuses and awards, if material, in the accounting period earned. Components assess the materiality threshold.

11.2.4. When DoW employees accrue paid leave, Components incur an expense and a liability for the salary payable when the leave is taken.

11.2.5. Accrue all unused annual leave (including restored leave, compensatory time, and credit hours earned) and associated fringe benefit costs. For financial statement purposes, reflect all pay increases and unused leave balances at least quarterly. Unused annual leave in GF is typically unfunded until used, but must be funded in WCFs.

11.2.6. Personnel should not accrue sick leave, home leave, or compensatory time for travel, as the DoW does not reimburse unused balances. These entitlements are expensed as taken.

11.2.7. Accrue Social Security, retirement funds, Thrift Savings Plan (TSP), and group health and life insurance programs in the same manner as gross compensation (refer to Volume 8).

11.2.8. Accrue other benefits such as relocation-related real estate costs and personnel allowances in the period earned.

11.2.9. Accrue payments to the OPM for reemployed annuitants and severance pay for former employees in the same manner as gross compensation.

11.2.10. Accrue recruitment and relocation bonuses and retention allowances in the period earned.

11.3    Pensions

11.3.1. Pension benefits include all retirement, disability, and survivor benefits financed through a pension plan, including unfunded pension plans. Three defined benefit retirement plans: CSRS, FERS, and Military Retirement System (MRS) cover DoW civilian and military employees.

11.3.2. Recognize the pension liability when the employee’s services are rendered and report the liability in the Components’ financial statements.

11.3.3. Defined contribution plans (e.g., TSP) do not create pension liabilities.

11.3.4. Components recognize a pension expense equaling the employee service cost for the applicable accounting period, less employee contributions, if any, for DoW Civilian pension plans (CSRS and FERS).

11.3.5. Calculate the pension expense and liability using actuarial estimates for MRS. Refer to Volume 12 for more information.

11.3.6. Maintain official communication between OPM and the DoW Office of the Actuary to support pension expense and any related liability.

11.4    Other Retirement Benefits

11.4.1. An employer provides Other Retirement Benefits (ORB) outside the pension plan to a former employee or the employee’s beneficiary upon retirement. ORB includes all retirement benefits other than pension plan benefits, such as retirement health care benefits.

11.4.2. Recognize the ORB liability when the employee’s services are rendered. Report the liability in the Components’ financial statements.

11.4.3. Account for and report the ORB expense, such as medical costs for retirees, in the Component financial reports in a manner similar to that used for pensions.
11.5    Other Postemployment Benefits

11.5.1. Components provide Other Postemployment Benefits (OPEB) to former or inactive employees (e.g., temporarily laid off or disabled), their beneficiaries, and covered dependents, outside of traditional pension or ORB plans. These benefits can include salary continuation, severance, counseling, training, continued healthcare/other benefits, unemployment compensation, workers' compensation, and veterans' disability compensation paid by the employer entity.

11.5.2. For OPEB, such as those under the Federal Employees’ Compensation Act (FECA), recognize expense and liability when a future outflow or other sacrifice of resources is probable and measurable based on events occurring on or before the reporting date.

11.5.3. FECA provides workers’ compensation benefits to federal employees injured in the performance of duty. Workers’ compensation benefits include wage-loss benefits for total or partial disability, monetary benefits for permanent loss or loss of use of a body part, medical benefits, and vocational rehabilitation. Agencies’ direct reimbursements finance the FECA program.

11.5.4. The FECA fund pays benefits on behalf of Federal entities as costs are incurred and bills the entity annually for the previous period. Include annual budget estimates for the fiscal year beginning in the next calendar year equal to the costs (approximately 15 months) for the appropriation-funded agencies.

11.5.5. The Department of Labor sends each agency the actuarial liability estimates for future workers’ compensation benefit amounts for both the current and prior years. The current amount is the new balance in the Actuarial FECA Liability.

11.5.6. The Actuarial FECA Liability entry must be supported by specific documentation.

11.6    Auditability and Internal Procedures

Each Component must develop and implement internal operating procedures to ensure complete, consistent, timely, accurate, valid, and relevant financial data. The Component must also maintain appropriate supporting records to provide an appropriate footnote disclosure in the financial statements if personnel-related liabilities are unfunded. Components must disclose according to Volume 6.

title: Section 12.0: Component Debt
content:
12.0    COMPONENT DEBT

Debt incurred by DoW Components is generally associated with direct and guaranteed loans, and housing programs determined to be necessary to carry out the DoW’s mission, including mortgage agreements accepted pursuant to the Family Housing Program (FHP) and the Homeowners Assistance Fund (HAF).

12.1    Loans and Loan Guarantees

The Department must pay the debt on direct loans if borrowers (e.g., foreign governments, county or city governments, ship owners, or housing builders) default. For loan guarantees, the Department must pay the amount of outstanding principal guaranteed. The accounting policy for loans and loan guarantees is provided in Volume 12.

12.2    Housing Program Debt

12.2.1. Family Housing Program. The Defense FHP offers housing referral services to military and civilian families, which include managing private rentals for overseas personnel, leasing private housing, and guaranteeing rental, mortgage, and mortgage insurance payments on privately owned homes.

12.2.2. Homeowners Assistance Fund. Under 42 U.S.C. § 3374, the SecWar can aid owners of one- or two-family dwellings near military installations slated for closure, in part or whole. This assistance may involve acquiring negotiated title to their properties from the owners. This statute establishes the HAF, which receives its funding through annual Congressional appropriations. DoDD 4165.50E outlines the overall policy for the HAP. Detailed guidance on HAP benefits, domestic and foreign, is provided in regulations published by the Secretary of the Army (as the DoW Executive Agent for HAP) and codified in 32 CFR Part 239.

12.3    Accounting Policy for Debt Associated with Housing Programs

The liability for amounts owed on housing acquired under FHP and HAP programs will be equal to (1) borrowings from other Federal Agencies and the public to construct or acquire the properties, or (2) the mortgages assumed when title passes to the DoW. Liabilities for borrowings from other Federal Agencies and non‑federal organizations will be recorded at the amounts obtained. Amounts paid to financial organizations to obtain the borrowings must be treated as a current period operating expense.

title: Section 13.0: Other Liabilities
content:
13.0    OTHER LIABILITIES

Components report these liabilities on the Balance Sheet as “other liabilities” as they are often immaterial and therefore do not warrant separate reporting. See Volume 6 for financial reporting requirements for other liabilities. Each Component must develop and implement internal operating procedures to implement this overarching policy in a manner that ensures accurate, complete, and relevant financial data.

13.1    Unearned Revenue

13.1.1. Advances and Prepayments

Advances and prepayments are amounts received in advance for goods and services that will be delivered at a future date. When advance fees or payments are received by DoW Components, such as for large-scale, long-term projects, revenue should not be recognized until the goods and services are provided (regardless of whether the fee or payment is refundable. Liability for advances and prepayments includes advances received that are transfers of assets from the public and other federal entities to cover future expenses or the acquisition of other assets. The DoW Components receiving an advance or prepayment must record the amount received as a liability until payment is earned (goods or services have been delivered or contract terms met). After the payment is earned (performance has occurred), the DoW Components must record the appropriate amount as revenue and reduce advances and prepayments liability accordingly.

13.1.2. The two major activities for which DoW receives advances are as follows:

13.1.2.1. Reimbursable Activities. DoW provides services to other federal agencies and to the public on a reimbursable basis. When a non-federal customer enters into a reimbursable agreement with DoW, the customer is required to pay for services in advance unless exempted by law. Generally, non-DoW entities are required to pay in advance.

13.1.2.2. DWCF Activities. The appropriation language for DoW’s DWCF permits the fund to receive advances for supplies and services. Therefore, the DWCF business entities may be advanced funds identified in the DWCF customer orders during the fiscal year, as required, to enable the DWCF activity to pay for its costs of operation.

13.2    Nonfiduciary Deposit Funds

13.2.1. Deposit funds are, in general, monies that do not belong to the Federal Government. Nonfiduciary deposit funds are deposit funds that do not meet the definition and characteristics of fiduciary activities in SFFAS 31. While awaiting disposition, nonfiduciary deposit funds are reported separately on the entity’s financial statements.

13.2.2. Deposit funds must be recorded as a liability because those assets do not belong to the Federal Government. The liability includes, but is not limited to, currency and coin on hand, cash on deposit at designated depositories (excluding Disbursing Officer held cash), negotiable instruments on hand, military payment certificates, and unsupported undistributed collections. Such funds are not available for paying salaries, grants, or other expenses of the Federal Government.

13.2.3. See TFM Volume I for more details on deposit fund accounts and the Treasury’s FAST Book for a full list of DoW deposit accounts.

13.3    Clearing Accounts

Clearing accounts represent amounts known to belong to the Federal Government but held temporarily in this account until additional information is collected for the disposition or reclassification of these amounts. Clearing accounts may be used to record unmatched transactions from the public when there is a reasonable presumption that the amounts belong to a Federal Government account other than miscellaneous receipts in the Treasury or to record unmatched transactions between Federal agencies, including IPAC transactions.

13.4    Contingent Liabilities

A contingent liability must be recognized in financial reports if a past event (e.g., contract breach) makes a probable and measurable future resource outflow. This applies when a legal claim is likely to be settled in the claimant's favor, and a settlement amount can be estimated. If a specific amount within a range is the best estimate, that amount is recognized; otherwise, the minimum amount in the range is recognized, with the nature and range of the contingency disclosed. If these recognition conditions aren't met, but a loss is at least reasonably possible, the contingent liability should be disclosed in the financial statement notes.

13.5    Legal contingencies

13.5.1. Legal contingencies arise from litigation, claims, and assessments. It is the Component management’s responsibility, with legal counsel’s advice, to assess the likelihood of adverse outcomes for legal cases and decide whether to recognize them as liabilities and to disclose them in the notes to the financial statements.

13.5.2. In accordance with SFFAS 5 and SFFAS 12, the only available categories to assess contingent losses based on the likelihood of the loss are Probable, Reasonably Possible, and Remote. When legal counsel cannot indicate whether the unfavorable outcome is probable or remote (e.g., unable to express an opinion), the Component should categorize the outcome as Reasonably Possible and disclose the notes to the financial statements.

13.6    Contract Progress Payments

When a DoW contractor requests a progress payment, a measurable liability is created for the DoW. Progress payment requests expected to be paid within one year are recorded as "Accounts Payable." The estimated amount of costs incurred by the contractor expected to remain unpaid for over a year until asset delivery is recorded as "Other Liabilities."

title: Section 14.0: Environmental and Disposal Liabilities
content:
14.0    ENVIRONMENTAL AND DISPOSAL LIABILITIES

14.1    Recognize Environmental and Disposal Liabilities

The Component must recognize environmental and disposal liabilities on the financial statements as a result of past transactions or events when the future outflows or expenditures of resources for environmental cleanup, closure, and/or disposal actions are probable and can be reasonably estimated.

14.2    Liability And Expense Recognition

The liability and expense should be recognized when both (1) Congress has appropriated or authorized resources, and (2) an exchange occurs (contractor performs repairs), or nonexchange amounts are unpaid as of the reporting date (direct payments to disaster victims), whichever applies, in accordance with SFFAS 5.

14.3    Liabilities for Environmental Cleanup

Refer to SFFAS 5 to address liabilities for environmental cleanup resulting from an accident, natural disaster, or other one-time occurrence. Refer to SFFAS 6 for the standards related to the timing of recognition of environmental and disposal liabilities and related inter-period operating expenses. Disclosure of the total estimated cost is required

14.4    Cleanup Costs

Cleanup costs associated with government-acknowledged events (such as toxic waste damage caused by nonfederal entities and natural disasters) do not meet the definition of a “liability” until, and to the extent that, the government formally acknowledges financial responsibility for the cost from the event and an exchange or nonexchange transaction has occurred.

14.5    Estimating Cleanup Cost

Cleanup costs must be estimated when the associated Property, Plant, and Equipment (PP&E) is placed in service. The estimate must be referred to as the “estimated total cleanup cost. As the Component pays cleanup costs, it must recognize the payments as a reduction in the liability for cleanup costs. These include the cost of PP&E or other assets acquired for use in cleanup activities. Refer to SFFAS 6 to recognize the total cleanup cost for Stewardship PP&E and general PP&E. The estimated environmental and disposal liabilities associated with the total cleanup cost for Stewardship PP&E must be consistent with the treatment of the acquisition cost of Stewardship PP&E (i.e., expensing in the period placed in service). Refer to SFFAS 6 for the estimated environmental and disposal liabilities associated with PP&E placed in service after September 30, 1997. Refer to SFFAS 5 to recognize the liability for the estimated cleanup cost if the environmental and disposal liability is not associated with an asset having a useful life. No amounts may be recognized as expense in the period of implementation. The amounts involved must be disclosed and, to the extent possible, the amount associated with current and prior periods should be noted. The offsetting charge for any liability for asbestos-related cleanup costs related to general PP&E in service at the date of implementation must be made to the net position of the entity. The amount of the adjustment must be shown as a “change in accounting principle” in any statement of changes in net position that may be required.

14.5.1. Estimates must be evaluated and revised periodically (at least annually) to account for material changes due to inflation or deflation and changes in regulations, plans, and/or technology.

14.5.2. For asbestos (both friable and non-friable) related environmental and disposal liabilities associated with PP&E, the initial date of the standard implementation is the effective date for the systematic liability recognition. Asbestos-related environmental and disposal liabilities associated with PP&E placed in service after September 30, 2012, must be systematically recognized over the remaining useful life of the PP&E.

14.5.3. Environmental and disposal liabilities that are unique in nature have different recognition criteria.

14.5.3.1. An environmental and disposal liability for military range cleanup, including unexploded ordnance, arises only after a formal decision to close the range or if hazardous waste migrates off-range. This guidance is based on the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) conditional exemption (40 CFR 266.202), which excludes military munitions used for their intended purpose—such as training military personnel or explosives and munitions emergency response specialists, research and development (R&D), and on-range destruction during clearance—from the definition of solid waste. However, this exemption does not cover on- range disposal or burial of munitions and contaminants that are not a result of product use.

14.5.3.2. Environmental and disposal liabilities for conventional munitions are recognized for the total estimated disposal cost when they are determined to be excess or obsolete as of the financial reporting date. As consumable inventory, a liability for conventional munitions only arises when they become excess or obsolete, requiring special disposal actions. Obsolescence occurs when munitions are no longer needed due to changes in technology, laws, or operations. The determination of excess or obsolete status must be supported by documentation of management's decision to permanently remove the asset from service and terminate its use.

14.5.3.3. Environmental and disposal liabilities for both stockpile and non- stockpile chemical agents and munitions, including those that are buried, must be recognized when the probable and reasonably estimable criteria have been met with TR2. Under 50 U.S.C. § 1521, the DoW is required to dispose of all chemical weapons and materiel, which includes the existing stockpile as well as non-stockpile items like binary chemical weapons, miscellaneous chemical warfare materiel, recovered chemical weapons, and former production facilities. Proper action is also necessary to mitigate the risks to human health and the environment from buried chemical agents and munitions.

14.5.3.4. When an entity permanently removes an asset from service, it must recognize the full environmental cleanup cost liability for its disposal, closure, or shutdown. If the removal is not permanent, or if there is no documented decision to permanently remove an asset from service, the full liability for cleanup costs associated with PP&E is not recorded, and the liability and associated cleanup costs continue to accumulate.

14.5.3.5. Overseas environmental and disposal liabilities, which are cleanup, closure, and/or disposal costs from operating overseas installations, are governed by DoDI 4715.08 and international agreements (per DoDD 5530.3). Considered "Government Related Events" under SFFAS 5, these liabilities are recognized when the event creating them occurs. The specific requirements for recognition are based on applicable SFFAS standards, DoW Issuances (like DoDI 4715.05), and international agreements.

14.5.3.6. When estimating the disposal cost of assets containing hazardous waste, stakeholders may recognize non-environmental costs that are considered immaterial to the total cost of removing or disposing of the asset(s) as an environmental and disposal liability.

14.5.3.7. Both friable and non-friable asbestos-related cleanup, closure, and/or disposal costs must be estimated in accordance with TB 2006-1, as amended by TB 2011-2. Asbestos-related cleanup, closure, and/or disposal costs are the expenses associated with removing, containing, or disposing of asbestos-containing materials from property or the materials themselves. These costs are incurred during the permanent or temporary closure or shutdown of associated PP&E, typically when cleanup is deferred until the end of an asset's useful life or performed at regular intervals.

14.5.4. When multiple reporting entities are involved with general PP&E and its cleanup, accounting responsibility is clearly defined. Federal Accounting Standards Advisory Board (FASAB) Interpretation 9 clarifies that during the asset's useful life, the entity that owns the asset must recognize inter-period operating costs and accrue the cleanup liability within the financial statements. At the time of transfer, the asset and its associated liability are derecognized by the original owner and recognized by the entity designated responsible for cleanup.

14.5.5. Changes in environmental and disposal liability cost estimates are recognized as current period expenses, with corresponding liability adjustments. Current period cleanup costs are also expensed and accrued as an environmental and disposal liability. Material error corrections from prior period operations require a prior period adjustment, restating comparative financial statements, and are reflected in the Statement of Changes in Net Position without current period expense recognition. Such adjustments, including those for estimated liabilities, arise from mistakes or misuse of facts that materially misstate financial statements. Disclosures must include involved amounts, noting current and prior period allocations where possible. Immaterial adjustments are recognized as current period events.

14.5.6. The risk of material misstatement of accounting estimates normally varies with the complexity and subjectivity associated with the process, the availability and reliability of relevant data, the number and significance of assumptions made, and the degree of uncertainty associated with those assumptions.

14.6    Environmental and Disposal Liability Estimates

14.6.1. Environmental and disposal liabilities are generally developed based on accounting estimates, because the extent of the environmental cleanup, closure, and/or disposal costs cannot be determined until completing cleanup/disposal operations. The accounting estimates are subject to Statement on Auditing Standards No 122/AU-C Section 540. Organizations that prepare accounting estimates must retain adequate documentation of quality review, estimator and reviewer qualifications, data sources, estimating methodologies, substantiation including the cost models, and internal control procedures.

14.6.2. The environmental cleanup, closure, and/or disposal costs that are probable and reasonably estimable must be estimated based on site-specific information using engineering estimates, comparison with similar sites, contaminants, equipment, parametric methodologies, or cost models validated in accordance with DoDI 5000.61. Once the DoW Component generates a cost estimate, the liability must be recognized and any uncertainty disclosed in the notes to the financial statements.

14.6.2.1. A cost estimate produced from a site-specific study is generally more reliable because it is based directly on environmental conditions at the site. However, understanding that DoW Components often include multiple sites on an individual contract, supporting documentation required to justify individual unpaid obligation transaction-level details does not need to be at the site level.

14.6.2.2. If a site-specific study is not available, the Component must assess if the site is similar to others where remediation has been completed, or a comprehensive study exists. If there is no investigation or comparable site data, costs are not considered reasonably estimable. In this case, the DoW Component should recognize the anticipated costs of future studies as an environmental and disposal liability until a site-specific study is completed.

14.6.2.3. If an acceptable cleanup technology is not available to address the site, then the Component must recognize the estimate to contain the hazardous waste and other relevant costs, such as the costs for future studies, as an environmental and disposal liability. The Component must also disclose the range of uncertainty in the notes to the financial statement.

14.6.2.4. When using cost models for environmental and disposal liability estimates, Components must accumulate relevant and reliable data, ensure estimates are prepared by qualified personnel and reviewed/approved by the appropriate authorities, and sustain the model's use by regularly compiling documentation to support cost factors (at least annually). This documentation must be available for audit. Decisions to update cost factors should be based on the impact of new information. Components must also compile documentation supporting the reasonableness of cost factors used by estimation software, obtain assurance from the service provider that the software has been validated, and compare prior estimates with actual results to assess the reliability of both the estimation process and the reasonableness of estimates developed.

14.6.3. Environmental and disposal liability estimates must be developed to include all event-driven environmental liability sites in the current asset/site universe and must include all asset-driven cleanup, closure, and/or disposal costs. Environmental and disposal liability estimates must be comprehensive, encompassing a wide range of potential costs. These include the compensation and benefits for government personnel directly involved, the cost of employing external contractors and consultants, and direct disposal costs such as demilitarization, material handling, and transportation. Estimates must also cover the costs of any dedicated facilities, machinery, and equipment, along with their associated operating and maintenance expenses, and any R&D for alternative remediation technologies. Furthermore, the calculation must include payments to regulatory agencies, permits and licenses, planning and design efforts, and costs to restore landscaping damaged by remediation. For the Defense Environmental Restoration Program, which is a statutorily defined program, associated program management costs must be included in the liability. These costs, which cannot be attributed to individual sites, are to be reported as rolled-up cost-to-complete estimates at the program level, covering the Future Years Defense Program (FYDP) and beyond; post-FYDP costs are estimated by applying the average percentage of program management costs from the FYDP to the remaining site-level requirements. All of these various cost estimates must be supported with appropriate documentation. Refer to DoDM 4715.20.

14.6.4. Environmental and disposal liability estimates must be reviewed annually and revised when there is evidence that significant changes in the cost measurement have occurred, such as changes in scope, ownership, regulation, or technology. The Component must retain contracts and invoices supporting the transaction-level details for combined multiple sites to support future audit requirements.

14.6.5. A portion of estimated total cleanup costs must be recognized as an expense during each period the PP&E is in operation. This must be accomplished systematically and rationally based on use of the physical capacity of the associated PP&E, whenever possible. If physical capacity is not applicable or estimable, the estimated useful life of the associated PP&E may serve as the basis for systematic and rational recognition of expense and accumulation of the liability.

14.6.6. Components must establish and maintain a complete and current universe of environmental and disposal liabilities.

14.6.7. After an initial baseline has been established, DoW Components must maintain site universes.

14.6.8. Components must establish and maintain environmental and disposal liability universe baselines for event-driven and asset-driven environmental and disposal liabilities:

14.6.8.1. Event-driven environmental and disposal liabilities. Components define the history, timeline, and activities employed in the environmental surveys to demonstrate that a due care approach was taken, in accordance with TR 2, to establish an initial baseline using current factors (e.g., technology, cost, and the regulatory environment. Documentation must be readily available to support the baseline, allowing auditors to verify the completeness of established cleanup site universes.

14.6.8.2. Asset-driven environmental and disposal liabilities. Refer to SFFAS 6. If an environmental and disposal liability applies to only a subset of the PP&E asset universe, Components must first review the entire universe and justify excluding non-applicable subcategories.

14.6.9. DoW Components must identify and account for environmental and disposal liabilities that are non-routine at the time of equipment disposal, in accordance with TR 11.

14.7    Environmental and Disposal Liability Disclosures

14.7.1. Financial statement disclosures provide pertinent information in notes or narratives about the amounts reported on the face of the financial statements. Refer to Volume 6. Disclosure requirements for liabilities, including environmental and disposal liabilities, differ depending on the underlying event and the probability and measurability (reasonably estimable) of loss. Key determinants of probable are the likelihood of contamination, whether the contamination is government-related, whether the government is legally liable or the government acknowledges the financial responsibility, and whether remediation technology exists. The classifications of likelihood are probable, reasonably possible, and remote.

14.7.2. Environmental and disposal liabilities meeting the criteria in TR 2 for “probable” and “reasonably estimable” must be recognized on the Balance Sheet. The recognition of environmental and disposal liabilities requires disclosure.

14.7.3. Environmental and disposal liabilities that don't meet the “probable” and "reasonably estimable" criteria for recognition, but for which there's a reasonable possibility of loss, are considered contingent liabilities.

14.7.4. DoW Components must disclose Intragovernmental Liabilities Not Covered by Budgetary Resources separately from Liabilities Covered by Budgetary Resources in accordance with Volume 6. Liabilities Covered by Budgetary Resources are liabilities incurred that are covered by realized budgetary resources as of the Balance Sheet date. Budgetary resources encompass not only new budget authority but also other resources available to cover liabilities for specified purposes in a given year. Available budgetary resources include new budget authority, unobligated balances of budgetary resources at the beginning of the year or net transfers of prior year balances during the year, spending authority from offsetting collections (credited to an appropriation or fund account); and recoveries of unexpired budget authority through downward adjustments of prior year obligations.

14.7.4.1. Liabilities are considered covered by budgetary resources if they are to be funded by permanent indefinite appropriations, which have been enacted and signed into law and are available for use as of the Balance Sheet date, provided that OMB may apportion the resources without further action by the Congress and without a contingency having to be met first.

14.7.4.2. Liabilities Not Covered by Budgetary Resources include liabilities incurred for which revenues or other sources of funds necessary to pay the liabilities have not been made available through Congressional appropriations or current earnings of the reporting entity.

14.7.5. DoW reports environmental litigation liabilities separately from other environmental and disposal liabilities in the notes to the financial statements. DoW Components must report estimates of certified third-party damage claims that are probable or reasonably possible.

14.7.6. Documentation to support the environmental and disposal liability recognition and disclosures, including management reviews, must be retained for the life of the liability. Once the liability has been eliminated, the documentation must be retained according to applicable retention and disposal instructions in their DoW Component records retention requirements.

14.8 Accounting Procedures for Recording Environmental and Disposal Liabilities

Refer to the SFIS and Volume 1 for the requirements for Standard Line of Accounting (SLOA)/Accounting Classification compliance for DoW business systems to meet statutory requirements and additional requirements implemented by the OMB and the Treasury. Environmental and disposal liabilities reported in the financial statements must reflect the liability as of the Balance Sheet date (i.e., as of September 30, or as of June 30), not an earlier date. Thus, when the annual evaluation of the environmental and disposal liabilities is performed as of a date earlier than September 30, DoW Components must develop, document, and execute a process for performing roll forward procedures. These procedures are to determine if any changes that meet the “probable” and “reasonably estimable” criteria occurring during the roll forward period have a significant impact on the estimates to be reported as of September 30.

14.8.1. Roll Forward Procedures: Environmental and disposal liabilities reported in the financial statements must reflect the liability as of the Balance Sheet date (i.e., as of September 30, or as of June 30), not an earlier date. Thus, when the annual evaluation of the environmental and disposal liabilities is performed as of a date earlier than September 30, DoD Components must develop, document, and execute a process for performing roll forward procedures. Refer to the Supplemental for more information on roll forward procedures.

14.8.2. Refer to the Supplemental for more information.

14.8.3. Quantitative Determination of Significant Amounts in the Roll Forward Period.

title: Section 15.0: Payment Integrity
content:
15.0    PAYMENT INTEGRITY

The DoW Payment Integrity portfolio comprises separate Payment Integrity programs that report improper payment and unknown payment risk assessments or statistical estimates. These programs include disbursements related to pay and benefits, commercial goods and services, health care, military retirement, and travel, which collectively encompass the majority of payments made by DoW annually in accordance with the Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (PIIA). Refer to the Federal Government PaymentAccuracy.gov website for a complete listing of DoW Payment Integrity programs. PIIA repealed the Improper Payments Information Act of 2002, the Improper Payments Elimination and Recovery Act of 2010, the Improper Payments Elimination and Recovery Improvement Act of 2012, and the Fraud Reduction and Data Analytics Act of 2015. The requirements for compliance with PIIA are described in the OMB Circular A-123, Appendix C, and OMB Circular A-136, or their successor publications.

15.1    Program Payment Integrity Activities by Phase

15.1.1. The Component categorizes programs with annual outlays exceeding $10 million as either Phase 1 or Phase 2. A program is designated as Phase 1 if its combined total of improper and unknown payments is unlikely to surpass the statutory threshold. This threshold is defined as either 1) payments exceeding both 1.5% of program outlays and $10 million annually, or 2) payments exceeding $100 million, irrespective of the improper payment percentage.

15.1.2. Phase 1 Payment Integrity Activities Performed by the DoW Components. PIIA requires that federal agencies assess all programs with annual outlays greater than $10,000,000 for IP risk at least once every three years. The purpose of an improper payment (IP) risk assessment is to adequately conclude whether the program is likely to make total annual IPs plus unknown payments (UP) above or below the statutory threshold and thus may be susceptible to significant improper payments for the given year. The results of the IP risk assessment help identify weaknesses in internal controls that, if strengthened, could prevent future IPs and UPs from occurring. Establishing and maintaining effective internal controls, including an internal control system that prevents IPs and UPs from being made and promptly detects and recovers any IPs that are determined to be recoverable, should be a priority.

15.1.3. Phase 2 Payment Integrity Activities Performed by the DoW Components. If a program's risk assessment determines that its annual improper and unknown payments are likely to exceed the statutory threshold, it enters 'Phase 2'. In the following fiscal year, the program must report statistically valid estimates for both improper and unknown payments to reflect the total annual amount for the program.

15.1.3.1. Programs reporting IPs for the first time must produce a Sampling and Estimation Methodology Plan (S&EMP). A program’s S&EMP should have a mechanism for identifying, accounting for, and estimating the annual IPs and the annual UPs separately. Once a program has submitted a S&EMP to OMB, the program does not need to resubmit a S&EMP unless an update to the plan is warranted (i.e., if the program is impacted by any significant legislative, funding, structural, or guidance changes).

15.1.3.2. Programs must perform an adequate reconciliation of any population, such as the disbursement systems used in the creation of the S&EMP. The reconciliation process should be documented in the S&EMP.

15.1.3.3. If a program is in Phase 2, has established a baseline, and reports an IP and UP estimate that is below the statutory threshold, it will automatically move back into Phase 1 the following FY unless the OIG of DoW issued a noncompliance finding for the program in the previous year and that the finding demonstrated that the program IP and UPs estimate was inaccurate and inappropriate given the program characteristics.

15.1.4. Components must sample, conduct post-payment reviews, estimate the amount of improper payments and unknown payments using statistically valid sampling methodologies, and report improper payments and unknown payments to the OUSW(C) for reporting in the consolidated Agency Financial Report (AFR) and the annual OMB Payment Integrity data call.

15.2    Compliance With PIIA Requirements

The OIG DoW, on an annual basis, will evaluate the Department’s compliance with the requirements under PIIA. The Department is not considered compliant under PIIA if one or more of its programs are found non-compliant with one or more PIIA requirements. If the OIG DoW determines that a program is non-compliant for any requirement, then the final OIG report must provide concrete recommendations to the program or DoW Component with specific actions the program must take to achieve compliance with the requirement. DoW Intelligence Agencies that have a standalone PIIA Compliance audit conducted by their own Inspector General are excluded from incorporation into the Department’s overall PIIA portfolio that is reported publicly, OUSW(C), FMPR Payment Integrity team maintains executive oversight and the DoW Intelligence Agencies must follow the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, National Intelligence Program, PIIA guidelines and reporting requirements. Classified payments are excluded from public reporting. The PIIA requirements are:

15.2.1. Publish a Payment Integrity section in the Other Information section of the consolidated DoW AFR for the most recent fiscal year and post the consolidated AFR and any accompanying materials required by OMB. DoW Components are not required to include payment integrity information in their individual AFRs. DoW Components must include the following statement under the Payment Integrity section in their individual AFRs: “DoW reports payment integrity information (i.e., improper payments) at the agency-wide level in the consolidated DoW Agency Financial Report.

15.2.2. Conduct a program-specific risk assessment for each DoW program or activity and adequately conclude whether the program is likely to make IPs plus UPs above or below the statutory threshold.

15.2.3. Publish IP and UP estimates for programs susceptible to significant improper and unknown payments in the accompanying materials to the consolidated DoW AFR.

15.2.4. Publish corrective action plans (CAPs) for each program susceptible to significant improper and unknown payments for which an estimate above the statutory threshold was published in the accompanying materials to the annual financial statement.

15.2.5. Publish a reduction target for each DoW program that has reported IP and UP estimates above the statutory threshold, demonstrated improvements to payment integrity or reached a tolerable improper payment or unknown payment rate, and develop a plan to meet the established reduction target.

15.2.6. Report an IP and UP estimate of less than 10 percent for each DoW program and activity for which an IP and UP estimate was published in the accompanying materials to the annual financial statement.

15.3    OUSW(C) Roles and Responsibilities

15.3.1. FMPR Directorate Role

The DCFO Financial Management Policy Reporting (FMPR) Directorate manages the DoW Payment Integrity portfolio. The FMPR Directorate provides oversight to the DoW Components to ensure compliance with the authoritative guidance on Payment Integrity. Additionally, FMPR must be notified by the audit agency of any stand‑alone audits regarding Payment Integrity.

15.3.2. The FMPR Directorate holds a wide range of responsibilities related to Payment Integrity within the DoW. The Directorate must interpret and guide DoW Components to ensure compliance with authoritative regulations. The FMPR Directorate also coordinates efforts to reduce monetary loss, compiling and submitting quarterly reports to OMB for any high-priority programs that project over $100 million in improper payments. A key part of their role is to establish and report baselines for payment integrity, then work with DoW Components to set reduction targets and develop plans to meet them. They are responsible for reviewing and consolidating all payment integrity data from the Components, reporting the final results in the consolidated DoW AFR and to OMB through the Annual Data Call. Furthermore, the FMPR Directorate prepares and submits all DoW-wide reports on Payment Integrity and serves as the primary liaison for annual OIG DoW and Government GAO audits, ensuring timely information transmission and implementation of auditor recommendations. They also provide administrative and technical support to the DoW PIIA Senior Accountable Officials Steering Committee, which oversees the Payment Integrity program. Finally, the FMPR Directorate is responsible for keeping the Payment Integrity policy within the DoW Financial Management Regulation current and for retaining all documentation submitted by DoW Components, in accordance with official financial records retention policies. For additional information on FMPR retention requirements, refer to OSW Records Disposition Schedules.

15.4    DoW Component Roles/Responsibilities

15.4.1. The DoW Components ensure that their payments are valid, accurate, and complete. Additionally, the DoW Components ensure that their payments are subjected to post- payment reviews that align with the Department’s Payment Integrity lines of effort.

15.4.2. For each DoW program under Phase 1, conduct a program-specific risk assessment to determine if the DoW program or activity is susceptible to significant improper payments.

15.4.3. For each DoW program under Phase 2 that has been determined to be susceptible to significant improper payments, develop a statistically valid S&EMP. In addition, implement the S&EMP to produce statistically valid improper payment and unknown payment estimates for all DoW programs and activities determined to be susceptible to significant improper payments. Report annual results of improper payments and unknown payments to OUSW(C), FMPR, for adjudication, consolidation, and reporting in the Payment Integrity section of the consolidated DoW AFR and to OMB through their Annual Data Call.

15.4.4. For programs or activities determined to be susceptible to significant improper payments and unknown payments above the statutory threshold designated by OMB, identify the root causes of improper payments and unknown payments and develop cost-effective CAPs that eliminate the root causes of improper payments and unknown payments and prevent and reduce improper payments and unknown payments. Submit results on a quarterly basis to OUSW(C), FMPR, for consolidation and reporting in accordance with OMB for high-priority programs. High- priority programs must provide quarterly Payment Integrity Scorecard reporting on PaymentAccuracy.gov.

15.4.5. Implement a cost-effective payment recovery program to recover improper overpayments that resulted in monetary losses.

15.4.6. Support the annual OIG DoW performance audit and relevant GAO audits in a timely manner by furnishing all required provided-by-client documentation, providing responses to auditor’s inquiries, and implementing auditor recommendations. Provide support for all ad-hoc requests from external oversight bodies (i.e., OMB, GAO, and Congress). Notify OUSW(C), FMPR of any stand-alone audits regarding Payment Integrity that directly impact their Component. Retain documentation submitted by the DoW Components.

15.5    OMB Circular No. A-123 Appendix C

DoW Components must implement the requirements in OMB Circular No. A-123, Appendix C, or its successor publication.

15.6    OMB Circular No. A-136

15.6.1. The Department must implement the requirements in OMB Circular No. A-136, or its successor publication. The Department must complete the annual OMB Data Call and include a link to PaymentAccuracy.gov in its consolidated AFR. Key responsibilities include contacting OMB by September 1st to gain access to the Data Call and reviewing its guidance to determine applicable requirements. If recovery audits are conducted and the contractor recommends actions to prevent overpayments, the Department should report on these actions in the AFR.

15.6.2. High-priority programs are required to provide in the annual consolidated DoW AFR a summary of their payment integrity activities and results.

title: Section 16.0: Revenue and Other Financing Sources, Gains and Losses
content:
16.0    REVENUE AND OTHER FINANCING SOURCES, GAINS AND LOSSES

16.1    Revenue

16.1.1. The DoW generates revenue from its normal operations and may experience gains or losses from unusual or nonrecurring transactions. Revenue is defined as an inflow of resources that the government either demands, earns, or receives as a donation, resulting in an increase in assets, a decrease in liabilities, or both, which ultimately increases the Net Position. A prime example of how a decrease in liabilities impacts revenue is the reduction of “Liabilities for Advances and Prepayment” after the delivery of goods or services.

16.1.2. Exchange and Nonexchange Revenues

16.1.2.1. DoW activities (WCF within the Military Departments and Other Defense Organizations, and construction agents) earn exchange revenues when they provide goods and services at cost to other government entities and the public. They must recognize revenue at the actual price received or receivable as soon as the value is delivered and post exchange revenue at the actual price that is received or receivable under the established pricing arrangement.

16.1.2.2. Nonexchange revenues are inflows of resources that the government demands or receives by donation.

16.1.2.3. Cost of goods sold must be recorded when exchange revenues are generated by providing goods and services. Costs must be recorded in the appropriate accounts, such as Cost of Goods Sold for Inventory Sales or Operating Expenses/Program Costs for services sales. The cost of goods sold account is discussed in Section 17.

16.1.2.4. Nonappropriated Funds (NAF) Activity Revenues must be accounted for in accordance with Volume 13. NAF Activities are not included in federal financial statements and are non-federal activities for budgetary and proprietary accounting purposes. They follow the standards of the FASB rather than FASAB.

16.1.2.5. Refunds are recoveries of overpayments and can result from errors in paying invoices or items returned to the vendor, not revenue.

16.1.3. Reimbursements and Collections

16.1.3.1. The Component requires specific legal authority to retain collections from providing reimbursable goods and services; otherwise, all funds collected must be transferred to a miscellaneous receipt account. The expenses incurred for this work must be recorded in full and cannot be reduced or offset by reimbursements. See Volume 11 for additional information about reimbursements.

16.1.3.2. The Component must record revenue in the financial records, collect it promptly, and deposit it in the appropriate Treasury account.

16.2    Exchange Revenue Recognition and Measurement

16.2.1. Exchange revenues are earned when both parties in a transaction sacrifice and receive value, such as with user charges or intragovernmental cost reimbursements. The revenue recognized from these transactions is the price received or receivable for the exchange.

16.2.2. Revenue from advance payments must be deferred until the related goods or services are provided. Upon receipt, these funds must be recorded as an increase to cash and a liability, such as "unearned revenue," and this liability is only cleared once performance is complete.

16.2.3. A receivable must be recorded when revenue is recognized, and payment is not received. If the full amount is not expected due to credit losses, returns, allowances, or price redeterminations, bad debt expense must be recognized. An appropriate allowance for estimated bad debts must be established.

16.3    Exchange Revenue Disclosures

16.3.1. Each DoW Component that provides goods or services to the public or another government agency must disclose information about exchange revenue.

16.3.2. If increased prices for the exchange revenue may cause reduced demand, the entity must provide an estimate of the possible revenue foregone and provide calculation assumptions.

16.4    Nonexchange Revenue Recognition and Measurement

16.4.1. Nonexchange revenues, such as taxes, fines, and donations, stem from the government's power to demand payment. They are recognized in the financial results of operations only when a specifically identifiable, legally enforceable claim exists, collection is probable, and the amount is measurable. Detailed guidance on reporting these revenues can be found in Volume 6.

16.4.2. Donations from non-federal entities, whether financial, such as cash or securities, or non-financial, such as land or buildings, are recognized as nonexchange revenue at their estimated fair market value. However, no value is recognized for donations of heritage assets or stewardship land, unless they are classified as multi-use heritage assets, which must be recorded at fair market value.

16.4.3. The Component must deposit collections not authorized for retention as miscellaneous receipts into the Treasury's GF, regardless of whether they are exchange or nonexchange revenue. If the underlying asset is predominantly nonexchange, the revenue is nonexchange. While the collecting entity is responsible for measuring any nonexchange revenue, it is the legally entitled recipient entity that must formally recognize it, as detailed in SFFAS 7.

16.5    Nonexchange Revenue Disclosures

Each DoW Component must disclose nonexchange revenue.

16.6    Other Financing Sources

The DoW Component must categorize appropriations used, asset transfers from other government entities, and imputed financing from cost subsidies as “other financing sources.”

16.6.1. Appropriations

DoW Components do not consider appropriations a financing source until they use them. When appropriations are available for apportionment, the Component recognizes them in its capital accounts as ‘unexpended appropriations.’ The Component then reduces this balance as it uses the funds or makes adjustments for changes like rescissions and transfers. The Component recognizes the net change in unexpended appropriations as a change in its net position. Once used, appropriations become a financing source in determining the net results of operations. DoW Components ‘use’ appropriations when they receive goods and services, provide benefits and grants (which the Component provides when grantees meet the requirements), and establish the related liability.

16.6.2. Imputed Financing

16.6.2.1. Government entities frequently receive goods and services from other government entities without fully reimbursing them or incur costs like pensions that are paid by other entities. These transactions create imputed costs for the provider and imputed financing for the recipient. Recognizing these imputed costs and their corresponding offsets is crucial when such costs contribute to government goods or services provided for a fee.

16.6.2.2. WCFs must recognize these subsidized costs as an imputed financing source equal to the imputed cost. This offsets any effect of imputed cost on net results of operations for the period.

16.6.2.3. GFs do not recognize imputed financing. However, OMB requires GFs to recognize certain imputed costs. These exceptions include: employee pension, post-retirement health, and life insurance benefits; postemployment benefits for terminated and inactive employees, such as unemployment and workers' compensation under the Federal Employees’ Compensation Act; and losses from litigation proceedings that the Treasury Judgment Fund pays.

16.6.2.4. DoW Component imputed costs can include military personnel costs, retirement benefits, other postemployment benefits, unreimbursed tenant’s costs, and unreimbursed environmental cleanup costs, when administered outside the DoW reporting entity.

16.7    Transfers

For unreimbursed intragovernmental asset transfers, the receiving entity must recognize a transfer-in as an additional financing source, while the transferring entity recognizes a transfer-out as a decrease in its result of operations. The transfer must be recorded at the asset's book value; if the book value is unknown, the asset's estimated fair market value on the transfer date is used. Trading partners should record reciprocal transfers in the same accounting period to avoid reconciliation differences. Refer to the procedures for more on PP&E transfers and refer to OMB Circular A-11 for guidance on the budgetary impact of transfers.

16.8    Gains or Losses

16.8.1. The Component must recognize gains or losses for unusual or nonrecurring transactions, such as the sale, exchange, or disposition of government assets (excluding inventory held for sale). A loss is also recognized when inventory is reclassified as excess, obsolete, or unserviceable because its value falls below its acquisition cost. The difference between an asset's sale proceeds and its book value is recognized as a gain or loss upon sale. This principle applies to assets, PP&E, receivables, and investments where the selling entity retains the proceeds.

16.8.2. Base Realignment and Closure gains and losses are discussed in Volume 12.

16.8.3. Record unrealized holding gains/losses on securities available for sale in accordance with FASAB’s ASC 321-10-35; fair value hedges, cash flow hedges, and accounting for a hedge of a net investment in a foreign operation under ASC 815‑20‑25; and foreign currency matters under ASC 830-10.

16.9    Volume 4 Appendix

Refer to the appendix within the Supplemental. The appendix provides accounting standards used for classifying transactions that finance the DoW cost of operations and a significant number of lesser transactions aligned to SFFAS 7. This appendix is divided into the following groups: nonexchange transactions; exchange transactions that produce revenue; other financing sources; revaluation gains and losses; and transactions not recognized as revenues, gains, or other financing sources.

title: Section 17.0: Expenses and Miscellaneous Items
content:
17.0    EXPENSES AND MISCELLANEOUS ITEMS

Expenses represent a cash outlay, consumption of assets, and/or the incurrence of liabilities during a period of providing goods, rendering services, or carrying out other normal operating activities related to the entity’s programs and missions, which results in a decrease in the entity’s net position. Accounting systems must be capable of reporting transactions in sufficient detail to support budget preparation and cost accounting requirements.

17.1    Exceptions to Cash Outlays

While most expenses require cash outlays, exceptions include depreciation, other losses, and bad debt expenses. Miscellaneous non-cash items can also arise from extraordinary transactions, prior period adjustments, and changes in actuarial liabilities.

17.2    Unusual or Nonrecurring Transactions

Costs from extraordinary or unexpected events are classified as miscellaneous items. However, unusual or nonrecurring transactions, or those from an entity's incidental activities, should be recognized as a gain or loss rather than revenue or expense.

17.3    Budgetary Accounts

An expense typically involves the use of budgetary or other resources. When goods and services are ordered and received, they are recorded as expended authority in the budgetary accounts and as an expense in the proprietary accounts, supporting financial control over resources and accurate accounting during budget execution.

17.4    DWCF Expenses

The treatment of expenses by some DWCF activities differs compared to the treatment of appropriation-funded activities. Expenses are costs accumulated in asset accounts such as Construction in Progress (CIP) or Inventory Work in Process and are subsequently billed to customers. Expenses are also costs to the activity or cost center, similar to appropriated funded activities. Refer to Volume 11 for DWCF policy.

17.5    Presentation in Financial Statements

17.5.1. Expense Recognition

Expenses are commonly reported at the time they are incurred, not when invoices are received. Goods and services (costs) acquired from or provided to other government trading partners or programs (i.e., intragovernmental) must be recorded separately from those purchased from nonfederal entities (i.e., the public).

17.5.2. Program Costs

Program costs, as required by Volume 6 for the Statement of Net Cost, encompass the full costs of program outputs, including direct costs, costs directly traced or allocated on a cause-and- effect basis, and nonproduction costs. These costs must also include services provided by other entities, even if not fully reimbursed, and costs paid by other entities that accounting standards require to be recognized within the financial statements.

17.5.3. Production and Nonproduction Costs

The Component must report costs related to the production of outputs separately from nonproduction costs on the Statement of Net Cost. Nonproduction costs are reported as a separate item in the financial statements and are addressed in the SFFAS 4.

17.5.3.1. The cost of acquiring, constructing, improving, reconstructing, or renovating heritage assets. Costs associated with multi-use heritage assets are capitalized and depreciated over the expected useful life if they meet the capitalization criteria.

17.5.3.2. The acquisition cost of acquiring stewardship land.

17.5.3.3. The cost of maintenance not performed but delayed to a future period (deferred maintenance) reported in the Required Supplementary Information (RSI) section of the financial statements. Refer to Volume 6.

17.5.4. Expenses and Miscellaneous Items

Operating expenses, which include personnel costs, contractual services, and OM&S, can also include allocations of prior capital outlays (depreciation/amortization) or cost recovery for operations. Also known as program costs, these expenses are tied to specific programs or functions and often require a budgetary entry to record obligations from the unexpended obligation (undelivered order) to the expended authority (delivered order). Examples include personnel, travel, communications, contractual services, and other program expenses. DWCF activities typically record these expenses to a cost of goods sold account to match costs with revenue.

17.5.5. Property, Plant and Equipment

Costs for PP&E acquired or constructed for a project must be capitalized if the acquisition cost exceeds the Department’s threshold, the items are not for sale in the ordinary course of operations, are intended for entity use, and have a life expectancy of over two years. Conversely, an asset may be expensed if it falls below the purchasing agency's capitalization threshold or has a useful life of less than two years, even if acquired from another federal agency.

17.5.6. Work in Process Account

WIP accounts must accumulate the costs of goods or services. The WIP cost amounts and applicable inventory accounts serve as the basis for calculating the cost of goods sold.

17.5.7. Depreciation, Amortization and Depletion Account

Depreciation, Amortization and Depletion are used to record the allocation of the cost of an asset (tangible or intangible) over the period of time benefited or the asset’s useful life.

17.5.8. Benefits Expense

17.5.8.1. The employer's contribution to various employee benefit programs including retirement funds, life insurance, Voluntary Separation Incentive Payments (VSIP), FECA, unemployment, Social Security, and Medicare, constitutes a benefit expense. This expense must be recorded in the entity's General Ledger by the program and/or administering agency as it is incurred for benefit payments.

17.5.8.2. Employer contributions to the Thrift Savings Plan are nonfederal expenses. The account must be supported by subsidiary accounts to show the types of transactions for which entitlement benefits were incurred.

17.5.8.3. Administrative expenses incurred for benefit payments are generally nonfederal expenses. This includes (but is not limited to) costs for retirement, life insurance, health insurance, VSIP, FECA, unemployment, entitlements, and insurance guarantees (i.e., flood insurance).

17.5.9. Cost of Goods Sold Account

The cost of goods sold account is used to record the cost of goods or services sold from inventory by various DoW activities, including DWCF activities and other entities authorized to provide services to federal and nonfederal organizations. While predominantly used by revolving fund activities, this account must also be used by appropriated fund activities to support their reimbursable programs.

7.5.10. Imputed Costs Account

All DoW activities receiving goods or services without reimbursement from outside their reporting entity must use the Imputed Cost account. Refer to SFFAS 55 for the recognition of significant inter-entity costs among federal agencies for business-type activities. Business-type activities, like the DWCF, are self-sustaining, financing operations through exchange revenues.

17.5.11. Future Funded Expenses

Future funded expenses are accrued expenses requiring future year appropriations. Examples include accrued annual leave (except for WCFs), accrued workers' compensation, upward re-estimates for credit reform loan programs, and projected future cleanup costs for hazardous materials associated with PP&E.

17.5.12. Expense Transactions Not Requiring Budgetary Resources

Some expense transactions, such as depreciation, imputed costs (paid by other entities), or future-funded expenses, do not require the use of current budgetary resources. For these, only proprietary accounts are used, often allocating costs over multiple reporting periods.

17.5.13. Losses

Losses are associated with transactions not incurred in the normal operation of the organization (such as the loss on the disposal of property).

17.5.13.1. Losses on Disposition of Assets Account

The Losses on Disposition of Assets account is used to record a loss incurred on the disposition of DoW-owned assets. Such losses can result from the sale, exchange, casualty, or retirement of assets. Losses are reported net of any received proceeds.

17.5.13.2. Components of Losses on Disposition of Assets Account

The Losses on Disposition of Assets account must be used only by DoW Components authorized to dispose of DoW property; however, any DoW Component having control over personal and real property may incur such losses due to events beyond its control. The effect of such losses must be recorded in Losses on Disposition of Assets in the Statement of Net Cost.

17.5.13.3. Other Losses

Other Losses must be used to record the loss on assets resulting from events other than disposition, such as investment losses and miscellaneous losses.

17.5.14. Extraordinary Items

Events are classified as extraordinary items when they are both unusual and infrequent, considering the entity's operating environment. The total amount of all extraordinary items is included in the Statement of Net Cost's applicable Gross Program Cost or Non-Production Cost lines, and their nature and amount must be disclosed in the financial statements.

17.5.15. Prior Period Adjustments

Circumstances may arise requiring an entity to adjust prior period financial statements due to a change in accounting principle or correction of a material error. Such circumstances include the retrospective application of a change in accounting principle or the correction of a material error in prior period financial statements pursuant to SFFAS 21. Refer to Volume 6 for information on reporting prior period adjustments in the financial statements.

17.5.15.1. Change in Accounting Principle

A change in accounting principle involves adopting a new, preferable GAAP, including new federal financial accounting standards, to produce more accurate and meaningful financial statements and disclosures. The term "accounting principle" encompasses both the principles themselves and their application methods. Unless otherwise specified in the transition instructions section of a new federal financial accounting standard, the cumulative effect of the change on prior periods should be reported as a change in accounting principle, with the adjustment made to the beginning balance of the cumulative results of operations in the Statement of Changes in Net Position. The nature of the changes in accounting principle and its effect on relevant balances should be disclosed in the current period. Financial statements of subsequent periods need not repeat the disclosure.

17.5.15.2. Correction of Errors

If material errors are discovered after financial statements have been issued, corrections must be made. For comparative statements, the error should be corrected in the earliest affected period presented by adjusting individual financial statement amounts. If the error occurred before the earliest period shown, its cumulative effect should be reported as a prior period adjustment to the beginning balance of cumulative results of operations in the Statement of Changes in Net Position for the earliest period presented. The nature of the error and the effect of its correction must be disclosed. Importantly, prior period financial statements should only be restated for errors that would have caused them to be materially misstated.

title: Section 18.0: Managerial Cost Accounting
content:
18.0    MANAGERIAL COST ACCOUNTING

18.0.1. Managerial cost accounting standards provide reliable and timely information on the full cost of federal programs, projects, activities, and outputs. This information is the foundation for accurate and consistent cost accounting, and it clarifies the relationship between cost accounting, financial reporting, and budgeting. Cost accounting information is also crucial for DoW program managers and stakeholders, aiding in informed decisions regarding budget control, performance measurement, pricing, program evaluations, and economic choices. As an integral part of the financial management system, managerial cost accounting concepts provide a basis for accounting, recognition, and measurement.

18.0.2. The five fundamental elements of managerial cost accounting are as follows: First, costs of activities must be accumulated and reported on a regular basis for management information purposes. Second, responsibility segments should be established to match costs with outputs. Third, the full costs of government goods and services need to be determined. Fourth, the costs of goods and services provided among Federal entities must be recognized. Finally, appropriate costing methodologies should be used to accumulate and assign costs to outputs. Agencies have flexibility in designing a cost accounting methodology that meets both internal and external user needs. Refer to SFFAS 4.

18.0.3. Managerial cost accounting helps an organization determine at what point a program might experience a cost overrun given its current spending plan. It also clarifies the full costs to deliver goods and services by organization, line of business, or region. Ultimately, this information provides insight into how effectively the organization is managing its resources for mission success and cost efficiency, and how well it has met its strategic goals with the resources available.

18.1    Assignment and Methodologies

Managers must establish appropriate procedures for collection, measurement, analysis, interpretation, and communication of consistent cost information with a system or the use of cost assignment approaches that link financial expenses to an organization's outputs. The primary method for assigning costs is by directly tracing them whenever feasible and economically practical. If direct tracing isn't possible, costs should be assigned based on a cause-and-effect relationship or, as a last resort, allocated on a reasonable and consistent basis. While no specific costing methodology is mandated by SFFAS 4, the standard requires that once a methodology for accumulating and allocating costs is chosen, it must be used consistently and guided by the USSGL and the SFIS.

18.2    Systems, Sources and Cost Finding

18.2.1. A system is a continuous and systematic process designed to accumulate and assign costs from a common data source to various objects, either routinely or as managers require. This data source can include a wide variety of financial and non-financial information to support cost, financial, and budgetary accounting.

18.2.2. When data systems cannot provide the necessary cost information, or for non- recurring needs like budget estimates and special analyses, personnel can use cost-finding techniques such as analytical or sampling methods and special studies. These techniques should not, however, replace consistent and regular managerial cost reporting when it is available.

18.3    Reporting and Analysis

Reporting and analysis of reliable cost information offers a deeper understanding of programs, including their costs, changes over time, and overall efficiency. This data supports budgetary, financial, and managerial decisions. Aligning planned and actual performance data brings additional benefits, such as capturing the full costs of products and manpower, creating transparency in pricing, and ensuring consistent reporting for historical analysis and forecasting.

18.4    Users

All stakeholders, regardless of their function, require accurate reporting to identify cash, disbursements, collections, and the full cost of resources, activities, capabilities, and operations. For DoW Reporting Components, this is particularly crucial for making better decisions at the cost element level, knowing the cost of operations and activities, and linking budget planning to actual expenditures. This level of reporting also enables responses to both external and internal cost inquiries and makes costs visible to DoW leadership, component leadership, operational commanders, and program managers.

18.4.1. Internal Users

Government managers are the primary users of cost information, as they are responsible for carrying out program objectives. Program managers use this data to control costs, make resource acquisition decisions, improve the efficiency of program activities, and prepare budget proposals for agency heads and Congress. Concurrently, financial managers, including accountants and budget analysts, rely on cost information to calculate unit costs, analyze variances, formulate standard costs, compile financial reports, and analyze cost behavior for decisions such as whether to buy or lease. Additionally, franchise activity managers use it to set prices or reimbursements. At the executive level, government leaders utilize cost information to evaluate overall program performance, assess future resource requirements for financial plans and budgets, and develop proposals to the President and Congress on resource allocations and program modifications.

18.4.2. External Users
