2.4.1.2. Civilians concurrently employed in more than one position must use the same identifier (SSN or ITIN) across every position. Person identifier data must support the capability to correct and update a person's identity information, per DoWI 1444.02, Volume 1.

2.4.2. Individual Employee Pay Records

2.4.2.1. Each employee must have an individual pay record maintained as part of the master pay record. Except for multiple appointments, only one pay record may be active at any time for each authorized position. If more than one pay record is maintained, the rationale must be thoroughly documented and an audit trail maintained. Sufficient information on active pay records must be retained or accessible at the servicing PRO to support manual input, payment, and performance of other required administrative functions.

2.4.2.2. The pay record must contain all transaction information related to payments and deductions, with an audit trail to the authorizing source document, subject to paragraph 4.5. The pay record must contain information on rates of pay pertaining to the categories listed in this paragraph.

2.4.2.3. The pay records must be supported by T&A, leave records, and personnel records. T&A records contain all hours for a pay period based on the effective work schedule. All hours worked (regular and premium) and leave taken (paid and unpaid) are used to compute pay. Leave records include annual, sick, and any other leave earned, taken, lost, forfeited, restored, or advanced, including appropriate unused leave balances. The pay record must contain other information, such as year-to-date and quarter-to-date totals, as necessary, to compute pay and prepare reports.

2.4.2.4. Year-to-date information must be maintained for the current and prior pay years. Pay records must be dispositioned per the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), General Records Schedule (GRS) 2.4: Employee Compensation and Benefits Records.

2.4.3. Payroll Substantiating Document File

2.4.3.1. Under a centralized civilian payroll function, separate document files are required and maintained for each employee. The servicing PRO must maintain documents applicable to PRO functions and responsibilities. The Customer Service Representative (CSR)/employing activity must maintain documents applicable to CSR responsibilities.

2.4.3.2. All source documents that substantiate the employee's entitlement to compensation, leave, benefits, and authorizations, or that support deductions, whether maintained in hardcopy or electronic format, must be safeguarded from improper or unauthorized access or use. Payroll-related documents, whether maintained by the PRO or the CSR, must be dispositioned per NARA, GRS 2.4. Each agency may establish a specific document retention policy; however, the policy must not impose a lesser retention requirement than NARA requirements.

2.4.3.3. All source documents must be readily available for research. Active and inactive files must be dispositioned per NARA, GRS 2.4 for current employees and NARA, GRS
2.5    for separated employees.

2.4.4. Retention sites must control source documents to ensure timely processing of payroll documents, auditing, and reconciliation of individual pay accounts. Local document control procedures may be used as long as appropriate control and access are maintained.

2.4.5. Personnel Actions

2.4.5.1. DCPS is integrated or interfaced with the personnel system the employee's agency uses. DCPS must use the information the personnel system authorizes as the basis for pay, leave entitlements, and some deduction calculations.

2.4.5.2. The servicing HRO must maintain source documentation for actions originating with the Human Resources Office (HRO). Where the systems do not permit interface of the actions, the servicing HRO must provide the servicing PRO a hardcopy or electronic copy of the document, which the servicing PRO also must maintain.

2.4.6. Appropriate controls must be established for all payroll functions.

2.4.6.1. The controls must ensure the timely, correct, complete, accurate, and properly authorized processing of payroll documents, including the items in paragraphs 2.4.6.1.1 through 2.4.6.1.5.

2.4.6.1.1. An authorized official must approve, in writing or through electronic signature (made by entering designated codes into an automated system under safeguards that prevent unauthorized use), corrections and other adjustments to data in official records, as set out in paragraphs 2.6.1.1.1 through 2.6.1.1.3.

2.4.6.1.1.1. Records of all changes made after records have been approved or certified must be generated and maintained.

2.4.6.1.1.2. Manual corrections to documents made after the documents have been approved or certified must be made in a way that does not obliterate the original entries. A designated authorizing official must approve the corrections.

2.4.6.1.1.3. Automated system changes to data must be made so that an audit trail is maintained to show, or reference, documents showing the original and new data and the authorization for the change. Such changes may be made only based on properly approved documents authorizing the changes.

2.4.6.1.2. Separation of duties applies to the PRO and system development personnel. To minimize opportunities for unauthorized, fraudulent, or otherwise irregular acts, the payroll duties listed in this paragraph must be separated so that no one person performs all phases of a transaction without the possibility of intervention or review by another person.

2.4.6.1.3. Access to the items listed in this paragraph must be restricted to authorized personnel.

2.4.6.1.4. Employees must not maintain or service their own payroll or personnel records. This internal control must be incorporated into the security system software that governs access to DCPS records. Employees may provide authorizing source documentation to the servicing CSR or input data using an electronic self-service application. The employee transactions maintained by the CSR or input by the employee through such an application are listed in this paragraph.

2.4.6.1.5. To detect inappropriate data at the earliest time and to the extent practical, data entered into DCPS must be subjected to computerized edits at the time of entry.

2.4.7. PROs must ensure that payroll data is complete and accurate. DCPS and the HRO must each reconcile employee records to ensure that shared data matches.

2.4.7.1. Reconciliation of common data (for example, work schedule, salary, and date of birth) between the human resources system and DCPS must be accomplished at least every 4 months. The servicing HRO reviews the reconciliation and annotates any mismatches. The servicing HRO resolves mismatches where possible and provides supporting documentation to the servicing PRO to resolve payroll record errors. The servicing PRO must ensure thorough reviews of and necessary corrections to the DCPS database. The servicing PRO must complete the payroll portion of the reconciliation within 10 workdays after receiving the annotated reconciliation documentation from the servicing HRO. The servicing PRO must maintain historic records to ensure timely compliance with this reconciliation requirement.

2.4.7.2. Based on the predetermined schedule, DCPS must generate and transmit reconciliation files to the appropriate personnel system host. The DCPS manager establishes and publishes the schedule in conjunction with the personnel system manager.

title: Section 3.0: Time and Attendance (T&A)
content:
3.0    TIME AND ATTENDANCE (T&A)

3.1 Responsibilities of Employing Agency, Approving Officials, and Timekeepers

3.1.1. Approving Official Responsibilities

3.1.1.1. When approving T&A, all supervisors, other equivalent officials, or higher-level managers must certify, to the best of their knowledge, that work schedules are accurately recorded. The supervisor should be aware of an employee's work schedule, leave taken, and any absence from duty and must review and approve the T&A to ensure its accuracy. Supervisors must ensure that exceptions to the employee's normal tour of duty are recorded in a timely and accurate manner.

3.1.1.2. The supervisor may assign responsibility for observing daily attendance or accurately recording T&A data to a timekeeper or, in limited circumstances, to the individual employee. The supervisor remains ultimately responsible for the timely and accurate reporting of the T&A per applicable policies, regulations, instructions, and bargaining agreements. The supervisor must inform the timekeeper when an employee is on leave or has worked any type of premium work. The supervisor may assign an alternate timekeeper to maintain T&A during the absence of the primary timekeeper.

3.2    T&A Requirements

3.2.1. The period shown on the T&A must correspond to the length of a pay period. For example, if payment is made for a two-week period, then the T&A must cover a two-week period.

3.2.2. Work Schedules and Alternate Work Schedules (AWS)

3.2.2.1. The work schedule defines the basic work requirement as the number of hours, excluding overtime, an employee must work or account for by charging leave. Generally, a full-time employee's basic work requirement is 80 hours per pay period. Attendance and absence must be consistent with the individual's employment status. The agency must maintain an approved work schedule for each employee showing planned arrival and departure for each day. When an employee's work schedule differs from the agency-wide schedule or reflects an AWS, the supervisor, or the official most knowledgeable of the employee's schedule, must approve it before the period it takes effect. If not approved in advance, the supervisor must approve it as soon after the start of the pay period as possible.

3.2.2.2. Material variances or deviations, as determined by the flexible work schedule, must be approved by the supervisor before the change occurs, or promptly after if not feasible beforehand. Supervisors must verify that the dates and the material variances or deviations have been recorded in the T&A.

3.2.3. Temporary Assignment (TDY)

3.2.3.1. For an employee on TDY, the hours worked and hours of leave must be recorded on the T&A. All time actually spent away from the permanent duty station during the basic workweek must be recorded at the employee's permanent duty station as time worked or leave taken. The travel order must support entries on the T&A for regular time.

3.3    T&A Recording

3.3.1. Scheduled starting and ending times of the day for each employee or group of employees must be established and recorded. The day an employee's shift begins is designated as the day of work for night and shift-differential purposes. These requirements are modified for employees working a flexible or compressed work schedule under the AWS plans.

3.3.2. T&A approvals must give management assurance that supervisors or other authorized officials know they are accountable for approving an employee's work time and absences. Employees must either initial or sign for indicated absences or submit an approved application for leave. A supervisor may require a medical certificate or other evidence of illness when granting sick leave. The employing activity must retain such certification.

3.3.3. All leave types are charged to the employee by days, hours, or fractions of hours. Timecards must clearly indicate whether annual leave taken is charged against the employee's current leave account or a separate account established for restored leave. The employee's regular leave account is charged unless the annual leave taken is identified as charged to the restored leave account.

3.3.4. Recording Daylight Savings Time

3.3.4.1. Civilian employees working a tour of duty when Daylight Savings Time begins are credited with the actual number of hours worked. The hour lost is charged to annual leave, compensatory time used, credit hours used, or leave without pay, as the employee requests. Employees may also be allowed to work one hour beyond the end of their shift.

3.3.4.2. Civilian employees working a tour of duty when standard time begins are credited with the actual number of hours worked. Time worked in excess of 8 hours, or the regular tour of duty hours, must be paid as overtime, compensatory time earned, or recorded as credit hours.

3.4    T&A Certification

3.4.1. All T&A and supporting documents must be reviewed and approved by the supervisor or designated alternate certifier. The supervisor or designated alternate certifier must understand the responsibility for ensuring report accuracy and must have knowledge of the time worked and absence of the employees for whom approval is given.

3.4.2. Certification, Controls and Approval of T&A

3.4.2.1. The certification of T&A constitutes authorization for the expenditure of Government funds. Each employee's T&A must be certified correct at the end of the pay period by the employee's supervisor, acting supervisor, other equivalent official, or a higher-level manager authorized to act as an alternate certifier. Certification ordinarily must not be made earlier than the last workday of a pay period. When an early cutoff is unavoidable, such as when a legal holiday falls on a Friday or Monday, additional controls must be in place, operating, and demonstrated in the system design. If the certifier lacks personal knowledge of employees' presence and absence, the certifier must have a reasonable basis for relying on internal controls to ensure accuracy and legal compliance, which must include periodic testing of those controls. Certification of T&A documents must be based on knowledge from personal observation, work output, or timekeeper verification; checking data against other independent sources such as validating starting and ending times of work, using sign-in and sign-out sheets or time clock entries; reliance on other internal controls; or a combination of controls.

3.4.2.2. When an early cutoff is used, additional controls must ensure that any change in certified attendance or absence occurring after the cutoff date is identified and reported before pay computation, or reported for the next pay computation. The employee may initial the corrected entries or submit OPM Form 71, Request for Leave or Approved Absence, or a locally approved electronic leave request, as appropriate.

3.4.3. Approval

3.4.3.1. Approvals must be made individually for each employee, and a signature must accompany each T&A.

3.4.3.2. A single supervisory or designated alternate certifier signature may approve the information recorded for all employees listed on a multiple-employee T&A report only when three prerequisites are met:

3.4.3.2.1. The data elements required by the agency must appear on the report for each employee listed on the report;

3.4.3.2.2. Supporting documents required for the information on the report must be reviewed by the supervisor or designated alternate certifier; and

3.4.3.2.3. The supervisor or designated alternate must initial or sign each page of the report and either sign the last page or enter an approval code into an automated system.

3.4.3.3. When a paperless T&A system is used and T&A data is contained in an electronic file displayed on a terminal, the supervisor may enter a single automated code to approve the information in the file. Before approving the T&A, the supervisor, or designated alternate certifier, must review supporting documents and computerized files. The system must generate a record of any change made to a file when approved by someone other than the original approving official and send it to the original approving official or other designated person.

3.4.4. Certification of the T&A must not be delayed to obtain the employee's initials or signature for requested leave when the employee is unavailable. The employee must submit a request for leave (OPM Form 71, when required) upon return to duty to confirm the requested leave.

3.4.5. Maintenance and Approval of T&A by Employee

3.4.5.1. Employees may maintain their own official T&A only in the following situations:

3.4.5.1.1. The employee is the timekeeper;

3.4.5.1.2. Employees work flexible hours outside the hours of the timekeeper and supervisor;

3.4.5.1.3. An employee is working alone at a remote site;

3.4.5.1.4. Employees are based at the same location as their supervisors and timekeepers but are frequently away during working hours; or

3.4.5.1.5. When the employing organization determines that individual timekeeping by all employees is warranted, it must maintain documentation demonstrating that the T&A reporting system has sufficient capacity and internal controls to ensure timely and accurate recording of T&A by these individual employees.

3.4.5.2. Employees are generally prohibited from approving their own T&A. Exceptions apply only when it is not feasible for an employee's T&A to be approved by a supervisor. In such cases, the Component head, or designee, must grant official written authorization for the employee to approve his or her own T&A. An employee may be authorized to approve his or her own T&A under the following circumstances: the employee works alone at a remote site for long periods; the employee is based at, but frequently away from, the location of their supervisor and timekeeper during working hours; or the employee is the head of an organization within an agency that has no supervisor on site.

3.4.5.3. To provide reasonable assurance that employees are working when scheduled, supervisors must take reasonable measures (such as occasional telephone calls during scheduled work times, or assessing the reasonableness of output for the time spent) to determine the accuracy of T&A data submitted by individuals who maintain their own T&A. The supervisor is responsible for the accuracy of that data.

3.5    T&A Reporting

3.5.1. T&A data must be transmitted to the payroll system, as required, using positive (100 percent) reporting or exception reporting. Under positive reporting, all T&A data is reported to the payroll system for each employee. Under exception reporting, only exceptions to the employee's scheduled tour of duty are reported. When reporting to the payroll system by source-data automation, positive reporting is required for each employee.

3.5.2. Regardless of the reporting method, controls must ensure that all required T&A data, including current-period corrections and prior-period adjustments, is properly reviewed and approved by the supervisor and reported in a timely and accurate manner.

3.5.3. If any required T&A data is missing for an employee, the PRO generates a charge against the employee's annual leave balance. If the annual leave balance is insufficient to support the employee's regularly scheduled tour of duty, the PRO must charge any remainder to another leave category to fulfill the scheduled tour. The PRO must correct the employee's pay and leave record upon submission of the certified T&A data.

3.6    Adjustments or Corrections

3.6.1. Adjustments or corrections required because of changes after T&A information was approved must be processed promptly and be traceable to the pay period to which the correction applies. Electronic corrections for current-period corrections and prior-period adjustments must be made per the PRO's established procedural guidance. T&A corrections for pay periods no longer available electronically require a hard copy of the certified T&A for each pay period, certified by the supervisor and forwarded to the PRO, which processes the manual correction. An authorizing official must approve all changes.

3.7    Record Retention

3.7.1. Management may require employees and timekeepers, if any, to attest to or verify T&A information. T&A information that supports financial or cost reporting should be auditable. Employing activities must establish a uniform practice for the locations at which T&A reports and related supporting documentation are maintained. T&A reports, together with approved leave applications, overtime approvals, military orders, jury-duty certification, or other supporting documents, may be retained by the timekeeper or supervisor or sent to a designated storage location.

3.7.2. Sufficient internal controls must be established to prevent unauthorized changes to completed T&A, regardless of where they are retained.

title: Section 4.0: Pay Administration
content:
4.0    PAY ADMINISTRATION

4.1    General Provisions on Pay

4.1.1. Pay and Payroll Data

4.1.1.1. Payroll computations must be based on statutorily authorized entitlements per Title 5 U.S.C., Title 5 C.F.R., and other statutory or regulatory requirements stated herein. Payment of any entitlement must be supported by one or more of the following source documents, as appropriate: Standard Form (SF) 50, Notification of Personnel Action and/or other similar personnel documents; certified copies of travel orders; T & A reports, including any necessary supporting documents such as sign-in and sign-out registers or OPM Form 71, Request for Leave or Approved Absence; and authorizations or approvals of overtime and compensatory time worked.

4.1.1.2. If the servicing Human Resources Office (HRO) electronically transmits pay entitlement data from source documents to the servicing PRO, the servicing HRO must send the source documents back to the PRO on request. The servicing HRO must ensure the integrity and accuracy of the pay computation data, establish effective controls, and ensure all data transmits successfully. The servicing HRO must retain source documents, with transmittal and control data, for audit purposes per the National Archives General Records Schedule 2.4.

4.1.1.3. The PROs must ensure an employee's compensation is consistent with their grade, position classification, other entitlements, and employment location. For example, an agency may not pay any foreign area allowances, regardless of authorizing documents, to an employee assigned to stateside duties; the servicing PRO must request the servicing HRO clarify or correct the documents.

4.1.1.4. The servicing PRO must ensure pay computations are based on the completed time and attendance records maintained for each employee. The servicing PRO must complete computations as soon as possible after the close of the pay period.

4.1.1.5. The servicing PRO, the servicing HRO, and the CSR must communicate to ensure all appropriate entitlement information is considered for each pay computation and that computations are supported by the appropriate documentation. At least every 4 months, personnel and pay data must be reconciled and discrepancies corrected. The functional area that entered the incorrect data has primary responsibility for reconciling discrepancies in common data. For additional information, see Section 2.

4.1.2. The servicing HRO must notify the servicing PRO of employee pay changes. The servicing PRO must inform each employee in writing of gross pay changes, total pay, allowances, deductions, and net pay. The information may be included on the employee's Leave and Earnings Statement (LES).

4.2    Premium Pay

4.2.1. Each employing activity is responsible for controlling overtime. Supervisors must ensure funds targeted for their employing activity will cover overtime worked. Overtime approval or disapproval must be consistent with direction from the Deputy Secretary of War. The employee is paid only approved overtime as certified on the employee's time and attendance report. Normally, employees must request approval to work overtime in writing before performing the work (5 U.S.C. § 5542).

4.2.1.1. An employee must receive advance written approval for compensatory time worked, made per Section 3. Compensatory time off is an alternative form of payment for overtime work. For applying pay cap limitations or liquidating compensatory time, the dollar value of the compensatory time equals the overtime pay the employee would otherwise have received for the same number of overtime hours. Pay limitations apply as follows: Biweekly Premium Pay Cap. If invoking the biweekly cap, an employee cannot receive credit for compensatory time worked if the basic rate of pay equals or exceeds the maximum rate for grade GS-15, step 10, or Level V of the Executive Schedule. An employee whose basic rate is less than the maximum rate of GS-15, step 10, or Level V of the Executive Schedule, may earn compensatory time. However, it may only be credited to the extent that the monetary value of the compensatory time does not cause the total rate of pay to exceed the maximum earnings limitations under 5 CFR 550.106(c). Annual Premium Pay Cap. If invoking an annual premium pay cap, an employee may only receive credit for compensatory time to the extent that the monetary value of the compensatory time does not cause the total rate of pay to exceed the maximum earnings limitations. See 5 CFR 550.106(c). FLSA Considerations. The granting of compensatory time off in lieu of overtime pay under 5 U.S.C. § 5542 must not violate the overtime pay requirements of FLSA. For instructions on compensatory time off for nonexempt employees, refer to 5 CFR
551.531. For FLSA exempt employees, refer to 5 CFR 550.114.

4.2.1.2. When an FLSA exempt or nonexempt employee separates, dies, or transfers to another DoW Component, or moves to a non-DoW agency, the losing Component must pay for any unused compensatory time balances at the overtime rate in effect when the employee earned the compensatory time. Title 32 National Guard technicians are not paid for unused compensatory time. See DoWI 1400.25-V550, 5 C.F.R. 550.114, and 5 C.F.R. 551.531.

4.3    Foreign and Non-Foreign Allowances and Differentials

4.3.1. Foreign Area Allowances and Differentials

4.3.1.1. Within DoW, only three of the five FTA elements are authorized for payment: the miscellaneous expense portion, the lease penalty expense portion, and the subsistence expense portion. DoW does not authorize payment of the wardrobe expense portion or the pet shipment and required quarantine portion. The FTA standard is governed by DSSR Chapter 200,
section 240 and DoWI 1400.25-V1250.

4.3.1.2. Within DoW, only three of the five HSTA elements are authorized for payment: the miscellaneous expense portion, the lease penalty expense portion, and the subsistence expense portion. DoW does not authorize payment of the wardrobe expense portion or the pet shipment and required quarantine portion. The HSTA standard, including the required 12-month service-agreement certification, is governed by DSSR Chapter 200, section 250 and DoWI
1400.25-V1250.

4.3.1.3. DoW does not authorize payment of the education allowance. DoW does authorize reimbursement of transportation costs for dormitory-student family members of eligible employees between the overseas duty station and the DoW Education Activity (DoWEA) approved school. The education-allowance standard is governed by DSSR Chapter 200, section 270, 5 U.S.C. 5924, and DoWI 1400.25-V1250.

4.3.1.4. Before a representation allowance is payable, the employee's position must first be designated as eligible by the Deputy Under Secretary of War for Civilian Personnel Policy. A voucher of expenses incurred is the basis for payment. The representation-allowance standard and allowable items are governed by DSSR Chapter 300 and DoWI 1400.25-V1250.

4.4    Other Pay, Differentials, and Allowances

4.4.1. Supervisory Differential

4.4.1.1. Authority to approve supervisory differentials under 5 U.S.C. § 5755 and 5 CFR 575, subpart D is delegated through the DoW Component and its chain of command to the official who exercises personnel-appointing authority (normally the head of an installation or activity). Only the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of War may approve a supervisory differential for an individual appointed to a Schedule C position, as defined by 5 CFR Part 213. The agency may authorize a supervisory differential for a GS employee who supervises one or more non-GS employees when a subordinate would be paid more than the supervisor absent the differential. The DoWI 1400.25-V575 contains additional guidance.

4.4.2. Defense agency employees required by law or regulation to wear uniforms during official duties may be reimbursed a uniform allowance at the rates posted in the DoWI 1400.25-V591. The agency's authorized management official must approve payment of a uniform allowance. Uniform allowances are not considered wages.

4.4.3. Government-Provided Home-to-Work Transportation

4.4.3.1. DoW employing activities must not report on a calendar-year basis. They must report for the 12-month period from November 1 through October 31. The value of benefits received in November and December is considered paid in the next year, as authorized by IRS Publication 15-B.

4.4.4. Under 10 U.S.C. §§ 1596 and 1596a, the Secretary of War may pay FLPP to eligible DoW employees performing intelligence or non-intelligence duties that require foreign language proficiency. FLPP is not basic pay for any purpose and does not count toward retirement, TSP, FEGLI, or any other basic-pay-related benefit, and is not pay for lump-sum leave payments under 5 U.S.C. §§ 5551 or 5552. FLPP is a discretionary, continuing payment for the aggregate limitation on pay. FLPP must not be paid if the employee is in LWOP or other unpaid status for more than 10 consecutive workdays, or in an extended paid absence for more than 30 consecutive workdays.

4.4.4.1. Under 10 U.S.C. § 1596, the Secretary of War determines the annual rate of intelligence FLPP. FLPP may be paid in addition to pay under 10 U.S.C. § 1602. See the DoWI 1400.25-V2016. The Secretary of War may pay special pay to a DoW employee who: has been certified as being proficient in a foreign language identified by the Secretary of War as being a language in which proficiency by civilian personnel of the DoW is important for the effective collection, production, or dissemination of foreign intelligence information; and is serving in a position, or is subject to assignment to a position, in which proficiency in that language facilitates performance of officially assigned intelligence or intelligence-related duties.

4.4.4.2. Under 10 U.S.C. § 1596a, the Secretary of War may prescribe special pay for a DoW employee, but the pay may not exceed 5 percent of the employee's pay. This special pay is in addition to any other pay or allowances to which the employee is entitled. See the DoWI 1400.25-V2016. The Secretary of War may pay this special pay to a DoW employee who: has been certified by the Secretary of War to be proficient in a foreign language identified by the Secretary of War as being a language in which proficiency by civilian personnel of the DoW is necessary because of national security interests, is assigned duties requiring proficiency in that foreign language, and is not receiving special pay under 5 U.S.C. § 1596.

4.5    Recruitment, Relocation, and Retention Incentives

4.5.1. Recruitment Incentive

4.5.1.1. The incentive must be included with regular salary payments and separately identified on the LES.

4.5.1.2. A demotion or separation for cause, or a rating less than "Fully Successful" or equivalent, terminates the service agreement. An employee who fails to complete the service period for these reasons, or otherwise fails to fulfill the agreement, must repay any portion of the incentive attributable to uncompleted service. The servicing PRO prorates the authorized recruitment incentive across the service period to determine the amount attributable to completed and uncompleted service, and must recover the amount owed per the debt collection regulations (see Volume 16). The servicing HRO must notify the servicing PRO of the recruitment incentive repayment or debt via SF 50 data.

4.5.1.3. The servicing HRO must document each recruitment incentive using information derived from an SF 50.

4.5.2. Relocation Incentive

4.5.2.1. The incentive must be included with regular salary payments and separately identified on the LES.

4.5.2.2. If the employee is demoted for cause, separates for cause, or receives a less than "Fully Successful" or equivalent rating, the service agreement terminates. An employee who fails to complete the service period for these reasons, or otherwise fails to fulfill the agreement, must reimburse DoW for all benefits received under the agreement in excess of the amount attributable to completed service. The servicing PRO must prorate the full authorized relocation incentive across the service period to determine the amounts attributable to completed and uncompleted service. The servicing PRO must recover the amount owed per agency debt collection regulations (see Volume 16). The servicing HRO must notify the servicing PRO of the repayment/debt via SF 50 data.

4.5.2.3. The servicing HRO must document each relocation incentive via an SF 50.

4.5.3. Retention Incentive

4.5.3.1. The incentive must be included with regular salary payments and separately identified on the LES.

4.5.3.2. If an employee is demoted for cause, separates for cause, or receives a less than "Fully Successful" or equivalent rating, the service agreement terminates. An employee who fails to complete the service period for these reasons, or otherwise fails to fulfill the agreement, must reimburse DoW for all benefits received under the agreement in excess of the amount attributable to completed service. The employee may retain any retention incentive payments attributable to completed service and is entitled to any portion owed by the agency for completed service. The amount owed must be recovered per agency debt collection regulations (see Volume 16). The servicing HRO must notify the servicing PRO of the repayment/debt via SF 50 data.

4.5.3.3. The servicing HRO must document each retention incentive via an SF 50.

4.5.4. DoW Student Loan Repayment Program

4.5.4.1. The servicing PRO must remit the student loan repayment directly to the lender under the terms, limitations, and conditions of the written service agreement. The payment is made in a lump sum, periodically, or in biweekly installments, and is in addition to basic pay or any other compensation payable to the employee.

4.5.4.2. DoW is not responsible for any late fees or penalties assessed by loan holders before, during, or after the student loan repayment agreement.

4.5.4.3. The servicing HRO must document each student loan repayment action via an SF 50 and must transmit the SF 50 and a copy of the service agreement to the servicing PRO to begin payments.

4.6    Lump-Sum Leave Payments

4.6.1. Computation of Lump-Sum Payment

4.6.1.1. DFAS must pay lump-sum leave at the end of the pay period in which it receives the separation transaction; the payment may or may not be combined with regular pay depending on receipt timing. DFAS must identify the payment separately and apply flat 25 percent federal withholding, except when the exemptions claimed on Form W-4 exceed the regular pay, in which case DFAS must combine the lump-sum leave with the regular pay and compute taxes as a single payment. Lump-sum annual leave payments are not subject to FEHB, FERS, FEGLI, or TSP deductions and are subject to offset for debts owed to the United States (5 CFR 550.1205).

4.6.2. DoW must make a lump-sum payment of restored annual leave under 5 U.S.C. § 6304(d)(3) to any DoW employee moving to a non-DoW federal agency or to a DoW position not located at an installation being closed or realigned, as required by 5 U.S.C. § 5551. The servicing HRO must notify the servicing PRO via SF 50 data when the employee is no longer authorized restored leave under this authority. The lump-sum calculation uses the rate of pay at the time of separation or transfer to the non-BRAC installation.

4.7    Severance
4.7.1. Payments

4.7.1.1. The servicing PRO must pay authorized severance payments based on the information processed on an SF 50. Severance payments are subject to withholding for income and OASDI/Medicare taxes (5 CFR 550.709(b)).

4.7.2. Severance pay is taxable in the year the employee receives it, is included on the employee's Form W-2, and is subject to government and state withholding. If an employee dies, the servicing PRO must report any severance pay paid to beneficiaries on Form 1099-MISC.

4.7.3. If an agency reemploys a former employee in federal service, severance pay is discontinued effective on the date of reemployment. The losing agency must report the total amounts paid to the gaining activity or agency, which uses that information to track the lifetime severance cap of one year's pay at the rate received immediately before separation (5 U.S.C. § 5595(c)).

4.8    Advanced Pay

4.8.1. Foreign Post Assignment

4.8.1.1. The disbursing officer (or the officer's overseas agent) supporting the servicing PRO for the overseas area must pay foreign-post pay advances; outside the continental U.S., a disbursing officer who is a deputy to the continental U.S. office may pay. Payment may be included in the next regular biweekly pay or made as a single lump-sum. An employee may request an advance 3 weeks before the estimated departure date or up to 2 months after arrival, and must submit the request on the SF 1190, which serves as the request, authorization, and voucher document.

4.8.1.2. The HRO responsible for the employee must verify eligibility for an advance by confirming the travel orders and the pay grade and step at the foreign post. If the HRO does not confirm the foreign pay grade or step, the servicing PRO may use the employee's current gross pay at the time of the advance. The HRO must counsel each eligible employee on the authorized purposes of the advance, repayment requirements, anticipated expenses at the foreign assignment, and application procedures.

4.8.2. Collection of Advance Payments

4.8.2.1. Repayment is collected by payroll deduction over a maximum of 26 pay periods. Deductions must begin the first pay period after receipt of the advance or after arrival at the foreign post, whichever is later. The losing agency must forward a copy of the SF 1190 to the gaining PRO for collection.

4.8.2.2. The servicing PRO may accept partial or lump-sum repayments in addition to payroll deductions.

4.8.2.3. When an employee separates or transfers, the outstanding advance balance is due in full. Advances are recoverable from the employee or the employee's estate by deduction from accrued pay, retirement credit, other amounts due from the Government, or other methods provided by 5 U.S.C. § 5514 and 31 U.S.C. § 3716.

4.8.2.4. The Defense Debt and Claims Management Office, DFAS Indianapolis Center, may waive the Government's right of recovery of an erroneous pay advance per DoWI
1340.23    and 5 U.S.C. § 5584.

4.8.3. Other Requirements or Conditions for Advances

4.8.3.1. An employee is authorized only one outstanding advance at a time, regardless of how often assigned to a foreign area. An employee who becomes eligible for a second advance must liquidate the first advance before requesting the first payment of the second.

4.8.3.2. More than one member of a household may be eligible for an advance.

4.8.3.3. Allotments and assignments of advances are not authorized.

4.8.3.4. Advances are paid to employees of another federal agency on a reimbursable basis only if an agreement exists between that agency and DFAS to make similar payments to DoW employees.

4.8.3.5. The servicing office may require the employee to submit statements and documents establishing the need for, and use of, an advance.

4.8.3.6. Management must develop controls to ensure only authorized employees obtain an advance and that complete accountability procedures exist for the disbursement and collection of pay advances. Accounting records must include current, accurate, and complete records of obligations, receivables, and collections.

4.8.4. Agencies may authorize an additional advance payment when circumstances warrant and the employee has not received the maximum possible advance for the employee's pay grade. Exceptional circumstances include a substantial understatement of the maximum advance authorized, inadequate or inappropriate counseling on the purpose of the advance, and unforeseeable events significantly increasing the employee's cash-outlay needs at the foreign assignment location.

4.8.5. The head of an agency may provide for advance payment of basic pay to a newly appointed employee (5 CFR 550.203). DoW delegates this authority to officials who exercise personnel-appointing authority (normally the head of an installation or activity), through and subject to the DoW Component heads, to be used on a case-by-case basis (DoWI 1400.25-V550).

4.9    Awards

4.9.1. General Title 5 U.S.C., Chapter 45

4.9.1.1. A time-off award cannot be transferred between DoW Components or outside DoW. Managers and supervisors should ensure the employee can use the award before leaving the granting Component. DoW Components may establish procedures to accommodate the transfer of time-off awards within their respective Components. A time-off award cannot be converted to a cash award, and unused awards are lost when an employee separates or transfers to another agency or component (5 CFR 451.104(f)).

4.9.1.2. The servicing HRO must process awards on an SF 50 and issue them to the servicing PRO as authorization for payment of cash awards or granting of time-off awards. Awards are paid in the same manner as the employee's net pay and are not distributed to the worksite.

4.9.1.3. Time-off awards must be posted to the employee's record and reduced when the time off is taken or forfeited. Use of a time-off award reported before notification of the award must be reflected as a negative balance in the civilian payroll system. If the servicing HRO does not post a time-off award to the employee's record within two pay periods of a negative balance appearing in the civilian payroll system, the use is treated as a time-and-attendance error.

4.9.2. Payment of Awards

4.9.2.1. Cash award payments are subject to federal, state, and local income tax withholding. The civilian payroll system automatically applies the IRS supplemental-wage federal withholding rate (set by the IRS; see IRS Publication 15) to these special earnings. The servicing PRO must compute applicable state, local, and OASDI/Medicare withholding from the employee's current master record, and must not withhold state and local taxes for employees assigned to overseas duty locations unless the employee requests it.

4.9.2.2. To pay an award to a separated employee, the agency must reestablish the employee on the payroll using the last known master account record information for applicable deductions and mailing address.

4.9.2.3. Cash award payments must be included on the employee's LES and Form W-2.

title: Section 5.0: Mandatory Deductions
content:
5.0    MANDATORY DEDUCTIONS

5.1    Mandatory Deductions

5.1.1. Mandatory payroll deductions withheld from a DoW employee's pay must include sufficient information to establish the deduction, adequate documentation and certification, payment to the appropriate recipient for the correct amount, and a provision of law or court order supporting the deduction.

5.1.2. DFAS must retain deduction authorizations in the PRO or at a designated storage site per National Archives General Records Schedule 2.

5.2    Order of Precedence

5.2.1. Available Pay

5.2.1.1. If the next deduction in the order of precedence is a mandatory deduction, the PRO must use the remaining available pay to make a partial deduction, and the employee's net pay is then zero.

5.2.1.2. If the next deduction in the order of precedence is a voluntary deduction, the PRO must not make that deduction or any later deduction, and must pay the employee's remaining available pay as net pay.

5.3    Retirement Deductions

5.3.1. Civil Service Retirement System (CSRS), CSRS-Offset, and Federal Employees Retirement System (FERS) Administration and Recordkeeping

5.3.1.1. When the PRO receives notification of an employee's death, the PRO must send the IRR to OPM within 5 days of the date final pay is computed. OPM must receive the deceased employee's records and associated applications within 30 days from the date of death.

5.3.1.2. IRRs not maintained in a mechanized manner must be stored in a lockable metal file cabinet or a secured facility with access limited to employees whose official duties require it. Manually maintained IRRs must be posted manually, then stored electronically and kept separately from the record itself, per OPM requirements.

5.3.1.3. Manual records must be disposed of by shredding.

5.3.1.4. More than one IRR may be submitted with an SF 2807/3103. The PRO must not delay transmitting completed retirement records while preparing other IRRs for forwarding to OPM.

5.3.1.5. When possible, correct any errors detected on the IRR before submission to OPM. If an error is detected after the IRR is sent to OPM, prepare an SF 2806-1 (CSRS) or SF 3101 (FERS), Notice of Correction of Individual Retirement Record.

5.3.1.5.1. If a retirement over-deduction occurs from a current employee's pay, the PRO must make an adjustment during the next payroll cycle: decrease the current retirement deductions from the employee's current pay-period earnings and make a corresponding adjustment in the employer's contributions.

5.3.1.5.2. If a retirement under-deduction occurs, or deductions were not made for a period when an employee was covered by CSRS or FERS, the employee must be afforded due process rights before being indebted for the erroneous pay (see Volume 16). If deductions were made for a non-appropriated fund (NAF) retirement plan when CSRS or FERS deductions were required, the PRO must adjust the NAF retirement and Social Security deductions and contributions in the next pay period, offsetting these amounts against what should have gone to CSRS or FERS to determine the net amount to withhold from the employee's current-period pay.

5.3.1.5.3. When excess retirement amounts have been deducted from a former employee's pay and the IRR SF 2806 (CSRS) or SF 3100 (FERS) has not yet been forwarded to OPM, the PRO must correct the amount in the current calendar year and correct the accumulated deductions posted on the SF 2806/3100 before forwarding to OPM.

5.3.1.5.4. If a retirement over-deduction is found after the SF 2806/3100 was sent to OPM, the PRO must prepare and submit the SF 2806-1/3101 to OPM.

5.3.1.5.5. If an over-deduction from a former employee's pay results in excess employer retirement contributions, the PRO must deduct the excess from the next pay period's submission of the Retirement and Insurance Transfer System (RITS) file.

5.3.1.5.6. When an insufficient retirement amount has been deducted from a former employee's pay and the SF 2806/3100 has not yet been submitted to OPM, the PRO must note the deficiency on the SF 2806/3100. If the SF 2806/3100 has been submitted, the PRO must prepare another SF 2806/3100 annotated "Supplemental" in the upper left margin.

5.3.1.5.7. When an under-deduction from a former employee's pay results in insufficient employer retirement contributions, the PRO must normally include the shortfall in the RITS file for the next pay period.

5.3.1.5.8. When excess retirement amounts have been deducted from a transferred employee's pay and the SF 2806/3100 has not been forwarded to OPM, the PRO must correct the amount in the current calendar year and correct the total accumulative deductions posted on the SF 2806/3100 before forwarding.

5.3.1.5.9. If a retirement over-deduction is found after the SF 2806 was forwarded to another PRO within DoW, the PRO must prepare and submit an SF 2806-1 to the gaining PRO.

5.3.1.5.10. When an over-deduction from a transferred employee's pay results in excess employer retirement contributions, the PRO must deduct the excess employer contributions from the RITS file for the next pay period.

5.3.1.5.11. When an insufficient retirement amount has been deducted from a former employee's pay and the SF 2806 has not yet been forwarded to another PRO within the same component, the losing PRO must note the under-deductions on the SF 2806. The losing PRO must prepare and forward a supplemental SF 2806 to the gaining PRO if the SF 2806 was previously submitted.

5.3.1.5.12. The PRO must correct the "Service History" portion of the SF 2806 if the error is detected before the record is sent to another PRO within the same component. If the error is detected after the record is submitted, the losing PRO must prepare and submit an SF 2806-1 to the gaining PRO.

5.3.1.5.13. The PRO must report CSRS or FERS deductions withheld from a retroactive salary payment for a separated employee by preparing a supplemental SF 2806/3100 and forwarding it to OPM on an SF 2807/3103.

5.3.1.5.14. For a current employee, the PRO must include CSRS or FERS deductions withheld from a retroactive salary payment in the current-year salary deduction on the SF 2806/3100 maintained for the employee.

5.3.1.5.15. A losing PRO must report CSRS or FERS deductions withheld from a retroactive salary payment for an employee transferred to another PRO within the same component by preparing a supplemental SF 2806/3100. The losing PRO must send the SF 2806 to the gaining PRO on an SF 2807. The losing PRO must send the SF 3100 to OPM on an SF 3103.

5.3.1.6. Employee deductions and employer contributions for CSRS or FERS must be reported separately to OPM each pay period. PROs reporting to OPM via the RITS must report deductions and contributions per the procedures in Section 10. Employer contributions must be charged to the appropriation(s) from which the employee's salary is paid.

5.3.2. DoW Employees Covered by Retirement Systems for Non-Appropriated Fund Instrumentalities (NAFI)

5.3.2.1. Employees who elect to retain coverage under a NAF retirement system must have their SF 50 annotated as "5-Other" for the retirement code. The SF 50 must state that the employee has elected to retain coverage under a NAF retirement system.

5.3.2.2. Employee retirement deductions, employer contributions, employee contributions to applicable 401(k) plans, and loan repayments must be made biweekly and submitted to the appropriate NAF employee benefit system. FICA contributions must be withheld and reported per current U.S. Department of the Treasury guidance.

5.3.3. Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences (USU) Faculty Retirement

5.3.3.1. A total of 15 percent of the employee's total salary must be contributed to the employee's selected retirement plan (TIAA/CREF or Fidelity Investments): USU contributes 10 percent and the employee contributes a mandatory 5 percent through payroll deduction.

5.3.3.2. Part-time employees, visiting foreign employees holding H-1 and J-1 visas, faculty whose titles carry the prefix "Visiting," Visiting Scientists, and Postdoctoral Fellows are not eligible to participate in TIAA/CREF or Fidelity Investments upon employment with USU.

5.4    Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) Tax

5.4.1. Authority

5.4.1.1. If an employee transfers between DoW Components, the gaining PRO must count Social Security and/or Medicare taxes already deducted by the losing PRO so as not to exceed the maximum Social Security and/or Medicare tax liability due for that payroll year. On a transfer, the PRO must include Social Security and/or Medicare year-to-date wages and taxes on the SF 1150, Record of Leave Data.

5.5    Federal Income Tax Withholding (FITW)

5.5.1. General

5.5.1.1. An EIN, assigned by the appropriate IRS District Director, identifies the tax accounts of employers. Only one EIN per Payroll Office (PRO) is authorized to report all federal and Social Security and/or Medicare taxes. The PRO must collect federal and Social Security and/or Medicare taxes from employee wages and report all taxes using IRS Form 941, Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return. For withholding and reporting guidance, consult the current Circular E.

5.5.2. If an employee submits a new W-4, the PRO must change the withholding effective the next pay period. Retroactive adjustments are not permitted, even if the employee claims the W-4 on file is erroneous and submits a corrected one.

5.5.3. As forms become superseded or obsolete, the PRO must move them from the active file to an inactive file. The PRO need not send IRS forms such as the 941 or W-4 to the IRS District Director, but must, on request, show that the information is on file as a supporting record.

5.5.4. Tax Payments - Payment of Withheld Tax

5.5.4.1. The PRO that makes the tax collection must prepare and issue the W-2 to the employee.

5.5.4.2. The disbursing office must disburse all withheld taxes based on the information the PRO provides and the payroll frequency. It remits federal income, Social Security and/or Medicare taxes withheld from wages, plus the employer's Social Security and/or Medicare contributions, through EFTPS.

5.6    State Income Tax Withholding (SITW)

5.6.1. Withholding Authority

5.6.1.1. DoW requires employees to complete a withholding certificate as the basis to properly withhold state taxes. The certificate must specify whether the employee is subject to the tax, the employee's residence and regular place of employment, and any exemptions and allowances. The certificate remains in effect until the employee submits a new one. If an employee does not furnish a withholding certificate for a designated state, the PRO must withhold the maximum amount applicable to the employee's annual compensation.

5.6.1.2. The state, city, or county income or employment tax withheld from the compensation of an employee or member of the Armed Forces must, at a minimum, approximate the tax required to be withheld. The PRO may accomplish withholding by one of the following methods: applicable tax withholding rate(s) specified in the state, city, or county instructions; any other percentage or formula method; or a calculated, fixed amount deducted each pay period from the compensation of the employee.

5.6.1.3. Reciprocal agreements between states may modify state withholding requirements; they generally relieve nonresident employees of tax liability to the state of employment and relieve the employer of the duty to withhold. Agencies must conform to the withholding provisions of applicable Treasury-state and reciprocal agreements. If an employee is subject to withholding in more than one state, the PRO must use separate deduction codes to identify the tax remittance for each state.

5.6.1.3.1. Reciprocal agreements between states may affect automatic withholding by duty station. In all disputed cases, the PRO must withhold tax and advise the employee to negotiate the tax liability directly with the proper taxing authority.

5.6.1.4. When a state provides for discretionary allotment withholding, the PRO must withhold state taxes only for employees who have a legal obligation to pay and who elect such withholding. This applies whether or not Treasury has a withholding agreement with the state.

5.6.1.4.1. Employees must request the allotment on a proper withholding certificate.

5.6.1.4.2. Employee tenure does not affect the allotment.

5.6.1.5. Employees located in foreign areas must determine the need for state and local taxes. Before submitting a request, the PRO must advise the employee to:

5.6.1.5.1. Obtain assistance from the employing activity legal staff available to him or her; or

5.6.1.5.2. Contact the appropriate state or local income tax office about the applicability of withholding taxes while on an overseas assignment, preferably before departure from the continental United States (CONUS). If the employee determines a withholding liability applies, the PRO must honor the request.

5.6.1.6. The PRO must comply with the agreement, regulations, and instructions of the state concerned.

5.6.1.6.1. The PRO must base the allotment amount on either the amount (in whole dollars) set by an employee; or the withholding certificate filed by an employee and the state withholding tables or formulas.

5.6.1.6.2. The PRO must pay withheld state income taxes to each state concerned as that state prescribes.

5.6.1.7. Employees are subject to mandatory withholding under Treasury-state withholding agreements, but an employee may claim exemption under certain conditions. The PRO must require the use of state-furnished tax exemption certificates, if available; and give the employee’s name, SSN, and basis for the claimed exemption to the designated taxing state official.

5.6.2. The PRO must send W-2 copies to states that have negotiated agreements with the Secretary of the Treasury for employees subject to mandatory state withholding or who may elect withholding under state law (see TFM, Volume 1, Part 6, Chapter 5000).

5.6.2.1. The PRO must record the amounts withheld each pay period on the employee's pay record when a special payment occurs; otherwise, the system automatically updates the records.

5.6.2.2. The PRO must compute the total of withheld state taxes and deposit it per Treasury's Federal Account Symbols and Titles (FAST) Book II, crediting the appropriate deposit account regardless of the employee's employing activity.

5.6.2.3. The PRO must correct a clerical error from a prior pay period in the current calendar year if the employee is still on the payroll. For an under-deduction, the PRO must follow due process to collect the taxes paid on the employee's behalf; for an over-deduction, the PRO must refund the over-deducted amount on the next regular payroll cycle. The PRO must not make any adjustment if the employee is no longer on the payroll or the error was in a prior calendar year.

5.6.2.4. The PRO must comply with the state's current tax law on payment frequency (biweekly, monthly, or quarterly) and must not make payments more often than the state requires.

5.6.2.5. The disbursing officer must issue payment based on an approved voucher prepared by the PRO, and the PRO must prepare the required tax payment documents.

5.6.2.6. The PRO must balance the amounts reported on each state W-2 with year-to-date control totals for state taxes withheld and state taxable wages. These amounts must balance before the W-2s are distributed to employees and forwarded to the states.

5.6.2.7. Collection of a state or local government tax levy is authorized by 5 CFR Part 582. The DFAS Cleveland center is the designated agent to accept legal process for DoW civilian employees for state or local tax levies. Send all state income tax liens to: DFAS Garnishment Law Directorate, P.O. Box 998002, Cleveland, OH 44199-8002.

5.6.2.8. DoW Components must advise employees that information returns will be sent to the state and other taxing authorities of the employee's place of employment (and, in some cases, place of residence) when those authorities request the information. Components may release only information properly releasable under the Privacy Act of 1974 (5 U.S.C. § 552a) or the applicable notice of routine use.

5.6.2.9. The PRO must retain the following records of state tax deductions: the EIN assigned by the state; the amounts and dates of all payments and wages subject to state tax withholding; employees' names, addresses, and SSNs; and the dates and amounts of tax deposits made.

5.6.2.10. The HRO must retain the employee's state withholding allowance certificate, kept until superseded or canceled, and the dates of employment.

5.7    City and Local Income Tax Withholding

5.7.1. Withholding of city, county, or employment tax from federal employees subject to tax whose regular place of federal employment is within a city or county that has a proper agreement with the Secretary of the Treasury is authorized by 5 U.S.C. § 5520; withholding is also required if the employee is a resident of the city or county. Each DoW employee must complete a city or local tax withholding certificate as the basis for proper withholding, and an out-of-state employee's consent to withholding is required when applicable.

5.7.1.1. The PRO must apply the policies and procedures prescribed for each state when determining the employee wages subject to mandatory city and county withholding.

5.7.1.1.1. The PRO must withhold tax from the wages of federal employees who reside in cities or counties that have entered into withholding agreements.

5.7.1.1.2. The PRO must withhold tax from the wages of federal employees whose regular place of federal employment is within a city or county where they are subject to tax. Employees who reside in a state other than the state in which the city or county is located are exempt from mandatory withholding.

5.7.1.1.3. Where local ordinances tax only wages for services performed within the city or county (in most cases only for non-resident employees), an employee eligible to exclude part of annual income must submit a withholding certificate specifying the amount or percentage, and the PRO must reduce withholding accordingly. If the employee does not file a certificate, the PRO must withhold tax based on the employee's total compensation. The PRO must not adjust withholding if the employee performs less than 25 percent of services outside the city or county.

5.7.1.2. Employees must submit withholding certificates and provide all information needed to deduct city or county income taxes. If an employee does not provide a certificate, the PRO must withhold tax at the highest level that applies to the employee's annual wages. The PRO must not withhold any tax from the wages of out-of-state employees until they present a form consenting to withholding.

5.7.1.3. Employing activities may use a withholding or exemption certificate furnished by a city or county only if it contains all required information. If the form is incomplete, employing activities may use Treasury's Fiscal Service (FS) Form 7311, Employee Withholding Certificate for Local Taxes (see TFM, Volume 1, Part 6, Chapter 5000).

5.7.1.4. An employee who does not reside in the state where the city or county (place of employment) is located is exempt from mandatory withholding; the PRO may withhold tax with the employee's consent, and the employee must submit a withholding certificate.

5.7.1.5. Employees may make discretionary allotments for the payroll deduction of taxes of their city or county of residence when employed outside that location. Withholding taxes for the city or county of employment does not affect the employee's discretionary allotment.

5.7.1.5.1. An employee may make a discretionary allotment for withholding even if the city or county does not have a withholding agreement.

5.7.1.5.2. The PRO must set the allotment amount by the city or county withholding method or deduct a whole-dollar amount set by the employee, and the employee must submit a proper withholding certificate.

5.7.1.6. The PRO must account for discretionary tax deductions as prescribed for mandatory withholdings.

5.7.1.7. The PRO must withhold tax by one of these methods: the city or county tax withholding rate set in the city or county instructions; the prescribed percentage or formula method; or a set amount computed and deducted from the employee's pay each pay period.

5.7.1.8. The PRO must deduct, at a minimum, an amount nearly equal to the tax required by the city or county.

5.7.2. The PRO must record amounts withheld each pay period in the employee's pay record when a special payment occurs; otherwise, the system automatically updates the record.

5.7.2.1. The PRO must compute the withheld city or county income tax (below state or territorial tax) and the total amount withheld each pay period, and credit the withheld tax to the appropriate deposit fund account for city and county tax.

5.7.2.2. The PRO must apply the same instructions used for the withholding of state taxes when correcting city or county tax errors.

5.7.2.3. The PRO must apply the same instructions used for paying out withheld state tax when paying out withheld city or county tax.

5.7.3. Recordkeeping

5.7.3.1. The PRO must keep all records of city or county income tax deductions, including the EIN assigned by the city or county; the amounts and dates of all wages subject to city or county tax withholding; employees' names, addresses, and SSNs; the dates and amounts of city or county tax paid; and copies of all returns filed.

5.7.3.2. The employing activity must retain city tax withholding authorization certificates for each employee until superseded or canceled. When a DoW employee's gross pay is not sufficient to permit all required deductions, deductions must be withheld in the order of precedence: (1) defined benefit retirement deductions (CSRS, FERS, CSRS-Offset, Title 32 National Guard, NAFI employee retirement contributions); (2) OASDI (Social Security, under FICA); (3) Medicare tax (under FICA); (4) federal income tax; (5) health insurance premiums; (6) basic group life insurance premiums (FEGLI, state life insurance); (7) state income tax; (8) local income tax; (9) collection of debts owed to the United States (continuous levy under the Federal Payment Levy Program, salary offsets); (10) court-ordered collection/debt (child support, alimony, bankruptcy, commercial garnishments); (11) optional benefits (see Section 12); (12) other voluntary deductions and allotments; and (13) IRS paper levies. The taxability of each compensation type and the annual FICA rates and maximum taxable earnings are set each calendar year by the Social Security Administration.

title: Section 6.0: Leave and Other Absences
content:
6.0    LEAVE AND OTHER ABSENCES

6.1    General Requirements and Responsibilities

6.1.1. PROs and payroll systems areas must meet the following objectives: maintaining leave records and balances for each employee as provided in paragraph 6.1.3, Recording accrued and accumulated leave. Accrued leave is leave earned by an employee during the current leave year that is unused at any given time in that year. Accumulated leave means unused leave remaining to the credit of an employee at the beginning of the leave year, reporting all leave taken, and reporting accurate data on leave use and accruals in order to simplify the collection of leave- related debts and preparation of financial reports.

6.1.2. A leave record must be maintained for each employee to show: rate of accrual for each type of leave, hours or days accrued, and type of leave used, hours or days of leave advanced by leave type, and leave balances.

6.1.3. Rate of Leave Accrual

6.1.3.1. To ensure proper accrual rates, the civilian payroll system must contain accurate information on each employee’s type of appointment and the types of leave hours or days to which the employee is entitled. The system must accurately record leave earned for each type of leave using the correct rates effective for the proper times.

6.1.3.2. Annual and sick leave earned for each pay period must be posted to the employee’s leave record. The leave record must also reflect all leave used during the same pay period.

6.1.4. To support the time and attendance record, employees must request approval of leave. The supervisor or other designated official should approve leave before it is taken. If leave cannot be approved in advance due to an unusual or emergency situation, the supervisor should review it for approval or disapproval as soon as possible after it is taken. See GAO-03-352G, Maintaining Effective Control over Employee Time and Attendance Reporting. Supervisors designated to approve leave must document leave used in writing, showing the dates, times, and types of leave taken.

6.1.5. Heads of DoW Components and their designees may establish minimum charges for leave per DoWI 1400.25-V630. The minimum charge for leave is 1 hour unless an agency determines a need for a minimum charge of less than 1 hour or establishes a different minimum charge through negotiations. In any case, the agency may not charge for leave in increments of less than 6 minutes. See 5 CFR 630.206.

6.2    Annual Leave

6.2.1. General Annual

6.2.1.1. To ensure proper documentation of leave, any annual leave earned must be posted to the employee’s record in a pay period before charging the leave taken during the same pay period.

6.2.2. Restoring Forfeited Annual Leave

6.2.2.1. If restoration is based on exigency of the public business, DoW must delegate the responsibility for determining that a need is important enough to prevent use of annual leave subject to forfeiture to the lowest practical level. Those who approve exigencies must establish termination dates for the exigencies. See 5 CFR 630.305, 5 CFR 630.306(a)(2), and DoWI 1400.25-V630.

6.2.2.2. The payroll system must maintain separate restored leave accounts for each calendar year. The servicing Human Resources Office (HRO) must identify the reason for restoration and the category of leave restored and provide that information to the CSR in writing. DoW must credit restored annual leave to a separate leave account that identifies the date of restoration, the date of forfeiture, the amount credited for use, the amount of usage, and the unused balance. Restored annual leave is not included in, and does not increase, the maximum annual leave carryover for an employee. See 5 U.S.C. § 6304(d)(2).

6.3    Administrative Leave (Excused Absence)

6.3.1. Employees serving as blood donors may be excused from work without charge to leave for the time necessary to donate blood, for recuperation after donation, and for necessary travel to and from the donation site. This provision does not cover an employee who gives blood for personal use or receives compensation for giving blood.

6.3.2. If an employee is unavoidably or necessarily absent for less than one hour, or tardy, the agency may, for adequate reason, excuse the employee without charge to leave.

6.3.3. An employee may be granted excused absence to take an examination (for example, the certified public accountant examination) in their functional area if securing the certification or license would enhance the employee's professional stature and benefit the DoW. This provision does not cover time spent preparing for such examinations.

6.3.4. Employees may be excused to attend conferences or conventions when it is determined that the attendance will serve the best interest of the Federal service. Such absences may be restricted to situations in which the employee is an official representative of the organization involved or is a contributor on the agenda. Employees may not be excused to attend conferences or conventions of political parties or partisan political groups or committees.

6.3.5. Representative leave hours must be reported using 4 separate categories: term negotiations, mid-term negotiations, dispute resolution, and general labor-management relations. Absence charged as representative leave may be subject to local negotiated agreements or supervisory approval.

6.3.6. Employees authorized a PCS move within DoW may be granted excused absence before departing the old duty station and after arriving at the new duty station to accomplish personal tasks resulting from the move (for example, to open or close personal bank accounts or to obtain driver's licenses or car tags). Employees coming to the DoW from other federal agencies may also be granted excused absence after being placed on the DoW employment roll. This provision does not cover time involved in complying with PCS requirements such as obtaining passports and vaccinations, meeting government housing authority requirements, or being present for packing and receiving household goods. Accomplishing tasks conditional to the PCS is considered official duty.

6.3.7. Employees under notice of separation or change to lower grade for any reason except personal cause may be granted excused absence for job searches and interviews. Employees competing for positions within DoW may also be granted excused absence for merit placement interviews.

6.3.8. Excused absence may be granted to permit an employee to attend the initial counseling session (for example, drug, alcohol, or financial) resulting from a referral under the Employee Assistance Program. This provision does not include the official duty status an employee is in during the initial referral to the Employee Assistance Program.

6.3.9. Excused absence may be granted to employees participating in management-sponsored volunteer projects (for example, education mentorship or tutoring programs). This provision does not apply to time spent on volunteer activities not sponsored by management. Volunteer activity not sponsored by management may be promoted through established leave programs and the flexibility offered through alternative work schedules.

6.3.10. Excused absence may be granted to employees to assist in emergency situations declared by, or requested from, authorized officials. This provision does not cover employees who respond to emergencies in National Guard or Reserve status.

6.3.11. Excused absence may be granted to an employee to undergo medical examinations required by appropriate military authorities for enlistment or induction into the Military Services. This provision does not cover travel time outside the commuting area or situations in which the employee receives military compensation, can use military leave, or undergoes additional tests, examinations, or treatments for conditions discovered or suspected as a result of the examinations.

6.3.12. Invited Medal of Honor holders may be granted excused absence to attend or participate in events such as the inauguration of the President of the United States, Congressional Medal of Honor Society conventions, and services on Memorial Day or Veterans Day.

6.4    Court Leave and Jury Duty

6.4.1. When an employee is called for court service as a witness or juror, the employee must present the court order, subpoena, or summons, if one was issued, to the supervisor as far in advance as possible.

6.4.2. Certificate of Attendance and Collection of Fees Paid

6.4.2.1. Unless otherwise allowable under this section, an employee in a pay status may not retain fees received for jury duty or witness services. The employee must submit any fees received to their employing activity by money order or personal check.

6.4.2.2. The employee must also submit a certificate of attendance from the clerk of the court to the employing activity. The certificate must show the dates of jury duty or witness service and the amount of fees the court paid, separately identifying fees and other allowances or expenses. If the certificate does not identify allowances separately, all monies received are treated as fees for jury duty or witness service and must be collected.

6.4.3. If fees are paid incorrectly to an employee serving in a nonofficial capacity, the employee may not retain the fees. The employee must turn the fees in to the CSR at the employing activity.

6.4.4. Monies submitted to the CSR for jury duty or witness service fees must be accounted for on a DoW (DD) Form 1131, Cash Collection Voucher. The servicing PRO must credit these monies to the appropriation and accounting classification that paid the employee's salary during the jury duty or witness service. See 5 U.S.C. § 5515.

6.4.5. Fees not submitted in a timely manner are subject to payroll deduction. The payroll deduction to collect the fees must be made in the next regular pay period. See 5 U.S.C. § 5515.

6.5    Shore Leave

6.5.1. The time and attendance report must reflect shore leave taken.

6.6    Military Leave

6.6.1. Military Leave

6.6.1.1. If a civilian employee changes their tour of duty from part-time to full-time in the middle of the FY, the servicing PRO must determine the number of days of military leave the employee used during that FY. For an employee who increases the hours in their workweek, the days of used leave are subtracted from the days authorized under the current tour of duty.

6.6.2. To substantiate all types of military leave charges, the employee must submit a copy of their military orders or other documentation directing them to report to active military duty. On return to civilian status from military leave, the employee must submit a certified verification of attendance. If an employee has separate sets of orders, or orders covering separate periods with a return to civilian status between them, military leave must not be charged for the time the employee is in civilian status.

6.7    Furlough

6.7.1. Shutdown Furlough

6.7.1.1. Public Law 116-92 authorizes employees to receive retroactive pay in a shutdown furlough. If a furlough occurs mid-pay-period and an employee receives a partial paycheck, the servicing PRO must apply deductions using the order of precedence in Section 5,
Table 4-1. Furloughed employees receive pay for any hours worked before the lapse in appropriations.

title: Section 7.0: Miscellaneous Actions (Special Actions)
content:
7.0    MISCELLANEOUS ACTIONS (SPECIAL ACTIONS)

7.1    Unemployment Compensation for Federal Employees (UCFE)

7.1.1. Employing Activity Responsibilities

7.1.1.1. The PRO must provide exact wage data through the HRO to the SESA so the SESA can determine the former employee's weekly and maximum unemployment benefit amounts. The PRO must accurately report all monetary information affecting the claim, such as lump sum annual leave payments, severance pay, annuity pay, or incentive pay.

7.1.1.2. The servicing HRO is the central point of contact for all UCFE matters. The PROs must refer all inquiries they receive (such as state queries, telephone calls, and requests for UCFE documentation) to the servicing HRO. The servicing HRO must contact the PRO for any additional information.

7.1.2. On receipt of the ETA 931, the HRO must report the employee's non-pay status to the SESA, including the LWOP starting and ending dates and any other pertinent data. For non- pay status of more than 30 days, the SF 50 provides the LWOP information; for LWOP of 30 days or less, the biweekly interface extract provides it to the HRO. The HRO must indicate whether an employee on LWOP is awaiting an on-the-job injury approval or disability retirement from the Office of Workers' Compensation Programs (OWCP). If an employee is awaiting an OWCP determination, the SESA is responsible for contacting the OWCP for any data it needs.

7.2    Claims from Employees for Additional Compensation

7.2.1. Claims Submission

7.2.1.1. The PRO may approve and pay claims received from the claimant when there is no question of law or fact.

7.2.1.2. The PRO must act on any claim it receives from OPM, including claims originally received by the DCMO and forwarded to OPM for final review, per the instructions in the letter or order transmitting the claim. The PRO must pay any resulting amount as part of the regular payroll.

7.2.1.3. Claims not received through OPM that the PRO denies administratively must be returned to the claimant with a letter explaining in detail why the claim was disapproved. If the employee appeals, the PRO must forward the claim to OPM via the DCMO with a transmittal letter the PRO prepares.

7.3    Back Pay Under 5 U.S.C. § 5596 (The Back Pay Act)

7.3.1. General

7.3.1.1. The HRO must determine an employee's entitlement to back pay and document the determination in the Remarks section of the SF 50.
