7.3.1.2. If a settlement agreement or order uses an undefined term of art like "back pay" without defining it, DFAS will apply the regulatory or statutory definition and process the back pay under the Back Pay Act unless the agreement or order expresses a contrary intent.

7.3.2. Correcting an Unjustified or Unwarranted Personnel Action

7.3.2.1. When an employee has been separated, DoW must complete corrective action on the date DoW reasonably sets for the employee's return to duty and must notify the employee of the return date in writing. Until that date, the erroneous action remains in effect. If the employee fails to report on the date set, DoW may charge annual leave, LWOP, or absence without leave from the date set for return until the employee returns to work. An employee who resigns instead of returning to duty is still entitled to back pay up to the date the employee is considered separated from federal service, since there is no requirement that the employee return to duty.

7.3.3. Deductions of Erroneous Payments From Back Pay

7.3.3.1. The PRO must transfer the recovered annuity amount to the retirement system.

7.3.3.2. The order of precedence for deducting erroneous payments from back pay awards, when the net amount of back pay is insufficient to cover all the deductions, is as follows: retirement annuity payments, refunds of retirement contributions, severance pay, then any lump sum payment for accrued annual leave.

7.3.4. Back Pay and Offsetting UCFE

7.3.4.1. If a reinstated employee is entitled to back pay, the HRO must determine whether the employee applied for unemployment compensation via the UCFE program within the last 52 weeks. If the employee applied for or received unemployment compensation, the HRO must promptly notify the SESA of the back pay payment date, the amount, and the period covered.

7.3.4.2. DoW will not deduct unemployment compensation paid during the back pay period from the back pay award unless state law requires the employer (rather than the employee) to reimburse the state for overpayments. A state agency may also determine an overpayment occurred and notify the federal government as the employing agency. See 65 Comp Gen 865 (1986) and DoWI 1400.25-V850.

7.3.5. Tax Withholding and Reporting in Back Pay Matters

7.3.5.1. A settlement or order may require an employing agency to issue a lump sum payment to the employee in lieu of back pay or as an award of damages. To ensure proper tax reporting and withholding, employing agencies must identify the nature of each lump sum payment as wages or non-wages. The PRO must review the nature of the payment before processing and must contact the agency if the identity or apportionment of the payment is in question.

7.3.5.1.1. If a settlement or order requires an employing agency to pay a lump sum and the payment is not clearly identified as damages or attorney fees, the payment is generally considered wages for tax purposes. A lump sum representing wages must be submitted to the PRO as an individual award to ensure proper processing. Federal and state taxes, OASDI, and Medicare taxes are withheld from wage payments, which are reported on IRS Form W-2, Wage and Tax Statement.

7.3.5.1.2. DFAS Vendor Pay (or other appropriate vendor pay office) processes lump sum payments of damages, which are reported on IRS Form 1099-MISC, Miscellaneous Income, with no taxes withheld.

7.3.5.2. Treasury operates the Judgment Fund under 31 U.S.C. § 1304, and back pay awards may be paid from it. Treasury regulations require the agency that submits the payment request to issue the tax reporting. For employees paid by DFAS, DFAS will issue the tax reporting on behalf of the employing agency even when the award of back pay or damages is made from the Judgment Fund. See 31 CFR 256.51.

7.4    Continuation of Pay (COP) (Injury Compensation)
7.4.1. Buy Back of Leave

7.4.1.1. The PRO must recover any gross amount paid for leave used during a period retroactively covered by OWCP compensation. Certain deductions are recoverable by payroll adjustment. The amount recovered from the employee or OWCP depends on whether payment for leave is paid in the current or prior year.

7.4.1.2. The amount collected for leave payments made in the current calendar year is the net pay plus deductions for the following bonds, savings allotments, alimony/child support, rent, indebtedness to the United States, and other deductions the employee received value but not otherwise collected.

7.4.1.3. Current deductions reversed in the payroll system (if applicable and if the moneys are recovered) are: CSRS or FERS; OASDI and/or Medicare; Federal, state, and local taxes; FEHB (if the OWCP payment is for more than 28 days); FEGLI (basic and optional); TSP; union dues; charitable contributions; and military service credit deposits and civilian service credit deposits.

7.4.1.4. The PRO must adjust earnings-to-date in the payroll system for items other than the reversed deductions. Amounts collected from the employee or OWCP must be identified as a cash refund on a voucher for disbursement or collection.

7.4.1.5. The amount collected for leave payments made during a prior year is the gross amount less CSRS/FERS, OASDI or Medicare, TSP, FEHB (if the OWCP payment is for more than 28 days), and FEGLI (basic and optional). The PRO must post the credit to CSRS/FERS as a separate credit line item on the SF 2806, Individual Retirement Record CSRS, or the SF 3100, Individual Retirement Record FERS, fiscal side, indicating the year of the adjustment with an explanation in the "Remarks" column. Adjustments are unauthorized for federal, state, and local income taxes.

7.4.1.6. When an employee separates or at the end of the payroll year, the PRO must prepare a W-2, as appropriate, but may not include any tax adjustments for a prior year. The PRO must prepare a certified statement to accompany the current year's W-2 stating that a prior-year refund was paid in the amount of $XX.XX, but that the gross wages shown on the current year W-2 were not reduced by the amount of the refund.

7.4.1.7. If circumstances permit, the employee may repay the amount due (after recovery of the amount repaid by OWCP) through partial payroll deductions. The PRO must not reverse deductions under subparagraph 7.4.1.3 until the full amount is paid.

7.4.1.8. Credit the full amount of leave used during the buyback period to the employee's leave account. The PRO must not recredit leave bought back until the total amount is repaid.

7.5    Emergency Evacuation Payments

7.5.1. Purpose

7.5.1.1. The DD 2461, Authorization for Emergency Evacuation Advance and Allotment Payments for DoW Civilian Employees, authorizes and records emergency payments to employees and dependents. The PRO is responsible for maintaining this record of payments on the employee's permanent pay account. In appropriate cases, information on this form may be disclosed to other federal agencies (SSA, IRS, and OPM), to state and local taxing or welfare authorities, and to certain private organizations for crediting payments to the employee's account. The PRO must receive DD 2461 before making payment of amounts due the evacuated civilian employees or family members.

7.5.1.2. Compute the employee's payments at the rate they are entitled to immediately before the order of evacuation or departure. Adult family members or designated representatives may receive payments as allotments. The PRO must make all advance payments (and any necessary adjustments) per the DoW component's procedures.

7.5.2. Transmission of Data to Safe-Haven Post

7.5.2.1. After authorities issue an evacuation order, the PRO must immediately forward all significant payroll data from the evacuated installation to the safe-haven post.

7.5.2.2. The physical conditions and circumstances at the evacuation installation determine the method and timing for transmitting data. Safeguarding and preserving payroll, leave, and travel records is a primary concern because the records are still needed after the conditions that gave rise to the emergency evacuation are resolved. Take all necessary steps to safeguard and preserve the records at the safe-haven post.

7.5.3. To the extent possible and practicable, the PRO must pay employees and dependents remaining at the evacuated installation per the normal fiscal procedures of that installation. A special advance payroll may be prepared per normal payroll procedures and charged against the appropriate funds available to the evacuated installation for authorized advance payments.

7.5.4. Actions After Evacuation

7.5.4.1. The PRO with jurisdiction over the employee's account must review the account for necessary adjustments at the earliest possible date after the evacuation is terminated (or earlier if circumstances apply), after the employee returns to the duty station, or when the employee is officially reassigned. See 5 CFR 550.408.

7.5.4.2. The PRO must adjust the employee's pay based on the rates of pay, allowances, or differentials, if any, to which the employee would otherwise be entitled. Adjustments must reflect any advance payments the employee received. If the employee is indebted for any part of the advance payment(s) made to the employee, dependent(s), or designated representative, the PRO with jurisdiction over the account must recover the debt unless there is an approved waiver. See 5 CFR 550.408.

title: Section 8.0: Department of War Education Activity (DoWEA) Employees
content:
8.0    DEPARTMENT OF WAR EDUCATION ACTIVITY (DOWEA) EMPLOYEES

8.1    TP Pay Plan

Educators, administrators, and ISS employees who hold a Teaching Position (TP) as defined in 20 U.S.C. § 901 are governed by the policies and regulations the DoWEA prescribes. Educators (teachers, social workers, guidance counselors, school psychologists, and nurses) earn a school year salary based on 190 duty days and typically receive compensation over 22 or 26 pay periods per the employee's written election. Administrators (school principals and assistant principals) and ISS employees earn a school year salary based on 222 duty days, paid over 26 pay periods. These employees do not earn annual, sick, or home leave under Title 5 U.S.C., but are entitled to educator's leave under 20 U.S.C. § 904.

8.1.1. School Year Duty Days

8.1.1.1. The school year for educators consists of 190 duty days and includes no less than 175 days of classroom instruction. The 190 duty days include the days required before and after the first and last day of school when educators must prepare for the opening and closing of school. The school year calendar may be adjusted after the school year begins with no change in school year salary, as long as 190 duty days are required and no less than 175 days of classroom instruction are provided. If the school year extends beyond 190 duty days, the educator receives compensation at the appropriate daily rate as of the 191st working day. If an emergency precludes completion of a full school year at one or more schools, the educators must be furloughed, separated, or salary continued until the full school year salary has been paid out.

8.1.1.2. The school year for administrators consists of 222 duty days and includes no less than 175 days of classroom instruction. The 222 duty days also include any time services are required for a majority of educators at the school. The school year calendar may adjust after the school year begins with no change in school year salary, as long as the required 222 duty days for principals and assistant principals and no less than 175 days of classroom instruction remain. If the school year extends beyond 222 duty days during a given school year, the administrator receives compensation at the appropriate daily rate as of the 223rd working day. If an emergency precludes completion of a full school year at one or more schools, the administrators must be furloughed, separated, or salary continued until the full school year salary has been paid out.

8.1.1.3. The school year for an ISS employee consists of 222 duty days, the same schedule as administrators. ISS employees coordinate their 222-day schedule with their supervisors at the start of the school year.

8.1.1.4. Overseas school year calendars DoWEA issues may vary due to local customs and holidays. The calendars identify the first and last duty days of the school year, instructional days, and exception days for educators and students. DoWEA must provide a copy of school calendars to the servicing PRO and to the DFAS Information and Technology (I&T) Office no later than 4 weeks before the first duty day of the new school year. Submit calendars and updates by email to the PRO (dfas.indianapolis-in.jfv.mbx.dodea@mail.mil) and DFAS I&T (dfas.indianapolis-in.ztb.list.cin-dcps-dodea@mail.mil) as soon as possible.

8.1.2. The Defense Civilian Personnel Advisory Service (DCPAS) Wage and Salary Division (WSD) establishes the rates of basic compensation for teachers and TP employees in the DoW. DCPAS WSD issues Pay Plan salary schedules in April or May of the current school year, effective retroactive to August 1 of the current school year (the prior calendar year). Use the prior school year salary schedules until the WSD issues salary schedules for the current school year. Separate salary schedules are issued for educator, management, specialist, and administrator overseas school year positions, further differentiated by step and academic salary lane.

8.1.3. Step increases for educators, administrators, and ISS employees are similar to step increases for General Schedule (GS) employees. Steps 1 through 14 are regular step increases and steps 15 through 18 are longevity steps. Substitute teachers are not eligible for step increases.

8.1.3.1. A full-time educator assigned to a 190-day position may receive a regular step increase (steps 1 through 14) if they have been in a pay status at least 150 duty days during their last previous school year as an educator.

8.1.3.2. A full-time educator assigned to a 190-day position may receive a longevity step increase (steps 15 through 18) if they have been in a pay status at least 150 duty days during each of the previous 4 school years as an educator.

8.1.3.3. A half-time educator assigned to a 190-day position may receive a regular step increase (steps 1 through 14) if they have been in a pay status at least one-half of 150 duty days during each of the previous 2 school years. A half-time educator may receive a longevity step increase (steps 15 through 18) after being in a pay status at least one-half of the 150 working day minimum during each of the previous 8 school years.

8.1.3.4. A full-time administrator assigned to a 222-day position may receive a step increase (steps 1 through 10) if they have been in a pay status at least 175 duty days during their last previous school year as an administrator.

8.1.3.5. A full-time ISS employee assigned to a 222-day position may receive a regular step increase (steps 1 through 14) if they have been in a pay status at least 175 duty days during their last previous school year as an educator.

8.1.3.6. A full-time ISS employee assigned to a 222-day position may receive a longevity step increase (steps 15 through 18) if they have been in a pay status at least 175 duty days during each of the previous 4 school years as an educator.

8.1.3.7. A half-time ISS employee assigned to a 222-day position may receive a regular step increase (steps 1 through 14) if they have been in a pay status at least one-half of 175 duty days during each of the previous 2 school years. A half-time educator may receive a longevity step increase (steps 15 through 18) after being in a pay status at least one-half of the 175 working day minimum during each of the previous 8 school years.

8.1.3.8. A full-time educator assigned to a 190-day position may receive an annual step increase (or service credit toward a longevity step) for the last satisfactory year of service, plus an additional annual step (or service credit) for the first year of absence, only upon return to duty after successfully completing a program of study or employment of one or more years under the Administrative Reemployment Rights Program.

8.1.3.9. Step increases take effect August 1 of each school year following completion of the school year. The step increase is not payable until the educator returns to duty for the subsequent year. When moving to a higher or lower salary schedule, there is no change to the effective date of step increases.

8.1.4. Arrival at Post

8.1.4.1. Newly recruited educators from the Continental United States are appointed with the understanding that they will serve for an entire school year or a specified partial month. When an educator arrives late to the post of assignment through no personal fault (for example, transportation or processing delays), the educator is administratively excused and paid as though the educator arrived on time and served during the lost time. DoWEA dates the offer letter 14 days before the reporting date. Educators not so described who arrive late at the post of assignment after the start of the school year do not receive compensation for the duty days before the day of arrival unless granted paid leave by a supervisor.

8.1.4.2. Educators who arrive at their post of assignment before the start of the school year normally are not entitled to compensation until the start of the school year. Educators who are required to report at their post of assignment and perform work before the start of the school year receive compensation at the daily salary rate from the prior school year salary schedule for each day worked. This salary is not subject to retroactive adjustment.

8.1.5. Educators who are unable to depart promptly after the end of the school year for personal reasons or because of circumstances beyond their control (for example, lack of available transportation) are not entitled to compensation for the period between the end of the school year and the date of departure. Educators who are required to perform work after the end of the school year are paid at the daily rate of their salary for each day worked.

8.1.6. While enroute during a permanent change of station (PCS) between school years, an educator is in a non-pay status and receives appropriate per diem payments per the DoW Joint Travel Regulations (JTR). While enroute during a PCS between school years, a principal or assistant principal otherwise in a non-pay, non-duty status remains in a non-pay status and receives appropriate per diem payments per the DoW JTR.

8.1.7. Work at More Than One Post of Assignment

8.1.7.1. When educators PCS during the school year, the servicing office must ensure that, after working the scheduled duty days during the remaining pay periods at the new post of assignment, the educator receives the full school year salary as entitled. If the total number of days actually worked during the school year (including paid leave at the former and new duty stations) exceeds 190 days, the educator receives compensation at the daily rate for any days worked in excess of 190 days.

8.1.7.2. When administrators or ISS employees PCS during the school year, the servicing office must ensure that, after working the scheduled duty days during the remaining pay periods at the new post of assignment, the administrator or ISS employee receives the full school year salary as entitled. If the total number of days actually worked during the school year (including paid leave at the former and new duty stations) exceeds 222 days, the employee receives compensation at the daily rate for any days worked in excess of 222 days.

8.1.8. Substitute Teachers

8.1.8.1. A substitute teacher receives the flat daily rate prescribed under Salary Schedule A. The minimum increment paid for substitute work is one-half day.

8.1.8.2. The Salary Schedule for "Other Compensation" provides the daily rate for a summer school substitute teacher, which is two-thirds of the regular school year substitute teacher rate established for the prior school year. This salary is not subject to retroactive adjustment. The prior school year rate for a 2025 summer school substitute teacher, for example, is published in the 2024-2025 salary schedules. The minimum increment earned and paid is one- half day, the equivalent of one-third of the regular substitute teacher rate. Substitute teachers who teach an academic enrichment K-8 program during the summer recess period receive a stipend as authorized by the memorandum of understanding (MOU).

8.1.9. Educators, administrators, and ISS employees may be entitled to certain allowances and differentials, such as government quarters, living quarters allowance (LQA), temporary quarters subsistence allowance (TQSA), separate maintenance allowance (SMA), post allowance, post differential, or storage of household goods. An educator employed as a substitute is not entitled to government quarters, quarters allowance, post allowance, post differential, or storage of household goods.

8.2    Leave

8.2.1. Accrual of Leave

8.2.1.1. Under 20 U.S.C. § 904, educators (excluding substitute teachers) are entitled to cumulative leave with pay, also referred to as educator leave. If the school year consists of less than 8 months, the leave accrues at the rate of 1 day for each calendar month worked or partial month. If the school year includes more than 8 months, an employee who serves the entire school year is entitled to 10 days of cumulative educator leave with pay for the school year. The full school year accrual is credited to the employee's leave record when the school year begins (normally in August) or whenever the employee enters on duty under DS Regulation 5630.4, DoDDS Absence and Leave.

8.2.1.2. Administrators and ISS employees may earn 13 days of cumulative educator leave with pay under 20 U.S.C. § 904 and DS Regulation 5301.4. The credit reflects on the employee's leave record each year on August 1.

8.2.1.3. If an educator, administrator, or ISS employee separates for any reason before the school year ends, any leave credited but not earned is subtracted from the leave balance. If already used, the servicing office must establish a debt and take appropriate collection action.

8.2.1.4. Educators and ISS employees regularly employed on a part-time basis earn leave in an amount proportionate to the leave earned by a full-time employee. Part-time ISS employees, such as those in a job-sharing arrangement, earn 6.5 days per year (or one-half day (4 hours) per pay period if less than 8 months remain in the school year).

8.2.1.5. Substitute teachers employed on a temporary intermittent basis are not entitled to earn leave.

8.2.1.6. Educators and administrators who perform activities during the summer recess period do not earn leave.

8.2.2. Leave Usage

8.2.2.1. The minimum charge for educator leave is one-half day, and additional charges are in multiples of one-half day. An administrative authority may use discretion to excuse an occasional absence from duty of less than one-half day for adequate reasons without charge to educator leave. Report leave charges to the PRO and record them on the employee's timecard.

8.2.2.2. An educator, administrator, or ISS employee may use accrued educator leave during the school year with appropriate advance notice and prior supervisor approval, an educator, administrator, or ISS employee may use up to 3 days of leave in a given school year for any purpose. Educator leave used for any purpose normally may not be used during orientation week or the first or last week of the school year. An exception may be made when an employee is accepted for an educational program and must report before the end of the school year.

8.2.2.3. Using accrued educator leave during any summer recess period is not permissible. An absence during a summer recess period is without pay.

8.2.2.4. Except for unique tours of duty established by the host nation (for example, Bahrain), Saturdays, Sundays, regularly scheduled holidays (including U.S. and host nation holidays), and other administratively authorized non-workdays are not normally days of leave, per 20 U.S.C. § 904(b). Leave Without Pay (LWOP) is therefore not charged to an educator, administrator, or ISS employee who is in a non-pay status immediately preceding or following a scheduled holiday.

8.2.3. Under unusual circumstances, an educator, administrator, or ISS employee may receive up to 30 days of advanced educator leave (above the amount already credited for the current school year) for use on any scheduled duty day within the school year. Such an advance is subject to subsequent earning of educator leave or repayment upon separation for leave advanced but not earned. The immediate supervisor may approve requests for up to 10 days of advance educator leave. Submit requests for more than 10 days to the Director for Student Excellence or District Superintendent, as appropriate. Submit approved requests to the PRO upon receipt from the approving official.

8.2.4. An educator's or ISS employee's immediate supervisor may approve an LWOP request of up to 3 days. The Director for Student Excellence or District Superintendent may approve LWOP requests over 3 days but less than 30 days. The Director for Student Excellence may approve LWOP requests of 30 days or more. For administrators, the District Superintendent must approve LWOP requests over 3 days but less than 30 days, and the Director for Student Excellence or their delegate must approve LWOP requests over 30 days.

8.2.5. Conversion of Leave

8.2.5.1. A federal or District of Columbia employee who transfers without a break in service from a different leave system to an educator, ISS employee, or administrator position receives credit for sick leave held immediately before the effective date of the conversion, transfer, promotion, or reappointment. Sick leave so credited is included in the employee's balance of educator leave.

8.2.5.2. No annual leave is credited to an educator, ISS employee, or administrator's balance of educator leave when the employee transfers without a break in service from a different leave system. The employee receives a lump-sum payment for accrued annual leave from the previous employer. Administrators who converted from GS or General Merit positions to Salary Schedules K and L on October 11, 1987, received annual leave credit during the initial conversion.

8.2.6. Transfer and Recredit of Educator’s Leave

8.2.6.1. When an educator, administrator, or ISS employee is separated and reappointed to another educator, administrator, or ISS employee position without a break in service of more than 3 years, the employee's educator leave must be certified to the employing agency for credit as sick leave on the SF 1150, Record of Leave Data.

8.2.6.2. If an educator, administrator, or ISS employee accepts temporary federal employment in a non-educator position during a recess period, the educator-leave account must not be transferred to the summer position's leave account. Sick leave earned during the temporary summer employment must be credited, and any unused sick-leave balance must be transferred to the educator-leave account when the employee returns to duty in their regular educator or administrator position.

8.2.7. Liquidation of Leave Upon Separation

8.2.7.1. Any annual leave earned under a different leave system and remaining to the credit of an educator, administrator, or ISS employee on separation must be liquidated by a lump-sum payment per 5 U.S.C. § 5551 and 20 U.S.C. § 904(f).

8.2.7.2. Lump-sum payment to liquidate educator leave on separation is prohibited. Educator leave that may not be liquidated includes leave earned by an educator, administrator, or ISS employee, and the leave balance under subparagraph 8.2.5.1.

8.2.8. Sabbatical Leave

8.2.8.1. The Director for Student Excellence may authorize yearlong educator leave at half-pay (sabbatical leave) for an educator, administrator, or ISS employee for educational purposes when the Director determines the course of study is appropriate. An SF 50 is not required. The approved training request must reflect that the employee will be in an LWOP status for one-half of each day during the yearlong period.

8.2.8.2. Educators and administrators granted sabbatical leave at half-pay must continue to receive life insurance and health benefits coverage as if in full pay status. Retirement contributions are deducted for only one-half year, but the employee is entitled to a full year of retirement credit. Educator leave is neither earned nor deducted from the employee's leave account during the training period. Any pay step increase that would have been authorized must be processed as if the employee had worked a full school year.

8.3    Pay Status During School Year and Summer Recess

8.3.1. An educator's school year consists of 190 duty days. In most overseas locations these duty days fall on the normal workweek (Monday through Friday). An educator does not work every Monday through Friday during the school year because of exception days (for example, winter and spring recess, federal holidays, and certain host-nation holidays). As a result, the school year may include 22 pay periods spanning about 213 Monday-through-Friday days between the educator's first and last duty day, typically 21 full pay periods plus 3 additional days in the 22nd pay period.

8.3.2. During summer recess, while school is not in session, educators are ordinarily in a non-pay status. Educators returning to duty for the following full school year are entitled to continued LQA payments during summer recess while in non-pay status (see DSSR Chapter 100, Quarters Allowances, and Chapter 700, DoW Teachers). The servicing HRO must notify the servicing PRO of any change in an educator's status, such as transfer, resignation, or retirement.

8.4    Compensation

8.4.1. Educators With a 190-Day School Year

8.4.1.1. For an educator on non-paid absence, such as LWOP or absence without leave (AWOL), biweekly pay is reduced by 1/190th of the school year salary for each scheduled duty day in a non-paid status. Because educators are not paid for federal holidays or recess periods, biweekly pay is not reduced when the educator is in a non-paid status before or after an exception day.

8.4.2. Administrators With a 222-Day School Year

8.4.2.1. In addition to basic pay, administrators assigned to foreign areas where the cost of goods and services is substantially higher are entitled to a post allowance (see 20 U.S.C. § 906). To compute the foreign post allowance, divide the total annual amount payable by 365 calendar days (366 days in a leap year).

8.4.2.2. For an administrator on non-paid absence, such as LWOP or AWOL, biweekly pay is reduced by 1/222nd of the school year salary for each scheduled duty day in a non-paid status. Because administrators are not paid for exception days, biweekly pay is not reduced when the administrator is in a non-paid status before or after a federal holiday or recess day.

8.4.3. ISS Employees With a 222-Day School Year

8.4.3.1. ISS employees build their own calendar, scheduling 222 duty days within the 260-to-262-day school year. The remaining 38 or 39 days are considered non-workdays for this regulation. The ISS employee sets the schedule, then obtains supervisor approval. An ISS employee who schedules work on a federal holiday does not receive holiday pay and still has the same number of non-workdays (38 or 39). However, an employee who schedules work on a holiday or Sunday when normal school operations are in session is entitled to the appropriate premium pay. For example, if school is in session on Sundays by local custom and the employee's approved schedule includes Sunday, the employee is entitled to Sunday premium pay; if Sunday is not normally a workday for school staff, the employee is not. Calculate biweekly pay as follows: Duty Days and "Daily Rate" or "222 Rate" for ISS Employees. The number of duty days in the school year to ISS employees is 222. The ISS employee’s daily rate, or "222-Rate," is the school year salary divided by 222 days. School Year Days and "School Year Rate" or "260 Rate" for ISS Employees. The school year days for ISS employees will total between 260 and 262 days, depending on the calendar year. Thus, the days during the school year include days that fall within and outside of the school year for educators. The school year days for ISS employees include 222 duty days and exception days that occur on Monday through Friday during the regular school year. Exception days include federal holidays (e.g., Labor Day) and school recess days (e.g., spring recess) when ISS employees are not normally scheduled to work. However, due to the schedule flexibility, ISS employees may elect to work on a federal holiday (but will not receive holiday pay) and schedule non-workdays on days that other educators generally work. Use the number of school year days to determine an ISS employee’s school year rate, or "260-Rate." The school year rate is the daily rate used to provide uniform payment for each biweekly pay period. Multiply the school year rate by 10 days to determine the ISS employee’s biweekly basic pay amount. Formula for ISS Employee’s Biweekly Pay. ISS employees typically receive compensation over 26 pay periods. Use the following to calculate the biweekly pay: School Year Salary ÷ (260, 261, or 262 School Year Days) = School Year Rate, and School Year Rate × 10 Days = Biweekly Pay.

8.4.3.2. In addition to basic pay, ISS employees are entitled to a post allowance under 20 U.S.C. § 906. To compute the foreign post allowance, divide the total annual amount payable by 365 calendar days (366 days in a leap year).

8.4.3.3. For ISS employees on non-paid absence (for example, LWOP or AWOL), biweekly pay reduces by 1/222nd of the school year salary for each scheduled duty day the ISS employee is in non-paid status. Because ISS employees are not compensated for scheduled non- workdays, no reduction of biweekly pay is needed when the ISS employee is in non-paid status before or after an exception day.

8.4.3.4. When an ISS employee separates (resigns, retires, or dies) before the end of a school year, the school year salary must be adjusted to the number of actual duty days worked, including any days in paid leave status, by multiplying the 222-Rate daily rate by duty days worked. Any difference between the adjusted school year salary and the salary already paid must be reconciled.

8.4.4. Premium Pay, Sunday Work, and Holiday Work

8.4.4.1. Educators and administrators are not eligible for overtime pay or compensatory time off.

8.4.4.2. Educators appointed to a 190-day position whose regular tour of duty requires Sunday work are entitled to basic pay plus a premium of 25 percent of the daily rate (190-Rate). Administrators on a 222-day position whose regular tour of duty requires Sunday work (where part of the 190-duty-day school year or within summer school session) are entitled to basic pay plus a premium of 25 percent of the regular daily rate (222-Rate). An ISS educator who works on a Sunday when normal school operations are in session is entitled to the appropriate premium pay.

8.4.4.3. Educators appointed to a 190-day position whose regular tour of duty requires work on a federal holiday are entitled to basic pay plus premium pay equal to the daily rate. Administrators on a 222-day position whose regular tour of duty requires work on a federal holiday (where part of the 190-duty-day school year or within summer school session) are entitled to basic pay plus premium pay equal to the daily rate. An ISS employee who schedules work on a federal holiday usually does not receive holiday pay; but an ISS employee who works on a federal holiday when normal school operations are in session is entitled to the appropriate premium pay.

8.4.5. Employment During the Summer Recess Period

8.4.5.1. Educators are in non-pay/non-duty status during the summer recess period but may receive pay for certain duties performed then. An educator who participates in a non- summer, school-related activity (for example, agency-sponsored and approved training, early return, and late departure) during summer recess is compensated at a daily rate of 1/190th of the prior school year salary. An educator who participates in a summer school-related activity (for example, teaching) usually receives two-thirds of the daily rate of the prior school year salary, though exceptions are possible and the notification for teaching summer school may state a different amount. The minimum increment earned and paid for summer recess activities is one- half day. Educators who work an academic enrichment K-8 program during summer recess receive a stipend as authorized by the MOU. This period of employment is exempt from dual-pay provisions per 5 U.S.C. 5533(d)(7)(D) and is not subject to CSRS, FERS, FEGLI, or TSP deductions (see DoWEA AI 5303.1).

8.4.5.2. An administrator or ISS employee who participates in a non-summer, school-related activity (for example, agency-sponsored and approved training) during summer recess in excess of the 222-day work year is compensated at a daily rate of 1/222nd of the prior school year salary. An administrator or ISS employee who participates in a summer school-related activity receives two-thirds of the daily rate of the prior school year salary. The minimum increment earned and paid for summer recess activities is one-half day. This period of employment is exempt from dual-pay provisions per 5 U.S.C. 5533(d)(7)(D) and is not subject to CSRS, FERS, FEGLI, or TSP deductions (see DoWEA AI 5303.1).

8.4.6. Post Allowance

8.4.6.1. Under 20 U.S.C. 906, full-time educators, administrators, and ISS employees assigned to a foreign area where the cost of goods and services is substantially higher are eligible, in addition to basic pay, to receive a post allowance. The amount is a flat rate based on the employee's basic salary, family size, and post assignment, and appears on the SF 1190, Foreign Allowances Application, Grant and Report. If an employee's annual salary is adjusted, the post allowance may also be adjusted, in which case the daily rate must be recomputed.

8.4.7. Extra Duty Program for Educators

8.4.7.1. The extra duty program applies to certain DoWEA employees under the pay plan who are assigned extra duty assignments, such as coaching or activity sponsorship, in addition to regular school duties (see DoWEA AI 1417.01, Extra Duty Assignments). Educators receive extra duty compensation only for assignments conducted and completed outside the educator's duty day. When a selected educator performs an extra duty assignment, the educator and school principal must sign an MOU identifying the assignment and stating the duties, hourly range, amount of compensation, and a prohibition on performing duties during regular duty hours. Administrators are not eligible for extra duty assignments; any extra duties an administrator performs are voluntary. Compensatory time and holiday pay are not authorized forms of extra duty compensation.

8.4.7.2. The DCPAS WSD publishes the compensation rate for completing an extra duty assignment as part of the yearly DoWEA salary schedules (Schedule for Other Compensation). Before receiving extra duty compensation, the educator must complete the activity and perform the minimum number of established hours for it. The administrator must certify satisfactory completion and authorize compensation, and must forward a memorandum to the PRO as soon as possible, no later than May 31, to enable payment by the end of the school year.

8.4.7.3. The Director of DoWEA determines an appropriate hourly range for completing each type of authorized extra duty activity. The DCPAS WSD establishes the hourly ranges for extra duty compensation.

8.4.7.4. If the administrator determines an extra duty assignment was completed satisfactorily in less time than the approved MOU identified, compensation must be reduced and the educator must be paid at the rate established for the appropriate lower hourly range. When the hours worked fall short of the original range, or completion is less than acceptable to the administrator, the educator is paid less than the approved MOU amount on a pro rata basis.

8.4.7.5. Substitute teachers are paid for completing an extra duty assignment at the rate published by the DCPAS WSD.

8.4.8. Accelerated Deductions

8.4.8.1. FEGLI and FEHB premium deductions for an educator on a 190-day work schedule accelerate so that the total annual premiums are deducted over 22 pay periods rather than 26 pay periods. This lets the employee maintain coverage and pay no additional premiums during the summer recess non-pay status. The coverage period usually runs from the first duty day of the school year until the day before the first duty day of the next school year. Accelerated premium deductions are not required for an administrator or ISS employee on a 222-day work schedule.

8.4.8.2. If an educator resigns at the close of the school year and has elected FEGLI and/or FEHB coverage, the actual separation date is delayed so the employee keeps coverage throughout the period covered by accelerated premium deductions; coverage for an educator employed a full school year continues until the day before the first duty day of the next school year. If the educator separates before the end of the school year, the resignation must specify an earlier coverage-termination date and the employee must acknowledge that coverage continues only 31 days after separation. An educator who separates early is reimbursed proportionately if the separation date precedes the end of the prepaid FEHB coverage period. If an educator converts to or is appointed to a 222-day or calendar-year schedule, accelerated premium deductions may need to be refunded where the conversion takes effect during the prepaid coverage period and withholding in the new position causes duplicate premium payments.

8.4.8.3. Educators enrolled in the FSAFEDS Program and paid over 22 pay periods may elect to accelerate these allotments. The Federal LTC Program does not offer accelerated payments to educators paid over 22 pay periods. For periods of non-pay status, the educator receives a "Bill for Uncollected Payroll Premium."

8.4.9. Other Deductions

8.4.9.1. Allotments of pay for labor organization dues take effect the second pay period in October of each school year for an educator who is a bargaining unit member. The allotment is the dues amount the employee identifies on the SF 1187, Request for Payroll Deductions for Labor Organization Dues, or the amount on a list issued by each local or regional bargaining unit, divided by 12 full pay periods unless all parties agree otherwise.

8.4.9.2. Educators who enter the dues withholding agreement when fewer than 12 full pay periods remain in the school year have their dues allotments prorated over the remaining full pay periods within the dues withholding period.

8.4.9.3. An SF 1187 authorization for dues withholding remains in effect when a Not to Exceed (NTE) employee converts to an excepted service position in the bargaining unit before the NTE appointment expires.

8.4.9.4. After each pay period, the PRO must prepare and electronically forward the remittance to the designated labor organization, accompanied by a report listing the names and amounts withheld.

8.4.9.5. An educator's dues withholding authorization carries forward automatically to the next school year unless the employee notifies the PRO to stop the deduction. To cancel labor organization dues deductions, an educator must submit an SF 1188, Cancellation of Payroll Deductions for Labor Organization Dues, to the PRO no later than September 1. Proper completion and timely submission of the SF 1188 is the employee's responsibility. An SF 1188 received after September 1 processes for the next school year.

8.4.9.6. No later than 2 weeks before withholding is to begin, the local or area units of the labor organization must forward a list of employees who have requested dues withholding. The list must identify the bargaining unit name or number, location, address, points of contact, and phone numbers, and must include each employee's name, Social Security Number, location assigned, and amount of dues to withhold for that school year.

8.4.9.7. Savings and other allotments authorized in Section 12 deduct over the number of full pay periods in the school year.

8.4.9.8. An educator, administrator, or ISS employee may elect a percentage or a dollar TSP deduction per the guidelines in Section 12. If the employee elects percentage withholding, TSP deductions are also taken from the annual retroactive salary adjustment each year.

8.4.10. DoWEA employs retired military officers and noncommissioned officers as educators in its overseas JROTC program. The school year salary of JROTC instructors is set using the comprehensive Schedule for Educators and Specialist (Schedule C).

8.4.11. DoWEA employees may apply for a waiver of erroneous payments of pay and allowances by following the procedures in Section 9. The PRO must forward DoWEA employee applications to the DoWEA Human Resources Division, Classification and Compensation Section, for adjudication rather than to the Debt and Claims Management Office at DFAS.

title: Section 9.0: Underpayments, Collection of Non-DoW Debts, Garnishments, Bankruptcy Action, and Tax Levies
content:
9.0    UNDERPAYMENTS, COLLECTION OF NONDOW DEBTS, GARNISHMENTS, BANKRUPTCY ACTION, AND TAX LEVIES

9.1    Underpayments

9.1.1. General

9.1.1.1. All salary payments must be paid per the time and attendance reported and certified by the employee's supervisor. Reported time and attendance that is less than an employee's normal work schedule is presumed to accurately reflect the employee's hours of work and non-work. Any time and attendance errors must be corrected and certified to adjust underpayments.

9.1.2. Special Payments

9.1.2.1. An employing activity must submit a request to the PRO for a special payment. The PRO must request copies of substantiating and supporting documentation to process the special payment. The PRO makes the final determination on whether a special payment is appropriate and will process a special payment only under the following circumstances:

9.1.2.1.1. A special payment may be issued to correct a salary underpayment when an employee has received less than 90 percent of their regular biweekly pay and allowances. The request must be made by the commanding officer/director and must include a certified (or corrected) time and attendance report. PRO Directors may waive the 90 percent rule when extenuating circumstances exist.

9.1.2.1.2. A special payment may be issued to pay an employee erroneously omitted from the payroll. Before processing, the PRO must verify the individual's employment using the SF 50, Notification of Personnel Action. The request must be made by the commanding officer/director and must include a certified and corrected time and attendance report and any necessary source documents to support deductions.

9.1.2.1.3. A special payment may be issued to an employee placed in LWOP status for payroll processing when LWOP is approved for conversion to advanced annual, sick, or donated leave. The commanding officer/director may request the special payment after determining a financial hardship exists and that the employee has received less than 90 percent of their regular biweekly pay and allowances. The request must include a certified and corrected time and attendance report.

9.1.2.1.4. A special payment may be issued to a beneficiary entitled to receive a deceased employee's unpaid compensation under 5 U.S.C. § 5582. The PRO may issue the special payment only after the employing activity's human resources office submits sufficient documentation to support the payment. For computation and more on deceased employee unpaid compensation, see Section 11.

9.1.2.2. A special payment requested for the following reasons will not be processed:

9.1.2.2.1. The PRO will not honor a request for partial payment of salary before the regular pay date.

9.1.2.2.2. The PRO will not process a request for special payments for overtime or other premium pay earned but not reported, and therefore not paid in the corresponding pay period. However, authorization for a special payment for other reasons will include payment of any unpaid premium pay for the corresponding pay period.

9.1.2.3. The PRO must compute special payments to current and former employees using the "gross-to-net" method. Gross-to-net payments represent the regular biweekly pay and allowances normally due the employee (plus unpaid premium pay for the corresponding pay period, if applicable) less required deductions and withholdings withheld from the employee's biweekly pay. Gross-to-net special payment computations apply as follows:

9.1.2.3.1. If the employee received less than 90 percent of their biweekly pay, the employee is entitled to the difference between what was paid and what should have been paid. The PRO will deduct additional amounts for applicable items unless previous payroll processing has satisfied those deductions. The employee is responsible for existing voluntary allotments not deducted during the previous processing. All deductions and withholdings must resume the following pay cycle, including voluntary allotments.

9.1.2.3.2. If the employee received no biweekly pay, the gross entitlements, less applicable deductions and withholdings, are payable to the employee. The PRO must exclude deductions for voluntary allotments. The employee is responsible for existing voluntary allotments. All deductions and withholdings must resume on the following pay cycle, including voluntary allotments.

9.1.2.3.3. An employee's final pay may be issued as a special payment. The gross entitlements, less required deductions and withholdings are payable to the employee. The employee is responsible for voluntary allotments. Under 5 U.S.C. § 5514, when an employee separates by resignation, retirement, death, or termination of appointment, the employee's final pay (including lump-sum leave payments) will be applied to the extent necessary to liquidate any previously established debt. See Volume 16.

9.1.2.4. Employees will receive special payment disbursements in the same manner as their net pay, by electronic funds transfer (EFT). If the employee has a waiver of the EFT requirement for payroll disbursements, the PRO will send a U.S. Treasury check via express mail to the employee's address of record. Payments are normally issued within 3 business days after the PRO receives the special payment request and required supporting documentation.

9.1.2.5. For special payments made after the last regular pay period of the tax year but before the end of the calendar year, the PRO must withhold federal, state, and local taxes and Social Security/Medicare from the special payments. When computing or deducting Social Security, the PRO must ensure the employee has not reached maximum withholdings for the year. The PRO must forward the withholdings to the applicable offices as soon as possible. The PRO will include all deductions and contributions for Social Security/Medicare and federal, state, and local taxes for canceled checks or special payments.

9.1.2.6. The PRO will process updates to ensure special payments or canceled checks are included in the history totals. After the final pay period of the tax year, if the PRO identifies incorrect reporting on the W-2, the PRO will issue the W-2c and the IRS Form 941-X, Adjusted Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return or Claim for Refund, per IRS Publication 15, (Circular E), Employer's Tax Guide.

9.1.2.7. Special payments for TSP participants are subject to TSP deductions provided the employee has not reached the maximum contribution level established by law. TSP deductions withheld from special payments after the last regular pay period in the tax year, but before the end of the calendar year, will be combined with the next pay cycle for reporting and submission to the Federal Retirement Thrift Investment Board.

9.2 Collection of Non-DoW Debts by Salary Offset; Judgments Against Employees for Debts Owed to the Federal Government

9.2.1. Non-DoW Federal Creditor Agencies

9.2.1.1. When non-DoW federal creditor agencies (except the IRS or U.S. Courts) identify DoW employees with outstanding debts, those agencies must address their salary offset requests to the Secretary of War designee for such collection, DFAS Cleveland (CL): DFAS-AHADC/CL, 1240 East 9th Street, Cleveland, OH 44199-8002. A request for offset must include certification that due process rights have been afforded to the indebted employee by the non-DoW creditor agency. Debts established in the payroll system for non-DoW employees serviced by DFAS who later become DoW employees must be transferred systematically to the employing DoW agency for continued collection.

9.2.2. Government Travel Charge Card (GTCC) Contractor

9.2.2.1. The travel charge card contractor must forward delinquent debts to the DFAS-CL Salary Offset Project Office.

9.2.2.2. Undisputed 120-day-old delinquent accounts referred for salary offset must contain the full balance of the account, regardless of whether some individual charges relate to an official travel document. In addition to the delinquent charges, the amount referred for salary offset must include any late fees assessed and costs of collection.

9.2.2.3. The file must include the travel charge card contractor's financial institution and account routing information to facilitate electronic transmission of delinquent amounts collected.

9.2.2.4. Any delinquent debt the travel charge card contractor has already forwarded to a private collection agency must not be included in the salary offset process. Likewise, a travel charge card contractor must not refer any delinquent debt already submitted to DFAS for collection by salary offset to a private collection agency.

9.2.2.5. The Salary Offset Project Office must process the request for initiation of travel charge card delinquent debt salary offset in the same manner as federal salary offset requests from other federal agencies.

9.2.2.6. The Salary Offset Project Office must manage the debt balance during the salary offset process. If changes to the debt balance occur, the travel charge card contractor must immediately advise the Salary Offset Project Office of those changes.

9.2.2.7. The PROs must provide reports listing the collection transactions to the Salary Offset Project Office for each collection file to monitor amounts collected and remaining debt balances due.

9.2.3. Under 31 U.S.C. § 3716(h) and 31 CFR 285.6, a state may enter into a reciprocal agreement with the Department of Treasury to collect unpaid state debt by offset of federal non-tax payments. DFAS does not offset non-tax state debts from federal employee salaries.

9.2.4. When a U.S. Court determines that a federal employee is indebted to the United States and enters a judgment against the employee, PL 97-276, section 124 (published as a note to 5 U.S.C. § 5514) allows collection of the debt by deduction from the employee's current pay account. The employee's consent is not required. Any federal agency requesting salary offset under this authority must send a request for offset to the PRO with a copy of the judgment. The PRO may request DFAS Office of General Counsel (OGC) to review the judgment if questions arise. After confirming the validity or interpretation of the judgment, the PRO will:

9.2.4.1. Compute the amount to be collected each pay period using the percentage specified in the offset request. The maximum amount deducted for a pay period may not exceed 25 percent of the employee's disposable pay, unless a greater percentage is necessary to recover the amount owed within the time of anticipated employment. Deductions may be made from basic pay, special pay, incentive pay, or, for an individual not entitled to basic pay, other authorized pay.

9.2.4.2. Collect the total unpaid balance as specified in the offset request. This amount may include accumulated interest and administrative charges. The agency requesting offset should notify the PRO approximately 90 days before completion of the judgment offset with the final judgment amount, which includes the balance of accrued interest charges.

9.2.4.3. Forward a copy of the offset request to the employee with written notification of the deduction amount and the pay period the deduction will start.

9.2.4.4. Apply final pay (salary and lump-sum leave) to any unliquidated debt balance if the employee retires, resigns, dies, or if employment otherwise ends.

9.2.4.5. Forward payment each pay period to the agency requesting salary offset.

9.3    Child Support, Alimony and Commercial Garnishments

9.3.1. DFAS serves as the paying agency for DoW and for non-DoW federal agencies. In this capacity, DFAS-OGC, Garnishment Law Directorate, is the designated agent for service of the legal garnishment process for agencies paid by DFAS. Submit court orders, related documents, and forms for child support, alimony, and commercial garnishments to the Garnishment Law Directorate by mail, fax, or online through the askDFAS module: DFAS Office of General Counsel, Attn: Garnishment Law Directorate, PO Box 998002, Cleveland, OH 44199-8002. Upon review of the court order, DFAS will process the garnishment deduction in the payroll system. Cancellation of the order is automatic on the date of separation from DoW, upon death of the employee, or upon court notification that the garnishment is terminated. The employee cannot voluntarily stop court-ordered deductions.

9.3.2. Commercial Garnishments

9.3.2.1. Under 15 U.S.C. § 1673(a)(1), involuntary withholding for collection of a commercial debt is limited to a maximum of 25 percent of the employee's disposable earnings; state law prevails when it provides a maximum collection percentage less than 25 percent. If the employee already has a child support or alimony withholding order in effect, and the total deduction for child support and alimony equals or exceeds 25 percent of the employee's disposable pay, the PRO will not process any commercial debt deduction. Further limitations on the amount to be garnished are in 5 CFR 582.402. There is no limit on the percentage for garnishment for federal, state, or local tax obligations, or for bankruptcy court orders.

9.3.3. Involuntary state tax levies will be processed similar to commercial garnishments and are submitted to the Garnishment Law Directorate to begin legal review. The PRO can establish voluntary state tax levies as allotments.

9.4    Bankruptcies

9.4.1. This section applies to DoW employees who have filed a bankruptcy petition under 11 U.S.C., Chapter 7 or Chapter 13. The law waives the U.S. Government's sovereign immunity for compliance with payroll deduction orders issued by the bankruptcy courts (11 U.S.C. § 106); collections will be processed per the court order. DFAS serves as the paying agency for DoW and non-DoW federal agencies, and DFAS-OGC, Garnishment Law Directorate, is the designated agent for service of personal bankruptcy cases for agencies paid by DFAS. Submit bankruptcy notices and Chapter 13 withholding orders to the Garnishment Law Directorate by mail, fax, or online using the askDFAS module: DFAS Office of General Counsel, Attn: Garnishment Law Directorate, PO Box 998002, Cleveland, OH 44199-8002.

9.4.1.1. Upon notice or actual knowledge of the filing of a bankruptcy petition, when the employee has listed the United States as a creditor, the PRO files a proof of claim with the bankruptcy court for all Chapter 13 filings and, if requested by the bankruptcy trustee, for Chapter 7 cases.

9.4.2. Chapter 13 Bankruptcies (The Plan)

9.4.2.1. Once the bankruptcy court confirms a Plan, it usually orders the employer to pay a specific amount of an employee's income to the trustee named in the order. Payment to the trustee will be made per the employee's normal pay cycle. Bankruptcy law authorizes withholding up to 100 percent of the employee's disposable earnings, as directed by the court- ordered wage order.

9.4.2.2. If the United States is both the employer and creditor when the individual files bankruptcy under Chapter 13, the government's priority under 31 U.S.C. § 3713 may be asserted absent a judicial determination to the contrary. The appropriate PRO must timely file Official Form 410, Proof of Claim, with the bankruptcy court.

9.5    Tax Levy for Unpaid Federal Income Tax

9.5.1. Authority

9.5.1.1. After the PRO receives a levy, the PRO must not allow employees to increase or add any voluntary allotments. Changes that increase existing voluntary allotments are authorized only after the total tax liability is paid or arrangements are made with the IRS.

9.5.2. When the IRS serves Form 668-W, Notice of Levy on Wages, Salary, and Other Income, the PRO will take immediate action to implement the levy. Once the PRO processes the levy, it continues in effect until the collection is complete or the IRS releases the levy.

9.5.2.1. The PRO must follow the instructions on the 668-W and provide notice to the employee that a levy has been received.

9.5.2.2. The levy attaches to the employee's take home pay minus the allowable exceptions. Unless the IRS instructs otherwise, the employee's payroll deductions in effect when the levy was received will be allowed when determining take home pay. However, a voluntary allotment may be disallowed if the deduction is so large it defeats the levy. The IRS may notify the PRO when different procedures apply to specific employees. To determine take home pay, the levy attaches to the gross amount of the employee's accrued wages or salary, less the following deductions: Social Security/Medicare; retirement; FEHB; FEGLI; garnishments for child support or alimony; overpayments due the U.S. Government; and allowable personal exemptions on the
668-W.

9.5.2.3. After the PRO makes the first deduction for the levy against the employee's pay, the PRO must follow the instructions on the 668-W and return Part 3 of the form to the IRS.

9.5.2.4. If the employee has been reassigned to an organization serviced by another PRO, the losing PRO must inform the IRS District Director of the employee's new address. The losing PRO must mail the complete levy package to the new PRO for processing.

9.5.2.5. If the employee has moved from overseas, transferred to another federal agency, separated, or retired, the PRO will return the levy to the IRS District Director and provide the employee's new address on the 668-W.

9.5.2.6. If the PRO receiving the levy has no record that payroll service has been furnished for the employee, the PRO must annotate that fact on the bottom of the levy and return the levy to the IRS District Director.

9.5.3. An employee may arrange with the IRS to liquidate a delinquent federal income tax debt through voluntary biweekly payroll deductions. The IRS Form 2159, Payroll Deduction Agreement, must be submitted to the PRO to initiate the deduction process.

9.6    Pay Corrections and Tax Reporting

9.6.1. A payment made to correct an underpayment of earnings ("corrective payment") is reported as wages in the year the corrective payment is issued, even if the underpayment occurred in a prior calendar year. The PRO must process the corrective payment in the current pay cycle and report it as gross wages subject to Social Security/Medicare taxes on the employee's current year W-2. Social Security/Medicare tax must be withheld from the corrective payment. The gross wages must be reported as current quarterly earnings on the IRS Form 941, Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return. For separated employees, the PRO may be required to prepare the IRS Form W-2c, Corrected Wage and Tax Statement, if a W-2 was previously issued.

9.6.2. Tax Reporting

9.6.2.1. For active employees, the PRO must follow the debt collection procedures in Volume 16 to establish a debt for the overpaid earnings. If the employee repays the debt, in whole or in part, in the same year the overpayment occurs, the PRO must record the repaid amount as a reversal in base pay, gross pay, net pay, or other pay as applicable. This action is required to recover income tax withholding and Social Security and Medicare taxes for the repaid wages and to correct the yearly gross income.

9.6.2.2. The PRO must follow the same procedures for active employees in subparagraph 9.6.2.1 but must reestablish the employee on the payroll before processing the required reversals. If a W-2 was previously issued to the separated employee, the PRO must prepare a W-2c.

9.6.2.3. If an active employee repays an overpayment of earnings paid in a prior year, Social Security/Medicare wages and taxes may need to be corrected. If the year of repayment is still within the 3-year statute of limitations for Social Security or Medicare tax refunds, the PRO must prepare a W-2c and W-3c for the prior year to reduce the gross wages subject to Social Security/Medicare (box 3). Wages reflected in box 1 of the W-2c must not be corrected. No adjustments are made for income tax withholding or additional Medicare tax withholding. Per Circular E, the PRO will prepare the 941-X to correct errors on the 941 and retain copies of the corrected forms. If the repayment is beyond the 3-year statute of limitations, the PRO will not make corrections to the prior year W-2 and the 941.

9.6.2.4. The PRO must prepare a tax certificate for the employee representing the repaid wages in the year of repayment. The amount entered on the certificate is the total of the reverse deductions plus the amount the employee repaid. The employee may be entitled to a deduction (or a credit, in some cases) for the repaid wages on the employee's income tax return for the year of repayment. For additional information, see 26 U.S.C. § 1341 and IRS Publication 525, Taxable and Nontaxable Income.

9.6.2.5. For separated employees, the PRO will follow the procedures for active employees but will retain copies of the W-2c and the 941-X to balance annual federal tax deposits.

title: Section 10.0: Records, Files, and Reports
content:
10.0    RECORDS, FILES, AND REPORTS

10.1    Records and Files

10.1.1. Payroll Documentation

10.1.1.1. Deductions for CSRS and FERS, life insurance, and health benefit programs with employer contributions are paid to OPM each pay period. The PRO must submit a consolidated SF 2812-A to OPM biweekly through the Retirement and Insurance Transfer System (RITS) to report these deductions. For RITS, see subparagraph 3.3.3.

10.1.1.2. The PRO must reconcile payments to deduction recipients on a cyclical basis, at least annually, with the amounts withheld plus any related employer contributions shown by the pay or other records, to confirm correct amounts are reported to those authorized to receive the deductions and contributions. Payroll records must provide a clear audit trail from the gross pay calculation to the employee's net pay, by pay period and year-to-date.

10.1.1.2.1. Each DoW PRO must keep a record, for each calendar year, of the total amounts withheld from employees' salaries and the total employer contributions for FEGLI. The PRO must keep these records in a ledger or other appropriate form, or as file copies of the vouchers used to report the information to OPM.

10.1.1.2.2. The PRO must keep a record of employee deductions and employer contributions for health benefits by each enrollment code number. The PRO and the health benefit carrier must submit the enrollee data in this record to the National Finance Center FEHB Centralized Electronic Enrollment Reconciliation Clearinghouse (CLER) system quarterly. The HRO and the PRO must review any error codes identified in CLER and resolve the discrepancies by comparing the coverage reported by the PRO, the coverage reported by the carriers, the SF 2809, and the SF 2810 sent in support of the coverage.

10.1.1.2.3. The HRO must maintain a record of traditional and Roth TSP deductions and agency contributions for each employee.

10.1.2. Retroactive Computations Involving Former PROs

10.1.2.1. When retroactive payroll computations involve one or more former PROs, the consolidated PRO holds overall responsibility for the adjustment process. If a former PRO is involved, the consolidated PRO must contact each former PRO to obtain the necessary information.

10.1.2.2. If the consolidated PRO cannot obtain the documentation needed to perform the retroactive calculation, it may take one or more of the following steps: Request Archived Documents From the National Personnel Records Center (NPRC). When copies of the SF 135, Records Transmittal and Receipt, are unavailable at the employee’s former office, the current PRO must complete a National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) Optional Form 11, Reference Request - Federal Records Centers, with all available information. The employee’s name, Social Security number (SSN), known places of employment, names and PRO numbers of applicable PROs, and year(s) for which the records are requested must be included in the description and remarks section of the form. Contact the appropriate HRO. If the NPRC cannot locate the records, the PRO must prepare a memorandum to the appropriate HRO requesting copies of the SF 50, Notification of Personnel Action, or other related pay and/or leave information. Since there may have been consolidations of both the PRO and the appropriate HRO prior to the Defense Civilian Pay System (DCPS) consolidations, it is imperative that both offices work together to obtain information that will assist in the determination of pay and leave adjustments for the employee. Contact the Employee. If the PRO cannot locate documentation from the NPRC or the appropriate HRO, the PRO must contact the employee for the necessary documentation. If the employee has copies of the SF 50 and/or the Leave and Earnings Statement (LES), the PRO may accept this information and use it to reconstruct the pay and/or leave records. Contact OPM. If the transmittal letters to OPM and/or copies of the retirement records cannot be located, the PRO may submit a request to OPM in writing to procure the necessary copies of the records. The PRO may use the information on the retirement records for reconstruction of pay information for adjustments.

10.2    Reports

10.2.1. DoW civilian payroll systems must generate reports at regular intervals, as needed, or to meet special requirements. The PRO must support management by generating reports that provide the information needed to ensure the system's integrity. Individuals who create reports must correct errors caused by inaccurate reading or entry of data. Discrepancies in reporting, transmitting, or depositing funds must be resolved promptly. Per GAO-03-352G, Maintaining Effective Control Over Employee Time and Attendance Reporting, reports must be: prepared accurately, promptly, and distributed to the appropriate recipients to ensure receipt when the information will be of maximum benefit; based on, supported by, and periodically validated against appropriate detailed information in the payroll system; sent in a timely manner to officials who authorized, or were responsible for, processing payroll transactions, and reviewed by those officials for completeness and accuracy; discussed periodically with users and modified or eliminated as appropriate to meet user needs; and retained and disposed of in accordance with NARA General Records Schedule 2.0, Human Resources, which includes: NARA General Records Schedule 2.4, Employee Compensation and Benefits Records, and NARA General Records Schedule 2.5, Employee Separation Records, with sensitive data handled in accordance with the provisions of the Privacy Act. See 5 CFR Part 2606.

10.2.2. As-Required Reports

10.2.2.1. The losing PRO must prepare an SF 1150 at the time of the employee's separation if the employee transfers within DoW to another PRO or to another federal agency. All blocks on the SF 1150 must reflect accurate data. Besides transferred leave data, the form's Remarks section reports other employee information, including year-to-date wages for Social Security and Medicare tax purposes, year-to-date TSP deductions, the last deduction for FEHB and FEGLI, the date through which insurance deductions were made, and overseas or territorial differential data.

10.2.2.2. DFAS is responsible for:

10.2.2.2.1. DFAS must retain the employer's copy of the W-2c in the PRO.

10.2.2.2.2. DFAS must attach IRS Form 941-X, Adjusted Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return or Claim for Refund, to the current quarterly IRS Form 941, Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return, and enter the adjustment amount on the 941. The PRO must maintain copies of both forms.

10.2.2.2.3. DFAS must retain a copy of the W-2c and the Form 941-X in the current-year quarterly tax folder to balance annual federal tax deposits.

10.2.3. Biweekly Reports

10.2.3.1. The LES must show gross pay, deductions, net pay, and employer contributions for the current pay period and cumulative totals for the current year. The LES must reflect accrued and used leave balances for the pay period and year-to-date. The LES must be made available electronically through the DFAS myPay web application, or mailed to the employee's non-work address, every pay period.

10.2.3.2. To process RITS transactions, the PRO must provide the disbursing office with the payroll system-generated hardcopy of the payroll for personal services certification and summary, the SF 2812-A, and any disbursement vouchers for cash payments.

10.2.3.2.1. Cash payments received from employees, such as military deposits and health benefits payments, are current transactions, collected and disbursed from a holding account. The total of the payroll for personal services certification and summary plus cash disbursement vouchers must equal the total on the SF 2812-A. Cash collections for health benefit indebtedness from pay accounts not carried forward from former PROs must be reported to OPM separately on a supplemental SF 2812-A.

10.2.3.2.2. The disbursing office must ensure voucher amounts agree and the vouchers contain proper certifying signatures before authorizing transmission of the file to OPM. The delay between creating the system file and transmission is a necessary internal control for disbursing government funds. If the file is transmitted before the payment date, OPM must warehouse the data until the settlement date.

10.2.3.3. RITS can report on a regular biweekly basis and report adjustments in a supplemental off-cycle mode. Regular biweekly reporting is the preferred method, and the PRO must fully use the payroll system's automated capabilities to do so. Use of a supplemental reporting cycle must be limited to the greatest extent possible.

10.2.3.4. Adjustments for accounts not transferred to the consolidated PRO are accounts that were inactive on former PRO records and did not convert to the consolidated office. Responsibility for these adjustments now rests with the consolidated payroll operation under DFAS PRO operations. These adjustments may involve correcting a retirement plan, cash collection for military deposits, or health benefit indebtedness.

10.2.3.4.1. The PRO must report these retirement-plan correction adjustments to OPM on a hardcopy SF 2812-A citing the PRO number that originally reported the deductions and contributions. The PRO must prepare and forward to OPM corrected retirement records and registers citing the former PRO. The PRO must forward copies of the SF 2812-A, registers, and records to the departmental reporter for the former PRO so cumulative balances can be adjusted.

10.2.3.4.2. The PRO must report cash collections for military deposits on a hardcopy SF 2812-A citing the PRO number that originally reported the deductions and contributions. The PRO must prepare and forward to OPM corrected retirement records and registers citing the former PRO. The PRO must forward copies of the registers, records, and SF 2812-A to the departmental reporter for the former PRO so cumulative balances can be adjusted.

10.2.3.4.3. The consolidated PRO must report cash collections for health benefit indebtedness via RITS as a supplemental SF 2812-A using the consolidated PRO number.

10.2.3.5. Adjustments for accounts transferred to the consolidated PRO are accounts that were active on former PRO records and converted to the consolidated office. These adjustments may be for accounts that have become inactive since consolidation or that are still active. As part of the consolidated payroll operation, the DFAS PRO is responsible for these adjustments. Records for both the former and consolidated PROs may need correction, depending on the effective date of the correction.

10.2.3.5.1. The adjustment may involve both hardcopy reporting via the SF 2812-A and reporting via RITS. The PRO must report adjustments effective before the transfer to the consolidated office to OPM via the SF 2812-A, citing the former PRO number, and must prepare and forward to OPM corrected retirement records and registers for the portion applicable to the former PRO. The PRO must forward a copy of the SF 2812-A, registers, and records to the departmental reporter for the former PRO so cumulative balances can be adjusted. The PRO must correct the portion applicable to the consolidated PRO through the payroll system and report it via the RITS regular biweekly cycle. The PRO must correct adjustments for accounts that have become inactive since consolidation through the payroll system by reactivating the account.

10.2.3.5.2. The PRO must report cash collections for military deposits via RITS during the regular reporting cycle. The PRO must correct collections for accounts that have become inactive since consolidation through the payroll system by reactivating the account. Correction through the payroll system is necessary to maintain the proper sequencing of system-assigned register numbers.

10.2.3.5.3. The PRO must report cash collections for health benefit indebtedness via RITS during the regular biweekly reporting cycle.

10.2.3.6. The PRO must forward a biweekly report to each creditor agency of the collections made for the pay period. This report must include, at a minimum, the non-DoW agency to which the collections apply, the PRO name and address, the employee's name, the amount collected for each employee, the period the collection applies to, and the total collections remitted to the non-DoW agency.

10.2.3.7. The PRO must forward a biweekly report of employees with salary offsets for non-DoW federal agencies to the DFAS site that originally forwarded the salary offset request to the PRO. This report must include, at a minimum, the employee's name, SSN, creditor agency, amount of the last biweekly collection, pay date of the last collection, and the debt balance. For employees with more than one debt to a non-DoW federal agency, the PRO must provide this information for each debt.

10.2.3.8. Each pay period, the PRO must prepare a listing for each recipient of withheld union dues.
