15.2.6.1. The DoW Component responsible for reviewing and accepting recommended adjustments must retain adequate documentation to support any adjustment processed. Each completed adjustment file must include the preparer's identity, approval, and confirmation that the adjustment was posted.

15.2.7. All stakeholders must incorporate internal controls into their operations to maintain complete, consistent, and accurate data for contract files and related entitlement and accounting records throughout the life of the contract, as discussed in section 2.0.

15.3    STREAMLINED CONTRACT CLOSEOUT

15.3.1. Agencies and DoW Components must partner closely to identify potential contracts for closeout under the NDAA authority and must maintain a documented record of all contracts closed under that authority. The Deputy Chief Financial Officer policy memorandum, "National Defense Authorization Act Contract Closeout Authority (FPM 19-06)," dated May 14, 2019, contains procedural implementation guidance and is available on the Office of the Deputy Chief Financial Officer/Financial Management Policy and Reporting website under Dual Purpose Policy Memos & Other Information (Common Access Card-enabled).

15.3.2. After a contract is closed out by a negotiated settlement modification, the payment or accounting offices concerned must adjust and close any open finance and accounting records related to the contract.

title: Section 16.0: Junior Reserve Officer Training Corps (JROTC) Instructor Pay
content:
16.0    JUNIOR RESERVE OFFICER TRAINING CORPS (JROTC) INSTRUCTOR PAY

16.1    REIMBURSEMENT RESPONSIBILITIES

16.1.1. The host school pays JROTC instructors, and the sponsoring Military Service reimburses the school 50 percent of the MIP. JSIPS sets the MIP the Military Services use to reimburse the host school.

16.1.2. The Secretary of the Military Department concerned (or designee) may pay additional instructor funds to a school when funds are available and the Military Department determines, following periodic reviews, that the school is in an educationally and economically deprived area and that such action is in the national interest.

16.2    REIMBURSEMENT REQUIREMENTS AND PROCESS

16.2.1. The JIRO authorizes reimbursement to schools only for instructors certified as qualified by the cognizant Military Service, for whom the Military Service has authorized funding, and who fill positions authorized by the Military Service.

16.2.2. School Reimbursement Process

16.2.2.1. The reimbursement to the school generally equals 50 percent of an instructor's MIP. The Secretary of the Military Department concerned may pay the school more than 50 percent of the amount the school paid the member if the needs criteria in paragraph 16.1.2 are met, as prescribed in 10 U.S.C. § 2031(d)(2). The JIRO must ensure documentation supporting these reimbursements is retained per Volume 1, section 9.0, is readily available to support future audits, and is of sufficient quality for an independent third party, such as an outside auditor, to understand and verify the basis of the reimbursement.

16.2.2.2. Schools must provide banking information through the System for Award Management when new to the JROTC program or when previously provided banking information changes.

16.3    JROTC UNIT ESTABLISHMENT AT SCHOOLS

16.3.1. An authenticated copy of the countersigned contract between a school and the Military Service must be provided to the JIRO to verify and document that schools requesting payment are active JROTC program participants.

16.3.2. Authorized officials occupying the positions stated in the contract between a school and the Military Service must supply the current address of the school employing each instructor.

16.4    JIRO

16.4.1. The school is the employing organization and pays the full amount due the JROTC instructor, not less than the MIP. Each JROTC instructor negotiates his or her own contract with the school. The Military Service JIRO authorizes reimbursement to the school for up to 12 months per academic year, only while the instructor is under a valid contract and receiving a salary at or above the MIP. Reimbursement generally equals 50 percent of an instructor's MIP (see subparagraph 16.2.2.1).

16.4.2. Each school must forward a copy of the DD 2767 to the JIRO within 30 days of the instructor's employment. Reimbursements for that instructor are withheld until the JIRO receives the form.

16.4.2.1. Each school must submit a DD 2767 annually for JROTC instructors continuing employment at the school in the upcoming academic year.

16.4.2.2. The form must be received before the end date of an instructor's current contract to ensure uninterrupted reimbursement.

16.4.2.3. Schools are reimbursed only when a current form is on file at the JIRO.

16.5    SEPARATIONS, TRANSFERS, DECERTIFICATIONS, AND
DISESTABLISHMENTS

16.5.1. Each employing school must forward a DD 2767, or termination letter, containing the applicable date to the JIRO immediately upon the separation or death of an instructor. An instructor separates when he or she resigns the position at a specific school. If the JIRO does not receive timely notification, the JIRO must adjust future reimbursement to the school to reflect the actual period the instructor performed JROTC instructor duties and to collect any over- reimbursement.

16.5.2. An instructor transfers by resigning the position at one school and accepting a position at another. Transfers must be processed as a separation from one school and a new hire at another. Both the losing and gaining schools must forward a DD 2767 to the JIRO. The instructor must immediately forward an updated DD 2754 to the JIRO. Locality pay is adjusted per the JSIPS locality table for the new school. The pay scale for relocations and transfers is based solely on grade and highest academic degree held. Relocation assistance allowance may be available for JROTC instructors who relocate to fill hard-to-fill locations per 10 U.S.C. § 2031(e)(1).

16.5.3. A Military Service may, for cause, decertify a JROTC instructor for employment eligibility. The IMD must immediately notify the JIRO of decertified instructors currently under contract with a school. The JIRO must adjust future reimbursement to the school to reflect the actual period the instructor performed JROTC instructor duties and collect any over- reimbursement.

16.5.4. A JROTC unit is normally disestablished when the Military Service determines the unit will not meet its standards or cannot maintain the statutory minimum student enrollment. Disestablishment voids the contract between the Military Service and the school and terminates instructor pay reimbursements; the JIRO must authorize final reimbursement to, or initiate collection action from, the school.

16.6    FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT

16.6.1. Each Military Service holds and manages its JROTC funds. The JIRO concerned must authorize and assign the funds to the proper line of accounting and verify the accuracy of each JROTC instructor's pay computation and associated reimbursement amount for each school before disbursement by the designated paying office. The JIRO also monitors budget execution throughout the instructor's assignment.

16.6.2. Based on JIRO authorization and verification of fund availability, military pay operations certifying officers must certify payment and submit the certification to the designated paying office for all school disbursements. Certifying officers must be appointed per Volume 5,
section 5.0. Reimbursement to DoDDS must be made via a separate IPAC transfer citing the applicable appropriation provided for DoDDS.

16.6.3. Reimbursement to the school must be made only after the JIRO concerned has verified the payroll data, authorized fund availability, and received concurrence from the appropriate accounting office, and after military pay operations has provided certification. The DFAS designated paying office disburses funds for school reimbursements based on an SF 1034, Public Voucher for Purchases and Services Other Than Personal, for each Military Service payment to the school districts. Funds must be sent via EFT to the school's financial institution, except reimbursements to DoDDS schools, which are transferred via the IPAC system.

16.7    IDENTIFICATION AND COLLECTION OF JROTC-RELATED DEBTS

16.7.1. The JIRO must identify debts. A debt accrues when a school or school district is over-reimbursed for an instructor's pay, such as when an instructor transfers to another school, separates from the instructor program, or dies, or when a contract ending date is changed to shorten the contract period.

16.7.2. Debt Collection Process

16.7.2.1. A debt is collected by a fully documented adjustment to the school's reimbursement for the next calendar month, with one exception: when a debt is owed by a school that no longer has JROTC instructors and is not due further reimbursements, collection action must follow Volume 16, section 5.0.

16.7.2.2. When a school has no future reimbursement to adjust or offset, the JIRO must initiate collection action directly from the school through a demand letter. See Volume 16,
section 5.0 for policy requirements and guidance. Amounts collected must be forwarded to the JIRO as the debt collection office.

16.7.2.3. After the JIRO completes all related actions specified in Volume 16,
section 5.0, uncollected debts 90 days delinquent must be referred to the DFAS Debt Management Office, which refers debts delinquent over 120 days to the Bureau of the Fiscal Service for further collection action, as prescribed in 31 U.S.C. § 3716(c)(6)(A).

title: Section 17.0: Payment Recovery Audits
content:
17.0    PAYMENT RECOVERY AUDITS

17.1    GENERAL

17.1.1. All programs or activities, as defined by OMB Circular A-123, Appendix C, with annual payments exceeding $1 million must implement and use a cost-effective recovery audit and activities program to recover improper payments. Recovery audit requirements apply to all payment types except intra-governmental transactions.

17.2    DOW RECOVERY AUDIT AND ACTIVITIES PROGRAM
17.2.1. Applicability

17.2.1.1. If a Component concludes that implementing this review for a program or activity is not cost-effective, it must submit a quantitative justification to OUSD(C)/ODCFO/FMPR for approval.

17.2.1.2. When determining the cost-effectiveness of recovery audit contingency contracts, any DFAS resources used to assist the recovery audit contractor must be considered, including the cost of providing government records, researching claims, and recovering amounts due the government. See OMB Circular A-123, Appendix C, for cost-effectiveness criteria for a recovery audit and activities program.

17.2.1.3. Recovery audits must be implemented to ensure the greatest financial benefit to the Component. In most cases, combining payment recovery activities, predominantly internal controls, yields the most cost-effective results. Recovery audit and activities, coupled with the financial management roles and responsibilities for all PIIA-established programs, ensures timely overpayment corrective actions and streamlined recoupment.

17.2.1.4. Components must report the results of their recovery audit and activities program per section 17.3 and OMB Circular A-136, Financial Reporting Requirements.

17.2.2. Annual Plan Submission

17.2.2.1. Components expending $1 million or more annually for each program and activity must reassess their annual recovery audit plan to determine its validity and provide any updates or improvements no later than August 31 of each year, for use during the upcoming fiscal year (FY), to: OUSD(C)/ODCFO/FMPR, 1100 Defense Pentagon, Suite 3D150, Washington, DC 20301-1100.

17.2.2.2. At a minimum, this plan must include a cost-effectiveness analysis; the estimated total dollar amount of payments by program or activity for the current FY; any collection/recovery audits and/or risk mitigation activities the Component plans to use beyond its current DoW recovery audit and activities program; the dollar amount of payments the Component plans to review using these additional activities or audits; what entity will perform the recovery audits (internal, external, or contractor resources); the proposed methodology; and the period of review.

17.2.2.3. If the Component head determines that recovery audit activities are not cost-effective for certain categories of disbursements (see paragraph 17.4.2), this plan must include the quantitative justification.

17.2.3. Annual recovery targets must be set for each established recovery audit and activities program. DoW must establish annual targets for each Department-established PIIA program (Civilian Pay, Military Pay for each Branch, Commercial Pay, Travel Pay, Retired and Annuitant). Targets must be based on the rate of recovery (improper contract overpayments recovered divided by improper contract overpayments identified) and set to show an increase in recoveries over time. Each Component must provide its annual recovery targets to OUSD(C)/ODCFO/FMPR for review and approval (see paragraph 17.2.2). OUSD(C)/ODCFO/FMPR then submits targets to OMB for review as part of the annual approval of Agency Financial Reports (AFR) and Performance and Accountability Reports (PAR), with the OMB Annual PIIA Tables and Data call submission.

17.3    REQUIRED REPORTING

17.3.1. Components must report annually on their recovery audit and activities programs. Components must consult with DFAS Enterprise Audit Support & Compliance to ensure proper coverage of improper payments and payment recovery actions and to prevent duplicate reporting. Components must inform OUSD(C)/ODCFO/FMPR of any suspension or limitation in Component monitoring or oversight activities. To meet the AFR reporting schedule, this reporting is due no later than the dates established in the annual Consolidated DoW Recovery Audit and Activities Program Plan.

17.3.2. OMB Circular A-136 Required Reporting

17.3.2.1. DoW must report per the annual update to OMB Circular A-136, Financial Reporting Requirements. The AFR or PAR must address actions taken on auditor recovery recommendations and fraud reduction reporting; instances of potential fraud discovered through recovery audit activities must be reported per Volume 5, section 6.0.

17.4    SCOPE OF DOW RECOVERY AUDIT ACTIVITIES

17.4.1. All programs and activities expending $1 million or more annually, including grant, benefit, loan, and contract programs, must be considered for recovery audits. All classes of contracts and contract payments, and all other payment types (excluding intra-governmental transactions), must be considered for recovery audit activities. Components that disburse payments must review payment categories, identify those with higher potential for recoverable payment errors to ensure the greatest financial benefit to the government, and determine the overall cost-effectiveness of recovery audits.

17.4.2. Agencies may exclude payments from certain programs from recovery audit activities if the agency determines recovery audits are not cost-effective for identifying and recovering overpayments, or if other mechanisms to identify and recover overpayments are already in place. If an agency excludes a class of payments or contracts from payment recovery activities or audits, its annual plan and annual report must include the justification (see paragraphs 17.3 and 17.4).

17.4.3. Beyond identifying and documenting specific overpayments resulting from payment errors, any entity performing recovery audits must analyze why the payment errors occurred and, where appropriate, recommend cost-effective controls to prevent such overpayments. These results must be presented to management regularly. The Component should consider the analysis and related recommendations as part of its management improvement program. The Component must provide such information to DFAS, the DoDIG, and, where applicable, the Inspector General (IG) of the Military Service.

17.5    ROLE AND RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE DOW COMPTROLLER’S OFFICE

17.5.1. To facilitate compliance with OMB Circular A-123, Appendix C, the ODCFO assigned reporting responsibility for this function to the OUSD(C), FMPR Directorate. This function is part of OUSD(C) oversight responsibility for DoW's annual recovery audit reporting in the AFR.

17.5.2. The Comptroller's FMPR Directorate must serve as the Executive Agent (EA) for the DoW Payment Integrity program; provide oversight to the DoW Components to ensure compliance with the PIIA and/or OMB Circular A-123, Appendix C, requirements; review the Components' annual recovery audit plan submissions for completeness; review the annual submission of recovery audit reports to ensure the reporting requirements are met; prepare and submit Department-wide recovery audit results and mandatory reports as described in OMB guidance, and any related information, for submission to OMB, publication in the AFR, and other required reporting; and prepare the Department-wide recovery audit and activities plan reassessment, based on pertinent overpayment recovery methods or improvements identified by the Components during the FY, for submission to the DoDIG.

17.6    ROLE AND AUTHORITY OF THE OFFICE OF THE IG

17.6.1. Nothing in this policy may be construed to impair the authority of an IG under the Inspector General Act of 1978, as amended, or any other law. However, because the recovery audit program required by this policy is an integral part of Components' internal control over payments, and therefore a management function, independence considerations normally preclude the IG and other Component external auditors from carrying it out.

17.7    SOURCES TO PERFORM RECOVERY AUDITS

Recovery audits may be performed by Component employees, by any other Component, department, or agency of the U.S. Government acting on behalf of the Component, by private- sector contractors performing recovery audit services under contracts awarded by the Component, or by any combination of these options.

17.8    RECOVERY AUDIT SERVICES PERFORMED BY CONTRACTORS

17.8.1. When Components determine that using external post-payment recovery audit contractors (a recovery audit contingency contract) is the most cost-effective plan, they must update their recovery audit plan with the detailed cost-effectiveness breakdown, including the contract terms, and submit it to OUSD(C) FMPR for approval before executing the contract. These private-sector firms may, with the consent of the employing Component, communicate with the Component's contractors to verify potential payment errors they have identified. To avoid confusion with established accounts receivable and debt management processes, Components must coordinate with the DFAS, Enterprise Solutions and Standards, Accounts Receivable Office (JJA) at 8899 East 56th Street, Indianapolis, IN 46249 to determine whether direct communication with the Component's contractors is authorized.

17.8.2. Component contracts for private-sector recovery audit services are limited to contingency contracts that pay the contractor a negotiated percentage of the total amount collected by the United States for valid claims of overpayment. However, certain recovered payments may not be available to pay recovery audit costs (for instance, amounts recovered from interim improper payments under ongoing contracts if still needed to make subsequent payments under the contract, or amounts recovered from closed accounts). Components may allow contracted recovery auditors to establish a presence on, or visit, the property, premises, or offices of any subject of recovery audits.

17.8.3. The recovery audit contractor may, with the consent of the contracting Component, notify entities (including individuals) of potential overpayments made to those entities, respond to questions concerning potential overpayments, and take other administrative actions on overpayment claims made, or to be made, by the Component.

17.8.4. Beyond provisions describing the scope of recovery audits (and any other provisions required by law, regulation, or Component policy), any contract with a private-sector firm for recovery audit services must include provisions that prohibit the recovery audit contractor from having the authority to make a final determination on whether any overpayment occurred or whether to compromise, settle, or terminate an overpayment claim; requiring production of any additional records or information from the Component's contractors; using or sharing sensitive financial information not officially released for use by the general public, except for an authorized purpose of fulfilling the recovery audit contract; and disclosing any information that identifies an individual, or could reasonably be used to identify an individual, for any purpose other than as authorized for fulfilling its responsibilities under the payment recapture audit contract.

17.8.5. Components must require the recovery audit contractor to safeguard the confidentiality of sensitive financial information that has not been released for use by the general public and any information that could be used to identify a person.

17.8.6. At a minimum, each contract for recovery audit services must require the contractor to, at least quarterly, provide reports to the DoW disbursing Component on the root cause conditions causing identified overpayments and recommendations to mitigate such conditions; notify the DoW disbursing Component of any identified overpayments pertaining to any Component beyond the scope of the contracts; and report potential instances of fraud immediately to the DoW disbursing Component for which it is performing the contract.

17.9    RECOVERY AUDIT COLLECTION ACTIVITY

Actual collection activity must be carried out by federal employees, or nonfederal entities expending federal awards, as appropriate. However, Components or nonfederal entities may use another private-sector entity, such as a private collection agency, to perform this function if permitted by the applicable laws and regulations governing collection of amounts owed to the Federal Government.

17.10    DISPOSITION OF AMOUNTS RECOVERED

17.10.1. Contingency fee contracts must preclude any payment to the contractor performing recovery audit services until the Component actually collects the recoveries.

17.10.2. All funds collected, and all direct expenses incurred, as part of the recovery audit and activities program must be accounted for specifically. The identity of all funds recovered must be maintained to facilitate crediting recovered funds to the correct appropriations, to identify applicable time limitations on the appropriated funds recovered, and to allow required reporting per OMB Circular A-136.

17.10.3. Overpayments identified by a recovery auditor, but subsequently determined not to be collectable or not to be improper, are not considered "collected" for the disposition purposes outlined in this section.

title: Section 18.0: Purchase Card Payments
content:
18.0    PURCHASE CARD PAYMENTS

18.1    GENERAL

18.1.1. Authoritative Guidance *

18.1.1.1. The Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment (OUSD(A&S)) and the DoW Component Program Managers (CPM) oversee the purchase card program, including policy formulation and procedural guidance. The Defense Contract Management Agency participates in operational oversight of the purchase card program DoW Components administer.

18.2    PURCHASE CARD POLICY

18.2.1. Overview

18.2.1.1. A purchase card charge authorizes the card-issuing bank to pay the merchant or contractor consistent with the GSA master contract and this Regulation. An authorized purchase satisfies a bona fide need at a fair and reasonable price and meets all legal and regulatory requirements. Individuals responsible for purchase card violations (abuse, delinquency, internal fraud, or misuse) are subject to administrative and disciplinary actions per DoW GPC Policy and Component personnel policies and procedures.

18.2.1.2. Purchase card open market transactions are limited to the applicable micro-purchase thresholds prescribed by FAR 2.101, 10 U.S.C. § 3573, and DFARS PGI 213.201(g). See DoW GPC Policy for current DoW micro-purchase thresholds. Any increase to a cardholder's delegated authority requires issuance and acceptance of a new Government Purchase Card Delegation of Procurement Authority Letter.

18.2.2. Per 10 U.S.C. § 4754(b)(14)-(15), the purchase card program is subject to periodic audits by the DoW Inspector General and the Military Services' audit agencies to determine compliance with agency policy.

18.2.3. Purchase Card Accountable Officials

18.2.3.1. Within DoW, purchase card accountable officials are military members or civilian employees appointed in writing as cardholders, approving/billing officials, and certifying officers. Such appointments, made per Volume 5, section 5.0 (10 U.S.C. § 2773a and 31 U.S.C. § 3528), establish pecuniary liability under the law governing accountable officials, other than those potentially liable under 10 U.S.C. § 4754(c). Accountable officials must provide information, data, or services to certifying or disbursing officers in support of the payment process and must attest to the accuracy of information and data supporting payment to the card-issuing bank. DoW purchase card program accountable officials must be appointed within the Joint Appointment Module (JAM) of the Procurement Integrated Enterprise Environment (PIEE). JAM-issued certifying officer appointments satisfy the DD Form 577, Appointment/Termination Record-Authorized Signature, appointment and distribution requirements of Volume 5, section
5.0. If an Electronic Data Interchange-enabled invoice is rejected and converted to a manual payment, the JAM-rendered DD Form 577 validates the certifying officer's appointment.

18.2.3.2. Foreign national employees cannot serve as purchase card certifying officers or accountable officials unless they are direct hire employees of the United States Government. Before making such appointments, commanders must consider the potential consequences when Status of Forces Agreements or other treaties do not subject direct hire local nationals to the same pecuniary liability or disciplinary actions as other DoW employees. If such appointments are necessary, commanders must consider other management controls to compensate for the lack of pecuniary liability. Refer to Volume 5, section 1.0 for policy on accountable officials and foreign national personnel.

18.2.4. Per 31 U.S.C. § 3325, the head of an executive agency may delegate the authority to assign personnel to perform purchase card invoicing, reviewing, approving, and certifying responsibilities at the accountable official level. When authority is delegated, DoW Components must:

18.2.4.1. Designate each billing office, approving/billing official, and certifying officer within the Component's activities to receive the official purchase card billing statements; and

18.2.4.2. Delegate the authority to certify official purchase card billing statements per Volume 5, sections 1.0 and 5.0.

18.2.5. Purchase Card Refunds and Credits

18.2.5.1. The terms "rebate" and "refund" are used interchangeably throughout the CFR, OMB guidance, existing legislation, and this section. Purchase card billing statement payments must occur as soon as administratively possible when the refund offered exceeds the cost of funds as defined in 5 C.F.R. § 1315.8. DoW takes advantage of refund offers only when economically justified and advantageous to DoW, and follows the guidelines for taking discounts and refunds/rebates in 5 C.F.R. § 1315.8, FAR 32.906(e), and OMB Circular A-123, Appendix B,
Section 7. Billing statements are paid for the amount certified. See section 3.0 for additional refund/rebate policy.

18.2.5.2. Refunds attributable to purchase card use may be credited to operation and maintenance and research, development, test and evaluation accounts of DoW that are current when the refunds are received (see the statutory note "Crediting of Refunds" within 10 U.S.C. § 4754). Per OMB Circular A-123, Appendix B, Section 7, rebates/refunds can be used for any legitimate purchase by the appropriation or account to which they were returned, or as otherwise authorized by statute. Transaction credits - funds sent back to DoW from the contracted bank from returned items, billing errors, overpayments, duplicate payments, or erroneous payments - must be credited to the original appropriation from which they were disbursed. See the Guidebook, Chapter 9, for DoW GPC refund validation requirements.

18.2.6. If an account number is compromised, or a card is lost or stolen, the cardholder must notify the approving/billing official, certifying officer, agency/organization program coordinator (A/OPC), and the card-issuing bank to close the account immediately.

18.3    INTERNAL CONTROLS

18.3.1. All DoW Component purchase card program policies, implementing procedures, and enterprise risk management programs must include internal controls to prevent, detect, and report improper purchase card transactions. Refer to DoW GPC Policy and OMB Circular A-123, Appendix B, section 2.4.1 and Attachment 6, for terminology and definitions of improper or incorrect purchase card transactions.

18.3.2. Managers at all levels must maintain effective internal controls within the purchase card program and ensure adequate separation of duties of participants under their control. The management accountability and internal control requirements prescribed by DoW GPC Policy, and those in sections 1.0 and 8.0, apply to the operation of a DoW Component purchase card program.

18.3.3. Cardholder, approving/billing official, certifying officer, A/OPC, and Resource Manager (RM)/Financial Manager (FM) access to government and the card-issuing bank's purchase card data and processing systems must be limited to that necessary to accomplish required tasks while maintaining proper separation of duties. Refer to DoW GPC Policy for specific requirements when such personnel transfer to other duties or depart from the organization.

18.3.4. Commanders and supervisors at all levels must ensure compliance with this section and DoW GPC Policy. Military and civilian personnel who violate this section or DoW GPC Policy are subject to administrative and disciplinary action. When an official directs a cardholder to purchase items or services later determined to be violations, that official may be subject to personal financial liability and disciplinary action per OMB Circular A-123, Appendix B, Section 3, sections 2.5 and 2.10. See DoW GPC Policy for disciplinary action policies and requirements within the Government Charge Card Program.

18.3.5. Per 10 U.S.C. § 4754(b)(7), this Regulation, records management policies, and DoW GPC Policy, documentation must be maintained at all levels to support purchase card program integrity and facilitate reconciliation and payment of purchase card transactions.

18.3.5.1. Cardholders must establish clear audit trails for purchase card transactions by maintaining a purchase log with an entry containing all fields required in DoW GPC Policy for each purchase requirement, and by maintaining transaction supporting documentation in the card-issuing bank's Electronic Access System. This makes cardholder billing statements, purchase log entries, and supporting documentation available to the approving/billing official and certifying officer, fulfills electronic GPC disbursing office record retention requirements, and supports auditability.

18.3.5.2. On termination of a cardholder or approving/billing official account, management must ensure safeguards are in place to meet retention requirements.

18.3.5.3. Per the Guidebook, PIEE/JAM is the mandatory enterprise tool for issuing and retaining GPC program appointments.

18.3.5.4. The minimum supporting documentation for the DoW GPC program is account billing statements, cardholder purchase log, request to purchase or request for payment, verification of availability of funds as defined by the DoW Component's policy, proof of acceptance, vendor invoice, receipts, or order confirmations, approval documentation, cross references to any related contract, delivery or task order, or purchase order, and supporting documentation for any credit received (e.g., items returned).

18.4    RESPONSIBILITIES

18.4.1. Reconciliation and account certification of Statements of Account received from the card-issuing bank is a coordinated responsibility among the cardholder, approving/billing official, and certifying officer. Every individual involved in the purchase card process must report suspected purchase card non-compliances, improper transactions, or violations through the proper chain of command and per component policies (refer to DoW GPC Policy for definitions of these transactions). They must also complete required initial and refresher training per DoW GPC Policy, Component policy, and Volume 5, section 5.0, and comply with the additional responsibilities for contingency operations and contracting events in the Guidebook, Appendix A.

18.4.1.1. Commanders and supervisors at all levels have the authority and responsibility to ensure military and civilian personnel under their supervision use purchase cards only as authorized. They must address purchase card non-compliances, improper transactions, and violations.

18.4.2. The Heads of DoW Components (or their designees) may delegate their authority in writing to appoint cardholders, approving/billing officials, A/OPCs, component program managers (CPMs), and certifying officers (see Volume 5, section 5.0 for additional policy on appointments). Heads of DoW Components must also manage commanders, directors, or other designated officials and their delegated authority for performing their duties and responsibilities per DoW GPC Policy.

18.4.3. The CPM serves as the Service's or Agency's functional representative with the Program Management Office and must develop and maintain hierarchies, ensure subordinate CPMs and A/OPCs perform their functions and roles, and interface with DoW-level program offices on card-issuing bank performance issues per DoW GPC Policy.

18.4.4. A/OPCs serve as the Agency's functional representatives and, as identified in DoW GPC Policy, are appointed with responsibility for the management, administration, day-to-day operation, and integrity of the purchase card program. The A/OPC works jointly with the RM/FM to set and maintain cardholder spending limits based on estimated purchase requirements for the period or a budgetary limit. The A/OPC may also assist the RM/FM in providing guidance to the cardholder on any legal or regulatory restrictions on the funds provided.

18.4.5. Commanding Officer or Director

18.4.5.1. The military officer in command or the civilian director in charge of an activity has overall responsibility for implementing this section's purchase card financial management policies. They have disciplinary authority over cardholders and approving/billing/certifying officials and must investigate all allegations of purchase card violations. They must establish activity procedures permitting rapid investigation and resolution of purchase card violations, convene or order an investigation per Volume 5, section 6.0, and take all appropriate actions resulting from each investigation.

18.4.5.2. When the Head of the DoW Component has delegated authority, the commanding officer or director must appoint accountable officials per Volume 5, section 5.0.

18.4.6. The review official is an individual the commanding officer or director may appoint to perform pre- and/or post-payment reviews and other duties per Volume 5, section 5.0. The A/OPC may not be appointed as the review official.

18.4.7. The certifying officer is responsible for the accuracy of payments, including designation of the proper appropriation(s) or other funds, certified to the disbursing office and disbursing officer. The certifying officer is liable for any illegal, improper, or erroneous payment processed by DoW resulting from an inaccurate or misleading certification. The certifying officer's appointment must meet the minimum qualifications and eligibility requirements in Volume 5, section 5.0. The certifying officer and approving/billing official duties may be performed by the same appointed person, as discussed in Volume 5, section 2.0. See Figures 23 - 1 and 23-2 for the monthly review checklist and certification statements. Purchase card certifying officers' responsibilities, identified in Volume 5, section 5.0 and DoW GPC Policy, include but are not limited to:

18.4.7.1. Ensure transactions meet the legal requirements for authorized purchase card purchases.

18.4.7.2. Ensure adequate documentation is available for individual transactions and cardholders have reconciled all transactions with purchase log entries.

18.4.7.3. Ensure the facts presented in documents for payment are complete and accurate, including designation of the proper appropriation(s) or other funds.

18.4.7.4. Verify the accuracy of computation of a voucher before certification.

18.4.7.5. Ensure internal controls exist to prevent submission of duplicate invoices for the same transaction.

18.4.7.6. Ensure all items and services have been received and procedures are in place to dispute, within the designated dispute timeline, transactions for items or services not received by the next billing cycle.

18.4.7.7. Ensure the cardholder is familiar with the servicing bank's dispute process and implement dispute procedures when warranted. Refer to subparagraph 18.5.3.4 on disputed transactions.

18.4.7.8. Ensure the cardholder billing statement and all original supporting documentation (receipts, logs, invoices, delivery orders, and approvals) is retained to comply with record retention requirements. This retention must capture and leverage the origination of electronic data in automated systems so it may be shared across DoW platforms.

18.4.8. The approving/billing official is the individual, appointed by the commanding officer, director, or designee, with oversight responsibility for cardholders to ensure all purchase card transactions are necessary and for official government purposes only.

18.4.8.1. Approving/billing officials must provide information and data to certifying or disbursing officers in support of the payment process and must attest to the accuracy of information and data provided to a purchase card certifying officer in support of a payment to the card-issuing bank. They are accountable and may be held pecuniarily liable for erroneous payments resulting from inaccurate information and data, including designation of the proper appropriation(s) or other funds, provided to a purchase card certifying officer, if the erroneous payment results from negligence in performing assigned duties.

18.4.8.2. The approving/billing official must review each cardholder's billing statement monthly to verify the cardholder was authorized to purchase the items, the government received the items, and all accountable property (including pilferable items as defined by the DoW Component) has been properly recorded on government property accountability records per component property accountability policy and DoDI 5000.64, "Accountability and Management of DoW Equipment and Other Accountable Property." The capitalization threshold and accountability requirements for property, plant, and equipment purchased are in Volume 4, sections 24.0-28.0. Each approving/billing official must have a reasonable span of control over cardholders per DoW GPC Policy. The approving/billing official's responsibilities in DoW GPC Policy include but are not limited to:

18.4.8.2.1. Coordinate purchase card limits and MCC exclusions with the RM/FM and A/OPC for cardholders under their purview.

18.4.8.2.2. Ensure each cardholder fulfills the responsibilities identified in DoW GPC Policy.

18.4.8.2.3. Review and reconcile the cardholder's billing statements and approve the statement when the cardholder cannot perform this function. The approving/billing official and certifying officer may use the purchase card checklist (Figure 18-1 in the Procedures Supplement) to document due diligence in billing statement reviews.

18.4.8.2.4. Verify all transactions are legal, proper, and mission essential per the FAR, DFARS, and DoW policies and regulations.

18.4.8.2.5. Ensure monthly Statement of Account accuracy and forward it with all original supporting documentation (receipts, logs, invoices, delivery orders, and approvals) to the certifying officer.

18.4.8.2.6. Resolve any questionable purchases with the cardholder.

18.4.8.2.7. Notify the A/OPC of any personnel changes that may require cardholder or managing account closure.

18.4.8.2.8. Notify the A/OPC and certifying officer (if not the approving/billing official) of any planned approving/billing official reassignment to other duties or departure from the installation or activity.

18.4.8.2.9. Notify the A/OPC and certifying officer (if not the approving/billing official) of any lost or stolen cards, in addition to the cardholder notifying the card-issuing bank.

18.4.8.2.10. Complete service and agency-specific training.

18.4.9. Authorized Cardholder

18.4.9.1. A cardholder must ensure funds are available before making the purchase.

18.4.9.2. A cardholder must review the monthly cardholder Statement of Account as described in paragraph 5.2.

18.4.9.3. A cardholder who uses the card to make unauthorized transactions may be liable for any illegal, improper, or erroneous payment resulting from those transactions and may be subject to pecuniary liability (including reimbursing the Government for unauthorized or erroneous purchases through salary offset) or appropriate adverse personnel actions.

18.4.9.4. If an erroneous charge is not disputed timely, the cardholder may also be held accountable.

18.4.10. The convenience check account holder is a military member or civilian employee appointed as prescribed in DoW GPC Policy. In addition to the authorized cardholder responsibilities in subparagraph 18.4.9, the account holder must order, receive, store, safeguard, inventory, reconcile, and dispose of check stock. Convenience check account financial management policy is in paragraph 18.6. The account holder must complete tax reporting for the convenience checks they issue and obtain a signed IRS Form W-9, Request for Taxpayer Identification Number and Certification, so that an IRS Form 1099-MISC, Miscellaneous Information, can be issued to the convenience check payee. Reporting requirements are in subparagraph 18.6.2. The account holder must not perform the functions of approving/billing officials or certifying officers on the managing account for which they are a check writer. The commanding officer, director, or designee with oversight responsibility must cancel the convenience check privileges of cardholders who improperly use convenience checks.

18.4.11. The RM/FM is the individual designated by a component to record formal commitments and obligations in the accounting system. The RM/FM must establish commitments in advance in amounts no less than the periodic purchase limits authorized for commercial purchase cards or at the individual requirement level. The RM/FM, with the assigned A/OPC, establishes advance reservations of funds or commitments, which must be considered when setting office, managing account, or cardholder purchase limits. Policy for recording obligations for the transactions in this section is in Volume 3, section 8.0. RM/FM responsibilities for the purchase card program, referenced in DoW GPC Policy, include coordinating funding and spending limits with approving/billing officials and A/OPCs, including advice on legal or regulatory constraints on the use of funds; providing approving/billing officials and cardholders official notification of funding; assigning default and alternate lines of accounting (LOAs) and ensuring they are entered into the card-issuing bank's system for electronic invoicing, receipt, and processing; providing reallocation authority to cardholders and approving/billing officials when necessary; receiving and correcting invoice rejects with the certifying officer's assistance; assisting with resolving delinquent accounts and providing payment information when requested; and coordinating with responsible officials to ensure unrecorded purchases are recorded in the period they occur and the miscellaneous obligation is reversed timely as referenced in Volume 3, section 8.0.

18.4.12. Entitlement Office

18.4.12.1. The entitlement office must verify the amount certified for payment on the invoice matches the amount certified on the certified disbursement voucher.

18.4.12.2. The entitlement office must validate that sufficient funds have been obligated in the accounting records.

18.4.12.3. The entitlement office must notify the certifying officer and RM/FM within one business day of invoices rejected, including a detailed reason for the rejection. Upon resubmission of the rejected transactions, processing must include the Standard Document Number or contract number of the original transaction.

18.4.13. The disbursing office verifies the certifying officer's DD Form 577 is completed in the PIEE/JAM and disburses payments to the card-issuing bank. The disbursing office must not replicate the reconciliation process before making payment on certified purchase card billing statements. The disbursing office makes an advice of payment available to the bank. See Volume 5, section 9.0 for additional disbursing policy.

18.5    STATEMENT RECONCILIATION AND CERTIFICATION

18.5.1. The cardholder must ensure receipt and acceptance and properly document all purchases. Independent acceptance by an individual other than the cardholder is required for accountable property purchases and self-generated purchases (purchases lacking a documented request to purchase from someone other than the cardholder). Accountable property, as identified in DoDI 5000.64, includes sensitive, classified, and pilferable property-type items. Refer to the Guidebook for additional circumstances that may require independent acceptance and the use of the Wide Area Workflow module within the PIEE when the purchase card is used as a payment method against a contract.

18.5.1.1. Local procedures may specify additional circumstances (for example, based on cost) requiring evidence of acceptance by an individual other than the cardholder. The approving/billing official must verify acceptance documentation exists and may also physically verify acceptance. Recording, tracking, and management of pilferable, sensitive, high-valued, or otherwise accountable property obtained with the purchase card must be per component property accountability policy and DoDI 5000.64.

18.5.2. Cardholder Review

18.5.2.1. Each cardholder must reconcile the Statement of Account, ensure a purchase log entry exists for each transaction or purchase, and retain supporting documentation as specified in DoW GPC Policy to ensure accurate and timely payments. Cardholders must review their statements to identify discrepancies and, as appropriate, attempt to resolve the issues with the merchant or, per bank procedures, dispute the transactions or report the external fraud (see subparagraph 18.5.3.4).

18.5.2.1.1. Under the billing discrepancy provisions of the GSA master contract, the cardholder must report fraud to the card-issuing bank, the A/OPC, the commanding officer or director, and the local procurement fraud investigative authority for investigation and adjudication. The cardholder must also comply with the bank's fraud reporting procedures.

18.5.2.1.2. Known or suspected fraudulent transactions not authorized by the cardholder must not be approved for payment. If the bank does not remove the fraudulent transaction by the end of the billing cycle, the invoice must be manually processed, excluding the transactions in question, and then certified for payment. If the transaction has already been paid, the bank issues a transaction credit on the next billing statement per the SmartPay contract. Cardholders must identify in the system the reason transactions are deemed fraudulent and the date they were reported to the bank. The cardholder must attempt to review and reconcile all transactions during the billing cycle in which they occur so that fraudulent transactions are never included in the corresponding cardholder Statement of Account.

18.5.2.2. If the cardholder cannot resolve the discrepancy by obtaining a credit from the merchant, the cardholder must officially dispute the transaction with the card-issuing bank per subparagraph 18.5.3.4.

18.5.2.3. The cardholder must sign and date the Statement of Account (preferably electronically) and forward it, with the necessary supporting documentation, to the approving/billing official for action. Figure 18-2 in the Procedures Supplement contains the language for the cardholder's certification statement.

18.5.2.4. If the cardholder cannot review the Statement of Account upon receipt, the cardholder must make the Statement of Account and supporting documentation available to the approving/billing official or certifying officer for timely review.

18.5.3. The approving/billing official must review each transaction made by cardholders under their managing account to ensure all supporting documentation is available and correct. The approving/billing official must ensure cardholder reviews were completed properly; ensure billing discrepancies were resolved with the merchant, disputed, or reported as fraud as necessary; ensure acceptance and documentation of all accountable property; verify all transactions were necessary government purchases; and perform any other functions required by DoW GPC Policy and other component policies and procedures.

18.5.3.1. Under billing discrepancy provisions of the GSA master contract, known or suspected fraudulent transactions not authorized by the cardholder must not be certified for payment and must be reported to the card-issuing bank, A/OPC, commanding officer or director, and the local fraud investigative authority for investigation and adjudication. Refer to subparagraph 18.5.2.1.2 for additional guidance on the review and handling of fraudulent transactions. If the cardholder has not done so, the approving/billing official should ensure fraudulent transactions are disputed per applicable card-issuing bank procedures and reported as fraudulent per the card-issuing bank and component fraud reporting procedures.

18.5.3.2. The Government is contractually obligated to pay the card-issuing bank for all purchase card transactions made by an authorized cardholder other than those successfully disputed or resulting from external fraud. This includes transactions made by an authorized cardholder in violation of purchase card policies (for example, unauthorized or incorrect as defined by OMB Circular A-123, Appendix B, section 2.4.1). Report these purchase card violations to the A/OPC, appropriate authorities, and management officials for investigation and corrective action per component policies and procedures.

18.5.3.3. For transactions determined to be purchase card violations, the approving/billing official must authorize payment for any items that cannot be returned and pursue corrective action by reporting the matter to the A/OPC and management officials per Component policies and procedures.

18.5.3.4. For questionable transactions, the approving/billing official must determine as rapidly as possible whether there is potential fraud or the transaction is otherwise disputable. Lack of supporting documentation alone must not trigger a finding of fraud or impropriety unless the identity of the item or service, or other facts, would lead a reasonable person to believe the transaction was fraudulent or unauthorized. If the transaction is determined not to be external fraud or otherwise disputable, it must be approved for payment. The approving/billing official must continue to follow up to obtain documentation sufficient to show the transaction is no longer questionable. The follow-up should involve the cardholder, appropriate management, and bank officials, as necessary.

18.5.3.5. When the approving/billing official is appointed collaterally as the certifying officer, the official must also complete the requirements in subparagraph 18.5.4.1.

18.5.4. The certified billing statement is the official invoice for payment purposes.

18.5.4.1. The certifying officer must review and certify the billing statement (preferably electronic) and forward it to the designated entitlement or disbursing office for timely payment processing. Figure 18-2 in the Procedures Supplement contains the language for the certifying officer's certification statement. See Volume 5, section 5.0 for additional policy on certification requirements.

18.5.4.2. The certifying officer must not certify a known or suspected fraudulent transaction not authorized by the cardholder. The certifier must not certify payments for transactions generated by an unauthorized user, such as a merchant entering the wrong card number, or transactions occurring after the card or card number is reported lost or stolen. The certifying officer must follow agency procedures for addressing all fraudulent or abusive transactions or other purchase card misuse.

18.5.4.3. Under 31 U.S.C. § 3528, a certifying officer certifying a voucher (purchase card billing statement) is responsible for the information, computation, and legality of a proposed payment under the appropriation or fund. A certifying officer must ensure all transactions are legal, proper, correct, and satisfy a bona fide need per government policies, rules, and regulations. Because payments are made to the financial institution, the certifying officer must certify the legality and accuracy of the information on the amount owed the financial institution.

18.5.5. Per DoW GPC Policy, the DoW may certify invoices for payment of micro- purchases before verifying that all items billed have been received and accepted. As part of the monthly Statement of Account reconciliation, the cardholder must annotate instances of non- receipt of recently ordered goods or services on each statement. Each approving/billing official must establish a system and related procedures to flag and track all transactions certified for payment without verification of receipt and acceptance. These procedures must ensure receipt and acceptance of all transactions reconciled and approved for payment are verified no later than 45 days after the invoice date. If there is no documented evidence verifying receipt and acceptance after the 45-day period, the cardholder must protect the Government's rights by disputing the transaction. The cardholder must notify the bank of any item in dispute and has 90 calendar days from the date the transaction was processed or posted to the account. The cardholder must file a formal dispute.

18.5.6. The designated entitlement office must pay purchase card invoices (preferably electronic) upon receipt of the certified billing statement. The entitlement office must observe the prompt payment clock, which starts when the invoice is made available to the DoW on the card- issuing bank's website, not when invoices are transmitted to the entitlement office. The entitlement office must ensure only the amount certified for payment by the certifying officer is processed for payment.

18.5.7. A transaction dispute may occur when the Government questions the validity of a transaction on the cardholder Statement of Account. Transactions should be disputed only after all attempts have been made to resolve the issue directly with the merchant. Reasons to dispute a transaction include: the cardholder did not authorize the transaction, the amount is incorrect, the quality or service is unacceptable, the information is erroneous or duplicates an existing transaction, or the material was returned or service was cancelled and the merchant did not issue a credit within 30 days. The cardholder must dispute the transaction as soon as possible per the timetable and provisions in the tailored task orders with the card-issuing bank, the DoW GPC Policy, and local procedures.

18.5.7.1. For items billed but not received, the cardholder must contact the merchant to validate shipment. For non-shipment, items must be officially disputed only if the merchant fails to credit the account in the next billing cycle or the items are not ultimately received.

18.5.7.2. Approving/billing officials must monitor discrepancies between cardholder items billed and items received and accepted to ensure any remaining discrepancies are disputed.

18.5.7.3. Fraudulent transactions include those made on lost or stolen cards or compromised card numbers, or initiated by unauthorized third parties. They do not follow the dispute process and must be reported as fraudulent per the card-issuing bank fraud reporting procedures, DoW GPC Policy, and Component procedures.

18.5.8. To reduce transaction processing fees, DoW activities must summarize accounting data, where systems capabilities are available to prevent duplication of LOAs, before submitting certified billing statements and accounting data to the designated entitlement office. Specifically, DoW activities must "roll up" disbursing data by LOA to eliminate duplicate LOAs on one certified billing statement.

18.5.8.1. Approving/billing officials and certifying officers must ensure complete summarization of billing statements with no duplicate LOAs before certifying and submitting the billing statements for payment. The level of appropriation data summarization must be consistent with the advance reservation of funds and the data for entry into the accounts payable, disbursing, and accounting systems to maintain positive funds control, match each planned disbursement with a recorded obligation (as described in section 2.0 and Volume 3, section 8.0), and prevent unmatched disbursements.

18.6    CONVENIENCE CHECKS

18.6.1. Convenience check use must be minimized and designated as a purchase instrument of last resort. Checks must be used only if the merchant offering the goods or services does not accept or cannot process the purchase card, no other merchant can reasonably be located, and paying for the items by the traditional procurement method is not practical.

18.6.1.1. A discrete account must be set up to issue convenience checks. Convenience checks and normal purchase card accounts may be issued under a single managing account but must not be commingled. Transactions reported during the billing cycle for the convenience check and purchase card accounts appear on the cardholder's Statement of Account.

18.6.1.2. Each component must issue instructions on convenience check use. Individuals delegated as convenience check account holders must be appointed in writing. At a minimum, the appointment letter must state the check writer's specific duties, any limitations on the scope of authority (including dollar limitations), and an acknowledgement of the check writer's duties and responsibilities. Convenience checks must not be used for employee reimbursements, cash advances, cash awards, travel-related transportation payments, meals, or payroll or salary payments. Refer to DoW GPC Policy for additional convenience check requirements and restrictions on use.

18.6.2. IRS Form 1099 Requirements

18.6.2.1. The Defense Finance and Accounting Service (DFAS) has tax-form issuance and IRS reporting responsibilities for the DoW convenience check program.

18.6.2.2. DFAS obtains the universe of DoW convenience check payment data from the GSA contracted bank responsible for convenience check accounts and provides it to the applicable A/OPC, Account Manager, and Convenience Check Account Holder to determine the tax reporting requirements and complete specifically identified data not available to, or captured by, the contracted bank. The Convenience Check Account Holder must ensure the data is completed and returned to DFAS.

18.6.2.3. A/OPCs, Account Managers, and Convenience Check Account Holders that do not return the requested information to DFAS are responsible for their own tax-form issuance and IRS tax reporting.

18.6.3. Requests to establish a convenience check account must be justified in writing and per the provisions in DoW GPC Policy. A specific individual must be designated as the account holder responsible for that account via the proper application forms and delegation of authority letters. Those forms must be submitted through the DoW activity's existing purchase card hierarchical structure.

18.6.4. The authorized threshold for convenience checks is one half of the applicable micro-purchase threshold (41 U.S.C. § 1902, statutory notes). See DoW GPC Policy and FAR
2.101 for alternative thresholds for declared contingencies or emergency-type operations within or outside the United States. To maintain effective internal controls, approving/billing officials, payment review officials, and certifying officers must not perform the functions of convenience check custodian or cashier. Additional conditions on convenience check use are as follows:

18.6.4.1. Convenience checks must be issued for the exact payment amount. Purchases, payments, or other amounts must not be split among more than one check to keep amounts below the applicable micro-purchase threshold or other assigned limits.

18.6.4.2. Convenience checks must be used for official government purposes only.

18.6.4.3. Convenience checks must not be issued as an "exchange-for-cash" vehicle to establish cash funds.

18.6.4.4. If convenience checks are mailed to payees, local internal controls must be in place to avoid duplicate payments to them.

18.6.4.5. The issuing activity bears all administrative costs of convenience checks. Fees for convenience check use are specified in the GSA contract. At DoW Component election, the costs of purchasing convenience checks may be expressed as a (a) percentage, (b) number of basis points, or (c) fixed fee.

18.6.4.6. Convenience checks are negotiable instruments and must be treated like cash for security purposes. Local policies and procedures must safeguard against physical loss, theft, or potential forgery. Checks must be accounted for by recording transactions as they occur in the check register or purchase log to maintain control of number sequence.

18.6.5. The convenience check account holder must reconcile the Statement of Account against the holder's supporting documentation as part of the monthly billing cycle, per the standard purchase card payment practices in section 5.0.

18.6.5.1. Convenience check accounts and transactions must be reviewed per the Guidebook, which requires review and approval of each convenience check case (transaction) generated by the bank's data mining review tool; the tool identifies all convenience check transactions for review. Reviews must ensure each transaction was authorized, properly funded and approved, appropriate for Government use, does not exceed allowable limits, includes supporting documentation, and meets any other requirement of Component policies. Suspected violations must be reported to the appropriate management and investigative authorities per established policies (see DoW GPC Policy for terminology and definitions of the specific categories of unauthorized or inappropriate transactions).

18.6.5.2. The dispute process is not available for convenience checks. Any concerns over a purchase made with a check must be resolved directly with the merchant. The account holder is solely responsible for securing restitution or credit on disputed purchases.

18.6.6. The military officer in command or the civilian director in charge of an activity responsible for implementing the purchase card financial management policies of this section must ensure each convenience check account is reviewed annually by an individual other than the convenience check account holder. The review must validate compliance with DoW and component policies and procedures for physical security of checks; timely and accurate completion of IRS Form 1099 tax reporting requirements by DFAS mandated deadlines; completion and effectiveness of data mining case reviews of convenience check transactions, including review of transaction supporting documentation; and minimization of convenience check use.

title: Section 1.0: General
content:
1.0    GENERAL

1.1    Purpose

Volume 11 of the DoW Financial Management Regulation (FMR) provides guidance on reimbursement operations, including project orders and the assessment of fees for services provided by DoW Components. The authority for these reimbursable operations comes from the Office of the Under Secretary of War (Comptroller) and is authorized by U.S. law. It is important to note that this volume does not authorize sales to private parties or apply to user fees associated with the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) or the Privacy Act.

Additionally, Volume 11 establishes the primary financial management policy for the DoW Defense Working Capital Funds (DWCF). It outlines the foundational rules for all DWCF activities, covering their establishment, financing, operation, and overall lifecycle management. This includes policies for budgeting, cost accounting, revenue, and specific requirements for major activities like Supply Management and Depot Maintenance.

1.2    Authoritative Guidance

Refer to Volume 11 authoritative guidance document on the FMR webpage.

1.3    Definitions

Refer to Volume 11 definitions in the Glossary.

1.4    Procedures

Refer to the Volume 11 Supplemental for procedures, tables, figures and appendices throughout this volume and sections.

title: Section 2.0: Reimbursement Guidance
content:
2.0    REIMBURSEMENT GUIDANCE

2.1    General Guidance

2.1.1. A seller’s reimbursements are amounts earned and collected for materials sold or services furnished because of a reimbursable agreement. A seller’s reimbursable obligations are financed by offsetting collections. Components credit these offsetting collections to an expenditure account in payment for goods and services provided by that account. Credit the specific appropriation or fund account for the collection only when it is authorized by law. Refer to Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Circular A-11, Section 20 for further details.

2.1.2. The Treasury Financial Manual (TFM) provides the requirements for accounting, reporting, and reconciliation of Intra-governmental Transactions (IGTs).

2.1.3. The TFM provides the requirements for using G-Invoicing, a data exchange utility that facilitates the exchange of information between federal entities that includes lines of communication when sharing data and exchanging information on IGT Buy/Sell activity. It also serves as an agreement broker and mechanism by which federal entities arrange and negotiate the terms of the Interagency Agreement (IAA) electronically. All IGT Buy/Sell activity must have implemented G-Invoicing by October 1, 2025. Refer to the IPAC System Enforcement Control Timeline within the TFM, Volume 1, Part 2, Chapter 4700, for further details. Treasury requires G-Invoicing for recording and reporting on IGT Buy/Sell transactions unless other guidance (such as OMB policy) requires a completed agreement for certain IGT types, such as assisted acquisitions.

2.1.4. Non-Economy Act orders for intra-governmental work and services must be executed in accordance with the detailed guidance provided in Section 18 of this volume.

2.2    Disposition of Collections

2.2.1. Collections must be credited to the appropriation that procured the services or materiel being sold when specifically authorized by law as outlined in this volume. Statement of Federal Financial Accounting Standards (SFFAS) No.7

2.2.2. Collections for unfunded costs such as labor of military personnel, depreciation of capital assets and interest, must be deposited into the General Fund of the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts or by other DoW issuances.

2.2.3. Collections received after an appropriation cancels must be deposited in Treasury Account 3200, "Collections of Receivables from Canceled Accounts.” Refer to Volume 4.

2.2.4. Disposition of collections for FMS must be in accordance with Volume 15.

2.3    Billing Standard

2.3.1. The price to be charged for goods and/or services furnished by the Department depends on whether that good and/or service is provided to, or for the benefit of a DoW Component, a non-DoW federal agency, a private party, or FMS customer. Therefore, the ordering DoW Component activity that requisitions or orders a good or service must inform the performing DoW activity of the identity of the intended recipient for the requisitioned goods or services. Volume 4 requires that the ordering activity must review all charges from the performing activity to ensure that amounts due agree with the reimbursable order and are supported with a copy of the order or contract and evidence of performance.

2.3.2. DoW Components performing work or services on a customer order must bill the ordering DoW Component, other federal agency, or the public for earned reimbursements (performance of work or services, or delivery from inventory) within 30 calendar days after the month in which performance occurred. The payment due date must not be more than 30 calendar days from the date of the invoice. Bills rendered are not subject to audit by the customer prior to payment.

2.3.3. The accurate reporting of reciprocal balances, and proper elimination of reciprocal activity between trading partners, requires accurate documentation of accounting events. Unreconciled items occur when federal entities or trading partners are unable to account for and reconcile differences when buying and selling goods and services. Volume 6 provides guidance for trading partner exchange of data, eliminating intra-governmental transactions from the DoW quarterly and annual financial statements, and providing Treasury elimination information for use in preparing the Government-wide financial statements.

2.4    Determining Amounts to be Reimbursed

DoW Components must adhere to the guidance when determining amounts collected as reimbursements. Components may use alternative reimbursement rules described in this volume and in other DoW issuances as applicable.

2.4.1. DoW Components providing prepaid or reimbursable support must require that cost information is quantifiable and provided to all parties. In addition, support must only be reimbursable when the specified support increases the seller’s incremental direct costs and the seller’s actual indirect costs of providing support. For any costs that apply to a customer order, DoW Components are prohibited from augmenting their appropriations by charging customers for costs that do not incrementally increase their direct cost. A seller can waive reimbursement from buyers that use or benefit from available support when charges would be less than the anticipated expense of billing and disbursing funds. DoW Components designated as a Combatant Command support agent will provide administrative and logistics support to Combatant Command headquarters and the subordinate unified command headquarters, as documented in agreements on a non-reimbursable basis, in accordance with DoD Directive (DoDD) 5100.03 “Support of the Headquarters of Combatant and Subordinate Unified Commands.” Refer to DoD Instruction (DoDI) 4000.19 for additional guidance.

2.4.2. An order placed or agreement made under the Economy Act obligates an appropriation of the ordering entity. The amount obligated is deobligated to the amount of costs incurred and billed by the performing entity before the end of the period of availability of the appropriation. According to OMB Circular A-11 “Section 20 - Terms and Concepts,” the Economy Act allows federal agencies or DoW Components to do work for each other. As costs for this work are incurred, the Economy Act authorizes the collections credited directly to the expenditure account that provided the goods and services for reimbursement. Refer to section 4 for further details.

2.4.3. A project order placed with and accepted by a separately managed DoW-owned entity for services, material, or the manufacture of material, provide support for a valid and recordable obligation of the ordering entity. Project order appropriations remain available to pay an obligation in the same manner as appropriations remain available to pay an obligation to a commercial manufacturer or private contractor. Refer to Section 2 for further details.

2.4.4. Customers may not place orders with DWCF activities for the purpose of extending the life of their appropriations or avoiding any statutory limitation or restrictions pertaining to those funds. Additional guidance applicable to all working capital funds can be found in Volume 3.

2.4.5. As provided in Volume 13, Morale, Welfare, and Recreation (MWR) Utilization Support and Accountability (USA) and Uniform Funding and Management (UFM) are two mechanisms for provision of Appropriated Funds (APFs) support to Nonappropriated Fund Instrumentalities (NAFIs). The MWR USA and UFM practices involve use of NAFs for MWR expenses that, according to funding policies in DoDI 1015.15, should be borne by APFs. MWR USA enables NAFIs to use Nonappropriated Funds (NAFs) to execute such expenses, subject to subsequent APF reimbursement under MOAs. Unlike MWR (USA) practices (which involve reimbursement from APFs), under UFM practices, APFs may be transferred into NAF accounts prior to expenditure. Funds appropriated to DoW and available for MWR programs are treated as NAFs for all purposes under UFM MOAs and remain available until expended. Refer to Volume 13 supplemental guidance for more information.

2.4.6. Direct Civilian Labor

2.4.6.1. A DoW Component must be reimbursed for direct civilian labor costs when performing a service or furnishing materials to another entity. If the performing Component has appropriated funds for that purpose, then reimbursement is not required. Unless the organizations using appropriation are prohibited from directly charging civilian pay.

2.4.6.2. DoW Components, other federal agencies, and the public must be charged for civilian labor performed for their benefit.

2.4.6.3. Civilian personnel fringe benefit rates must be computed. These rates are updated annually and published by Office of Under Secretary of War, Comptroller (OUSW(C)), Deputy Comptroller Program/Budget (P/B) on the Financial Management Reports web page, listed by fiscal year (FY) under the DoW Reimbursable Rates heading. Refer to the Civilian Personnel Fringe Benefit Rates (Tab D).

2.4.7. Direct Military Labor

2.4.7.1. A DoW Component must fund the cost of direct and indirect military labor used to perform services for, or the furnish materials to, another DoW Component through their applicable military personnel appropriations. Under 10 U.S.C. § 2571, internal DoW support, including military labor, may be provided with or without reimbursement. DoW policy generally prohibits reimbursement of military labor between DoW Components. However, DoW Components must reimburse Defense Working Capital Fund (DWCF) activities for the cost of military labor as prescribed in this volume. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) military labor supporting civil works activities or Support for Others Program activities must be charged using the military composite rates applicable to non-DoW organizations, consistent with the Volume 11 Supplemental.

2.4.7.2. Public Law 11847, division A, section 8049 permanently authorizes the use of certain operation and maintenance appropriations to reimburse pay, allowances, and related expenses for National Guard and Reserve members who provide intelligence or counterintelligence support to Combatant Commands, Defense Agencies and Joint Intelligence Activities. These activities fall within the National Intelligence Program (NIP) and the Military Intelligence Program (MIP). Intel reimbursement rates (Rate Billable to DoW Entities) are published annually by OUSW(C), Program and Budget under the subsection “DoW Reimbursable Rates.”

2.4.7.3. Military labor provided in support of any non‑DoW entity must be reimbursed unless there is explicit authority for the Department to provide such support on a non‑reimbursable basis. This includes support to Federal, State, Territorial, Tribal, and local government entities; private organizations; foreign governments; and international organizations. Components must apply the reimbursement rules prescribed in the Volume 11 Supplemental and applicable statutory authorities.

Reimbursement for direct military labor is required under 10 U.S.C. § 277 for support provided to civilian law enforcement agencies, including support provided under 10 U.S.C. § 272 and 10 U.S.C. § 274 when military personnel perform labor associated with those activities, unless there is explicit authority to provide the support on a non-reimbursable basis. See Volume 11 Supplemental for details on military labor reimbursement for support to civilian law enforcement agencies and the required waivers. Reimbursement is also required under 10 U.S.C. § 2012 for military labor provided to non‑profit organizations unless a statutory waiver applies. Interagency support provided under the Economy Act (31 U.S.C. §§ 1535–1536) must be reimbursed at full cost, including the cost of military labor. When DoW provides military labor or services of value to non‑DoW entities, reimbursement must be collected consistent with 31 U.S.C. § 9701. Components must ensure reimbursement is collected in accordance with these statutory requirements and the Secretary of War’s policy prohibiting discretionary non‑reimbursable support to non‑DoW entities.

2.4.7.4. Military labor charged to non-DoW organizations must use the applicable annual reimbursement rates published by the OUSW(C), Program and Budget. These include the Rate Billable to Other Federal Entities and the Rate Billable to Foreign Military Sales (FMS) Entities, each which contains distinct cost elements and reimbursable requirements. Rate application must follow the Department’s compensation rules, including the 30-day month computation method and leave factors when applicable to Other Federal Entities, and time-worked billing rules and leave/holiday factors when applicable to FMS. Refer to OUSW(C), Program and Budget guidance published online under the subsection DoW Reimbursable Rates.

2.4.7.5. Military labor charged to non-DoW organizations must include full-cost recovery elements as required by law and regulation. For Other Federal Entities, reimbursement must include the medical acceleration factor. For FMS Entities, reimbursement must include both the medical acceleration factor and the Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care per-capita normal cost, consistent with the Arms Export Control Act requirement to recover the full cost of providing the service. Refer to Volume 15 for FMS reimbursement procedures.

2.4.7.6. Military Services must furnish the data required to compute the DoW Reimbursement Rates annually, in coordination with the President’s Budget submission, and must apply the reimbursement rules prescribed in the Volume 11 Supplemental, and applicable statutory authorities.
