3.5.6. Annual Reviews. The DFAS will conduct an annual review of the DCA operations and transactions, including the purchase and sale of investments. The objective of the review will include compliance with the DoW and the Treasury policies and procedures, and adequacy of internal controls.

title: Section 4.0: Direct Loans and Loan Guarantees
content:
4.0    DIRECT LOANS AND LOAN GUARANTEES

This section establishes the DoW policies for direct loans and loan guarantees for non- Federal borrowers. The policies for credit programs reflect the requirements of the Federal Credit Reform Act of 1990 (FCRA) as amended. The major purposes of the FCRA are to: (a) measure more accurately the costs of Federal credit programs; (b) place the cost of credit programs on a budgetary basis equivalent to other Federal spending; (c) encourage the delivery of benefits in the most appropriate form to meet the needs of beneficiaries; and (d) improve the allocation of resources among credit programs and between credit and other spending programs.

4.1    Accounting Standards

4.1.1. Netting Subsidy Re-estimate Amounts (within Cohorts). To calculate subsidy costs, components begin by estimating the expected cash flows and inflows over the life of the loans for each cohort year. Expected cash flows are then discounted to the point of the loan disbursement to determine the net present value. The subsidy cost represents the net present value cost of making or guaranteeing new loans.

4.1.1.1. The data used for budgetary subsidy cost estimates are updated, or re- estimated, annually after the end of the fiscal year to reflect actual loan performance and to incorporate any changes in assumptions about future loan performance. Re-estimates must be made immediately after the end of each fiscal year, if any loans in the cohort are outstanding.

4.1.1.2. OMB Circular No. A-11, Part 5, Section 185.6 (f), “Reestimate Increases/Decreases,” states that in cases where agencies execute a risk category on a loan-by-loan basis, increases or decreases in subsidy cost for different loans within the same cohort and risk category will be netted against each other. Loans that require increased subsidies should draw on the excess from any risk categories within the cohort where the re-estimate shows a subsidy decrease. A negative or downward subsidy re-estimate should be recognized as a direct reduction in expense, not as a revenue, gain, or other financing source.

4.1.1.2.1. If the netting within the cohort indicates a net increase in the subsidy cost of the cohort since the last estimate or re-estimate, an obligation in the amount of the net increase (plus interest) must be recorded against permanent indefinite budget authority available to the program account for this purpose.

4.1.1.2.2. If the netting within the cohort results in a net downward re- estimate, there is no overall increase in subsidy cost for the cohort, and hence no additional appropriated subsidy for the program account. To keep the correct balances in the financing account, an obligation and a financing disbursement in the amount of the net decrease (plus interest on the re-estimate) must be recorded in the financing account.

4.1.1.2.3. Within the financing account, any amounts borrowed for downward re-estimates for individual loans not needed for/transferred to loans with upward re- estimates are transferred to a miscellaneous receipt account.

4.1.1.3. The DFAS maintains separate accounting records for each loan and loan guarantee with all accounting transactions. All projects having a downward re-estimate, whether they are in a cohort with an upward re-estimate project, borrow the gross amount of their respective downward re-estimates from the Treasury’s Bureau of the Fiscal Service. The borrowed funds received by a downward re-estimate project is transferred to the amount needed to fund an upward re-estimate project in the same cohort, with any net remaining funds paid to the Treasury.

4.1.1.3.1. The downward re-estimate project records such intracohort transfers as a credit to USSGL account 427100 “Actual Program Fund Subsidy Collected” with an offsetting debit to USSGL 427100 recorded by the upward re-estimate project. Consequently, the total re-estimate amount included in Line 4120 “Federal Sources” on the SF 133 “Report on Budget Execution and Budgetary Resources” is the sum of the net cohort balances.

4.1.1.3.2. The Treasury, primarily through the Fiscal Service, provides detailed accounting and reporting guidance for Federal credit programs through the Guide for Basic Accounting and Reporting for Direct Loan Programs without Collateral in Federal Credit Program and the Guide for Basic Accounting and Reporting for Loan Guarantee Programs without Collateral in Federal Credit Program.

4.2    Credit Reform Fund Controls

4.2.1. Fund Control. Leaders of DoW agencies must prescribe, by regulation, a system of administrative control of funds. For credit programs and resources, systems for administrative control of funds must ensure that internal controls include objectives specific to compliance with the Antideficiency Act (ADA). Additional detailed guidance can be found in OMB Circular No. A-11, Part 4, Section 150.

4.2.2. Antideficiency Act Violations. ADA violations for direct loans, guaranteed loans, and financing accounts are reportable to the President, through the Director of the OMB, to the Comptroller General, and to Congress. For additional information, refer to Volume 14. For examples of ADA violations refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

4.3    Credit Apportionment and Reapportionment

All Treasury Appropriation Fund Symbols (TAFS) and all program, financing, and liquidating accounts are required to be apportioned, except in the case of a TAFS that is exempt from apportionment per OMB Circular No. A-11, Part 4. Refer to Volume 3.

4.4    Report on Budget Execution and Budgetary Resources (SF 133)

4.4.1. Coverage. Unless otherwise specified by the OMB, the Report on Budget Execution and Budgetary Resources must be prepared to provide current data on each credit account, whether apportioned or not. Current reporting requirements are published in OMB Circular No. A-11, Part 4.

4.4.2. Timing of Reports. The SF 133 must be submitted electronically through the Treasury’s Governmentwide Treasury Account Symbol (GTAS) Adjusted Trial Balance System at the end of November, July, August, and each quarter or such other time period specified by the OMB for each open TAFS. Optionally, the SF 133 is submitted through the GTAS for the additional monthly reporting in November, July, and August for expiring TAFSs. This facilitates analysis and ensures consistent presentation of budget execution information so that Government- wide totals are meaningful. A copy of the SF 133 for each calendar quarter must be submitted to the Committee on Appropriations, House of Representatives.

4.5    Direct Loans

The DoW Component must record an obligation of subsidy in the program account when it signs a binding contract, in accordance with the provisions of OMB Circular No. A-11, Part 5, 'Federal Credit.' Subsidy funds must be paid from the program account to the financing account when the direct loan is to be disbursed to the borrower. Note that the subsidy is not recalculated at the time of loan disbursement. Rather, any change in estimated subsidy caused by an interest rate change or a change in estimates for other components of subsidy cost is made at the beginning of the fiscal year after the fiscal year in which the loan is disbursed. If, at that time, the subsidy amount increases, permanent indefinite budget authority is available to fund the increase, pursuant to section 504(f) of the Federal Credit Reform Act (FCRA) of 1990. If the subsidy amount decreases, a payment must be made to a receipt account.

4.6    Guaranteed Loans

The DoW Component must record the obligation of subsidy in the program account when a binding contract has been signed, in accordance with the provisions of OMB Circular No. A-11, Part 5, “Federal Credit.” The DoW Component must pay subsidy funds from the program account to the financing account when the third-party lender disburses the guaranteed loan to the borrower. Note that the subsidy is not recalculated at the time of loan disbursement. Rather, the DoW Component makes any change in the estimated subsidy caused by an interest rate change or a change in estimates for other components of subsidy cost at the beginning of the fiscal year after the fiscal year in which the loan is disbursed. If, at that time, the subsidy amount increases, permanent indefinite budget authority is available to fund the increase, pursuant to section 504(f) of the FCRA of 1990. If the subsidy amount decreases, the DoW Component must make a payment to a receipt account.

4.7    Computation of Interest Expense and Interest Income

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for: Instructions for Computations of Interest Expense and Interest Income for Direct and Guaranteed Loan Programs; Frequency of Interest Computations; Weighted Average Interest Rate; and Procedure and Due Dates for Computing Interest Expenses and Income Related to Borrowing for Direct Loan and Guaranteed Loan Financing Accounts.

4.8    Credit Reform USSGL Accounts and Definitions

Credit reform accounts and definitions were established in the USSGL to implement requirements of the FCRA of 1990 (as amended) and are intended to account for direct loans and loan guarantees. DoW entities must follow the Standard Financial Information Structure (SFIS), which is based on the Treasury USSGL. For more complete information, visit the SFIS website.

title: Section 5.0: Grants and Cooperative Agreements
content:
5.0    GRANTS AND COOPERATIVE AGREEMENTS

5.1    DoW Statutory Authorities for Use of Grants

A DoW Component may use grants when the SecWar delegates the statutory authority, or when a statute grants the authority directly to the Head of the DoW Component. Title 32, Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) § 21.420 lists the types of statutory authority the DoW may use to award assistance instruments.

5.2    Grants Financial Management

5.2.1. Financial Management Information System

5.2.1.1. The DoW Component must ensure the availability of a financial management information system capable of recording and monitoring grant transactions and providing, by transaction, a delineation of the federal and grantee breakout of program costs.

5.2.1.2. The system must enable the DoW Component to quickly identify the basic categories of funds involved, along with the related obligation and expenditure rates, and provide for ensuring fund availability prior to awarding financial assistance and obligating funds.

5.2.2. Record Retention. The DoW Component must maintain grant-supporting financial management documentation in accordance with the requirements in its DoW Component records retention requirements.

5.2.3. Recording and Reviewing Commitments and Obligations. Accounting for funds under a grant must start with the commitment of funds prior to their obligation by an awarding official. The awarding official must be a DoW grants or agreements officer with a statement of appointment that meets the requirement in 32 CFR §§ 21.435-21.465. After funds commitment, budgetary obligations must be recorded upon execution of the agreement or other obligating document approved by the awarding official that sets out the amount and purpose of the award, the performance period, the performance obligations of the parties to the award, and other terms. A legal obligation to disburse grant funds, in accordance with the terms of the agreement, occurs upon execution of an agreement or other obligating document. Refer to Volume 3 for more information.

5.2.4. Volume 10 provides detailed payment provisions for grants and other instruments of assistance.

5.2.4.1. Timing and Frequency

5.2.4.1.1. 32 CFR § 22.810 prescribes the timing and frequency of grant payments. In general, it is Governmentwide policy to minimize the time elapsing between any payment of funds to a grantee and the grantee’s disbursement of the funds for program purposes. For States, payments are governed by Treasury-State Cash Management Improvement Act agreements and default procedures codified in 31 CFR § 205 and I Treasury Financial Manual (TFM) 4A - 2000 Overall Disbursing Rules for All Federal Agencies.

5.2.4.1.2. The assisting DoW Component must account for payments made to grantees to cover part or all their anticipated expenses or advance payments as advances. This accounting treatment continues until the grantee performs under the award, meaning the grantee meets the requirements to use the funds in accordance with the grant agreement. Refer to Volume 4 for more information.

5.2.4.1.3. The DoW Component should require payments as reimbursements when the grantee cannot meet the requirements in subparagraphs 5.2.4.1.1 and 5.2.4.1.2, when the DoW Component sets a specific grant condition per 2 CFR § 200.207, or when the grantee requests this payment method. The DoW Component may also use reimbursement for any construction grant, or if private market financing or Federal loans fund the major portion of the construction project, and the Federal award constitutes a minor portion of the project.

5.2.4.2. Method. It is a government-wide requirement to use EFT in the payment of any grant to the maximum extent practicable under 32 CFR § 22.810.

5.2.4.3. Process. Disbursing offices must follow the policies and procedures in Volume 10 for payment provisions for grants.

5.2.4.4. Withholding Payments. The DoW Component may withhold payments for allowable costs when:

5.2.4.4.1. The grantee failed to comply with the project objectives, Federal statutes, regulations, or the terms and conditions of the Federal award. If the grant is not otherwise suspended, the DoW Component must release the payment to the grantee upon the grantee’s compliance. If the grant is suspended, the DoW Component will make payment adjustments according to 2 CFR § 200.342;

5.2.4.4.2. The grantee is delinquent in a debt to the United States as defined in OMB Circular No. A-129. In this situation, the DoW Component must provide reasonable notice to the grantee that payments will not be made for obligations incurred after a specified date until the indebtedness to the Federal Government is paid; or

5.2.4.4.3. The grantee has a sustained audit finding which resulted in amounts due to DoW. The DoW Component must promptly record the amount due from the grantee upon entitlement as an accounts receivable, even if the decision to collect is subject to administrative appeal or litigation. Interest must begin to accrue no later than 30 days after the date the grantee was notified of the debt and continues to accrue while an appeal is underway.

5.2.4.5. Interest from Advanced Payments. A DoW Component may allow grantees to retain interest earned up to $500 per year for their administrative expenses. Grantees must remit any additional interest earned on DoW advance payments, required to be deposited in interest-bearing accounts, annually to DoW using either an Automated Clearing House network or a Fedwire Funds Service payment.

5.2.5. Recording of Expense

5.2.5.1. When the grantee that received the advance has performed under the grant, the DoW Component must record an expense in an amount equal to the cost of the services performed or cost incurred and reduce the advance account by that amount. The grantee must provide sufficient documentation to support the cost of the services performed or cost incurred, consistent with the grant.

5.2.5.2. The DoW Component must account for payments to grantees for reimbursement of work performed or costs incurred as expenditures and expenses incurred, or as reductions of liabilities if the expenses were recorded previously.

5.2.6. Accruals. The DoW Component must recognize and report balances due or advanced to grantees at the end of the reporting period and apply cost-benefit considerations to the process of estimating and validating accruals.

5.2.6.1. Accrual estimates must be treated as follows:

5.2.6.1.1. Amounts issued as advances must be adjusted, even if grantees have not yet reported expenses incurred; and

5.2.6.1.2. Where there is no advance or no remaining advance, the DoW Component must estimate amounts payable to grantees.

5.2.6.2. The DoW Component must document and maintain support for the data and assumptions used to develop grant accrual estimates and follow internal control guidance in Federal Accounting Standards Advisory Board Technical Release 12.

5.2.7. Accounts Receivable

5.2.7.1. At the termination or closeout of a grant, the DoW Component must establish an accounts receivable for any disallowed expenses, improperly applied funds, unused funds, and any other amount due to the DoW according to the grant's terms and conditions.

5.2.7.2. When a grantee has a sustained audit finding that resulted in amounts due to DoW, the DoW Component must promptly record the amount due from the grantee upon entitlement as an accounts receivable, even if the decision to collect is subject to administrative appeal or litigation. Interest must begin to accrue no later than 30 days after the date the DoW Component notifies the grantee of the debt and continues to accrue while an appeal is underway.

5.2.8. Debt Collection. A DoW Component establishes a debt when it determines it has overpaid a grantee under the terms and conditions of the grant. Volume 10 and Volume 16 describe the treatment of debt collection.

5.3    Real Property and Equipment

5.3.1. Grantee Purchased Real Property or Equipment. A DoW Component must provide prior approval to grantees to purchase real property or equipment with federal funds. Generally, title to real property or equipment vests with the grantee upon the grantee’s acquisition and DoW does not account for its reversionary interest in real property and equipment (32 CFR § 34.21(a) and (b)). The title must be conditional, subject to the following:

5.3.1.1. The grantee must use the real property or equipment for the authorized purposes of the grant until funding ceases, or until the property or equipment is no longer needed for the grant. Use in other projects must be limited to those under federally sponsored projects (i.e., awards) or programs that have purposes consistent with those authorized for support by the DoW Component;

5.3.1.2. The grantee cannot encumber the property without approval of the DoW Component; and

5.3.1.3. The grantee must use the real property or equipment following the terms of the grant and dispose of the property or equipment following disposition instructions from the DoW Component, consistent with 32 CFR § 34.21(d) and (e).

5.3.1.4. At grant close-out, the DoW Component must follow subparagraph 5.2.7 to account for any outstanding proceeds from the disposition of real property or equipment.

5.3.2. Federally-owned Property. Title to Federally-owned property remains vested in the DoW (32 CFR § 34.22) and:

5.3.2.1. The DoW Component must establish appropriate general ledger accounting controls and property records and include the assets in its financial statements. The asset must be recorded at acquisition cost to the grantee and depreciated in accordance with guidance in Volume 4.

5.3.2.2. If DoW has no further need for the property, it must declare the property excess and report it for disposal following the instructions in Volume 4 for Excess Items Disposition, unless the DoW Component has statutory authority to dispose of the property by alternative methods.

5.3.3. Exempt Federally-owned Property. Exempt Federally owned property means property acquired under a grant when the DoW has chosen to vest title to the property to the grantee without further obligation to the Federal government, based on explicit terms and conditions of the grant. A DoW Component may exercise this option only when statutory authority exists.

5.4    Supplies

Title to supplies will vest in the grantee upon acquisition. If there is a residual inventory of unused supplies exceeding $5,000 in total aggregate value upon termination or completion of the project or program and the supplies are not needed for any other Federal award, the grantee must retain the supplies for use on other activities or sell them. In either case, the grantee must compensate DoW, following the requirements in 32 CFR § 34.24. The grantee may deduct and retain $500 or ten percent of the proceeds, whichever is less, for selling and handling expenses. At grant close-out, the DoW Component must follow subparagraph 5.2.7 to account for compensation received from grantee residual inventory.

5.5    Intangible Property

Intangible property applies to a patent, patent application, copyright, or other intangible property acquired, but not developed or produced, under the grant. When the grantee no longer needs the intangible property for the originally authorized grant purpose, the DoW Component must arrange for the disposition of the intangible property, following the requirements in 32 CFR § 34.25. At grant close-out, the DoW Component must follow subparagraph 5.2.7 to account for the remaining proceeds from disposition of intangible property.

5.6    Other Required Reporting

5.6.1. Improper Payment. An improper payment is any payment that should not have been made, or that was made in an incorrect amount under statutory, contractual, administrative, or other legally applicable requirements. An improper payment also includes any payment that was made to an ineligible recipient or for an ineligible good or service, or payments for goods or services not received (except for such payments authorized by law).

5.6.1.1. Questioned costs, including those identified in audits, are not an improper payment until reviewed and confirmed to be improper as defined in OMB Circular No. A-123 Appendix C.

5.6.1.2. Grant programs are subject to the payment integrity requirements in Volume 4.

5.6.2. Public-Private Partnership Reporting. Grants which meet the definition of public- private partnerships (P3), risk-sharing arrangements or transactions with expected lives greater than 5 years between public and private sector entities, may be subject to disclosure under SFFAS 49. Volume 6 and SFFAS 49 provide detailed information about P3 reporting.

5.6.3. Grants, Loans, Credits, and Contingent Liabilities Involving Foreigners. 1 TFM 2 - 4500 requires electronic submission of several reports pertaining to foreign obligors to the Treasury. Refer to Volume 6 and Volume 16 for more details.

title: Section 6.0: Financial Liability for Government Property, Lost, Damaged, Destroyed, or Stolen
content:
6.0    FINANCIAL LIABILITY FOR GOVERNMENT PROPERTY, LOST, DAMAGED, DESTROYED, OR STOLEN

6.1    Applicability

The requirements within this section apply to all government property regardless of whether the government property is recorded in an Accountable Property System of Record. This
section does not apply to loss, damage, destruction, or theft of Government Furnished Property, Contractor Acquired Property, and property acquired by a contractor because of partial, advance, progress, or performance-based payments in the possession of a third party, to include contractors. Loss, damage, destruction, or theft of such property must be processed in accordance with the terms and conditions of the accountable contract or third-party agreement to which the lost, damaged, destroyed, or stolen property was accountable.

6.2    General Requirements

6.2.1. Initiation of General Inquiries and Investigations

6.2.1.1. Upon discovery of loss, damage, destruction, or theft of government- owned property (real or personal) of any value, the first line supervisor or, in the case of military, immediate superior within the chain of command, must conduct a general inquiry to determine if the situation warrants a formal investigation. A DD Form 200 is not required for general inquiries. Loss, damage, destruction, or theft of supply system materiel must be processed in accordance with paragraph 6.5.

6.2.1.2. An investigation must be conducted for all loss, damage, destruction, or theft of government-owned equipment with initial unit acquisition cost (value) of $5,000 or greater; all sensitive, classified, or leased (Refer to Volume 4) property regardless of initial acquisition cost; and any real property (see Department of Defense Instruction (DoDI) 5000.64 for more information). Investigations may also be conducted when circumstances warrant. For example, when the loss, damage, destruction, or theft of small amounts of property occurs frequently enough to suggest a pattern of wrongdoing, then an investigation may be warranted.

6.2.2. DD Form 200. The DD Form 200 is the required documentation for investigations and must be used to document the facts and circumstances of the loss, damage, destruction, or theft. The person conducting the investigation must complete blocks 1 through 11 of the DD Form 200. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

6.2.3. Review. Upon completion of the investigation, the DD Form 200 must be forwarded to the appointing authority for review. The appointing authority must determine if a financial liability officer or a financial liability board is needed to investigate. The general criteria for appointing a financial liability officer or board and the responsibilities of a financial liability officer or board regarding inventory losses are contained within the Volume 12 Supplemental. General Counsel and/or the member’s commander must be consulted before statements are taken from anyone if there is a suspected violation of the Uniform Code of Military Justice
(10 U.S.C. §§ 801-806).

6.2.4. Evidence of Theft. Cases involving stolen government-owned property must be referred to local security and/or law enforcement officials, in accordance with agency procedures.

6.2.5. Notification and Examination. When financial liability is recommended, the individual must be notified and given the opportunity to examine the findings and recommendations, obtain representation, make a rebuttal statement, and present any mitigating factors that may have contributed to the negligence or abuse. If damage to government housing is involved, an individual also must be given the opportunity to request a waiver of the financial liability in accordance with
10 U.S.C. § 2775.

6.3    Approving and Appointing Authority

Due Process. The appointing and approving authorities must act on the DD Form 200 once an individual has been properly notified and given the opportunity to respond to the findings. Failure of individuals involved to respond to recommendations of financial liability is not a sufficient reason for the appointing and approving authorities to delay the approval process if the individuals were given a reasonable opportunity to reply, as discussed in the Volume 12 Supplemental.

6.4    Government Housing Liability

Military Personnel Liability for Government Housing Determination of Proximate Cause. A member of a Military Service must be held liable to the U.S. for the loss, damage or destruction of family housing or an unaccompanied personnel housing unit assigned to such member, including equipment and furnishings therein, when a determination is made that the loss, damage or destruction was proximately caused by the abuse or negligence of the member, a dependent of the member, or a guest either of the member or the member’s dependent.

6.5    Supply System Material

This section applies to personal property defined as “supply system materiel” and contains procedures to be followed when inventory losses are discovered. The provisions of this section are applicable to all activities accountable for supply system material, including stock fund and other inventories (e.g., appropriated fund).

6.5.1. Inventory. Physical inventories must be performed in accordance with the provisions contained herein and in Department of Defense Manual (DoDM) 4140.01, Volume 5.

6.5.2. Causative Research. Causative research must be conducted for all inventory discrepancies that meet any of the criteria specified in Defense Logistics Manual (DLM) 4000.25, Volume 2. For inventory discrepancies that do not meet the criteria for performing causative research, a justification for adjusting the inventory and accounting records and relief from property accountability must be provided by means of an inventory adjustment document.

6.5.3. Resolved Inventory Losses

6.5.3.1. Accountability. The data developed by post count validation, pre- adjustment research, and causative research must be utilized to prepare correcting documentation so that the inventory accounting systems may be updated. These adjustments must be processed in accordance with this Regulation and DLM 4000.25, Volume 2.

6.5.3.2. Statistics. The type of inventory losses must be categorized and accumulated by category to identify trends or problem areas in accounting or supply system procedures in accordance with DLM 4000.25, Volume 2.

6.5.4. Unresolved Inventory Losses Not Meeting the Criteria for an Investigation

6.5.4.1. Accountability. Relief from property accountability and justification for the adjustment of the inventory and accounting records to the inventory on hand must be provided by means of an inventory adjustment document. The detailed data requirements and procedures for preparing and processing the inventory adjustment document must be as prescribed in the appropriate DoW Component implementing documents.

6.5.4.2. Authority for Adjustment. If the cause or probable cause of the discrepancy has not been determined, and the discrepancy does not qualify for causative research, this paragraph must be cited as authority for relieving the accountable officer of accountability.

6.5.4.3. Statistics. The type of inventory losses must be categorized and accumulated by category to identify trends or problem areas in accounting or supply system procedures in accordance with DLM 4000.25, Volume 2.

6.5.5. Unresolved Inventory Losses - Causative Research Indicates No Personal Responsibility

6.5.5.1. Accountability. See subparagraph 6.4.4.1.

6.5.5.2. Statistics. See subparagraph 6.4.4.3.

6.5.6. Unresolved Inventory Losses - Causative Research Indicates Evidence of Personal Responsibility

A financial liability investigation must be used to support the adjustment of the inventory and accounting records to the actual inventory on hand and to relieve the accountable officer of accountability.

6.5.7. Criteria for an Investigation. A financial liability investigation must be initiated on all unresolved inventory discrepancies for each stock number that meets any of the criteria identified in the Volume 12 Supplemental.

title: Section 7.0: Foreign National Employees Separation Pay Account, Defense
content:
7.0    FOREIGN NATIONAL EMPLOYEES SEPARATION PAY ACCOUNT, DEFENSE

7.1    Authoritative Guidance

7.1.1. The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for Fiscal Years 1992 and 1993 authorized a trust fund account to accumulate funds to finance obligations for separation payments to foreign national employees of the DoW. The NDAA for Fiscal Year 1995 extended this authorization to include foreign nationals employed by a foreign government, for the benefit of DoW, under any of the following agreements that provide for separation pay: (1) a contract, (2) a treaty, or (3) a memorandum of understanding with a foreign nation. 10 U.S.C. § 1581, “Foreign National Employees Separation Pay Account,” provides for the establishment and operation of this account. The use of the term “foreign national employees” in this section is meant to apply to both foreign national direct and indirect hire employees. 10 U.S.C. § 1592 establishes that funds in the “Foreign National Employees Separation Pay Account, Defense” account may not be used to pay severance pay to a foreign national employed by DoW that provides for payment of separation pay if the separation of the employment of the foreign national is the result of the closing of, or the curtailment of activities at, a United States military facility in that country at the request of the government of that country.

7.1.2. This guidance applies to all DoW appropriations. This guidance does not apply to activities under the Defense Working Capital Fund (DWCF). DWCF activities must continue to make necessary foreign national employee severance payments under established DWCF procedures. This guidance also does not apply to the FMS Trust Fund. The FMS Trust Fund activities must continue to accrue and disburse separation pay to their foreign national employees from the FMS Trust Fund. Use of nonappropriated funds (NAF) to pay for severance or separation entitlements, accrued during periods of employment with appropriated funded (APF) entities is prohibited.

7.2    Policy

7.2.1. Calculations. Foreign national employees' separation pay must be determined and calculated at the installation level in accordance with applicable host country agreements. These amounts must be obligated in the full amount of the liability that accrues during the fiscal year, without regard to whether the amount is currently payable. Disburse these amounts from the Treasury “Foreign National Employees Separation Pay Account, Defense,” 097X8165. The applicable Treasury receipt account is 097X8165.001, “Employing Agency Contributions, Defense.” Find additional guidance on obligations for separation allowances for foreign national employees in Volume 3.

7.2.2. The Director, DFAS, must administer the account as well as perform related accounting functions.

7.2.3. Transfers into the “Foreign National Employees Separation Pay Account, Defense” must be made following procedures in the procedures/guidance document.

7.2.4. Deobligations. Each DoW Component must notify its supporting DFAS site of all deobligation transactions, adjustments, and corrections, in a timely and accurate manner. The respective site will record adjustments and corrections in the accounting records.

7.3    Subsequent Disbursements

7.3.1. Validation of Funds Availability. Local disbursing offices and the Department of State (DoS) may continue to make disbursements for foreign national employee separation payments, when approved by DFAS, using DoW cross-disbursement procedures. Each DoW Component and non-DoW office (e.g., DoS) must coordinate its disbursement/cross-disbursement actions with the supporting DFAS site to validate the availability of funds prior to disbursement. A positive balance in the account is necessary prior to payment; therefore, both DoW and non- DoW activities will verify from the supporting DFAS site that sufficient funds are available prior to submitting vouchers to servicing disbursing offices for employee payments.

7.3.2. Cross-Disbursements. When cross-disbursement procedures are used, the appropriate DFAS site must be advised prior to each actual disbursement. Find additional guidance on cross-disbursement transactions in Volume 3.

7.4    Responsibilities

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

title: Section 8.0: International Agreements
content:
8.0    INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENTS

8.1    General
This section establishes the financial procedures that must be followed when DoW Components initiate, develop, and request formal review of international agreements and any annexes, appendices, amendments, or modifications thereto. It does not cover Foreign Military Sales (FMS) transactions and contracts entered into under the provisions of the Federal Acquisition Regulation or agreements associated with security assistance programs. Such transactions are implemented under provisions identified in Section 15.

8.1.1. International Agreement Document. This term includes any document, among others, identified as an international agreement, memorandum of understanding, memorandum of agreement, memorandum of arrangement, exchange of notes, exchange of letters, or technical arrangement with one or more foreign governments (including their agencies, instrumentalities, or political subdivisions) or with an international organization.

8.1.2. International Agreement Design for Coordination. Each international agreement submitted for coordination must contain a fiscal, legal and policy memorandum in accordance with DoDI 5530.03, “International Agreements,” paragraphs 5.2.b., or a Summary Statement of Intent (SSOI) in accordance with paragraph 5.2.b.(5). Refer to Volume 12 Supplemental for detail regarding these memoranda.

8.2    Legal Considerations

Legal authority information is critical to the preparation of an international agreement and is the basis for determining the legal authority for entering into the agreement and subsequent financial requirements. Any agreement that involves the obligation of U.S. appropriated funds must have an underlying legal authority for the use of such funds; the agreement itself cannot create such an authority. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for detailed information regarding these legal considerations.

8.3    Fiscal Considerations

8.3.1. Availability of Financing Sources. There are two general prohibitions on the use of appropriated funds for international agreements. In addition, the legal section must identify any other applicable prohibitions. It is implicit in the identification of the financing sources set forth in the Volume 12 Supplemental that funds are available. It is desirable, however, to include in the fiscal information section a certification that all legal and policy prohibitions on the use of funds have been complied with. The general prohibitions are as follows:

8.3.1.1. No funds designated by the Congress for North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) or major non-NATO cooperative research and development under 10 U.S.C. § 2350a may be used to procure equipment or services from any foreign government, foreign research organization, or other foreign entity (including NATO participants) to the agreement.

8.3.1.2. U.S. Government military assistance funds (i.e., Foreign Military Financing, FMS loans, and FMS credits) are not available to finance a foreign participant’s share of the cost of a cooperative project authorized by section 27 of the Arms Export Control Act or a cooperative development project with a major non-NATO ally under 10 U.S.C. § 2350a.

8.3.2. Financial and Nonfinancial Contributions. A contribution to an international agreement may be financial, nonfinancial, or both. Nonfinancial contributions may be in the form of defense articles or defense services needed for the cooperative project. If the contribution is nonfinancial, a price analysis must be made to ensure the valuation assigned to such nonfinancial contribution is fair and reasonable. The fiscal information section must summarize the results of such an analysis. The price analysis must be based on prior cost experience for the nonfinancial contribution to be provided. When a foreign contribution is in the form of foreign currency or the awarding of a contract in a foreign country, the foreign currency contribution generally must be valued at the exchange rate current at the time that the agreement is prepared. There must be no subsequent modification of the valuation because of changes in the currency exchange rate. The fiscal memorandum or SSOI must display the value of the currency in terms of U.S. dollars.

8.3.3. Valuation of Nonfinancial Contributions. The value of all nonfinancial (background data/information, software, services, military and civilian labor, materiel, equipment, and facilities) contributions to an agreement is to be determined and considered for the evaluation of equitableness of the proposed project. The fiscal memorandum or financial section of the SSOI must describe the nonfinancial contributions, indicate their value, and state the method used in determining the valuation. The nonfinancial contributions must also be valued in terms of U.S. dollars in the fiscal memorandum or SSOI. The alternatives for determining the value of nonfinancial contributions can be found in the Volume 12 Supplemental.

8.3.4. Reasonable and Necessary Expense. Any obligation of DoW appropriations under an international agreement must be supported by a showing that it is a reasonable and necessary expense required for the accomplishment of DoW missions, unless the use of DoW funds for other than a DoW mission specifically is authorized by statute.

8.4    Proposed Agreement

8.4.1. Financial Policies and Appropriate Cross References. An international agreement must contain language that implements the requirements established by U.S. law and regulation. This section discusses the financial policies that must be followed and provides appropriate cross references to other parts of this Regulation that provide more specific guidance.

8.4.2. Fund Availability Qualification. Because agreements may involve future years for which Congress has not yet appropriated funds, all agreements that require that DoW provide financial contributions must contain a funds availability clause to prevent a premature recording of an obligation against a future year’s appropriation.

8.4.3. Reconciliation of Agreement Dollar Value to Financing Sources. An international agreement must set forth the dollar value of the agreement and portions of the dollar value that must be borne by each participant. This cost sharing may be in the form of monies or nonfinancial contributions. A preliminary requirement is to ensure that any obligations that the Department may be required to incur in implementation of the agreement have been identified in the fiscal information section. Nonfinancial contributions, described in the scope section, may be valued in the fiscal information section as part of the overall financial contributions, or described solely in the scope section without valuation in the financial information section. The financial information in the fiscal memorandum or SSOI will value all financial and nonfinancial contributions identified in the international agreement.

8.4.4. Adherence to Prescribed Pricing Rules

8.4.4.1. If an international agreement provides for nonfinancial contributions, there must be assurance that proper pricing procedures have been followed. Subparagraphs 8.3.2 and 8.3.3 discuss special requirements that may be applicable to certain agreements. The text of an agreement must be reviewed carefully to ensure compliance with these paragraphs. An area of special pricing attention is charges for existing DoW technical data and computer software, or the use of equipment or facilities.

8.4.4.2. Equipment and facilities provided for use in the furtherance of the purpose of an international agreement should be based on an amortized rate. This amortized rate should be based on the cost and useful life of the equipment or facilities and applied to the length of time the equipment or facilities will be used in the furtherance of the purpose of the international agreement. Standard rates, if available, can also be used.

8.4.5. Determination of Program Equitableness

8.4.5.1. 2350a and 22 U.S.C. § 2767, and in accordance with DoDI 5530.03, international agreements involving cost sharing should be equitable. The United States and the other participants to an international agreement must contribute their equitable share of the full cost in funds or in defense articles or services needed to execute the cooperative project and must receive their equitable share of the results of the cooperative project in the form of defense articles or services. A participant’s cost share must be proportionately equal to the benefits it receives. In many cases, “equitable” will mean equal, but the sharing need not be exactly equal to meet the equitable standard; minor deviations are permissible so long as the cost sharing is fair based on the totality of the circumstances involved, and not in contravention of other law or regulation. Any such deviation will be cited clearly in the SSOI and approved by the relevant DoW officials during their routine coordination of international agreements. Further details of meeting the requirements for equitability are provided in the Volume 12 Supplemental.

8.4.5.2. The SSOI or fiscal memorandum to a proposed international agreement, must clearly explain why the agreement is considered equitable. Prior to approval of all proposed international agreements, a determination of agreement equitability must be made by the approving DoW officials. It is critical that sufficient detail and information be provided to clearly demonstrate to approving officials that the proposed international agreement is equitable.

8.4.5.3. Calculation of Expected Contribution. In support of an equitability determination by DoW approving officials, the expected contribution must be calculated and presented in the SSOI or supporting documentation using one of the methods identified in the Volume 12 Supplemental:

8.4.6. Sales and Transfers of Technical Data Developed Under an Agreement – Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

8.4.7. Taxes, Duties, and Similar Charges – Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

8.4.8. Advance of DoW Funds

8.4.8.1. An advance constitutes a disbursement of DoW funds before an authorized DoW official has certified that materials have been delivered or ordered services performed. An agreement must not provide for DoW advance payments, unless the conditions for such advances, as set forth in Volume 4, are met. An advance to a foreign country is authorized only when required for compliance with the laws and ministerial regulations of the foreign country and is further required by the agreement.

8.4.8.2. When possible, advances must be made for no more than the amount necessary to fulfill the DoW share of project expenses for one month. Advances and prepayments must not exceed the amount necessary to fulfill the DoW share of project expenses for a current fiscal quarter. If monies are paid in advance and deposited into commercial banks, provision must be made to ensure that the agreement requires: Payment of interest at competitive rates; Timely identification of interest earned by each party; and Interest disposition in accordance with the participants’ instructions.

8.4.8.3. The DoW share of funding required to support an international project must be obtained in full by appropriation, and no part of such funding must be derived from interest earnings on U.S. contributions. In view of this policy, the U.S. Government share of interest earned on U.S. advance payments must be returned to the Treasury Miscellaneous Receipts Account 3210, “General Fund Proprietary Receipts, Defense Military, Not Otherwise Classified.” The interest must not be used to reduce a future call for funds, nor used for any project cost that would result in funding derived outside the appropriation process.

8.4.8.4. Advances of DoW funds in excess of 90 days or $5 million require consultation with the Treasury. Contact with the Treasury must be through the OUSW(C).

8.4.9. Billing Requirements. When payments are to be made, the agreement or subsequent financial arrangements must include information identified in the Procedures document.

8.4.10. Special Types of Agreements

8.4.10.1. Agreements for Reciprocal Exchange of Materials or Services. These agreements must set forth the time period allowed for exchange of materials and services. They also must set forth financial settlements that must be made if the exchange does not take place. DoW services or materials provided are priced in accordance with Volume 11.

8.4.10.2. Cooperative Research, Development, Test and Evaluation (RDT&E), Technical Data Exchange, Co-production, Licensed Production, and Related Standardization Agreements That Are Not Implemented through the Security Assistance Program. Full costs must be identified and shared equitably. Cost sharing may be accomplished through the following:

8.4.10.2.1. Pooling of monies and designation of a lead country to manage the program, collect cash, and award contracts. Specific shares of program cost are set forth in the agreement.
8.4.10.2.2. No pooling of monies or designation of a lead country. Specific efforts to be accomplished by each participating country and estimated costs of such efforts are set forth in the agreement.

title: Section 9.0: Funding Civilian Separation Incentives and Civilian Personnel Transition Initiatives
content:
9.0    FUNDING CIVILIAN SEPARATION INCENTIVES AND CIVILIAN PERSONNEL TRANSITION INITIATIVES

9.1    Overall Funding Policy

9.1.1. For this policy, the term “civilian separation incentives” means resignation and retirement incentives and outplacement subsidies that may be used to encourage designated civilian employees to separate voluntarily from DoW.

9.1.2. Available separation incentives include Voluntary Separation Incentive Pay (VSIP), VSIP Phase II, Voluntary Early Retirement Authority (VERA), and Voluntary Reduction in Force (VRIF). The DoW activities may pay up to $25,000 (before taxes and deductions) from appropriations, funds, or accounts available for such purposes for the voluntary resignation, early retirement, or optional retirement of a designated civilian employee.

9.1.3. Outplacement subsidies are used as an incentive for other Federal agencies to hire employees displaced by reduction in force (RIF) or transfer of function. DoW activities may pay up to $20,000 from appropriations, funds, or accounts available for such purposes. The payment is for Permanent Change of Station (PCS) costs incurred by another Federal agency when that agency hires any DoW employee in a surplus skill category who is subject to RIF. See the DoW
FMR.

9.1.4. Audit Readiness/Internal Procedures. Each DoW Component must develop and implement internal operating procedures and/or guidance to implement this overarching policy in a manner that ensures accurate, timely, and relevant reporting of financial data. Relevant records supporting financial statements must be maintained and made available during financial statement audits.

9.1.5. Recording Funding Obligations. Funds for separation incentives and outplacement subsidies must be obligated when an employee accepts the offer of an incentive payment. The obligation must be recorded in DoW Standard General Ledger account 640000, “Benefits Expense,” and reported as object class 13.0, “Benefits for former personnel” for separation incentive and object class 12.1 for outplacement subsidies. Refer to the Office of the DCFO SFIS for additional information on account descriptions, and OMB Circulars, Circular No. A-11,
Section 83 for additional information on object class codes.

9.2 Specific Funding Policies for Different Types of Employees

9.2.1. Civilian Separation. A DoW Component that offers civilian separation incentives to an employee, to induce the voluntary separation of that employee to create a vacancy for another employee of the same DoW Component, must fund the resulting separation payments from the applicable appropriation, fund, or account that otherwise is available to pay for salaries and expenses of that DoW Component. The source of Voluntary Separation Incentive Payments funds may include a DWCF for employees of a DWCF-funded activity. DoW central account funding is not provided.

9.2.2. Foreign Military Sales Trust Fund – Refer to Volume 12 Supplemental.

9.2.3. Placements Outside the Department. DoW activities may pay up to $20,000 (subject to the availability of funds) in outplacement subsidy for Permanent Change of Station (PCS) costs associated with placement of a surplus DoW employee with another Federal Agency as authorized under 5 U.S.C. § 5724 and DoDI 1400.25, Volume 1702. When the gaining Federal agency accepts a DoW Component-offered outplacement subsidy, the DoW activity must notify the gaining agency that DoW funds may be billed up to $20,000 per employee or for the actual PCS costs, whichever is less. The notification must include the DoW fund citation to be billed and the address of the fiscal station paying the subsidy. Payment must be made by the applicable DoW activity based upon documentation of the amounts paid or to be paid to the employee by the gaining Federal Agency.

9.3    Controls over Available Funds

Controls must be established to ensure that sufficient funds are available to cover projected requirements for employee acceptance of incentive offers and outplacement subsidies each quarter. ADA provisions apply to the DoW Component appropriations, funds, and accounts. Therefore, if available funds are projected to be inadequate to cover anticipated incentive program acceptances and outplacement subsidies, appropriate action must be taken. In this regard, the DoW Components either must cancel or withdraw incentive offers prior to employee acceptance or obtain additional funds.

title: Section 10.0: Privatization of War Utility Systems
content:
10.0    PRIVATIZATION OF WAR UTILITY SYSTEMS

10.1    DoW Utility Systems

As permitted under the authority of 10 U.S.C § 2925, the Secretary of a Military Department is allowed to transfer utility systems. This authority does not extend to utility projects operated by the Army Corps of Engineers under its civil works authority. The policy is driven by DoDI 4170.11, "Installation Energy Management," which establishes utilities privatization as the preferred strategy for modernizing and recapitalizing these critical systems. Consequently, the Military Services are mandated to attempt privatization of such utility systems at all Active and Reserve Component installations, both within and outside the United States. However, there are specific exceptions to this mandate: privatization is not required for installations scheduled for closure, for systems that the Secretary of the Military Department certifies as exempt for security reasons, or in cases where privatization would be uneconomical. The USW for Acquisition and Sustainment (A&S) is assigned primary responsibility for overseeing this instruction.

10.2    Conveyance of Utility Systems

10.2.1. Consideration and Determination. Subsection 2688(c)(1) of 10 U.S.C. provides that the Secretary of a Military Department concerned may require as consideration for a conveyance an amount equal to the fair market value (as determined by the Secretary) of the right, title, or interest of the United States conveyed. Such consideration may take the form of a reduction in charges for utility services provided or a lump sum payment. Subsection 2688 does not itself constitute authority for the Secretary of a Military Department to convey a utility system without any consideration or cause to be inapplicable to authorities that govern disposal of DoW real property and personal property. The Secretary concerned may authorize a contract for utility services to have a term more than 10 years, but not to exceed 50 years. The determination of cost effectiveness must be made using a business case analysis that includes an independent estimate of the level of investment that should be required to maintain adequate operation of the utility system over the proposed term of the contract or contract renewal. The business case analysis must also demonstrate how a privatized system will operate in a manner consistent with energy resilience and cybersecurity requirements and associated metrics provided to the conveyee to ensure that the reliability of the utility system meets mission requirements.

10.2.2. Reduction in Charges. A reduction in charges for utility services provided is acceptable consideration when the services are provided by the utility or entity obtaining the utility, and the reduction in charges is provided to the military installation at which the utility system is located at the time of conveyance. In such circumstances, a reduction in charges for utility services provided is an exchange of dissimilar assets that does not result in a credit to an appropriation. The consideration (reduction) in such an exchange is considered an “Other Asset” (Account 199000), and the recorded asset is reduced by charges to “Operating Expenses/Program Costs” (Account 610000) over the life of the contract for utility services. Corresponding asset disposal losses must be recognized as described in Volume 4.

10.2.3. Lump Sum Payment – Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

10.3    Conveyance Authorization and Agenda

10.3.1. Same Utility Service Procurements. Before utility conveyance proceeds may be used to procure the same utility services as those provided by the utility system conveyed, the organization receiving the funds must submit the proposed distribution of funds to Assistant Secretaries of the Military Departments’ Financial Management and Comptroller (FM&C) for approval. The FM&C must notify the supporting DFAS site of approved funds distributions.

10.3.2. Savings and Conservation Projects and Improvements. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

title: Section 11.0: Energy and Water Savings and Revenue Management
content:
11.0    ENERGY AND WATER SAVINGS AND REVENUE MANAGEMENT

11.1    Financial Management Policy, Incentives, and Revenues
The Congress has enacted a series of measures aimed at strengthening energy and water security, resilience, and sustainability within the DoW. This section establishes the financial management policy for identifying, retaining, and utilizing energy and water cost savings, as well as financial incentives and revenues derived from the sale of electricity. It provides comprehensive guidance on the receipt and use of utility incentives and water cost savings for conservation efforts; the availability and application of energy cost savings; the implementation of energy savings contracts and related activities; the sale of electricity generated from alternative energy and cogeneration facilities; and DoW participation in programs designed to manage energy demand or reduce energy consumption during peak periods. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for more detailed steps and procedures.

11.2    Energy Savings and Incentives Received from Utilities

11.2.1. Extended Availability from Energy Savings. Energy savings amounts with extended availability must be transferred to extended availability accounts for execution.

11.2.1.1. An extended availability account must be established for each appropriation for which energy cost savings have been identified and for which a period of extended availability is established.

11.2.1.2. Transfers to extended availability accounts must be made by a SF 1151, “Nonexpenditure Transfer Authorization,” or other authorized Service-specific method that incorporates all SF 1151 requirements (refer to Volume 14). Reprogramming actions will not be required in the case of such transfers.

11.2.1.3. The level that uses the accounts, such as the command, installation, Military Department, Defense Agency, and/or OSW level Accounting, must establish appropriate controls, and oversight for amounts in extended availability accounts to optimize funds executability.

11.2.2. Financial Incentives - Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

11.3    Revenues from the Sale of Electricity

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for Sale of Electricity; Use of Proceeds from the Sale of Electricity; and Congressional Notification.

11.4    Budgeting and Energy Savings on Utility Payments

Each military department must include the portion of the guaranteed savings due to the contractor for payment under an Energy Savings Performance Contract (ESPC) or to the utility for payment under an Utility Energy Service Contract (UESC) in its utility requirements submitted in budget requests for the length of the ESPC or UESC entered by that military department. The total utility requirements submitted as part of budget requests must include the entire amount of guaranteed savings provided in an ESPC or performance assurance savings provided in an UESC, including amounts for contract payments and amounts to be retained by installations. The total of the amounts requested must not exceed those that would have been requested in the absence of the ESPC. The Secretary concerned, or designee, must specify the procedures for identification of such amounts by installations, facilities, or operating locations at which ESPCs or UESCs for that military department are in existence. In accordance with the OMB Circular No. A-11, Appendix B, “Budgetary Treatment of Lease-Purchases and Leases of Capital Assets,” the costs of ESPCs may be scored on an annual basis, consistent with the guidance provided in OMB Memorandum M-98-13, “Federal Use of Energy Savings Performance Contracting,” and OMB Memorandum M-12-21, “Addendum to OMB Memorandum M-98-13 on Federal Use of Energy Savings Performance Contracts and Utility Energy Service Contracts.”

11.5    Use of Balances Available Resulting from Energy Cost Savings

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

11.6    Accounting for Energy Cost Savings

11.6.1. 10 U.S.C. § 2912. The energy cost savings amounts realized in accordance with 10 U.S.C. § 2912 remain as unobligated balances available for obligation at the end of the fiscal year and the succeeding fiscal year.

11.6.2. Unobligated Balance Transfers. Unobligated balances covered by subparagraph 11.6.1 must be transferred to extended availability accounts on an SF 1151 or other authorized Service-specific method that incorporates all SF 1151 requirements (see subparagraph 11.1.1). The authority and policy to be cited for the transfer is 10 U.S.C. § 2912(e).

11.6.2.1. The SecWar may transfer amounts that remain available for obligation to other funding accounts of the DoW if the purpose for which such amounts will be used is specified in the Volume 12 Supplemental.

11.6.2.2. Amounts transferred to a funding account of the Department under subparagraph 11.5.2.1 will be available for obligation for the same period as amounts in that account.

11.6.2.3. At the end of each fiscal year, the SecWar must submit to Congress a report detailing any funds transferred pursuant to subparagraph 11.5.2.1 during that fiscal year, including a detailed description of the purpose for which such amounts have been used.

title: Section 12.0: Fiscal Policy for Base Closure and Realignment
content:
12.0    FISCAL POLICY FOR BASE CLOSURE AND REALIGNMENT

12.1    Policy

DoW Components are responsible for implementing all base closure and realignment action including preparation of an economic analysis in accordance with Volume 2, and must administer the allocations of base closure funds. DoW Components are to deposit the proceeds in the appropriate account authorized by law. If transfer funds were deposited into the wrong account, a suspense account, or other interim account, an SF 1080, “Voucher for Transfers Between Appropriations and/or Funds,” must be used to transfer funds to the proper account. Refer to the Procedures document for: DoW Base Closure Account 1990 and DoW Base Closure Account 2005; DoW Overseas Military Facility Investment Recovery Account; and Reserve Account.

12.2    Budget and Accounting Responsibilities

12.2.1. Requests for Funds

12.2.1.1. DoW Components DoW Base Closure Account Financial Plan. The Military Departments and Defense Agencies, in cooperation with, and at the direction of, the USW for A&S or designee, the Director, OSW Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) Office, must submit a financial plan to the Director, Military Personnel and Construction, OUSW(C), Program/Budget (P/B), supported by a “DoW Base Closure Account Financial Plan,” (Format 460-BC), to request allocations of base closure funds. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for more information. Host DoD Components are responsible for coordination with all affected tenant activities, including Defense Agencies, Defense Medical Facilities Office, Reserve Components, and nonappropriated fund activities. Tenant activities must identify specific base closure program requirements to their host DoD Component.

12.2.1.2. Director, Military Personnel and Construction. This office must initiate the SF 132, “Apportionment and Reapportionment Schedule,” for the appropriate base closure account for submission to the OMB for its approval.

12.2.2. Funds Distribution

12.2.2.1. Director, Military Personnel and Construction. Upon OMB approval of the SF 132 for the base closure account, this office must provide a Fund Authorization Document to the applicable component for recording in the agency-level accounting records.

12.2.2.2. Director, Defense Finance and Accounting Service. The Director of DFAS must obtain and record, in the departmental-level accounting records, a Financial Management Service 6200, “Appropriation Warrant,” for the base closure accounts. Refer to the
Exhibit in the Volume 12 Supplemental.

12.2.3. Plan Execution - Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

12.3    Reporting Responsibilities

12.3.1. DoW Components. The DoW Components must prepare and submit reports to the appropriate DFAS site on the status of its allotments. At a minimum, these reports must offer detail for each subaccount specified in a Fund Authorization document provided by OSW (refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental). Submit these reports in accordance with a schedule of due dates to be provided by the DFAS.

12.3.2. Defense Finance and Accounting Service. DFAS must establish base closure accounts with the Treasury and manage associated transactions, such as posting SF 1151 "Nonexpenditure Transfer Authorizations." This function also requires the preparation of various departmental-level reports, including appropriation and fund status reports as mandated by Volume 6, and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) reports for all base closure accounts. Additionally, it involves offering the consolidation of financial reports to produce Treasury Index 97 financial reports on a pass-through basis. This guidance can be supplemented with additional procedures as necessary, subject to the approval of OUSW(C).

12.4    Administration of Base Closure Funds

12.4.1. Appropriated Fund Activities. Expenses, losses, or other events occurring at an appropriated fund activity as a direct result of a DoW base closure action, which result in a cash outlay, are eligible for reimbursement from the applicable DoW Base Closure Account. Expenses, losses, or other events not resulting in a cash outlay by an appropriated fund activity are not eligible for reimbursement. Expenses, losses, or other events that result in a cash outlay (vice expenses, losses, or other events that do not result in a cash outlay) are dependent largely upon the unique circumstances in existence at a particular activity subject to closure. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for general guidance on Expenses that Ordinarily Result in a Cash Outlay and Losses that Do Not Ordinarily Result in a Cash Outlay.

12.4.2. Disposition of DoW Base Closure Assets - Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

title: Section 13.0: Transferring, Disposing, and Leasing of Real Property and Personal Property
content:
13.0    TRANSFERRING, DISPOSING, AND LEASING OF REAL PROPERTY AND PERSONAL PROPERTY

This section provides financial policy for the disposal, transfer, and leasing of real property, as well as the transfer and lease of personal property. Financial policy for the disposal of personal property is addressed in Volume 11.

13.1    Policy

Leases: Non-excess Property and Personal Property. The Secretary of a Military Department may lease non-excess real and personal property under its control that is not needed for a public use for the time that it is leased in accordance with 10 U.S.C. § 2667. 10 U.S.C. § 2667 provides the same authority to the SecWar with respect to property under the control of a Defense Agency. Throughout this section and the corresponding section in the Supplemental, the term "Secretary concerned" will mean the Secretary of a Military Department, with respect to matters concerning that Military Department; and the SecWar, with respect to matters concerning the OSW Components of Defense Field Activities. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

13.2    Reporting Requirements to Congress

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental

title: Section 14.0: Educational Assistance Programs
content:
14.0    EDUCATIONAL ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS

14.1    Overview of Educational Assistance Programs

The DoW provides several Educational Assistance Programs that establish a legally binding entitlement for eligible individuals, including active-duty service members, reservists, survivors, and their dependents. These programs serve the dual purpose of aiding in military recruitment and retention while also facilitating the readjustment of service members to civilian life and providing educational support for their families. While the authorization of these entitlements constitutes a binding contract with the Federal Government, it may require a separate, subsequent appropriation of funds. This section provides specific guidance on the financial operations, transaction recording, and accounting standards for managing these programs, and additional details can be found on the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (DVA) website.

14.1.1. Veterans’ Education Assistance Program (Post-Vietnam). The Veterans’ Education Assistance Program (VEAP) (38 U.S.C. § 3201) is an educational benefit for service members who entered service between January 1977 and June 1985. This program was terminated on April 1, 1987. However, the Services may be required to budget and submit payment for unfunded liabilities as determined by the DoW Board of Actuaries on a year-by-year basis.

14.1.2. Montgomery GI Bill – Active Duty. The Montgomery GI Bill – Active Duty (MGIB-AD) (38 U.S.C. Chapter 30), also known as “Chapter 30,” provides education benefits to veterans and service members who have met the minimum requirements of their obligated period of active duty. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for Eligibility Requirements; Benefits; and Budget Submission Guidance.

14.1.3. Montgomery GI Bill – Selected Reserve. The Montgomery GI Bill Selected Reserve (MGIB-SR) 10 U.S.C. Chapter 1606 program offers up to 36 months of education and training benefits. Refer to 10 U.S.C. § 16132(a). Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for Eligibility Requirements; Period of Entitlement; Benefits; and Budget Submission Guidance.

14.1.4. Post-9/11 GI Bill. The Post-9/11 GI Bill (38 U.S.C. Chapter 33) provides education and job training to qualifying Veterans or members of the Armed Forces who served on active duty after September 10, 2001, and have met the minimum requirements of their obligated period of active duty. The DVA funds the Post-9/11 GI Bill. Such members are also entitled to transfer the Kicker of this benefit to a spouse or dependent children if conditions to transfer the basic benefit are met. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for Eligibility; Benefits; and Budget Submission Guidance.

14.2    Funding for Educational Assistance Programs

The Veterans Educational Assistance Act of 1984 established a trust fund to finance DoW education liabilities on an actuarially sound basis. The DoW Education Benefits Fund (EBF) is a trust fund used to accumulate funds for transfer to the DVA to cover the DoW share of benefits. The DoW funds the MGIB-AD benefits, the MGIB-SR basic and Kicker benefits, and the VEAP benefits. The DoW Office of the Actuary performs actuarial valuations and provides actuarial support and expertise for the EBF. Refer to the Education Benefits Valuation Report, which is updated annually. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for more information and guidance on the fund; payments; transfers; deposits; and Table 14-1 for Active-Duty Critical Skill “Kicker” benefits.

14.3    Fund Transfers of Military Personnel Appropriations

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

14.4    Payroll Deductions

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

14.5    Refunds or Erroneous Deductions from Active-Duty Members

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

14.6 Collection of Educational Debts Owed to the Government by Selected Reserve

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

title: Section 15.0: Military Personnel Entitlement Programs
content:
15.0    MILITARY PERSONNEL ENTITLEMENT PROGRAMS

Entitlement Programs are legally established benefits available to any person or unit of government meeting eligibility requirements established by law. Authorizations for entitlements constitute a binding obligation on the part of the Federal Government, and eligible recipients may have legal recourse if the obligation is not fulfilled. Legislation authorizing entitlements does not necessarily include a corresponding appropriation of funds, thus subsequent enactment of appropriations may be necessary. This section prescribes the accounting policy for three entitlement programs established for DoW military personnel. The entitlement programs are the MRF, the Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund (MERHCF), and the Voluntary Separation Incentive Fund.

15.1    General Accounting Policy for Entitlement Programs

15.1.1. Payment of Benefits. Entitlement programs are divided into three categories according to the events that give rise to benefit payments: payments based on individual eligibility, payments required by law, and reimbursable events. These categories are accounted for as follows:

15.1.1.1. Individual Eligibility. When the program is administered by a federal agency, entitlement benefits based on individuals meeting eligibility requirements of a program must be recorded as a liability and an expense when the eligibility requirements are met (as determined by program officials). The recorded liability and expense must cover all expected payments for the current period of eligibility. Payments to recipients reduce the recorded liability.

15.1.1.2. Compliance with Statutory Laws. When payments are authorized (through appropriation and allotment of funds) for disbursement pursuant to legal requirements with no specific action required of the recipients, a liability and expense must be recorded when the appropriated funds are allotted to the applicable program. The recorded liability and expense must cover the total amount to be disbursed. As payments are made, the liability must be reduced.

15.1.1.3. Reimbursable Events. When payments are based on the occurrence of a specific event for which costs are reimbursable under an entitlement program, a liability must be recorded when the event occurs. If the reimbursement is based on end-of-period reports from program administrators, an estimated amount must be accrued at the end of a reporting period.

15.1.2. Identifiable Refunds. When the expense for payments made under an entitlement program exceeds the appropriation (permissible for certain programs under special statutory authority), the source of the related funds must be clearly identified. If the funds were borrowed, the appropriate liability account must be established.

15.1.3. Suspension of Payments. When substantiated doubt exists on the continued entitlement of a military retiree or annuitant to receive benefit payments and payments on an account are suspended, the DFAS must cease obligating on the subject account for retired pay, retainer pay, or annuitant benefits. Previously obligated amounts must be deobligated to the extent of recoveries on previous payments or amounts held in a suspense account. Although this procedure is directed primarily at suspected death status accounts, it applies equally to other situations that may terminate entitlement. Examples of other situations include (but are not limited to) employment by a foreign government, renouncing U.S. citizenship, remarriage of a surviving spouse, and certain student annuitants dropping out of school.

15.2    Military Retirement Fund

15.2.1. Overview of the Military Retirement Fund

The Military Retirement Fund (MRF) is a statutory trust fund established under 10 U.S.C. §§ 1461–1467 to finance, on an actuarially reasonable basis, the Department of Defense (DoD) and the Coast Guard liabilities for military retired pay and survivor benefit programs. The MRF constitutes an entitlement authority under 2 U.S.C. § 622(9). Authorization of these entitlements represents a binding obligation of the Federal Government and may require subsequent appropriations. This section prescribes the accounting policy applicable to the MRF. Additional statutory and programmatic details are available from the DoD Office of the Actuary (OACT) and the DoD Agency Financial Report.

15.2.2. Military Retirement Fund Structure.

The MRF finances retired pay and survivor benefit liabilities through normal cost contributions, Treasury contributions for unfunded liabilities, and interest earnings on its investments in Treasury securities. The DoD Board of Actuaries approves the actuarial methods and assumptions used to determine the required contributions.

15.2.3. Funding for the Military Retirement Fund The MRF is financed through normal cost contributions—a combination of accrual payments from DoD’s Military Personnel, Reserve Personnel, and National Guard Personnel appropriations, combined with payments from Treasury to finance concurrent receipt—along with Treasury contributions for unfunded liabilities and interest earnings on investments in Treasury securities. The DoD Office of the Actuary, under the direction and oversight of the DoD Board of Actuaries, performs actuarial valuations and determines contribution requirements to ensure the fund balance remains actuarially reasonable.

15.2.4. Normal Cost Contributions

Funds the present value of future pension benefits accrued during the year. Amounts payable to the MRF must be determined using actuarial methods and assumptions approved by the DoD Board of Actuaries. These contributions consist of accruing cost payments from DoD and contributions from Treasury to finance concurrent receipt. DoD Components must include sufficient funds in MILPERS budgets to meet their required contributions.

15.2.5. Unfunded Liability Contributions

Treasury contributions for unfunded liabilities must be determined using actuarial methods approved by the DoD Board of Actuaries and deposited to the MRF in accordance with statutory requirements.

15.2.6. Investment of Fund Balances

MRF balances not needed for current payments must be invested in Treasury securities, consistent with 10 U.S.C. § 1467.

15.2.7. Accounting Requirements

Liabilities must be recorded consistent with federal accounting standards, including SFFAS 5 and SFFAS 33. DFAS must prepare trust fund financial statements in accordance with Volume
6A.

15.2.8. Administrative and Operational Requirements

Additional guidance on accrual calculations, obligations, transfers, investment workflows, and reporting requirements is contained in the Volume 12 Supplemental

15.3    Medicare‑Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund

15.3.1. MERHCF Purpose

Overview of the Medicare‑Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund

The Medicare‑Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund (MERHCF) is a statutory trust fund established under 10 U.S.C. §§ 1111–1117 to finance, on an actuarially reasonable basis, uniformed services retiree health care liabilities for Medicare‑eligible beneficiaries, including dependents and survivors. MERHCF constitutes an entitlement authority under 2 U.S.C. § 622(9). Authorization of these entitlements represents a binding obligation of the Federal Government and may require subsequent appropriations.
