This section prescribes the accounting policy applicable to MERHCF. Additional statutory and programmatic details are available from the DoD Office of the Actuary (OACT) and the DoD Agency Financial Report.

15.3.2. MERHCF Structure - MERHCF finances Medicare‑eligible retiree health care liabilities through normal cost contributions, Treasury contributions for unfunded liabilities, and interest earnings on investments in Treasury securities. The DoD Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care (MERHC) Board of Actuaries approves the actuarial methods and assumptions used to determine required contributions.

15.3.3. Funding for the Medicare‑Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund

MERHCF is financed through normal cost contributions from Military Personnel, Reserve Personnel, and National Guard Personnel appropriations; Treasury contributions for unfunded liabilities; and interest earnings on investments in Treasury securities. The DoD Office of the Actuary, under the direction an oversight of the DoD MERHC Board of Actuaries, performs actuarial valuations and determines contribution requirements to ensure the fund remains actuarially reasonable.

15.3.3.1. Normal Cost Contributions - Normal cost contributions must be based on per‑capita rates developed by the DoD Office of the Actuary and approved by the DoD MERHC Board of Actuaries. DoD Components must include sufficient funds in MILPERS budgets to meet required contribution levels.

15.3.3.2. Unfunded Liability Contributions - Treasury contributions for unfunded liabilities must be determined using actuarial methods approved by the DoD MERHC Board of Actuaries and deposited to MERHCF in accordance with statutory requirements.

15.3.3.3. Investment of Fund Balances - MERHCF balances not needed for current payments must be invested in Treasury securities, consistent with 10 U.S.C. § 1113.

15.3.3.4. Accounting Requirements - Liabilities must be recorded consistent with federal accounting standards, including SFFAS 5 and SFFAS 33. DFAS must prepare trust fund financial statements in accordance with Volume 6A.

15.3.4. Administrative and Operational Requirements

Additional guidance on accrual calculations, obligations, transfers, reimbursements, investment workflows, and reporting requirements is contained in the Volume 12 Supplemental.

15.3.5. Responsibilities

15.3.5.1. Assistant Secretary of War for Health Affairs (ASW(HA)). Approves and issues procedures for the management and operation of MERHCF and provides guidance and operational direction to the Defense Health Agency (DHA).

15.3.5.2. Director, DHA. Implements DoW policy for MERHCF, directs reviews of legislative changes for potential impacts, and oversees execution reviews.

15.3.5.3. Department of War Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care Board of Actuaries. Provides advice on actuarial matters, reviews actuarial valuations of MERHCF, and reports annually on its actuarial status to the Secretary of War, and not less than once every four years (quadrennial report), to the President and Congress.

15.3.5.4. Chief Actuary, DoW Office of the Actuary. The DoW Office of the Actuary (OATC), Chief Actuary, reports on the actuarial status of MERHCF, provides cost estimates to OMB and participating Services, and reviews legislative changes for actuarial impact.

15.3.5.5. USW(C). The USW(C) prepares the total unfunded liability amortization payment plus the total normal cost contribution for certification by the Secretary of War to the Secretary of the Treasury.

15.3.5.6. Director, DFAS. Manages MERHCF’s investments, establishes the necessary accounts, develops financial management processes, performs accounting, reports financial activities for required financial statements, and supports financial audits.

15.3.5.7. Secretaries of the Military Departments. Provide personnel data as requested and conduct all fund transfers, accounting, reconciliation, and other administration relating to the operation of MERHCF.

15.3.5.8. Administering Secretaries for the Participating Uniformed Services. The Administering Secretaries for the participating Uniformed Services include the Secretary of Homeland Security (for USCG) and the Secretary of Health and Human Services for PHS and NOAA. The Administering Secretaries for the participating Uniformed Services calculate and transfer their normal cost contributions to MERHCF and provide personnel data as requested.

15.3.6. MERHCF Accounts

The DoW MERHCF (097X5472, “Department of War, Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund”) is classified as a Special Fund and uses specific receipt, expenditure, and investment accounts. Amounts deposited are immediately available for investment, payment of benefits, and administrative costs. DFAS is responsible for making amounts available from the fund to cover all qualifying expenses.

15.3.7. MERHCF Assets

15.3.7.1. Contributions. Payment from DoW appropriations and other uniformed services (USCG, NOAA, and PHS), and the Treasury to fund future benefits.

15.3.7.2. Unfunded Actuarial Liability Payment. Payments from a permanent indefinite general fund appropriation, 097X0850, to fund future benefits payable from MERHCF attributable to service rendered prior to October 1, 2002 (i.e., the unfunded actuarial liability), and to cover actuarial gains and losses.

15.3.7.3. Investment Income. Income earned on the invested portion of the fund.

15.3.7.4. Return of Prospective Payment Transfers. Amounts returned to the fund that were previously transferred but found to be in excess of what was needed.

15.3.8. Accounting for MERHCF Revenues

DFAS records investment earnings. All contributions from DoW, other uniformed services, and the Treasury must be based on determinations by the DoW OACT under methods approved by the DoW MERHCF Board. Prior to each fiscal year, the Secretary of War shall certify the amortization payment and normal cost contributions due to the fund.

15.3.9. Reimbursements of Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care

The Fiscal Year 2005 National Defense Authorization Act provides permanent, indefinite appropriations from the Treasury to finance the cost of Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care (MERHC) accruals beginning in fiscal year 2006, rather than from MILPERS annual appropriations. Therefore, the per capita normal cost for MERHC accruals is not billable to other DoW Agencies or Federal Agencies. However, under 22 U.S.C. § 2761(a)(1)(C) of the Arms Export Control Act, these costs must be included in the rate billed to foreign countries or international organizations for the sale of defense services. These reimbursements must be deposited into the Treasury Miscellaneous Receipts account 304100.

15.3.10. Investment of MERHCF Cash Balances

DFAS is responsible for investing cash balances of MERHCF not required to meet current withdrawals. Investments are limited to Market-Based U.S. Government Special Securities issued by the Treasury. The income on such investments must be credited to receipt account 097X5472.002, “Earnings on Investments, DoW Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund,” and form a part of MERHCF.

15.3.11. Accounting for MERHCF Outlays

15.3.11.1. DFAS must make amounts available from the fund for payment of qualifying expenses. These expenses fall into two categories:

15.3.11.1.1. Purchased Care. Healthcare purchased from non-DoW providers.

15.3.11.1.2. Direct Care. Healthcare services provided to Medicare-eligible beneficiaries directly in DHA MTFs.

15.3.11.2. DHA determines the annual prospective payment amounts required from the fund for these categories. These amounts are based on the estimated costs of providing services to Medicare-eligible beneficiaries. Throughout the year of execution, an execution review is conducted to compare prospective payments against the earnings from the actual care provided. An established 10% variance threshold governs this reconciliation. Variances falling within this +/- 10% threshold are mutually waived. For variances that exceed the threshold, only the amount of the variance in excess of the 10% band is reconciled through adjustments to future prospective payment calculations. The results of this review are used to inform future fund requirements, and funds determined to be in excess of requirements may be returned to the MERHCF in accordance with 10 U.S.C. § 1113.

15.3.12. MERHCF Financial Reporting Requirements

DFAS is responsible for preparing all required financial reports for MERHCF, including the SF 133 (Report on Budget Execution and Budgetary Resources), the Status of Funds report, and all Federal financial statements as required by OMB Circular No. A-136 to support the DoW Agency-wide financial statements. The financial statements must recognize a liability for the present value of future MERHC benefits for eligible participants.

15.4    Voluntary Separation Incentive Fund

15.4.1. Overview of the Voluntary Separation Incentive Fund

15.4.1.1. The Voluntary Separation Incentive (VSI) Fund was established under
Section 662 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Years 1992 and 1993 (Public Law 102‑190) to finance VSI payments on an actuarially reasonable basis. VSI provides annual payments to eligible active‑duty Service members with more than six but fewer than 20 years of service who voluntarily separate during authorized force‑shaping periods. Authorization of these benefits constitutes a binding obligation of the Federal Government and may require subsequent appropriations. This section prescribes the accounting policy applicable to the VSI Fund. Additional statutory and programmatic details are available from the Department of Defense Office of the Actuary (OACT).

15.4.1.2 VSI Benefit Structure - VSI payments are annual installments paid for twice the number of years of active service. The DoD Board of Actuaries determines actuarial assumptions and required amortization payments to ensure the VSI Fund remains actuarially reasonable using OACT as the operational organization performing the calculations.

15.4.2. Funding for the VSI Fund

The VSI Fund finances VSI liabilities through amortization payments and interest earnings on Treasury securities. The DoD Office of the Actuary performs an annual actuarial valuation and determines the required amortization amount to ensure the fund remains actuarially reasonable.

15.4.2.1 Amortization Payments - DoD Components must include sufficient funds in Military Personnel appropriations to make required amortization payments to the VSI Fund. Amortization amounts must be determined using actuarial methods and assumptions set by the DoD Board of Actuaries and must be obligated and transferred consistent with statutory requirements.

15.4.2.2 Investment of Fund Balances - VSI Fund balances not needed for current payments must be invested in Treasury securities, consistent with statutory requirements governing DoD trust funds. Interest earnings must be credited to the VSI Fund and used to finance future benefit liabilities.

15.4.2.3 Accounting Requirements - Liabilities must be recorded consistent with federal accounting standards, including SFFAS 5 and SFFAS 33. DFAS must prepare trust fund financial statements for the VSI Fund in accordance with Volume 6A.

15.4.3. Administrative and Operational Requirements

Additional guidance on amortization payments, investment workflows, and reporting requirements is contained in the Volume 7 Military Pay Policy.

title: Section 16.0: DoW Rewards Program
content:
16.0    DOW REWARDS PROGRAM

16.1    Responsibilities

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

16.2    Implementing the Program in the Field

16.2.1. Rewardable Information. Eligible persons may receive a reward for providing information or non-lethal assistance that benefits (1) an operational activity of U.S. or allied forces in combined operations against international terrorism outside the U.S. or (2) force protection of U.S. or allied forces in combined operations.

16.2.2. Payment Approval Amounts. Tactical Rewards Officers can authorize rewards up to $10,000. A Combatant Commander (CCDR) is permitted to approve rewards up to $1,000,000. For rewards greater than $1,000,000 and up to $2,000,000, approval from the USW Policy (USW(P)) is necessary. Rewards exceeding $2,000,000 but not surpassing $5,000,000 require the authorization of the SecWar or the Deputy SecWar, or, through a separate written delegation, the USW(P). Statutorily, if any proposed reward (whether pre-approved or otherwise) exceeds $2,000,000, consultation with the Secretary of State is mandated for the SecWar. Table 1 in DoDI O-3000.13 outlines these approval limits. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for further guidance on approving officials; approval level; rewards lists; payments; coordination; and requests for additional funds.

16.3    Policy

16.3.1. Allocation of Funds. The USW(C)/CFO will ensure DoW funds for the Rewards Program (RP) are correctly allocated to WHS for control and execution. Geographic combatant commanders will inform the Director, Joint Staff of any necessary inter-theater fund allocations.

16.3.2. Improper Usage of Funds. U.S. citizens, officers or employees of the U.S. federal, state, or local government, or employees of a U.S. Government contractor are not eligible for rewards under the DoW RP. CCDRs should be cautious about rewarding foreign security force members due to potential risks such as extortion, corruption, negative perceptions, or undermining U.S. law or DoW human rights policies related to training and equipping foreign security forces. The USW(P) can grant exceptions to this rule for specific countries and will review these waivers annually. Requests for such approvals should be directed to the Assistant Secretary of War for Special Operations/Low-Intensity Conflict (ASW SO/LIC). Previously approved waivers remained valid under this guidance.

16.3.3. Delivery, Transporting and Safeguarding of Funds. Any funds made available for the DoW RP will be delivered, transported, and safeguarded consistent with Volume 5.

16.3.4. Appointment of Paying Agents. The Disbursing Officer will appoint Paying Agents responsible for delivering funds under the DoW RP in accordance with Volume 5. Allied forces members will receive the same training as U.S. paying agents and sign a statement of understanding. Since the DoW cannot hold foreign nationals and other non-U.S. citizens pecuniarily liable for fund losses, the appointing authority must carefully consider the necessity and risk when appointing them as paying agents. The responsible agent must record all funds given to and returned by allied forces paying agents on DD Form 1081, “Statement of Agent’s Officer’s Account,” as specified in Volume 5. Upon completing authorized payments, the paying agent must return the paid vouchers, negotiable instruments, and any remaining funds to the disbursing officer along with a properly filled out DD Form 1081.

16.3.5. Documentation of Payments. DoW RP payments will be executed and recorded in accordance with Volume 5 and Volume 10.

16.3.6. Circumventing Limits. The DoW prohibits circumventing monetary limits and approval requirements by dividing a single reward into multiple smaller rewards or by other methods. However, the DoW allows splitting payments of approved expenses for administrative purposes (for instance, paying a vendor 50 percent at the start of a project and the remaining 50 percent upon completion).

16.3.7. Clearance of Accounts. The DoW Component must clear accounts maintained under the RP consistent with Volume 5.

16.3.8. Certification of Payments. Payments made under the DoW RP will be certified in a manner consistent with Volume 5.

16.3.9. Audits and Program Reviews. The DoW RP will undergo periodic audits by internal bodies like the DoW Inspector General and other audit agencies, as well as external groups such as the Government Accountability Office and congressional oversight committees. Officials managing the RP must cooperate fully with these reviews, audits, or investigations.

16.4 Payments and Rewards through Government Personnel of Allied Forces

Execution of Rewards through Allied Government Personnel. The SecWar, geographic combatant commanders, and all delegated officials may use their authorities to offer and make rewards, acting through government personnel of allied forces. However, they may not pay rewards through allied government officials after the payment date authorized by 10 U.S.C. § 127b. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for information on payment requests; appointments of paying agents; and limitations.

16.5    Information Dissemination

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

16.6    Reports and Notifications

16.6.1. Annual Report. According to 10 U.S.C. § 127b, by February 1 each year, the SecWar must report to the Senate and House Armed Services Committees on the administration of the RP for the previous fiscal year. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

16.6.2. Report on Designation of Countries for which Rewards may be Paid. Within 15 days of designating a country for operations or activities eligible for rewards under this section, the SecWar must report to the Senate and House Armed Services Committees. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

16.7    Waivers

16.7.1. Requests for Waivers or Exceptions to Law. A DoW Component must submit requests for waivers or exceptions to any provision of law that would otherwise prohibit, restrict, limit, or constrain the execution of the reward program through ASW SO/LIC, the USW(C)/CFO, and DoW General Counsel to the SecWar for approval.

16.7.2. Requests for Waivers or Exceptions to Guidance. A DoW Component must submit requests for waivers or exceptions to this guidance through ASW SO/LIC to the USW(C)/CFO for approval.

title: Section 17.0: Food Service Program Responsibilities
content:
17.0    FOOD SERVICE PROGRAM RESPONSIBILITIES
In accordance with 37 U.S.C. § 1011, the SecWar must establish meal rates for all personnel authorized to dine at military messes, including uniformed members, civilian employees, retirees, and their dependents. The OUSW(C) is responsible for the financial management policy herein and must establish these rates annually. The primary purpose of these rates is to ensure full reimbursement to the concerned appropriations for both food costs and operating expenses. However, the Secretary may reduce a meal rate by the amount attributable to operating expenses when the Secretary determines it is in the best interest of the United States. The policies in this section govern the specific meal charges for all classes of diners, and all DoW Components must implement them. DFAS is responsible for developing the necessary implementation procedures. DoW Components may not issue policies that supplement this guidance without prior written approval from the OUSW(C). The OUSW(C) publishes official rates on its reimbursable rates website.

17.1    Reimbursable Meals and Meal Service (Operating) Charges

The provisions of this section must be used to determine use of the DoW discount meal rate (the cost of the food only) or the DoW standard meal rate (the cost of both the food and the non-training/readiness food service operating expenses). Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for available meal services.

17.2    Meal Charges

Reimbursement charges for persons authorized to eat in an appropriated fund dining facility vary depending on the status of each person. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for more information on the five major categories of personnel: officers; enlisted personnel; military dependents; Federal civilian employees; and others.

17.3    General Provisions

17.3.1. Personnel, Other Than Enlisted Personnel. Personnel, other than enlisted personnel, may receive a meal from an appropriated fund dining facility, provided no increase in direct resources results from feeding such personnel and appropriate meal charges are collected consistent with paragraph 17.2.

17.3.2. Commanding Officer Responsibility. The commanding officer of the DoW installation, at which an appropriated fund dining facility is located, is responsible for assuring that meals are provided only to authorized personnel within the capabilities and availability of existing appropriated fund dining facilities.

17.3.3. Temporary Duty Orders. Temporary duty orders must indicate the food allowance/per diem status of travelers to assist in determining the appropriate meal charge to be assessed.

17.3.4. Service Academies. Service academies (i.e., Army, Navy, and Air Force) are to use the food service charges contained within the DoW Reimbursable Rates, “Food Service Charges at Appropriated Fund Dining Facilities.

17.3.5. Civilian and Military Personnel of a Foreign Government. Civilian and military personnel of a foreign government must furnish meals in accordance with specific arrangements made between the U.S. Government and the foreign government. Charges for food costs and related food service operating expenses must be made on the same basis as they would be for U.S. Government personnel of equal rank.

17.4    Disposition of Funds

Each Military Service is responsible for the program, budget, and accounting for obligations, expenditures, revenues, and food service operating expenses and all meals in accordance with this section. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for Recording; Collections; and Discounted and Standard Meal Rate Distribution.

17.5    Accounting for Food Allowances

17.5.1. Information Requirements. Information requirements have been established to ensure that data are maintained, and that information is reported for use in determining and administering food allowances. These requirements prescribe procedures for counting meals furnished to personnel in appropriated fund dining facilities under the daily food allowance and authorized reimbursable programs. They are designed to assist in monitoring food costs and allowances and making the accumulation of data more consistent throughout the Department under the Food Service Program established by DoDM 1338.10.

17.5.1.1. The recording and reporting of obligations/expenditures against the daily food allowance portion of the operations and maintenance appropriations are as set forth in Volumes 2 and 3.

17.5.1.2. The data reported must support budget requests based on furnishing meals to entitled enlisted personnel by each Military Service, after consideration of the absentee rate, without regard to the member’s parent Military Service.

17.5.2. Counting the Number of Persons’ Furnished Meals. Except for mass feeding situations as set forth in the Volume 12 Supplemental, all personnel authorized to eat in appropriated fund dining facilities must identify themselves with a meal card, DoW Common Access card, or travel orders issued by a DoW Component before receiving a meal from the dining facility. Enlisted personnel on Basic Allowance Subsistence or receiving the meal portion of per diem, as well as all officers, civilian employees, official visitors, dependents, and guests authorized to eat on a reimbursable basis, must be required to identify themselves as to the category of entitlement (authorized to eat on a reimbursable basis) and status (per diem or non-per diem). They must reimburse DoW at the appropriate meal rate before receiving a meal from an appropriated fund dining facility. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for more information.

17.6    Food Service Operating Expense Reporting Requirements
The OUSW(C) P/B Office establishes meal rates annually for personnel authorized meals on a reimbursable basis. The Military Services are required, in coordination with OUSW(C), to report the cost of food served to service members and food service operating expenses.

title: Section 18.0: Military Academy Dining Hall Operations
content:
18.0    MILITARY ACADEMY DINING HALL OPERATIONS
18.1    Policy

This section promulgates the policy that implements 37 U.S.C. § 422 which authorizes funding for the operation of cadet and midshipmen dining halls at the military academies and prescribes associated reporting requirements.

18.1.1. Authorization Determination: Each Military Department operates an academy dining hall to provide complete food service support to the cadets or midshipmen as an integral part of the activities of its academy.

18.1.1.1. The superintendent of each academy is authorized to determine who may be authorized to eat in the academy dining hall and the regulations incident thereto within guidelines issued by the secretary of the cognizant Military Department.

18.1.1.2. Charges for meals furnished to other than cadets and midshipmen will be established by the Under Secretary of War (Comptroller) (USW(C)) and the reimbursable rate for “Food Service” issued annually.

18.1.1.3. All collections for food costs must be deposited into the nonappropriated fund described in subparagraph 8.1.2.2. The charge for operating expenses will be collected and deposited under the same rules that are applicable to appropriated fund food service activities as prescribed by Section 17.

18.1.2. Subsistence Allowance Amount

18.1.2.1. The SecWar prescribes the amount of the subsistence allowance for cadets and midshipmen.

18.1.2.2. The amount prescribed is allocated by the Military Departments from the current military personnel appropriation to a nonappropriated fund at each academy based on the number of cadets and midshipmen present for training.

18.1.2.2.1. Each nonappropriated fund is used to procure the food and food products necessary to provide subsistence for the cadets and midshipmen.

18.1.2.2.2. Nonappropriated funds must be established as a NAFI and administered as a Program Group V – Supplemental Mission Fund in accordance with DoWI 1015.15.

18.1.2.2.3. The nonappropriated fund must be audited in accordance with DoWI 7600.06 if the annual revenues in the fund exceed the threshold established therein.

18.1.2.2.4. The nonappropriated fund must not be used for any purpose other than subsistence procurement. All other charges associated with dining service must be charged against appropriated funds.

18.1.3. Subsistence Allowance – Leave Status

The subsistence allowance that is not earned for any cadet or midshipman on leave or otherwise away from the academy, and not subsisted at Government expense, will be credited to the cadet/midshipman’s pay account.

18.1.4. Subsistence Allowance – Temporary Duty Status

The subsistence allowance that is not earned for any cadet or midshipman on temporary duty, and subsistence-in-kind that is furnished at the temporary duty location, will not be collected by the nonappropriated fund.

18.2    Responsibilities and Reporting Requirements

18.2.1. Internal Control and Procurement Requirements. Under overall policy supervision by the secretary of the cognizant Military Department, the superintendent of each academy is responsible for:

18.2.1.1. Assuring the efficient and effective management of the academy dining hall and its NAF for the purchase of subsistence items. In connection with this responsibility, the superintendent must install an accrual accounting system that permits an objective, constructive evaluation of the dining hall operation.

18.2.1.2. Assuring that the procurement procedures maintain the same degree of integrity as those procurement actions taken in accordance with the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR). In the event any question arises regarding the proper procurement procedure, the FAR will be used as a guide.

18.2.2. Reporting Requirements. An annual report on meal operating expenses in the military academy dining halls should be submitted in accordance with the guidance contained in Volume 11.

18.3    Annual Reimbursable Rates

The annual reimbursable rates for military academy dining halls are located on the USW(C) public website, listed by Fiscal Year (FY) under the following headings: Financial Management, Reports, DoW Reimbursable Rates.

title: Section 19.0: Financial Management for Defense Health Program Resources
content:
19.0    FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT FOR DEFENSE HEALTH PROGRAM RESOURCES

19.1    General

19.1.1. The Defense Health Program (DHP) appropriation (Treasury Federal Account Symbols and Titles (FAST) 0970130) funds medical operations of the Defense Health Agency (DHA) and the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences (USUHS); and consists of Operation and Maintenance (O&M), RDT&E, and Procurement funds.

19.1.2. The DHP does not fund military medical personnel costs or operational healthcare for field/numbered medical units, hospital ships, and shipboard medical operations. Funding for operational healthcare remains the responsibility of the Military Departments.

19.1.3. Military Construction (MILCON) is a separate appropriation, however, the Assistant Secretary of War for Health Affairs (ASW(HA)) executes and reports on MILCON for medical facilities as part of DHP's financial statements.

19.2    Responsibilities

19.2.1. The ASW(HA) is the DHP funds holder. ASW(HA) allots budget authority, issues execution policy, develops the Unified Medical Program, and enters into reimbursable agreements with other federal agencies. The ASW(HA) exercises authority, direction, and control over the DHA and USUHS, and any other subordinate officials that may be assigned.

19.2.2. The Deputy Assistant Secretary of War, Health Resources Management and Policy, serves as the DHP Senior Accountable Official, overseeing financial reporting, internal controls, and execution policy in accordance with all applicable laws and regulations.

19.2.3. Military Departments and Combatant Commands (CCMD) are responsible for engaging with ASW(HA) for the advance planning and coordination of mission expansions or force restructurings that result in increased demand on DHP resources. Changes that were not programmed for within the DHP may result in requirements being under-resourced. Military Departments and CCMDs will generally be responsible for transferring sufficient funds to the DHP to support increased demands on DHP healthcare resources, documented in a corresponding Memorandum of Agreement, and properly integrated by the DHP during normal programming cycles.

19.3    Expenses Chargeable to the DHP

See Volume 12 Supplemental Procedures for additional items.

19.3.1. Civilian Payroll. Civilian payroll for personnel assigned to DHA and USUHS.

19.3.2. Communications and Utilities. Charge DHP for telephone services and other communication services that support the medical mission. Charge DHP for utilities obtained from commercial sources and all base-produced utilities. Utilities include fuel for heating and cooling.

19.3.3. Immunizations Funded with DHP:

19.3.3.1. Routine Vaccines: These are vaccines required to maintain warfighters (including expeditionary civilians) in a "Fully Medically Ready" status, in accordance with DoDI 6025.19, ASW(HA) policy, and DHA immunizations guidance. All warfighters are required to have these vaccines regardless of deployment status.

19.3.3.2. Directed (Pre-Deployment): These are vaccines directed by CCMDs and approved by ASW(HA) for an imminent deployment.

19.3.3.3. Immunizations for PCS: Vaccines required and approved by ASW(HA) for entry into a specific geographic Area of Responsibility (AOR) will be provided to warfighters and their eligible dependents.

19.3.3.4. Immunizations for Leisure Travel: Provided at no cost to Service members/ dependents. Provided on a reimbursable basis to civilian employees.

19.3.3.5. Immunizations for the Activated and Inactivated Reserve Component (RC): Effective FY 2027, RC Service members may obtain those vaccines required to maintain their “Fully Medically Ready” status, in accordance with DoDI 6025.19, ASW(HA) policy, and DHA immunizations guidance. MTFs must provide the vaccines on a non-reimbursable basis.

19.3.4. Autopsies and Forensic Pathology Investigations. The Armed Forces Medical Examiner, funded through the DHP appropriation, conducts autopsies and forensic pathology investigations under the authority of 10 U.S.C. § 1471 and in accordance with DoDI 5154.30.

19.3.5. TRICARE Contracts. 10 U.S.C. § 1079 authorizes TRICARE contracts for spouses’ and children’s medical care; 10 U.S.C. § 1086 authorizes health benefits for certain members, former members, and their dependents; 10 U.S.C. § 1097 authorizes medical care for retirees, dependents, and survivors (alternative delivery of healthcare). 10 U.S.C. § 1092 authorizes studies and demonstration projects relating to the delivery of health and medical care.

19.3.6. Sustainment, Restoration, and Modernization (SRM). SRM of DHA MTFs and
USUHS.

19.3.7. Healthcare Services Contracts. Personal and non-personal healthcare service contracts supporting the DHA, MTFs, or USUHS. Healthcare provider personal service contracts follow the terms and restrictions in Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS) 237.104 (b)(ii), and DoDI 6025.5, “Personal Services Contracts (PCSs) for Health Care Providers (HCPs).”

19.3.8. Hyperbaric and Hypobaric Chambers. Chambers used for clinical treatment. DHP does not fund chambers used for aircrew physiological training.

19.4    Expenses Not Chargeable to the DHP

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for additional items.

19.4.1. Transportation of Human Remains.

19.4.2. Non-prescription Items. DHP does not fund non-prescription items such as sunscreen, hand sanitizer, lip balm, and tissue for distribution to non-DHP-funded organizations. These are personal expense items. DHP can only fund these items (e.g., hand sanitizer, masks) for staff and patients within DHP-funded organizations.

19.4.3. Veterinary Services Provided to Privately-Owned Pets. Installation Veterinary Services’ primary purpose is to provide healthcare to DoW working animals. DoW veterinary clinics may provide some services to pets but must ensure that costs for DoW working animals are segregated from those provided to pets. Typically, Non-Appropriated Fund Instrumentalities (NAFI) must cover the expenses related to pets and proportionately share in the costs of custodial services and utilities, consistent with DoDI 1015.15.

19.4.4. Clothing, Supplies, or Equipment for Contingency or Other Military Operations. Military Departments or other appropriations that fund the contingency must fund these expenses.

19.4.5. Contingency Support Medical Activities. Military Department or other contingency appropriations must fund:

19.4.5.1. Deployed medical facilities and biological/chemical warfare medical supplies deployed with personnel.

19.4.5.2. Pre-deployment, employment, and redeployment of medical combat support personnel, equipment, and supplies.

19.4.5.3. Immunizations carried by personnel for potential use during the deployment.

19.4.6. Medical Care at Deployed Locations for Exercises and Contingencies. Charge costs to Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS)/CCMD exercise or contingency funds. Include medical care provided to members at local indigenous medical facilities, medical supplies (e.g., pharmaceuticals, orthopedic braces), and urgent/emergency care at the deployed location.

19.4.7. Medical Participation in JCS/CCMD Exercises. Charge JCS/CCMD Exercise funds for the deployment of medical personnel, the cost of supplies used during the exercise, shipping, and the resupply cost of supplies upon return.

19.4.8. Aeromedical Evacuation (AE) Airlift in Support of Peacetime and Contingency Operations. AE airlift is not a DHP expense. Per the FY 2021 President’s Budget, these funds are managed by the Air Force for both peacetime (including Special Assignment Airlift Missions and contingency operations. During contingency operations, the appropriation funding the contingency will be charged for the AE contingency airlift (from contingency area to first overseas MTF). Air Force O&M funds pay only those AE contingency airlift costs billed by the Transportation Working Capital Fund (WCF) from the first overseas fixed MTF to CONUS. After the contingency designation is formally withdrawn, Air Force O&M funds then become responsible for all future AE airlift costs from that former contingency area.

19.4.9. Automated External Defibrillators and Naloxone. AEDs and Naloxone for installation use outside of the MTF (e.g., for fire and security personnel) are funded by the requesting organization. Funds provided to the local MTF Medical Logistics office by the requesting organization enable the MTF to procure the item on behalf of the requesting organization on a reimbursable basis.

19.4.10. Humanitarian Assistance and Civic Assistance. Per 10 U.S.C. § 401 and DoDI 2205.02, in specific instances, humanitarian civic assistance activities may be provided in conjunction with authorized military operations of the Armed Forces. Commanders ensure that expenses providing humanitarian civic assistance to a foreign country are paid for out of funds specifically appropriated for such purpose.

19.4.11. Military Spiritual Resiliency Programs. The DHP does not fund Military Department chaplain resiliency programs and initiatives. Funding is the responsibility of the Military Departments.

19.4.12. Health and Wellness Centers, Fitness Staff, and Athletic Trainers. Military Department appropriations fund wellness center exercise equipment, appliances for healthy cooking demonstrations, supplies, facilities, maintenance, and support staff. Military Department also funds fitness staff, athletic trainers, health and wellness educators, health promotions staff, etc., assigned to units, installation gymnasiums, or health and wellness centers.

19.4.13. Miscellaneous Non-clinical Programs. The DHP does not fund Military Department non-clinical programs designed to enhance general readiness and performance. This includes activities like physical fitness, unit teambuilding, mindfulness training, and other resilience efforts that occur outside of a medical setting and are not part of a formal treatment plan for a health condition.

19.4.14. Tactical Combat Casualty Care. Military Department fully fund and support trauma training and skills sustainment platforms (hospital and pre-hospital) to include installation, workforce, equipment, and information technology. See DoDI 1322.24, “Medical Readiness Training.”

19.5    Other Healthcare Accounting Matters

Refer to Volume 12 Supplemental for the full list.

19.5.1. Sexual Assault Prevention and Response (SAPR). The Director, DoW Human Resource Activity (DHRA) manages the Defense-wide O&M appropriation that funds the SAPR program. The Military Departments, OSW, JCS, DSCA, U.S. Special Operations Command, DHA, and DHRA are allocated funds supporting SAPR activities. Multiple Program Elements (PE) execute funds.

19.5.2. Integrated Primary Prevention. The Military Departments and DHA receive Defense-wide O&M to prevent self-directed harm and prohibited abusive or harmful acts including, sexual assault, harassment, suicide, retaliation, domestic abuse, and child abuse. These efforts include prevention strategy development, policy, oversight, manpower, research, programs, evaluation, and training.

19.5.3. Suicide Prevention. The Defense-wide O&M appropriation funds suicide prevention efforts. Military Departments and DHA receive funds. Multiple PEs fund these efforts.

19.5.4. Drug Demand Reduction Program/Urinalysis Program. The Defense-wide Counternarcotic appropriation funds routine drug testing of military personnel and civilian employees. The Deputy Assistant SecWar for Counternarcotics and Stabilization Policy within the OUSW for Policy manages the program. Multiple PEs execute funding.

19.5.5. Family Advocacy Program. The Defense-wide O&M appropriation funds the Family Advocacy Program (FAP). The FAP addresses domestic abuse, child abuse and neglect, and harmful behaviors between children and youth.

19.6    Uniform Billing Office Operations

19.6.1. The DHP has statutory authority to bill and collect for healthcare services. Collections stem primarily from three distinct reimbursement programs:

19.6.1.1. Third-Party Collections (TPC) Program. 10 U.S.C. § 1095 established the TPC program. For beneficiaries with health insurance other than TRICARE, MTFs and TRICARE submit claims to health insurance companies for care provided to DoW beneficiaries. Collections must be deposited in the current O&M appropriations of the MTF that provided the care.

19.6.1.2. Medical Services Account (MSA) Program. The MSA program involves billing and collection for medical and dental services provided to a wide range of patients, including other government agencies, DoW civilian employees and contractors, employees of NAFs or DoW schools, Secretarial designees, authorized foreign military members, and civilian emergency patients. The MSA is governed by multiple authorities, including 10 U.S.C. § 1074a, 10 U.S.C. § 1079b, 10 U.S.C. § 1085, 14 U.S.C. § 506, and 38 U.S.C. § 8111.

19.6.1.2.1. Collections from the U.S. Coast Guard. In lieu of the reimbursement required under 10 U.S.C. § 1085, the Secretary of Homeland Security, as per 14 U.S.C. § 506, makes prospective payment for the actuarial valuation of treatment that MTFs provide to current and former members of the Coast Guard, and their dependents.

19.6.1.2.2. Collections from the Department of Veterans Affairs. DoW and the VA established agreements under the authority of 38 U.S.C. § 8111 permitting the VA to reimburse DoW for healthcare services provided to VA beneficiaries. Collections must be deposited in the current O&M appropriations of the MTF that provided the care.

19.6.1.3. Medical Affirmative Claims (MAC) Program. 42 U.S.C. § 2651 – 2653 and 10 U.S.C. § 1095 govern the MAC program and authorizes DoW to recover expenses from liable third parties for medical care costs incurred on behalf of covered beneficiaries.

19.6.2. MHS Modified Payment and Waiver Program (MPWP). Pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 1079b, the MPWP provides financial relief for medical bills incurred by civilian non- beneficiaries treated in MTF on or after June 21, 2023. The program features an income-based sliding fee scale, a catastrophic fee waiver to prevent severe financial harm, and a discretionary waiver based on the readiness value of the care provided. All patient applications for financial relief under this authority are centrally processed and adjudicated by the DHA's Debt Adjudication Office. Discretionary waivers of $600 or more require reporting to the Internal Revenue Service and issuance of a Form 1099-C (prepared by DHA).

19.7 DHP Budget Activity Groups (BAGS) and Program Elements (PE) Structure

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

title: Section 20.0: Contingency Operations
content:
20.0    CONTINGENCY OPERATIONS

20.1    General Guidance

20.1.1. This chapter promulgates financial policy for small, medium, and large-scale campaign level military contingency operations related to the Department of War (DoW). These might include, but are not limited to, support for peacekeeping operations, foreign disaster relief (FDR) efforts, and noncombatant evacuation operations (NEO). Note that the term “contingency operation,” as used in this chapter, is more encompassing than the specific definition contained in 10 U.S.C. § 101(a), paragraph 13. Explicitly excluded from this chapter are peacetime civil emergencies occurring within the United States, the guidance for which is included in DoDD 3025.18, “Defense Support of Civil Authorities (DSCA).” Also excluded from this chapter are steady-state DoW humanitarian assistance activities.

20.1.2. Budgeting for Contingency Operations. DoW Components normally do not budget for contingency operations as discussed in this section. Therefore, DoW Components must accomplish directed contingency operations using funds available to the cognizant command or unit, independent of the receipt of specific funds for the operation. The SecWar issues the authority for DoW Components to expend available funds. Since the FY 2010 President’s Budget, estimates for the Global War on Terror and Overseas Contingency Operations are included with the submission of the President’s Budget.

20.1.3. An Execute Order from the SecWar. An execute order from the SecWar is both the authority for the commander of a Combatant Command (CCMD) to initiate military operations and the authority for DoW Components to expend available funds to carry out the order. Planning orders and alert orders from the Chairman, of the Joint Chiefs of Staff (CJCS) constitute authority for a commander of a CCMD to expend funds available to that commander of a CCMD and authority to direct a military component to expend funds available to that component for forces assigned to the commander of a CCMD. Refer to Joint Publication 5-0, Joint Operation Planning, for information on joint operation order types.

20.1.4. DoW Policy Requirements. DoW policy requires that controls, accounting systems, and procedures provide, in financial records, proper identification and recording of costs incurred in supporting contingency operations. For such operations, data must be collected and records maintained to support bill development and the distribution of reimbursements to the applicable organizations.

20.1.5. Emergency Supplemental Funding

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

20.1.6. Elimination of Potential Duplicative Efforts. DoW officials having responsibility for reviewing and approving purchases for which the source of funding is derived from a transfer account like the Overseas Contingency Operations Transfer Fund (OCOTF) must, to the greatest extent possible, review transactions to: (1) eliminate the potential for duplicating the procurement of goods and services and (2) ensure that contractors are reimbursed for only those services and goods provided to the government.

20.1.7. Allowable Contingency Operations Cost. The funding derived from a contingency transfer account is available only for those incremental costs incurred in direct support of a contingency operation. As such, funds that are transferred into a Component’s baseline appropriation are not to be used to finance activities and programs that are not directly related to the incremental cost of the contingency. In addition, the funds transferred to a Component’s appropriation are not to be used to procure durable and expendable items in excess of what is required. Furthermore, those durable items procured with transferred funds are to be retained in support of the contingency even after the Component/unit has completed its tour of duty to support the contingency. Those durable items in the inventory, such as office equipment and expendable supplies that have not been consumed, should be made available to Components/units that are replacing the Component/unit that is departing the contingency operation area.

20.1.8. Fiduciary Responsibility. It is vital for civilian and military personnel authorized to obligate and expend funds in support of a contingency operation, using resources derived from the transfer of funds from a centrally funded transfer account (e.g., OCOTF), to employ a fiduciary approach to ensure that the funds are used in a prudent manner. Contingency funds are not to be used for purchases that are improper or are in excess of government requirements or which might bring embarrassment to the U.S. Government. Furthermore, special attention must be given by the Components’ approving officials when the government purchase card is used for purchases to be funded with funds derived from a contingency operations transfer account. Approving officials are responsible for reviewing and reconciling cardholders’ statements and for verifying that all transactions were necessary government purchases made in accordance with the FAR and all other government policies and procedures. See Volume 10 for more information.

20.2    Supplemental Information

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for additional information on references, responsibilities, types of estimates, reporting, contingency-specific definitions, justification, and the COST estimate tool. Cost reporting requirements for submission, inclusions, and consolidation of cost reports are in the Supplemental. Guidelines to assist the DoW Components in determining baseline and incremental costs for contingency operations and the process for reimbursement and distribution are provided in the manual. Details on base-funded overseas contingency operations and foreign disaster relief are also in the Supplemental.

20.3    General Funding Responsibilities

20.3.1. Service Component. Each service Component command must collect all applicable costs related to specific contingency operations and report these costs to the respective MILDEP Senior Financial Manager, who will then submit them to the DFAS for consolidation. If a contingency operation lacks financing, the Department will pursue all available options to obtain the additional funding required to ensure that participation in the operation does not reduce the readiness of U.S. Forces.

20.3.2. U.S. Transportation Command and the Defense Logistics Agency. Except as provided in paragraph 20.6 below, all requests for transportation or other services to a Working Capital Fund (WCF) Activity, such as the U.S. Transportation Command and the Defense Logistics Agency, must include a funding source. If a WCF activity receives a valid order (e.g., an execute or deployment order or a commander of a CCMD operations order) that directs action without a funding source, the parent MILDEP of the subordinate command receiving the services must provide funding to finance the request.

20.4    Special Funding Mechanisms

20.4.1. General. Congress revised 10 U.S.C. § 127a to include special funding mechanisms for operations that lack advance funding. The statute requires the SecWar to designate and identify such operations to Congress. When the SecWar designates an operation, DoW Components must immediately notify their subordinate organizations and establish procedures and controls for these special funding mechanisms.

20.4.2. Special Funding Mechanisms Participating Units. Under certain conditions, WCF organizations may not require units participating in such designated operations to reimburse (provide funded customer orders for) goods and services at the time the units order them. These procedures apply only to units participating in the covered operation, and only to requirements that are directly attributable to the operation; would not have been incurred but for the operation; and have not been financed previously through an appropriation, supplemental funding, reprogramming, or a reallocation of existing appropriations.

20.4.3. General Restrictions. The legal restrictions of the Anti-Deficiency Act (ADA) still apply to the Department, and WCF cash must remain positive under these restrictions. Therefore, the following general rules apply. Before a WCF activity accepts an unfunded customer order, its commander must determine that the activity can fill the order without violating the ADA. If filling the order without funded customer payment would violate the Act, the WCF activity must notify the requesting DoW Component to either issue a funded order or arrange to transfer sufficient cash to the supporting activity to cover the requested service or supplies.

20.4.4. WCF Activities. When a participating unit of the U.S. Armed Forces orders goods or services from a WCF activity and those goods or services meet the criteria addressed in subparagraphs 20.4.2 and 20.4.3, the unit providing the unfunded customer order to the performing WCF activity must, in each such request, notify the performing WCF activity that the order, or specified portion thereof, is in support of a designated operations and that a funded customer order for the goods or services is not required.

20.4.5. WCF Activity Unfunded Customer Orders. The WCF activity filling the unfunded customer order must separately account for all such filled orders and report those costs monthly to the DoW Component Senior Financial Manager of the requesting activity. The DoW Component's Senior Financial Manager must, in turn, separately report the cumulative amounts of these unfunded orders to DFAS in accordance with this section's provisions. Pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 127a, DFAS must account for these amounts separately, which the DoW will then use to determine the funds required for transfer to the WCF activities to restore their balances to previous levels.

20.4.6. WCF Priorities. To ensure the WCF activity uses its cash reserves for the highest priority requirements, the commander of the activity must notify the Principal Deputy USW(C), in writing, and wait 5 workdays before filling the unfunded customer order.

20.4.7. Guidance on Reporting. As needed, the OUSW(C) will provide additional guidance on reporting the use of this authority for designated operations that become eligible for the special funding mechanisms available under 10 U.S.C. § 127a.

20.5    Cost Collection

20.5.1. Special Program Codes. Upon being alerted of an impending contingency operation, each participating DoW Component must establish a unique special program code to capture costs. The OUSW(C) Operations Directorate must issue a Standard Financial Information Structure (SFIS) code for contingency operations. The SFIS Values Library Service webpage maintains a list of contingency codes. Additionally, the Joint Staff must issue a three-digit CJCS Project Code, which provides precedence for supply requisitions and facilitates cost capturing and reporting.

20.5.2. Accounting System(s). Each organization that supports a contingency operation must capture related obligations and disbursements in its accounting system(s) at the lowest possible level of the organization. This provides tracking of obligations and disbursements for affected appropriations.

20.5.3. Costs Related to Contingency Operations. Organizations may incur costs related to a contingency operation both in the area of responsibility and in other locations. The organization that incurs costs in support of the operation, whether directly or indirectly, must transmit information on all such costs to the appropriate DoW Component Senior Financial Manager.

20.5.4. Cost Accounting Systems. DoW Components must not establish cost accounting systems solely for the purpose of determining costs for contingency operations; instead, they must use the data from existing systems as applicable.

20.5.5. Incremental and Billable Costs. DoW Component Senior Financial Managers must determine incremental and billable costs.

20.6    Billing

DoW Components determine their billable incremental costs. Billable incremental costs will be less than the full incremental cost when the performing DoW Component has determined to supplement or enhance their support beyond the level agreed to by the requesting organization. The DoW Component headquarters are responsible for transmitting to DFAS, on a monthly basis, a Contingency Operations Cost Report, standardized SF 1080 for each UN Letters of Assist or incurred cost for which payment is requested, and sufficient supporting documentation such as receipts, invoices, copies of requisitions approved by the organization supported (e.g., UN, State Department, or other), when required by the billed organization. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for billing requirements and procedures for DoW and Non-DoW Transportation Rates for the Contingency Operations and United Nations Process.

20.6.1. DFAS administers centralized billing and reimbursement distribution activities in support of contingency operations. For the billing function, DFAS must consolidate the bills from the Components for monthly transmittal to the U.S. Mission to the UN (USUN) or other organizations, as required, along with copies of the Component Contingency Cost Reports. In addition, DFAS must prepare a monthly status report on amounts billed and reimbursements received for each applicable peace operation. In accordance with the provisions of Sections 607 and 630 of the Foreign Assistance Act (FAA), other applicable U.S. statutes, and the requirements of the billed organization, DFAS must submit only billable costs to the applicable agencies or international organizations.

20.6.2. The DoW Components must transmit billing information with sufficient supporting documentation to satisfy the payee of the validity of the charges. They must also include detailed lists of transactions supporting the billed amount with each bill rendered.

20.6.3. With respect to services and commodities provided under section 607 of the FAA, the Department may spend only those reimbursements it receives within 180 days after the end of the fiscal year in which the costs were incurred. The Department cannot use payments received after this 180-day period to defray costs it has already incurred providing the requested assistance.

20.6.4. The responsible DoW Component must credit payments received for assistance under the UN Participation Act, and unsolicited payments from the UN for UN-Determined Costs for Participating Troops, to the account or accounts that incurred the costs or to the accounts currently available for such purposes.

20.6.5. Given the legal restrictions on using reimbursed expenses, each DoW Component must identify and report all reimbursable billable expenses to DFAS on a timely basis, including sufficient supporting documentation as required by the billed organization, to ensure the Department recoups its costs.

20.7    Noncombatant Evacuation Operations (NEO)

20.7.1. Protection of U.S. Citizens and Nationals

20.7.1.1. The DoW conducts Noncombatant Evacuation Operations (NEOs) to assist the Department of State (DoS) in evacuating U.S. citizens, DoW civilian personnel, and designated host-nation (HN) and third-country nationals (TCNs) whose lives are in danger, moving them from a foreign nation to an appropriate safe haven. The United States Government (USG) will consider evacuating TCNs and host country nationals on a case-by-case, space-available, and reimbursable basis. Although the USG normally considers evacuations in connection with hostile action, it may also conduct them in anticipation of, or in response to, any natural or man-made disaster.

20.7.1.2. Upon receipt of a request from the President, or the DoS, the Department will protect U.S. citizens and nationals and designated other persons and assist in evacuating these persons from threatened areas overseas. In accordance with Executive Order 12656, as amended on February 9, 1998, the Department is authorized to deploy and use military forces to protect U.S. citizens and nationals and designated other persons in support of their evacuation from threatened areas overseas. The DoS has the lead responsibility for such evacuations.

20.7.2. Memorandum of Agreement (MOA). The MOA between the DOS and Defense, “DOS/DoW Cost Responsibility Matrix and Definitions,” dated September 2, 1997, defines departmental cost responsibilities when an evacuation occurs. The content of the MOA is included in the Volume 12 Supplemental and must be used to determine all NEO cost responsibilities. In general, DoW will fund protection-related costs, and DOS will fund evacuation-related costs. The DoW Component supporting the protection operation must fund the costs of its deployment, unless otherwise specified.

20.7.3. Cost to Transport DoW Noncombatants. Pursuant to 31 U.S.C. § 1535 (the Economy Act), all costs that the DoW incurred to assist in evacuating personnel from threatened areas are billable and reimbursable, except for the costs to transport DoW noncombatants to safe havens. If, however, the DoS incurs costs for transporting DoW noncombatants to safe havens, the applicable DoW Component must reimburse the DoS for those costs.

20.7.4. Contingency Operations Cost Report. After the evacuation is completed, the finance and accounting office of the supporting DoW Component must collect the cost data and submit the following documents, through its Component Senior Financial Manager, to DFAS: an SF-1080 for all reimbursable evacuation costs, supporting cost documentation (e.g., flying hours, medical costs, or food for evacuees), and a Contingency Operations Cost Report. The DoW Component must work with the DoS and DFAS to submit the bills for reimbursement from the DoS, Attn: Bureau of Finance and Management Policy, Washington, DC 20520-7427.

20.8    Follow-Up

If billed organizations require additional information relating to submitted bill(s), DFAS must assist the billed organization to ensure that the necessary information is provided by the appropriate Component.

20.9    Large Scale Contingencies

20.9.1. Preparing Budget Estimations Guidance. DoW may be involved in a range of operations from very large to small-scale contingencies. The following guidance is to be used in addition to that found throughout this regulation for purposes of preparing budget estimations, cost reporting and billing associated with large-scale, campaign level, contingency operations. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

20.9.2. Spending Constraints. Each DoW Component must ensure that detailed guidance is disseminated to the appropriate subordinate organization levels to ensure the accuracy and reporting of costs. The DoW Components are responsible for employing a fiduciary approach to ensure that the funds are used in a prudent manner. As operations mature, steps should be taken to evaluate and establish spending constraints.

title: Section 21.0: Burdensharing and Overseas Relocation Contributions by Foreign Allies
content:
21.0    BURDENSHARING AND OVERSEAS RELOCATION CONTRIBUTIONS BY FOREIGN ALLIES

21.1    Responsibilities

This chapter addresses burden-sharing, host nation, and mutually beneficial contributions provided under various statutory authorities. Pursuant to 10 U.S.C. §§ 2350j and 2350k, and NDAA FY 2016 § 2804, this section prescribes policy and responsibilities for the acceptance, receipt, use, and reporting of burdensharing and relocation contributions by foreign allies in the DoW.

21.1.1. Under Secretary of War for (Policy)

The USW(P) has policy and management responsibility for burdensharing agreements or arrangements. In addition, the USW(P) will work with the DFAS – Trust Funds Accounting and Reporting Division (TFAR) (DFAS-ESS/Trust Funds) on burden-sharing program requirements that impact DFAS responsibilities, as appropriate.

21.1.2. Under Secretary of War (Comptroller)

21.1.2.1. The USW(C) serves as the single departmental point of contact with the Departments of State and Treasury for all matters involving the acceptance, receipt, administration and distribution of contributions of funds from foreign countries and organizations for burdensharing, overseas relocation, and Kuwait mutually beneficial contributions.

21.1.2.2. The USW(C) is responsible for coordination and approval of military construction projects that are subject to 10 U.S.C. §§ 2350j and 2350k, and NDAA FY 2016 § 2804, as amended. In addition, the USW(C) is responsible for reviewing and submitting to the Congress those reports required by 10 U.S.C. §§ 2350j and 2350k, NDAA FY 2016 § 2804, as amended, and any reports required from annual authorization and appropriation acts.

21.1.3. Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment (USW(A&S))

USW(A&S) has policy and oversight responsibility for Host Nation Funded Construction (HNFC) provided by burdensharing agreements or arrangements under 10 U.S.C §§ 2350j and 2350k, and NDAA FY 2016 § 2804, as amended. USW (A&S) is responsible for authority reviews in locations with multiple HNFC agreements and technical reviews of HNFC Congressional notification packages, including project lists and project documentation.

21.1.4. Director of Defense Finance and Accounting Service (DFAS)

The DFAS Director is responsible for recording and reporting the collection of receipts for burdensharing, relocation, and mutually beneficial contributions, and for the distribution of receipts, as prescribed by the USW(C), in support of burdensharing, overseas relocation, and mutually beneficial programs.

21.1.5. Commanders of the Geographic Combatant Commands (CCDRs)

The cognizant CCDR with area of responsibility for the contributing country is responsible for financial management oversight and may delegate to another CCDR or subordinate commanders. This applies to burdensharing contributions for projects other than military construction, and military construction projects that are funded with burdensharing contributions. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

21.1.6. Assistant Secretaries for Financial Management and Comptroller (FM&C)

The cognizant Assistant Secretary (FM&C) has responsibility to review and approve the distribution of funds received from foreign countries and regional organizations for the purposes outlined in this Regulation. For funds supporting overseas geographic CCDR equities, the FM&C will ensure full distribution to the cognizant CCDR with area of responsibility for the contributing country or designated service component in that region. These responsibilities may be delegated below the Assistant Secretary level. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

21.2    Notifications of Monetary Contributions

The DoW Components must notify the DFAS-EASS/Trust Funds of all potential monetary contributions prior to acceptance of such contributions. All notifications must indicate the applicable statute (i.e., § 2350j for burdensharing contributions or 10 U.S.C. § 2350k for overseas relocation and FY 2016 NDAA § 2804, as amended, for mutually beneficial contributions). Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

21.3    Accounting

21.3.1. Burdensharing Credits

Burdensharing contributions must be credited to one or more of the special fund accounts which have been established in the U.S. Treasury for monetary contributions accepted by the SecWar or designee under 10 U.S.C. §. 2350j . Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for a listing of the accounts.

21.3.2. Overseas Relocation

21.3.2.1. Relocation contributions must be credited to one or more of the trust fund accounts which have been established in the U.S. Treasury for monetary contributions accepted by the SecWar or designee under 10 U.S.C. §. 2350k. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for a listing of the accounts.

21.3.2.2. The DFAS disbursing office or Financial Services Office must transmit copies of deposit tickets for these investments to the DFAS-Indianapolis (DFAS-IN)/EASS Trust Funds. DFAS-EASS Trust Funds manage and track the investments and earnings.

21.3.3. Mutually Beneficial

Mutually Beneficial contributions must be credited to the special fund account, which has been established in the U.S. Treasury for monetary contributions accepted by the SecWar or designee under the authority of FY 2016 NDAA § 2804, as amended. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for a listing of the account.

21.4    Availability of Contributions

Contributions are available for the payment of costs specified in 10 U.S.C. § 2350j or § 2350k, or FY 2016 NDAA § 2804, as amended. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for additional information regarding the availability of burdensharing and relocation contributions.

21.5    Reporting Requirements

As needed, the USW(C) will provide guidance to ensure necessary information is collected to comply with any congressional reporting requirements.

title: Section 22.0: Disposition of Non-DoW Personal Property
content:
22.0    DISPOSITION OF NON-DOW PERSONAL PROPERTY

22.1    Disposition of Unclaimed Property General Policy

22.1.1. The Secretary of any Military Department, and the Secretary of Homeland Security, under such regulations as they may respectively prescribe, may each by public or private sale or otherwise, dispose of all lost, abandoned, or unclaimed personal property that comes into the custody or control of the Secretary’s department, other than property subject to 10 U.S.C. §§ 7712, 8392, or 9712. Property subject to paragraph 22.3 is exempted from the requirements. Requirements for the disposition of personal property of deceased members of the Army and Air Force are in the Volume 12 Supplemental. Requirements for the disposition of personal property of deceased members of the Navy and Marine Corps are in the Volume 12 Supplemental.

22.1.2. Property may not be disposed of until a diligent effort has been made to find the owner (or the heirs, next of kin, or legal representative of the owner). A diligent effort to find the owner (or the heirs, next of kin, or legal representative of the owner) must begin, to the maximum extent practicable, not later than 7 days after the date on which the property comes into the custody or control of the Secretary having immediate jurisdiction. The period for which that effort is continued must not exceed 45 days.

22.1.3. Notice of the time and place of the intended sale or other disposition must be sent by certified or registered mail to the applicable owner (or heirs, next of kin, or legal representative of the owner) at their last known address. If the owner (or the heirs, next of kin, or legal representative of the owner) is determined but not found, the property may not be disposed of until the expiration of 45 days after the date the notice is sent to the owner (or the heirs, next of kin, or legal representative of the owner).

22.1.4. When a diligent effort to determine the owner (or heirs, next of kin, or legal representative of the owner) is unsuccessful, the property may be disposed of without delay. If the property has a fair market value of more than $300, it may not be disposed of until 45 days after the date it is received at the point of storage designated by the Secretary.

22.2    Distribution of Proceeds

The proceeds from the sale of lost, abandoned, or unclaimed personal property found on a military installation must be credited to the operation and maintenance account that funds the operations of that installation and be used to reimburse the installation for any costs incurred during the collection, transportation, storage, protection, or selling of the property. Any proceeds which remain after the reimbursement of installation expenses must be utilized to support Morale, Welfare and Recreation (MWR) activities under the jurisdiction of the armed forces that are conducted for the comfort, pleasure, contentment, or physical or mental improvement of members of the armed forces at such installation. The net proceeds from the sale of other property under paragraph 22.1 must be deposited into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts.

22.3    Restrictions

No property covered by this section may be delivered to the Armed Forces Retirement Home by the Secretary of a Military Department, except papers of value, sabers, insignia, decorations, medals, watches, trinkets, manuscripts, and other articles valuable chiefly as keepsakes.

22.4    Claims for Proceeds

The owner (or heirs, next of kin, or legal representative of the owner) of personal property whose proceeds were credited to a military installation may file a claim with the SecWar for an amount equal to the proceeds less costs referred to in paragraph 22.2. Amounts to pay the claim must be drawn from the MWR account for the installation that received the proceeds. The owner (or heirs, next of kin, or legal representative of the owner) may file a claim with the SecWar for proceeds deposited at Treasury as well. Unless a claim is filed under this section within 5 years after the date of the disposal of the property to which the claim relates, the claim may not be considered by either the SecWar or a court. The responsibility of the SecWar to consider such claims has been delegated to the USW for Personnel and Readiness.

22.5 Army and Air Force Disposition of Personal Property of Deceased Members

22.5.1. General Policy

Upon the death of a person subject to military law and under the jurisdiction of the Army or Air Force, or upon the death of a resident of the Armed Forces Retirement Home; the commanding officer must permit the legal representative or the surviving spouse of the deceased, if present, to take possession of the effects of the deceased that are then in camp, air base, or quarters. If there is no legal representative or surviving spouse present, the commanding officer must direct a summary court-martial to collect the effects of the deceased that are then in camp, air base, or quarters. The summary court-martial may collect debts due the decedent by local debtors and pay undisputed local creditors of the deceased (to the extent permitted by the monetary assets of the deceased in the court’s possession). Receipts for payments made from the estate of the deceased must be filed with the court’s final report to the Department of the Army or Air Force.

22.5.2. Distribution of Personal Property

As soon as practicable after the collection of the personal effects and monetary assets of the deceased, the summary court-martial must, at the expense of the United States, send the personal effects and monetary assets to one of the living persons, in the order of precedence shown on the following list, whom the court finds:

22.5.2.1. The surviving spouse or legal representative.

22.5.2.2. A child of the deceased.

22.5.2.3. A parent of the deceased.

22.5.2.4. A brother or sister of the deceased.

22.5.2.5. The closest next of kin of the deceased.

22.5.2.6. The beneficiary named in the will of the deceased.

22.5.3. Time Limits

If the summary court-martial cannot dispose of the effects as stated in paragraph 22.5.1 because there are no persons in any of the categories listed, or because the addresses of such persons are not known or are not available, the court may convert the effects of the deceased into cash by public or private sale. However, the sale may not occur until 30 days after the date of death of the deceased. Items listed in paragraph 22.5.2 may not be sold.

22.5.4. Final Disposition of Personal Effects

As soon as practicable after the effects have been converted into cash, the summary court-martial must relinquish custody of all cash and all receipts relating to cash transactions to the executive part of the Department of the Army or Air Force. Wills or other papers of value, an inventory of personal effects, and articles whose sale is not permissible also must be placed under the jurisdiction of the executive part of the Service of which the deceased was a member. All items received by the executive part of the Army or Air Force must be delivered to the Armed Forces Retirement Home.

22.6. NAVY AND MARINE CORPS DISPOSITION OF PERSONAL PROPERTY OF
DECEASED MEMBERS

22.6.1. General Policy

The Secretary of the Navy must retain custody of money or other personal property of a deceased member of the Naval Service and make a diligent effort to determine and locate the heirs or next of kin of the deceased member. Property remaining unclaimed 2 years after the death of the member must be sold, and the proceeds, together with any other monetary assets of the member held in custody, must be deposited into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts.

22.6.2. Recoupment

Within 5 years after the date the money and proceeds are deposited into the Treasury, any claim that is presented and supported by competent proof must be certified to Congress for consideration. After the 5 years, claims may not be accepted, and the requestor must be notified that the time limit for submitting a claim has expired.

title: Section 24.0: Operation and Use of General Gift Funds
content:
24.0    OPERATION AND USE OF GENERAL GIFT FUNDS

The SecWar and Secretaries of the Military Departments have the authority to accept, hold, administer, and spend gifts made for the benefit or in connection with various institutions and individuals under their jurisdiction. These gifts include money, real property, personal property, or services for the establishment, operation, or maintenance of schools, hospitals, libraries, museums, cemeteries, and other institutions, as well as for the benefit of wounded or injured members of the armed forces (including members performing full-time National Guard duty), civilian employees, dependents, and survivors of members or employees who are killed.

24.1    DESIGNATIONS

The SecWar and the Secretaries of the Military Departments may approve additional Acceptance Authority designations under their jurisdiction. The Office of the Secretary of War (OSW) designations are as follows:

24.1.1. USW(C)

All authority and responsibility granted to the SecWar associated with the acceptance and use of gifts has been delegated to the USW(C).

24.1.2. USW(C) Designations

The USW(C) prescribes additional designations of gift Acceptance Authority to OSW Components. On behalf of the SecWar, the USW for Acquisition and Sustainment (A&S), USW Personnel and Readiness (P&R), Administration and Organization Policy, DoW Defense Agencies, Joint Staff, Commanders of Combatant Commands, and Washington Headquarters Services (WHS) have the authority and responsibilities associated with acceptance and use of such gifts of real property or personal property and may authorize the development of additional procedures for implementing policy in this chapter. The Director of the WHS also has the authority to accept such gifts of services for the benefit of individuals at facilities under his or her authority. All gifts over $500,000 must be accepted by the USW(C).

24.2    Responsibilities

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

24.3    Acceptance

24.3.1. Acceptance of Gifts for Military Musical Units; Accounting for Missing Persons; Museum Programs; U.S. Service Academies; and the USUHS can be found in the Volume 12 Supplemental.

24.3.2. Circumstances to Decline Acceptance. Acceptance Authorities must decline gifts under the circumstances identified in the Volume 12 Supplemental.

24.3.3. DoW Personnel. DoW personnel must not solicit, fundraise for, or otherwise request or encourage the offer of a gift. Acceptance Authorities must not accept gifts offered contrary to this policy. Notwithstanding this general prohibition, the SecWar may solicit from a bona fide collector a gift for the use and benefit of a military museum program.

24.3.4. Related Expenses. Acceptance Authorities may pay all necessary expenses in connection with the conveyance or transfer of a gift.

24.3.5. Offers from Prohibited Sources. Acceptance Authorities must use increased sensitivity and scrutiny when gifts are offered from prohibited sources. Acceptance of gifts from prohibited sources may cause embarrassment to the DoW or the appearance of influencing official decisions or actions of the Department. Acceptance Authorities must consult with their appropriate Ethics Official before accepting such a gift valued more than $10,000 to determine whether the donor is involved in any claims, procurement actions, litigation, or other matters involving the Department that must be considered prior to gift acceptance.

24.3.6. Acknowledgment of Future Gifts. Acceptance Authorities may acknowledge offers of future gifts and advise the donors that acceptance will occur after the actual presentation of the gifts only when they determine that such acceptance will likely occur.

24.3.7. Acceptance through Intermediaries. Acceptance Authorities must not accept gifts offered indirectly through an intermediary if they cannot accept such gifts if offered directly from the source.
