24.3.8. Accepting Gifts to Benefit Certain Members, Dependents, and Civilian Employees. - Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

24.3.9. Acceptance of Property Gifts with Naming Rights.

24.3.9.1. The Secretary concerned may delegate the authority to accept gifts with the condition of naming rights only to a civilian Presidential appointee in a position requiring Senate confirmation. This authority may not be further re-delegated.

24.3.9.2. The Secretary concerned must issue uniform regulations governing the circumstances under which gifts conditioned on naming rights may be accepted, appropriate naming conventions, and suitable display standards. The naming conventions and suitable display standards must be in accordance with Unified Facilities Criteria (UFC) 3-120-01 and other implementing guidance issued under the purview of the USW(A&S).

24.4    Receipt

24.4.1. Monetary Gifts. All monetary gifts must be forwarded to the DFAS office servicing the Acceptance Authority via mail or an EFT. DoW officials must contact DFAS for EFT deposit information.

24.4.2. Gift Fund Accounts. - Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

24.4.3. Accounting Transactions. Accounting entries for monetary, non-monetary, and service-type gifts are specified within the U.S. Standard General Library.

24.5    Records and Reports

24.5.1. Records. Acceptance Authorities must keep accurate, auditable, and timely records of all gifts and provide this information for periodic audits. The receiving organization must obtain and retain the required documentation and information for all gifts received, including the date non-monetary gifts were transferred to property records and the unique identifier or data element, if applicable (see property accountability requirements in paragraph 24.7). For audit purposes, the supporting documentation for monetary and non-monetary gifts must be retained in accordance with the policy in Volume 1. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

24.5.2. Reports

24.5.2.1. DFAS Standards and Compliance (Corporate Reporting) must develop and require a standardized report for Acceptance Authorities or designees to report the following information to DFAS on a quarterly basis. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

24.5.2.2. Acceptance Authorities must report the information in the reports for all monetary gifts and real property gifts along with personal property gifts and services with a unit value of $5,000 or more to the DFAS office servicing each Secretary (Defense, Army, Navy, and Air Force) not later than 10 days after the end of each quarter. Monetary, real property, and personal property gifts must be reported separately.

24.6    Investments

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for DFAS responsibilities for investments.

24.7    Property Accountability

Acceptance Authorities must establish procedures for receiving, accounting, and disposing of real and personal property gifts. Property accountability procedures must be addressed or referenced in general gift acceptance procedures. Property accountability procedures must be consistent with policy prescribed in DoDI 4165.14, DoDI 4165.70, DoDI 4165.71, DoDI 4165.72, and DoDI 5000.64.

title: Section 25.0: DoW Branding and Trademark Licensing Program
content:
25.0    DOW BRANDING AND TRADEMARK LICENSING PROGRAM

25.1    Responsibilities

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

25.2    Accounting and Reporting

25.2.1. Accounting

25.2.1.1. Fees received in a fiscal year must remain available for obligation in such fiscal year and the following two fiscal years.

25.2.1.2. The excess of licensing fees collected over annual costs may be expended to support MWR activities. The law does not require that the excess be obligated in the fiscal year collected. The excess may be used in the following two fiscal years to offset those fiscal year costs of the licensing program or may be expended in support of the DoW Component’s MWR activities.

25.2.1.3. Funds not obligated or made available to MWR activities before September 30 of the second fiscal year following the year collected must be reallocated (transferred) to TAS R3210, “General Fund Proprietary Receipts, Defense Military, Not Otherwise Classified.”

25.2.1.4. Additional TASs may be used to separately track unobligated funds carried forward from the fiscal year of collection through the following two fiscal years.

25.2.1.5. Each DoW Component must ensure that all royalty reports received from licensees and/or licensing agents are promptly reviewed, and any questions resolved. Copies of royalty reports must be retained in accordance with Volume 1.

25.2.2. Reporting. Each DoW Component operating a trademark licensing program must provide the Manager, DoW Branding and Trademark Licensing Program (BTLP), with the following financial reports. The Manager, BTLP, may issue guidance prescribing the required format of the reports and the specific information to be provided. For information on quarterly and annual reports, refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

title: Section 26.0: Collection and Retention of Conference Fees from Non-Federal Sources
content:
26.0    COLLECTION AND RETENTION OF CONFERENCE FEES FROM NON-FEDERAL SOURCES

26.1    Policy

Federal Laws and Regulations. Although 10 U.S.C. § 2262 authorizes the retention of conference fees, all other applicable Federal laws and regulations must be followed regarding conferences and conference planning. These Federal authorities include the Joint Travel Regulations, the FAR, the DFARS, and the JER. This authority does not increase or affect any other currently existing conference authority. Guidelines related to determining conference fees are available on the DoW Cost Guidance Portal that resides on the DoW Costs Assessment and Program Evaluation web page. Access to the web page requires a DoW Common Access Card (CAC). Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for use of contracts, reimbursement, and ethics and fiscal guidance.

A “conference” is defined in the Joint Travel Regulations as a meeting, retreat, seminar, symposium, or event that involves attendee travel. The term conference also applies to training activities in accordance with 5 CFR § 410.404. Conferences subject to this authority are also often referred to as conventions, expositions, workshops, or exhibitions that typically involve topical matters of interest to, and the participation of, multiple agencies and/or non-governmental participants. The DoD Conference Guidance 4.0 identifies exemptions to the defined list of conferences.

26.2    Responsibilities

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for OUSW(C), DFAS, and DoW Component responsibilities.

26.3    Accounting and Reporting

26.3.1. Accounting

26.3.1.1. Accounting for collections into appropriations is covered in the DoW United States Standard General Ledger Transaction Library, on the Office of the DCFO SFIS web page.

26.3.1.2. Except when conference planning services at no cost to the government are used and the government entity does not directly collect fees, amounts collected in accordance with 10 U.S.C. § 2262 with respect to a conference must be credited to the appropriation or account from which the costs of the conference are paid and must be used to pay or reimburse those costs of the Department with respect to the conference. Record conference fees collected as an appropriation reimbursement.

26.3.1.3. The registration fees collected must remain with the year that funds for the conference are obligated. In the event registration fees are collected in one fiscal year, but the conference is conducted in the next, the fees collected must remain in the year the conference expenses were obligated and must be available for the same purpose and time period of the appropriation.

26.3.1.4. Components, agencies, and activities that collect conference fees into appropriations may not augment those appropriations. Accordingly, any fees collected that exceed actual conference costs must be deposited into the Treasury as Miscellaneous Receipts (i.e., Receipt Account 3210).

26.3.2. Reporting

26.3.2.1. In accordance with DoW's Conference Policies and Controls, all DoW- sponsored conferences are required to be reported through a central DoW Conference Tool. This data is used to generate the annual reports that are posted publicly and support the Department's ongoing oversight of conference activities. Conference fees are not reported as a separate entity; they are reported within conference expenses as a net of any fees or revenue received through the conference, not to include costs.

26.3.2.2. In accordance with OMB Memorandum M-17-08, "Promoting Efficient Spending to Support Agency Operations,” agencies must report conference expenses on a dedicated space on their official website. Conference expenses are defined as all direct and indirect conference costs paid by the Government, whether paid directly by agencies or reimbursed by agencies to travelers or others associated with the conference, but do not include funds paid under Federal grants to grantees. Conference expenses include any associated authorized travel and per diem expenses, hire of rooms for official business, audiovisual use, light refreshments, registration fees, ground transportation, and other expenses as defined by the Federal Travel Regulations.

26.3.2.2.1. By January 31 of each year, the agency must describe all agency-sponsored conferences from the previous fiscal year where the net expenses for the agency associated with the conference were in excess of $100,000. This description must include:

26.3.2.2.1.1. Total conference expenses incurred by the agency for the conference.

26.3.2.2.1.2. The location of the conference.

26.3.2.2.1.3. The date of the conference.

26.3.2.2.1.4. A brief explanation of how the conference advanced the mission of the agency.

26.3.2.2.1.5. The total number of individuals whose travel expenses or other conference expenses were paid by the agency.

26.3.2.2.2. In addition, for any instances where the net expenses for an agency-sponsored conference exceeded $500,000, the website must include the agency-designated official's rationale and approval. The website must also include information in the appropriate format (e.g., narrative) about the total net conference expenses for the fiscal year incurred by that agency, as well as a general report about conference activities throughout the year.

26.3.2.2.3. In reporting this data, agencies must exclude any information that is considered to be sensitive, that is prohibited from public disclosure by statute or regulation, or that may jeopardize national security or the health, safety, or security of conference attendees, organizers, or other individuals.

title: Section 27.0: Financial Institutions and Military Banking Facilities on DoW Installations
content:
27.0    FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND MILITARY BANKING FACILITIES ON DOW INSTALLATIONS

27.1    Responsibilities

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

27.2    General Policy Provisions

27.2.1. Financial Institutions (FI) on DoW Installations

27.2.1.1. No more than one bank and one credit union are permitted to operate on a DoW installation except where they already existed as of May 1, 2000, or the installation was affected by BRAC. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for information that pertains to installations affected by BRAC.

27.2.1.2. Upon the request of an installation commander and with the approval of the Secretary of the Military Department concerned (or designee), duly chartered FI may be authorized to provide financial services on DoW installations to enhance the morale and welfare of DoW personnel and facilitate the administration of public and quasi-public funds. Arrangements for the provision of such services must be in accordance with this section.

27.2.1.3. FIs may be established on DoW installations only after approval by the Secretary of the Military Department concerned (or designee), the appropriate regulatory agency as required, and in accordance with 32 CFR § 230.

27.2.1.4. Except in limited situations overseas, only banks insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and credit unions insured by the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund, or by another insurance organization specifically qualified by the Secretary of the Treasury, may operate on DoW installations. These FIs may either be State or federally chartered; however, U.S. credit unions operated overseas must be federally insured.

27.2.1.5. Military Banking Facilities (MBF) may be established on DoW installations when a demonstrated and justified need cannot be met through other means, pending the availability of FIs willing to perform these functions. Normally, MBFs are only authorized at overseas locations. MBFs may be considered for use at domestic DoW installations only when the cognizant DoW Component cannot obtain financial services from a state or federally chartered FI authorized to operate in the installation state. MBFs may be designated during mobilization as an emergency measure. The Director, DFAS, may recommend the designation of MBFs to the Treasury.

27.2.1.6. The installation commander must approve the expansion of financial services (to include in-store banking) requiring the out grant of additional space or logistical support. Any DoW activity considering expanding the availability of financial services must coordinate requests with the installation Banking Liaison Officer (BLO) prior to the commander’s consideration.

27.2.1.7. No DoW Component must perform retail banking operations. Solicitations for such services must be issued, and proposals accepted, according to the policies identified in this section.

27.2.1.8. If an FI or MBF operates on a DoW installation, installation commanders must not seek financial services from any entity other than the on-base FI or MBF.

27.2.1.9. Military disbursing offices, NAFIs (including MWR activities and the Military Exchange Services), and other DoW Component activities requiring financial services must use on-base FIs and MBFs to the maximum extent feasible.

27.2.1.10. NAFIs (including MWR activities and the Military Exchange Services) that desire and are authorized to provide currency accommodation exchange services to individuals must acquire all foreign currency for this purpose from the servicing MBF at the MBF accommodation rate and sell it at a rate of exchange no more favorable than the customer rate available at the MBF.

27.2.2. Security

27.2.2.1. The installation commander (or designee), officials of the on-base FIs, and installation security authorities must establish an understanding of each entity’s responsibilities on all matters of asset protection.

27.2.2.2. Establish a written agreement outlining the security procedures that the FI follows and the role that installation security authorities play regarding alarms, movement of cash, and criminal activity response procedures to be followed (e.g., vandalism or robbery).

27.2.2.3. Cash and other assets in on-base FIs are the property of those FIs. Except for MBFs operated under contract, maintenance of alarms and the guarding and/or escorting of cash is the sole responsibility of the on-base FI. The installation commander may decide that providing for the guarding or escorting of cash is desirable or necessary.

27.2.2.4. The use of armored vehicles for transportation of cash is the sole responsibility of the on-base FI and MBF, and use must be coordinated with the installation commander to permit access to DoW installations and facilities.

27.2.3. Central Locator Services. Military locator services will be provided per the Privacy Act guidelines contained within the Volume 12 Supplemental (Figure 33-1) and associated fees, if any, are to be paid by the FI in accordance with Volume 11. See the Locate Military Members website to obtain information on how to locate a military member, retiree, or facility. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for information and guidance on Advertising and Personal Solicitation; Automatic Teller Machine (ATM) Service; Staffing; Departure Clearance; Operating Agreements; Installation Financial Services; In-Store Banking; and Domestic MBF.

27.2.4. Advertising and Personal Solicitation. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

27.2.5. ATM Service. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

27.2.6. Domestic and International Treasury General Accounts. In cases where authorization is required for the on-base FI or MBF to act as a Treasury General Account (TGA) domestic depositary (or, on overseas installations, an International Treasury General Account (ITGA) depository), the FI must satisfy the risk management standards established by the Secretary of the Treasury. On-base FIs and MBFs must accept deposits for credit to the TGA (or ITGA) when authorized.

27.2.7. Staffing. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

27.2.8. Departure Clearance. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

27.2.9. Operating Agreements. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

27.2.10. Installation Financial Services. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

27.2.11. Banking Liaison Officer. Each installation commander having an on-base FI or MBF must appoint a BLO. The BLO’s name and duty telephone number must be displayed prominently at each FI and MBF location on the installation. The responsibilities of BLOs must be assigned to comptroller or resource management personnel. Employees, officials, or directors of a FI or MBF may not serve as BLOs. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for BLO responsibilities.

27.2.12. In-Store Banking. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

27.2.13. Domestic MBF. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

27.3    Banks Operating on Domestic DoW Installations

27.3.1. General Policy. U.S. banks may operate on DoW installations, in accordance with this section, when required by installation commanders to promote the morale and welfare of installation personnel and to help facilitate installation operations. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for Establishment and Terminations.

27.3.2. Solicitations. The Secretary of the Military Department concerned (or designee), or the installation commander with advice from the cognizant Secretary of the Military Department (or designee), must conduct solicitations, to include pre-proposal conferences, for on-base banking. Subject to the criteria for selection outlined in the Volume 12 Supplemental, the preferred sources of on-base financial services at domestic installations are federally insured, state- chartered or federally insured, federally chartered banks operating in the local area. The Volume 12 Supplemental addresses distribution of the solicitation only and does not preclude any federally insured, state-chartered or federally insured, federally chartered bank from responding at any stage (from local distribution in the Volume 12 Supplemental to publication in SAM.gov and FI trade journals as outlined in the Volume 12 Supplemental ) of the solicitation process. Do not commit to any bank regarding its proposal until the appropriate regulatory agency makes a designation if a designation is required. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for more information on solicitations.

27.3.3. Termination. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for more information.

27.3.4. Use of Space, Logistical Support, and Military Real Property for Banks Operating on Domestic DoW Installations.

27.3.4.1. Lease Terms. The consideration for a lease must be determined by an appraisal of fair market rental value in accordance with 10 U.S.C. § 2667. Periodic reappraisals must be based upon the fair market rental value exclusive of the bank improvements made. Coordinate with USW(A&S) or designee. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

27.3.4.2. Logistical Support

27.3.4.2.1. The bank must be housed in a building accessible to DoW personnel on the installation and in a location permitting reasonable security.

27.3.4.2.2. Banks must perform all maintenance, repair, improvements, alterations, and construction on the banking premises.

27.3.4.2.3. Banks must pay for all utilities (i.e., electricity, natural gas or fuel oil, water, and sewage), heating and air conditioning, intra-station telephone service, and custodial and janitorial services including garbage disposal and outdoor maintenance (such as grass cutting and snow removal) at rates set forth in the lease, operating agreement or other written agreement between the installation and the bank.

27.3.5. Land Leases. A lease for the construction of a bank must be at the appraised fair market rental value. Charges must apply for the term of the lease not to exceed 25 years, subject to periodic review every 5 years to assess changes in fair market value. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

27.3.6. Construction. Banks may construct buildings subject to provisions found in the Volume 12 Supplemental.

27.4    FIs and MBFs Operating on Overseas DoW Installations

General Provisions of Financial Services Overseas. The Department acquires financial services overseas for use by authorized persons and organizations from the following sources.

27.4.1. MBFs operated under contract and authorized by the pertinent status of forces agreement, other intergovernmental agreements, or host-country law.

27.4.2. Domestic and foreign banks located on overseas DoW installations. Each such institution must be:

27.4.2.1. Chartered to provide financial services in that country.

27.4.2.2. A party to a formal operating agreement with the installation commander to provide such services.

27.4.2.3. Identified, where applicable, in the status of forces agreements, other intergovernmental agreements, or host-country law. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for more information on Establishment, Terminations, Logistical Support, Operations, and other Overseas Banking Offices.

27.5    Credit Unions Operating on Domestic DoW Installations

U.S. credit unions may operate on DoW installations, in accordance with this section, when required by installation commanders to promote the morale and welfare of installation personnel and to help facilitate installation operations. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for more information on Establishment; Termination; Use of Space, Logistical Support, and Military Real Property for Domestic Credit Unions; Land Leases; Construction; and ATM service.

27.6    Overseas Credit Unions

27.6.1. Credit union services to authorized persons and organizations, as permitted by Status of Forces agreements, other intergovernmental agreements, or host-country law, may be provided by domestic on-base credit unions operating under a geographic franchise.

27.6.2. The extension of credit union service overseas must be in accordance with this
section as it relates to domestic credit unions and aligned with applicable status of forces agreements or other intergovernmental agreements, or host-country law.

27.6.3. Where permitted by the status of forces agreements or other intergovernmental agreements, or host-country law, only federal credit unions or federally insured state-chartered credit unions may operate on overseas DoW installations. The ultimate decision to provide services overseas rests with the credit union itself. Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental for more information on Establishment; Logistical Support Services; Travel; and Operations.

title: Section 28.0: Direct Acceptance of Gifts by Members of the Armed Forces, Department of War Employees and Their Families and Survivors
content:
28.0    DIRECT ACCEPTANCE OF GIFTS BY MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES, DEPARTMENT OF WAR EMPLOYEES AND THEIR FAMILIES AND SURVIVORS

28.1    Gift to Covered Employees

Pursuant to the authority in 10 U.S.C. § 2601(a), covered members of the armed forces in the DoW and covered employees of DoW, their family members, and their survivors may accept gifts directly from nonprofit organizations, private parties, and other sources outside the DoW when, while performing military duties or performing duties as a civilian employee on or after September 11, 2001, they incur an injury or illness: (1) as a direct result of armed conflict; while engaged in hazardous service; in the performance of duty under conditions simulating war; or through an instrumentality of war; (2) in an operation or area designated as a combat operation or combat zone by the SecWar; (3) that results in enrollment in a Warriors in Transition program, as defined in section 738(e) of the NDAA for Fiscal Year 2013 (Public Law 112-239, 10 U.S.C. § 1071); or (4) under other circumstances determined by the Secretary concerned to warrant treatment like members covered by the first criterion of this section.

28.2    Impermissible Gifts

The authority in 10 U.S.C. § 2601a does not apply to gifts from foreign governments or international organizations or their representatives, nor does it apply to gifts that: (1) are accepted in return for being influenced in the performance of an official act; (2) are solicited or coerced;
(3) are accepted in violation of any other statute or regulation, including 18 U.S.C. § 201, 18 U.S.C § 209, 5 CFR § 2635 and 5 CFR § 3601; or (4) will reflect adversely on the DoW.

28.3    Criteria for Gift Acceptance

Refer to the Volume 12 Supplemental.

title: Section 1.0: General
content:
1.0    GENERAL

1.1 Nonappropriated Fund (NAF) accounting applies to all NAF Instrumentalities (NAFIs) and their supporting Accounting Offices (AOs). NAFs are separate from appropriated funds (APFs) of the U.S. Department of the Treasury (Treasury). NAFs must not be commingled with APFs and must be managed separately from APFs, even when used to support a common program.

1.2    Authoritative Guidance

Refer to the authoritative guidance document on the FMR webpage.

1.3    Definitions

Refer to the Glossary of terms document on the FMR webpage.

1.4    Procedures

Refer to the Supplemental document listed throughout this volume.

title: Section 2.0: Introduction to Nonappropriated Fund Accounting
content:
2.0    INTRODUCTION TO NONAPPROPRIATED FUND ACCOUNTING

2.1 The chart of accounts for NAFs must be established to comply with Federal Accounting Standards Board (FASB) and Department of Defense Instruction (DoDI) 1015.15 reporting requirements and is maintained on the DoD NAF Accounting website. NAF accounting systems used by the Military Exchanges are exempt from using the NAF chart of accounts; the Exchanges use the separate Defense Resale Activities chart of accounts, available on the DoD NAF Accounting website.

2.2 For reporting purposes that require the level of materiality to be quantified, materiality must be defined as a minimum of one percent of the total assets in the Balance Sheet for each NAFI. The one percent threshold does not preclude entities from making necessary adjustments to financial statements for transactions that may fall below the threshold. For NAF activities required to report on a consolidated basis, the threshold of materiality must be a minimum of one percent of the assets in the consolidated Balance Sheet.

2.3 AOs must prepare an end-of-month trial balance of the general ledger accounts to ensure total debits equal total credits.

2.4 The annual accounting reporting period for DoD NAFIs begins October 1 of each year and ends September 30 of the following year. The Military Exchanges use the National Retail Federation reporting period and fiscal year that begins in February and ends the following January per DoDI 1015.15. This divides the year into four quarters of 13 weeks grouped into two 4-week "months" and one 5-week "month."

2.5 Financial reports must be prepared annually for each NAFI and must include notes to accompany the financial statements. The DoD Procedures, Guidance, and Instructions for Section 6 explains the following NAFI financial reports: Balance Sheet; Reconciliation of Net Worth; Statement of Income and Expense; and Statement of Cash Flows.

2.6 Financial reports must include full and adequate disclosure of financial and accounting information per Section 6 reporting requirements (for example, disclosure of fund equity adjustments and eliminating entry transactions between NAFIs); this includes Military Service Headquarters, Major Command or Region, and installation NAFIs.

2.7 Since NAFI business operations are similar to the private sector, financial statements are prepared and presented to comply with accounting standards promulgated by FASB. All other accounting literature not included in the Codification is considered non‑authoritative.

2.8 NAFIs must use the accrual basis of accounting, by recognizing income and expenses when earned or incurred.

2.9 AOs provide centralized professional accounting services to NAFIs. AO responsibilities include maintaining the books of original entry, general ledger, and related subsidiary ledgers; maintaining fixed asset and payroll records; preparing disbursement vouchers and checks after assuring fund availability and paying NAFI liabilities; preparing and distributing required periodic financial reports; preparing an annual AO operating budget; reconciling supported NAFIs' bank accounts; computing and billing service fees to recover operating costs; reviewing documentation for completeness and accuracy; providing documentation to auditors; preparing aged accounts receivable reports; maintaining awareness of changes affecting financial reporting; and reviewing fund equity or net worth adjustment requests and forwarding them to the approval authority designated by each Military Service.

2.10 NAFIs must establish and operate internal control programs in accordance with the Office of Management and Budget Circular A-123, “Management’s Responsibility for Enterprise Risk Management and Internal Control,” and the statute it implements, the Federal Managers’ Financial Integrity Act of 1982.

2.11 Each Military Service is required by DoDI 7600.06 to have independent certified public accountants conduct an annual financial audit of NAFIs with annual income or expenses exceeding $10 million. NAFIs in Program Group VI – Special Purpose Central Funds, and NAFIs supporting highly sensitive operations, must have audits at least annually regardless of the dollar threshold of revenues and expenses.

Companion reference: For detailed procedures, implementation guidance, definitions, and the full data tables, see the Supplemental for Volume 13, Section 2.

title: Section 3.0: Nonappropriated Fund Standard General Ledger
content:
3.0    NONAPPROPRIATED FUND STANDARD GENERAL LEDGER

3.1 This section prescribes policy for the NAF Standard General Ledger (NAFSGL), maintained on the DoD NAF Accounting website. The NAFSGL is a modified version of the United States Standard General Ledger used for accounting and financial statement reporting to ensure financial statement information is consistent for all NAFIs. The NAFSGL provides for standardization and traceability from the financial statements through the general ledger balances to the source documentation for audit purposes. At a minimum, the Office of the Under Secretary of War (Personnel & Readiness) must update and publish the NAFSGL before 1 October of each year. Policies in this section apply to all NAFIs and their supporting accounting offices, except the Military Exchanges, which include Army and Air Force Exchange Service, Navy Exchange Service Command, and Marine Corps Exchange.

3.2 The general ledger accounts are self-balancing (total debits equal total credits) and provide for accounting of business events. The NAFSGL contains a Chart of Accounts and basic common account code elements: the Installation, NAF, Activity, Cost Center, Site, APF/NAF, and General Ledger Account Code (GLAC). Each Military Department uses the accounts required for its particular financial operations. NAFIs and Military Departments may not have to use all accounts.

3.3 The NAFSGL uses an eight-digit account numbering system for the GLACs. Within the NAFIs, the NAFSGL supports financial statement reporting at the Program Group level and the consolidated Military Department level. All data must summarize to the four-digit DoW standard GLAC and be traceable to the NAFIs using subaccounts. The general ledger accounts are grouped into the following major summary categories: 1000 Assets; 2000 Liabilities; 3000 Net Worth/Equity; 4000 Operating Income; 5000 Operating Expenses; 6000 Non-Operating Income; 7000 Non-Operating Expenses.

3.4 Account for assets in the 1000 series of accounts. Current asset accounts consist of cash, investments, receivables, inventories, and other assets reasonably expected to be converted to cash or consumed during the normal operating cycle (12 months or less). Long-term asset accounts consist of NAFI-titled fixed assets, APF-titled fixed assets, and other long-term assets. Section 4 contains additional information on assets.

3.4.1. Cash and investments are liquid assets that can be quickly used to carry out operations. Cash consists of coins, paper currency and readily negotiable instruments, cash in bank, foreign currencies, revolving cash funds, cash held in petty cash or change funds, imprest funds, savings, restricted cash for current operations, and certificates of deposit with an original maturity of three months or less. Investments consist of interest-bearing deposits, certificates of deposit with an original maturity greater than three months but no more than 12 months, and marketable securities. NAFIs must exclude employee retirement cash and investments (employee 401K, employee retirement, and employee post-retirement medical) from a consolidated presentation, because they would distort available NAF.

3.4.2. Fixed assets are property, plant, and equipment purchased, donated, or transferred to NAFIs that have an expected life of two or more years. Fixed assets consist of buildings, land, land improvements, vehicles, aircraft, boats, furniture, fixtures and equipment, information technology, livestock, assets in progress, fixed assets in-transit when ownership passes to the NAFI before receiving the asset, and accumulated depreciation. NAFIs must report material donations of assets and services in the financial statements. NAFIs must not include donated artifacts in the financial statements unless the NAFI: (1) uses or intends to use the artifact in its primary operations outside its educational function; or (2) sells or intends to sell the artifact and use the proceeds for something other than purchasing another artifact for educational purposes.

3.4.3. Other long-term assets are assets not identified in other asset categories. They consist of long-term pension benefit assets, receivables, long-term prepaid expenses, certificates of deposit (more than 12 months), marketable securities, long-term contributions, long-term franchise fees, intangible assets, and long-term royalty and trademark fees. Report pension benefit asset information when the pension plan is overfunded and classified as a long-term asset; refer to FASB Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) Topic 715, "Compensation-Retirement Benefits," and Section 8 for reporting guidance. NAFIs must classify and report cash and investments restricted for long-term purposes on the balance sheet as other long-term assets.

3.5 Account for liabilities in the 2000 series of accounts. Current liability accounts are due, or will become due, on demand within 1 year and consist of accounts payable, wages payable, interest payable, post-retirement benefit obligations (12 months or less), and other liabilities. Long-term liability accounts are due more than 12 months from the Balance Sheet date and consist of loan liabilities, capital lease liabilities, post-retirement benefit obligations (more than 12 months), and other long-term liabilities. Section 4 contains additional information on liabilities.

3.5.1. Report the current post-retirement benefit obligation when the pension plan is underfunded (plan assets are less than the plan benefit obligation) and classified as a current liability, as determined and provided by the pension provider. This includes any other post- retirement benefit plan, such as retiree health care. The benefit obligation is the accumulated post- retirement benefit obligation. Refer to FASB ASC Topic 715 and Section 8 for reporting guidance.

3.5.2. Report the long-term post-retirement benefit obligation when the pension plan is underfunded (plan assets are less than the plan benefit obligation) and classified as a long-term liability, as determined and provided by the pension provider. This includes any other post- retirement benefit plan, such as retiree health care. The benefit obligation is the accumulated post- retirement benefit obligation. Refer to ASC Topic 715 and Section 8 for reporting guidance.

3.6 Account for Net Worth/Equity in the 3000 series of accounts. Net Worth consists of retained earnings, transferred equity, workers' compensation reserves, equity reserves, undistributed profits and net income, unrealized gains and losses, and other equity transactions. The pension cost liability account records any adjustment made to existing pension balances on the Balance Sheet. Post these adjustments as an offset to the equity account on the Balance Sheet, as either an addition or reduction to Net Worth. Account for these temporary adjustments in the Net Worth section of the Balance Sheet the same way as unrealized gains and losses on investments per FASB ASC Topic 320, "Investments-Debt Securities." Do not include these temporary adjustments in the net worth calculation. Refer to ASC Topic 715 for reporting guidance.

3.7 Classify income as either operating (4000 series) or non-operating (6000 series).

3.7.1. Account for operating income in the 4000 series of accounts. Examples of operating income accounts include gross sales income, participation fees income, concessionaire income, rental income, amusements income, gaming income, reimbursement income, and other operating income. Section 5 contains additional information on income.

3.7.2. Account for non-operating income in the 6000 series of accounts. Examples of non- operating income include interest income, rebates income, subsidy income, exchange dividend income, unusual or infrequent income, and other non-operating income.

3.8 Classify expenses as either operating (5000 series) or non-operating (7000 series).

3.8.1. Account for operating expenses in the 5000 series of accounts. Examples of operating expenses include purchases, cost of goods sold, depreciation expense, wage expense, tax expense, retirement expense, supplies expense, communication expense, utilities expense, travel expense, claims expense, entertainment expense, bad debt expense, unemployment compensation and other employee benefit expense, and other operating expense. Section 5 contains additional information on expenses.

3.8.2. Account for non-operating expenses in the 7000 series of accounts. Examples of non-operating expenses include interest expenses, unusual or infrequent expenses, costs incurred in acquiring historical artifacts, and other non-operating expenses.

Companion reference: For detailed procedures, implementation guidance, definitions, and the full data tables, see Supplemental for Volume 13, Section 3.

title: Section 4.0: Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth
content:
4.0    ASSETS, LIABILITIES, AND NET WORTH

4.1 This section prescribes the accounting policy and related requirements for NAF assets, liabilities, and net worth. NAFI programs and facilities must be operated, maintained, and funded as an integral part of the DoW personnel and readiness program. Policies in this section apply to all NAFIs and their supporting AOs, including the Military Exchanges (Army and Air Force Exchange Service, Navy Exchange Service Command, and Marine Corps Exchange).

4.2 The NAFSGL chart of accounts, including definitions and GLACs for asset, liability, and net worth accounts, is maintained on the DoD NAF Accounting website. NAF accounting systems used by the Military Exchanges are exempt from this chart of accounts; the Military Exchanges use the separate Defense Resale Activities chart of accounts available on the DoD NAF Accounting website.

4.3 The NAFSGL contains eight asset categories: Cash; Investments (refer to DoDI 1015.15); Receivables; Inventories; Other Current Assets; NAFI-Titled Fixed Assets; APF-Titled Fixed Assets; and Other Long-Term Assets. Accounting requirements for these categories are in paragraphs 3.1 through 3.7.

4.4    Cash

4.4.1. NAF cash must be maintained in financial institutions that are U.S. federally insured or designated by the Treasury. Cash consists of coins; paper currency; readily negotiable instruments such as money orders, checks, and bank drafts on hand or in transit for deposit; demand deposits with banks or other financial institutions; and foreign currencies translated into U.S. dollars at the exchange rate on the financial statement date. All sales of merchandise or services using credit cards must be recorded as cash at the time of sale.

4.4.2. Designated accounting personnel must reconcile all bank statements or reports monthly and report any discrepancies immediately to NAFI management. To maintain separation of duties, the person performing reconciliations must not be anyone associated with the collection or disbursement of funds.

4.4.3. The AO must designate a custodian to maintain the records and control the blank check stock; for security, this person must not be a check writer. Checks must be sequentially pre- numbered and stored in a locked container that is either a built-in vault or a burglary-resistant safe with a minimum two-hour fire rating. For additional guidance on securing blank check stock, refer to Volume 5, Section 3.

4.4.4. Check signing equipment has three components: a signature plate, a machine key, and the machine. The signatory must maintain the signature plate, and a designated person other than the signatory must maintain the key and a usage log; the authorized operator must record the beginning and ending readings, date, and initials in the log for each use. Other media, such as digitized signatures, are acceptable. For comprehensive guidance on check signing, refer to Volume 5, Section 7.

4.4.5. When a signatory changes, the NAFI must destroy the signature plates and notify the bank. A certificate of destruction must be prepared, signed by two witnesses and the successor signatory, and maintained in the AO. Refer to Volume 5 for additional information on destroying signature media.

4.4.6. Increases to a change fund must be requested in writing from the NAFI custodian (see DoDI 1015.15 for the definition of NAFI custodian). The AO then issues a check for the approved amount and increases the appropriate asset account.

4.4.7. The NAFI manager or designee must replenish change funds at the end of the day with cash received from operations, provided all daily net receipts are deposited in total, and must ensure all checks cashed from these funds are deposited daily. The NAFI manager or designee must not exchange dollars for foreign currency except as provided in Volume 5, Section 13.

4.4.8. Each NAFI must comply with the following requirements when establishing a petty cash fund.

4.4.8.1. Each manager within a NAFI must appoint petty cash custodians in writing.

4.4.8.2. A petty cash fund must not exceed one month's requirements.

4.4.8.3. Any single transaction must not exceed $500, and transactions must not be fragmented to circumvent this limit. The Military Service proponent for NAF financial management may approve a higher limit for purchases made in foreign currency when currency rates warrant; this increase must be reviewed annually.

4.4.8.4. In foreign locations, a NAFI may maintain one petty cash fund in the local foreign currency and one in U.S. dollars. If a NAFI gives cash bingo prizes in both dollars and foreign currency, it must establish two bingo petty cash funds.

4.4.8.5. NAFIs must not use petty cash funds to cash checks or to pay salaries and wages.

4.4.8.6. The AO provides the fixed petty cash amount to the appointed custodian, who completes a petty cash voucher to support each disbursement. The custodian must submit a replenishment request with vouchers and receipts (or equivalent) to the AO as needed, but no later than the last day of each month, and the AO must issue a reimbursement check payable to the custodian by name.

4.5    Receivables

4.5.1. Receivables are amounts owed to NAFIs for sales of merchandise, services, or dues, and may arise from APFs, Uniform Funding and Management (UFM) processes, employees, members, customers, and organizations for dues, fees, charges, rentals, credit sales (except credit- card sales recorded as cash per paragraph 3.1), or travel advances. NAFIs must maintain receivable records that accurately identify each debt and its debtor and must reconcile receivable subsidiary records monthly to the general ledger control accounts. Refer to the NAFSGL for the complete listing of receivable accounts and their definitions.

4.5.2. NAFIs with internal credit systems must prepare an aged customer accounts receivable report that, at a minimum, identifies amounts over 30 days (second billing statement), over 60 days (third billing statement), and over 90 days (fourth billing statement).

4.5.3. NAFIs must create and use an allowance for doubtful accounts (credit losses), determining and recording the estimated uncollectible accounts receivable at the end of each reporting period based on a review of historical average write-offs, per ASC 326-20-30 and ASC 450-20-25-2. NAFIs must maintain supporting documentation for the calculation and associated adjustment for audit purposes and must adjust the allowance to cover accounts expected to become uncollectible during the next reporting period.

4.6    Inventories

4.6.1. Inventories must be valued and recorded at cost, per ASC 330-10-30. The DoW Components must prescribe the cost-determination method (for example, first in first out, last in first out, or moving average), apply it consistently, and disclose it in the notes to the financial statements; the Military Exchanges must use the retail inventory method for retail merchandise. Costs that can be associated with specific items (freight, distribution, purchase charges, insurance, and handling) are included in merchandise cost; otherwise, they are recorded against the appropriate expense account. Purchase discounts must be deducted from the price billed and merchandise recorded net of discounts, with discounts lost and excise taxes recorded in the applicable operating expense account.

4.6.2. Immaterial losses of inventory resulting from spoilage, breakage, obsolescence, rejection, or constant customer complaint items are absorbed in cost of goods. Material losses are recorded in a Spoilage and Breakage expense account for the applicable operation.

4.6.3. Merchandise held on consignment is maintained and accounted for by the consignor; per ASC 606, NAFIs do not record this inventory in the general ledger and recognize revenue only once consignment tickets are sold to a third party, at which point selling costs and amounts due the consignor are expensed. NAFIs must physically inventory consigned merchandise for accountability monthly or at the end of an event for tickets, whichever comes first. Tickets purchased for resale must be recorded as inventory in the general ledger.

4.6.4. NAFIs must physically count inventories.

4.6.5. At least annually, an individual independent of the NAFI conducting the count must observe the physical inventory counts to verify the inventory and confirm the accuracy of the accounting records. Observations may be staggered throughout the year when observing all counts at once is impractical.

4.7    Other Current Assets

4.7.1. Other Current Assets are short-term prepaid expenses that are payments and expenditures made in contemplation of future benefits or performance. Other Current Assets also consist of prepayments for supplies, contracts, insurance, franchise fees, deposits, and advance payments that are not material enough for a separate line item disclosure. Prepaid expenses are accounted for in multiple accounts in the Other Current Assets category (refer to the NAFSGL for a complete list of accounts and definitions).

4.8    NAFI-Titled Fixed Assets and APF-Titled Fixed Assets

4.8.1. Fixed assets purchased with NAFs, donated, or transferred to a NAFI with a useful life of two or more years and an acquisition cost of $7,500 or more must be capitalized. Services with more stringent capitalization thresholds may follow their internal policy. This applies to a single item, or to multiple identical items purchased or transferred to the NAFI at the same time.

4.8.1.1. All Services must set the minimum capitalization threshold for assets purchased in quantity at a purchase cost equal to or greater than $7,500; Services with more stringent thresholds may follow their internal policy. The assets must be identical items with a useful life of two or more years and must meet all fixed-asset criteria in paragraph 3.6.1. Whole- room capitalization and composite purchase capitalization are both permitted for assets purchased in quantity.

4.8.2. When an asset is traded in at the time of purchase, the new asset is recorded at the amount of the monetary consideration paid, plus the trade-in allowance for the old asset. The acquisition cost and accumulated depreciation of the traded-in asset are removed from the accounting records. If the trade-in allowance is less than the book value of the old asset, then a loss will result. These losses are recorded in the “Other Non-Operating Expense” GLAC of the NAFI. If the trade-in allowance is more than the book value of the old asset, then the difference is subtracted from the acquisition cost of the new asset. No gain is recognized.

4.8.3. Assets-in-progress include all costs attributable to a construction project, such as new building construction, renovation of existing buildings, and fixed assets purchased as part of the project. The DoW Components must use construction-in-progress to accumulate the cost of real property construction projects. The AO transfers the accumulated cost to the appropriate fixed asset account and begins depreciation on the date of receipt shown on the receiving document when no installation is required, the date installed when required, or the date the asset is available for use. NAFI management establishes facility depreciation periods per the guidance in Volume 4. Fully depreciated buildings remain on the NAFI accounting books until the asset is sold or retired.

4.8.4. Record donations of assets and services material to the financial statements. Assets donated or transferred without the expenditure of funds are recorded at the fair market value on the date the asset was donated or transferred. If the fair market value cannot be determined, then the amount recorded is the book value of the donated asset in the donor's accounting records. Donated artifacts should not be included in the financial statements unless the NAFI: 1) uses or intends to use the artifact in its primary operations outside of its educational function, or 2) the NAFI sells or intends to sell the artifact and use the proceeds for something other than purchasing another artifact for educational purposes.

4.8.5. When NAFIs exchange assets without monetary consideration (a nonmonetary exchange), the gaining NAFI records the assets received at the net book value of the losing NAFI, with the offsetting entry to the Realized Gains and Losses for Sale of Fixed Asset Income GLAC on both NAFIs.

4.8.6. APF property obtained for free is recorded separately from other fixed assets because title and control remain with APFs. For APF fixed assets expected to benefit more than one accounting period, acquisition-related costs (repairs, transportation, installation) and subsequent outlays that extend useful life are recorded and depreciated over the asset's useful life. For APF fixed assets held one year or less, all costs are expensed in the period the asset is held.

4.8.7. Fixed assets acquired through the Utilization Support and Accountability (USA) process, the UFM process, or 10 United States Code (U.S.C.) § 2492 authority are NAFI assets unless APF-titled, and proceeds from their disposition revert to the NAFI. Refer to DoDI 1015.15 for further information on the USA and UFM processes and 10 U.S.C. § 2492 authority.

4.8.8. Artifacts are historical treasures or heritage assets held primarily for educational purposes in a museum, with measures taken to preserve them. Costs incurred to acquire artifacts must be recorded as a non-operating expense and must not be recognized as part of asset value or depreciated.

4.8.9. A unique aspect of NAF accounting is that some assets, particularly buildings, are purchased with NAFs and used exclusively by the NAFI while title rests with the U.S. Government. NAF-procured property or facilities may be transferred to APF for maintenance when Military Service regulations allow. On receipt of approved documentation from NAFI management, record these items in the NAF property records and general ledger as APF-Titled Fixed Assets and begin depreciation. Assets acquired by Memorandum of Agreement that transfers title and maintenance to an APF are not depreciated in the NAF accounting records.

4.8.10. The NAFI may receive title to fixed assets and may make payment for fixed assets before the NAFI has physical possession of the property. Typically, this happens when property destined for a NAFI overseas is delivered to a stateside port for over‑water transportation by government means. Payment is made based on the receipt at the port and is recorded in the appropriate fixed asset account. When asset reaches final transit location, begin depreciation on the date of receipt shown on the asset receiving document in cases where no installation is required, the date installed (if required), or the date the asset is available for use.

4.8.11. Disposal means the NAFI activity manager or custodian has physical control of an item and disposes of it. The NAFI activity manager or custodian must prepare and approve documents for the disposition of fixed assets. When property is transferred to APFs, the transfer must be evidenced on the form required by APFs.

4.9. A physical inventory of all fixed assets must be conducted at least annually and observed by at least one individual independent of the NAFI conducting the count, to verify the inventory and confirm the accuracy of the accounting records. When performing the inventory all at once is impractical, the NAFI may schedule and conduct it by area.

4.9.1. Property subsidiary ledgers serve as property control records and must, at a minimum, list each piece of property, its acquisition date, acquisition value, useful life, depreciation to date, and current book value. The ledger may be automated or manual, but automation must be used when available. The NAFI must prepare the documentation needed to change ledger data even when no general ledger entry is required, such as a fixed asset transferred between locations within the same NAFI.

4.10. DoW Components must use the straight-line method of depreciation and must prescribe and disclose the useful lives of assets in the notes to the financial statements. All tangible fixed assets except construction-in-progress must be depreciated over their expected useful lives, and all NAF activities recognize depreciation of their fixed assets as an operating expense. Refer to Volume 4 for the requirement to subtract salvage value from acquisition cost before computing depreciation.

4.10.1. For NAF capital assets whose titles transfer to APFs but that the NAFI still uses, continue to depreciate them on the NAFI books until fully depreciated. Fully depreciated assets still in use must be reported on the balance sheet until disposed of by sale or retirement.

4.10.2. In the case of constructed real property, depreciation will commence when the building is available for use, regardless of whether the building is fully occupied.

4.10.2.1. If an asset remains in use beyond its estimated useful life, the NAFI must retain it in the property accountability or management system and in the accounting records, reflecting both its recorded cost and accumulated depreciation until disposition.

4.10.2.2. Depreciation of real property must not be accelerated at installations approved for realignment, closure, or re-stationing. On actual closure of the facility, the NAFI must expense the undepreciated value in the applicable extraordinary expense account.

4.10.3. In accordance with ASC 350-40-35-4, internal-use software will be amortized on a straight-line basis unless another systematic and rational basis is more representative of the software’s use. Software acquired for research and development with no alternative future use will be amortized over the period of the project as opposed to the normal life-cycle amortization. Refer to Volume 4 for detailed guidance.

4.11    Other Long-Term Assets

4.11.1. Other Long-Term Assets include those not identified in other asset lines of accounting that are held for longer than 1 year. Other Long-Term Assets consists of long-term pension benefit assets, long-term receivables, long-term prepaid expenses, long-term leases and capital leases, certificates of deposit (more than 12 months), marketable securities, long-term contributions, long-term franchise fees, intangible assets, and long-term royalty and trademark fees.

4.12    Accounting Requirements for Liabilities

4.12.1. The NAFSGL contains two liability categories: Current Liabilities and Long-Term Liabilities. Current liabilities are due, or will be due, on demand within one year; long-term liabilities are due over a period longer than one year from the balance sheet date. Accounting requirements for liabilities are in paragraphs 4.1 through 4.3.

4.12.2. Liabilities arise from the acquisition of goods or services. Accounts payable must be recognized upon receipt of services or when accepting title to goods. Under accrual accounting, accrued liabilities are recorded for goods or services which have been provided but for which invoices have not yet been received; and therefore, not yet included in accounts payable.

4.12.3. Contingencies are existing conditions involving uncertainty as to possible gain or loss that are resolved when one or more future events occur or fail to occur. Loss contingencies are accrued when the outcome is probable and the amount is reasonably estimable, and gain contingencies are not recorded, per ASC 450-20-25. When a contingency is identified, the AO must footnote the year-end Military Service level consolidated financial statements to explain the contingency and the potential gain or loss.

4.13    Payment of Liabilities

4.13.1. The NAFI manager or designee is responsible for approving the disbursement of NAFs. The AO must not make disbursements without the approval of the NAFI manager or designee, or as otherwise authorized in this Regulation.

4.13.2. NAFIs must submit the following documents, properly prepared and authenticated, to the AO to support payment for procurements. A procurement document, e.g., purchase order (PO), contract, blanket purchase agreement, or similar documents; a DoD (DD) Form 250, Material Inspection and Receiving Report, or other signed document that provides evidence goods were accepted or services were received; and a vendor invoice or claim for payment.

4.13.3. For overseas shipments, the AO must receive a vendor invoice and proof of shipment before payment; these payments may be made before receipt or acceptance of the goods.

4.13.4. When a NAFI purchases goods or services from another NAFI, it must submit a DD 1149, Requisition and Invoice/Shipping Document, or similar form to the AO to support the transaction.

4.13.5. NAFI purchases of goods or services from the Government (for example, bills from APFs) are not usually supported by a procurement instrument; the NAFI must submit a DD 250 or other signed document to the AO to support payment.

4.13.6. A vendor invoice represents a claim against NAF. All invoices must be date- stamped at the time of receipt and must meet the Prompt Payment Act criteria in 5 Code of Federal Regulations 1315. Refer to Volume 10 for additional information on contract payments.

4.14    Accounting Requirements for Net Worth

4.14.1. Net Worth (Equity) consists of capital invested in NAFIs plus or minus net income or loss since inception. Transactions into and out of equity are limited to net income, net losses, entries associated with establishing the fund, and certain adjustments. Adjustments are rare and may include certain accounting principle changes, prior period adjustments greater than one percent of the assets in the consolidated balance sheet (or less than one percent but deemed material), and distribution of capital. The NAFSGL contains one net worth/equity category; accounting requirements are in paragraphs 6.1 and 6.2.

4.14.2. When a new NAF organization with preexisting capital is authorized, the capital is recorded as equity (for example, when a private association converts to a membership association). Equity is disestablished when a NAF organization is dissolved.

4.14.3. Equity may be distributed by declaring dividends to other NAF organizations (for example, dividends paid by installation restaurants) or through special grants for new construction and facility improvements. The declaration of dividends by the Military Exchanges and the distribution of grants must be recorded and reported as decreases in equity. The receipt of Military Exchange dividends and of grants that support recurring operations must be recorded as non- operating income, while the receipt of grants for capital items must be recorded as equity transactions. Equity is transferred as cash or other assets.

4.13.4. Transfers into and out of the Other Equity or Earnings general ledger account are limited to the following: net income; net losses; declaration of dividends by Military Exchanges; prior year material corrections; components of other comprehensive income (loss) prescribed by ASC 220-10-45-10A; entries associated with the establishment, disestablishment, or consolidation of NAFIs; and distribution and receipt of capital.

Companion reference: For detailed procedures, implementation guidance, definitions, and the full data tables, see Supplemental for Volume 13, Section 4.

title: Section 5.0: Income and Expenses
content:
5.0    INCOME AND EXPENSES

5.1 This section prescribes DoD NAF income and expense policies. NAFI programs and facilities must be operated, maintained, and funded as an integral part of the DoW personnel and readiness program. These policies apply to all NAFIs and their supporting AOs, including the Military Exchanges (Army and Air Force Exchange Service, Navy Exchange Service Command, and Marine Corps Exchange), except that Exchanges are not required to use the NAFSGL.

5.2    Income Standards

5.2.1. In accordance with ASC, Topic 605, Subtopic 10, Section 25, NAFIs must recognize revenue (classified as “income” in the NAFSGL) when it is realized or realizable.

5.2.2. The AO must record income in the appropriate NAFI's financial records on a consistent basis, in the appropriate cost center, and in the operating cycle in which the income is earned, per DoDI 1015.15.

5.3    Expense Standards

5.3.1. NAFIs must recognize costs as an expense in the period that the income with which they are associated is recognized (the matching principle).

5.3.1. Using the accrual method, AOs must record expenses on a consistent basis, in the appropriate cost center, and in the operating cycle in which the expense was incurred. Refer to Volume 4 for further guidance on accrual accounting.

5.4    Accounting for APF Support to NAFIs

5.4.1. Title 10 U.S.C. § 2241 is the basic statutory authority to provide APFs to support Morale, Welfare, and Recreation (MWR) functions. MWR USA and UFM are the two mechanisms for providing APF support to NAFIs. Both involve use of NAFs for MWR expenses that, per DoDI 1015.15, should be borne by APFs. Under MWR (USA), NAFIs use NAFs to execute such expenses subject to later APF reimbursement under Memoranda of Agreement (MOAs). Under UFM, APFs may be transferred into NAF accounts before expenditure; funds appropriated to DoW and available for MWR programs are treated as NAFs for all purposes under UFM MOAs and remain available until expended (10 U.S.C. § 2491). Other statutory authorities available to NAFIs are 10 U.S.C. §§ 2492, 7459, 8478, and 9459.

5.4.2. MWR (USA) Recording

5.4.2.1. The AO must record funds received from appropriated sources for expenses covered by MWR (USA) as MWR (USA) income.

5.4.2.2. The AO must record authorized expenses (the amount subject to APF reimbursement), as they occur, in the applicable expense accounts so that MWR (USA) support is identifiable, per DoDI 1015.15.

5.4.3. UFM Recording

5.4.3.1. The AO must record UFM funds received in the cash account with a contra entry to the Unearned Income (liability) account identified as UFM.

5.4.3.2. The AO must record authorized expenses, as they occur, in the applicable expense accounts so that UFM support is identifiable, per DoDI 1015.15, and reduce the cash account as applicable in the same reporting cycle.

Companion reference: For detailed procedures, implementation guidance, definitions, and the full data tables, see Supplemental for Volume 13, Section 5.

title: Section 6.0: Financial Reporting
content:
6.0    FINANCIAL REPORTING

6.1 These policies apply to DoD NAFIs and their supporting AOs. They apply to the Military Exchanges, except for policies related to the NAFSGL.

6.2 The DoW Components are responsible for the fair presentation in the financial reports of financial position, results of operations, and the program and personnel information included, and for compliance with NAF program laws and regulations.

6.3 The supporting AO is responsible for compiling the necessary information from accounting and payroll systems and for preparing financial statements and reports. The AO is also responsible for the integrity of those systems and the accuracy of the data produced. Refer to Section 2 for definitions, reporting requirements, and accounting standards.

6.4 The principal financial statements used to convey information to users are the Balance Sheet, Statement of Income and Expense, Reconciliation of Net Worth, and Statement of Cash Flows.

6.5 The NAFSGL Financial Statement Mapping to the financial statements is maintained on the DoD NAF Accounting website. The working versions of all statements and notes must include line numbers as shown there.

6.6 Retain all records relating to payments to individuals and firms according to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Topic Number 305, “Recordkeeping.”

6.7 International Balance of Payments (IBOP) Program is an accounting of a country’s international transactions for a particular period of time. NAFIs are subject to the IBOP reporting guidance prescribed in DoDI 4105.67, “Nonappropriated Fund (NAF) Procurement Policy and Procedure,” and Volume 6.

Companion reference: For detailed procedures, implementation guidance, definitions, and the full data tables, see Supplemental for Volume 13, Section 6.

title: Section 7.0: Nonappropriated Fund Payroll
content:
7.0    NONAPPROPRIATED FUND PAYROLL

7.1 This chapter provides the standard NAF policy for DoD NAF payroll and applies to DoD NAF employees. NAF employees are not paid from funds appropriated by Congress but from funds generated by NAFIs. NAF employees are Federal employees, but they are not covered by most laws administered by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), unless specifically provided by statute. Policy in this chapter applies to all NAFIs, NAF Human Resources (HR), NAF payroll offices, and their supporting AOs.

7.2    Payroll Oversight

7.2.1. Defense Civilian Personnel Advisory Service, NAF Personnel Policy Division is responsible for developing, coordinating, and publishing DoD-wide civilian HR policy concerning NAF employees. DoD NAF HR policy is found in DoDI 1400.25, with volumes in the 1400 series.

7.2.2. All NAF payroll systems, whether being designed, implemented, or in use, must operate per the authoritative guidance document on the FMR webpage and Volume 1.

7.2.3. AOs must ensure all payroll information (including accrued payroll and benefits) passes to the accounting system, whether systemically or manually; update the appropriate NAFSGL accounts; and meet the reporting requirements in DoDI 1015.15 and Volume 13, Section 6. AOs must also compile the financial statements.

7.2.4. The NAF payroll office has primary responsibility for all payroll processing and must work closely with the supporting NAF personnel office, NAFIs, and NAF employees.

7.3    Payroll Deductions

7.3.1. Payroll deductions or withholdings from an employee's pay must be properly authorized by the employee (or made per applicable laws), adequately documented, and paid when due to the appropriate recipient in the authorized amount.

7.3.2. The payroll office must withhold taxes from civilian employees' wages and remit them to tax jurisdictions wherever the Federal Government has entered withholding agreements. State and local taxes must be withheld from the pay of enlisted personnel compensated from NAF for off-duty work.

7.3.3. NAFIs located in foreign countries must neither pay to, nor collect for, any foreign country or political subdivision any tax unless the United States has consented to that levy by treaty, convention, or Executive agreement.

7.4.4. The payroll office will withhold a set percentage of an employee’s salary each pay period to pay the employee’s share of Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) contribution. FICA also requires that the NAFI contribute a set percentage of an employee’s salary to the Social Security Trust Fund and the Medicare Trust Funds.

7.5.5. If the gross salary of an employee is not sufficient to permit all deductions to be made, then deductions will be made in the order of precedence established by the OPM Personnel Policy Memorandum, PPM-2008-01, “Order Of Precedence When Gross Pay Is Not Sufficient To Permit All Deductions,” dated July 30, 2008. NAFIs must consult policy, legal staff, and collective bargaining agreements to ensure the proper order of precedence is followed.

7.4    Employee Retirement Accounting

7.4.1. NAF HR/payroll offices are responsible for providing and processing forms for employees retiring under the Civil Service Retirement System (CSRS) or the Federal Employee Retirement System (FERS). OMB Circular A-130, Appendix II prescribes electronic processes and digital signatures whenever possible, and in the Government's best interest. NAF HR/payroll offices must fulfill the following CSRS or FERS responsibilities (for more on portability retirement, refer to Volume 8).

7.4.2. NAF HR/payroll offices must prepare and maintain a Standard Form (SF) 2806 (CSRS) or an SF 3100 (FERS), Individual Retirement Record, for each employee subject to CSRS or FERS. Each SF 2806/SF 3100 must be correct, complete, clear in every detail, and properly certified to ensure timely, accurate closeout when an employee separates or transfers to another agency's paying jurisdiction.

7.4.3. NAF HR/payroll offices must maintain adequate control over retirement records and associated monetary balances.

7.4.4. NAF HR/payroll offices must promptly send claims and records to OPM (CSRS/FERS Retirement Records, Office of Personnel Management, Retirement Operations Center, P.O. Box 45, Boyers, PA 16017-0045).

7.4.5. NAF HR/payroll offices must withhold retirement deductions from employees' salaries, make agency contributions, and send the deductions and contributions to OPM for deposit. Deductions begin on the day the employee acquires retirement-system coverage and must be prorated for partial pay periods. FICA contributions must be withheld and reported per current Treasury guidance. Employee retirement deductions, employer contributions, employee contributions to applicable 401(k) plans, and loan repayments must be made biweekly and submitted to the appropriate NAF employee benefit system. Thrift Savings Plan (TSP) deductions and the employer's matching contributions must be forwarded to the TSP.

7.5    Leave Accrual

7.5.1. Annual leave accrual is material and must be recognized as a liability and expensed monthly in the individual NAFI's accounting records. The individual leave records or annual leave report, showing the accumulated leave balance for all employees, must serve as the subsidiary ledger to the appropriate NAFSGL account for each NAFI.

7.5.2. Monthly sick leave accrual is not a liability to the NAFI. The NAFI must recognize sick leave used as an expense monthly in its accounting records.

7.6 NAFIs must accrue the estimated liability for a business-based action when probable and accrue a separation allowance monthly where applicable. (DoDI 1015.15 requires NAFIs to set aside and invest funds regularly to ensure cash is available to pay severance benefits for U.S. and Foreign National employees on separation; DoDI 1400.25, Volume 1405 sets the eligibility criteria, exclusions, conditions, and computation and payment requirements.)

7.7 All payroll disbursements must be paid to NAF employees by electronic fund transfer (EFT) unless the head of the agency or designee grants a waiver. The head of the agency or designee may waive the EFT requirement on receipt of written certification from the employee stating that the employee has no account with a financial institution or describing another extenuating circumstance.

7.8 NAF payroll offices must keep records sufficient to support all NAF payroll transactions. Employment-tax records must be retained for 4 years after the tax due date or the date the tax was paid, whichever is later (IRS Publication 15). Aggregate records of payroll disbursed each pay period (base pay, additions to and deductions from pay, and leave balances) must be stored and transferred to the National Personnel Records Center for 56 years' retention (National Archives and Records Administration General Records Schedule 2.4).

7.9 All DoD NAF organizations must follow the internal control standards in OMB Circular A-123; DoDI 1015.15, subparagraph 6.7.3; DoDI 5010.40; and DoDI 7600.06 for payroll operations and for the methods and procedures adopted to process and audit payrolls.

Companion reference: For detailed procedures, implementation guidance, definitions, and the full data tables, see Supplemental for Volume 13, Section 7.

title: Section 8.0: Accounting for Defined Benefit Pension and Other Postretirement Plans
content:
8.0    ACCOUNTING FOR DEFINED BENEFIT PENSION AND OTHER POSTRETIREMENT PLANS

8.1 This section provides requirements to account for single-employer defined benefit pension and other postretirement plans. Its policies apply to DoD NAFIs, their supporting Accounting Offices, and Military Services Exchanges. This section does not apply to Military Department plans considered multi-employer. Each NAFI and its supporting Certified Public Accounting firm must fully review the exceptions and variables associated with pension accounting before implementation.

8.2 NAFIs must report pension plan assets and liabilities annually in conformance with FASB ASC Topic 715, "Compensation-Retirement Benefits." The current published version of ASC Topic 715 is the superseding authority for the accounting addressed in this section.

8.3 The Military Departments must calculate the funded status of a benefit plan as of the year- end statement date (measurement date). Funded status is the difference between the projected benefit obligation and the plan assets at fair value.

8.4 Temporary equity adjustments to pension balances must not be included in the net worth determination. Post these adjustments as an offset to the equity account, treated in the same manner as unrealized gains and losses on investments per ASC Topic 320, "Investments-Debt Securities."

8.5 At a minimum, the NAFI must disclose additional information about certain effects on net periodic benefit cost and the amount and timing of any plan assets expected to be returned to the Military Departments and NAFIs. See ASC Topic 715 for the full disclosure requirements.

Companion reference: For detailed procedures, implementation guidance, definitions, and the full data tables, see Supplemental for Volume 13, Section 8.

title: Section 1.0: General
content:
1.0    GENERAL

1.1    Overview

This volume prescribes the Department of War (DoW) requirements for the administrative control of funds and compliance with the Antideficiency Act (ADA). It defines the statutory restrictions and the implementing executive branch requirements that govern fund control, explains the legal framework of the ADA, and establishes the consequences for violations.

The detailed policies, procedural guidance, and the complete ADA violation process are prescribed in this Volume. This volume establishes the authoritative, legally based policy for the administrative control of all DoW appropriations and funds. It defines what constitutes a violation of the ADA and related funding statutes and establishes the legal consequences of such violations. This volume serves as the foundational rulebook that all DoW implementation policies and procedural guides must follow.

1.2    Authoritative Guidance

Refer to the Volume 14 authoritative guidance document on the FMR webpage.

1.3    Definitions

Refer to the Glossary.

title: Section 2.0: Administrative Control of Funds Policy
content:
2.0    ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROL OF FUNDS POLICY

2.1    Defense-wide Appropriations

Unless otherwise specified, for purposes of this volume, the Office of the Under Secretary of War, Deputy Comptroller (Program/Budget) is considered a “DoW Component” for matters involving Defense-wide (Treasury Symbol “97”) appropriations.

2.2    Administrative Control Systems

DoW Components must:

2.2.1. Design systems for the administrative control of funds so that formal administrative subdivisions of funds are placed at the highest practical organizational level consistent with effective and efficient management.

2.2.2. Restrict the use of limitations on available funds to those necessary to comply with statutory provisions, such as those imposed by the appropriate DoW Authorization or DoW Appropriations Act, or to address specific management requirements.

2.3    Reporting Requirements for Administrative Control Systems

DoW Components must establish a reporting system for the administrative control of funds process to provide data for reviewing the efficiency (e.g., obligation rate) with which funds are used. Reporting requirements must be established separately from a formal administrative subdivision of funds limitation when a need exists for accumulating data below the allocation level.

2.4    Delegations of Authority

All delegations or redelegations of authority or functions under this volume must be made in writing.
